Why must cyanide water handling be controlled?

What is Area F22?.q: Why does loaded carbon need acid washing before elution?
What is Area F22?.a:
To remove scale that blocks the carbon's pores.

As carbon sits in leach slurry, calcium and magnesium carbonates deposit on and inside it. That is worse here because the process water is hypersaline and lime is added for pH. Scale blocks the pores where gold sits and gets in the way of the hot caustic cyanide solution during elution, so gold strips poorly. It also lowers carbon activity when the carbon goes back to CIL.

Dilute hydrochloric acid (about 3 percent) dissolves the carbonate scale. On CIL4 the acid wash and elution happen in the same single column, made of SAF2205 duplex stainless steel: acid wash, water rinse, then the caustic cyanide pre soak and elution. Acid waste goes to the final tails tank.

f.q: Why is the CIL4 column made of duplex stainless steel?
f.a:
Because it sees both hot chloride bearing solutions and acid. The column does acid wash with dilute HCl, then elution at well above 100 C under pressure, with caustic and cyanide. The plant water is saline too.

Ordinary austenitic stainless steels like 316 are prone to chloride pitting and stress corrosion cracking in hot chloride service. Duplex stainless SAF2205 has higher strength and much better resistance to chloride stress corrosion and pitting, so one vessel can safely do both jobs.

The existing concentrate circuits use separate acid wash columns instead. It is the same reasoning as choosing duplex for seawater heat exchangers.
f: Why is the elution column kept under pressure?
What temperature does CIL4 elution run at?
How is acid kept out of the elution heater circuit?

f.q: Where does the acid wash waste go?
f.a:
To the final tails tank. The reference lists the final tails tank as receiving CIL4 tails, acid wash waste and fine carbon waste, which are then pumped to the Fim III TSF.

The MEL also lists acid effluent and fine carbon pumps (F30-PP-496 and 497) for this kind of duty on the concentrate side.

Mixing the small acid stream into the large alkaline tails flow neutralises it quickly. Acid and cyanide must never meet in an enclosed space, because acid turns cyanide into HCN gas, so the rinse step and the routing of acid waste are designed to keep them apart until the acid is diluted in the tails.
f: Why must acid and cyanide solutions be kept apart?
How is the acid rinse step sequenced in the column?
What is in the fine carbon waste stream?

f.q: What happens if acid washing is skipped?
f.a:
In general, scale keeps building up on the carbon with every cycle. Elution gets less effective, so more gold stays on the stripped carbon and goes back to CIL as inventory rather than production. Carbon activity falls, so in CIL4 the carbon adsorbs gold more slowly and soluble gold losses to tails can rise. Scale can also build up in the regeneration kiln, and some scale does not burn off.

On this plant acid wash is a programmed step in the CIL4 elution sequence (carbon in, acid wash, rinse, pre soak, elution, cooling, carbon out), so it is not normally skipped. If it is, the CIL metallurgist would want to know.

Why does scale reduce elution efficiency?
What does the elution sequence do if a step faults?

What is Area F22?.q: What handover symptom shows the carbon regeneration kiln is underperforming?
What is Area F22?.a:
In general, the clearest sign is falling carbon activity: regenerated carbon that adsorbs gold slowly. In CIL4 that shows as poorer adsorption, higher solution gold in the later tanks and rising soluble losses, confirmed by lab activity tests.

Kiln specific signs would be temperature not reaching setpoint, carbon throughput low so barren carbon backs up in the kiln feed hopper, quench or barren carbon pump problems, or the kiln stopping because the mercury abatement system tripped.

The CIL4 regeneration kiln (F22-KN-411) is a vendor package (Lochhead) with its own PLC, tied to the DCS through an overall regeneration sequence. The kiln vendor panel and DCS trends are where the CRO would look first.

f.q: How is carbon activity measured?
f.a:
This is general lab practice; the reference does not describe the site method.

A sample of regenerated carbon is contacted with a standard gold cyanide solution under fixed conditions, and the lab measures how fast or how much gold it takes up, compared with fresh carbon. The result is often expressed as a percentage of fresh carbon activity or as a rate constant.

Low activity means fouled pores, from organics, scale or poor regeneration. Comparing loaded, eluted and regenerated carbon samples shows whether the problem is acid washing, elution or the kiln.

The CIL metallurgist and the plant lab would run and interpret these tests.

How often are carbon activity tests done?
What regeneration temperature restores activity?

f.q: Why must the mercury abatement system run with the kiln?
f.a:
Because heating carbon drives off mercury. Gold ores in this region carry mercury, which dissolves in the leach and loads onto carbon with the gold. In the kiln it vaporises into the off gas.

The control philosophy says the mercury abatement system must run whenever the kiln runs, and its drives are in the same regeneration sequence. The MEL describes it as a package with a knock out box, off gas cooler, demister and an adsorption vessel with sulphur impregnated carbon, which captures mercury vapour.

So if abatement trips, the kiln stops: you never run the kiln without it. It is an environmental and health control.

How is mercury exposure monitored around the kiln?
What else is driven off carbon in the kiln?

f.q: What heats the CIL4 regeneration kiln?
f.a:
Electricity. The MEL describes F22-KN-411 as a horizontal kiln, electrically heated, with 102 elements at 28 kW each, about 2.86 MW of heating.

This is separate from the CIL4 elution heater, which is LPG fired (the TPE package) with a burner management system and heats the eluate through heat exchangers. So LPG feeds elution, while the kiln runs on electric elements.

Electric heating gives good temperature control along the kiln and no combustion gases mixing with the carbon off gas, which simplifies the mercury abatement. The kiln package has its own vendor PLC, screw feeder and local panel.

How does the kiln screw feeder control carbon rate?
Why is the kiln atmosphere kept low in oxygen?

What is Area F22?.q: What happens to carbon after it leaves the regeneration kiln?
What is Area F22?.a:
It is cooled, sized and sent back to CIL4.

Hot carbon from the kiln (F22-KN-411) drops into the quench, the CIL4 carbon quench hopper (F22-HP-446), where water cools it. The barren carbon pump (F22-PP-490, a recessed impeller slurry pump) then sends it to the CIL4 carbon sizing screen (F21-SC-420), which removes fines. The sized carbon goes to the last CIL4 tank, where solution gold is lowest, to start its counter current trip upstream again.

Fresh carbon to make up losses is added through a hoist, bag splitter and the quench hopper, so it joins the regenerated carbon at this point. The whole loop is run by the regeneration sequence, with the kiln on its vendor PLC.

f.q: Why is hot carbon quenched in water straight from the kiln?
f.a:
In general, three reasons. Carbon leaves the kiln at several hundred degrees, and if it meets air while hot it can burn, losing carbon and activity. Quenching in water stops that immediately. It cools the carbon so it can be handled and pumped as a slurry. And it wets the pores so the carbon is ready to adsorb when it goes back into CIL.

The quench can cause some thermal shock and breakage, which is one reason the carbon passes a sizing screen before returning to the tanks.

On CIL4 the quench is the carbon quench hopper (F22-HP-446), also used as the entry point for fresh carbon.
f: How much carbon breaks into fines in each cycle?
Why does dry carbon float in leach tanks?
How is the quench water supply controlled?

f.q: Why does carbon enter CIL4 at the last tank?
f.a:
Because the circuit is counter current. Barren carbon has the most capacity to adsorb, so it goes where the solution has the least gold left, the last tank (TK-418), to scavenge those last traces before the slurry leaves to tails.

It is then advanced upstream tank by tank, meeting progressively richer solution and loading up as it goes, until it is pulled out loaded from the first adsorption tank (TK-413).

That keeps a driving force for adsorption in every tank, exactly like a counterflow heat exchanger, where the coldest coolant meets the coolest product. Putting barren carbon at the front would leave the tail end with saturated carbon and lose gold.
f: How is barren carbon distributed into the last tank?
What happens if barren carbon goes to the wrong tank?
How do spool pieces route carbon between tanks?

f.q: What does the CIL4 carbon sizing screen remove?
f.a:
Fines and broken carbon. The sizing screen (F21-SC-420, a flat vibrating screen with a polyurethane deck in the MEL) sits on the barren carbon return to the last CIL4 tank.

Regeneration, quenching and pumping break some carbon into small pieces. If those went back into CIL4 they could pass through the 1.0 mm intertank screens, load gold as they travel downstream, and leave with the tails, taking gold to the TSF.

Removing them before the carbon enters the circuit stops that loss. The fine carbon waste goes to the final tails tank. CIL3 has its own new barren carbon sizing screen for the same reason.

How much fine carbon is lost each month?
Can fine carbon be sold or recovered for its gold?

What is Area F23?.q: Why are booster pumps needed to send tailings to the TSF?
What is Area F23?.a:
Because one set of pumps cannot deliver enough head for the whole trip to the Fim III TSF (WBS T03).

The final tails pumps (F23-PP-466 to 469, duty/duty/duty/standby) lift the tails out of the final tails tank, and the MEL lists three FIM III booster pumps (F23-PP-651 to 653) at a booster station along the line, with their own gland seal water pumps and potable water tank. The reference does not give the pipeline length or lift.

In general, a long tailings line loses a lot of pressure to friction, plus any rise to the dam crest. Splitting that across pumps in series keeps each pump within its pressure and wear limits, like stages in a multistage pump. Slurry pumps wear fast at very high heads, so boosting part way is usually more reliable.

f.q: How do pumps in series add head on a long tails line?
f.a:
In general, pumps in series pass the same flow, and their heads add. The first pump raises pressure enough to push slurry to the booster station; the booster adds more to finish the trip to the dam.

Slurry pumps have practical limits on discharge pressure, set by casing rating and wear, which climbs steeply with head. Splitting the duty keeps each pump in a sensible range.

Control has to match them: if the booster runs faster or slower than the upstream pumps, its suction pressure drops or rises, so booster stations usually control on suction pressure or flow. The reference gives each tails line a flowmeter, density and pressure measurement.
f: How is booster pump speed matched to upstream pumps?
What happens if the booster suction pressure drops?
Why does slurry pump wear rise with head?

f.q: Why does the booster station have its own gland water pumps?
f.a:
The MEL lists gland seal water pumps for FIM III booster pumps 1 and 2 (F23-PW-651 to 654) at the booster station, plus a potable water tank there.

The reference does not explain why. In general, gland water must be injected at a pressure above the pump's discharge pressure to keep slurry out of the packing. At a booster station that pressure is high, and the station is away from the main plant gland water system, so it gets its own dedicated pumps.

The plant control philosophy applies: low gland water flow blocks a slurry pump starting, and trips it after a delay when running.
f: Why must gland water pressure exceed pump pressure?
What is a Maric constant flow valve for?
How is the remote booster station monitored?

f.q: How is a leak detected on the tailings pipeline?
f.a:
By comparing flows at each end. Each tailings line has a flowmeter, density and pressure measurement at the plant end, and the reference specifies a second flowmeter near the deposition end for leak detection.

If more slurry leaves the plant than arrives at the dam, beyond normal measurement tolerance, the difference points to a leak or burst. The DCS can alarm on that mismatch.

A falling discharge pressure with steady pump speed can also indicate a leak. Tailings leaks are an environmental issue, since the slurry carries residual cyanide, so a leak alarm normally means stopping pumping and inspecting the line under the site response procedure.
f: What flow mismatch triggers a leak alarm?
Why does residual cyanide make tailings leaks serious?
How is the tailings line patrolled for damage?

What is Area F23?.q: What would a blocked final tails line look like on shift?
What is Area F23?.a:
In general you would see pressure and flow disagreeing. Discharge pressure on the final tails pumps climbs while flow on the line flowmeter drops; pump power or speed changes as the controller tries to hold flow; and the flowmeter near the deposition end shows less than the plant end, or nothing.

Upstream, the final tails tank level rises because the pumps cannot move enough slurry, and since tank level sets pump flow setpoints, the pumps are already being driven harder.

Causes include sanding from low velocity, scale, a closed or failed valve, or debris. It is serious: if tails cannot be pumped, the whole plant has to stop. The response is to stop feed per procedure, not to keep forcing the pumps.

f.q: Why does low velocity cause a slurry line to sand up?
f.a:
Every slurry has a deposition velocity, below which the heavier particles drop out and form a bed on the bottom of the pipe. Once a bed forms, the open area shrinks, friction rises and the bed can grow until the line blocks.

Velocity drops when flow is cut, when a pump slows, or when density rises. That is why the control philosophy uses dual hopper level control in some places: one loop on pump speed, another adding water at a lower setpoint, to keep the line above minimum velocity.

On a long tails line, running below minimum velocity for long periods is a common cause of blockages. Design velocity margins come from slurry testwork.
f: How does density change deposition velocity?
What does dual level hopper control prevent?
How is a sanded slurry line cleared?

f.q: What happens to the plant if final tails cannot be pumped?
f.a:
Final tails is the exit for everything: about 3,164 t/h of solids at design. If it cannot be pumped, the final tails tank fills in minutes, then CIL4 backs up, then the tails thickener, and so on upstream.

So in general the plant has to cut feed or stop in a controlled way, starting from the front end. That is why the tails pumps run three duty plus one standby: losing one pump should not stop the plant.

The handover card on the tails pump arrangement says it plainly: if tails cannot be pumped, the whole plant stops. Restart sequences then work backwards from downstream.

How does a controlled plant shutdown proceed?
Why do restart sequences start from downstream?

f.q: How are tailings lines flushed after a shutdown?
f.a:
The reference covers the protection rather than a flushing procedure. Slurry pumps have actuated dump valves that fail open on power loss, so lines drain rather than letting slurry settle and bog the pump and pipe.

In general, on a planned stop the tails line is flushed with water before pumps stop, so the line is left full of water, not settling slurry. On an unplanned stop, drains and dump points let slurry out at low points, and the line may be flushed on restart.

The exact routine for the tails lines would be in the site operating procedures. The control room operator or tailings operator would know it.
f: Why do dump valves fail open on loss of power?
Where does drained slurry go at the low points?
How long does a tailings line flush take?

What is Area F23?.q: How does the final tails tank buffer flow variation before the TSF?
What is Area F23?.a:
By acting as a small surge vessel with level control on the pumps.

The final tails tank (F23-TK-404, about 8.6 m diameter by 10.1 m in the MEL) collects CIL4 tails, acid wash waste and fine carbon waste, about 3,164 t/h of solids at 54.5 percent solids. Tank level sets the tailings pump flow setpoints: as level rises the pumps speed up, as it falls they slow down.

It is not a large buffer. My rough estimate from the dimensions is under 600 m3 gross, which is only around 10 minutes of tails flow, so it smooths short swings rather than covering outages. Each pump line has its own flowmeter, density and pressure measurement, and the pumps run three duty and one standby.

f.q: Why does tank level set the tailings pump flow setpoint?
f.a:
It is a cascade. The level controller is the master and sets the setpoint of the pump flow controllers, which drive the pump speeds.

That way the pumps follow what comes in from CIL4 without the tank overflowing or running empty, while the flow loops hold a steady velocity in each pipeline. Flow control on the line protects against sanding, since flow is held above a minimum, and gives smoother operation than driving pump speed directly from level.

It is the same idea as a surge drum feeding a pipeline: level sets the flow target, the flow loop handles the fast stuff.
f: What minimum flow is held in each tails line?
How are the three duty tails pumps shared?
What happens if the tank level transmitter fails?

f.q: What enters the final tails tank besides CIL4 tails?
f.a:
The reference lists acid wash waste and fine carbon waste as well as CIL4 tails.

Acid wash waste is the dilute HCl used to wash carbon before elution. Mixing it into the large alkaline tails flow neutralises it. Fine carbon waste is carbon fines removed by the sizing screens; it goes to tails rather than back into CIL.

In general, other streams like spillage returns may also end up there, but the reference only names these.

Everything in the tank goes to the Fim III TSF, and the decant water returns to the plant as cyanide water, treated with hydrogen peroxide to a WAD cyanide target.
f: How is decant water treated before reuse?
Why is fine carbon sent to tails instead of recycled?
What does WAD cyanide measure in decant water?

f.q: Why do the final tails pumps run three duty and one standby?
f.a:
Because three pumps are needed to carry the design flow, and losing tails pumping stops the whole plant.

The MEL lists four final tails pumps, F23-PP-466 to 469, and the reference gives the arrangement as duty/duty/duty/standby. Each pump line has a flowmeter, density and pressure measurement. With one standby, a pump can trip or be taken out for maintenance without cutting throughput.

Slurry pumps on tails duty wear quickly, so rotating maintenance through a standby unit is normal. It is the same N plus 1 logic you would apply to critical cooling water pumps.
f: How are tails pumps rotated for even wear?
What gland water do the final tails pumps use?
How is a standby tails pump brought online?

What is Area F24?.q: Why does the plant need separate saline and process water systems?
What is Area F24?.a:
The premise needs a tweak: on this plant process water is the saline water. What F24 really separates is several water qualities, each for duties that can tolerate it.

Process water: saline (SG about 1.07), mainly recycled flotation tails thickener overflow, topped up from Bore Water Dam 2 by saline pumps. Used for most process duties: dilution, sprays and the HP process water and mill water systems.

Scheme water: fresh pipeline water (SG 1.00), expensive, kept for jobs that cannot take salt, such as UFG gland seals, elution and reagent make up.

Raw water: the Raw Water Tank, fed from Bore Water or Saline Dam 3, supplying the LP and HP gland water pumps.

Plus cyanide water (TSF decant), potable and fire water. Each has its own tanks and pumps so qualities do not mix.

f.q: Where does the plant's saline water come from?
f.a:
From borefields and dams. The reference lists saline sources including the Kaltails borefield (N02), the Eastern Borefield and the offsite roaster saline transfer dam.

Within the plant, the Process Water Tank (F24-TK-401) is mainly fed by flotation tails thickener overflow, with top up from Bore Water Dam 2 (South Dam) by three saline pumps that trip on dam low low level. The Raw Water Tank is fed from Bore Water or Saline Dam 3 through booster pumps.

Fresh water is scarce in the Goldfields, so running the plant on saline water is a basic design choice. That is why corrosion resistant materials and reagent behaviour get so much attention.
f: What is in the N02 Kaltails borefields WBS scope?
Why do the saline pumps trip on dam low low level?
How much make up water does the plant need?

f.q: Which duties must use fresh scheme water?
f.a:
Scheme water, fresh from the Goldfields pipeline (SG 1.00), is reserved for duties where salt would cause problems.

The reference and cards mention gland seals on the UFG mills, elution (the CIL4 column uses scheme water for elution and cooling steps), reagent make up, and safety showers. In general, anything where salt would corrode equipment, scale heat exchangers, upset chemistry or harm people gets scheme water.

Because it is expensive and limited, scheme water use is watched closely. The MEL lists a scheme water booster pump in F24 and a UFG gland seal water scheme water tank in F28.
f: Why does elution need fresh water rather than saline?
How is scheme water use measured on site?
What happens to UFG mills if scheme water fails?

f.q: Why are some F24 water pumps made of super duplex steel?
f.a:
The MEL lists the raw water pumps, raw water booster pump and scheme water booster pump in F24 as super duplex stainless steel, and the gland seal pumps with titanium impellers.

The reason is chloride corrosion. Saline bore water attacks ordinary stainless steels through pitting and crevice corrosion, especially where flow is fast or stagnant. Super duplex and titanium resist chlorides far better, so they last in saline service.

It is the same choice you see in seawater cooling systems. For pumps handling slurry, rubber or hard metal linings deal with wear, but clear saline water pumps need corrosion resistant metallurgy.
f: Why does chloride cause pitting in stainless steel?
Why do gland seal pumps use titanium impellers?
How are saline water pipelines protected from corrosion?

What is Area F24?.q: What would low instrument air pressure cause across the plant?
What is Area F24?.a:
In general, nearly every pneumatic valve and instrument on the plant depends on instrument air: control valve actuators and positioners, knife gate valves on the cyclones, actuated pump suction, discharge and dump valves, flotation air valves, and the CIL4 pneumatic slurry bypass gates.

Low pressure first means sluggish or erratic valve movement, then valves drifting to their fail positions. Valve watchdog timers flag fail to open or close, sequences pause, and process loops lose control. A major loss trips large parts of the plant.

Instrument air comes from the plant and instrument air compressors (F24 for new plant, F81 existing), dried and filtered, with receivers as a short buffer. Low header pressure alarms give early warning.

f.q: What are valve fail positions and why do they matter?
f.a:
Every actuated valve is designed to go to a defined position when it loses air or power: fail open, fail closed, or fail last. The choice depends on what is safest for the process.

For example, the control philosophy says slurry pump dump valves fail open on power loss, so lines drain rather than sanding up. A reagent dosing valve would usually fail closed so chemicals stop flowing.

So on an instrument air failure, the plant moves to a known state. Knowing a valve's fail position tells you what will happen when air is lost. The control valve list records each valve's fail position.
f: Where are valve fail positions recorded on site?
What happens to cyclone knife gates on air loss?
How does a valve watchdog timer work?

f.q: How is instrument air kept clean and dry?
f.a:
In general, compressed air passes through dryers, usually refrigerated or desiccant, to remove moisture, and filters to remove oil and particles, before going into the instrument air header. Receivers store air to smooth demand and give a short ride through if compressors trip.

The MEL lists three plant air compressors in F24 (oil injected rotary screw with integral dryers). Instrument air is kept separate from plant air, which is used for tools and blowing down, because instruments and valve positioners need clean, dry, oil free air at stable pressure.

Wet or oily air fouls positioners and solenoids, a common source of valve faults.
f: What does wet instrument air do to a positioner?
How often are instrument air dryers serviced?
Why is plant air kept separate from instrument air?

f.q: What backs up instrument air during a compressor trip?
f.a:
The reference does not detail it. In general, instrument air systems have duty and standby compressors that start automatically on low pressure, and air receivers that hold enough stored air to keep valves working for a short time while a standby starts. Some sites give instrument air priority, shutting off plant air users first when pressure falls.

The DCS and field I/O also ride through power dips on UPS, and the emergency generator starts automatically on an outage, which helps restore compressors.

For how the F24 and F81 systems back each other up, ask the electrical or utilities maintenance planner or the control room operator.
f: How long can air receivers hold the valves up?
What does the emergency generator power on site?
Which air users are shed first on low pressure?

What is Area F24?.q: How do F24 services differ operationally from the existing F75/F81 areas?
What is Area F24?.a:
The main difference is age and who built them, not how you operate them.

F24 is the new Growth Project air and water services area. The MEL lists the new Process Water Tank (F24-TK-401, about 18 m diameter), the Raw Water Tank (F24-TK-501), saline water pumps 1 to 3, raw water and booster pumps, HP process water pumps, mill water pumps, LP and HP gland seal water pumps, and plant air compressors 1 to 3.

F75 (water services existing) and F81 (air services existing) are the old FIM services that continue to supply existing plant.

Both run on the same Yokogawa DCS and site templates, so pumps and valves use the same Auto, Manual and Local modes and interlock rules. How the old and new systems are interconnected is not described in the reference.

f.q: What does the new Process Water Tank supply?
f.a:
The Process Water Tank (F24-TK-401) feeds the process water distribution through duty/standby pumps. The reference says it is mainly fed by flotation tails thickener overflow, with top up from Bore Water Dam 2.

In general, process water serves the big process duties: dilution at mills and cyclone hoppers through the mill water system, HP process water for sprays, launder sprays, trash screen sprays and hose points, and other process make up.

The MEL lists mill water pumps 1 and 2 and HP process water pumps 1 and 2 in F24, which take from that supply. Saline water quality limits it to duties that tolerate salt.
f: What is the difference between HP process water and mill water?
Why is thickener overflow the main process water source?
What happens if the Process Water Tank runs low?

f.q: How do LP and HP gland water differ?
f.a:
The reference says the lower portion of the Raw Water Tank supplies the LP and HP gland water pumps; the MEL lists LP gland seal water pumps 1 and 2 and HP gland seal water pumps 1 and 2, multistage vertical pumps with titanium impellers.

In general, gland water must be injected at a pressure higher than the slurry pump's discharge pressure, or slurry pushes into the packing. Most slurry pumps run at moderate pressure and can use the LP supply. High head pumps, such as cyclone feed or tailings pumps, need a higher pressure supply, the HP system.

Each pump's gland line then has a manual isolation, actuated valve, Maric constant flow valve and flow switch or flowmeter.
f: Why does gland water draw from the lower Raw Water Tank?
What happens when gland water flow is lost?
Which pumps need HP rather than LP gland water?

f.q: Do new and old air systems share a common header?
f.a:
The reference does not say. It lists F24 air and water services as new, with plant and instrument air compressors, and F81 as existing air services, but does not describe how they connect.

In general, on a brownfield expansion the new and old compressed air systems are often linked by a tie in with isolation valves, so one can support the other, but they can also be kept separate by area.

To find out, check the compressed air P&IDs for the F24 and F81 areas, or ask the utilities maintenance planner or the control room operator.
f: Where are the compressed air P&IDs kept?
How many compressors normally run on the new system?
What alarm warns of low instrument air pressure?

What is Area F28?.q: Why install two new IsaMills in F28 instead of one larger one?
What is Area F28?.a:
The reference gives the outcome, so the reasoning here is partly general.

Timing is the clearest reason. UFG 2 was installed in Stage 1, when part of the concentrate still went to the offsite roaster. UFG 3 came in Stage 2 so all concentrate could be treated at FIM. Two mills let the capacity arrive with each stage.

Two mills also give redundancy and turndown. Each M15,000 IsaMill (F28-MUF-402 and 403) draws about 3.5 MW and takes about 30 t/h nominal, up to about 46 t/h. If one is down for media top up or maintenance, the other keeps running, with UFG 1 and the filters as relief. One giant mill would mean an all or nothing outage.

It is like installing two pumps instead of one big one.

f.q: Is the M15,000 the largest IsaMill size available?
f.a:
The reference only gives the size used here: Glencore IsaMill M15,000, 3.8 MW installed, about 3.5 MW drawn, alongside the older M3000 (UFG 1, 1,120 kW).

In general the number in the model name refers to the internal grinding volume in litres, so an M15,000 has about 15 cubic metres. It is one of the larger models in the range, but I cannot confirm from the plant documents whether it is the largest available today.

For model range and capacity questions, the Glencore IsaMill vendor documentation, or the site's UFG process engineer, would be the right source.
f: How does grinding volume relate to IsaMill power?
Why does UFG 1 use a much smaller M3000 mill?
Who is the vendor support contact for the IsaMills?

f.q: What happens to UFG capacity when one F28 mill is down?
f.a:
Capacity roughly halves on the new mills. With UFG 2 or 3 offline, the remaining one can run up to about 46 t/h at P80 12 microns, and UFG 1 adds about 10 to 13 t/h. Anything beyond that goes from the filter feed tanks to the vacuum belt filters and the concentrate stockpile.

At the nominal concentrate rate of about 75 to 78 t/h, that means some concentrate is filtered and stockpiled rather than leached. A handover like 'UFG 2 offline for media top up, excess con going to filters' describes exactly this.

The stockpiled concentrate is deferred gold, treated later when UFG capacity is available.
f: How long does an IsaMill media top up take?
How is stockpiled concentrate reclaimed for UFG?
What product size does one mill give at 46 t/h?

f.q: How is concentrate split between UFG 2 and UFG 3?
f.a:
The MEL lists separate feed pumps for each UFG circuit in F35: UFG circuit 1 feed pump (F35-PP-435), UFG circuit 2 feed pump (F35-PP-448) and UFG circuit 3 feed pump (F35-PP-449), drawing from the filter feed tanks. In F28 each mill also has its own feed hopper and feed pump.

The control philosophy says the UFG feed pumps run on flow control, with density and mass flow measurement. So in general the split is set by the flow setpoints on each circuit, typically equal on UFG 2 and 3 in normal running, with UFG 1 brought in at high concentrate rates.

For the actual setpoint practice, ask the control room operator.
f: Why are the UFG feed pumps on flow control?
How is mass flow to each UFG mill calculated?
What happens to the split if one feed pump trips?

What is Area F28?.q: What handover sign would point to grinding media wear issues in F28?
What is Area F28?.a:
Media problems usually show through mill power and media consumption.

The control philosophy says media is added through a positioning knife gate to hold a mill power draw setpoint. So signs of a media issue include power struggling to hold setpoint, the media hopper (F28-HP-426 or 436) emptying faster than usual, product size drifting coarser on the particle size analyser, or media showing up where it should not, such as broken beads in the discharge or product.

The MEL lists media dewatering screens (F28-SC-442 and 452, 0.8 mm sieve bends) and Isacharger pumps for each mill, which handle media charging.

Shell vibration alarms can also point to mechanical issues like worn discs. The UFG maintenance planner tracks media consumption.

f.q: What does the Isacharger pump do?
f.a:
The MEL lists a UFG Mill 2 Isacharger pump (F28-PW-421) and a UFG Mill 3 Isacharger pump (F28-PW-431). The reference does not describe how they work.

In general, an Isacharger is the media charging system for an IsaMill: ceramic media is mixed with water and pumped into the mill, so media can be added while running without manual handling. That matches the control philosophy, where media is metered in through a positioning knife gate to hold a mill power setpoint.

For the details of the charging sequence and hopper arrangement, check the UFG P&IDs or the IsaMill vendor manual, or ask the UFG process engineer.
f: How is media delivered to the UFG media hoppers?
What sets the media addition rate in the DCS?
Why is media charged wet rather than dry?

f.q: What are the media dewatering screens for?
f.a:
The MEL lists a media dewatering screen for each new mill (F28-SC-442 and 452), static sieve bends with 0.8 mm openings in 316 stainless.

The reference does not describe their duty. In general, a static sieve bend lets water and fine slurry drain through while retaining larger particles, here ceramic media. It is used to separate media from water, for example when media is charged as a slurry or recovered from the mill during maintenance, so it can be reused rather than lost.

The UFG process engineer or the P&IDs would confirm exactly where they sit in the circuit.
f: How does a static sieve bend separate solids?
Can recovered media be reused in the mill?
What size are the IsaMill ceramic beads?

f.q: Why does broken media hurt downstream equipment?
f.a:
In general, ceramic media is hard and abrasive. Whole beads are retained in the IsaMill by its product separator, but broken pieces can be small enough to escape with the product.

Escaped media fragments can wear pumps, cyclones and pipe bends, collect in hoppers and tank bottoms, and in the leach they act like abrasive grit on agitators and intertank screens. Lost media also has to be replaced, adding cost.

Media breakage rises with poor quality media, wrong media size for the duty, or mechanical problems in the mill. That is one reason media consumption and product oversize are watched.
f: How is media consumption measured per tonne?
What does the IsaMill product separator do?
Why does media quality vary between suppliers?

What is Area F28?.q: What feeds into F28 and where does its product go next?
What is Area F28?.a:
Feed comes from the concentrate thickener side; product goes to the concentrate leach.

Feed: final concentrate is thickened in 30-TH-61, then held in filter feed tanks A and B (700 m3 each in the MEL) at about 60 percent solids. UFG circuit feed pumps (F35-PP-448 for UFG 2, F35-PP-449 for UFG 3) send it through static trash screens to each mill's feed hopper (F28-HP-424 and 434) and feed pump. Each mill runs in closed circuit with its own cyclone cluster (24 x 100 mm cyclones).

Product: cyclone overflow at about 17 to 18 percent solids, P80 about 9 microns, goes to the UFG product hopper (F28-HP-430) and UFG product pumps (F28-PP-409 and 410), then to the concentrate pre leach thickener 30-TH-31 and on to CIL2.

f.q: Why do the UFG mills run in closed circuit with cyclones?
f.a:
So that only particles that are fine enough leave, and coarser ones go back for more grinding.

Each mill discharges to a hopper, and a discharge pump feeds its cyclone cluster. Cyclone overflow, the fine product at about 17 to 18 percent solids, goes forward; underflow at about 48 percent solids returns to the mill. That gives a tighter product size distribution than a single pass, and stops coarse particles escaping to the leach where their locked gold would not be exposed.

The control philosophy says the UFG 3 discharge hopper density is controlled by water addition, swapping to level control if level is low, and the cyclone valves operate on pressure or level deadband.
f: Why are the UFG cyclones only 100 mm in diameter?
What is the UFG cyclone underflow density target?
How does closed circuit grinding affect energy use?

f.q: What does the pre leach thickener do with UFG product?
f.a:
It thickens it before the leach. UFG product arrives dilute, at about 17 to 18 percent solids, because the cyclones need dilute feed for fine classification. Sent straight to CIL2, that much water would cut residence time badly.

The concentrate pre leach thickener (30-TH-31, a 27 m high rate thickener, repurposed from FIM Flotation Tailings Thickener No. 2) raises it to about 52 to 58 percent solids underflow. Duty/standby VSD underflow pumps (F30-PP-415 and 416) run on a cascade from bed pressure or density to flow, and can recycle to the feed box.

The overflow recovers water. The underflow goes to the CIL2 leach feed box.
f: What flocculant dose does fine UFG product need?
Why does fine ground concentrate settle slowly?
Where does pre leach thickener overflow water go?

f.q: How is UFG product sampled for size?
f.a:
The MEL lists product sample pumps for each new mill, UFG Mill 2 product sample pump (F28-PP-494) and UFG Mill 3 product sample pump (F28-PP-495), both peristaltic pumps.

The control philosophy says the UFG circuit has an online particle size analyser, a vendor package reporting to the DCS. In general the sample pumps deliver a continuous sample of product slurry to the analyser, which measures the size distribution and reports P80 against the 9 micron target.

Peristaltic pumps suit small, abrasive sample flows because only the hose touches the slurry. Lab sizing of composite samples is used to check the analyser.
f: How often does the online size analyser report?
Why use peristaltic pumps for slurry samples?
What happens if the size analyser is offline?

What is Area F30?.q: Why was CIL2 repurposed for leach duty and CIL3 for adsorption specifically?
What is Area F30?.a:
The reference records the change but not the reasoning, so this is general practice applied to the design.

Separating leach and adsorption lets each run in its best conditions. CIL2 can run very aggressive leaching, pH 11.75 to 12.5, cyanide up to 6,500 ppm in the later tanks, heavy oxygen through lances and new injection pumps on the first two tanks, and lead nitrate, without carbon in the way. With no carbon there, the carbon is not abraded by oxygen injection pumps, and dissolving gold is not competing with fouling of carbon by fine reactive sulphides.

CIL3 then does adsorption only, with carbon at about 20 g/L and no oxygen.

The order simply follows the slurry flow: CIL2 tanks come first, and CIL3 tails go on to CIL4.

f.q: Why does CIL3 run without any oxygen addition?
f.a:
The reference states that CIL3 is adsorption only with no oxygen; the reasoning is general.

Oxygen is needed to dissolve gold. By the time slurry leaves CIL2, the leach has done its work, with design extraction of about 90 percent. CIL3's job is to catch the dissolved gold on carbon, and adsorption does not need oxygen. Skipping it saves oxygen supply and equipment.

Some leaching still continues with the residual cyanide and dissolved oxygen in the slurry, and CIL3 tails go on to CIL4, where oxygen is added again. The oxygen plant supplies both CIL2/3 and CIL4 from the PSA unit with liquid oxygen backup.
f: How much oxygen does the concentrate leach consume?
Does any leaching continue in the CIL3 tanks?
How are CIL3 carbon concentrations measured?

f.q: What is leach then CIL compared with plain CIL?
f.a:
In plain CIL, carbon is in every tank from the start, so leaching and adsorption happen together throughout the train. In leach then CIL, the first tanks leach without carbon, then the following tanks hold carbon.

On this plant both arrangements appear. CIL4 is leach then CIL in one train: 2 leach tanks, then 6 adsorption tanks. The concentrate circuit takes the idea further: CIL2 is a whole leach train (seven tanks, 32A to 32G), then CIL3 is a whole adsorption train (seven tanks, 62A to 62G).

The card describes it as working like a leach then CIL train. The benefit is dedicated conditions for each step.
f: Why does CIL4 have only two leach tanks?
How are carbon and slurry moved through CIL3?
What would plain CIL do to concentrate leach costs?

f.q: Why was a seventh tank added to both trains?
f.a:
The reference gives CIL2 as tanks 30-TK-32A to 32F plus a new 32G, and CIL3 as 62A to 62G, with 62G added in the enabling works per the MEL and the as built PFD. The older PDC design basis used six CIL3 tanks.

It does not state the reason. In general, adding a tank to each train increases residence time, about one sixth more volume per train at 1,685 m3 per tank, giving more leach time in CIL2 and more adsorption stages in CIL3. That supports the higher design leach extraction agreed for CIL2/3 (90 percent) and lower soluble losses.

For the design history, ask the process engineering team.
f: When was CIL3 tank 62G installed?
How do agitator sizes compare between CIL2 and CIL4?
What does enabling works mean in project terms?

What is Area F30?.q: What would a handover flag if concentrate leach residence time dropped?
What is Area F30?.a:
In general it would flag the causes rather than the residence time itself.

Typical notes: concentrate feed rate above normal, more tonnes through the same tanks; pre leach thickener underflow density low, below about 52 percent solids, so more water and volume; a CIL2 tank out of service or bypassed; or levels running low.

The consequence is less time for leaching, so lower gold extraction against the design 90 percent, and more gold carried through CIL3 to CIL4, where the conditions are much weaker. Cyanide and oxygen use per tonne may also shift.

The response is usually to restore underflow density, check thickener performance, and confirm all tanks are in circuit. The CIL metallurgist would watch residue assays closely.

f.q: How long is the CIL2 leach residence time at design?
f.a:
The reference gives the inputs but not the result, so this is my rough estimate.

CIL2 has seven tanks of 1,685 m3, about 11,800 m3. The design feed is about 104 t/h of solids at about 49 percent solids. Using a solids SG near the concentrate's 3.93 and saline water at SG 1.07, the slurry flow comes out at roughly 130 m3/h. That gives a residence time in the order of 90 hours, three to four days, before allowing for freeboard and dead volume.

That long time fits a concentrate leach, which needs it for fine, reactive sulphide concentrate. Check the PDC or ask the metallurgist for the official figure.
f: Why does concentrate leaching need days, not hours?
How does tank freeboard reduce live volume?
What feed rate does CIL2 see at nominal grade?

f.q: What does low pre leach thickener underflow density do to CIL2?
f.a:
It sends more water into CIL2 with the same solids. The design underflow is about 52 to 58 percent solids, and CIL2 feed about 49 percent.

More water means more slurry volume through fixed tanks, so leach residence time drops. It also dilutes reagents: cyanide is ratioed to solids mass flow, so the dose per tonne holds, but the concentration in solution falls, which can slow leaching. Lime and lead nitrate behave similarly.

The underflow pumps run on a cascade from bed pressure or density to flow, so the loop should slow pumping to rebuild density. Persistent low density points to flocculant problems or thickener overload.
f: How is lead nitrate dosed at the leach feed box?
What causes the pre leach thickener to overload?
How is cyanide ratioed to solids mass flow?

f.q: Can a CIL2 tank be bypassed for maintenance?
f.a:
The reference does not describe bypass arrangements for CIL2. It mentions pneumatic slurry bypass gates only for CIL4, operated locally.

In general, leach trains are built with launders and bypass gates or spool pieces so a tank can be taken out of service while slurry flows around it, at the cost of reduced residence time. The tank is then drained and isolated before any work inside.

To find out what CIL2 has, check the F30 P&IDs or ask the CIL area supervisor. Any work on a cyanide tank goes through isolation, draining, cleaning and gas testing.
f: How are CIL4 slurry bypass gates operated?
What gas testing is required before tank entry?
How long does it take to drain a CIL tank?

What is Area F30?.q: What thickener feeds F30 and what tank codes mark its tanks?
What is Area F30?.a:
The concentrate pre leach thickener, 30-TH-31, feeds the leach. It is the old FIM Flotation Tailings Thickener No. 2, a 27 m high rate thickener, repurposed in Stage 2 to thicken UFG product to about 52 to 58 percent solids before CIL2. The concentrate thickener 30-TH-61, ahead of UFG, also sits in F30.

Tank codes use the TK equipment code with legacy numbers:

CIL2 leach tanks: 30-TK-32A to 32F, plus the new 32G.
CIL3 adsorption tanks: 30-TK-62A to 62G.

Each is 12.7 m diameter by 13.5 m high in the MEL, about 1,685 m3. The MEL writes them with an F prefix (F30-TK-62A), while older drawings often omit it (30-TK-32A).

f.q: Why do some drawings show 30-TK-32A and others F30-TK-32A?
f.a:
Both refer to the same tank. The existing FIM plant used tags like 30-TK-32A, with the area number and a letter suffix. The Growth Project numbering spec puts F, for FIM, in front of every area code, so in project lists like the MEL the same tank appears as F30-TK-32A.

You will see both styles because older drawings and the existing DCS may still use the legacy form, while new documents use the F prefix. The low numbers and letters (32A, 62G) mark them as legacy equipment; new Growth Project items start at 401.

When searching documents or the DCS, try both forms.
f: How are new Growth Project tags numbered?
Why do legacy tanks use letters like A to G?
Where is the master tag register kept?

f.q: How is CIL2 feed transferred from the pre leach thickener?
f.a:
The pre leach thickener underflow is pumped by duty/standby VSD underflow pumps (F30-PP-415 and 416 in the MEL) on a cascade loop: bed pressure or density sets a flow controller, which drives pump speed. They can recycle to the thickener feed box.

The underflow goes to the CIL2 leach feed box, where milk of lime and lead nitrate are added. Cyanide is ratioed to the solids mass flow on the CIL2 feed. The MEL also lists concentrate leach transfer pumps (F30-PP-426 and 427).

Design feed is about 104 t/h of solids at about 49 percent solids.
f: Why is lead nitrate added at the leach feed box?
How is milk of lime dosed to CIL2?
What do the concentrate leach transfer pumps move?

f.q: Where do CIL3 tails go after the last tank?
f.a:
To CIL4. Slurry leaving the last CIL3 tank passes a carbon detection meter (with a reference probe), then goes to the CIL3 tails hopper, where cyanide water is added. Duty/standby VSD pumps (CIL3 tails pumps F30-PP-428 and 429 in the MEL) send it to the CIL4 feed box.

In CIL4 the concentrate residue gets more leaching and adsorption, and its residual cyanide keeps working on the combined flotation tails slurry. Any dissolved gold that escaped CIL3 has another chance on CIL4 carbon.

After CIL4 everything goes to the final tails tank and the TSF.
f: What does the CIL3 carbon detection meter detect?
Why is cyanide water added at the CIL3 tails hopper?
How does CIL3 residue affect CIL4 cyanide demand?

What is Area F34?.q: Why keep the smaller UFG1 mill instead of retiring it along with offsite roaster?
What is Area F34?.a:
Because it is useful spare capacity at very little cost.

In Stage 2, UFG 2 and 3 do the normal duty. When concentrate production is high, they run at maximum (about 46 t/h each) and the excess goes to UFG 1 (F34-MUF-01, an M3000 IsaMill, 1,120 kW, about 10 t/h, 13 design). Only beyond that does concentrate go to the filters and stockpile.

The design grade case makes about 104 to 107 t/h of concentrate, and UFG 1, 2 and 3 plus the filters are sized for it. Without UFG 1, more concentrate would be filtered and stockpiled instead of leached.

The mill and its cyclones, pumps and gland water system already exist, and the MEL shows a new product hopper and pump added to tie it into the Stage 2 circuit.

f.q: How does UFG 1 compare in size with UFG 2 and 3?
f.a:
UFG 1 (F34-MUF-01) is an IsaMill M3000 with 1,120 kW installed, taking about 10 t/h (13 t/h design). The MEL notes a closed circuit with a feed rate of about 51 m3/h, and classification cyclones in pods of 4 inch cyclones, 26 in total.

UFG 2 and 3 (F28-MUF-402 and 403) are M15,000 IsaMills with 3.8 MW installed and about 3.5 MW drawn, taking about 30 t/h fresh feed nominal each and up to 46 t/h, with 24 x 100 mm cyclone clusters.

So each new mill is roughly three times UFG 1's power and throughput. All three target the same product, P80 about 9 microns.
f: Why do UFG 1 cyclones use 4 inch pods?
Does UFG 1 use the same ceramic media as UFG 2?
How old is UFG 1 compared with the new mills?

f.q: What trash protection does UFG 1 have?
f.a:
The reference says UFG 1 has a vibrating 1.0 mm mesh screen, while UFG 2 and 3 have inclined static wedge wire trash screens. The MEL lists a cyclone feed screen (F34-SC-01) in the UFG 1 area.

Trash such as wood fibre and plastic would block the IsaMill's product separator and internal screens, so every UFG mill has a screen ahead of it, on top of the main trash screens after the primary cyclones.

A vibrating mesh screen handles fine trash well but needs more maintenance than a static screen. Its condition is part of UFG 1's readiness when it is called into service.
f: Why use static screens on UFG 2 and 3 instead?
What happens to an IsaMill if trash gets inside?
How is a vibrating mesh screen cleaned?

f.q: When does UFG 1 come into service in Stage 2?
f.a:
When concentrate production is more than UFG 2 and 3 can handle. The Stage 2 operating philosophy says UFG 2 and 3 run normally; at high concentrate rates they run at maximum and the excess goes to UFG 1; anything beyond UFG capacity goes to the vacuum belt filters and stockpile.

In practice that means UFG 1 is called on during high sulphur ore, or when one of the new mills is down, for example for a media top up or maintenance.

The decision to start it would be the control room operator's, guided by concentrate rates and UFG 2 and 3 loading. Its feed comes through the UFG circuit 1 feed pump (F35-PP-435).
f: How long does UFG 1 take to start from standby?
What checks are done before starting UFG 1?
How is UFG 1 kept ready when not running?

What is Area F34?.q: What would reduced UFG1 throughput mean for overall treatment capacity?
What is Area F34?.a:
Normally very little, because UFG 1 is not part of the base duty in Stage 2. UFG 2 and 3 handle the normal concentrate.

It matters at high concentrate rates or when one new mill is down. Then UFG 1 is the next relief, about 10 t/h (13 design). If its throughput is reduced, more concentrate goes to the vacuum belt filters and the concentrate stockpile instead of being ground and leached.

That concentrate is not lost, but its gold is deferred until it can be reclaimed and treated, and the filters have their own capacity limit.

The design grade concentrate case of about 104 to 107 t/h needs all three mills plus the filters, so in that case UFG 1 availability matters.

f.q: What happens to concentrate that goes to the filters instead?
f.a:
It is dewatered on the existing vacuum belt filters (55 m2) to a cake below 10 percent moisture and placed on the concentrate stockpile in F35. The stockpile has a transportable moisture limit of about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w, which matters if it is to be moved in bulk.

The reference does not describe how stockpiled concentrate is later brought back into the process. In general it would be reclaimed and repulped when UFG capacity is available, or historically trucked offsite.

So filtering is a relief path, not a treatment route; the gold waits on the stockpile.
f: How is filter cake moisture kept below 10 percent?
Can stockpiled concentrate be repulped for UFG?
Does stored concentrate lose any gold value?

f.q: Why is stockpiled concentrate called deferred gold?
f.a:
Because the gold is still there but has not been produced. Concentrate on the stockpile carries its locked gold; until it is ground and leached, none of that gold reaches the goldroom.

From an accounting view, the gold has left the mill feed but is held as inventory on the stockpile, so plant recovery and gold output for the period look lower even though the gold is not lost.

There are some risks while it waits, in general: sulphide concentrate can oxidise in air, which can raise cyanide consumption when it is finally leached, and stockpiles need managing for dust and runoff.
f: How is concentrate inventory valued each month?
Why does oxidised concentrate consume more cyanide?
How is stockpile runoff and dust controlled?

f.q: What limits UFG 1 to about 10 to 13 t/h?
f.a:
Mainly its power. UFG 1 is an M3000 IsaMill with 1,120 kW installed. To reach the target product near P80 9 microns the new mills use about 116.5 kWh per tonne. Dividing 1,120 kW by about 116 kWh/t gives roughly 10 t/h, which matches the quoted rate. That is my calculation from the design figures.

Pushing more tonnes through would give each tonne less energy and a coarser product, the same trade off as on the bigger mills.

Its classification cyclones and pumps are sized to match. The 13 t/h design figure gives some headroom, probably at a slightly coarser product.
f: How does specific energy set IsaMill throughput?
What is the UFG 1 product size at 13 t/h?
Can UFG 1 power be increased with more media?

What is Area F34?.q: How does UFG1 output combine with the new F28 mills?
What is Area F34?.a:
The MEL shows that the project added a new UFG Mill 1 product hopper (F34-HP-405) and a UFG Mill 1 product pump (F34-PP-443) to the existing UFG 1 circuit. That is how UFG 1's ground product is collected and pumped forward in Stage 2.

The reference does not spell out where that pump discharges. Since all UFG product feeds the concentrate pre leach thickener (30-TH-31) ahead of CIL2, the most likely route is that UFG 1 product joins the UFG 2 and 3 product there, either directly or through the UFG product hopper.

To confirm, check the F34 and F28 P&IDs or the Stage 2 concentrate PFD, or ask the control room operator.

f.q: Why does UFG 1 have its own classification cyclones?
f.a:
Because each IsaMill runs in closed circuit. The MEL lists the UFG 1 classification cyclones (F34-CY-01) as pods of 4 inch cyclones, 26 in total.

Mill discharge goes to the cyclones; fine overflow goes forward as product, and coarse underflow returns to the mill for more grinding. That keeps coarse particles from escaping to the leach, where their locked gold would stay locked, and sharpens the product size distribution.

Small diameter cyclones are used because the cut size is very fine, around 10 microns. UFG 2 and 3 do the same with their own 24 x 100 mm clusters.
f: Why does a smaller cyclone give a finer cut size?
How are blocked small cyclones detected?
What density does UFG cyclone feed run at?

f.q: Does UFG 1 product size match UFG 2 and 3?
f.a:
The design target is the same for all UFG product: P80 about 9 microns, range 9 to 12. The reference gives UFG 1 at about 10 t/h (13 design) without a separate size figure.

In general, an older, smaller mill can match the size if it runs at a similar specific energy per tonne. At 1,120 kW and about 10 t/h, UFG 1 is close to the new mills' 116.5 kWh/t, so it should be comparable at its normal rate. Pushed towards 13 t/h it would likely run a little coarser.

The online particle size analysers and lab sizing would show the real comparison. The UFG metallurgist would know.
f: How is UFG 1 product size measured online?
What happens to leach recovery at P80 12 microns?
Does UFG 1 use the same media size as UFG 2?

f.q: How is UFG 1 feed taken from the filter feed tanks?
f.a:
The MEL lists a UFG circuit 1 feed pump (F35-PP-435), a peristaltic pump, in the concentrate handling area F35. The new mills have their own UFG circuit 2 and 3 feed pumps (F35-PP-448 and 449).

Concentrate comes from filter feed tanks A and B (700 m3 each, at about 60 percent solids, with a balance line). The UFG 1 feed passes its vibrating 1.0 mm mesh screen and goes to the UFG mill feed hopper (F34-HP-01) and feed pump (F34-PP-01).

A peristaltic pump suits the small, controlled flow UFG 1 needs, about 10 t/h, since its output follows speed closely.
f: Why use a peristaltic pump for UFG 1 feed?
How are filter feed tank levels controlled?
What does the UFG 1 feed hopper do?

What is Area F35?.q: Why keep vacuum belt filters running when UFG treats most concentrate?
What is Area F35?.a:
Because they are the relief path when concentrate exceeds what the UFG mills can treat.

In Stage 2, UFG 2 and 3 handle the normal duty, and UFG 1 picks up excess at high concentrate rates. Anything beyond that, from high sulphur ore, a mill offline for media top up or maintenance, or a UFG upset, has to go somewhere. The existing vacuum belt filters (55 m2) dewater it to cake below 10 percent moisture, and it goes to the concentrate stockpile.

Without them, excess concentrate would back up into the concentrate thickener and filter feed tanks, and flotation would have to cut mass pull or the plant would have to cut feed. It is like a relief valve to a holding tank: rarely the main path, but essential when needed.

f.q: How much filter capacity does F35 have?
f.a:
The reference gives the existing vacuum belt filters as 55 m2 producing cake below 10 percent moisture; the MEL lists equipment for filter 1 and filter 2 (filtrate, final filtrate and washdown pumps), and concentrate filter feed pumps 1 and 2.

It does not give a tonnage capacity for the filters. The design statement is that UFG 1, 2 and 3 plus the filters are sized for the design grade concentrate case of about 104 to 107 t/h.

In general, belt filter capacity depends on cake formation rate, which depends on particle size, slimes content and vacuum. For a t/h figure, ask the concentrate area metallurgist.
f: Why do two vacuum belt filters share the duty?
What does filtrate get recycled to?
How is vacuum produced on the belt filters?

f.q: What are the deslime cyclones in F35 used for now?
f.a:
The MEL lists the deslime cyclones (F35-CY-01) as in service: pods of 4 inch cyclones, 36 in total, with a feed rate of about 126 m3/h.

In Stage 1 the reference says the concentrate sent offsite was deslimed and filtered, so these cyclones removed the ultrafine slimes that blind filter cloths. The Stage 2 description does not say how they are used now.

Since the filters remain as a relief path, it is likely the desliming step remains available ahead of them. Ask the concentrate area metallurgist or the control room operator for current practice.
f: Where do the slimes from desliming go?
Why do slimes blind vacuum filter cloths?
Is desliming needed for concentrate going to UFG?

f.q: How big are filter feed tanks A and B?
f.a:
The MEL lists filter feed tank A (F35-TK-01A) and filter feed tank B (F35-TK-01B) as 700 m3 tanks each. The reference says they run at about 60 percent solids with a balance line between them, so they act as one buffer.

They hold the concentrate thickener underflow and feed both the UFG circuit feed pumps and the concentrate filter feed pumps. That makes them the hub of the concentrate side: from here concentrate goes to grinding, or to the filters when UFG is full.

Agitation keeps the solids suspended at that density, so agitator health matters; a stalled agitator in a 700 m3 tank at 60 percent solids would quickly sand up.
f: What does the balance line between tanks A and B do?
How are filter feed tank levels kept in range?
What agitator protections do these tanks have?

What is Area F35?.q: What handover note flags filter capacity being exceeded?
What is Area F35?.a:
Typical signs that concentrate is arriving faster than it can be filtered:

Filter feed tank levels rising in tanks A and B. Cake coming off wet, above the 10 percent moisture target. Filter cloths blinding or vacuum falling. The concentrate thickener bed and torque climbing because underflow cannot be pulled away. The concentrate stockpile growing, or wet cake that would fail the transportable moisture limit (about 6.1 to 8.3 percent).

A note might read 'filters can't keep up, FFT levels high' or 'cake wet'. That usually means UFG capacity is short as well. The fallback is to reduce concentrate production, by trimming flotation mass pull, or to cut plant feed, a decision for the CRO and supervisor.

f.q: What makes filter cake come off too wet?
f.a:
In general, a few things.

Feed: more fines or slimes in the concentrate, which pack tightly and hold water, or lower feed density.

Filter: blinded or damaged cloth, low vacuum from leaks or vacuum pump problems, or belt speed too fast for the cake to dewater.

Load: pushing more tonnes over the filter than it can handle, giving a thick cake that does not drain.

The fixes are washing or changing cloths, checking vacuum, slowing the belt, and confirming desliming is working. Wet cake matters because it may exceed the stockpile's transportable moisture limit.
f: How is belt filter speed set for cake moisture?
How often are filter cloths replaced?
What does a vacuum leak look like on the filter?

f.q: What happens when filter feed tanks run high?
f.a:
They are the buffer between the concentrate thickener and both the UFG mills and the filters, 700 m3 each. If they run high, the buffer is nearly full, so any further imbalance has nowhere to go.

In general the thickener underflow pumps then have to slow, the concentrate thickener bed builds, rake torque rises and overflow can get dirty, losing fine gold bearing concentrate. If it continues, flotation mass pull or plant feed has to come down.

High tank levels also make solids suspension harder. The response is to increase draw to UFG and filters where possible and reduce incoming concentrate.
f: How does the concentrate thickener respond to backing up?
What alarm warns of filter feed tank high level?
How is flotation mass pull trimmed in an upset?

f.q: Who decides to cut mass pull when the concentrate side is full?
f.a:
The reference does not assign that decision. In general, the control room operator makes the immediate call to protect equipment, for example trimming flotation air or reagents, or cutting plant feed, following the operating procedures and supervisor guidance. The process metallurgist sets the longer term strategy for how hard to pull flotation versus what the concentrate side can treat.

The flotation expert system adjusts level, air and reagents within its limits, but a deliberate cut in mass pull to protect the concentrate side is an operations decision.

Ask the shift supervisor or metallurgist how it is handled here.
f: How does cutting mass pull affect plant recovery?
Can the flotation expert system limit concentrate rate?
What does the shift supervisor check first in an upset?

What is Area F35?.q: What happens to concentrate stockpiled at F35 during upset conditions?
What is Area F35?.a:
It waits there until it can be treated, but the reference does not describe how it is brought back.

What the documents say: excess concentrate beyond UFG capacity goes through the vacuum belt filters to the concentrate stockpile, as cake below 10 percent moisture, with a transportable moisture limit of about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w if it is to be moved in bulk.

In general, stockpiled concentrate is later reclaimed by loader, repulped with water and fed back into the concentrate circuit when UFG capacity is free, or in the past was trucked offsite. While it sits, it is gold inventory rather than production.

For the actual reclaim route and how often it is used, ask the concentrate area supervisor or the metallurgist.

f.q: Can stockpiled concentrate oxidise while it waits?
f.a:
Yes, in general. Fine sulphide concentrate exposed to air and moisture slowly oxidises, forming iron and other sulphates and some acidity. It can also heat up in large piles.

Oxidised concentrate can behave differently when finally treated: soluble oxidation products consume more cyanide and lime in the leach, and some surface coatings can affect leaching. The longer it sits and the wetter it is, the more oxidation.

So stockpiling is best kept short. The metallurgist would track the age of stockpiled concentrate and adjust reagents when it is reclaimed.
f: How does oxidised concentrate affect cyanide use?
Can a concentrate stockpile self heat?
How is stockpile runoff collected and treated?

f.q: Why does stockpiled concentrate need to stay under its TML?
f.a:
Because above the transportable moisture limit, fine concentrate can liquefy when vibrated or compacted during transport. Water held between particles gets squeezed until the material flows like a slurry, which can shift a load in a truck or spill.

The reference gives the stockpile TML as 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w and the filter target as below 10 percent moisture, so cake usually needs to dry further, or be managed, before any bulk haulage.

For onsite rehandling the risk is lower, but wet concentrate is still sticky, hard to handle and prone to slumping. The TML is set by lab testing of the specific material.
f: How is the TML of a concentrate tested?
How does concentrate dry out on a stockpile?
What happens if a load exceeds its TML?

f.q: How is concentrate on the stockpile accounted for?
f.a:
The reference does not cover this. In general, metallurgical accounting tracks the concentrate sent to the stockpile as tonnes and grade, from weighed or metered filter feed and assays, and carries it as an inventory of contained gold.

When it is reclaimed and treated, that gold moves from inventory into production. Regular surveys of the stockpile volume check the tonnes, and moisture and grade samples keep the gold estimate honest.

How it is done on this site would be the process metallurgist's or the metallurgical accountant's area.
f: How often is the concentrate stockpile surveyed?
How are concentrate grades assayed for accounting?
How does inventory change affect monthly recovery?

What is Area F65?.q: Why does the concentrate side need its own carbon circuit separate from F22?
What is Area F65?.a:
Mainly because the carbon is very different and the equipment already existed.

CIL3 carbon loads to about 4,490 g/t at design, versus roughly 332 to 579 g/t for CIL4. Mixing them would dilute the rich carbon, and elution efficiency and gold accounting are easier when each stream is stripped on its own. The volumes differ too: CIL3 has about 202 t of carbon in circuit at 20 g/L, while CIL4 runs a much larger flow at 12.5 g/L.

F65 reuses the existing concentrate carbon equipment: two split AARL elution circuits with separate acid wash columns, heat exchangers, and regeneration kilns No. 3 and 4 in the MEL. Stage 2 added a new CIL3 loaded carbon pump, screen and transfer hopper. CIL4 got its own new column and kiln in F22, sized for its duty.

f.q: How much carbon does each circuit strip per batch?
f.a:
The reference does not give strip sizes or frequencies for either circuit. It gives carbon in circuit for CIL3 (about 202 t at 20 g/L) and the CIL4 concentration (12.5 g/L), plus the CIL4 elution volume of 5 bed volumes of eluate.

In general, a strip batch is a fixed column load of carbon, often a few tonnes up to around 10 or more, and the number of strips per day is set by how much loaded carbon the circuit makes.

For the actual batch size and strip frequency on F65 and F22, ask the elution operator or the CIL metallurgist.
f: What is a bed volume in elution terms?
How does carbon advance rate set strip frequency?
What limits how many strips a day a column can do?

f.q: What existing equipment does F65 still use?
f.a:
The MEL lists a lot of existing F65 equipment in service: primary heat exchangers No. 1 and 2 and recovery heat exchangers No. 1 and 2, elution circuit No. 1 and 2 water pumps, elution caustic and cyanide dosing pumps, lean eluate tanks, an elution water tank, heater oil tanks, carbon rinse screens, stripped carbon dewatering screens, carbon regeneration kilns No. 3 and 4 (F65-KN-61 and 62) with their quench tanks, barren carbon pumps, a carbon transfer pump and a venturi wet scrubber.

New in Stage 2 are the CIL3 loaded carbon pump (F65-PP-481, recessed impeller), CIL3 loaded carbon screen (F65-SC-471) and CIL3 loaded carbon transfer hopper (F65-HP-461).
f: What does the venturi wet scrubber clean in F65?
Why does elution use primary and recovery exchangers?
How old are the existing elution circuits in F65?

f.q: Why are high carbon loadings an advantage for elution?
f.a:
Because elution cost and capacity scale with tonnes of carbon, not ounces of gold. Each strip handles a fixed column load of carbon and uses roughly the same heat, water, caustic, cyanide and acid regardless of how much gold is on it.

So carbon loaded to about 4,490 g/t, as in CIL3, delivers many more ounces per strip than carbon at a few hundred g/t, as in CIL4. Fewer strips per ounce means lower cost and less carbon handling and attrition.

The trade off, in general, is that very high loadings need efficient elution to avoid leaving gold behind, and carbon held at high loading represents a lot of gold inventory.
f: Why does CIL4 carbon load so much less than CIL3?
What happens if elution leaves gold on carbon?
How is loaded carbon grade measured before stripping?

What is Area F65?.q: What symptom in a handover suggests F65 elution efficiency is dropping?
What is Area F65?.a:
In general, the clearest sign is gold left behind: a higher than usual gold assay on stripped (barren) carbon after elution. Other signs are lower pregnant eluate grades, strips taking longer, or temperature not reaching setpoint during the hot elution step.

Downstream effects follow: carbon going back to CIL3 still carrying gold, which lowers its capacity, and loaded carbon backing up in CIL3 if strips cannot keep pace, showing as higher carbon loadings in the first tanks.

Common causes are heater or heat exchanger problems, incomplete acid washing leaving scale, pre soak issues with caustic or cyanide strength, or flow problems through the column. The elution operator and CIL metallurgist would review the strip records.

f.q: Why does elution temperature matter so much?
f.a:
Gold desorbs from carbon much faster at high temperature. The AARL method relies on hot water, well above 100 C, after a caustic cyanide pre soak, to strip gold into the eluate. The column is pressurised so the solution does not flash to steam.

A few degrees low and elution slows noticeably, so more gold stays on the carbon in the time available. That is why temperature control on the eluate line is central to the elution sequence.

On F65 the existing circuits use heat exchangers (primary and recovery) and heater oil tanks in the MEL; on CIL4 the LPG fired heater works through heat exchangers with a temperature controller on the eluate line.
f: What heats the existing F65 elution circuits?
Why is the elution column pressurised?
How does the recovery heat exchanger save energy?

f.q: What happens if stripped carbon still holds gold?
f.a:
It goes back to CIL3 still partly loaded. That gold is not lost, but it is not produced either: it becomes circulating inventory. The carbon also has less capacity to pick up new gold, so adsorption efficiency in CIL3 falls, and soluble gold losses to CIL3 tails can rise (CIL3 tails go on to CIL4, which gives some second chance).

If the residual gold is high, the metallurgist may decide to re strip the carbon.

Regeneration in the kiln does not remove gold; it burns off organics. So poor elution passes straight through to the carbon going back to the tanks.
f: When would carbon be re stripped in elution?
How is stripped carbon sampled after elution?
What residual gold on carbon is acceptable?

f.q: How are the existing elution heaters heated?
f.a:
The reference does not say how the existing F65 elution circuits are heated. It describes the CIL4 heater as LPG fired.

The MEL lists heater oil tanks No. 1 and 2 (F65-TK-67 and 68) and primary and recovery heat exchangers in F65. In general, that arrangement points to a thermal oil system: a heater warms a circulating oil, and the oil heats the elution solution through the primary heat exchangers, while the recovery heat exchangers pass heat from outgoing hot eluate to incoming cold solution.

To confirm the heater type and fuel, check the F65 P&IDs or ask the elution operator.
f: Why use thermal oil instead of direct firing?
What maintenance do heat exchangers need here?
How is elution heater temperature controlled?

What is Area F65?.q: What downstream equipment receives eluate coming out of F65?
What is Area F65?.a:
The reference does not map the F65 eluate route in detail, so this answer combines what it does say with general practice.

In split AARL elution, the solution coming off the column goes to different places by stage. The rich pregnant eluate goes to electrowinning, where gold plates onto cathodes, and the cathode sludge is smelted to doré in the goldroom (F66). The later, weaker fraction is saved in the lean eluate tanks (the MEL lists F65-TK-61 and 62) for the first stage of the next strip.

After electrowinning, the spent eluate still holds some gold and cyanide, so the reference sends a portion to CIL2, and spent eluate is also part of the CIL4 feed.

Which electrowinning cells serve the F65 circuits is not stated; ask the goldroom supervisor.

f.q: What is spent eluate and where does it go?
f.a:
Spent eluate is the solution left after electrowinning has taken most of the gold out of the pregnant eluate. It still carries some gold, cyanide and caustic.

The reference says a portion of spent eluate returns to CIL2, and spent eluate is listed as part of the CIL4 feed with the flotation tails thickener underflow and CIL3 tails.

Returning it to a leach recovers the remaining gold onto carbon and reuses the cyanide and alkalinity, instead of treating it as waste. It also helps the water balance, since the eluate was made with scheme water.
f: How much gold is left in spent eluate?
Why is eluate made with fresh scheme water?
Does spent eluate change CIL2 cyanide control?

f.q: How does lean eluate get reused in the next strip?
f.a:
In split AARL, not all the eluate from a strip is pregnant enough to send to electrowinning. The later, weaker fraction, lean eluate, is saved in a lean eluate tank.

At the next strip it is used first, after the pre soak, to start eluting the fresh loaded carbon. Because it already contains caustic and cyanide and some gold, it saves reagents and water, and the fresh water used later in the strip becomes the next batch of lean eluate.

The MEL lists lean eluate tanks in F65 (F65-TK-61 and 62) and in F22 for CIL4 (F22-TK-442). On CIL4, pregnant eluate goes to the circulation tanks, then diverts to the lean eluate tank when they are full.
f: Why does split AARL save water compared with plain AARL?
How many bed volumes of eluate does a strip use?
What sets when eluate switches to the lean tank?

f.q: What happens to cathode sludge in the goldroom?
f.a:
In electrowinning, gold deposits on stainless steel cathodes as a loose sludge. In the goldroom (F66) the sludge is washed off, dried, mixed with fluxes and smelted, and the molten metal is poured into doré bars, a gold and silver alloy sent to the refinery.

The fluxes form a slag that takes up base metals and impurities. The gravity EW cells are clean in place, so their sludge is washed out without removing cathodes.

The goldroom is a high security area with controlled access. The refinery then separates gold from silver and other metals.
f: What fluxes are used to smelt goldroom sludge?
Why does doré contain silver as well as gold?
How is goldroom security managed on site?

What is Area F66?.q: Why are there separate electrowinning cells for gravity gold and CIL4 gold?
What is Area F66?.a:
The two solutions are very different, so they get their own cells. Gravity electrowinning treats the pregnant solution from the Acacia intensive leach reactor: a small daily batch of about 14.5 m3 at roughly 1,100 to 1,800 ppm Au. CIL4 electrowinning treats eluate from the CIL4 elution column, a much larger volume at a lower grade.

Mixing them would dilute the rich ILR solution and tie the gravity batch timing to the elution timing. Keeping them apart also lets the metallurgists account for gravity gold and leach gold separately.

In the equipment list the gravity cell is F66-EC-401 with rectifiers F66-ER-401A and B. The Stage 2 CIL4 cells are F66-EC-411 and 412, each with its own pair of rectifiers. It is the same reasoning as sizing a separate heat exchanger for each duty rather than forcing one unit to cover two very different flows.

f.q: How does electrowinning actually plate gold onto the cathodes?
f.a:
A rectifier converts AC to DC and drives current through the cell. Gold sits in the eluate as a gold cyanide complex. At the cathodes it picks up electrons and deposits as metal, mostly as a loose sludge on the cathode mesh. At the anodes water is oxidised and oxygen is given off.

The design current density for the gravity cell is 15 to 25 A/m2. Above that range you mostly waste power on side reactions such as hydrogen evolution and get poorer quality deposit. Solution flow matters too, because gold has to be carried to the cathode surface. The gravity design is 24 m3/h through each of its two compartments of 11 cathodes.
f: Why is current density limited rather than just turning up the amps?
What are the cathodes in these cells usually made of?
Is the gas given off at the anodes a hazard in the cell room?

f.q: Why does the gravity solution have a barren target below 5 ppm Au?
f.a:
The design runs gravity electrowinning for about 10 hours per batch until the solution is below 5 ppm Au. The solution starts at around 1,100 to 1,800 ppm, so that target means more than 99 percent of the gold has been plated out.
