Any gold left in the barren solution is not won on that pass. It either recirculates through the circuit or is lost, depending on where the barren goes. The condensed reference does not say where the gravity barren is sent, so check the F66 P&ID or ask the metallurgist.

Treat 5 ppm as a design value. The live target and the actual barren assays are on the shift and lab records.
f: What happens if the batch is stopped before barren is reached?
Who samples the barren solution and how quickly are results back?
Why does plating slow down as the solution gets weaker?

f.q: Could the gravity cell take CIL4 eluate if the CIL4 cells were down?
f.a:
The plant reference does not describe any crossover between the gravity and CIL4 electrowinning circuits, so I can't tell you reliably whether it is possible or allowed.

In general terms it would be limited by volume and timing. The gravity cell is sized for a small, rich daily batch at 24 m3/h per compartment, while CIL4 eluate comes in much larger volumes. Mixing streams would also upset gold accounting between gravity and leach.

Ask the goldroom supervisor or the metallurgist. They will know whether a piping route exists and whether there is an approved procedure for it.
f: What contingency is there if a CIL4 eluate circulation tank fills up?
How long can pregnant eluate safely wait before electrowinning?
Do the existing EW cells in F66 have spare capacity?

What is Area F66?.q: What would a handover flag if electrowinning cell current dropped?
What is Area F66?.a:
Rectifier current is what plates the gold, so lower current means less gold deposited per hour. The batch takes longer or the barren grade comes out higher.

A useful handover would say which cell and which rectifier (for example F66-ER-401A or B on the gravity cell), whether the rectifier tripped or is running at reduced output, what the cell voltage did, whether solution flow was normal, and what the latest barren assay showed. It should also say whether the batch was extended.

Common causes are a rectifier fault, corroded busbar or cathode contacts, cathodes shorting, or a solution problem. Think of it like a motor suddenly drawing less current: either the supply has changed or the load has, and voltage tells you which.

f.q: Why would cell voltage change if the current dropped?
f.a:
A rectifier on current control raises its voltage to push the set current through the cell. If resistance in the circuit rises, from poor busbar contacts, corroded cathode hangers or scaling, the rectifier eventually hits its voltage limit and the current falls. So high voltage with low current points to resistance.

Low voltage with low current points more to the rectifier itself, such as a fault, a derate or a trip of one unit. A short between an anode and a cathode usually shows as a voltage drop with current held up, while that cathode stops plating properly.

This is general electrowinning behaviour. The project's alarm limits are not in the condensed reference.
f: What does a cathode to anode short look like on the trends?
How are busbar contacts kept clean in a corrosive cell room?
Why does the gravity cell have two rectifiers instead of one?

f.q: How would you confirm whether gold is still plating properly?
f.a:
The direct check is solution assays. Compare the gold in the cell feed with the barren leaving it. If the drop across the cell is shrinking or the batch is not reaching barren, plating has slowed.

The equipment list includes a gravity and CIL4 electrowinning sampler cabinet, F66-XM-493, so routine samples come from a fixed point. The lab turns those into assays.

Alongside that, trend rectifier current and voltage, solution flow and temperature. Good current with poor gold removal suggests the current is going into side reactions or a short. Low current explains the slow plating by itself. The design barren for gravity is below 5 ppm Au, but use the live target from the metallurgist.
f: How long does a gold solution assay usually take to come back?
Why can high current still give poor gold removal?
Does solution temperature affect electrowinning efficiency?

f.q: Who should be called if an EW rectifier trips on shift?
f.a:
A rectifier is electrical plant, so a trip goes to the shift electrician, and the control room operator logs it. The goldroom or elution supervisor should be told too, because the batch timing and security arrangements around the cells may be affected.

Do not reset protection or open rectifier panels yourself unless you are authorised. Protection trips are there for a reason and the rectifier output is high current DC.

The reference does not set out a specific F66 call out procedure. Check the area's shift instructions or ask the control room operator who the on call contacts are.
f: What electrical hazards are specific to electrowinning cells?
Can the batch continue on one rectifier if the other has tripped?
What gets recorded in the shift log after a rectifier trip?

What is Area F66?.q: What happens to cathode sludge before it reaches the smelting furnace?
What is Area F66?.a:
The condensed reference does not spell out the goldroom steps, but the equipment list for F66 shows the route. There are high pressure cathode spray water pumps (F66-PW-62A) to wash sludge off the cathodes, a sludge dewatering cone (F66-TK-64), a sludge filter press (F66-FI-61) and its pump, a sludge drying oven (F66-OV-62), a mercury retort oven (F66-OV-66), calcine ovens and furnace, and two bullion smelting furnaces (F66-SF-01 and 02).

In general the sludge is washed off, dewatered, dried, retorted to drive off mercury, then mixed with fluxes and smelted. The slag takes base metals and the gold and silver are poured as doré.

The exact sequence and recipes are goldroom procedures. Ask the goldroom supervisor for the current method.

f.q: Why does sludge go through a mercury retort before smelting?
f.a:
Many gold ores carry traces of mercury. It dissolves in cyanide along with the gold, loads onto carbon and plates out in electrowinning, so it ends up in the cathode sludge.

If wet sludge went straight to a furnace, the mercury would vaporise into the goldroom air, which is a serious health hazard. A retort heats the sludge in a closed vessel, the mercury boils off and is condensed and collected. The F66 equipment list shows retort vacuum pumps (F66-PV-01A and B) and a retort chiller heat exchanger, which fits that arrangement.

The same concern is why the CIL4 regeneration kiln has a mercury abatement system that must run with the kiln.
f: Where does the recovered mercury go once it is collected?
How is goldroom air monitored for mercury vapour?
Why does mercury follow gold through the cyanide circuit?

f.q: What fluxes are added when smelting the dried sludge?
f.a:
The reference does not give the goldroom flux recipe. The F66 equipment list does show flux ducting, so flux handling is part of the setup.

In general gold smelting uses a mix of borax, silica, sodium nitrate and soda ash. Borax and silica form a fluid glassy slag. Nitrate oxidises base metals such as copper, iron and zinc so they report to the slag. Soda ash helps fluidity.

The right mix depends on what is in the sludge. The ILR solution carries noticeable copper (about 303 ppm in the design), so base metal load matters. The goldroom supervisor will know the current recipe.
f: Why does copper in the sludge lower the doré purity?
What happens to the slag after a smelt?
How is the doré bar sampled for its gold content?

f.q: Why is the goldroom so tightly controlled for security?
f.a:
Everything that comes out of the goldroom is close to pure value: dried sludge, calcine and doré bars hold a large share of the site's gold in a small, portable mass. That makes it the highest theft risk on the plant.

Goldrooms in general use restricted access lists, two person rules, CCTV, sealed containers, weighed and recorded transfers, and strict sampling chains of custody so the bullion count matches the metallurgical accounts.

The site's specific security rules are not in the plant reference. Your supervisor or the goldroom security officer will brief you before you are given any access.
f: Who reconciles goldroom output with the plant metallurgical balance?
What is doré and how pure is it typically?
Why are cathodes handled only under supervision?

What is Area F72?.q: Why must cyanide and acid reagents be stored and handled separately?
What is Area F72?.a:
Acid and cyanide together release hydrogen cyanide gas, which is lethal at low concentrations. Cyanide is safe to handle only while it stays alkaline, so any acid contact, from a leak, a shared bund or a common drain, is a major hazard.

On this plant cyanide arrives as about 29 percent NaCN solution and is distributed by a pressurised ringmain. Hydrochloric acid is used for acid washing carbon before elution, with its own DOL dosing pumps and a separate dilute acid tank for CIL4. They sit in separate bunds and their spills must not meet.

Keep the same logic in mind with the elution sequence. The acid wash and the caustic cyanide pre soak are separate steps with a water rinse between them for the same reason.

f.q: Why is cyanide solution kept at high pH with caustic?
f.a:
Cyanide in water exists as either the cyanide ion or hydrogen cyanide, and pH decides the split. Around pH 9.2 it is roughly half and half. Above about 10.5 almost all of it is the ion, which stays in solution instead of gassing off.

So caustic is added to cyanide storage and mixing to keep it well alkaline, and lime holds the pH in the leach. Interestingly, the CIL4 design leach pH is 8.8 to 9.3, lower than a typical leach. That is one reason CIL4 has HCN gas monitors with a beacon and siren.

Think of pH as the pressure that keeps a dissolved gas in solution. Drop it and the gas comes out.
f: Why does CIL4 run at a lower pH than the concentrate leach?
What pH does the concentrate leach CIL2 run at?
What happens to cyanide if lime dosing to a leach tank fails?

f.q: Where on the plant would HCN gas monitors be located?
f.a:
The control philosophy calls for an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren on CIL4. The instrument list shows three HCN analysers there: AIT21211 covering CIL4 tanks 1 and 2, AIT21212 the mid tank section, and AIT21213 tanks 7 and 8.

In general you would also expect fixed HCN detection wherever cyanide is mixed, stored or dosed, around leach tank tops, elution areas and the cyanide unloading point.

For the full list of HCN detectors in other areas, search the instrument list for HCN, or ask the area's safety coordinator. Always follow the site gas response procedure if one alarms.
f: What should you do if an HCN beacon starts flashing near you?
Why are HCN monitors placed near the first leach tanks?
How often are fixed HCN detectors bump tested?

f.q: What does a cyanide ringmain do differently from a simple dosing line?
f.a:
A ringmain keeps cyanide circulating in a loop from the tank, past every dosing point and back. On this plant cyanide and caustic both use pressurised ringmains with DOL pumps and a mechanical back pressure valve on the return.

The back pressure valve holds the loop pressure, like a relief valve holding pressure in a hydraulic ring main, so each dosing point always has supply available. Each point then has its own flowmeter and control valve to take what it needs.

Compared with a dedicated pump per user, it means fewer pumps and the solution never sits stagnant in a dead leg, which matters for a reagent that can crystallise or degrade.
f: Why is a DOL pump fine on a ringmain instead of a VSD?
What happens to dosing if the ringmain back pressure valve fails?
How is a cyanide flow setpoint ratioed to the ore tonnage?

What is Area F72?.q: What handover symptom points to a reagent dosing pump failure?
What is Area F72?.a:
Most F72 dosing loops are flow controlled. Copper sulphate, PAX, frother and lead nitrate use VSD dosing pumps on flow control, with a g/t or flow setpoint. A failing pump shows as the flow PV falling below setpoint while the controller output climbs towards 100 percent and the VSD speed goes up with no gain in flow.

Downstream you see the process effect. Lost frother changes the froth, lost PAX shows as rising tails grade on the onstream analyser, lost cyanide shows on the CIL4 cyanide analysers, and lost lime shows as falling pH.

A good handover names the pump, what was seen on the flow trend, whether the standby was started, and what the process did meanwhile.

f.q: How does a dosing loop in g/t mode calculate the pump flow?
f.a:
In g/t mode the operator sets grams of reagent per tonne of ore. The DCS multiplies that by the live tonnage, from a weightometer or a slurry mass flow, and divides by the reagent strength to get a volumetric flow setpoint.

That flow setpoint goes to the flow controller, which adjusts the VSD to match. It is a ratio loop feeding a flow loop, much like a fuel to air ratio on a burner.

On this plant CIL4 cyanide can be set as g/t on thickener underflow tonnes and trimmed by the cyanide analyser. The CIL2 cyanide is ratioed to solids mass flow on the feed. The actual g/t setpoints are operating values set by metallurgy, not design numbers.
f: What happens to g/t dosing if the weightometer fails?
Why trim cyanide with an analyser on top of the ratio control?
Where does the slurry mass flow signal come from on this plant?

f.q: What does a frother dosing failure look like at the flotation cells?
f.a:
Frother keeps bubbles small and gives the froth enough stability to carry mineral over the lip. Without it bubbles coalesce, the froth goes thin, brittle and patchy, and mass pull drops.

On this plant frother (Luprofroth 168) is dosed to the rougher, scavenger, cleaner and cleaner-scavenger feeds, so a failure can affect several stages at once. The flotation expert system uses froth cameras and launder velocity cameras, so you would see froth speed and bubble size change on those screens before the assays catch up.

Check the frother pump flow trend first. Then confirm the tank level and that the dosing line is not blocked.
f: How quickly does flotation recover once frother is restored?
What do the froth cameras actually measure?
Can too little frother be confused with a low air problem?

f.q: Why might a dosing pump run but deliver no flow?
f.a:
The common causes are mechanical, the same as any small pump. The suction may be air locked or the tank empty. A strainer or line may be blocked. A valve may have been left shut after maintenance. On a diaphragm or peristaltic pump the diaphragm or hose may have failed.

Some reagents add their own problems. Caustic can freeze in cold weather, which is why the caustic tank immersion heater switches on below about 20 C and off above about 25 C. Strong solutions can crystallise in dead legs.

Check tank level, then suction and discharge valve positions, then the flowmeter itself, before blaming the pump.
f: How do you tell a faulty flowmeter from a genuine loss of flow?
Why does caustic need heating in a desert climate?
What maintenance keeps reagent dosing pumps reliable?

What is Area F72?.q: Which reagents in F72 most directly affect flotation performance?
What is Area F72?.a:
Three F72 reagents act directly on flotation. PAX (potassium amyl xanthate) is the collector, coating sulphide surfaces so they become water repellent and stick to bubbles. Copper sulphate is the activator, dosed at the SAG discharge and at the cleaner, helping PAX attach to pyrite. Frother (Luprofroth 168) gives a stable froth, dosed to rougher, scavenger, cleaner and cleaner-scavenger feeds.

Lime, cyanide, lead nitrate and oxygen in the same WBS area serve the leach circuits rather than flotation.

Because so much of this ore's gold is locked in pyrite and tellurides, flotation recovery of sulphide drives overall gold recovery. Small changes in collector and activator dosing can move gold recovery noticeably.

f.q: Why does copper sulphate activate pyrite for flotation?
f.a:
Pyrite surfaces in a grinding circuit pick up oxidation products and iron hydroxides, and in saline process water they can be hard for xanthate to grab. Copper ions from copper sulphate adsorb on the sulphide surface and form copper sulphide like sites that xanthate bonds to strongly.

Dosing at the SAG discharge gives the copper conditioning time through the grinding and classification circuit before the slurry reaches the rougher cells. The cleaner dose tops up activation for the reground or recycled material there.

The mechanism is general flotation chemistry. The dose rates in use are set by the metallurgists, not by the design criteria.
f: What happens if copper sulphate is overdosed?
Why add copper sulphate again at the cleaner stage?
Does saline process water affect flotation chemistry?

f.q: Why is PAX chosen as the collector instead of a weaker xanthate?
f.a:
Xanthates get stronger and less selective as the carbon chain gets longer. Amyl xanthate has a longer chain than ethyl or isobutyl versions, so it collects sulphides more powerfully, including slower floating, partly oxidised or composite particles.

On a refractory ore where the target is pyrite carrying gold, recovery of all sulphide matters more than rejecting a little extra gangue, so a strong collector makes sense. Grade is then lifted in the Jameson cleaning stage.

The reasoning is general practice. The specific testwork behind the choice is not in the condensed reference, so ask the metallurgist if you want the background.
f: How is PAX mixed from solids into a dosing solution?
Why does xanthate solution degrade if it is stored too long?
What safety hazard does PAX decomposition create?

f.q: What happens if too much frother is added?
f.a:
Excess frother makes the froth too stable. It drains poorly, so it carries entrained gangue and water over the lip and concentrate grade falls. Launders can overflow, and froth that will not break down causes trouble in concentrate hoppers and pumps.

The design already allows for froth in the pumping: froth factors of 2.0 on rougher concentrate, 1.6 on scavenger, 2.5 on cleaner and 2.0 on cleaner-scavenger concentrate. Overdosing pushes beyond what those allowances cover.

So frother is a balance. Too little and the froth collapses, too much and you pump air and lose grade.
f: What is a froth factor and how does it affect pump sizing?
How does stable froth cause concentrate pumps to lose suction?
Who sets the frother dose rate on shift?

What is Area F78?.q: Why does regenerated carbon need reactivation instead of just washing?
What is Area F78?.a:
Acid washing and thermal regeneration remove different foulants. The acid wash, with dilute HCl in the elution column, dissolves inorganic scale such as calcium carbonate that builds up from lime and saline water.

Organic foulants are the other problem. Flotation reagents, oils, frother and humic material soak into the carbon's micropores and block the sites where gold cyanide adsorbs. Acid does not shift them. Heating the carbon to high temperature in a low oxygen, steamy atmosphere drives them off and reopens the pores.

That matters here because CIL4 treats flotation tails carrying residual reagents. It is like cleaning a heat exchanger: a chemical clean takes the scale, but some fouling only comes off with a different method.

f.q: What temperature and atmosphere do regeneration kilns typically use?
f.a:
In general carbon regeneration kilns run at around 650 to 750 C with steam and very little oxygen. Steam helps strip the organics, and keeping oxygen out stops the carbon itself from burning away. Residence in the hot zone is usually in the order of 15 to 20 minutes.

The condensed plant reference does not give the kiln setpoints. The equipment list does show the new CIL4 kiln F22-KN-411 is a horizontal, electrically heated kiln with 102 elements at 28 kW each, 2,856 kW in total.

For the actual operating temperatures, check the kiln vendor documentation or ask the elution operators.
f: Why does too hot a kiln lose carbon?
How is the kiln temperature measured and controlled?
What does the kiln vendor PLC look after compared with the DCS?

f.q: What does the regenerative thermal oxidiser in F78 do?
f.a:
The F78 equipment list includes a regenerative thermal oxidiser (F78-WC-72) with its heat exchanger, feed fans and combustion air fan, plus carbon filters F78-FI-71 and 72. The reference only says the existing kilns have off gas treatment.

In general an RTO burns the organic vapours driven off the carbon at high temperature so they are not released, and recovers heat through ceramic beds or an exchanger to cut fuel use. Carbon filters typically polish the gas, for example to capture mercury.

So the kiln does the cleaning and the RTO and filters deal with what comes off. For details of the F78 set up ask the area process engineer.
f: Why must off gas treatment run whenever the kiln is running?
What would a carbon filter fan trip mean for the kiln?
How is mercury captured from kiln off gas?

f.q: Why is carbon quenched in water after leaving the kiln?
f.a:
Carbon leaves the kiln red hot. If it met air at that temperature it would burn and lose mass, and it is also a burn hazard to handle. Dropping it into water cools it instantly and keeps it ready to pump as a slurry.

The equipment list shows a carbon quench tank for kiln No. 5 in F78 (F78-TK-70). The CIL4 regeneration sequence also includes a quench tank and barren carbon pump, which send carbon back to the adsorption tanks via the carbon sizing screen.

Quenching also helps wet the reopened pores so the carbon starts loading quickly when it returns to the circuit.
f: Why is regenerated carbon screened before it returns to the tanks?
Where does fine carbon broken in the kiln end up?
How is fresh carbon added to make up for losses?

What is Area F78?.q: What would declining carbon activity look like in the gold recovery data?
What is Area F78?.a:
You would see it first in adsorption performance. Dissolved gold in the later adsorption tanks rises, the gold in solution profile down the tanks flattens, and soluble gold losses to tails increase. Loaded carbon grades may fall even though the feed has not changed.

For CIL4 the design adsorption efficiency is 88 percent within a range of 84 to 92. A steady slide below that, with leach extraction holding up, points at the carbon. These are design figures, so compare against the metallurgists' current targets.

The lab also runs activity tests on regenerated carbon samples. Falling activity there, ahead of the plant numbers moving, is the earliest warning.

f.q: How does the lab measure carbon activity?
f.a:
A common method contacts a carbon sample with a standard gold cyanide solution for a fixed time, then measures how much gold was taken up. The rate is compared with fresh carbon tested the same way and reported as a percentage of fresh activity.

Samples are normally taken from barren carbon before and after regeneration, so you can see what the kiln restored. Fouled carbon loads slowly even if its total capacity looks fine.

This is general practice. The site's own test method, frequency and action limits are set by the metallurgy lab, so ask them for current results.
f: What activity level usually triggers a regeneration review?
Why does carbon lose activity over many cycles even with good regen?
How is carbon sampled from the barren carbon stream?

f.q: Why does solution gold in the last CIL tank matter so much?
f.a:
Whatever gold is still dissolved in the last tank leaves with the tails. Once it goes to the tailings storage facility it is lost for good.

CIL4 is big: its design feed is about 3,164 t/h of solids, so even a small rise in solution gold multiplies into a lot of gold over a day. That is why the last tanks are watched closely and why carbon activity and carbon concentration (12.5 g/L design) matter.

Think of the adsorption train like the last stages of a multi stage heat exchanger. If the final stage is weak, the outlet temperature drifts and that loss is gone from the system.
f: How often is solution gold measured down the CIL4 train?
What does the Carbon Scout measure in each adsorption tank?
Why does CIL4 have space for a future extra tank?

f.q: What else besides poor regeneration can lower adsorption efficiency?
f.a:
Several things. Low carbon concentration in a tank reduces the surface available. The CIL4 design is 12.5 g/L, and the Carbon Scout tracks it per tank. Short residence hurts too. CIL4 design total residence is 12.8 h, already below the 14 h ideal, so higher flow eats into margin.

Organic fouling from flotation reagents, carbon lost through worn intertank screens, poor mixing, and preg robbing material in the ore can all reduce adsorption. Uneven carbon advance between tanks also leaves some tanks overloaded.

Ask the metallurgist which of these is being tracked. Most show up first on Carbon Scout data and solution assays.
f: What is preg robbing and does this ore have it?
How is carbon advanced from one CIL4 tank to the next?
What sign shows an intertank screen is losing carbon?

What is Area F78?.q: How does F78 differ in role from the new F22 kiln?
What is Area F78?.a:
F78 is the existing carbon regeneration area. The equipment list shows kiln No. 5 (F78-KN-65) there with its dewatering screen, feed hopper, quench tank, barren carbon pump, carbon filters and a regenerative thermal oxidiser for off gas. Existing kilns No. 3 and 4 sit in F65. These serve the existing elution circuits on the concentrate side, CIL2 and CIL3.

F22 is the new CIL4 carbon circuit built in Stage 2. Its kiln F22-KN-411 is a new electrically heated horizontal kiln package with a vendor PLC, run in an overall regeneration sequence with a quench tank and barren carbon pump, and a mercury abatement system that must run with it.

So the job is the same, but the carbon inventories and circuits are kept separate.

f.q: Why keep CIL4 carbon separate from the concentrate circuit carbon?
f.a:
The two circuits load carbon to very different grades. CIL3 adsorption design loading is about 4,490 g/t, while CIL4 runs at 332 to 579 g/t. Each elution circuit is sized for its own carbon loading and volume.

Mixing carbon would blur gold accounting between the concentrate and tails circuits and could leave the larger CIL4 inventory diluting the high grade carbon. The concentrate side also sees much stronger cyanide.

So each side has its own loaded carbon screen, acid wash and elution, and regeneration. F65 and F78 serve the concentrate side and F22 serves CIL4.
f: Why is CIL4 carbon loading so much lower than CIL3?
How much carbon is held in the CIL3 circuit?
What happens to fine carbon screened out of each circuit?

f.q: Why is the new CIL4 kiln electrically heated rather than gas fired?
f.a:
The equipment list confirms F22-KN-411 is electrically heated, with 102 elements at 28 kW each. The reason for that choice is not recorded in the plant reference.

In general electric kilns avoid combustion gases in the kiln, give fine temperature control by switching element banks, and need no fuel train or burner management. The trade off is high power demand and element replacement. The CIL4 elution heater, by contrast, is LPG fired with a burner management system.

If you want the actual reasoning, the process engineer or the owner's project team would know.
f: How are kiln heating elements replaced and how often?
What happens to carbon in the kiln if power is lost?
Why does the CIL4 elution heater use LPG instead of electricity?

f.q: How many regeneration kilns does the plant have in total?
f.a:
The mechanical equipment list (Rev 0, December 2025) shows four. F65-KN-61 is kiln No. 3 and F65-KN-62 is kiln No. 4, both existing in the concentrate carbon area. F78-KN-65 is kiln No. 5, existing, in F78. F22-KN-411 is the new CIL4 kiln.

The existing kilns are listed as in service, and the CIL4 kiln as new. The numbering hints that kilns 1 and 2 existed historically but they are not in the current list.

Equipment status changes with the project, so confirm with the elution area operators or the maintenance planner which kilns are running.
f: Which elution circuit feeds each of the existing kilns?
Can one kiln cover another's carbon when it is down?
What maintenance does a regeneration kiln need?

Someone says 'it's in 25/26'. Which area.q: Why did the new plant replace F25/F26 with the F18 Jameson cells?
Someone says 'it's in 25/26'. Which area.a:
Stage 1 made the old FIM flotation circuit redundant. The new plant is designed for 25.5 Mtpa nominal, against 10.5 Mtpa for the old FIM circuit, so the old cells were too small and too many to integrate. The equipment list shows the F25 and F26 flotation cells and pumps as decommissioned in Stage 1.

The new cleaning duty went to two Glencore Jameson B6500/24 cells in F18. Jamesons are high intensity cells with a small footprint. They aspirate air naturally through downcomers so they need no blowers, and they handle fine particles well.

Fewer, larger, simpler units also means fewer pumps, agitators and instruments to maintain than a long bank of old tank cells.

f.q: How does a Jameson cell make bubbles without a blower?
f.a:
Feed slurry is pumped down a vertical downcomer through a nozzle. The plunging jet creates suction at the top of the downcomer and draws in air. The jet then shears that air into fine bubbles in intense mixing, so particles meet bubbles before they reach the tank.

On this plant the air rate depends on the total pumped flow through the downcomers, so the feed pump runs on a VSD on flow control. It works like a jet pump or venturi eductor: no flow through the nozzle, no suction.

That is why steady feed flow matters more on a Jameson than on a forced air cell.
f: What happens to aspiration if a downcomer nozzle wears?
Why are Jameson cells good at recovering fine particles?
How is froth depth controlled on a Jameson cell?

f.q: Why is half the cleaner tails recycled back to cleaner feed?
f.a:
Per the design, about 50 percent of cleaner tails returns to the cleaner feed hopper as an external recycle. It keeps the downcomer flow constant even when fresh feed varies, so aspiration and bubble generation stay steady.

It is like a minimum flow recirculation line on a centrifugal pump: the recycle keeps the machine at its design operating point however much fresh flow arrives. The recycle also gives particles a second chance to float.

The rest of the cleaner tails goes to the cleaner-scavenger Jameson. Its tails are also roughly half recycled, with the rest going to the flotation tails thickener.
f: What feeds the cleaner Jameson besides its own recycle?
Where does the cleaner-scavenger concentrate go?
How is the recycle split controlled between the two destinations?

f.q: How much bigger is the new circuit than the old FIM flotation?
f.a:
The old FIM circuit handled 10.5 Mtpa. The new plant's nominal design is 25.5 Mtpa, with a high throughput case of 28.35 Mtpa, so about two and a half times the old capacity.

The residence times shifted as well. The new rougher cells give 15.1 minutes, against 10 to 12 minutes in the existing plant. The scavengers give 21.4 minutes, against 29 to 32 minutes before, for a combined rougher plus scavenger time of 36.5 minutes.

Cell size changed too. The new FLS tank cells are 630 m3 each, while the old F26 east scavenger cells in the equipment list were 150 m3.
f: Why did rougher residence go up but scavenger residence go down?
How many cells are in the new rougher and scavenger banks?
What is the design mass pull from the rougher cells?

Someone says 'it's in 25/26'. Which area.q: What handover confusion arises from mixing up old and new cleaner areas?
Someone says 'it's in 25/26'. Which area.a:
The trap is that F25 and F26 are not all dead. The equipment list shows the old flotation cells and their pumps as decommissioned, but some equipment in those areas is still in service. Examples include the F25 flotation air compressors (F25-CM-31A to C) and air receivers, and several F26 sump pumps (F26-PS-01, 02, 03, 40 and 41).

So a note saying 'the cleaner area sump pump is down' could mean an F26 legacy sump pump or a new F18 one. Someone could chase the wrong unit, raise a work order in the wrong area, or, worse, isolate the wrong equipment.

Use the full tag in handovers and on the radio, and say 'new cleaner' or 'Jameson' when you mean F18.

f.q: Which F25 and F26 equipment is still in service?
f.a:
According to the mechanical equipment list, Rev 0, the in service items include the F25 flotation air compressors F25-CM-31A, B and C, the air receivers F25-RA-31A, 31B and 32, and the rougher column cavitation pumps F25-PP-19, 20 and 21 with sampling pump F25-PS-07.

In F26 the area sump pumps F26-PS-01, 02, 03, 40 and 41 are listed as in service. The old flotation cells, flotation feed and concentrate pumps, and the regrind mill are listed as decommissioned.

Status can change after the list was issued, so confirm in the field and with the area maintenance planner.
f: Why would the old flotation compressors still be in service?
What are rougher column cavitation pumps used for?
Who decides when legacy equipment is formally decommissioned?

f.q: Why is the full tag safer than an area nickname on a radio call?
f.a:
Nicknames like 'the cleaner sump' or 'the old cells' depend on what each person remembers, and the plant has old and new equipment doing similar jobs. A full tag such as F26-PS-41 points at one item only.

The full tag also ties straight to the equipment list, the P&ID and the isolation points. Anyone can look it up and get the same answer.

It is the same reason engineers quote part numbers rather than 'the big bearing'. When the outcome is an isolation or a start, ambiguity is where incidents start.
f: How do I find a tag's P&ID from the equipment list?
What should I do if a tag in the field differs from the drawing?
Why do some legacy tags have letters after the number, like 61A?

f.q: How do you check whether an old tag is decommissioned?
f.a:
The mechanical equipment list has a status column: in service, decommissioned, new, modified, removed or future. It also shows the stage of the change, which you can search in this app.

For the real current state, check the site maintenance system and the P&ID revision. Then look at the equipment itself, which should carry decommissioned or out of service tagging.

Never treat 'decommissioned' as meaning de-energised or safe. Follow the site isolation and test before touch procedure regardless of what the list says. The area maintenance planner can confirm the formal status.
f: What is the difference between decommissioned and removed?
Why can decommissioned equipment still carry stored energy?
Which MEL revision is the latest one in this app?

Someone says 'it's in 25/26'. Which area.q: Are F25 and F26 still available as backup cleaning capacity?
Someone says 'it's in 25/26'. Which area.a:
Not as designed. The mechanical equipment list shows the F25 and F26 flotation cells, their feed, concentrate and tails pumps, and the old regrind mill as decommissioned in Stage 1. The plant reference does not describe them as standby cleaning capacity.

The new cleaning circuit is the two F18 Jameson cells, cleaner and cleaner-scavenger. The as built flotation PFD also shows a dashed bypass sending rougher 1 concentrate straight to the final concentrate hopper.

Whether any of the old cells could physically be brought back is a question for the metallurgist and the area superintendent. It would need pumps, piping and control all reinstated.

f.q: What happens to cleaning if a Jameson cell is offline?
f.a:
The reference does not set out an operating strategy for losing a Jameson cell, so treat this as partly unanswered. What the documents show is that the two cells work in series: cleaner tails feed the cleaner-scavenger, whose concentrate returns to the cleaner. There is also a dashed bypass on the as built PFD sending rougher 1 concentrate to the final concentrate hopper.

In general, losing a cleaning stage means either lower concentrate grade, reduced mass pull upstream, or recirculating until it is back.

Ask the metallurgist or control room operator what the agreed response is.
f: Why does rougher 1 concentrate have a bypass to the final hopper?
How does lower concentrate grade affect the UFG mills?
What alarms would show a Jameson feed pump has stopped?

f.q: Why decommission old cells rather than keep them as spares?
f.a:
Keeping equipment as a usable spare costs money. Agitators, pumps, valves, blowers and instruments all need maintenance and testing, and old cells would need tying into the new circuit's pumping and control.

The old units also do not match the new duty. The old F26 east scavenger cells were 150 m3 each, while the new rougher cells are 630 m3, and the new cleaning circuit is built around the Jameson flowsheet with its recycle arrangement.

This is general reasoning. The project's own decision record is not in the reference, so ask the owner's team for the history.
f: Does any old FIM plant still run in the new flowsheet?
What happened to the old FIM ball mills?
Why was the FIM SAG mill kept when its ball mills were not?

f.q: What does decommissioned mean for isolation and safety?
f.a:
Decommissioned means taken out of service by a formal change. It does not guarantee every energy source is removed. Old equipment can still have live cables, connected pipework, trapped slurry or pressure, or a drive that could be re-energised by mistake.

Treat it like any other plant. Follow the site isolation procedure, verify zero energy, and test before touch. Never rely on a drawing or list status alone.

If you are planning any work around F25 or F26, the area maintenance planner and the permit issuer will confirm what is actually isolated.
f: What is test before touch and when is it required?
Who can issue a permit for work on legacy equipment?
How are redundant cables made safe on site?

What does the leading 'F' in every Growt.q: Why does the numbering system use a single letter for each site area?
What does the leading 'F' in every Growt.a:
The first letter is the WBS level 1 code: M Mining, F FIM Processing, T Tailings, N Non-Process Infrastructure and P Indirects. One letter tells you straight away which part of the project an item belongs to, without making the tag long.

It keeps tags compact enough to stencil on equipment and read on a screen, and it sorts cleanly in databases and lists. Everything in the processing plant then starts with F followed by a two digit area, such as F13 or F21.

It works like a part number family prefix. The first character narrows the search before you read anything else.

f.q: Do instrument tags also carry the F prefix?
f.a:
No. Instrument tags follow a different pattern: function letters, then the area digits, then the loop number, with no F prefix and no dashes. Examples from the instrument list are DIT13090, the cyclone feed pump discharge density transmitter, and LIT13076, the primary cyclone feed hopper level transmitter.

The instrument list links each instrument back to its parent equipment through a separate equipment number column, for example F13-PP-401 for that density transmitter.

So an F at the start of an instrument tag means flow, as in FIT, not FIM.
f: How are instrument loop numbers assigned within an area?
What does the X in a tag like DX13090 mean?
Why do some instruments share a loop number but differ in letters?

f.q: Why does the WBS split work into levels below the letter?
f.a:
Each level narrows the scope. Under F there are areas such as F66, and under F66 there are work packages: F66 010 general, F66 020 CIL4A/4B electrowinning and F66 030 gravity electrowinning.

Those packages carry the cost, schedule, contracts and documents for that scope. That lets the project track spending and progress at a useful level, and lets drawings and equipment be filed against a clear piece of work.

Think of it like a bill of materials for the whole project: the top assembly, then sub assemblies, then parts.
f: How does a WBS number differ from an equipment tag?
What WBS packages sit under the F72 reagents area?
Why do the WBS and equipment areas use the same codes?

f.q: What does the P for indirects cover in the WBS?
f.a:
The reference only says P stands for Indirects. It does not list the packages underneath.

In general, indirects are project costs that do not become a piece of plant. They cover engineering and design, project and construction management, temporary facilities and services, construction equipment, commissioning support, insurances and owner's costs.

You are unlikely to see a P code on any physical equipment. For the detail, look at the WBS source in this app or ask the project controls team.
f: Why are indirect costs tracked separately from plant costs?
What does the N for non process infrastructure include?
What does the M for mining cover in this WBS?

What does the leading 'F' in every Growt.q: What confusion could arise from misreading a tag's leading letter?
What does the leading 'F' in every Growt.a:
The letter F does several jobs in different tag types, which is where mix ups start. On equipment it means FIM, as in F21-TK-411. On an instrument the first letter F means flow, as in FIT13001. In cable circuit codes F means fire system and FO fibre optic.

Other letters overlap too. T is the tailings WBS letter but also temperature and transmitter in instrument tags. P is indirects but also pressure, and PS is both a sump pump and an electrical power supply code.

Older plant documents also show legacy tags without the F, like 30-TK-32A. Read the whole pattern, including the dashes and digits, not just the first letter.

f.q: Why do some older tags like 30-TK-32A have no F prefix?
f.a:
Those are legacy tags from the existing FIM plant, numbered before the Growth Project spec added the F prefix. You see both forms around the concentrate leach, for example 30-TK-32A for an original CIL2 tank and F30-TK-62A in project documents.

Many existing items in the equipment list are now shown with the F prefix and their original low numbers, such as F19-MS-61 for the FIM SAG mill. New items carry numbers from 401 upward.

When you see a tag without the F, add it mentally and search both ways in this app.
f: Why do existing tags keep their old low numbers?
What is the difference between tank 30-TK-32G and the others?
How do field tag plates show legacy versus new numbering?

f.q: How do you tell an instrument tag starting with F from an equipment tag?
f.a:
Look at the shape. An equipment tag is F, a two digit area, a dash, an equipment code, a dash and a number, as in F13-PP-401. An instrument tag starts with letters, then runs straight into a five digit area plus loop number with no dashes, as in FIT13001.

Motors are a third form. They are the equipment tag with the dashes removed, so F21PU001 has F then digits straight away.

So F then two digits and a dash means equipment. F followed by more letters means an instrument where F stands for flow.
f: What other suffixes hang off a motor tag besides VS and LCS?
How are valves tagged differently from the pipes they sit on?
Do vendor package instruments follow the same tag rules?

f.q: Could a T or N tag show up inside the process plant?
f.a:
The WBS says T03 covers the Fim III TSF, the tailings pipeline, distribution and the return water system, and N02 covers borefield pump stations, pipelines and RO and acid water treatment. Those mostly sit outside the plant fence.

At the interfaces the plant side items keep F codes. The final tails pumps F23-PP-466 to 469 and the FIM III booster pumps F23-PP-651 to 653 are all F23, even though they push into the T03 pipeline.

Whether any T or N tagged items sit inside the plant is not covered in the condensed reference. Search the equipment list or ask the area planner.
f: Where does the plant's tailings scope end and T03 begin?
What equipment sits in the N02 borefield pump stations?
Who maintains equipment that sits in T or N areas?

What does the leading 'F' in every Growt.q: How would you look up what a WBS letter like T or N stands for?
What does the leading 'F' in every Growt.a:
In this app, the glossary and area codes card set list them, and the WBS source document is available under sources. The Growth Project WBS gives level 1 as M Mining, F FIM Processing, T Tailings, N Non-Process Infrastructure and P Indirects, then breaks each into areas such as T03 Fim III TSF and N02 Kaltails Borefields.

For tag areas, the Plant Numbering Spec 2000-F00-STS-GE-10003 is the controlling document. It lists every F area code with its description, plus the equipment, electrical and instrument codes.

On site, document control can give you the current revision if you need to quote it.

f.q: What is the difference between the WBS and the plant numbering spec?
f.a:
The WBS breaks the project into scope packages for cost, schedule and contracts. For example F66 020 is CIL4A/4B electrowinning. The numbering spec defines how physical items are tagged, such as F66-EC-411 for CIL4 electrowinning cell 1.

They share the area codes, which is why F66 means the same thing in both. But a WBS number names a piece of work, while a tag names a piece of equipment.

As an engineer on the operating plant you will mostly use tags. WBS codes turn up on project documents, cost reports and commissioning packages.
f: Why does a commissioning package refer to a WBS code?
Can one WBS package contain equipment from several areas?
Who owns the numbering spec once the project hands over?

f.q: Where would I find a tag's P&ID or PFD reference?
f.a:
The mechanical equipment list has PFD and P&ID columns for each item, and the instrument list has a P&ID column too. Searching a tag in this app shows those fields.

For example, signals from the primary crusher 2 tramp magnet F12-MG-401 are on P&ID 2000-F12-PID-PR-10002. The silt trap raw water pressure transmitter PIT00001 is on 2000-F00-PID-PR-10100.

If a field is blank for an existing item, the legacy drawings may not have been reissued yet. Ask document control or the area engineer.
f: How do I read the drawing number format on a P&ID?
What is the difference between a PFD and a P&ID?
Where are the as built PFDs kept in this app?

f.q: What does the 2000 at the start of document numbers mean?
f.a:
The reference does not explain the 2000 prefix. Every project document quoted, from the PDC 2000-F00-DCR-PR-10002 to the P&IDs like 2000-F12-PID-PR-10002, starts with it, which suggests a project or contract number. I can't confirm that.

The rest of the number is easier to read from the examples: the area code, a document type such as PFD, PID, LST or REP, a discipline such as PR process or ME mechanical, then a sequence number.

Document control can tell you exactly what the 2000 stands for.
f: What document types appear in the third part of the number?
What discipline codes are used on project documents?
How do I tell which revision of a document is current?

In the WBS, what is T03?.q: Why is the TSF treated as a separate WBS area from the process plant?
In the WBS, what is T03?.a:
The TSF is a different kind of asset. It is a large earth dam and pipeline system run under dam safety and environmental approvals, built by civil and geotechnical contractors, and raised over many years. Keeping it under its own WBS letter separates its cost, schedule and contracts from the process plant.

The WBS breaks T03 into site development, tailings pipeline, the initial capital TSF, impoundment, tailings distribution, sustaining capital, return water pumping and return water pipeline.

The plant side stops at F23, final tailings handling, which pumps the tails out to T03. It is like a pump skid versus the pipeline it feeds: one owner for each, with a clear tie in.

f.q: Where is the battery limit between F23 and T03?
f.a:
The reference gives the scope on each side but not the exact tie in point. F23 covers the final tails tank, the four final tails pumps and the FIM III booster pumps F23-PP-651 to 653. T03 covers the tailings pipeline, distribution system and impoundment.

So the boundary is somewhere downstream of the booster pumps, typically at a flange or valve where the plant pipework meets the overland pipeline.

Check the F23 P&IDs, where battery limits are normally marked, or ask the area engineer.
f: Who operates the tailings pipeline outside the plant fence?
What instruments monitor the tailings line along its route?
Why do battery limits matter for isolations and permits?

f.q: What is the return water system in T03 used for?
f.a:
Water that separates from deposited tailings collects on the TSF and is pumped back to the plant. The WBS lists return water pumping and a return water pipeline under T03.

At the plant this water is called cyanide water: TSF decant return, which still carries some cyanide. The design treats it with hydrogen peroxide through inline mixers on the three decant water lines, controlled by an online WAD cyanide analyser and flowmeters, with a residual WAD target of about 1.5.

Returning decant cuts the demand for saline bore water and keeps water off the TSF.
f: Why is peroxide used to destroy cyanide in the decant water?
Where is cyanide water used in the plant?
What does WAD cyanide mean compared with total cyanide?

f.q: Why does a TSF need sustaining capital after it is built?
f.a:
A tailings dam is not built to full height on day one. It is raised in stages, called lifts, as tailings fill it. Each lift is a construction project of its own, which is why the WBS has a separate T03 sustaining capital package next to the initial capital.

Distribution pipework also gets extended and moved as the deposition points change, and return water systems need upgrades as the pond moves.

This is general practice. The T03 lift schedule and design are with the tailings engineering team, not the plant reference.
f: What is the difference between upstream and downstream dam raises?
Who monitors the TSF wall for stability?
How long is the Fim III TSF expected to last?

In the WBS, what is T03?.q: What handover symptom would indicate a tailings pipeline blockage to T03?
In the WBS, what is T03?.a:
The design gives each tailings line a flowmeter, density meter and pressure measurement, plus a second flowmeter near the deposition end for leak detection. A blockage shows as discharge pressure rising while flow falls, pump power changing, and the final tails tank level climbing because the pumps can't take the flow away.

Density creeping up before the event is a common lead in, because denser slurry settles faster. A flow mismatch between the plant flowmeter and the far end flowmeter points to a leak rather than a blockage.

A good handover gives the trend times, which line and pump, what was done (flush, standby pump), and the tank level at handover.

f.q: Why does a flow difference between two flowmeters point to a leak?
f.a:
It is a mass balance. In a sealed pipeline, what goes in at the plant should come out at the deposition end, give or take meter accuracy and changes in line inventory. If the far end flowmeter reads consistently lower, slurry is going somewhere else, which usually means a leak.

That is why the design puts a second flowmeter near the deposition end. A blockage behaves differently: both meters fall together and pressure rises at the pump end.

It is the same logic as comparing pump discharge flow with flow delivered to a remote tank on a water system.
f: How big a flow difference is needed before a leak alarm triggers?
What is done when a tailings pipeline leak is detected?
Why can a long slurry line hold a lot of inventory?

f.q: What causes slurry to settle out in a long tailings line?
f.a:
Every slurry has a deposition velocity. Below it, solids drop out and form a bed on the pipe bottom, which shrinks the flow area until the line blocks. Low flow, high density, coarse particles and long stoppages all push towards it.

The plant design guards against this elsewhere too. Dual hopper level control uses a second water addition loop to keep a minimum line velocity. Final tails pump flow setpoints come from tank level, so flow stays in range.

Lines are normally flushed with water before a planned stop for the same reason.
f: How long can a tailings line sit full before it needs flushing?
Why does high slurry density make pumping harder?
What is critical deposition velocity and how is it estimated?

f.q: What happens upstream if the final tails tank fills up?
f.a:
The final tails tank buffers between CIL4 and the tailings pumps. Its level sets the pump flow setpoints, so normally the pumps simply speed up to match. If the line is restricted and the pumps can't keep up, the level keeps rising.

Beyond that, high level alarms and process interlocks would act on the upstream feed, ultimately reducing or stopping flow from CIL4 and the plant. The specific interlock settings are not in the condensed reference.

Ask the control room operator what the high level response and timing are. It is a plant wide event, not just a tailings one.
f: What streams flow into the final tails tank?
How much surge time does the final tails tank give?
What is first out detection and how does it help after a trip?

In the WBS, what is T03?.q: What equipment moves tailings from F23 into the T03 system?
In the WBS, what is T03?.a:
From the final tails tank, four final tails pumps F23-PP-466 to 469 run duty, duty, duty, standby. They are horizontal centrifugal slurry pumps with gearboxes. Downstream are the FIM III booster pumps F23-PP-651, 652 and 653, with a sump pump F23-PS-410 at the booster pump station.

The tank receives CIL4 tails, acid wash waste and fine carbon waste, about 3,164 t/h of solids at 54.5 percent solids in the design. Each tailings line has a flowmeter, density meter and pressure measurement, and the tank level sets the pump flow setpoints.

Beyond the boosters the T03 tailings pipeline and distribution system take over to the Fim III TSF.

f.q: Why are three tails pumps duty with only one standby?
f.a:
At over 3,000 t/h of solids the duty is too big for one pump, so it is split across three running units with one standby that can step in for any of them. That keeps each pump in a sensible operating range and allows one to be maintained without stopping the plant.

The design notes that each line has its own flowmeter, density and pressure instruments, so the pumps appear to serve separate lines. The exact arrangement, and whether the boosters run in series with particular trains, is best confirmed on the F23 P&IDs.

Gland flow is monitored with a mag flowmeter on these pumps, and low gland flow blocks start.
f: How does the standby tails pump change over with a duty pump?
Why do the final tails pumps use gearboxes instead of direct drive?
What protects a tails pump from running dry?

f.q: How are the final tails pump speeds set?
f.a:
The design has the final tails tank level setting the pump flow setpoints. A level controller acts as the master and each pump's flow controller follows. The flow controllers adjust their pump drives to hit that flow.

This cascade lets the tank absorb short surges while the pumps track the average flow, like a surge tank ahead of a boiler feed pump.

Each line also has density and pressure measurement, so the control room can watch for a line heading towards blockage. Specific setpoints are operating values, not in the reference.
f: Why use level to flow cascade rather than level straight to speed?
What happens to the cascade if a line flowmeter fails?
How is minimum flow kept in a line at low plant throughput?

f.q: What other streams join the final tails tank besides CIL4 tails?
f.a:
The design lists acid wash waste and fine carbon waste going to the final tails tank alongside the CIL4 tails.

Acid wash waste comes from carbon acid washing with dilute HCl before elution. Sending it into a large alkaline tailings stream neutralises it. Fine carbon broken down in handling and screened out also goes to tails, since it is too fine to hold in the CIL screens.

Fine carbon carries some gold, so the metallurgists watch how much is lost this way. The CIL4 tails also have a carbon detection meter for screen breakthrough.
f: How much gold is lost on fine carbon going to tails?
Why is acid wash waste not neutralised separately?
What does the carbon detection meter on CIL4 tails tell you?

In the WBS, what is N02?.q: Why does the plant need a saline water supply alongside other water sources?
In the WBS, what is N02?.a:
Water volume is the driver. A plant treating around 25 Mtpa needs a huge amount of make up water, and fresh scheme water from the pipeline is limited and expensive. Local groundwater is saline, so the process circuit runs on saline bore water, SG about 1.07, with scheme water (SG 1.00) kept for duties that need clean water.

The reference lists saline sources as the Kaltails borefield (N02), the Eastern Borefield and the offsite roaster saline transfer dam. Most process water is recycled flotation tails thickener overflow, topped up from a bore water dam.

Grinding, flotation and leaching all tolerate saline water. Scheme water goes to gland seals on the IsaMills, parts of elution and similar clean duties.

f.q: Where is fresh scheme water used instead of saline water?
f.a:
The reference names several scheme water duties. The UFG IsaMills use scheme water for gland seal. The CIL4 elution sequence uses scheme water for the second elution stage and for cooling. Scheme water is listed separately from process water across the water services.

In general fresh water also goes to reagent make up where salts would cause problems, safety showers and potable supply.

Gland water for most slurry pumps comes from the Raw Water Tank via LP and HP gland water pumps, not necessarily from scheme water. Check the water services P&IDs for which source feeds which user.
f: Why does elution need fresh water instead of saline water?
What is the difference between raw water and scheme water?
Why do IsaMill glands use scheme water?

f.q: Does saline process water cause problems for equipment?
f.a:
Yes. Chlorides attack carbon steel and cause pitting and stress corrosion cracking in ordinary stainless steels, especially when hot. They also add to scaling. The instrument list even calls some streams hypersaline, such as the process water addition to the cyclone feed pump.

That shapes material choices. The CIL4 acid wash and elution column is SAF2205 duplex stainless, a grade with good chloride resistance. Rubber linings, coatings and HDPE pipe are common in saline services.

From a maintenance view, expect faster corrosion on unprotected steel, fittings and instrument parts than you would see with fresh water.
f: Why is duplex stainless better than 316 in chloride service?
How does saline water affect pump gland and seal life?
What corrosion protection is used on carbon steel tanks here?

f.q: How does the plant top up the process water tank?
f.a:
The Process Water Tank is fed mainly by flotation tails thickener overflow. When that is not enough it is topped up from Bore Water Dam 2 (South Dam) by three DOL saline pumps, which trip on dam low low level to protect them.

The Process Water Tank supplies the plant through duty and standby pumps. Separately, the Raw Water Tank is fed from the Bore Water or Saline Dam 3 via booster pumps, and its lower portion supplies the LP and HP gland water pumps.

So thickener overflow is the main supply and bore water is the make up.
f: Why do the dam top up pumps trip on low low level?
What happens if the thickener overflow clarity is poor?
How is the Process Water Tank level controlled?

In the WBS, what is N02?.q: What would a handover flag if borefield pump output dropped?
In the WBS, what is N02?.a:
Lower borefield output means less water reaching the bore water dams and the Raw Water Tank. A handover should give current dam and tank levels, which bores or pump stations are down, the expected repair time, and any water saving actions agreed.

The knock on effects matter. The process water top up pumps from Bore Water Dam 2 trip on dam low low level. The Raw Water Tank lower portion supplies the gland water pumps, and on this plant low gland water flow blocks slurry pump starts and trips running pumps after a delay. A long water shortage can therefore turn into a throughput problem.

The borefields are N02 non process infrastructure, so the call out may go to a different team than the plant.

f.q: Why would low raw water threaten the slurry pumps?
f.a:
Most slurry pumps rely on clean gland water to flush the shaft seal and keep abrasive slurry out of the packing. On this plant the gland water pumps draw from the lower portion of the Raw Water Tank.

The control philosophy protects the pumps. Each has a gland water flow switch, or a mag flowmeter on the big cyclone feed, thickener underflow and final tails pumps. Low gland flow blocks a start and trips a running pump after a delay.

So if raw water runs short, pumps start tripping on gland protection, which works like losing seal flush on a mechanical seal.
f: What is a Maric valve and why is it on gland water lines?
Why do the biggest slurry pumps get a mag flowmeter on gland water?
What damage does running without gland water cause?

f.q: Who looks after the borefield pumps and pipelines?
f.a:
The plant reference does not say which team operates or maintains the N02 Kaltails borefield. It only shows it as non process infrastructure, with pump stations, pipelines, an environmental control structure, diversion channel, dyke, RO and acid water treatment, and water wells.

On many sites borefields are run by a site services or water team separate from the process plant, often with remote monitoring.

Ask the control room operator who to call for borefield faults, or the area maintenance planner for who holds the maintenance responsibility.
f: Can the control room see borefield pump status remotely?
How many bores make up the Kaltails borefield?
What is the environmental control structure in N02 for?

f.q: How much water does the plant draw from the borefields?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not give borefield flow rates or the overall site water balance, so I can't give you a reliable figure.

The process design criteria tables and the plant water balance model would hold the design make up demand, split between bore water, scheme water and recycled water. The reference does show recycle is a big part of the picture: flotation tails thickener overflow is the main process water source and TSF decant comes back as cyanide water.

Ask the process engineer or the site water management team for current and design figures.
f: Why does recycling thickener overflow cut bore water demand?
How much water leaves the plant with the tailings?
What limits how much decant water can be reused?

In the WBS, what is N02?.q: What treatment does saline water go through before it is used on site?
In the WBS, what is N02?.a:
The WBS lists an RO system and acid water treatment under N02, so some of the borefield water is treated before use. The condensed reference does not describe that plant, its capacity or where its products go.

In general, reverse osmosis pushes saline water through membranes at high pressure to make a low salinity permeate, leaving a concentrated brine reject. Acid water treatment usually neutralises naturally acidic groundwater, often with lime, so it does not corrode pipelines and equipment.

Much of the process circuit runs on saline bore water as is, at SG about 1.07. For the details of the N02 treatment trains, ask the water services engineer.

f.q: What does reverse osmosis do to saline bore water?
f.a:
Reverse osmosis forces water through a semi permeable membrane at a pressure higher than the solution's osmotic pressure. Water passes through and most dissolved salts are held back. The output is a clean permeate stream and a concentrated brine reject that has to go somewhere.

High pressure pumps do the work, so the energy cost rises with salinity. Feed water is usually pretreated to stop scaling and fouling of the membranes.

It is a bit like a very fine filter where you have to push hard against the salt's natural pull. Plant specific details are not in the reference.
f: What happens to the brine reject from an RO plant?
Why do RO membranes need antiscalant dosing?
How much of the feed water does RO typically recover?

f.q: Why would bore water be acidic in the first place?
f.a:
In parts of the Western Australian Goldfields the groundwater is naturally both hypersaline and acidic. Oxidation of sulphide minerals in the ground and the chemistry of the old salt lake systems both contribute.

Acidic water dissolves metals, corrodes steel and would consume lime in the process, so it is neutralised before going into pipelines and process use.

This is general background. The actual quality of the Kaltails bore water is in the site water monitoring data, so ask the environmental or water team for the analyses.
f: What does acidic water do to carbon steel pipelines?
How is acidic water neutralised at scale?
Why does low pH water increase lime consumption in the plant?

f.q: Is saline process water ever used in the leach circuits?
f.a:
Yes, indirectly. The leach feeds are slurries, and their liquid is largely process water. CIL4, for example, is fed from flotation tails thickener underflow, whose liquor is saline process water. The PDC uses an SG of 1.07 for process water across the circuit.

Cyanide water, the TSF decant returned and treated with peroxide, also comes back into the process.

Saline water raises cyanide and lime consumption a little and affects corrosion, but leaching works in it. Where clean water is needed, as in parts of elution, scheme water is used instead.
f: Does saline water increase cyanide consumption in the leach?
Why is cyanide water added to the CIL3 tails hopper?
How does process water SG affect slurry density readings?

A conveyor runs from F12 into F13. Which.q: Why is a conveyor's area based on its head pulley rather than its tail end?
A conveyor runs from F12 into F13. Which.a:
The numbering spec ties a conveyor to the area it feeds, which is where its head pulley and discharge sit. The head end is where the conveyor delivers its product, so that is the area whose process depends on it.

It also tends to be where the action is. Most conveyors are head driven, with the drive, discharge chute, blocked chute switch and belt cleaners at the head, so the main maintenance and the process interlocks sit in the receiving area.

So a conveyor from F12 into F13 is an F13 conveyor. Think of it as belonging to its customer, much like a feed pump is usually listed with the vessel it feeds.

f.q: Is the conveyor drive always at the head pulley?
f.a:
Not always. Head drives are the most common because pulling the loaded belt from the head keeps tension low on the carry side. Long or steep conveyors may also have tail drives, intermediate drives, or dual drives at the head.

The numbering rule does not depend on where the drive is. The conveyor takes the area it feeds whatever its drive arrangement, and the motor tag follows the conveyor number.

Check the general arrangement drawing or the equipment list entry for a particular conveyor's drive layout.
f: Why does a head drive keep belt tension lower than a tail drive?
What is a take up and why does every conveyor need one?
How is a conveyor drive motor tagged on this project?

f.q: Which area's sequence controls a conveyor that crosses areas?
f.a:
Logically the downstream one. Plant sequences start downstream equipment first and work backwards, so a conveyor only starts once whatever it feeds is running. A trip stops the interlocked upstream equipment, so nothing keeps feeding a stopped belt.

For example, the stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to the stockpile high high switch and level alarm. That ties it to the area it delivers to.

This matches the numbering rule. The receiving area tag also tends to match where the conveyor sits in the control sequences. Exact grouping is in the control philosophy for each area.
f: Why do plant sequences start from the downstream end?
What is a start permissive on a conveyor?
What stops when the stockpile feed conveyor trips?

f.q: Do the conveyor's instruments take the same area number?
f.a:
Generally the instruments follow their parent equipment's area. The stockpile feed conveyor weightometer F12-WD-402 sits in F12 because that conveyor feeds the F12 crushed ore stockpile, and its instruments carry loop 12557. The SAG mill feed weightometer F13-WD-403 is in F13 with loop 13055.

The instrument list ties each instrument to its equipment number, so you can always trace back.

If an instrument area ever looks wrong, the equipment number column is the way to confirm which conveyor it belongs to.
f: What does a weightometer's tachometer measure?
Why do weightometers need calibration weights or chains?
How are pull wire switches tagged along a conveyor?

A conveyor runs from F12 into F13. Which.q: What confusion happens when a conveyor tag doesn't match its physical location?
A conveyor runs from F12 into F13. Which.a:
You can be standing in one area looking at equipment tagged for another. A conveyor tagged F13 may run most of its length through F12, so a fitter told it is in F12 might search the wrong area.

It gets more serious with isolations. The conveyor's drive, MCC and isolation point may sit in a different switchroom from where you are working. Pull wires are reset in the field along the belt, so you need to know where it physically runs, not just its tag area.

Always confirm against the tag plate and the isolation list for that exact tag, rather than assuming the area code tells you where to go.

f.q: How do you find which switchroom feeds a given conveyor?
f.a:
Start from the motor tag, which is the conveyor tag without dashes. The electrical single line diagrams show which switchboard and switchroom feed it, and the cable schedule links the motor's power cable to its starter. On this project MCCs are called switchboards, code SW, inside switchrooms, code SR.

The DCS also shows electrical SLD displays from the 33 kV incomers down to the 415 V MCC incomers, which helps the control room locate supplies.

For an isolation, always use the approved isolation list for that tag rather than reading it from drawings yourself.
f: What is the difference between a switchboard and a switchroom here?
How is the power cable to a conveyor motor tagged?
Who holds the isolation lists for each area?

f.q: Where are pull wire switches reset after a trip?
f.a:
In the field. The control philosophy says pull wires are reset locally, not from the control room. Someone has to walk the belt, find the tripped switch, confirm why it was pulled, and reset it.

A pull wire is a critical interlock. It trips the conveyor in every mode and cannot be bypassed. The reset is deliberately physical so a person checks the belt is clear before it can restart.

The conveyor also needs the trip cleared in the DCS and a restart through the normal start sequence with its siren.
f: How do you find which pull wire switch tripped on a long belt?
Why can't a critical interlock be bypassed from the DCS?
How long does a conveyor start siren sound before the belt moves?

f.q: Why does a conveyor trip stop the equipment feeding it?
f.a:
If a conveyor stops while the equipment upstream keeps running, material piles onto a stationary belt, chokes the transfer chute and spills. That means clean up, possible belt damage, and people working near moving plant.

So the control philosophy has a trip stop the interlocked upstream equipment. A stopped belt drops the feeder or conveyor ahead of it, and so on back up the line.

The microwave blocked chute switch works the same way. If the chute fills, it trips the belt after a short delay and the upstream chain stops with it.
f: What does a blocked chute switch detect and how?
Why does the blocked chute switch have a time delay?
How is a choked transfer chute cleared safely?

A conveyor runs from F12 into F13. Which.q: How would you tag a conveyor running from F13 into F14?
A conveyor runs from F12 into F13. Which.a:
By the rule it would take F14, the area it feeds, for example F14-CV-401 for a new item, since new numbers start at 401.

In practice you are unlikely to meet one. F14 is the gravity circuit and is fed by slurry, not conveyed ore. Gravity cyclones take feed from the primary cyclone feed and send underflow to the gravity scalping screens and Knelson concentrators. Treat the question as a test of the rule rather than a real belt.

The same logic gives the earlier example. A conveyor from F12 into F13 is tagged F13 because it feeds the milling area.

f.q: What would the number be for a new conveyor in an existing area?
f.a:
The numbering spec says new equipment and new instruments in existing areas start at 401, so they do not clash with legacy numbers. A new conveyor in an old area would start at CV-401, or the next free 4xx number.

You can see this in the equipment list. In F19, the existing FIM milling area, the old SAG is F19-MS-61 and the recycle conveyor is F19-CV-21, while a new ball charging magnet added by the project is F19-MG-405.

So a 4xx number in an old area is a quick sign of Growth Project equipment.
f: Why did the project not continue the old number sequence?
What existing conveyors are still in service in F19?
How are new items in existing areas shown on old P&IDs?

f.q: What tags would that conveyor's motor and LCS carry?
f.a:
Following the spec, the motor takes the equipment tag with dashes removed. A conveyor F14-CV-401 would have a motor F14CV401, a VSD F14CV401-VS if it had one, and a local control station F14CV401-LCS.

Its cables would carry circuit suffixes off the same base, such as F14CV401-P1 for the first power cable and F14CV401-C1 for a control cable.

The whole family hangs off one number, which makes it easy to trace from the field to the switchroom.
f: Why do some drives have a soft starter instead of a VSD?
What does an LCS let you do in Local mode?
How are pull wire switches linked to the conveyor's motor tag?

f.q: Why does gravity feed travel by slurry pipe instead of conveyor?
f.a:
By the time ore reaches gravity it is ground and mixed with water in the milling circuit. The gravity cyclones take slurry from the primary cyclone feed, and their underflow goes to scalping screens and then Knelson concentrators at about 54 percent solids.

Knelsons need a slurry feed to work. They spin it so heavy gold particles are caught in the bowl while lighter material washes through. Conveying ore dry at this point would make no sense.

Conveyors carry dry, coarse ore up to the SAG mill. After that, everything moves as slurry through pumps and pipes.
f: Why does gravity concentrate get taken from cyclone underflow?
What does the gravity scalping screen remove before the Knelsons?
How often does a Knelson flush its concentrate?

What is Area F00?.q: Why are HV power and buried services grouped under one general area code?
What is Area F00?.a:
These services cross every process area, so no single area code fits them. HV power, LV distribution, buried services and pipe racks all serve the whole site, and the WBS groups them as F00 010 general, F00 020 HV power distribution, F00 030 buried services, F00 040 piperacks and F00 050 LV power distribution.

Grouping them avoids splitting one cable route or pipe rack across several areas, with each area owning a piece of something that only works as a whole.

It is like a hydraulic system's main pressure header. It serves every actuator, so it belongs to the system, not to one cylinder.

f.q: What voltage levels make up the plant power distribution?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the electrical SLD displays run from the 33 kV incomers down to the 415 V MCC incomers. In between, the equipment list shows large motors at 3.3 kV, such as the cyclone feed pump F13-PP-401 and the existing primary crusher. Smaller drives run at 415 V, many on DOL starters.

The new SAG mill uses two low speed synchronous motors with variable frequency drives, supplied as part of the mill package, while the ball mill normally runs at a fixed speed of about 75 percent of critical.

For the full voltage structure and transformer list, the single line diagrams are the source. The site electrical engineer can walk you through them.
f: Why are big pumps run at 3.3 kV instead of 415 V?
What protection relays sit on the 33 kV incomers?
Why does the SAG mill run variable speed but the ball mill fixed?

f.q: Why must buried services be located before any digging?
f.a:
Buried services include HV and LV cables, earthing, communications, water and sometimes process lines. Hitting an HV cable can kill, and hitting a pipe can flood a trench or release process fluid.

Records are not always exact, especially around older plant, so sites require a formal excavation or ground disturbance permit, service location and often potholing before digging.

Follow the site ground disturbance procedure. The reference does not detail it, so your supervisor or the permit issuer will brief you on the local process.
f: What is potholing and when is it required?
Who keeps the buried services drawings up to date?
What should you do if you uncover an unmarked service?

f.q: What runs along the plant pipe racks?
f.a:
Pipe racks carry the shared services between areas. On this plant that includes the reagent ringmains, with cyanide and caustic on pressurised loops and milk of lime on its own ringmain. It also includes process, raw, gland and scheme water lines, plant and instrument air, and usually cable trays for power and instrumentation.

Slurry lines between areas may also run on racks where they can't be gravity launders.

The line list in this app shows each pipe, its service and its route reference, which is the best way to see what is on a particular rack.
f: Why are cyanide and acid lines kept apart on pipe racks?
How are pipe rack lines labelled so you can identify them?
What is the line list and how do I search it?

What is Area F00?.q: What handover issue arises from confusing F00 site services with process areas?
What is Area F00?.a:
The risk is underestimating the reach of an F00 fault. Trouble on an F00 HV feeder, LV distribution board or pipe rack line can affect several process areas at once, while a process area fault usually stays local.

A handover that only says 'power issue in F21' might hide that the root is an F00 feeder that also supplies other areas. Work on an F00 buried service can also sit physically inside a process area's boundary.

A clear handover names the F00 asset, the areas affected, and who owns the fault. With large drives, also note that the CRO must phone for approval before starting the mills, because the plant has no link to Parkeston Power Station.

f.q: What happens on site if the main power supply is lost?
f.a:
The control philosophy lists the backups. An emergency generator starts automatically and an essential generator is started manually. The DCS and remote IO are on UPS, so the control system keeps running and logging, and emergency lighting lasts 90 minutes.

On the process side, pump dump valves fail open on power loss so slurry lines drain rather than settle.
