Which loads go on emergency or essential power, such as agitators, thickener rakes or sump pumps, is shown in the equipment list emergency power column. The control room operator will know the restart order.
f: Which agitators must restart first after a power failure?
Why do pump dump valves fail open on power loss?
How long can a thickener rake stop before bogging becomes a risk?

f.q: Why must the CRO phone before starting the big mills?
f.a:
The control philosophy says there is no link to Parkeston Power Station. The CRO phones for approval before starting the mills, and the start sequence pauses for that confirmation.

A 20 MW mill start is a large step load on the power supply. Without automatic coordination, the power station needs warning so it can have generation ready, or the frequency and voltage could dip and trip other plant.

It is the same reason you would warn the people running a small generator before switching on a big motor.
f: How long does a SAG mill start sequence take?
What other drives need power station approval before starting?
What happens if the power station refuses a mill start?

f.q: Which loads stay on emergency power during an outage?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not list the emergency loads. The mechanical equipment list has an emergency power column for each item, so that is where to look for a definite answer.

In general emergency supply covers loads that prevent damage or harm when power is lost: thickener rakes, key agitators that would sand up, sump pumps, lube systems on large machines, lighting, and the control system.

Ask the electrical engineer or control room operator for the site's emergency load list and the order in which loads are restored.
f: Why do thickener rakes need emergency power?
What is the difference between emergency and essential generators?
How long will the UPS keep the DCS running?

What is Area F00?.q: What kind of documents carry the F00 area code?
What is Area F00?.a:
F00 marks site wide documents rather than area specific ones. Examples quoted in the reference are the Plant Numbering Spec 2000-F00-STS-GE-10003, the Stage 2 Process Design Criteria 2000-F00-DCR-PR-10002, and the control philosophies 2000-F00-REP-PR-10001 for Stage 1 and 2000-F00-REP-PR-10002 for Stage 2.

The mechanical equipment list 2000-F00-LST-ME-10001 and instrument list 2000-F00-LST-IC-11011 also carry F00, as do general PFDs and some P&IDs for site services, such as 2000-F00-PID-PR-10100 for silt trap raw water.

Area specific drawings carry their own area, such as 2000-F12-PID-PR-10002 for primary crushing.

f.q: How do you read a document number like 2000-F00-DCR-PR-10002?
f.a:
From the examples in the reference, the parts are a leading 2000, then the area (F00), then the document type (DCR, design criteria), then the discipline (PR, process), then a sequence number (10002).

Other types you will see are STS specification, REP report, LST list, PFD and PID. Other disciplines are GE general, ME mechanical, IC instrumentation and control, and PP piping.

The reference does not define the 2000 prefix itself. Document control can confirm the full coding scheme.
f: What does the revision letter or number on a document tell you?
Why do Stage 1 and Stage 2 have separate control philosophies?
Where is the document register for the project kept?

f.q: Why are area specific P&IDs numbered with their own area code?
f.a:
It lets you go from a tag to its drawing quickly. A tag such as F12-MG-401 tells you the area, and the P&IDs for that area carry the same code, here 2000-F12-PID-PR-10002.

It also keeps drawing sets manageable. Each area can be issued, revised and handed over on its own, which suits construction and commissioning in stages.

Site wide services that cross areas go on F00 drawings instead, so they are not split across many area sets.
f: How many P&IDs make up a typical area like F13?
What symbols on a P&ID show an interlock?
How do you follow a line from one P&ID sheet to the next?

f.q: Which F00 document should I read first as a new engineer?
f.a:
Start with the control philosophies, Stage 1 (2000-F00-REP-PR-10001) and Stage 2 (2000-F00-REP-PR-10002). They explain how each area is meant to run: drive modes, interlocks, sequences and control loops, which is what you need on shift.

Then use the Stage 2 Process Design Criteria for the design numbers, remembering they are design values, not live operating data. Keep the Plant Numbering Spec handy for decoding tags.

The cards and plant reference in this app are condensed from those documents, so they are a good first pass before the originals.
f: What is the difference between a design value and an operating value?
How do the Stage 1 and Stage 2 flowsheets differ?
What drive modes does the control philosophy define?

Decode F13-MS-401..q: Why does the tag format place the area code before the equipment type?
Decode F13-MS-401..a:
Putting the area first works like an address: it tells you where to go before what to look for. Every item in one area then sorts together in the equipment list, the DCS and the maintenance system, so all the F13 milling equipment sits in one block.

It also lines up with the WBS and the drawings. F13 equipment appears on F13 PFDs and P&IDs, so the area code takes you to the right drawing set.

The equipment code then narrows it to the type of machine, and the number picks out the individual unit. Street, then house type, then house number.

f.q: What does the equipment code tell you that the area code doesn't?
f.a:
The area code says where; the equipment code says what kind of machine. In F13 alone you have MS for the SAG mill, MB for the ball mill, CC for the pebble crushers, CY for the cyclone cluster, PP for process pumps and PS for sump pumps.

That matters for maintenance and spares. A code tells a planner which trade, which spares family and which maintenance strategy applies before they even open the equipment list.

The spec has a long list of mechanical codes and a separate list for electrical items such as SW, TR, VS and LCS.
f: Where can I see the full list of equipment codes?
Why are electrical items given their own code list?
What code do miscellaneous mechanical items get?

f.q: Could two items in different areas share the same number?
f.a:
Yes. The number only needs to be unique within its area and equipment code, so 401 turns up all over the plant. The equipment list has F12-CG-401 (primary crusher 2), F13-MS-401 (the SAG mill), F13-PP-401 (cyclone feed pump), F17-TH-401 (flotation tails thickener) and F66-EC-401 (gravity electrowinning cell).

Each is unique because the full tag, area plus code plus number, is different.

That is exactly why the number alone is never enough. 'Unit 401' could be any of those.
f: Why does almost every new area start its numbering at 401?
What tag is used for the old FIM SAG mill?
How are duty and standby pumps numbered in a pair?

f.q: What does the equipment list entry for F13-MS-401 say?
f.a:
The mechanical equipment list describes F13-MS-401 as a grate discharge SAG mill, 10.97 m diameter by 8.38 m EGL. It has a dual pinion ring gear drive, chrome moly shell plates and lifters with 6 mm rubber backing, and 125 mm grinding media, with a speed range of about 7.76 to 10.74 rpm.

The design criteria add 20 MW installed power, about 16.8 MW at the pinion, a speed range of 60 to 83 percent of critical, a 10.5 percent ball charge and a 27 percent total load.

These are design values. Live load, speed and power are on the DCS trends.
f: What does percent of critical speed mean for a mill?
Why does the SAG mill have rubber backing behind steel liners?
What are pebble ports and why are they 75 mm?

Decode F13-MS-401..q: What mistake could occur reading a tag without knowing its area code?
Decode F13-MS-401..a:
Without the area, a tag fragment can point to several machines. 'MS-401' only makes sense once you know it is F13, and 'PP-401' could be the F13 cyclone feed pump or a 401 pump in another area. Radio shorthand like 'the 401 pump' is how this goes wrong.

The consequences range from a work order on the wrong machine to the worst case, an isolation applied to the wrong drive while someone works on the one that is still live.

Old and new plant add to it. There are two SAG mills: the new F13-MS-401 and the existing FIM SAG F19-MS-61. Always read and quote the full tag.

f.q: How many SAG mills are on site and what are their tags?
f.a:
Two are in service in the new flowsheet. F13-MS-401 is the new SAG, 10.97 m by 8.38 m EGL with 20 MW installed. F19-MS-61 is the existing FIM SAG, 10.97 m by 4.27 m EGL with 12 MW, in the old FIM Area A.

Both feed the new ball mill and primary cyclone cluster. The FIM SAG discharge is pumped across by duty/duty transfer pumps to the new primary cyclone feed hopper.

The Mt Charlotte processing plant was made redundant in Stage 1, so it is no longer part of the flowsheet.
f: What happens to milling when the new SAG mill is relined?
Why does the FIM SAG mill discharge get pumped instead of gravity fed?
What stops the FIM mill transfer pumps automatically?

f.q: What is the safest way to confirm a tag before isolating?
f.a:
Check it three ways. Read the tag plate on the equipment itself, match it to the approved isolation list or permit for that exact tag, and confirm the isolation point, the switchboard, breaker or valve, carries the same tag reference.

Then prove it. After isolating, try to start the drive from its local control station under the site's test procedure to confirm the right one is dead.

Your site isolation procedure sets the exact steps. Never shortcut it because a tag 'looks right' on a drawing or someone named it on the radio.
f: What is a test for dead and when is it done?
Why are isolation lists tied to the full equipment tag?
Who can authorise an isolation on this site?

f.q: Which equipment numbers repeat across several areas?
f.a:
The 4xx range repeats everywhere because the spec starts new equipment at 401 in each area. Just in the equipment list: F12-CG-401, F12-FA-401, F13-MS-401, F13-MB-401, F13-PP-401, F13-CY-401, F17-TH-401 and F66-EC-401 all use 401.

Legacy numbers repeat as well. For example, 61 appears as F19-MS-61 (FIM SAG), F65-KN-61 (kiln No. 3) and F66-EC-61A (an electrowinning cell).

So a number is just the last piece of the address. It means nothing without the area and the code.
f: Why do some legacy numbers carry a letter suffix like 61A?
How are new and legacy tags shown together on P&IDs?
Does the instrument loop number also repeat across areas?

Decode F13-MS-401..q: What related tags would you expect for this SAG mill's motor and drive?
Decode F13-MS-401..a:
The equipment list shows the SAG mill drive as two motors, F13-MS-401A and F13-MS-401B, low speed synchronous motors with variable frequency drives, supplied with the mill.

Under the electrical rule a motor takes its parent number with the dashes removed, and its VSD adds -VS, so expect forms like F13MS401A for the motor and a -VS suffix for its drive. Its local control station would carry -LCS. Check the electrical load list for the exact form used on the mill motors.

Nearby you would also expect the SAG mill feed weightometer F13-WD-403 and loop instruments starting 13 on the instrument list.

f.q: Why does the new SAG mill have two motors?
f.a:
It has a dual pinion ring gear drive. Two pinions share the load on one large ring gear, each driven by its own motor. With 20 MW installed, splitting the power keeps each motor, pinion and gear mesh within practical size and load limits.

It also spreads tooth loading across two mesh points on the ring gear. That is the same reason big gearboxes use multiple planet gears instead of one massive pinion.

The ball mill also has a dual pinion drive, with motors F13-MB-401A and B in the equipment list.
f: How are the two pinion motors kept sharing load equally?
What is an inching drive used for on a mill?
How is the ring gear lubricated on a large mill?

f.q: Why does the SAG mill run on variable speed?
f.a:
The design speed range is 60 to 83 percent of critical speed. Speed changes how the charge tumbles: faster lifts it higher for more impact breakage, slower gives more grinding and less liner wear.

Operators and the expert system use speed to cope with changing ore hardness and feed size, and as liners wear and the lifter profile changes. Speed is one of the expert system inputs along with load, power, the SAG noise monitor and the feed size camera.

It is like adjusting a machine tool's speed to the material rather than running one fixed speed for everything.
f: What happens if the SAG mill runs too fast for its charge?
What does the SAG noise monitor listen for?
How does liner wear change the best mill speed?

f.q: What instruments watch the SAG mill's condition?
f.a:
The reference lists the expert system inputs: the SAG feed camera size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, mill load (weight), speed and power. Feed tonnage comes from the SAG mill feed weightometer, F13-WD-403.

Large mills also usually have bearing temperatures and lube oil pressures and flows, motor winding temperatures and gear mesh monitoring. These typically come from the mill vendor package and report to the DCS.

Search F13-MS-401 in the instrument list for the full set on this mill.
f: How is SAG mill load measured on a mill this size?
Why does a SAG mill get quieter when it is overloaded?
What trips the SAG mill on a lube system fault?

Why do new Growth Project equipment numb.q: Why choose 401 rather than continuing on from the highest existing number?
Why do new Growth Project equipment numb.a:
A fixed starting block is simpler and safer than tracking the highest legacy number. The existing plant has decades of numbering, often low numbers with letter suffixes like F19-MS-61 or F65-KN-62, and not every area has the same highest number.

Starting every new item at 401 guarantees no clash without a survey of every old tag. It also gives an instant visual cue: a 4xx number means Growth Project kit.

The gap also leaves room for any further legacy items found later, without running into the new range.

f.q: Does 401 apply to new instruments as well as equipment?
f.a:
Yes. The numbering spec says new equipment and new instruments in existing areas start at 401, so neither clashes with legacy items.

In brand new areas the instrument loops are numbered in their own sequence. The instrument list shows loops such as 13090 for the cyclone feed density and 21061 for CIL4 tank 1 DO and pH, with the area digits leading.

If you are unsure whether an instrument is new or legacy, the instrument list shows its stage and supplier.
f: How is an instrument loop number built from area and loop?
Do legacy instruments follow the same letter codes?
What does the stage column in the instrument list show?

f.q: Why do some new tags use 411 or 501 instead of 401?
f.a:
You will see blocks beyond 401: rougher cells F16-CF-411 to 413, CIL4 tanks F21-TK-411 to 418, the cleaner Jameson F18-CF-501 and cleaner-scavenger F18-CF-511, and the final tails pumps F23-PP-466 to 469.

The pattern suggests designers grouped related items into their own decades or hundreds within the new range, which keeps a system's equipment together. The condensed reference does not explain the rule behind those choices.

The point that matters is the same: anything 401 and up in that area is new equipment.
f: How are agitators numbered relative to their tanks?
Why do the CIL4 launders share numbers with their tanks?

f.q: What happens when an existing item is modified by the project?
f.a:
It keeps its original tag. The equipment list has a status column that includes modified alongside new, in service, decommissioned and removed.

For example, the electrowinning circuit No. 1 and No. 2 eluate circulation pumps F66-PP-61 and F66-PP-62 are listed as modified in Stage 1, but still carry their legacy numbers.

So a low number does not mean untouched. Check the status column and the latest P&ID revision before assuming an old item matches its old drawings.
f: What does a status of removed mean in the equipment list?
Which existing areas did the Growth Project modify the most?
Who holds the old drawings for legacy equipment?

Why do new Growth Project equipment numb.q: What confusion happens if a new tag accidentally duplicates an old number?
Why do new Growth Project equipment numb.a:
A duplicate tag breaks the one to one link between a label and a machine. Work orders, maintenance history and spares could attach to the wrong unit, and a duplicate in the field can lead to isolating one machine while work is done on the other.

Data systems suffer too. The DCS and historian need unique tag names, so a duplicate either fails to configure or overwrites another item, and trends end up showing the wrong equipment.

That is why the spec reserved 401 and up for new items. It removes the chance of a new tag landing on an existing number.

f.q: How would a duplicate tag show up in the DCS?
f.a:
In general a DCS will not accept two tags with the same name in one database. A duplicate is normally caught during configuration and renamed before commissioning.

The bigger risk is a mismatch between the DCS and the field. The screen can be correct while a tag plate on site is wrong or swapped, so the CRO and the field operator end up talking about different machines.

If a drive starts or stops when you did not expect it, or the OIS shows a different state from what you see, stop and report it.
f: How are field tag plates checked during commissioning?
What should happen if OIS status disagrees with the field?
What is loop checking and who does it?

f.q: What should you do if you find two items with the same tag plate?
f.a:
Stop and report it before any work goes ahead on either item. Tell your supervisor and the control room operator, and raise it with the area maintenance planner so the tags and records get corrected.

Do not apply an isolation until the correct item is confirmed against the drawings and the approved isolation list. Then test for dead.

Note it in the handover so the next shift does not hit the same trap.
f: Who fixes incorrect tag plates on site?
How do I check a tag against the P&ID in the field?
What gets recorded when a tagging error is found?

f.q: Why does maintenance history depend on unique tags?
f.a:
The maintenance system stores work orders, failure records, inspection results and preventive schedules against each tag. That history drives decisions like when to change a liner or whether a pump keeps failing for the same reason.

If two machines share a tag, their histories merge. One pump looks unreliable while the other appears never to fail, and planned maintenance may land on the wrong unit.

It is the same as keeping one service logbook for two different vehicles.
f: How are preventive maintenance intervals set for new equipment?
What is a functional location in a maintenance system?
Who enters failure data after a breakdown?

Why do new Growth Project equipment numb.q: How would you quickly tell Growth Project kit from legacy plant on a drawing?
Why do new Growth Project equipment numb.a:
The number is the quick cue: 4xx usually means Growth Project equipment, while low numbers like F19-MS-61 or F10-CG-01 are legacy plant. Tags without the F prefix, such as 30-TK-32A, are legacy too.

The PFD legends add stage information. SP1 and SP2 mark Separable Portion 1 and 2, the Stage 1 and Stage 2 contract scopes.

For certainty, look the tag up in the equipment list. Its status column (new, existing, modified, decommissioned) and stage column tell you exactly where it came from.

f.q: What do SP1 and SP2 mean on the PFDs?
f.a:
They stand for Separable Portion 1 and Separable Portion 2, which match the Stage 1 and Stage 2 contract scopes.

Stage 1 covered the new crusher, SAG, ball mill, gravity, flotation, UFG 2, the flotation tails thickener and final tails. Stage 2 added CIL4, UFG 3, the repurposing of CIL2 and CIL3, more elution and EW capacity, and extra reagent facilities.

So an SP2 label tells you that item was built under the later contract, which can affect which vendor documents and warranties apply.
f: What changed for the flotation tails between Stage 1 and Stage 2?
Why was the Growth Project split into two stages?
Which UFG mill came in Stage 2?

f.q: Is every 4xx item part of Stage 1?
f.a:
No. The 4xx numbers mark Growth Project equipment from either stage. The CIL4 electrowinning cells F66-EC-411 and 412 and their rectifiers are Stage 2, while the gravity electrowinning cell F66-EC-401 is Stage 1. All of CIL4 in F21 is Stage 2 scope.

The equipment list stage column gives the answer for each item, and the PFD legends show SP1 or SP2.

Some items are marked future, such as the CIL4 tank 9 discharge launder, which allows for the space reserved for an extra CIL4 tank.
f: Why does CIL4 have space for a future ninth tank?
What does future status mean for an item in the equipment list?
Which reagent facilities were added in Stage 2?

f.q: Why does it matter whether equipment is greenfield or brownfield?
f.a:
The control system splits the plant into four sections for ownership: Greenfields Stage 1, Greenfields Stage 2, Brownfield (modifications to the existing FIM plant) and Existing plant.

Greenfield equipment is new, built to the project's specifications and documents. Brownfield items are existing plant that the project changed, so you may need both old and new drawings. Existing plant may only have legacy documentation.

It affects who to ask, which drawings to trust and which warranty or vendor support applies.
f: Who owns the DCS configuration for brownfield areas?
How reliable are legacy drawings for existing plant?
What is a vendor package and how does it report to the DCS?

Equipment code 'CF'?.q: Why distinguish rougher and cleaner cells with the same equipment code?
Equipment code 'CF'?.a:
The equipment code describes the type of machine, not its duty. CF covers flotation cells and columns of any kind. The duty comes from the area and the number: F16 is rougher and scavenger flotation, F18 is cleaner and cleaner-scavenger.

So F16-CF-411 to 413 are the rougher cells, F16-CF-414 to 417 are the scavengers, F18-CF-501 is the cleaner Jameson and F18-CF-511 is the cleaner-scavenger Jameson. The technology differs, forced air tank cells against Jameson cells, but both are flotation cells.

It is like using one code for all pumps and letting the area and number say which service.

f.q: How do the F16 tank cells differ from the F18 Jameson cells?
f.a:
The F16 cells are FLS forced air tank cells, 630 m3 each. Each has an agitator to suspend the slurry and disperse air, and the air comes from low pressure blowers, F16-BW-401 to 405, with each cell's air on its own flow controller.

The F18 cells are Glencore Jameson B6500/24 units. They have no agitator or blower. Feed is pumped through downcomers where a plunging jet draws in air naturally. Their froth area is 22.2 m2 and they have wash water to clean the froth.

Tank cells give long residence for recovery. Jamesons give intense contact and froth washing for grade.
f: Why do the rougher agitators run reversible drives?
What does wash water do on a Jameson froth?
How is air pressure held on the flotation blower header?

f.q: Which CF tags are rougher cells and which are scavengers?
f.a:
In F16, F16-CF-411, 412 and 413 are rougher cells 1 to 3. F16-CF-414, 415, 416 and 417 are scavenger cells 1 to 4. All seven are 630 m3 tank cells.

Their agitators follow a parallel numbering: F16-AG-421 to 423 for the roughers and F16-AG-424 to 427 for the scavengers.

In F18, F18-CF-501 is the cleaner Jameson and F18-CF-511 the cleaner-scavenger Jameson, each with its own feed hopper, F18-HP-501 and F18-HP-511.
f: Why are rougher 1 and roughers 2 and 3 handled differently?
What does each scavenger cell's concentrate feed into?
How many flotation blowers normally run?

f.q: What does the code LF mean compared with CF?
f.a:
The numbering spec lists LF as flotation cells (slimes, existing). It is a legacy code kept for existing equipment, while CF covers flotation columns and cells in general and is used for all the new cells.

You are unlikely to meet LF on new drawings. If it turns up on an old drawing or in the equipment list, treat it as legacy plant and check its status, since most of the old FIM flotation was decommissioned in Stage 1.

The spec keeps a few legacy codes like this so existing tags stay valid.
f: What other legacy codes does the numbering spec keep?
Why does the spec say new miscellaneous items use XM, not WC?
Which old flotation equipment is still in service?

Equipment code 'CF'?.q: What handover symptom points to a specific CF cell losing its froth?
Equipment code 'CF'?.a:
Froth problems on one cell show first on the flotation expert system screens. The froth camera shows the bubbles changing and the froth slowing or collapsing, the launder velocity camera shows less froth crossing the lip, and the onstream analyser on that bank's concentrate stream shows a drop.

The usual causes are local. The air valve may have closed, which happens automatically if the agitator stops. The cell level may be too low, giving too deep a froth. The air flow controller or its mass flow meter may have failed.

A good handover names the cell tag, what the air flow, agitator status and level trends did, and what was changed.

f.q: Why does the air valve close if a cell agitator stops?
f.a:
The control philosophy interlocks each cell's air valve closed when its agitator stops. Air pumped into a still cell is not dispersed, so slurry settles around the rotor and stator and sands it in. The bearings also take a hit when the mechanism restarts against a settled bed.

It is a protective interlock, like stopping coolant flow to a machine that is not turning so you do not create a different problem.

The agitators are also meant to keep running whenever the cell holds slurry or water, which reduces how often this happens.
f: How do you restart an agitator in a cell full of settled slurry?
Why do the agitators use reversible drives?
What is the air flow setpoint based on for each cell?

f.q: How do the dart valves control the cell level?
f.a:
Each tank cell has two dart valves on its discharge, run on split range level control, either in series or in parallel. A dart valve is a plug that rises and falls in a seat, opening more flow out of the cell as the level rises above setpoint.

Split range means the controller output is shared between the two valves. One works over part of the range and the second joins in as more capacity is needed, giving fine control at low flow and full capacity when required.

The level setpoint sets the froth depth, which the expert system adjusts to balance grade and recovery.
f: How is level measured in a flotation tank cell?
Why does a deeper froth give higher grade but lower recovery?
What happens to downstream cells when one cell's level drops?

f.q: What does the launder velocity camera measure?
f.a:
It looks at the froth as it crosses the cell lip into the launder and tracks how fast it is moving. Froth velocity times lip length and froth depth gives an estimate of how much froth, and so mass, is reporting to concentrate.

The flotation expert system combines that with froth cameras and onstream analyser assays to set level, air and reagents. The design used lip loading and froth carry rates of 1.5 t/m/h and 1.5 t/m2/h.

It gives near real time feedback where assays only arrive every few minutes per stream.
f: What streams does the onstream analyser measure?
How does the expert system decide to change cell air?
What is lip loading and why does it limit a cell?

Equipment code 'CF'?.q: How would you identify which bank a given CF tag belongs to?
Equipment code 'CF'?.a:
Read the area first. F16 is the rougher and scavenger bank, F18 the cleaner circuit. Then read the number: in F16, 411 to 413 are roughers 1 to 3 and 414 to 417 are scavengers 1 to 4. In F18, 501 is the cleaner Jameson and 511 the cleaner-scavenger.

The equipment list description confirms it, for example 'ROUGHER FLOTATION CELL 1' against F16-CF-411, and the flotation PFD shows each cell in order along the bank.

The supporting tags follow the same blocks. Agitators run F16-AG-421 to 427 and concentrate launders run F16-VL-430 to 439.

f.q: Why are there three roughers but four scavengers?
f.a:
The scavengers need more time. Roughers take the fast floating, well liberated sulphides. Scavengers chase the slower floating, finer or composite particles left behind, which takes longer residence.

The design gives 1,890 m3 of rougher volume (15.1 minutes) and 2,520 m3 of scavenger volume (21.4 minutes), or 36.5 minutes together. With 630 m3 cells, that works out to three and four cells.

Splitting into several cells in series also cuts short circuiting, much like several smaller stirred tanks in series outperform one big tank.
f: Why does short circuiting reduce flotation recovery?
What is the design mass pull from the scavenger bank?
How does residence time change at the high throughput case?

f.q: Where does each rougher cell's concentrate go?
f.a:
Per the PDC mass balance and the as built PFD Rev 1 (September 2026), rougher 1 concentrate, about 4.4 percent mass pull at around 15.3 percent S, goes to the Jameson cleaner. The PFD also shows a dashed bypass straight to the final concentrate hopper.

Rougher 2 and 3 concentrate, about 2.4 percent mass pull at around 7.1 percent S, goes to the cleaner feed. Scavenger concentrate goes to the cleaner too.

Only cleaner concentrate feeds the final concentrate hopper in normal operation.
f: When would the rougher 1 bypass to the final hopper be used?
What is the final concentrate sulphur grade target?
Why does rougher 1 concentrate have a higher grade than 2 and 3?

f.q: What do the launder tags around the rougher bank refer to?
f.a:
The equipment list shows a VL launder for each cell's concentrate: F16-VL-430, 431 and 432 for roughers 1 to 3, and F16-VL-433 to 436 for scavengers 1 to 4.

Collection launders then combine streams. F16-VL-438 is the rougher 2 and 3 concentrate collection launder, and F16-VL-437 and 439 handle scavenger 1 and 2 concentrate collection. The flotation PFD also shows F16-VL-440 as the scavenger concentrate collection launder.

VL covers launders, sumps and kibbles in the numbering spec.
f: Why do flotation launders need sprays to keep froth moving?
How steep does a concentrate launder need to be?
Where do the collection launders discharge to?

Equipment code 'MB'?.q: Why do the SAG and ball mill get different codes despite both grinding?
Equipment code 'MB'?.a:
They are different machines doing different stages of grinding. The SAG mill takes crusher product, about P80 130 mm, and grinds mainly by ore breaking ore, helped by a 10.5 percent charge of 125 mm balls. It is grate discharge, with pebble ports and a screen to pull out critical size pebbles.

The ball mill is an overflow mill with a heavier 28.5 percent ball charge of smaller 65 mm media, finishing the grind towards P80 180 um in closed circuit with the cyclones.

Liners, media, spares, controls and maintenance all differ, so separate codes make sense. Think of a roughing cut and a finishing cut: same family, very different tools.

f.q: Why is the SAG mill grate discharge but the ball mill overflow?
f.a:
The SAG mill needs to get rid of critical size pebbles that build up because they are too big to grind easily but too small to act as media. Its grate, with 75 mm pebble ports and curved pulp lifters, lets slurry and pebbles out. The discharge screen then sends oversize, about 375 t/h in the design, to the pebble crushers.

The ball mill does not have that problem. An overflow design is simpler: slurry leaves over the discharge trunnion, the balls stay in, and a trommel catches scats.

The grate also lets the operators control SAG load by how fast material leaves.
f: What happens when SAG pebble ports wear larger?
Why do critical size pebbles slow a SAG mill down?
How do the pebble crushers return product to the circuit?

f.q: What other mill codes are used on this plant?
f.a:
The spec uses MS for SAG mills, MB for ball mills, MU for the existing ultra fine grinding mill and MUF for the new UFG mills. So you will see F13-MS-401, F13-MB-401, the UFG 1 IsaMill in F34, and the two M15000 IsaMills in F28.

MB is not only the big grinding mill. The lime slaking mills in the reagents area are also ball mills, F72-MB-411 and 412, small tyre driven units in the lime slaking package.

Read the area before assuming MB means the 20 MW ball mill.
f: How does an IsaMill differ from a ball mill?
What does the lime slaking mill actually do?
Why does the UFG circuit use ceramic media instead of steel?

f.q: How much power do the SAG and ball mill each draw?
f.a:
Both are 20 MW installed. The design pinion power is about 16.8 MW for the SAG and about 17.7 MW for the ball mill.

The modelled specific energies are 9.14 kWh/t for the SAG (7.68 in the high throughput case) and 9.68 kWh/t for the ball mill at a 180 um grind. Together that is close to 19 kWh/t of milling energy on the design basis.

These are design values. Actual power draw changes with ore hardness, load and liner condition, so check the DCS trends for live numbers.
f: How does ore hardness change the milling power needed?
What is pinion power compared with motor power?
Why does a coarser grind increase throughput?

Equipment code 'MB'?.q: What handover note would flag a ball mill overload condition?
Equipment code 'MB'?.a:
A ball mill overload usually builds over a shift. The handover would mention rising mill weight or bearing pressure, power that climbed then started to fall, a dull sound, higher circulating load, and maybe more scats or slurry spilling at the trommel.

The usual causes are too much fresh feed from the SAG mills, coarser or harder ore, or cyclones returning more underflow. The design circulating load is already 358 percent, so there is not much slack.

Actions normally include cutting feed, checking cyclone pressure and density, and confirming ball addition is not overcharging. Note the time of each change so the next shift can follow the trend.

f.q: Why can an overloaded mill draw less power, not more?
f.a:
Mill power comes from lifting the charge. The motor supplies torque to hold the charge's centre of gravity off to one side of the mill axis. In an overloaded mill the charge fills more of the shell, its centre of gravity moves closer to the axis, and the torque arm shrinks.

Slurry pooling makes it worse by cushioning the balls. So power can peak and then fall as load keeps rising, which can fool a controller that assumes more load means more power.

That is why mill weight is watched alongside power.
f: How is mill weight measured on a large ball mill?
What is slurry pooling and how is it cleared?
Why does mill power drop when liners wear?

f.q: How does circulating load affect ball mill loading?
f.a:
Cyclone underflow, the coarse fraction, goes back to the ball mill. The design circulating load is 358 percent of the overflow, so most of what the ball mill grinds is recirculated material, not fresh feed.

If the cyclones cut coarser, or fresh feed coarsens, more mass comes back and the ball mill loads up. Feed density and the number of cyclones open both affect where the cut sits.

It is like a recycle loop in a process plant. Small changes in the separator can swing the recycle flow a lot.
f: What is the design underflow density of the cyclones?
How does the cyclone feed density setpoint get chosen?
Why do both SAG mills feed one ball mill?

f.q: What are scats and where do they go from the ball mill?
f.a:
Scats are hard oversize that will not grind, mostly worn ball fragments and tough rock. They pass out of the mill discharge and get caught on the trommel.

The ball mill trommel has 19 by 40 mm slots and sends scats to a scats bunker. From there they are removed in bulk rather than returned to the circuit.

A sudden rise in scats can mean ball breakage, a change in ore, or a damaged trommel panel. Note it in the handover if it happens.
f: Why do worn balls need removing rather than regrinding?
How often is the scats bunker emptied?
What causes grinding balls to break in a mill?

Equipment code 'MB'?.q: What controls typically manage ball mill load and power draw?
Equipment code 'MB'?.a:
The ball mill normally runs at fixed speed, about 75 percent of critical. That leaves its load and power to be managed indirectly.

Ball addition is automatic, to a kg/t or a mill weight setpoint. The design ball charge is 28.5 percent, maximum 31. Fresh feed is set by the SAG mills, whose reclaim feeders follow the expert system. Circulating load comes from the cyclone cluster, where knife gate valves open or close cyclones on feed pressure and water addition controls density.

So you steer the ball mill through its feed and its cyclones rather than its speed, a bit like a fixed speed pump whose duty is set by the system around it.

f.q: Why is ball mill power mostly set by the ball charge?
f.a:
At fixed speed, mill power depends on how much charge is being lifted and where its centre of gravity sits. The balls are most of that mass, so the ball charge level largely sets power draw.

As balls wear, the charge drops and power falls. Topping up balls restores it. That is why ball addition can run on kg/t of ore or on a mill weight setpoint.

Ore and slurry add to the load, but they change faster. The ball charge is the slow, steady base.
f: How is the ball charge level measured during a shutdown?
What happens if the ball charge goes above its maximum?
Why is the ball mill structurally rated for 38 percent charge?

f.q: How is grinding media added to the ball mill?
f.a:
The design calls for automatic ball addition to either a kg/t or a mill weight setpoint, so media goes in steadily rather than in big batches. The equipment list shows 65 mm grinding media for the ball mill, against 125 mm balls for the SAG.

Ball charging systems usually lift balls from a storage bunker with a magnet and feed them into the mill feed chute. The FIM area has a ball charging magnet, F19-MG-405.

For the ball handling arrangement on the new mill, check the F13 P&IDs or ask the area operators.
f: Why use smaller balls in the ball mill than the SAG?
How are grinding balls delivered and stored on site?
What is a ball charging magnet and how does it work?

f.q: What changes when the ball mill is relined?
f.a:
The design sets out reline scenarios. While the ball mill is relined, the new SAG runs single stage, meaning the SAG works without the ball mill. Throughput and grind suffer during that time.

During a FIM SAG reline the new SABC circuit keeps running, and during a new SAG reline the FIM SAG runs with the new ball mill.

A reline is a planned shutdown with a liner handler, crane work and full isolations. The maintenance planner owns the schedule and the scope.
f: What does single stage SAG operation do to the grind size?
How long does a ball mill reline usually take?
What are Poly-Met liners made of?

Equipment code 'CG'?.q: Why use a gyratory crusher for primary crushing instead of a jaw crusher?
Equipment code 'CG'?.a:
Capacity is the main reason. The new crusher is designed for 2,634 t/h nominal and 3,135 t/h design, up to 3,436 t/h, taking run of mine ore with F99 around 1,000 mm, tipped directly from 250 t trucks on two sides. Gyratories crush continuously all the way round the mantle and handle that tonnage in one machine.

A jaw crusher only crushes on half its stroke and has a smaller feed opening per tonne. You would need several jaws plus feeders to match one big gyratory.

It is like comparing a reciprocating compressor with a rotary one for a big continuous duty: the rotary machine wins on throughput per unit.

f.q: What do OSS and throw mean on a gyratory crusher?
f.a:
OSS, the open side setting, is the widest gap between mantle and concave at the bottom of the crushing chamber. The mantle gyrates eccentrically, so the gap opens and closes as it moves round. Throw is how far it moves. The closed side setting is OSS minus throw.

The new crusher's design OSS is 165 mm with a 38 mm throw. The existing crusher runs 141 mm OSS. The design product is P80 130 mm.

A smaller setting gives finer product but less capacity and more power. It is like closing a valve to raise pressure drop.
f: Why does a tighter setting increase crusher power draw?
How is the crusher setting measured during operation?
What does P80 mean for crusher product?

f.q: How is the crusher gap adjusted automatically here?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the crusher gap is auto adjusted from a camera particle size analyser on the stockpile feed. If product coarsens, the gap is closed. The equipment list describes the new crusher as top service with a plant vision rock camera.

On a gyratory, the gap is changed by raising or lowering the mainshaft hydraulically, the hydroset system. Raising the mantle closes the gap.

It is a closed loop with a slow process measurement, a bit like trimming a valve from an analyser rather than a fast flow signal.
f: What does the stockpile feed camera actually measure?
How fast can the hydroset change the setting while running?
What protects the crusher if tramp steel enters the chamber?

f.q: How does the new crusher compare with the existing one?
f.a:
The new F12 crusher is an FLS 1300 x 1900 TSUV gyratory with 165 mm OSS, 38 mm throw and 600 kW. The existing F10 crusher is a 54-75 Mk II with 141 mm OSS and 450 kW.

The new circuit is designed for 2,634 t/h nominal and 3,135 t/h design. The existing crusher is rated at 1,844 t/h.

The new crusher feeds the new crushed ore stockpile, about 20,460 t live or 11 hours, while the existing one feeds its own stockpile of about 21,000 t live or 16 hours.
f: Why does the new crusher run a wider OSS than the old one?
Which SAG mill does each crusher stockpile feed?
Where is the new crusher controlled from?

Equipment code 'CG'?.q: What would a handover flag if the gyratory crusher choked or bridged?
Equipment code 'CG'?.a:
Bridging and choking look different. In a bridge, an oversize rock or a pile of rocks jams across the crusher throat and stops feed. The crusher runs but draws little power, the discharge chamber level falls and the ROM bin level rises. In a choke the crusher is overfed or packed, so power climbs and it may stall.

The handover should give the time and cause, how the rock breaker was used, any damage found, the truck delay, and whether the crusher was tripped. Truck traffic lights go red automatically from ROM bin level and crusher status, so dump trucks are held.

Nobody enters the crusher area to clear it by hand. That is the rock breaker's job, run remotely.

f.q: How do the truck traffic lights respond to a crusher problem?
f.a:
The control philosophy sets the PC2 truck lights automatically. Inputs are the truck radar, ROM bin level, the discharge chamber level and high high switch, whether the crusher is running, and the rock breaker position.

So if the crusher stops, the bin is full, the discharge chamber is high, or the rock breaker is out of its park position, trucks get a red light and do not tip.

It is an automatic permissive for the trucks, like a start permissive on a drive, keeping tipping in step with what the crusher can take.
f: Why does the rock breaker position affect the truck lights?
What is the live volume of the ROM bin?
How does the truck radar detect a waiting truck?

f.q: Why is a full discharge chamber a problem for the crusher?
f.a:
The crusher drops its product into the discharge chamber, and the apron feeder draws from there onto the discharge conveyor. If the chamber fills, product has nowhere to go and backs up into the crushing chamber. That packs the crusher, overloads it and can damage it.

So the discharge chamber has level measurement and a high high switch, which feed the truck lights and stop tipping. The apron feeder is interlocked to the discharge conveyor running, so a conveyor trip stops the feeder and the chamber starts filling.

It is the same as a blocked discharge on a positive displacement pump.
f: What trips the crusher discharge conveyor?
Why is the apron feeder interlocked to the discharge chamber low low?
How long can the crusher run with the apron feeder stopped?

f.q: Who operates the rock breaker and from where?
f.a:
The new crusher PC2 is run from the existing crusher control room using CCTV. The rock breaker is operated remotely by camera and parks automatically.

The equipment list describes the new unit, F12-RB-401, as a Rammer XL1200R boom with a 3288E hydraulic hammer, automatic lubrication, radio remote control and a BoomSafe smart boom automation system. The existing crusher has its own rock breaker, F10-RB-01.

The rock breaker has its own vendor PLC that reports to the DCS.
f: What does the BoomSafe system prevent the boom from doing?
Why must the rock breaker park before trucks tip?
How does the operator see into the crusher throat?

Equipment code 'CG'?.q: What maintenance is typically done on a gyratory crusher's mantle and concave?
Equipment code 'CG'?.a:
The mantle and concaves are manganese steel wear liners. They wear as the crusher works, the setting opens up, and the hydroset raises the mainshaft to compensate until the liners reach their wear limit. Then they are replaced.

Typical work includes measuring wear at shutdowns, changing the mantle (lifted out with the mainshaft) and replacing concave segments in rows, backing them with filler compound, plus spider bushing and eccentric lubrication checks.

The new crusher is a top service design with a top hung hydroset maintenance trolley, so main parts come out from above. Intervals and procedures are site specific, so ask the crusher maintenance planner.

f.q: How do you know when the mantle is worn enough to change?
f.a:
As liners wear, the gap opens, and the hydroset raises the mantle to hold the setting. The mainshaft position therefore tracks liner wear, and once it reaches the top of its travel the setting can no longer be held.

Other signs are coarser product on the stockpile feed camera, changes in power and pressure, and direct thickness measurements taken during shutdowns.

Wear limits and change intervals come from the crusher vendor and the site's maintenance history. The maintenance planner will have the current wear tracking.
f: What is the hydroset and how does it raise the mainshaft?
Why are concaves changed in rows instead of all at once?
How long does a gyratory mantle typically last?

f.q: What does top service mean on the new gyratory?
f.a:
A top service gyratory is designed so the main components, mainshaft, mantle and the hydraulic and eccentric parts, can be removed from above rather than from below the crusher. The equipment list notes the new crusher has a top hung hydroset maintenance trolley.

Access from above avoids working in the cramped space under the crusher and over the discharge chamber. It usually shortens shutdowns.

TSUV is the FLS model designation for this top service design.
f: What crane is used to lift the mantle out?
Why is working under a crusher considered high risk?
How is the crusher isolated before liner work?

f.q: How does the plant keep feeding the mill while the crusher is relined?
f.a:
There are two primary crushers in parallel: the existing F10 crusher and the new F12 crusher. Each feeds its own stockpile.

The stockpiles give buffer time. The new crushed ore stockpile holds about 20,460 t live, roughly 11 hours, and the existing one about 21,000 t, roughly 16 hours. The SAG mills draw from these while a crusher is down.

For longer outages, an emergency apron feeder can be fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader from dead stock or a ROM stockpile.
f: What is dead stock on a stockpile and how is it reclaimed?
Why is crushing availability only 65 percent in the design?
Which SAG mill does the emergency feeder supply?

Equipment code 'CY'?.q: Why are cyclones used for classification instead of screens at this stage?
Equipment code 'CY'?.a:
The flow is enormous and the cut is fine. The primary cyclone cluster takes about 14,400 t/h of solids, 13,233 m3/h of slurry, and cuts to produce overflow for a grind around P80 180 um. Screens at that size would need a huge area and wear quickly.

Cyclones do it in one compact Weir 800CVX13 cluster with no moving parts. Seventeen cyclones are installed, 15 on primary duty and 2 on gravity duty.

Screens are still used where the job suits them: the SAG discharge screen for pebbles, gravity scalping screens, and trash screens on the cyclone overflow to remove wood and debris.

f.q: How does a hydrocyclone separate coarse from fine particles?
f.a:
Slurry enters tangentially under pressure, about 82 kPa in the design, and spins inside the cone. Centrifugal force throws coarse and heavy particles to the wall, where they spiral down and out of the apex as underflow.

Fine particles and most of the water get dragged into an inner vortex that rises and leaves through the vortex finder as overflow. The design underflow is 77 percent solids and the overflow is 36.4 percent solids.

It is a centrifugal separator with no moving parts, using pump pressure for its energy.
f: What is the vortex finder and how does its size matter?
Why does underflow come out as a spray when healthy?
What wears fastest in a hydrocyclone?

f.q: Why are 2 of the cluster's cyclones on gravity duty?
f.a:
Gold is heavy, so it concentrates in cyclone underflow and circulates in the grinding loop. Taking two cyclones' underflow to the gravity circuit gives the Knelson concentrators a feed already enriched in free gold.

Each gravity cyclone underflow goes to its own gravity scalping screen, where oversize returns to the ball mill feed and undersize goes to the Knelsons. The cyclone feed valves are interlocked to their gravity screens.

Gravity design recovery is about 14 percent of feed gold, up to 20 percent, recovered early before it can be lost.
f: Why are gravity cyclone valves interlocked to the screens?
What size particles does the gravity scalping screen reject?
How much concentrate do the Knelsons make per day?

f.q: Why do trash screens follow the cyclones on overflow?
f.a:
Cyclone overflow carries wood, plastic, grit and other debris that came in with the ore. Left in, it blocks intertank screens in the leach, fouls flotation and UFG trash screens, and can end up on carbon.

The design has 4 linear trash screens, 3 running and 1 standby, with 1.0 by 1.0 mm apertures. About 27 t/day of wood, grit and trash is removed, and flotation feed comes from the trash screen underflow.

It is like a strainer ahead of a sensitive heat exchanger, protecting everything downstream.
f: What happens if a trash screen panel tears?
How is collected trash dewatered and disposed of?
Why does the UFG circuit have its own trash screens too?

Equipment code 'CY'?.q: What handover symptom shows a cyclone is roping and misclassifying?
Equipment code 'CY'?.a:
Roping is the classic overload. Healthy underflow leaves the apex as a hollow cone spray. When too many solids report to the apex it cannot discharge them, and the underflow narrows into a thick rope. Coarse particles that should go to underflow get pushed into the overflow instead.

The handover symptoms are a coarser grind at the flotation particle size analyser, very thick underflow, more coarse material on the trash screens and possibly lower flotation recovery. Roping cyclones can be seen in the field.

Usual fixes are more water to lower feed density, opening more cyclones, or reducing fresh feed. Note which cyclones were roping and what was changed.

f.q: Why does too high a feed density cause roping?
f.a:
A cyclone apex has a limited capacity to pass solids. As feed density rises, the solids sent to underflow rise too, until the apex is crowded. The underflow can't escape fast enough, the air core collapses, and the discharge becomes a rope.

Thick slurry also has higher viscosity, which slows particles settling to the wall and coarsens the cut.

That is why hopper water addition is used to control cyclone feed or overflow density. It is the first lever for preventing roping.
f: What is the air core in a cyclone and why does it matter?
How is cyclone feed density measured?
Can a worn apex cause roping at normal density?

f.q: How does the cluster decide how many cyclones are open?
f.a:
The control philosophy uses feed pressure. If pressure stays high for a set time, a knife gate valve opens one more cyclone. If it stays low, one closes. A minimum number must be open before the cyclone feed pump can start.

Hopper level cascades to the pressure setpoint, so pump speed and the cyclone count work together. Nominally 12 primary cyclones run, up to 14, with 1 standby.

It is like staging compressors on header pressure: add a unit when the demand pushes pressure up, drop one when it falls.
f: Why is a minimum number of cyclones needed before pump start?
How long a delay is used before opening another cyclone?
How are worn cyclones rotated out of service?

f.q: What instrument shows the grind size going to flotation?
f.a:
The instrument list includes a flotation particle size analyser, F16-AN-402, with soft tags such as XI16172 for its density reading. It gives an online size measurement on the flotation feed, which reflects cyclone performance.

The design grind target is P80 180 um, maximum 250, and 220 um in the high throughput case. Those are design values, so the metallurgists set the live target.

A rising P80 trend is often the first sign of roping or an overloaded circuit.
f: How does an online particle size analyser measure size?
Why does a coarser grind hurt flotation recovery?
How often does the particle size analyser update?

Equipment code 'CY'?.q: What operating parameter is usually adjusted to control cyclone cut size?
Equipment code 'CY'?.a:
Feed density is the main operating lever. The cyclone feed hopper has water addition that controls cyclone feed or overflow density. More water gives a finer cut, less water a coarser cut.

Feed pressure is the second lever, set through the cyclone feed pump speed and the number of cyclones open. Higher pressure generally gives a finer cut.

Hardware sets the range: apex and vortex finder sizes are changed at shutdowns, not on shift. The design runs at about 62 percent solids feed (65 in the high case) and around 82 kPa.

f.q: Why does adding water make the cyclone cut finer?
f.a:
Diluting the feed lowers its viscosity and reduces crowding between particles. Particles can then move to the wall more freely, so finer ones that would have been carried to the overflow now settle out to underflow. That shifts the cut size finer.

There is a trade off. More water means more volume through the cyclones and pumps, and it dilutes the overflow going to flotation.

On this plant the density loop adds process water at the cyclone feed hopper and holds a density setpoint.
f: What happens downstream if cyclone overflow gets too dilute?
How does the nucleonic density gauge on cyclone feed work?
Why is process water used for cyclone dilution, not scheme water?

f.q: How does the hopper level link to cyclone pressure?
f.a:
The control philosophy uses a cascade. The cyclone feed hopper level controller sets the pressure setpoint, and the pressure loop adjusts the pump speed. If the hopper level rises, the pressure setpoint goes up and the pump speeds up to draw it down.

There is Fast and Slow level tuning, so the hopper can either soak up surges or respond hard when needed.

Because the cyclone count also responds to pressure, a rising hopper ends up opening more cyclones. That spreads the extra flow across the cluster.
f: When would the operator switch to fast level tuning?
What happens if the cyclone feed hopper runs low?
Why does the cyclone feed pump have no installed standby?

f.q: Why change apex or vortex finder sizes rather than operating settings?
f.a:
Operating settings move the cut within a range. If the circuit consistently needs a different cut, or the cyclones are always roping or always too fine, the geometry is wrong for the duty. Changing the apex or vortex finder resets that range.

A larger apex passes more underflow and resists roping. A smaller vortex finder gives a finer cut. Both wear, so they get replaced anyway at intervals.

These changes are made at planned shutdowns by maintenance with metallurgy's agreement, not on shift.
f: How is cyclone component wear measured?
What material are cyclone liners usually made from?
Who decides on cyclone geometry changes?

What's the difference between 'PP' and '.q: Why do sump pumps get a different equipment code from process pumps?
What's the difference between 'PP' and '.a:
They do different jobs and are built differently. A process pump (PP) moves a main process stream continuously, like the cyclone feed pump F13-PP-401. Process pumps are usually horizontal centrifugal slurry pumps, often on VSDs, with gland water, actuated valves and duty or standby arrangements.

A sump pump (PS) clears spillage and washdown from an area sump and runs intermittently on level. On this plant they are mostly vertical cantilever pumps or submersible slurry pumps, like F13-PS-402 and F12-PS-401.

Different design, controls and maintenance strategy justify a different code. One catch: in the electrical code list PS also means power supply, so check context.

f.q: What types of sump pump are used on this plant?
f.a:
The equipment list shows two main types. Vertical cantilever pumps with belt drives and column lengths of about 1,500 to 2,100 mm, such as F13-PS-402, 403, 405 and 409. And Goodwin submersible slurry pumps, 90 kW, such as F12-PS-401 at the crushing area and F13-PS-404 at the mill discharge end.

The vertical pumps sit on sump pump frames, tagged PSF, such as F13-PSF-402, which support the pump over the sump.

Submersibles tend to go where the sump is deep or the duty is heavy, and cantilevers where a simple robust pump will do.
f: Why are sump pump frames given their own tag?
Why use belt drives on vertical sump pumps?
How is a submersible sump pump lifted out for maintenance?

f.q: Why do vertical cantilever pumps suit sump duty?
f.a:
A vertical cantilever pump hangs its impeller in the sump on a stiff shaft, with all bearings above the slurry. Nothing submerged needs lubricating or sealing, so it can tolerate running with air in the suction, called snoring, as the sump empties.

The motor sits up out of the wet area, so it is easy to inspect, and the whole pump lifts out in one piece.

That makes it a good fit for intermittent, dirty, start stop duty.
f: What is pump snoring and is it harmful?
What limits the column length on a cantilever pump?
How do you check a sump pump's impeller wear?

f.q: Does every process pump have an installed standby?
f.a:
No. The control philosophy covers duty/standby pumps with actuated valves, but not every service has one. The cyclone feed pump F13-PP-401 is a single large pump, and the equipment list shows F13-PP-402 as a spare wet end only, held for change out rather than installed.

Other services do have installed spares. The flotation tails thickener underflow pumps are duty/standby, and the final tails pumps run duty, duty, duty, standby.

Whether a pump gets a standby depends on its criticality, size and cost. Very large pumps are often single with a spare wet end.
f: How long does a cyclone feed pump wet end change take?
What happens to the mill if the cyclone feed pump trips?
How are duty and standby pumps rotated to even out wear?

What's the difference between 'PP' and '.q: What handover note would flag a sump pump running continuously?
What's the difference between 'PP' and '.a:
Sump pumps normally start on high level and run until the high clears, plus a run on time or until low level. One running continuously means water or slurry is arriving as fast as it can pump it, or the pump is not pumping properly.

Common causes include a leaking gland, a hopper or launder overflowing, a washdown hose left running, a burst pipe, or a worn or air locked pump that can no longer lower the level. A stuck level switch can also keep it running.

The handover should name the sump pump, the suspected source and what was checked, so the next shift does not start from scratch.

f.q: How do you find where the extra sump inflow is coming from?
f.a:
Walk the area that drains to the sump. Look for pump glands leaking heavily, hoppers or launders overflowing, burst hoses or pipe leaks, washdown hoses left on, and spillage from screens or chutes.

Then check trends in the control room. A tank or hopper level that has been sitting high, or a process pump that tripped and drained, often explains it.

If the source is a leak on process equipment, report it rather than fix it on the spot. It may need an isolation and a work order.
f: What gland leak rate is normal on a slurry pump?
How do area drains route back to the sumps?
Who should be told about a leaking process line?

f.q: What happens if a sump pump fails while the sump is filling?
f.a:
The sump fills and overflows onto the floor or into the surrounding bund, and a high high level alarm should come up in the control room. Slurry spilled on floors becomes a clean up job and a slip hazard, and in bunded reagent areas it can mean a contained spill.

Whether the upstream process trips on sump high high depends on the area's interlocks, which are not in the condensed reference.

Ask the control room operator what the alarm response is for that sump, and whether a portable pump is available.
f: How are spillages in bunded reagent areas handled?
Do any sump high levels trip upstream equipment?
What portable pumps are kept for emergencies?

f.q: Why do sump pumps have a run on time after high level clears?
f.a:
If a pump stopped the moment the level dropped below the high switch, a small inflow would bring it straight back, and the pump would start and stop every few minutes. That short cycling wears motors, starters and couplings.

So the control philosophy runs the pump on past the high level clearing, for a set run on time or until a low level, to pump the sump well down and space out starts.

It is the same idea as hysteresis on a thermostat.
f: How many starts per hour can a sump pump motor tolerate?
What sets the length of the run on time?
Why do some sumps use a low level switch instead of a timer?

What's the difference between 'PP' and '.q: How does a PP pump's control philosophy differ from a PS pump's?
What's the difference between 'PP' and '.a:
A process pump is usually in a continuous control loop. Many run on VSDs with speed set by a level or flow loop. The dual hopper control is a good example: loop A sets pump speed at the higher level setpoint, and loop B adds water at a lower setpoint to keep minimum line velocity.

Process pumps in duty/standby pairs have actuated suction, discharge and dump valves, with dump valves failing open on power loss. Gland water is proven by a flow switch or mag flowmeter, and low gland flow blocks starting.

A sump pump is simple on and off control: start on high level, then run until high clears plus run on time or low level.

f.q: How does dual hopper level control keep minimum line velocity?
f.a:
Two loops share the hopper. Loop A controls pump speed to a higher level setpoint. If inflow drops, the pump slows to hold level, but there is a minimum speed and flow below which slurry would settle in the line.

So loop B watches a lower level setpoint and adds water when the level falls to it. The extra water keeps the pump running fast enough to hold line velocity, at the cost of diluting the slurry a little.

It is like a minimum flow recirculation on a boiler feed pump, using makeup water instead of recirculation.
f: What happens to slurry density when loop B adds water?
Why is minimum line velocity so important for slurry pipes?
Which hoppers on this plant use dual level control?

f.q: Why do process pump dump valves fail open on power loss?
f.a:
When a slurry pump stops, the slurry in its suction and discharge pipes starts to settle. Left long enough it packs solid and the line has to be cleared by hand.

Dump valves drain the line to a sump or drain. Making them fail open on power loss means they drain the line even when nobody is available to act, for example during a site wide power failure.

It is a fail safe choice, like a spring return valve that goes to its safe position on loss of air.
f: Where does slurry from a dump valve drain to?
How is a dump valve closed again on restart?
What happens if a dump valve fails to open?

f.q: How is a standby process pump brought into service?
f.a:
The control philosophy says standby changeover is decided case by case, so there is no single rule. In general the standby is started through its own sequence: open the gland water, prove gland flow, open suction, start the pump, then open discharge. Meanwhile the duty pump stops and drains through its dump valve.

Some pairs may change over automatically on a duty pump trip, others manually by the CRO.

Check the area control philosophy or ask the control room operator for the arrangement on the pump you are interested in.
f: Why is gland flow proven before a slurry pump starts?
What is a Maric valve on a gland water line?
How often should a standby pump be run to keep it healthy?

Code 'SU' vs 'PS'. Which is the sump its.q: Why does the spec bother distinguishing the sump structure from its pump?
Code 'SU' vs 'PS'. Which is the sump its.a:
They are different assets with different owners and hazards. The sump (SU) is a civil or structural item: a concrete pit or steel box that collects spillage. The sump pump (PS) is a rotating machine with a motor, bearings and impeller.

They are maintained by different trades and inspected differently, and a single sump can be served by more than one pump. Work on each also needs different controls. Repairing the pump is a mechanical job with an electrical isolation. Cleaning out the sump can mean confined space entry.

The spec is blunt about it: SU is 'Sump (Sump Only! Not Sump Pump)'. Clearly people had mixed them up before.

f.q: Can one sump be served by more than one pump?
f.a:
Yes. The equipment list has examples like the FIM scavenger concentrators sump pumps 1 and 2, F26-PS-02 and F26-PS-03, both listed as in service.

Two pumps on one sump give a backup, or extra capacity for big washdown or spillage events. If the pumps get separate tags but the sump is one structure, an SU tag keeps the structure as a single asset.

Check the P&ID for which pumps share which sump. It is not always obvious from the names.
f: How do two pumps on one sump share duty?
Why do some areas have no sump pump standby?
How are sump high level alarms set?

f.q: What is a sump pump frame and why does it get its own tag?
f.a:
The numbering spec has a code for the pump sump frame, and the equipment list uses PSF, for example F13-PSF-402, a Type 1 sump pump frame, and F13-PSF-405, a Type 3 frame. It is the structural frame that holds a vertical sump pump in position over the sump.

It gets its own tag because it is a separate fabricated item, built and installed separately, with its own inspection and possibly its own lifting design.

Different frame types suit different pumps and sump depths.
f: How is a vertical sump pump lifted out of its frame?
What inspections does a sump pump frame need?
Why do sump pump frames come in different types?

f.q: What inspection does a concrete sump itself need?
f.a:
In general sumps are checked for silt and debris build up, wear and damage to linings, cracks or spalling in the concrete, the condition of grating and covers, and whether level switches are fouled or damaged.

Slurry is abrasive and process water here is saline, so concrete and steel embedments can deteriorate faster than in a fresh water plant.

Inspection often means a confined space entry. Follow the site's permit and isolation rules, including isolating the sump pump so it cannot start on level.
f: How often are sumps cleaned out on a plant like this?
What is used to remove heavy silt from a sump?
Why do sump level switches foul so easily?

Code 'SU' vs 'PS'. Which is the sump its.q: What handover issue arises from confusing a sump tag with its pump tag?
Code 'SU' vs 'PS'. Which is the sump its.a:
A work order raised against the wrong tag sends the wrong trade. 'Clean F13 sump' against a PS tag gets a fitter with spanners instead of a vacuum truck crew, and a pump fault logged against an SU tag may never reach a mechanic.

The bigger issue is safety. Cleaning a sump means isolating its pump so it cannot start automatically on level, and possibly a confined space permit. If the tags are confused, the isolation may be applied to the wrong item or missed altogether.

Quote the exact tag, and say whether you mean the structure or the pump.

f.q: Why does cleaning out a sump need the pump isolated?
f.a:
Sump pumps start automatically on high level. If someone is in or over the sump and the level rises, from washdown or a leak upstream, the pump can start without warning and draw in hoses, tools or people.

So the pump must be isolated and tested dead before any sump cleaning or entry, and the sources that drain into the sump should be controlled too.

Follow the site isolation and confined space procedures. Never rely on switching the pump to Manual or Local, because those are control modes, not isolations.
f: Why is a control mode never treated as an isolation?
How are inflows to a sump controlled during cleaning?
Who signs off a confined space permit for a sump?

f.q: Is a sump a confined space?
f.a:
Often, yes. A confined space is generally an enclosed or partly enclosed space not designed for people to occupy, with restricted entry, where there may be harmful atmosphere, engulfment or other hazards. Deep sumps, especially near cyanide or reagent areas where gas can collect, usually qualify.

Whether a specific sump is classified as a confined space is set by the site register, not by judgement on the day.

Check the site confined space register or ask the area supervisor before planning any entry.
f: What gas testing is done before entering a sump?
Why are sumps in leach areas a gas risk?
What rescue arrangements are needed for confined space entry?

f.q: How does silt build up in a sump affect the pump?
f.a:
Silt reduces the sump's working volume, so the pump starts and stops more often. It can bury the pump suction, so the pump either sucks dense slurry that overloads it or blocks altogether.

Settled material can also jam level switches or foul level probes, so the pump fails to start or keeps running.

A sump pump that trips on overload or keeps running without lowering the level is often a sign the sump needs cleaning, not that the pump has failed.
f: How do you tell a blocked suction from a worn impeller?
Why do some sumps have agitators or sparge pipes?
What is a sump high high alarm for?

Code 'SU' vs 'PS'. Which is the sump its.q: What would you check first if a sump was overflowing on shift?
Code 'SU' vs 'PS'. Which is the sump its.a:
Start with the pump. Is it running, and is it in the right mode? On the OIS check status, mode, level and any trip or first out alarm. In the field check whether the motor is turning, whether it is pumping, and whether the discharge valve is open.

If it is running but the level is still rising, the pump is either not pumping properly, from a blocked suction, worn impeller or air lock, or the inflow is more than it can handle. Then find the inflow source.

Report to the control room operator. Do not bypass level interlocks or run the pump in Local to get around a trip unless that is properly supervised for fault finding.

f.q: How can you tell if a sump pump is running but not pumping?
f.a:
The motor is running but the level does not fall. The motor current is lower than normal, often a sign of an air locked or blocked suction, and the discharge pipe feels empty or there is no flow at the outlet.

Common causes are a blocked suction or strainer, a worn or damaged impeller, a closed or blocked discharge, or a broken drive belt on belt driven pumps.

Compare with the pump's normal current if the control room can trend it. A big drop with no level change says the pump is not doing work.
f: What does motor current tell you about pump loading?
How do you check a belt drive without opening guards?
What causes impellers to wear unevenly?

f.q: What drive mode should a sump pump normally be in?
f.a:
Automatic. In Auto the DCS starts and stops it from the level signal, and the LCS can stop it but not start it.

Manual lets the CRO start and stop it from the OIS and allows LCS start and stop. Local allows an LCS start only and bypasses process interlocks and start permissives, though critical interlocks stay active. It is for fault finding and maintenance only, must be supervised, and has a timer that returns the drive to its target mode.

Mode changes are made from the OIS only, and they are bumpless.
f: Why does Local mode have a timer that returns the drive?
What interlocks stay active in Local mode?
Who is allowed to change a drive's mode?

f.q: Where does sump pump discharge usually go?
f.a:
In general sump pumps return what they collect to the process, usually into the nearest suitable hopper, feed box or tank, so spilled slurry is recovered rather than wasted.

On this plant the CIL4 area also has a static screen, a 1 mm sieve bend, for event pond and silt trap returns, which stops trash going back in with recovered spillage.

Check the area P&ID for each sump pump's destination. Where it goes matters when you are working out why a downstream level has jumped.
f: Why must spillage from leach areas stay in the leach circuit?
What is the event pond used for?
What does the silt trap catch before water is reused?

Code 'FA'?.q: Why use an apron feeder under the crusher rather than a belt feeder?
Code 'FA'?.a:
An apron feeder is built for heavy impact and big lumps. It is a chain of overlapping steel pans running on rollers, much like a crawler track, that can sit under a deep head of rock and take ore dropping straight onto it.

Under the crusher discharge chamber it carries crushed ore up to about P100 229 mm, and under the stockpile it takes the weight of thousands of tonnes above. A rubber belt feeder would be cut and torn by those loads.

The new crusher discharge feeder, F12-FA-401, is an 1800 x 6500 unit with a SEW gearbox, SALT chain and automatic lubrication. It is rated for a design of 3,135 t/h.

f.q: What does the D6 or D8 in the apron feeder description mean?
f.a:
The equipment list describes F12-FA-401 as D6 and the reclaim feeders as D8N. In general that refers to the chain and roller size class, borrowed from the equivalent bulldozer undercarriage, so a D8 chain is heavier than a D6.

Apron feeders often use tractor type track components because they are proven, heavy duty and widely available.

The reference does not explain these designations, so check the vendor data or ask the area maintenance planner for the exact chain specification.
f: Why do the reclaim feeders need a heavier chain than the crusher feeder?
How are apron feeder pans replaced?
What is the SALT chain mentioned in the equipment list?

f.q: Why do the reclaim feeders differ in size from the crusher feeder?
f.a:
They do different jobs. The two reclaim feeders, F13-FA-411 and 412, are 1,800 by 11,600 mm units with D8N chains, each designed for 2,017 t/h, 110 percent of nominal. They sit under the stockpile with a large head of ore pressing down.

The crusher discharge feeder F12-FA-401 is shorter, 1,800 by 6,500 mm with a D6 chain, but rated for the full design crushing rate of 3,135 t/h.

The longer reclaim feeders reach under the stockpile draw points and carry ore out to the SAG feed conveyor.
f: Why are two reclaim feeders used instead of one larger one?
What happens to SAG feed if one reclaim feeder stops?
How is the stockpile drawdown shape affected by feeder choice?

f.q: What is the emergency apron feeder used for?
f.a:
The design includes one emergency apron feeder, F13-FA-414, fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader. It lets the plant keep feeding the new SAG mill when ore can't be reclaimed from the stockpile, for example during reclaim feeder maintenance or when the live stockpile is drawn down.

The loader picks up ore from dead stock or a separate pile and tips it into the feeder hopper.

The equipment list shows it as 1,800 by 10,000 mm with a D6 chain, the same family as the other feeders.
f: What is live versus dead stockpile capacity?
How is loader fed ore blended with reclaimed ore?
What safety controls apply around a loader feed hopper?

Code 'FA'?.q: What handover symptom indicates an apron feeder chain problem?
Code 'FA'?.a:
Chain problems usually show up as noise and motion first: clunking or grinding as pans pass the sprockets, jerky or uneven movement, pans riding up or out of line, spillage under the feeder, or visible damage to links or rollers.

On the control side you might see motor current spikes or a higher average current for the same tonnage, or tonnage on the weightometer dropping or fluctuating while feeder speed stays the same. The position encoder can flag stalling or speed mismatch.

The handover should give the feeder tag, what was heard or seen, current and speed trends, and whether the autolube system is healthy.

f.q: What does the apron feeder position encoder tell the control system?
f.a:
The instrument list shows an incremental encoder on F12-FA-401. An encoder sends pulses as the shaft turns, so the control system knows the actual speed and whether the feeder is moving at all.

That lets the system compare commanded speed with actual speed. A stall, a broken drive or a slipping coupling shows up as a mismatch and can raise an alarm or trip.

It is the same as a zero speed switch or tachometer on a conveyor, but with more resolution.
f: What is an under speed switch on a conveyor for?
How does the feeder VSD respond to a stall?
Why use an incremental encoder instead of a simple speed switch?

f.q: Why does the apron feeder have an automatic lube system?
f.a:
The chain pins, bushings and rollers work under heavy load in a dusty, abrasive environment. Without regular grease they wear fast and the chain stretches.

An automatic lube system delivers small, frequent doses to each point while the feeder runs, which is far more consistent than manual greasing. It also keeps people away from moving equipment. The equipment list notes an Autolube system on the apron feeders.

A lube fault should be treated as a maintenance priority, not just an alarm to acknowledge.
f: How is a lube system fault shown on the OIS?
What does chain stretch do to an apron feeder?
How often do apron feeder rollers need replacing?

f.q: How is spillage under an apron feeder cleaned up safely?
f.a:
Spillage under feeders is a constant job on crushing and reclaim plants. The safe approach is to isolate the feeder and the equipment around it, and confirm zero energy, before anyone goes near the moving parts.

Cleaning around running feeders by hand is a classic way to get caught in rollers or under falling rock. Many sites use spillage conveyors, vacuum trucks or remote equipment instead.

Follow the site isolation and access procedures for that area. The reference does not give a specific procedure, so ask the area supervisor.
