f: Why is falling rock a hazard under a stockpile feeder?
What is a spillage conveyor and where is it used?
How is access to under feeder tunnels controlled?

Code 'FA'?.q: How is an apron feeder's speed controlled to match crusher throughput?
Code 'FA'?.a:
The feeders run on VSDs, with speed set by a tonnage loop. The crusher discharge apron feeder F12-FA-401 is speed controlled to a stockpile feed weightometer tonnage setpoint, using F12-WD-402 on the stockpile feed conveyor.

It is also interlocked: it stops if the discharge conveyor is not running, if the discharge chamber reaches low low, or if the head chute hits high high.

The reclaim feeders work the same way but to the SAG feed weightometer or a mill weight setpoint, normally set by the expert system, with a deadband to allow for the lag between feeder and weightometer.

f.q: Why is there a deadband on the reclaim feeder tonnage control?
f.a:
There is a transport delay between a change in feeder speed and the change reaching the weightometer further along the conveyor. If the controller reacted to every small error immediately, it would overcorrect, then chase its own correction, and the feed would hunt.

A deadband tells the controller to ignore small errors and only act when the tonnage is clearly off setpoint.

It is the same trick as a deadband on a level controller, trading a little precision for stability.
f: How long is the delay from reclaim feeder to the weightometer?
What is controller hunting and how is it spotted on trends?
Why is mill weight sometimes used instead of tonnage?

f.q: What stops the crusher discharge apron feeder automatically?
f.a:
The control philosophy lists its interlocks: the discharge conveyor not running, the discharge chamber reaching low low level, and the head chute high high.

The conveyor interlock stops the feeder dumping ore onto a stationary belt. The low low chamber interlock typically keeps a bed of ore in the chamber, which cushions the feeder pans from rock falling out of the crusher. The head chute high high stops a blocked chute from overfilling.

These are process interlocks. Like any drive, it also trips on critical interlocks such as pull wires and E-stops.
f: Why does the feeder need a rock bed left in the chamber?
What sensor detects a high high level in the head chute?
How is a head chute blockage cleared safely?

f.q: How does the expert system choose the SAG feed rate?
f.a:
The reclaim feeders are normally set by the expert system, which looks at the SAG feed camera size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, mill load, speed and power.

If the mill is underloaded and quiet, with power headroom, it raises feed. If load or power climbs towards limits, or the noise suggests the charge is packing, it cuts back. Coarser or harder feed usually means lower tonnage for the same load.

Operators can take it out of expert control and set tonnage or mill weight directly if needed.
f: What does the SAG feed size camera actually measure?
When would an operator take the mill off expert control?
How does harder ore change the SAG mill's best feed rate?

Code 'TH'?.q: Why do thickeners need both an agitator and a rake mechanism?
Code 'TH'?.a:
They don't, and the question mixes up two codes on the card. A thickener (TH) has a rake mechanism (RK) but no agitator. Agitators (AG) belong in tanks, where the job is to keep solids suspended. A thickener wants the opposite: solids settling into a dense bed.

The rake turns very slowly across the floor, pushing settled solids towards the central discharge cone. It also opens channels in the bed so water can escape upwards, which helps the bed compact. On F17 the rake mechanism is F17-RK-401 on the 60 m high rate thickener F17-TH-401, with a hydraulic rake drive and a separate rake lift system.

An agitator in a thickener would be like stirring a settling tank: it undoes the work.

f.q: What does the rake lift system do on the F17 thickener?
f.a:
If the bed gets too heavy, rake torque rises. Rather than stall the drive, the rake lift system raises the rake arms so they ride higher in the bed where the solids are softer. Once torque drops, the rakes are lowered again.

The equipment list shows a separate rake lift hydraulic power unit, F17-HU-414, and a rake lift hydraulic cylinder, F17-XM-573. Rake height is one of the vendor panel signals sent to the DCS.

It works like a clutch that slips before something breaks, buying time to fix the cause.
f: How high can the F17 rakes lift before they are fully raised?
What happens if the rakes stay lifted for a long time?
Why does the rake lift have its own hydraulic power unit?

f.q: Why is the F17 rake driven hydraulically?
f.a:
A thickener rake needs huge torque at very low speed. Hydraulic motors deliver that well, and the drive torque is directly proportional to hydraulic pressure, which gives a simple, accurate torque signal for protection.

The equipment list shows a rake drive hydraulic power unit F17-HU-406 with a 400 L reservoir, two rake drive hydraulic motors F17-HM-401 and 402, a rake drive oil cooling fan and an oil tank heater.

Relief valves in the circuit give overload protection, much like a relief valve on a hydraulic press.
f: Why does the rake drive oil tank need a heater?
How is hydraulic pressure turned into a torque reading?
What maintenance does a hydraulic rake drive need?

f.q: Where are agitators used instead of rakes on this plant?
f.a:
Anywhere solids must stay suspended. The rougher and scavenger flotation cells have agitators, F16-AG-421 to 427. The ILR solution tank has F14-AG-410, and the existing goldroom has eluate tank agitators such as F66-AG-61.

Leach and adsorption tanks also rely on agitation to keep slurry and carbon suspended and to mix in oxygen and cyanide. Reagent and filter feed tanks typically use them too.

The rule of thumb: agitators where you want everything mixed, rakes where you want solids to settle and be collected.
f: What happens to a CIL tank if its agitator stops?
Why do flotation cell agitators keep running when the cell is idle?
How are large tank agitators restarted after a power failure?

Code 'TH'?.q: What handover flag indicates a thickener rake torque alarm?
Code 'TH'?.a:
The vendor panel sends the DCS rake torque, bed level (SmartDiver), rake height, bed pressure as a measure of bed mass, and overflow clarity. A torque alarm handover should give the torque value and trend, whether the rakes lifted, and what bed pressure and underflow density were doing.

It should also say whether both underflow pumps were healthy, what flocculant was doing, whether the feed changed (more solids or coarser material), and what action was taken, such as increasing underflow draw or reducing flocculant.

A rising torque trend is an early warning. Caught early it is a pumping adjustment; left alone it can become a bogged thickener.

f.q: What usually causes rake torque to climb?
f.a:
Usually the bed is getting heavier or stiffer. The most common reason is underflow being drawn too slowly, from a pump problem, a blockage or a low flow setpoint, so solids accumulate.

Other causes are coarse sand settling fast near the centre, overdosed flocculant making a very dense bed, a change in ore that compacts more, or debris or scale building up on the floor.

Look at bed pressure and underflow flow first. If bed mass is rising while underflow flow has dropped, the cause is usually right there.
f: How does overdosing flocculant make the bed stiffer?
What happens to underflow density when the bed gets heavy?
Why can coarse sand be a problem in a tails thickener?

f.q: What happens if rake torque keeps rising after the rakes lift?
f.a:
Once the rakes are lifted and torque still climbs, the drive's protection will eventually stop it to prevent damage. A thickener with stopped rakes and a heavy bed can bog, meaning the solids set so hard the rakes cannot restart. Recovery then becomes a major job.

The usual response is to draw underflow harder, cut flocculant, and reduce or divert feed. The specific torque limits and steps are in the vendor and site procedures, not the condensed reference.

Ask the control room operator for the F17 high torque response.
f: How is a bogged thickener recovered?
Can feed be diverted away from F17 during an upset?
What torque percentage normally triggers a rake lift?

f.q: Why does bed pressure indicate how much solids are in the thickener?
f.a:
A pressure sensor near the floor reads the weight of everything above it. Water alone gives a known hydrostatic head. Settled solids are denser, so the extra pressure above the water head tells you how much solid is in the bed.

That makes bed pressure a good measure of bed mass, or inventory. The underflow pumps can cascade from bed pressure to keep inventory steady, rather than waiting for underflow density to change.

It is like reading tank contents from a bottom pressure gauge, with solids making the liquid heavier.
f: Why does saline process water affect the bed pressure reading?
How does the SmartDiver measure bed level?
What is the difference between bed level and bed mass?

Code 'TH'?.q: How is thickener underflow density typically controlled?
Code 'TH'?.a:
The design target is about 56 percent solids, range 50 to 62. The duty and standby underflow pumps, F17-PP-455 and 456, are on VSDs in a cascade. Bed pressure or density sets a flow setpoint, and the flow loop sets pump speed.

The underflow density transmitter is DIT17121 on the pump discharge. On start up or low flow, underflow recycles back to the thickener feed so the pumps and lines keep moving.

Flocculant is the other lever. In Stage 2 it is dosed to a feed solids ratio setpoint with an inline mixer for secondary dilution. Good flocculation gives a denser, faster settling bed.

f.q: Why control on bed pressure rather than underflow density alone?
f.a:
Underflow density is the result you want, but it lags. By the time density drops, the bed has already thinned. Bed pressure shows inventory building or falling earlier, so control is smoother.

The design lets the cascade run from either bed pressure or density, so the operator can choose. Pressure is useful for holding a steady bed, density for holding a target feed to CIL4.

It is like controlling a boiler on drum level as well as steam flow: watch the inventory, not just the output.
f: When would an operator switch the cascade to density control?
What is a typical bed pressure setpoint for this thickener?
How quickly does underflow density respond to a pump speed change?

f.q: What does the underflow recycle to the feed do?
f.a:
On start up, or when underflow flow is low, the underflow is sent back to the thickener feed rather than on to CIL4. The equipment list includes a recirculation feed box, F17-BX-410.

That keeps the pumps running above their minimum flow and the line velocity high enough to stop solids settling. It also stops thin, low density underflow being sent to CIL4 while the bed is still building.

It works like a minimum flow bypass on a centrifugal pump.
f: How does the operator know when to stop recycling underflow?
Why would low density underflow be bad for CIL4?
What happens to the thickener if both underflow pumps trip?

f.q: How does flocculant dosing affect underflow density?
f.a:
Flocculant is a long chain polymer that binds fine particles into larger flocs. Bigger flocs settle faster and compact into a denser bed, giving higher underflow density and clearer overflow.

Too little and fines stay suspended, overflow clarity drops and density falls. Too much costs money, can make the bed stiff and raise rake torque, and can carry over into process water.

In Stage 2 dosing follows a feed solids ratio setpoint through the inline mixer F17-XM-413, which adds dilution water so the polymer spreads evenly.
f: Why is flocculant diluted before it is added?
What does overflow clarity tell you about flocculation?
Can flocculant in process water upset flotation?

Code 'IL'?.q: Why does the gravity concentrate need a separate, more aggressive leach?
Code 'IL'?.a:
Gravity concentrate is mostly coarse free gold. Coarse particles dissolve slowly because they have little surface area for their mass, and ordinary CIL residence is too short to finish them. Left in the main circuit they would circulate in the grinding loop and some would be lost.

The concentrate is a small mass, about 14.4 t per day from the Knelsons. That makes it practical to leach intensively in a dedicated reactor with high reagent strength and strong contact. The design recovery is 92 to 98 percent.

The pregnant solution, about 14.5 m3 per batch at 1,100 to 1,800 ppm Au, goes straight to gravity electrowinning. It is a fast lane for the easiest gold.

f.q: Why does coarse gold leach so slowly in a normal tank?
f.a:
Cyanide dissolves gold at the particle surface, so the rate depends on surface area. A coarse particle has much less surface per gram than a fine one, so it takes far longer to dissolve completely.

In general a particle's leach time scales roughly with its size. A 500 um flake can need days in normal leach conditions, while fine gold dissolves in hours.

Intensive leaching speeds this up with higher cyanide and oxidant concentrations and vigorous contact. It is like increasing the driving temperature difference in a heat exchanger to transfer heat faster.
f: What oxidant is used to speed up gold dissolution?
Why does fine gold leach faster even in a weak solution?
Does coarse gold also cause sampling problems?

f.q: What happens to the ILR residue after leaching?
f.a:
After the solution is drained, the leached residue, about 40 percent solids in the design, is pumped out by the ILR discharge pump F14-PP-421, part of the Acacia package.

The condensed reference does not say where the residue goes. In general it is returned to the grinding circuit, so any gold left in it gets another chance in flotation and leaching rather than being lost.

Check the F14 P&ID or ask the metallurgist for the residue destination on this plant.
f: Is the ILR residue sampled before it leaves the reactor?
Why is residue returned to the mill instead of tails?
How is the reactor rinsed between batches?

f.q: How much gold does the gravity circuit recover?
f.a:
The design assumes gravity recovers about 14 percent of the feed gold, up to 20 percent. That covers gold caught by the Knelsons and then leached in the ILR at a design 98 percent recovery, within a 92 to 98 percent range.

On a nominal 1.11 Moz per year plant, that is a significant slice of production delivered quickly as gravity EW cathode.

These are design figures. Actual gravity recovery depends on how much free gold the ore carries, so ask the metallurgist for current results.
f: Why does gravity recovery vary between ore types?
What are the Knelson concentrators' design feed rates?
How is gravity gold kept separate in the metallurgical accounts?

Code 'IL'?.q: What handover note would flag an ILR batch cycle running long?
Code 'IL'?.a:
The design is one batch per day nominal, two maximum, on a 12 hour cycle. A batch running long should be flagged with the start time, which step it is stuck on (filling, leaching, solution transfer or residue discharge), and why if known.

Useful details include the reagent feed flows, such as the ILR cyanide feed FIT14121 and caustic feed FIT14122, any pump faults, and the latest solution assays.

The knock on effects matter. Knelson concentrate keeps arriving and is stored until the reactor is free, and gravity electrowinning waits for its next batch. The next shift needs to know how much room is left.

f.q: What happens to Knelson concentrate while the ILR is busy?
f.a:
Each Knelson cycle produces about 150 kg of concentrate, 48 cycles per day, roughly 14.4 t per day in the design. While a batch is leaching, that concentrate collects in the gravity concentrate hopper, F14-HP-420, part of the Acacia package.

A long batch means the hopper fills further. The condensed reference does not say what happens when it is full, but in general the Knelsons would need to be slowed or bypassed until there is room.

Ask the control room operator for the agreed response if the concentrate hopper is getting full.
f: How many tonnes does the gravity concentrate hopper hold?
Can the Knelsons run in bypass without making concentrate?
What alarms show the concentrate hopper is nearly full?

f.q: How is ILR leach completion judged?
f.a:
The package includes a pregnant solution sampler, F14-SA-406, and a residue discharge sampler, F14-SA-407, a single stage Vezin sampler. Solution samples show gold rising during the leach and levelling off when dissolution is done.

Most intensive leach systems run on a timed sequence based on testwork, with assays used to confirm performance afterwards. The design cycle is 12 hours.

Residue assays tell the metallurgist whether the batch left gold behind. Ask them how recent batches have performed.
f: How long do ILR solution assays take to come back?
Why use a Vezin sampler on the residue?
What residue grade would be considered a poor leach?

f.q: Who looks after the Acacia package controls?
f.a:
The control philosophy lists the ILR among the equipment that is DCS controlled, along with the Knelsons and EW cells, rather than running on its own vendor PLC. The control room operator runs the sequence from the OIS.

The package mechanical and process equipment, reactor, solution tank, pumps and samplers, comes from the vendor and is maintained under the area's maintenance plan.

For day to day questions start with the gravity area operator or CRO, and for performance the metallurgist.
f: What steps make up the ILR batch sequence?
Why is the ILR DCS controlled instead of on a vendor PLC?
Who should be called if an ILR pump trips mid batch?

Code 'IL'?.q: What reagents does the Acacia ILR use compared to standard CIL leaching?
Code 'IL'?.a:
The condensed reference does not list the ILR reagents. The instrument list shows cyanide feed (FIT14121), caustic feed (FIT14122) and a general reagent feed flow (FIT14082) on the ILR, so cyanide and caustic are confirmed.

In general, intensive leach reactors use high strength sodium cyanide, caustic soda to hold pH, and an oxidant such as hydrogen peroxide or a proprietary leach aid to speed dissolution. Standard CIL uses lower cyanide, lime for pH and oxygen. On this plant CIL4 runs at pH 8.8 to 9.3 with oxygen injection.

The ILR also has no carbon. Gold stays in solution and goes straight to electrowinning.

f.q: Why does the ILR send solution to EW instead of loading carbon?
f.a:
The ILR solution is small in volume and very rich, about 14.5 m3 at 1,100 to 1,800 ppm Au per batch in the design. That is ideal for direct electrowinning, which can plate it down to below 5 ppm in about 10 hours.

Loading it onto carbon would add an adsorption step, an elution and a regeneration for no gain. Carbon earns its place when gold is dilute in large volumes, as in CIL.

It is like skipping a storage tank when the flow can go straight to the user.
f: What cathodes does the gravity EW cell use?
Why is copper in the ILR solution a concern for EW?
Where does gravity EW barren solution go?

f.q: Why use caustic in the ILR but lime in the CIL tanks?
f.a:
Caustic soda is fully soluble and adds no solids, so it gives a clean, fast pH adjustment in a small batch reactor without forming scale. The cost is fine at the ILR's small volume.

Lime is much cheaper per unit of alkalinity, which matters across thousands of tonnes per hour in CIL. It adds calcium, which can scale pipes and carbon, and that is one reason carbon is acid washed.

This is general practice. The reference confirms caustic feed on the ILR and milk of lime dosing at the CIL feed.
f: How does calcium scale affect carbon activity?
What is milk of lime and how is it made on site?
Why is caustic heated in its storage tank?

f.q: Is the ILR a CS10000 or a CS8000?
f.a:
The documents disagree. The process design criteria and the flashcards describe an Acacia CS10000, 1 off, about 14.4 t per batch. Several entries in the mechanical equipment list for the reactor's solution tank, agitator, pumps and hopper say they are part of a CS8000 Acacia package.

It could be a naming or revision difference, or a change in the supplied unit. The reactor itself, F14-IL-403, is listed just as part of the Acacia package.

Check the vendor data book or the reactor nameplate, or ask the gravity area engineer, before quoting either figure.
f: Who should be told about a discrepancy between project documents?
Where can I find the Acacia vendor data book?
What is a technical query and when is one raised?

Code 'CN'?.q: Why does loaded carbon need elution before it can be regenerated?
Code 'CN'?.a:
Elution strips the gold off the carbon into solution. Regeneration then cleans the stripped carbon so it can adsorb again. Doing them in the opposite order would bake the gold into the kiln or lose it in carbon fines, and the regenerated carbon would go back to the circuit still loaded.

On CIL4 the single column does the whole split AARL sequence: acid wash, rinse, caustic cyanide pre soak, elution, cooling, then carbon out to the regeneration kiln.

One quirk: the CN code exists in the numbering spec, but the equipment list tags the actual columns as PR, pressure vessels. The CIL4 column is F22-PR-411, and the existing columns are F65-PR-61 to 64.

f.q: Why are the elution columns tagged PR in the equipment list?
f.a:
PR is the pressure vessel code. Elution runs hot and the column is pressurised to stop the solution flashing to steam, so the columns are designed and registered as pressure vessels.

The equipment list shows F22-PR-411, the CIL4 elution and acid wash column, 1.9 m ID by 12 m high. On the concentrate side, F65-PR-61 and 62 are acid wash columns and F65-PR-63 and 64 are elution columns.

So if you search for CN and find nothing, try PR. The spec code and the as listed code differ.
f: What inspections does a pressure vessel need by law?
Why is the CIL4 column made of duplex stainless steel?
How is carbon loaded into and out of the column?

f.q: What is the order of steps in a split AARL elution?
f.a:
For CIL4 the sequence is: carbon transfer in, acid wash with dilute HCl, water rinse, pre soak with caustic and cyanide, elution with lean eluate, elution with scheme water, cooling with scheme water, then carbon out.

The split refers to using lean eluate from the previous cycle first, then fresh scheme water. That uses less water and heat than a straight AARL.

Pregnant eluate goes to the CIL4 eluate circulation tanks and, when they are full, diverts to the lean eluate tank. The design uses 5 bed volumes of eluate.
f: Why is the acid rinsed out before the caustic pre soak?
What makes lean eluate useful for the first strip?
How long does a full elution cycle take?

f.q: Why is the CIL4 column used for both acid wash and elution?
f.a:
One column doing both saves a carbon transfer, another vessel and its pipework, and reduces carbon breakage from moving it. The CIL4 column is SAF2205 duplex stainless, chosen to handle both hot acid and hot caustic cyanide in saline conditions.

The existing concentrate side circuits use separate acid wash and elution columns, F65-PR-61 and 62 for acid wash and 63 and 64 for elution.

The trade off is that one column has to finish both steps before the next batch, so the cycle is longer per column.
f: Why does moving carbon between vessels break it down?
What happens to acid wash waste from the column?
How many elutions per day can the CIL4 column handle?

Code 'CN'?.q: What handover symptom shows low gold elution efficiency?
Code 'CN'?.a:
Low elution efficiency means gold stays on the carbon. A handover might note high gold on stripped carbon samples, lower pregnant eluate grades than usual, or electrowinning producing less gold than the carbon loading suggests.

Typical causes include low elution temperature from a heater fault, weak caustic or cyanide in the pre soak, a poor acid wash leaving calcium scale, short cycle times, or flow channelling through the carbon bed.

The handover should give the batch number, what the heater and temperature trends did, and any step that was cut short or repeated.

f.q: Why does elution temperature matter so much?
f.a:
Gold cyanide comes off carbon much faster at high temperature. A drop of a few degrees can noticeably slow the strip, leaving more gold on the carbon at the end of the cycle.

On CIL4 the heat comes from an LPG fired thermal oil heater, F22-HT-411, with a burner management system. A temperature controller on the eluate line sets the firing.

If the heater trips or underfires, the cycle can run on but deliver poor stripping. Check the temperature trend first when efficiency drops.
f: Why does the elution heater use thermal oil?
What trips the elution heater burner?
How long does it take to reheat the column after a trip?

f.q: How is barren carbon gold measured?
f.a:
A sample of the stripped carbon is taken after elution and sent to the lab, where it is ashed and assayed for gold. The result, in g/t, shows how much gold the elution left behind.

Comparing it with the loaded carbon grade gives the elution efficiency for that batch. Sites usually track it every batch.

This is general practice. The sampling point and the site's acceptable barren grade are set by the metallurgy team.
f: What loaded carbon grade does CIL4 carbon reach?
Why is carbon ashed before assaying?
How quickly are carbon assays reported?

f.q: What happens to gold left on barren carbon?
f.a:
It goes with the carbon through regeneration and back to the adsorption tanks. Most is not lost outright, but it sits in the circuit inventory instead of being produced, and it takes up adsorption sites.

Some is lost. Carbon that breaks into fines in the kiln and screens ends up in tails with its gold. Higher barren grades also mean the last adsorption tanks have less capacity, which can raise soluble losses.

So poor elution costs production now and recovery later.
f: Why does carbon in the last tank need to be the cleanest?
How much fine carbon is lost per elution cycle?
Does the kiln drive off any gold from the carbon?

Code 'CN'?.q: What temperature and pressure does an elution column typically run under?
Code 'CN'?.a:
The reference does not give elution temperature or pressure setpoints. It says the column is pressurised to stop flashing and heated by an LPG fired heater with a temperature controller on the eluate line.

In general AARL elutions run at around 110 to 130 C. The column is held at a pressure above the boiling pressure for that temperature, typically a few hundred kPa, so the solution stays liquid.

For the CIL4 setpoints check the elution package documents or ask the elution operators. Treat any number you hear as an operating value that may change with tuning.

f.q: What is flashing and why is it a problem in the column?
f.a:
Flashing is hot water boiling to steam when the pressure drops below its saturation pressure. Inside a carbon column that creates steam pockets that push solution around the carbon instead of through it, so stripping becomes uneven.

It also causes noise, vibration and water hammer, and steam released at a vent or flange is a burn hazard.

Keeping the column pressurised is like pressurising a cooling circuit to raise its boiling point.
f: How is column pressure held during elution?
What happens if the column pressure relief valve lifts?
Why is the column cooled before carbon is discharged?

f.q: How is heat recovered in the CIL4 elution circuit?
f.a:
The instrument list refers to F22-HE-412, a CIL4 elution recovery heat exchanger on the pregnant eluate feed. In general such an exchanger uses hot solution leaving the column to preheat cooler solution going in, which cuts LPG use.

The main heat input comes from the LPG fired thermal oil heater F22-HT-411. Thermal oil carries heat to the eluate through an exchanger, so the burner never heats the cyanide solution directly.

Check the F22 P&ID for the exact flow arrangement.
f: Why heat eluate through thermal oil instead of directly?
What fouls elution heat exchangers over time?
How is the thermal oil system protected from overheating?

f.q: What safety controls apply to the LPG elution heater?
f.a:
The reference says the LPG fired heater has a burner management system. In general a BMS runs a purge before ignition, proves the flame with a detector, and shuts the fuel off on flame failure, high temperature, low air or other faults. It also locks out restart until the fault is cleared.

These are safety functions. They must never be bypassed or forced to keep the heater running.

Gas leaks, unusual smells or repeated flame failures should go straight to the control room and the area supervisor.
f: What is a purge cycle and why must it complete?
How is the LPG supply isolated in an emergency?
Who is licensed to work on gas fired equipment?

Code 'WD'?.q: Why is the weightometer considered the main throughput signal on the circuit?
Code 'WD'?.a:
A weightometer measures the actual mass of ore going into the mill, live and continuously. Everything downstream is slurry, where tonnage has to be inferred from flow and density, so the belt scale is the cleanest throughput number the plant has.

The control system leans on it. The reclaim feeders are controlled to the SAG feed weightometer or a mill weight setpoint, and the crusher discharge apron feeder to the stockpile feed weightometer. Metallurgical accounting starts with tonnes treated.

Totals are kept per 12 hour shift and per day from 5:00 am, with wet tonnes converted to dry using a moisture input.

f.q: How does a weightometer convert belt load into tonnes per hour?
f.a:
Load cells under a set of weigh idlers measure the weight of belt and ore passing over them. That gives load per metre of belt. A tachometer measures belt speed. Load per metre times speed gives mass per second, which the transmitter converts to t/h.

The equipment list describes the SAG mill feed weightometer F13-WD-403 as a three idler, four load cell, fully floating weigh frame with a chain calibration weight and automatic reeler. Its instruments include a tachometer and transmitter.

The empty belt weight is tared out during zero calibration.
f: Why are lead in and lead out idlers needed around a weigh frame?
What does the tachometer on a weightometer measure?
How often is a weightometer zero checked?

f.q: Why are weightometer tonnes converted from wet to dry?
f.a:
Ore on the belt carries moisture, sometimes several percent. Metallurgical accounting, recoveries and grades all work in dry tonnes, so wet tonnes overstate throughput.

The control philosophy converts wet to dry using a moisture input, normally from routine moisture samples. If that moisture value is out of date, dry tonnes are wrong even when the scale is perfect.

It is like correcting a gas flow to standard conditions before comparing it.
f: Who enters the moisture value used for dry tonnes?
How is ore moisture sampled from a conveyor?
Why does wet season ore change the moisture correction?

f.q: Why do shift totals start at 5:00 am?
f.a:
The control philosophy sets the reporting day and 12 hour shift totals to start at 5:00 am, so all daily production numbers line up with that boundary.

The reference does not explain the choice of time. On most sites it matches the shift change roster, so each shift's totals belong to one crew.

When comparing tonnages from different reports, check they use the same 5:00 am day. Calendar day reports will not match.
f: How are shift totals reconciled with the daily mass balance?
Where in PI can I find shift and daily totals?
What happens to totals during a weightometer fault?

Code 'WD'?.q: What handover note results from a weightometer reading drift or fault?
Code 'WD'?.a:
A drifting weightometer feeds wrong numbers into control and accounting. The handover would say which scale is suspect and what it disagrees with: mill power, mill weight, feeder speed or stockpile levels that don't add up.

If the SAG feed scale reads low, the reclaim feeders push more ore than intended and the mill can overload. If it reads high, the mill runs light and throughput is lost. Either way the shift tonnes are wrong.

Good practice is to note the evidence, whether control was switched to mill weight, and whether a calibration check has been requested.

f.q: How is a weightometer checked with a calibration chain?
f.a:
A chain of known mass per metre is laid over the weigh idlers while the belt runs empty. The weightometer should read the chain's equivalent tonnage. Any difference shows a span error to correct.

The SAG mill feed weightometer F13-WD-403 has a chain calibration weight with an automatic reeler, so the check can be done without manual handling. The stockpile feed weightometer F12-WD-402 has on board calibration weights instead.

A zero check with the empty belt comes first, then the span check.
f: How often should a weightometer span check be done?
What is the difference between a zero and a span error?
Why are material tests sometimes used instead of chains?

f.q: What can make a weightometer read high or low?
f.a:
Common causes are material build up on the weigh idlers or frame, misaligned idlers, belt tracking off centre, changes in belt tension, and a slipping or failed tachometer.

Damaged load cells, water ingress, wind on exposed belts and loose fasteners on the weigh frame also cause drift.

Most of these are mechanical, so a quick inspection and clean often fixes it before anyone touches the calibration.
f: Why does belt tension affect a weightometer reading?
How do you safely clean a weigh frame on a running belt?
What alarms does a weightometer transmitter raise?

f.q: Can the mill keep running if its feed weightometer fails?
f.a:
Yes, with care. The reclaim feeders can be controlled to a mill weight setpoint instead of a tonnage setpoint, which keeps the SAG load steady without a tonnage signal.

Accounting will need estimated tonnes for the period, which the metallurgists usually back calculate from other data.

Switching control mode is the CRO's call. The handover should record when the fault started and when it was fixed, so the shift totals can be corrected.
f: How is mill weight measured on the SAG mill?
How are tonnes estimated when a weightometer is down?
Does the expert system work without a feed tonnage signal?

Code 'WD'?.q: Where on the circuit would you expect the most critical weightometers?
Code 'WD'?.a:
The equipment list shows the key ones. On mill feed: F13-WD-403 for the new SAG mill feed and F19-WD-60 for the FIM SAG mill feed. Between them they give total plant throughput.

Upstream: F12-WD-402 on the new stockpile feed conveyor, which controls the crusher discharge apron feeder, F10-WD-92 on the existing coarse ore stockpile feed, and F15-WD-03 on the Mt Charlotte coarse ore conveyor.

Inside the circuit, F13-WD-405 weighs recycle conveyor 2, the pebble stream. Further on, F35-WD-18 weighs concentrate to the concentrate stockpile.

f.q: Why weigh the pebble recycle conveyor?
f.a:
Pebbles are the critical size material the SAG mill rejects through its ports and discharge screen. In the design they are 16.6 to 28 percent of new feed, about 375 t/h of SAG discharge screen oversize.

Weighing them tells you how hard the SAG is working on that ore, how loaded the pebble crushers are, and when pebble ports are wearing larger. Rising pebble tonnage often means harder ore or worn grates.

It also lets the pebble crusher feeders and bypass logic respond to actual load.
f: What happens when the pebble crushers are bypassed?
How does grate wear change pebble tonnage?
Why does harder ore produce more pebbles?

f.q: How are the two SAG feed weightometers used together?
f.a:
Each SAG mill has its own feed weightometer, F13-WD-403 for the new SAG and F19-WD-60 for the FIM SAG. Adding them gives the total fresh feed to the grinding circuit.

In the design the new SAG takes about 1,833 t/h and the FIM SAG about 1,313 t/h, giving 3,146 t/h nominal to the cyclones and flotation, or 3,494 t/h in the high case.

Each scale also controls its own mill's feeders, so a fault on one affects only that mill's feed control.
f: Why does the new SAG take more feed than the FIM SAG?
What happens to ball mill feed if one SAG stops?
How is total throughput reported per shift?

f.q: Why is concentrate weighed going to the stockpile?
f.a:
Concentrate beyond UFG capacity is filtered on the vacuum belt filters and stockpiled. That stockpile holds valuable gold, so the tonnes going to it must be known for accounting.

The belt weigher F35-WD-18 does that, with a 150 kg calibration billet. Moisture also matters because the stockpile has a transportable moisture limit, 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w in the design, if it has to be moved off site.

Without the weigher, gold sitting in concentrate stockpiles would be hard to reconcile.
f: What is a transportable moisture limit and why does it matter?
When would stockpiled concentrate be reclaimed?
How dry do the vacuum belt filters make the cake?

Code 'MG'?.q: Why is tramp metal such a risk to crushers and mills?
Code 'MG'?.a:
Steel does not break like rock. A rock bolt, piece of mesh or a ground engaging tool tooth jammed in a crusher can overload the machine and damage liners, the mainshaft or eccentric. It can also rip a conveyor belt from end to end or jam a transfer chute.

The pebble crushers are the most exposed. They run at a 7 mm closed side setting, and the pebble stream also carries broken grinding media out of the SAG mill. Their cone crushers have hydraulic tramp relief, but repeated hits still cause wear and downtime.

That is why there are tramp magnets on the crusher discharge and recycle conveyors, plus a metal detector on recycle conveyor 2 that bypasses the pebble crushers.

f.q: Why are pebble crushers more at risk than the primary crusher?
f.a:
The primary crusher works at a 165 mm open side setting, so a lot of steel passes through or is crushed with less harm. The pebble crushers work at about 7 mm closed side setting, so almost any steel is uncrushable.

The pebble stream also concentrates steel. Broken and worn SAG balls (125 mm when new) leave through the pebble ports with the pebbles, alongside any tramp that got through the primary magnets.

So the recycle conveyors carry the highest steel load where the crusher can least tolerate it.
f: What happens inside a cone crusher when tramp relief opens?
How do worn SAG balls get through the pebble ports?
Why does steel in pebbles increase as grates wear?

f.q: What does the metal detector on the recycle conveyor do?
f.a:
F13-MD-401 sits on recycle conveyor 2 as an under belt and over belt detector. The equipment list gives its sensitivity as a 25 mm ferrous sphere, 35 mm non ferrous and 45 mm stainless steel, with an aperture of 250 to 500 mm.

It catches metal the magnets cannot pull out, such as manganese steel and stainless. On detection, the pebble crusher circuit automatically bypasses so the metal goes back to the SAG mill instead of into a crusher.

Magnets remove what they can, and the detector protects the crushers from the rest.
f: How long does the pebble bypass stay open after a detection?
Why is stainless harder to detect than ordinary steel?
Where does bypassed pebble material go?

f.q: How does the pebble crusher bypass work?
f.a:
The design has an automatic bypass on metal detection. The bypass gate also opens if a pebble crusher feed bin reaches High with both feeders stopped, or reaches High High.

In bypass, pebbles skip the crushers and return to the SAG mill feed. That protects the crushers and keeps the SAG running, but the mill has to grind those pebbles itself, which can reduce throughput.

The feeders start on bin high level and stop on low level, so the bins act as buffers between bypass events.
f: What does long term pebble bypass do to SAG throughput?
How big are the pebble crusher feed bins?
Can the operator force the bypass from the control room?

Code 'MG'?.q: What handover flag indicates the tramp magnet missed some metal?
Code 'MG'?.a:
Signs that tramp metal got through include steel found in chutes or at a crusher, pebble crusher tramp relief events, more frequent metal detector bypasses, a belt rip detector trip, or a sudden power spike at a crusher.

The handover should say what was found and where, any damage, and whether the magnet was running and its self cleaning belt working. Also note if there were status or fault alarms from the magnet.

Remember that magnets only catch magnetic steel. Manganese steel, such as many digger teeth and liners, and stainless steel go straight past, which is why the metal detector is there.

f.q: Why can't a magnet catch manganese steel or stainless?
f.a:
Hadfield manganese steel and austenitic stainless steels have a crystal structure that is essentially non magnetic, so a tramp magnet barely pulls on them.

Unfortunately those are common in mining: ground engaging tool teeth, crusher and mill liner pieces, and some fittings. They are also tough, which is exactly what makes them dangerous in a crusher.

A metal detector senses any conductive metal through eddy currents, so it covers the gap the magnets leave.
f: Where does manganese steel tramp usually come from?
How does an eddy current metal detector work?
Do work hardened manganese parts become magnetic?

f.q: How do you check a tramp magnet is working properly?
f.a:
The instrument list shows the primary crusher 2 tramp magnet F12-MG-401 sending system ready, system running and system fault signals to the DCS, with a remote select. So the first check is its status on the OIS.

In the field, see whether the self cleaning belt is running and steel is being discharged. A drop in collected steel when the ore source has not changed can mean the magnet is weak.

Field strength tests and coil checks are for electricians and the vendor, under isolation.
f: What does the remote select signal on the magnet do?
How often is a tramp magnet's field strength tested?
Why does the magnet need a heat exchanger?

f.q: What does the belt rip detector do if steel slices the belt?
f.a:
A long piece of steel caught at a chute can slit a belt lengthwise. Rip detection, often sensor loops embedded in the belt or detectors under the loading point, senses the damage and trips the conveyor before the cut runs the full length of the belt.

The control philosophy lists belt rip detectors among the standard conveyor protections, with belt drift switches, under speed sensors and blocked chute switches. A rip trip also stops interlocked upstream equipment.

Restarting after a rip trip needs a belt inspection. Never just reset and run.
f: How long does a full belt replacement take?
What other trips protect a conveyor belt?
Who decides whether a damaged belt can keep running?

Code 'MG'?.q: How is captured tramp metal removed and disposed of from the magnet?
Code 'MG'?.a:
The new magnets clean themselves. The equipment list describes F12-MG-401 and 402 as 65 kW self cleaning cross belt magnets, each with a 7.5 kW belt drive. A short belt runs across the magnet face and carries captured steel sideways off the conveyor, where it drops clear.

The recycle conveyor magnets F13-MG-403 and 404 are the same type, smaller.

Where the steel lands, a bin or chute beside the conveyor, and how it is emptied and sent for scrap is not covered in the condensed reference. Ask the area operators or check the general arrangement drawing.

f.q: Why does the tramp magnet need its own heat exchanger?
f.a:
An electromagnet is a large coil carrying current, and it generates heat continuously while energised. Too much heat damages the coil insulation and weakens the magnet.

The equipment list shows the primary crusher 2 tramp magnets with a 4.4 kW heat exchanger drive, so the coil is cooled, typically by circulating oil through a cooler.

It is the same reason transformers have cooling fins and fans.
f: What happens if the magnet's cooling fails?
How hot does a tramp magnet coil normally run?
Why are some magnets permanent instead of electro?

f.q: Where does the captured steel drop to?
f.a:
A self cleaning cross belt magnet throws steel off the side of the conveyor, usually into a chute, bin or bunker set below the magnet's discharge end.

The exact arrangement for F12-MG-401 and 402 and the recycle conveyor magnets is not described in the condensed reference.

Check the general arrangement drawing, or ask the crusher operators how often the tramp bins are emptied and where the scrap goes.
f: How is a full tramp bin detected?
Is the captured steel inspected before it is scrapped?
Why record what kind of tramp metal is caught?

f.q: Is it safe to remove metal stuck to the magnet by hand?
f.a:
No, not while it is running or energised. The magnetic field can pull tools and steel violently, the cross belt and conveyor are moving parts, and the magnet is suspended over a running belt.

Removing jammed steel needs the magnet, its cross belt and the conveyor below it isolated under the site isolation procedure. Note that de energising an electromagnet releases whatever it was holding.

If steel is wedged in the cross belt, report it and let it be cleared under a permit.
f: Why does de energising a magnet create a falling object risk?
What isolations are needed to work on a tramp magnet?
Can a magnet affect pacemakers or electronics nearby?

The motor on pump F21-PU-001 is tagged h.q: Why does the motor share the parent equipment's number instead of its own?
The motor on pump F21-PU-001 is tagged h.a:
The motor exists to drive that piece of equipment, so giving it the same number keeps one unbroken thread. From the pump F21-PU-001 you can find its motor F21PU001, its VSD F21PU001-VS, its local control station F21PU001-LCS and its cables F21PU001-P1 and -C2.

That makes it easy to trace from a mechanical problem to the electrical supply and back.

Note that F21-PU-001 is the numbering spec's illustration. PU is not in the equipment code list, and real pumps use PP, PS or PW. So the final tails pump F23-PP-466 would have a motor F23PP466. Where one machine has two motors, the equipment list adds a letter, as in F13-MS-401A and 401B.

f.q: How are equipment items with two motors tagged?
f.a:
The equipment list adds a letter suffix to the parent tag. The new SAG mill F13-MS-401 has motors F13-MS-401A and F13-MS-401B. The ball mill F13-MB-401 has F13-MB-401A and B. The old FIM SAG F19-MS-61 has F19-MS-61A and B.

Applying the motor rule, the electrical tags would drop the dashes and keep the letter.

Check the electrical load list for the exact form used on any particular drive, as the mill motors come as part of the mill vendor packages.
f: How are the two mill motors kept in step electrically?
Do the paired motors share one VSD or have one each?
Where is the electrical load list kept?

f.q: Why does the example use PU when the code list has PP?
f.a:
The numbering spec uses F21-PU-001 to show how motor, VSD, LCS and cable tags are built. It is a format example, not a real pump.

The mechanical code list has no PU. Pumps are split by duty: PP process, PS sump, PW water, PT transfer, PV vacuum, plus codes like PB bore pump, PF fuel pump and PO oil pump. Real CIL4 pumps also start at 401, not 001.

So learn the rule from the example, but use the real equipment list when looking for an actual pump.
f: What is the difference between a PT and a PP pump?
Which pumps in CIL4 carry the PP code?
What does the code CP mean for a pump?

f.q: Do auxiliary motors like lube pumps get their own tags?
f.a:
Yes. Auxiliary drives are separate equipment items with their own codes. The equipment list shows the flotation tails thickener rake drive pump F17-PO-408 and rake lift pump F17-PO-409, rake drive oil cooling fan F17-FN-492, and underflow pump gearbox fans F17-FN-455 and 456.

Each then has its own motor tag by the same rule, and its own starter and cables.

That matters for isolations. Stopping a main drive does not necessarily stop its auxiliaries, which may run on to protect bearings or gearboxes.
f: Why do some auxiliaries keep running after the main drive stops?
How are auxiliary drives interlocked with their main drive?
What happens if a mill lube pump fails while running?

The motor on pump F21-PU-001 is tagged h.q: What confusion could arise between an equipment tag and its motor tag?
The motor on pump F21-PU-001 is tagged h.a:
The equipment tag with dashes, F21-PU-001, is the pump, a mechanical item. The motor tag without dashes, F21PU001, is the electrical item. They are easy to blur in conversation and on work orders.

A work order on the wrong one sends the wrong trade. More importantly, isolating for mechanical work on the pump means isolating the motor's supply, so the isolation list refers to the electrical items. Getting the tags confused can mean isolating a different drive.

Read the dashes carefully. Dashes mean the machine, no dashes means its motor.

f.q: Which tag goes on an electrical isolation for a pump?
f.a:
Electrical isolation is applied at the motor's supply, typically its starter or feeder in the switchboard, so the isolation point is identified by the motor and switchboard references derived from the motor tag. The equipment tag identifies what is being worked on.

Site isolation lists normally link the two, so the permit names the pump and lists the electrical isolation points for its motor, plus any mechanical isolations such as valves.

Always use the approved isolation list for that tag, and test before touch.
f: Why do slurry pumps need valve isolations as well as electrical?
What is an isolation list and who approves it?
How is a VSD driven motor proven dead before work?

f.q: Why might a motor be swapped while the pump keeps its tag?
f.a:
Motors are often changed out for rewinds or repairs and replaced with a spare of the same rating. The tag belongs to the position in the plant, not the individual motor, so the new motor takes the same tag.

The individual motor is tracked by serial number in the maintenance system, so its own history follows it to the workshop and back.

That is why the tag plate on the machine matters more than any number on the motor itself.
f: How are rotable spares tracked in a maintenance system?
What checks are done when a spare motor is fitted?
Why do motors need alignment checks after a change out?

f.q: What does the VS suffix tell an electrician?
f.a:
It means the drive has a variable speed drive. On this plant VSDs are on a field network, and the E-stop acts through the VSD's Safe Torque Off input.

For an electrician that means more than one hazard. VSDs hold stored energy in DC bus capacitors after the supply is removed, and the motor can be fed from the drive, not straight from the switchboard. Isolation and discharge times matter.

Safe Torque Off stops the motor making torque but does not isolate it. It is not an isolation point.
f: Why is Safe Torque Off not an electrical isolation?
How long do VSD capacitors take to discharge?
What does the VSD field network report to the DCS?

The motor on pump F21-PU-001 is tagged h.q: What suffix would you look for to find a pump's VSD or local control station?
The motor on pump F21-PU-001 is tagged h.a:
Look for -VS for the variable speed drive and -LCS for the local control station, so F21PU001-VS and F21PU001-LCS.

Other starter types use electrical codes too. The spec lists SS for soft starter, LRS for liquid resistance starter and EOL for electronic overload. Low voltage DOL starters on this plant use electronic overloads on Modbus TCP, and the IsaMills use liquid resistance starters on the vendor PLC.

So the suffix tells you how the drive is started and controlled before you walk to the switchroom.

f.q: When is a soft starter used instead of a VSD?
f.a:
A soft starter ramps the voltage up at start to limit inrush current and mechanical shock, then the motor runs at full speed. It suits fixed speed drives that need a gentle start, such as large fans, compressors and some pumps.

A VSD is chosen when the speed needs to change in operation, such as pumps on level or flow control and dosing pumps on flow. Small fixed speed drives just use DOL starters.

It is the difference between a slow opening valve and a control valve.
f: What does DOL starting do to the power supply?
Why are dosing pumps on VSDs rather than DOL?
How does an electronic overload protect a motor?

f.q: What is a liquid resistance starter on the IsaMills?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the IsaMill motors use liquid resistance starters on the vendor PLC. In general an LRS starts a large wound rotor motor by putting an adjustable resistance into the rotor circuit. That resistance is made by electrodes in an electrolyte tank.

As the electrodes move closer, resistance falls and the motor accelerates smoothly with high torque and limited current. Once it is up to speed the rotor is shorted out.

It gives a gentle, high torque start for a heavy load without a large VSD.
f: Why does an IsaMill need a high torque start?
What maintenance does a liquid resistance starter need?
What does the IsaMill vendor PLC control?

f.q: How does an E-stop act on a VSD-driven motor?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the E-stop on a VSD drive is wired to its Safe Torque Off input. Pressing it removes the drive's ability to produce torque, so the motor coasts or is stopped without the drive being powered down.

E-stops are critical interlocks. They trip in every mode, including Local, and cannot be bypassed.

An E-stop is for stopping in an emergency, not for isolating. Work still needs a proper isolation.
f: Why can't an E-stop be used as an isolation?
Where are E-stops located on a typical pump?
How is a drive reset after an E-stop?

Cable F21PU001-P1 vs F21PU001-C2. What's.q: Why are power and control cables tagged with different letters?
Cable F21PU001-P1 vs F21PU001-C2. What's.a:
Power and control cables carry different energy and serve different purposes, so they need different handling. A power cable carries the motor's full voltage and current, for example 415 V or 3.3 kV. A control cable carries start, stop and status signals, often at low voltage but sometimes from a separate supply.

Separate letters let the cable schedule and the field markers show at a glance which is which. That guides segregation in trays, testing, isolation and fault finding.

The spec's circuit types are P power, N neutral, I instrumentation, C control, E earth, D digital, COM communications, DC direct current power, F fire system and FO fibre optic.

f.q: Why must power and instrument cables be kept apart?
f.a:
Power cables, especially those feeding VSDs, create electromagnetic fields that induce noise in nearby signal cables. Instrument signals such as 4 to 20 mA loops are small, so noise shows up as jumpy or false readings.

Standards set minimum separation distances and often separate trays or barriers between power and instrumentation, plus screened cables earthed at one end.

It is like keeping a sensitive pressure tapping away from a pulsing pump discharge.
f: Why are VSD motor cables especially noisy?
What is a screened cable and how is it earthed?
How does noise show up on a DCS trend?

f.q: What do the numbers after the letter mean?
f.a:
They count cables of that type to the same equipment. F21PU001-P1 is the first power cable to that drive, and F21PU001-C2 is the second control cable.

A drive can have several control cables, for example one for start and stop and another for status or interlocks, and sometimes more than one power cable.

The cable schedule lists each one with its route, size and both end terminations.
f: Why would a drive need two power cables?
What information does a cable schedule hold?
How are spare cores in a cable recorded?

f.q: What cable types does the numbering spec list?
f.a:
The spec lists ten circuit types: P power, N neutral, I instrumentation, C control, E earth, D digital such as Ethernet, COM communications, DC direct current power, F fire system and FO fibre optic.

Each cable tag is the equipment base tag plus the type letter and a number, so the tag tells you both what the cable serves and what it carries.

Fire system cables are often special fire rated types that must keep working during a fire. That is one reason they get their own letter.
f: What makes a fire rated cable different?
Why is earth given its own circuit type?
Where are DC power cables used on the plant?

Cable F21PU001-P1 vs F21PU001-C2. What's.q: What handover issue arises from isolating the wrong cable type?
Cable F21PU001-P1 vs F21PU001-C2. What's.a:
The main danger is assuming a drive is dead because its power cable is isolated. Control cables can carry voltage from a separate source: the DCS or remote IO supply, which is on UPS, an interposing relay panel, or an interlock loop from another drive.

Disconnecting the wrong control cable can also trip or disable another drive's interlock, or leave a safety circuit open without anyone realising.

Isolate from the approved isolation list for that equipment, which covers all energy sources, and test before touch. Never pick a cable by appearance.

f.q: Why can a control cable stay live after the motor is isolated?
f.a:
Control circuits are often powered from somewhere other than the motor feeder. On this plant the DCS and remote IO are on UPS, so their field signals can stay energised even during a power outage.

Interlock wiring can also bring voltage in from other equipment, for example a permissive from a downstream drive. Isolating the motor's power removes the motor hazard but not those circuits.

That is why electricians test every conductor they will touch, not just the main power cores.
f: How long does the UPS keep remote IO powered?
What is an interposing relay and why is it used?
How are foreign voltages shown on electrical drawings?

f.q: Who is allowed to work on or disconnect cables on site?
f.a:
In Australia, electrical work, including disconnecting and reconnecting cables, must be done by a licensed electrician under state electrical safety laws. Instrument work may be done by licensed instrument electricians.

Others may not open terminal boxes, remove cable glands or disconnect conductors, even on isolated equipment.

If you need a cable checked or moved, raise it through the area supervisor so the right trade and permit are arranged.
f: What is the difference between an electrician and an instrument tech?
What permit is needed to open a junction box?
Why is electrical work licensed separately?

f.q: How are cable tags physically marked in the field?
f.a:
In general each cable carries a marker with its tag at both ends, near the glands, and sometimes at points along the route such as where it enters a building or changes tray.

Individual cores are also numbered at terminations so they match the wiring diagrams.

The marker style used on this project is not in the condensed reference. If a cable is unmarked or the marker disagrees with the drawing, treat it as unknown and report it.
f: What should you do if a cable marker is missing?
How are cores identified inside a multicore cable?
Why are cables marked at both ends?

Cable F21PU001-P1 vs F21PU001-C2. What's.q: What does the FO cable code indicate, and where might you find one?
Cable F21PU001-P1 vs F21PU001-C2. What's.a:
FO is fibre optic. These cables carry data as light through glass fibres, so they are used for networks: links between switchrooms, DCS field control stations and remote IO panels, CCTV and communications.

Fibre is immune to electrical noise, works over long distances and provides electrical isolation between buildings with different earth systems.

You will find them in cable trays between switchrooms and control rooms, terminating in breakout trays. The electrical code list has FOB for a Fobot, a fibre optic breakout tray.

f.q: Why use fibre optic instead of copper for plant networks?
f.a:
Fibre carries light, so it is unaffected by electromagnetic noise from large motors and VSDs, which would corrupt copper data links. It can run several kilometres without repeaters, carries a lot of data, and isolates buildings electrically.

That electrical isolation matters during faults and lightning strikes, when copper links between buildings can carry dangerous voltages.

The trade off is that fibre needs special tools and skills to terminate and repair.
f: What happens to a fibre link if the cable is crushed?
Why is lightning a risk to copper network cables?
How is a broken fibre located along its route?

f.q: What happens to the DCS if a fibre link is cut?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not describe the DCS network redundancy, so the exact effect is not covered. In general DCS networks use redundant paths, so losing one fibre shifts traffic to the other with an alarm.

If both paths to a remote IO panel were lost, the outputs there would go to their configured fail safe states, and the CRO would lose indication for that area.

Ask the control systems engineer how the Centum VP network is laid out here and how communication failures are handled.
f: What is a fail safe state for a DCS output?
How does the CRO see a communication failure on the OIS?
Who maintains the plant control network?

f.q: What is a FOBOT in the electrical code list?
f.a:
The electrical code list has FOB as Fobot, a fibre optic breakout tray. It is where a multi fibre cable is split out into individual fibres and terminated onto connectors or patch leads.

Fobots sit in switchrooms, control rooms and network cabinets. They are the fibre equivalent of a terminal strip.

Fibre ends carry invisible laser light that can damage eyes, so never look into an open connector.
f: Why is laser light from fibre connectors an eye hazard?
What is a patch panel compared with a Fobot?
How are fibre cores labelled inside a Fobot?

Decode instrument tag FIT13001..q: Why do all the instruments in one control loop share the same loop number?
Decode instrument tag FIT13001..a:
A shared loop number ties every part of one control loop together. The sensor, transmitter, controller and final element all carry it, so you can find the whole loop from any one piece. The card's example is PT13001, PIC13001 and PCV13001.

A real example from the instrument list is loop 13090 on the cyclone feed pump discharge: DX13090 is the nucleonic density source, DE13090 the density element and DIT13090 the density indicating transmitter.

It works like an assembly number on a drawing. Every part of the assembly carries it, so the parts never get separated in the paperwork.

f.q: What is the difference between an element and a transmitter?
f.a:
The element is the part that senses the process, such as a flow tube, an RTD or a nucleonic detector. The transmitter converts what the element senses into a signal the DCS can read, usually 4 to 20 mA or a digital bus signal.

On loop 13090, DE13090 is the density element (the detector), DIT13090 is the transmitter, and DX13090 is the radioactive source on the other side of the pipe.

Sometimes element and transmitter are one device, such as a magnetic flowmeter with an integral display.
