What does the X in DX mean in the letter code?
How is a transmitter calibrated in the field?

f.q: What does a loop drawing show?
f.a:
In general a loop drawing shows one loop end to end: the field instruments, the junction box and terminals they wire through, the cable and core numbers, the remote IO or marshalling cabinet, and the DCS input or output card and channel.

Instrument techs use it to fault find and to run loop checks during commissioning.

The condensed reference does not cover this project's loop drawings, so ask the instrument team where they are kept.
f: What is a loop check during commissioning?
What is a remote IO panel and where are they located?
How do I find which RIO panel an instrument connects to?

f.q: Can one loop number cover more than one transmitter?
f.a:
Sometimes. The instrument list shows letter suffixes for related devices on one loop, such as LIT18051B on the cleaner flotation cell. In other places duplicate measurements get separate loops: the primary cyclone feed hopper has two level transmitters, LIT13076 and LIT13086.

Soft tags, which are calculated values with no device, can share an analyser's equipment. The CIL4 cyanide analysers have AIC21243 to 21247.

When in doubt, search the loop number and the equipment tag in the instrument list together.
f: Why does the cyclone feed hopper have two level transmitters?
What is a soft tag in the DCS?
How does a controller choose between two transmitters?

Decode instrument tag FIT13001..q: What handover symptom indicates a flow transmitter is faulty?
Decode instrument tag FIT13001..a:
A faulty flow transmitter usually shows as a reading that does not fit the process: flatlined, stuck at zero while the pump is running, very noisy, negative, or disagreeing with pump speed and other flows.

On this plant most slurry flows use magnetic flowmeters. They misread when the pipe is not full, when the electrodes are coated with scale, or when earthing is poor.

The bigger effect is on control. A flow loop, or a ratio such as reagent g/t that depends on it, will drive its valve or pump the wrong way. The handover should name the tag, the symptom, whether the loop was put in manual, and whether an instrument tech has been called.

f.q: Why do magnetic flowmeters suit slurry service?
f.a:
A magnetic flowmeter has an open, unobstructed tube with a lining and electrodes. A magnetic field across the pipe generates a voltage in the moving conductive slurry, proportional to velocity. There is nothing in the flow to wear or block.

That suits abrasive, solids laden slurries. The final tails pumps, for example, each have a magnetic flow indicating transmitter, such as FIT23417 on F23-PP-466.

They only work on conductive fluids, which saline process water easily is.
f: Why must a magnetic flowmeter run full of liquid?
What lining materials are used in slurry flowmeters?
How does pipe wear affect flowmeter accuracy?

f.q: What should the CRO do with a loop whose transmitter has failed?
f.a:
The usual step is to put the controller in Manual and hold its output at a sensible value, so the valve or pump does not chase a bad signal. Loops can run in Manual, Automatic or Cascade, and the mode changes are bumpless.

Then log it, raise a work request and call the instrument tech. If the transmitter feeds an interlock, the CRO should check with the supervisor before taking any further steps.

Never force or bypass an interlock to work around a failed instrument.
f: What does bumpless transfer mean for a control loop?
Who can authorise bypassing a process interlock?
How is a failed transmitter shown on the OIS?

f.q: How does saline water affect magnetic flowmeters?
f.a:
Conductivity is not the problem. Saline water is very conductive, which suits a magnetic flowmeter. The issues are scaling and corrosion.

Scale building up on the electrodes or lining can insulate the electrodes and cause drifting or erratic readings. Chlorides can attack electrode materials if the wrong grade is chosen, which is why electrode material selection matters.

Regular inspection and cleaning during shutdowns usually keeps them reading well.
f: What electrode materials resist chloride corrosion?
How is scale removed from flowmeter electrodes?
Why can scaling make a flowmeter read high?

Decode instrument tag FIT13001..q: How would you find the related controller or valve for FIT13001?
Decode instrument tag FIT13001..a:
Use the loop number. The controller would be FIC13001 and the valve FV13001 or FCV13001, all on loop 13001. Search the loop number in the instrument list, or follow the loop on the area P&ID.

The instrument list also gives the equipment the instrument belongs to and the P&ID number, so you can open the right drawing.

FIT13001 is the card's teaching example. Real F13 loops have numbers such as 13090 for cyclone feed density and 13076 for cyclone feed hopper level, so check the instrument list for actual loops.

f.q: What does the C in FIC or LIC stand for?
f.a:
In the letter code table, a C in the second or third position means control or controller. So FIC is a flow indicating controller and LIC a level indicating controller.

As a first letter C means conductivity, a measured variable, not control. The position of the letter decides its meaning.

The same pattern applies elsewhere: I is indicating, T transmitter, V valve, H high and L low when they follow the first letter.
f: What does a first letter W measure on this plant?
What does the N mean as a later letter in a tag?
What is the difference between an FIC and an FC?

f.q: Why are some DCS tags soft tags with no field device?
f.a:
Soft tags are values calculated or received inside the control system rather than wired from one field instrument. The instrument list shows XI16172 as the particle size analyser's density reading and AIC21243 to 21247 as CIL4 cyanide analyser concentrations, all soft tags.

They come from vendor packages, analysers that report several values over a network, or calculations such as slurry mass flow from flow and density.

They are as useful as real tags but depend on the source being healthy.
f: How is slurry mass flow calculated in the DCS?
What happens to a soft tag if its analyser fails?
Which vendor packages send soft tags to the DCS?

f.q: What do the letters ZSO and ZSC mean on a valve?
f.a:
Z is position, S is switch, O is open and C is closed, using the letter code table. So ZSO is the open position switch and ZSC the closed position switch on a valve.

The control philosophy uses them for valve monitoring. A watchdog timer flags a valve that fails to reach open or closed in time, and having both switches on or both off at once is flagged as a fault.

In the instrument list these appear as limit switches, for example on the F17 thickener feed valve.
f: What happens when a valve fails to open within its timer?
Why is both limit switches on treated as a fault?
What is a valve open permissive?

What does the first letter 'D' in an ins.q: Why is slurry density such a critical measurement across this plant?
What does the first letter 'D' in an ins.a:
Density turns volume into tonnes, and many controls depend on tonnes. On this plant slurry mass flow is calculated from a magnetic flowmeter and a nucleonic density gauge, using an operator entered solids SG. Reagent ratios such as cyanide g/t on thickener underflow tonnes use that number.

Density also controls performance directly. Cyclone feed density sets the cut size, thickener underflow density (56 percent nominal) sets how much residence CIL4 gets, and leach feed density affects residence and reagent use.

Process water here is saline, SG 1.07, so density calculations need the right water SG as well.

f.q: How does a nucleonic density gauge work?
f.a:
A sealed radioactive source on one side of the pipe sends gamma radiation through the slurry to a detector on the other side. Denser slurry absorbs more radiation, so less reaches the detector, and the transmitter converts that to density.

In the instrument list these appear as a source (DX), element (DE) and transmitter (DIT), for example loop 13090 on the cyclone feed pump discharge.

Nothing touches the slurry, so there is no wear, which is why nucleonic gauges are standard on slurry lines.
f: Why does the source decay require periodic recalibration?
How is the gauge shuttered for maintenance?
Why does pipe wall wear affect a nucleonic reading?

f.q: Why does the operator enter a solids SG for mass flow?
f.a:
A density gauge measures slurry density only. To work out percent solids and dry tonnes, the calculation also needs the SG of the solids and of the liquid.

The control philosophy has the operator enter the solids SG. If the ore changes and the SG is not updated, the tonnes and percent solids are wrong even though the gauge is fine. Concentrate is very different from tails. The design concentrate SG from the cleaner is 3.93.

So a wrong SG entry can quietly bias reagent dosing and accounting.
f: Who updates the solids SG values in the DCS?
How is ore SG measured in the lab?
What SG is used for flotation tails solids?

f.q: How does density affect residence time in CIL4?
f.a:
Leach tanks have a fixed volume. Thicker slurry carries more solids per cubic metre, so the same tonnage takes up less volume and stays longer in the tanks.

CIL4 design residence is 12.8 hours total, already below the 14 hour ideal, with 3.2 hours in the two leach tanks. The thickener underflow is designed for 56 percent solids, range 50 to 62. A drop in density shortens residence and can cut extraction.

It is like pipe velocity: more flow volume through the same pipe means less time inside it.
f: Why can't CIL4 feed density simply be raised much higher?
What is the CIL4 design leach extraction?
How does short residence affect cyanide consumption?

What does the first letter 'D' in an ins.q: What handover note flags a density gauge reading incorrectly?
What does the first letter 'D' in an ins.a:
A bad density reading shows as a value that does not fit: flatlined, jumping, or disagreeing with manual density checks and with what the pumps and cyclones are doing.

Causes include scale or wear changing the pipe wall, air or froth in the line, a partly empty pipe, a source that needs recalibration for decay, or an electronics fault. The controls acting on it then go wrong: water addition, cyclone cut, thickener pump speed and reagent ratios.

The handover should name the tag, the evidence such as a manual sample comparison, whether loops were put in manual, and whether the instrument tech was called. Nucleonic gauges are radiation sources, so only licensed people work on them.

f.q: How is a density gauge checked against a manual sample?
f.a:
A slurry sample is cut from a sample point near the gauge and weighed in a known volume, often with a pulp density scale or by weighing a container of fixed volume. That gives slurry density to compare with the gauge.

Several samples over a range of conditions are better than one, because a single grab can be unrepresentative.

This is general practice. Where sample points exist and who does the check are set by the site metallurgy and instrument teams.
f: What is a pulp density scale and how is it used?
Why can a single grab sample mislead you?
How often are density gauges checked on this plant?

f.q: What radiation safety rules apply around nucleonic gauges?
f.a:
In general nucleonic gauges are licensed sources under a site radiation management plan with a radiation safety officer. The source is shielded and the beam only runs across the pipe, so normal nearby work is safe.

Before anyone works on the pipe section or the gauge, the source shutter is closed and locked by an authorised person, and the area may be surveyed.

Never remove, cut or weld near a gauge without that clearance. Ask the site radiation safety officer for the local rules.
f: Who is the radiation safety officer on site?
What signs mark a nucleonic gauge location?
What happens if a gauge is damaged in an incident?

f.q: Why does froth or air in a pipe upset a density reading?
f.a:
A nucleonic gauge measures the bulk density of whatever is in the beam path. Air bubbles or froth lower that density, so the gauge reads low even if the solids content of the slurry has not changed.

That is common on flotation concentrate lines. The final concentrate pumps are froth pumps and carry a density gauge, DIT18027, so readings there need care.

The control effect is a falsely low density, which could trigger less water addition or a wrong mass flow.
f: How do froth pumps cope with air in the slurry?
Where should a density gauge be placed to avoid air?
Why do flotation concentrates carry so much air?

What does the first letter 'D' in an ins.q: Where would you expect the most process critical density instruments?
What does the first letter 'D' in an ins.a:
The instrument list shows nucleonic density gauges at the points that drive control and accounting. These include the cyclone feed pump discharge (DIT13090), the flotation tails thickener underflow (DIT17121), the final concentrate pumps (DIT18027) and the cleaner-scavenger tails pumps (DIT18237).

The UFG circuit has them on the mill feed and discharge pumps, such as DIT28033 and DIT28234. Each final tails pump has its own, such as DIT23418 on F23-PP-466.

Of these, cyclone feed and thickener underflow most directly affect performance: grind and CIL4 residence.

f.q: Why does each final tails pump have its own density gauge?
f.a:
The design gives each tailings line a flowmeter, density meter and pressure measurement. Density on each line shows the solids being pumped. Rising density warns of settling and blockage risk, and with flow it gives the tonnes sent to the TSF.

Together with the second flowmeter near the deposition end, it also supports leak detection.

The pumps are F23-PP-466 to 469, with density transmitters DIT23418, DIT23431, DIT23442 and DIT23453.
f: What density is too high for safe tailings pumping?
How is tailings tonnage to the TSF reported?
What triggers a tailings line flush?

f.q: How is UFG feed density used in the IsaMill controls?
f.a:
The UFG feed pump runs on flow control, with density and mass flow measured. Feed hopper water addition holds feed solids, or adds water to cool the mill if the discharge goes above 60 C.

Feed density matters because IsaMill grinding efficiency depends on the slurry being in the right range. Too thin wastes energy and too thick overloads the mill.

The UFG 3 discharge hopper density is also controlled by water addition, swapping to level control if the level runs low.
f: Why does the IsaMill need cooling above 60 C?
What is the IsaMill product size target?
How is grinding media added to an IsaMill?

f.q: Why measure density on the final concentrate going to the thickener?
f.a:
The final concentrate flow, combined with density, gives the tonnes of concentrate produced. That is a key metallurgical accounting number and sets the load on the concentrate thickener, UFG mills and concentrate leach.

The design concentrate rate is about 75 to 78 t/h at nominal grade, up to about 104 to 107 t/h at design grade.

Because that line carries froth, the reading needs checking against samples, as air in the line pulls the apparent density down.
f: What happens when concentrate exceeds UFG capacity?
How is the concentrate thickener feed diluted?
Why does higher head grade sulphur raise concentrate tonnes?

First letter 'L' in an instrument tag?.q: Why does level control drive so many pump speed loops on this plant?
First letter 'L' in an instrument tag?.a:
Most of the plant is slurry moving between hoppers, sumps and tanks, and pumps can't store anything. The simplest way to keep flows balanced is to hold each vessel's level steady and let the pump speed follow. If level rises, the pump speeds up; if it falls, the pump slows.

That way each pump automatically matches whatever flow arrives from upstream without anyone setting a flow. Examples include the primary cyclone feed hopper, where level cascades to cyclone pressure and pump speed, and the dual hopper scheme where loop A sets pump speed and loop B adds water to keep minimum line velocity.

Mechanically it is like a float valve on a header tank: level is the signal that balances in and out.

f.q: Why use a level to pressure cascade on the cyclone feed hopper?
f.a:
The cyclones need a steady feed pressure to classify well, while the hopper level has to absorb changes in mill discharge. A cascade lets the hopper level controller set the pressure setpoint, and a faster pressure loop drives the pump speed.

So pressure stays stable minute to minute, and only drifts slowly as the level controller asks for more or less throughput. Rising pressure also opens more cyclones through the knife gate valve logic.

The design adds Fast and Slow level tuning, so the operator can choose between soaking up surges and holding level tightly.
f: When would the operator choose fast level tuning?
Why does the cyclone feed hopper have two level transmitters?
What happens to cyclone pressure if the hopper runs low?

f.q: What does loop B add in a dual hopper level scheme?
f.a:
Loop A controls pump speed to hold a higher level setpoint. If inflow drops, the pump slows, but below a certain speed the line velocity would fall low enough for solids to settle.

Loop B watches a lower level setpoint and adds water when the level falls to it. The extra water keeps the level up so the pump can keep running at a safe speed.

It trades a little slurry dilution for keeping the pipe from sanding up, much like a minimum flow line protects a pump.
f: What water source is used for hopper level makeup?
How does extra dilution water affect downstream density?
Which hoppers on this plant use the dual level scheme?

f.q: How are sump levels detected for the sump pumps?
f.a:
Many sump pumps use simple level switches rather than a continuous transmitter. The instrument list shows LSH13064, a float level switch high on the coarse ore stockpile 2 sump pump F13-PS-402.

The control philosophy starts sump pumps on high level and runs them until the high clears plus a run on time, or until low level.

Float switches are cheap and robust but can stick or foul with slurry, which is a common reason a sump pump fails to start.
f: How is a stuck float switch detected?
Why use a run on timer instead of a low level switch?
What sump alarms come up on the OIS?

First letter 'L' in an instrument tag?.q: What handover flag indicates a level control loop is hunting or unstable?
First letter 'L' in an instrument tag?.a:
A hunting level loop shows on the trend as a level swinging up and down around setpoint, with the pump speed or valve output swinging with it. The handover would mention it if the swings were large or regular, or caused alarms or trips.

Typical causes are controller tuning that is too aggressive, a sticky control valve, a noisy level signal from turbulence or froth, or interaction with another loop such as a cascade or a downstream controller.

The note should name the loop, the period and size of the swings, and whether the loop was put in manual or the tuning changed. Tuning changes are for the control systems engineer, not a quick fix on shift.

f.q: What makes a control valve cause a loop to hunt?
f.a:
Stiction, or static friction, makes a valve stick and then jump. The controller keeps pushing until the valve breaks free, overshoots, then sticks again the other way. The trend shows a characteristic sawtooth on the output and a square wave on the process variable.

Worn actuators, tight packing and undersized positioners cause it. Slurry valves are prone to it because of wear and solids.

The valve watchdog timers in the control philosophy flag valves that fail to reach position, which can point to the same problem.
f: How does a valve positioner reduce stiction?
Why are slurry valves more prone to sticking?
What does a sawtooth controller output trend mean?

f.q: How does a noisy level signal upset a pump speed loop?
f.a:
If the level reading jumps around from turbulence, froth or splashing, the controller sees errors that are not real and drives the pump speed up and down to chase them. That wears the drive and pump, and can cause swings downstream.

Fixes include filtering the signal, relocating the transmitter or using a stilling well, and softer tuning. The cyclone feed hopper has two level transmitters, LIT13076 and LIT13086, which gives a cross check.

Think of it like a governor responding to a faulty speed sensor.
f: What is a stilling well and when is it used?
How much filtering is too much on a level signal?
Why do froth and air upset radar level readings?

f.q: Who is allowed to change controller tuning on site?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not set out who can change tuning. In general, controller tuning sits with the control systems or process control engineer, with changes recorded under a management of change process.

Operators normally adjust setpoints and switch loops between Manual, Automatic and Cascade, but not the tuning constants.

If a loop keeps hunting, log it and raise it with the control systems engineer rather than adjusting it on shift.
f: What is management of change for control settings?
How are tuning changes recorded in the DCS?
What do P, I and D do in a controller?

First letter 'L' in an instrument tag?.q: What equipment usually follows a tank's level transmitter in the loop?
First letter 'L' in an instrument tag?.a:
A level controller, LIC, takes the transmitter signal and compares it with setpoint. Its output then goes to whatever can change the level, usually a pump VSD on the outlet, a control valve (LCV or LV), or a water addition valve.

On flotation cells it is two dart valves on split range level control. On the cyclone feed hopper the level controller sets the pressure loop setpoint, which then drives the pump speed. In a dual hopper scheme a second level loop drives water addition.

So follow the loop number: LT, LIC and the final element all share it on the P&ID.

f.q: What is the difference between controlling level on inflow or outflow?
f.a:
Most plant tanks control level with the outflow, the pump or valve leaving the vessel, because the inflow comes from upstream and is not theirs to set. Speeding up the outlet pump when level rises balances the flow.

Some vessels control level on inflow instead, such as water makeup to a tank or water addition in the dual hopper scheme.

Picking the wrong one causes fights between loops. Each flow should have one controller in charge.
f: What happens when two loops fight over one flow?
Which tanks on this plant control level on water makeup?
How do process water tank pumps handle varying demand?

f.q: Why do flotation cells use dart valves instead of pumps for level?
f.a:
Tank cells in a bank discharge by gravity from one cell to the next, so their outlet is a valve, not a pump. A dart valve is a plug in a seat that rises to let more slurry out. It handles coarse, abrasive slurry well and gives a wide range.

Each cell has two dart valves on split range control, in series or parallel, to cover the full flow range smoothly.

The level setpoint sets froth depth, which the expert system adjusts.
f: Why does each flotation cell have two dart valves?
How does froth depth change concentrate grade?
What happens if a dart valve sticks open?

f.q: Where does a level controller get its setpoint from?
f.a:
It depends on the loop mode. In Automatic the operator sets it on the OIS. In Cascade another controller or system sets it, for example the flotation expert system setting cell levels, or a master loop in a cascade.

Loops can run in Manual, Automatic or Cascade, and mode changes are bumpless, so switching does not jolt the output.

The faceplate on the OIS shows the mode and where the setpoint comes from.
f: What does the flotation expert system adjust besides level?
How does bumpless transfer work when switching modes?
What are PV, SV and CV on a DCS faceplate?

First letter 'A' (e.g. AE, AIT)?.q: Why is online analysis needed in addition to lab assays?
First letter 'A' (e.g. AE, AIT)?.a:
Lab assays are accurate but slow. A sample has to be cut, prepared and analysed, and the result arrives hours later. Online analysers give readings every few minutes, fast enough to control the process while it is happening.

On this plant that includes pH and dissolved oxygen in the CIL4 leach tanks (such as AIT21061 on tank 1), the CIL4 cyanide analysers that trim cyanide dosing, the onstream analyser measuring Au and Fe on flotation streams, particle size analysers, HCN gas monitors, and the WAD cyanide analyser on decant water.

The lab still matters. Its assays calibrate the online instruments and provide the official accounting numbers.

f.q: How does the onstream analyser measure flotation streams?
f.a:
The OSA measures gold and iron, and infers sulphur from iron. Multiplexers, F16-SA-420 and 421 with six streams each, feed slurry from different streams to the analyser in turn, and de multiplexers send it back.

The design stream list includes flotation feed, rougher 1 concentrate, rougher 2 and 3 concentrate, scavenger concentrate and tails, cleaner feed, cleaner-scavenger tails, final concentrate and final tails.

The flotation expert system uses those results, plus froth and launder cameras, to set level, air and reagents.
f: How long does the OSA take to cycle through all streams?
Why is sulphur inferred from iron instead of measured?
What happens to flotation control if the OSA is down?

f.q: Why is lab assay still needed if analysers are online?
f.a:
Online analysers drift and need checking against a reference. Lab assays on the same samples calibrate them. The lab also measures things online instruments cannot, such as gold on carbon, fire assays on solids and full chemical analyses.

For metallurgical accounting, the official numbers usually come from lab assays on composite samples from the plant's samplers.

So online gives speed for control and the lab gives accuracy for accounting.
f: How often are online analysers calibrated to the lab?
What is a fire assay and why is it the reference?
Which samples feed the daily metallurgical balance?

f.q: What does the WAD cyanide analyser on decant water control?
f.a:
TSF decant water returns to the plant as cyanide water. The design treats it with hydrogen peroxide through inline mixers on the three decant water lines.

An online WAD cyanide analyser, with flowmeters, controls the peroxide dose so residual WAD cyanide stays near the design target of about 1.5.

Without that analyser, peroxide would have to be dosed blind, wasting reagent or letting cyanide through.
f: What is the difference between WAD and free cyanide?
Why does peroxide destroy cyanide?
Where is the treated decant water used?

First letter 'A' (e.g. AE, AIT)?.q: What handover symptom points to a faulty pH or cyanide analyser?
First letter 'A' (e.g. AE, AIT)?.a:
A faulty analyser usually shows as a reading that does not fit the process. It might be flatlined, drifting away from lab results, stuck at a limit, or changing when nothing else changes.

The dosing it controls then goes wrong. On CIL4, the pH controller on tank 1 opens the milk of lime valve, so a pH probe reading falsely low causes lime overdosing. The cyanide analysers trim cyanide dosing, so a bad reading over or under doses cyanide.

A handover should name the analyser tag, compare it with the latest lab or manual check, and note whether the loop was switched to manual or the backup used. CIL4 tank 2 is the pH backup for tank 1.

f.q: Why does a pH probe drift over time?
f.a:
pH probes use a glass membrane and a reference electrode. Slurry coats the glass, lime scale builds up, and the reference junction slowly gets contaminated, so the reading drifts and responds more slowly.

Regular cleaning and calibration against buffer solutions keeps them honest. In harsh slurry service probes are often cleaned automatically and replaced on a schedule.

The CIL4 leach tanks have pH measurement combined with DO in one analyser transmitter, and the Carbon Scout also samples leach tank pH, which gives a cross check.
f: How often are pH probes calibrated on this plant?
What does a slow responding pH probe look like on a trend?
Why is pH backup measured on CIL4 tank 2?

f.q: What does the Carbon Scout check besides carbon concentration?
f.a:
The Gekko Carbon Scout MK6 samples all CIL4 adsorption tanks for carbon in g/L. On the leach tanks it measures dissolved oxygen, pH and solids.

That gives an independent check on the fixed DO and pH analysers and on tank density. If the Carbon Scout and a fixed analyser disagree, one of them needs looking at.

It is a sampling system, so its results come at intervals rather than continuously.
f: Why does carbon concentration vary between CIL4 tanks?
How does the Carbon Scout take its samples?
What CIL4 carbon concentration is the design target?

f.q: What happens to cyanide control if the CIL4 analyser fails?
f.a:
The design sets CIL4 cyanide flow at the front end either by operator setpoint or as g/t on thickener underflow tonnes, trimmed by the cyanide analyser on tanks 1 and 2. If the analyser fails, the trim is lost but the base ratio control can keep dosing.

The operator would normally hold the ratio at a sensible value and rely on lab titrations until the analyser is fixed.

Ask the metallurgist what cyanide level to target in the meantime, as both underdosing and overdosing cost money and recovery.
f: How is free cyanide titrated in the lab?
Why are there extra cyanide addition points on CIL4 tanks?
What does too much cyanide in CIL4 tails cost?

First letter 'A' (e.g. AE, AIT)?.q: Where on the flowsheet would you expect the most analysis instruments?
First letter 'A' (e.g. AE, AIT)?.a:
Analysis instruments cluster where chemistry is controlled. The CIL4 leach tanks have DO and pH analysers (AIT21061 on tank 1, AIT21101 on tank 2), cyanide analysers, and three HCN gas monitors (AIT21211 to 21213) along the tank row.

Flotation has the onstream analyser covering nine streams and a particle size analyser on flotation feed. The UFG circuit has an online particle size analyser. The decant water has a WAD cyanide analyser.

The concentrate leach CIL2 and CIL3 also run on pH, cyanide and oxygen control, so expect analysers there too. Search the instrument list for AIT or AE in each area to see them all.

f.q: Why does CIL4 need dissolved oxygen measurement?
f.a:
Gold dissolution in cyanide needs oxygen. If DO is low, leaching slows even with plenty of cyanide. CIL4 gets oxygen from VSD injection pumps with flow control valves on both leach tanks, plus side lances on the leach tanks and first two adsorption tanks.

DO analysers alarm on high and low. Low means poor leaching; high can mean wasted oxygen.

Oxygen comes from the new PSA oxygen plant with liquid oxygen backup, so DO is also a check that supply is healthy.
f: How does the oxygen injection pump add oxygen to slurry?
What DO level is targeted in a leach tank?
What happens to CIL4 if the oxygen plant trips?

f.q: Why is particle size measured online after UFG?
f.a:
The UFG circuit grinds concentrate to a design P80 of about 9 um (9 to 12) so the gold locked in sulphides is exposed for leaching. An online particle size analyser shows whether the mills are hitting that target.

The IsaMills' media addition holds a power draw setpoint, and size data tells the operators whether that power is giving the right grind.

Too coarse and leach recovery drops. Too fine wastes energy, at a design specific energy of 116.5 kWh/t.
f: How does an IsaMill grind so fine?
Why does finer grinding improve concentrate leach recovery?
What controls the IsaMill power draw?

f.q: What does an HCN gas monitor do when it alarms?
f.a:
The CIL4 control philosophy specifies an HCN gas monitor with a beacon and siren. When the gas level crosses its alarm point, the beacon flashes and the siren sounds locally, and the alarm goes to the control room.

The local warning tells people nearby to move away upwind and follow the site gas response procedure.

The alarm settings and response steps are in the site procedures, not the condensed reference. Make sure you know them before working near the leach tanks.
f: What should you do if an HCN alarm sounds near you?
Why does lower leach pH increase HCN risk?
Where are personal HCN monitors required on site?

What does 'LAH' mean on a P&ID?.q: Why are alarms tiered, such as LAH versus LAHH, instead of one alarm?
What does 'LAH' mean on a P&ID?.a:
Tiers give time to act before something goes wrong. The plant follows ISA-18.2, with analogue alarms at LL, L, H and HH. An LAH is an early warning that the level is higher than normal. An LAHH means it is close to a limit and often comes with a trip or interlock.

With one alarm only, you either get warned too late to fix things or warned so early that it fires constantly and gets ignored.

Alarms also carry priorities: Logging, Low, High or Urgent. They are masked when the equipment is not running, so stopped plant does not flood the screen. It is like a two stage pressure warning on a boiler: first a warning, then the cut out.

f.q: What do the alarm priorities Logging, Low, High and Urgent mean?
f.a:
They rank how quickly the operator needs to act. A Logging alarm is recorded but does not demand attention. Low means attend when practical, High means act soon, and Urgent means act now because harm, damage or major loss is close.

ISA-18.2 expects each alarm to have a defined cause, consequence and response, and to be prioritised by consequence and time to respond.

The exact priority of each alarm is set in the site alarm database, which the control systems engineer maintains.
f: What is an alarm flood and how is it prevented?
Who decides an alarm's priority?
What is alarm rationalisation under ISA-18.2?

f.q: Why are alarms masked when equipment is not running?
f.a:
A stopped pump will show low flow, low pressure and low current, all of which would alarm if they were not masked. Those alarms tell the operator nothing useful and bury the alarms that matter.

The control philosophy masks alarms when their equipment is not running, so the alarm list shows only real problems.

It is like a car not warning about low oil pressure while the engine is switched off.
f: How does the DCS know a drive is running for masking?
Can masking hide a real fault on standby equipment?
What is a shelved alarm compared with a masked one?

f.q: What is the difference between an alarm and an interlock?
f.a:
An alarm tells the operator something needs attention and leaves the decision to them. An interlock acts automatically, tripping a drive or blocking a start, without waiting for anyone.

Often they work as a pair. An H alarm warns, then an HH trips. Interlocks come in three kinds here: critical (E-stops, pull wires, protection relays, never bypassed), process (trip in Auto and Manual, bypassable only by named users) and start permissives (block starting only).

First out detection records which trip happened first.
f: Who can bypass a process interlock and how?
What does first out detection show after a trip?
Why can a start permissive not trip a running drive?

What does 'LAH' mean on a P&ID?.q: What would trigger an LAH alarm during a shift?
What does 'LAH' mean on a P&ID?.a:
An LAH comes up when a level goes above its high alarm setpoint. Common causes on shift are a pump that has slowed, tripped or lost capacity, a blocked outlet or valve, more flow arriving than usual, or water addition left open.

Level controllers in Manual, or a controller that has reached full output, often lead to it. So can upstream changes, such as more mill throughput or a flotation upset sending more slurry to a hopper.

Instrument faults also cause it. A level transmitter coated with build up or reading falsely high will raise the alarm with nothing actually wrong. Check the trend before reacting.

f.q: How do you tell a real high level from a faulty transmitter?
f.a:
Look for corroborating signs. Is the pump speed or valve output at maximum? Did the inflow increase? Does a second transmitter, where there is one, agree? On the cyclone feed hopper there are two, LIT13076 and LIT13086.

In the field, a sight glass, a visual check or a level switch confirms it. A reading that jumped instantly or flatlined is more likely an instrument than a real rise.

If in doubt, treat it as real until proven otherwise.
f: What causes radar level transmitters to read falsely?
Why do some vessels have a separate HH level switch?
How is a level transmitter checked in the field?

f.q: What happens if a high level alarm is ignored?
f.a:
The level keeps rising to HH, which on many vessels trips equipment through a process interlock, for example stopping the upstream feed. If it keeps going, the vessel overflows, causing spillage, possible damage and lost production.

For example, the stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to the stockpile high high switch and level alarm, and the crusher apron feeder to the head chute high high.

So an LAH is the cheap warning. Ignoring it usually turns it into a trip and a clean up.
f: What gets tripped when a hopper reaches high high level?
Why are some HH trips hardwired switches?
How are alarm responses documented for operators?

f.q: Why might an LAH come up after a pump changeover?
f.a:
During a duty to standby changeover the outgoing pump stops before the incoming one is fully running and up to flow. The level rises in that gap. If the standby is slow to start, for example waiting on gland water flow to be proven, it can easily cross the high alarm.

Pumps here start through sequences, with gland water valves opened and proven first, and dump valves draining the stopped pump.

A brief LAH during a changeover is expected; one that keeps climbing means the new pump is not delivering.
f: How long does a slurry pump start sequence take?
Why must gland water be proven before starting?
What happens if the standby pump fails to start?

What does 'LAH' mean on a P&ID?.q: What operator action typically follows an LAH alarm?
What does 'LAH' mean on a P&ID?.a:
First acknowledge the alarm and look at the trend: how fast the level is rising and why. Then act on the cause. That might mean checking the outlet pump speed and status, starting a standby, freeing a blocked valve, reducing upstream feed, or closing water addition.

If the cause is not obvious, call a field operator to check the vessel and pump. Confirm in the field whether it is a real high level or an instrument fault.

Record what happened in the shift log. Never silence or bypass the alarm or its interlock to keep running. The specific response for each alarm should be in the site alarm response guide.

f.q: What does acknowledging an alarm actually do?
f.a:
Acknowledging tells the system that an operator has seen the alarm. It stops the flashing and the audible signal, but the alarm stays active on the list until the condition clears.

It does not fix anything or change any setting. Acknowledging without acting is a common trap during busy periods.

Under ISA-18.2 good practice, every alarm should have a defined response so acknowledging leads straight to action.
f: What is the difference between an active and a cleared alarm?
How are standing alarms managed on a DCS?
What is an alarm response guide?

f.q: When should a field operator be sent to check a level?
f.a:
Whenever the trend does not make sense, the cause is not visible on the OIS, or the level keeps rising after the obvious fixes. A field check confirms the actual level, whether the pump is running and pumping, and whether anything is blocked or overflowing.

Field checks matter most when the operator suspects an instrument fault, because acting on a false reading can cause a real problem.

The field operator should report back by radio using the full tag of what they checked.
f: What should a field operator check at a hopper?
How is a hopper overflow cleaned up safely?
Why use full tags when reporting by radio?

f.q: Why log alarms in the shift handover?
f.a:
A single LAH that was handled is not news, but repeated alarms show a trend. A pump losing capacity, an instrument drifting or a valve sticking often show up first as recurring alarms.

Logging them lets the next shift spot a pattern and lets maintenance plan work before it becomes a breakdown.

The PI historian keeps the alarm and trend data, so you can check the history rather than relying on memory.
f: How do I find alarm history in the PI historian?
What is a bad actor alarm?
Who reviews alarm statistics on site?

Electrical code 'SW' on the Growth Proje.q: Why are MCCs referred to as switchboards in this numbering system?
Electrical code 'SW' on the Growth Proje.a:
The numbering spec says MCCs are referred to as switchboards and uses one code, SW, for HV and LV switchboards and MCCs. MCC still appears in the electrical code list, but only with a note pointing to SW.

One code keeps tagging simple. An MCC is just a type of switchboard that holds motor starters, and on modern plants the line between an MCC and a distribution board is blurred anyway. One code avoids arguments over which label applies.

So if you hear 'MCC' on site, look for an SW tag in the documents.

f.q: What sits inside a typical LV switchboard on this plant?
f.a:
The control philosophy says LV direct on line starters use electronic overloads communicating on Modbus TCP, and VSDs sit on a field network. So an LV switchboard holds incomers, feeders, DOL starters with electronic overload relays, and possibly VSDs and soft starters.

The electrical code list also includes circuit breakers (CB), protection relays (IED), motor protection relays (MPR) and power quality meters (PQM), which are typical switchboard parts.

The SLD displays on the OIS run from the 33 kV incomers down to the 415 V MCC incomers.
f: What does an electronic overload report over Modbus?
Why are VSDs on a separate field network?
What is an IED in the electrical code list?

f.q: What voltage levels do the switchboards cover?
f.a:
The SLDs run from 33 kV incomers down to 415 V MCC incomers. In between, large motors run at 3.3 kV, such as the cyclone feed pump F13-PP-401, so there are HV switchboards at 33 kV and 3.3 kV and LV switchboards at 415 V.

Transformers (TR) step the voltage down between levels.

The SW code covers all of them, so the voltage comes from the switchboard's description, not its code.
f: Which motors on this plant run at 3.3 kV?
Where do the 33 kV incomers come from?
What is a ring main unit in the electrical list?

f.q: Can an MCC tag still appear in older documents?
f.a:
Yes. The code list keeps MCC with a note that MCCs are referred to as switchboards, so older or vendor documents may still say MCC. Existing plant areas may also have legacy MCC labels in the field.

Treat MCC and SW as the same kind of item and confirm the exact board by its full tag.

If a legacy label and a new tag disagree, check with the site electrical team before relying on either.
f: How are legacy electrical tags handled in brownfield areas?
Who keeps the electrical drawings up to date?
What does SUB mean in the electrical code list?

Electrical code 'SW' on the Growth Proje.q: What handover note flags a switchboard trip or fault?
Electrical code 'SW' on the Growth Proje.a:
A switchboard trip can stop many drives at once, so the handover should be specific. It should name the switchboard tag, whether the incomer or an outgoing feeder tripped, which protection operated if known, which drives were lost, and what first out showed.

It should also say whether the board was reset, by whom, and whether the cause was found. Repeated trips on the same board need electrical investigation, not just resets.

Remember the knock on effects. Process drives on that board will have tripped their interlocked upstream equipment, so check what still needs restarting in sequence.

f.q: Who is allowed to reset a switchboard protection trip?
f.a:
Protection trips on switchboards are reset by authorised electrical staff, normally after the cause has been checked. Resetting onto a fault can cause equipment damage or an arc flash.

The CRO can see the trip on the OIS through the SLD displays and the electrical status signals, but should call the shift electrician rather than reset it.

Your site will have its own electrical safety rules. The condensed reference does not give the authorisation list.
f: What is an arc flash and why is it so dangerous?
How does the CRO see switchboard status on the OIS?
What information does a protection relay record on a trip?

f.q: How do the switchroom fire systems interact with drives?
f.a:
The control philosophy lists switchroom fire alarms and sprinkler interlocks with lube and hydraulic pumps and conveyors with external lube. In general that stops equipment that could feed a fire, such as oil systems, when a fire is detected.

The fire indicator panel (FIP or FDP) handles detection and alarms.

The exact cause and effect matrix is not in the condensed reference. Ask the electrical or fire systems engineer for the area's fire interlocks.
f: Why stop lube pumps when fire is detected?
What is a cause and effect matrix?
How is a switchroom fire alarm handled by the CRO?

f.q: What does first out tell you after a switchboard trip?
f.a:
When many drives trip at once, the first out function records which trip happened first, so the root cause is not hidden among the knock on trips.

After a switchboard trip, first out will usually point at the electrical loss of supply rather than a process interlock. If instead it shows a process trip just before the board went, that is worth investigating.

The interlocks also have configurable time delays, so timestamps need reading carefully.
f: How are first out records reset?
Why do interlocks have configurable time delays?
Where is first out shown on the OIS?

Electrical code 'SW' on the Growth Proje.q: How does an SW switchboard differ physically from an SR switchroom?
Electrical code 'SW' on the Growth Proje.a:
A switchboard (SW) is the equipment: the cabinet line up of breakers, starters and protection that distributes power. A switchroom (SR) is the building that houses switchboards, usually along with VSDs, control panels and remote IO.

One switchroom typically holds several switchboards, often HV and LV, plus their transformers outside or nearby. The electrical code list also has SUB for a substation, the collective term for switchrooms and transformers together.

Think of the switchroom as the plant room and the switchboard as one of the machines inside it.

f.q: Why are switchrooms often raised or pressurised buildings?
f.a:
In general, switchrooms on mineral plants are raised so cables can enter from below and the floor stays above any flooding. They are often pressurised with filtered, air conditioned air to keep dust out and electronics cool.

Dust, especially conductive or abrasive ore dust, and heat shorten the life of switchgear and VSDs.

The design of this plant's switchrooms is not in the condensed reference, so check the electrical drawings for the details.
f: Why is air conditioning critical for VSD rooms?
How is cable entry sealed in a switchroom?
What happens if switchroom cooling fails?

f.q: What does a transformer tag TR connect between?
f.a:
A transformer steps voltage between levels, for example from 33 kV down to 3.3 kV for large motors, or down to 415 V for LV switchboards. Its tag uses the TR code from the electrical list.

The SLDs show each transformer between the switchboards it feeds and is fed from.

For a specific transformer, look up its tag in the electrical load list or ask the site electrical team.
f: Why are large transformers placed outside switchrooms?
What is a neutral earthing resistor for?
How is transformer oil temperature monitored?

f.q: What else is usually housed in a switchroom besides switchboards?
f.a:
Typically VSDs and soft starters, the remote IO panels (RIO) that connect field instruments to the DCS, UPS and battery systems, communications cubicles and network switches, fire detection panels and lighting distribution boards.

On this plant the DCS and RIO are on UPS, which usually lives in or near the switchrooms. Fibre optic links between rooms terminate in breakout trays there.

That is why a switchroom problem can affect both power and control for an area.
f: What is remote IO and why is it in the switchroom?
How long does the UPS support the DCS?
What is a communications cubicle used for?

Electrical code 'LCS'?.q: Why do drives need a local control station as well as control room control?
Electrical code 'LCS'?.a:
The control room runs drives through the DCS, but people working at the machine need a way to stop it immediately and, in the right mode, to run it locally. The local control station gives them that.

On this plant the LCS stop works in every mode, including Automatic. In Manual the LCS can start and stop the drive. In Local mode the LCS start is the only way to start, used for fault finding and maintenance. Local bypasses process interlocks and start permissives, keeps critical interlocks, and must be supervised.

It is like the local stop and jog buttons on a machine tool, even though the machine normally runs from a program.

f.q: What happens to interlocks when a drive runs in Local mode?
f.a:
Local mode bypasses process interlocks and start permissives, but critical interlocks stay active. So an E-stop, pull wire or protection relay will still trip the drive, but a process interlock such as a downstream equipment check will not.

That is why Local is only for fault finding and maintenance and must be supervised. A timer returns the drive to its target mode.

It is the most dangerous mode for the process, because the usual protections against spills and blockages are not acting.
f: Why does Local mode need supervision?
What does the Local mode timer return the drive to?
Which interlocks count as critical interlocks?

f.q: Why does the LCS stop still work in Automatic mode?
f.a:
Anyone at the machine must always be able to stop it, whatever the control room is doing. The control philosophy keeps the LCS stop active in Automatic, Manual and Local.

What changes between modes is who can start it. In Automatic only the DCS can start the drive, and the LCS start is disabled, so a local start cannot override plant logic.

Stopping from the LCS in Automatic will interrupt the sequence, so tell the control room when you do it.
f: What happens to a running sequence if a drive is stopped locally?
Is an LCS stop the same as an E-stop?
How does the CRO see that a drive was stopped locally?

f.q: What is on a typical local control station?
f.a:
In general an LCS has start and stop push buttons and often an emergency stop, plus indication lamps for running or fault. For conveyors the control philosophy calls for an E-stop at the LCS.

The equipment tag carries the -LCS suffix, so the station for a drive is easy to identify, for example F21PU001-LCS in the numbering spec example.

The exact button arrangement varies by drive type. Check the electrical drawings for a specific drive.
f: Where should an LCS be located relative to its drive?
Why do conveyors need an E-stop at their LCS?
How is an LCS E-stop reset?

Electrical code 'LCS'?.q: What handover issue arises if an LCS is left set to local mode?
Electrical code 'LCS'?.a:
On this plant the mode is selected from the OIS, not from a switch on the LCS. Local mode also has a timer that returns the drive to its target mode. So a drive cannot be left in Local indefinitely the way an old style local remote switch could be.

The risk is still worth flagging while it is in Local. Process interlocks and start permissives are bypassed, the DCS cannot start or stop it as part of a sequence, and it could be started into a full chute or a stopped downstream unit.

A handover should list any drives in Local or Manual, why, and who is supervising. Mode changes are bumpless.

f.q: How does a drive in Manual differ from one in Automatic?
f.a:
In Automatic the DCS starts and stops the drive from control logic and sequences, and the LCS can only stop it. In Manual the CRO starts and stops it from the OIS, and the LCS can start and stop it too.

Process interlocks and critical interlocks apply in both modes.

Sequences need drives in Auto or Manual to run. A drive in Local will hold up a group start.
f: Why would a CRO put a drive in Manual?
What happens to a group start if a drive is in Local?
Can the LCS change a drive's mode?

f.q: What is a start permissive and why is it bypassed in Local?
f.a:
A start permissive is a condition that must be healthy before a drive can start, such as gland water flow proven or a downstream unit running. It blocks the start but does not trip a running drive.

In Local mode, start permissives are bypassed along with process interlocks, so a maintainer can bump or test a drive that would otherwise be blocked, for example to check rotation after a motor change.

That is why Local needs supervision. The checks that normally protect the drive and process are not active.
f: Which pumps have low gland water as a start permissive?
What is a bump test after motor work?
Who can supervise a drive in Local mode?

f.q: How does a timer return a drive from Local mode?
f.a:
The control philosophy says Local mode has a timer that returns the drive to its target mode. If someone selects Local for fault finding and walks away, the drive does not stay with its interlocks bypassed.

The timer length and how the return is handled are set in the DCS configuration, not in the condensed reference.

Ask the control systems engineer how long the timer is for a given drive class.
f: What is a drive's target mode?
What happens if the drive is running when the timer expires?
Can the timer be extended for longer maintenance work?

Electrical code 'LCS'?.q: What safety function does an LCS typically serve during maintenance?
Electrical code 'LCS'?.a:
The LCS gives a person at the machine immediate stop control and, during maintenance, a way to test run the drive locally. Its stop works in every mode.

It is not an isolation point. Stopping a drive at the LCS does not make it safe to work on, because it can be restarted from elsewhere or by the control logic. Real isolation is done at the switchboard under the site isolation procedure.

After isolating, the LCS is commonly used to try to start the drive to prove the isolation worked. That proving step is part of the site procedure, so follow it exactly as written.

f.q: Why is an LCS stop not a safe isolation?
f.a:
An LCS stop only stops the drive through the control system. The motor supply is still live, and the drive can be restarted from the OIS or by plant logic in Automatic. A control fault could also start it.

Isolation removes and locks out the energy source, usually at the switchboard, with personal locks and danger tags, and then proves it dead.

Treat any stopped but not isolated machine as live.
f: What makes a proper electrical isolation?
What are personal danger locks and tags for?
Why can a stopped drive restart without warning?

f.q: Why try to start a drive after isolating it?
f.a:
The try step proves the isolation is on the right drive and actually removes power. If the drive starts, the wrong breaker was isolated or the isolation failed, and nobody has been exposed yet.

In general the try is done from the LCS, with everyone clear, and the start button returned to off afterwards.

Your site isolation procedure defines exactly how and when to do it. Follow that, not general practice.
f: What if a drive starts during the try step?
Who performs the try test in an isolation?
How are VSD drives proven dead after isolation?

f.q: What other stop devices sit near drives besides the LCS?
f.a:
Conveyors have pull wires along their length, reset in the field, plus belt drift, under speed, rip and blocked chute switches. E-stops are fitted at LCSs and other points.

E-stops, pull wires and protection relays are critical interlocks. They trip in all modes and cannot be bypassed. On VSD drives the E-stop acts through Safe Torque Off.

Start sirens and flashing lights also warn before crushers, feeders, conveyors and mills start.
f: Why are pull wires reset in the field?
How long does a start siren sound before a conveyor starts?
What is Safe Torque Off on a VSD?

Code 'VL'?.q: Why does one code cover launders, sumps and kibbles together?
Code 'VL'?.a:
They are all simple open or semi open vessels that collect or carry material, usually by gravity, with no moving parts. The numbering spec lumps them under one code, VL, so they don't each need their own.

A launder is an open channel that carries slurry or froth, a sump in this sense is a collection pit, and a kibble is a large bucket, a term from mining for a shaft bucket or material skip. The spec separately has SU for a structural sump.

On this plant VL is mostly launders: flotation concentrate launders, CIL4 tank feed and discharge launders, the ball mill discharge launder F13-VL-419 and the thickener overflow launder F17-VL-458.

f.q: Why does the thickener overflow launder have serrated lips?
f.a:
The equipment list notes serrated launder lips on F17-VL-458. Serrations, like a row of V notches, spread the overflow evenly around the thickener's circumference even if the launder is not perfectly level.

With a plain lip, a small tilt would send most of the overflow over the low side. That creates a strong local current that can pull solids up and spoil the overflow clarity.

It is the same reason V notch weirs are used for measuring and distributing flow.
f: What causes poor thickener overflow clarity?
Where does the thickener overflow go?
Why do the overflow launders have manual dart valves?

f.q: What do the CIL4 tank launders do?
f.a:
The equipment list shows a discharge launder on each CIL4 tank, F21-VL-411 to 418, plus feed launders on tanks 1 and 2, and a future launder for tank 9.

Slurry flows by gravity from tank to tank through the launders after passing the intertank screens, which keep carbon in its tank. Carbon moves the opposite way by pumping.

Pneumatic slurry bypass gates, operated locally, let a tank be bypassed. Removable spool pieces handle loaded carbon routing.
f: How is a CIL4 tank bypassed for maintenance?
Why do intertank screens sit at the launder entry?
What does the future tank 9 launder allow for?

f.q: What is a kibble used for on a plant like this?
f.a:
Kibble is a mining term for a large bucket, traditionally used in shaft sinking to haul rock and people. On a processing plant the term is less common. Where used, it usually means a bucket or skip for carrying material such as spillage, grit or scats.

The condensed reference does not show any specific kibble on the Growth Project.

If you meet a VL tag described as a kibble, check its equipment list entry and area drawing for its exact use.
f: What lifting rules apply to buckets and skips?
How is spillage collected and returned on the plant?
What does the equipment list show for VL tags in F13?

Code 'VL'?.q: What handover symptom indicates a launder is blocked or overflowing?
Code 'VL'?.a:
A blocked or overflowing launder shows as froth or slurry spilling over its sides, often with spillage on the floor below and a sump pump running hard. Downstream, the receiving hopper level drops while the upstream cell or tank level rises.

On flotation, a blocked concentrate launder can back froth up into the cell and stop concentrate reporting. The launder velocity camera may show froth slowing, and the onstream analyser stream for that concentrate may change.

Common causes are a froth that will not break down, coarse solids settling, spray water off, or debris. The handover should name the launder tag and what was done.

f.q: Why does over frothing cause launder overflow?
f.a:
A froth that is too stable does not break down in the launder. It stacks up, takes up far more volume than the slurry it carries, and spills over the sides.

Too much frother is the usual cause, though fine particles and some ore types also make froth tougher. The design allowed for froth in downstream pumping with froth factors such as 2.5 on cleaner concentrate, but launders still have a limit.

Sprays help knock it down. Reducing frother dose fixes the cause.
f: What is a froth factor in pump sizing?
How do launder sprays break down froth?
Why do fine particles make froth more stable?

f.q: How is a blocked launder cleared safely?
f.a:
Usually by restoring flow, such as turning on sprays or adding water, and by removing debris with long handled tools from a safe position. If anyone must reach into a launder or work near moving equipment, the feeding equipment must be isolated under the site procedure first.

Watch for hidden hazards: launders above agitated cells, slippery walkways and reagent splashes.

The site procedure for launder clearing is not in the reference, so check with the area supervisor.
f: Why are flotation cell tops a slip and fall hazard?
What PPE is needed around flotation reagents?
When does launder clearing need a permit?

f.q: Where does froth from the rougher launders end up?
f.a:
Per the design and the as built PFD, rougher 1 concentrate goes to the Jameson cleaner, with a dashed bypass straight to the final concentrate hopper. Rougher 2 and 3 concentrate collects in F16-VL-438 and goes to the cleaner feed. Scavenger concentrate collects through launders such as F16-VL-437, 439 and 440 and also goes to the cleaner.

Only cleaner concentrate normally reaches the final concentrate hopper F18-HP-414.

Each stream has its own sampler, so you can trace performance launder by launder.
f: What samplers are on the rougher concentrate streams?
Why does rougher 1 concentrate have a bypass?
How is concentrate pumped from the cleaner feed hopper?

Code 'VL'?.q: What keeps concentrate moving through a launder without settling out?
Code 'VL'?.a:
Mainly gravity and slope. Launders are built at a fall steep enough to keep solids moving, with slurry velocity high enough that particles do not settle. Coarse or dense material needs a steeper fall.

Flotation concentrate launders also handle froth, which flows poorly until it breaks down. Water sprays along the launder knock the froth down and add enough water to keep it flowing.

Good launder design avoids flat spots, sharp changes of direction and dead corners where solids can build up. It is like sizing a drain pipe at the right fall so it is self cleaning.

f.q: What happens if launder spray water is turned off?
f.a:
Froth stops breaking down, builds up and can overflow the launder or back up into the cell lip. Solids in the froth can also settle once the water is gone, especially if the concentrate is dense, like this plant's sulphide concentrate.

Sprays are usually set and left running, so a spray left off after cleaning or a blocked spray nozzle is a common cause of launder trouble.

Check sprays early when a launder starts to misbehave.
f: What water is used for launder sprays?
How are blocked spray nozzles cleaned?
Does spray water dilute the concentrate too much?

f.q: Why do dense sulphide concentrates settle in launders?
f.a:
Sulphide minerals such as pyrite are heavy. The design cleaner concentrate SG is 3.93, compared with about 2.7 for typical rock. Heavy particles settle fast when velocity drops.

So concentrate launders carrying high sulphur froth need good slope and enough water once the froth breaks down, or sludge builds up on the floor of the launder.

It is the same reason heavy slurry lines need higher minimum velocities.
f: What sulphur grade does the final concentrate carry?
How is minimum slurry velocity estimated?
Why does pyrite carry gold in this ore?

f.q: Are launders inspected for wear like pipes are?
f.a:
In general yes. Launders carrying abrasive slurry wear at the floor, bends and drop points, and are often rubber or polyurethane lined. Inspections look at lining condition, leaks, structural supports and build up.

On this plant the CIL3 launders in the equipment list mention internal coating systems on mild steel, which is typical for corrosive saline slurry service.

Inspection frequency comes from the maintenance plan, so ask the area maintenance planner for the schedule.
f: What lining materials are used in slurry launders?
How is a launder repaired without a long shutdown?
