Code 'SA' (as in F18-SA-403)?.q: Why is automated sampling needed for metallurgical accounting?
Code 'SA' (as in F18-SA-403)?.a:
Metallurgical accounting needs representative samples taken the same way every time. Gold grades are low and particles vary, so a poor sample gives a wrong answer, and multiplied by thousands of tonnes per hour that error becomes a lot of gold.

Automated samplers cut the whole stream at regular intervals, so every part of the flow has an equal chance of being sampled. Manual grab samples from slurry are inconsistent and often unsafe.

On this plant the code SA is used for samplers like the final concentrate sampler F18-SA-403. Others include the flotation feed composite sampler F16-SA-401 and the three stage CIL4 tails sampler that takes a shift composite.

f.q: What makes a sample representative of a slurry stream?
f.a:
The sampler must cut the full stream, at a constant speed, often enough, and with a cutter wide enough for the largest particles. If it only takes part of the stream, it can miss coarse or dense particles that segregate.

Multi stage samplers take a primary cut, then split it down with secondary and tertiary cutters to a manageable size. The CIL4 tails sampler has a linear crosscut primary (F21-SA-431) and rotary Vezin secondary and tertiary (F21-SA-432 and 433).

This follows general sampling theory. The design of each sampler sets how well it meets it.
f: What is a Vezin sampler and how does it work?
Why do coarse particles segregate in slurry flows?
How often does a primary sampler cut the stream?

f.q: Why does the OSA need its own samplers and multiplexers?
f.a:
The onstream analyser measures several streams with one instrument. Each stream needs a continuous sample delivered to it. Primary samplers such as the shark fin samplers on the rougher and scavenger concentrates (F16-SA-425 to 428) cut a sample from each stream.

Multiplexers F16-SA-420 and 421, six streams each, switch the samples into the analyser in turn, and de multiplexers send them back to the process.

Sample pumps and return hoppers, such as F16-PP-629 to 634 and F16-HP-451 and 452, move the samples around.
f: What is a shark fin sampler?
How long does the OSA spend on each stream?
Where does sampled slurry return to the process?

f.q: How do sampler assays feed the metallurgical balance?
f.a:
Shift or daily composite samples from the plant samplers are assayed in the lab. Combined with tonnages from weightometers and flow and density meters, they give the gold in each stream: feed, concentrate, tails and so on.

The metallurgists use those numbers in a mass balance to calculate recoveries and check that gold in equals gold out. Large mismatches point to a sampling or measurement problem.

That is why a sampler fault is reported quickly. A missed composite leaves a hole in the accounts.
f: What is a reconciled mass balance?
How are missing samples handled in the accounts?
Which samples are the official accounting samples?

Code 'SA' (as in F18-SA-403)?.q: What handover flag indicates a sampler is malfunctioning?
Code 'SA' (as in F18-SA-403)?.a:
Signs include empty or underfilled sample buckets at the end of a shift, an OSA stream showing no fresh data or flatlined results, sample lines blocked or spilling, and alarms from the sampler's control panel.

Many samplers report position. The final concentrate sampler F18-SA-403 has discharge valve open and closed limit switches, so a valve that does not reach position raises a fault.

The handover should name the sampler, what was found, whether the composite for that shift is valid, and whether a work order was raised. The metallurgists need to know if a shift's accounting sample was lost.

f.q: Why does a missed composite sample matter so much?
f.a:
The composite stands for a whole shift or day of production. Without it, the metallurgists have to estimate that period's grades, which weakens the accounting and recovery figures.

For streams like final tails, the composite is the main evidence of how much gold was lost. Guessing it is a poor substitute.

So tell the metallurgist as soon as a composite is known to be compromised, not at the end of the week.
f: How do metallurgists estimate a missing assay?
Who collects and labels shift composites?
What chain of custody applies to accounting samples?

f.q: What commonly goes wrong with slurry samplers?
f.a:
In general: cutters blocked by trash or coarse material, worn cutter lips that change the cut, pneumatic actuator or solenoid faults, sample lines and launders blocked, and sample buckets overflowing or not changed.

Pressure pipe samplers, like F18-SA-403, use a diaphragm valve on a nozzle, so valve wear or blockage is a typical fault.

Trash screens upstream help. Without them, wood and debris would block samplers constantly.
f: How is a sampler cutter inspected for wear?
Why does trash cause so many sampler blockages?
What is a pressure pipe sampler?

f.q: Who should be told when a sampler fails?
f.a:
The control room operator, so it is logged, and the metallurgist, because sampling data feeds the accounts and process control. Maintenance or the instrument team fix the sampler itself.

If the sampler feeds the onstream analyser, the CRO also knows the flotation expert system is working with less information.

The reference does not set out a specific call out list, so check the area shift instructions.
f: How does the flotation expert system cope with missing OSA data?
Who maintains the sampling systems on site?
How are sampler faults prioritised against other work?

Code 'SA' (as in F18-SA-403)?.q: How often does an Isa Sampler typically cut a sample?
Code 'SA' (as in F18-SA-403)?.a:
The condensed reference does not give sampler cut frequencies. Those are set in each sampler's configuration and the metallurgical sampling procedures.

What is documented is the equipment. F18-SA-403 is a pressure pipe sampler with a DN250 inlet and DN50 sample nozzle. The flotation feed sampler F16-SA-401 is a multi stage metallurgical composite sampler. The CIL4 three stage sampler takes a shift composite of tails.

In general, accounting samplers cut every few minutes so a shift composite holds many increments. Ask the metallurgist for the actual intervals.

f.q: What is the difference between SA, SM and CS sampler codes?
f.a:
The numbering spec lists SA as Isa sampler, SM as sampler and CS as concentrates sampler. In practice the project's equipment list uses SA widely for many sampler types, including shark fin, pressure pipe, Vezin and linear crosscut samplers, not only Isa brand units.

So do not read SA as a particular make. Check the equipment list description for what the sampler actually is.

The different codes probably reflect older or vendor naming carried into the spec.
f: Why does the project use SA for non Isa samplers?
What sampler types are used on the CIL4 tails?
How is the UFG product sampled?

f.q: Why do some streams need multi stage samplers?
f.a:
A primary cut from a big stream is still far too much material to send to the lab. The CIL4 tails, for example, carry over 3,000 t/h of solids. Secondary and tertiary samplers split the primary cut down while keeping it representative.

The CIL4 tails sampler uses a linear crosscut primary and two rotary Vezin stages. The CIL2 feed and CIL3 tails have primary and secondary samplers too.

Each stage must cut correctly, or the final sample stops being representative.
f: How big is a typical shift composite sample?
Why is the CIL4 tails sample so important?
Where are the CIL2 feed samplers located?

f.q: How is a pressure pipe sampler different from a cross cut sampler?
f.a:
A pressure pipe sampler takes its sample from a pumped pipe through a nozzle and valve, without opening the line. That suits pressurised or frothed streams like final concentrate, where F18-SA-403 is used.

A cross cut sampler moves a cutter right across a falling stream, usually at a launder or pipe discharge, so it takes the whole stream at intervals. That is closer to ideal sampling for accounting.

Each has its place, depending on whether a free falling stream is available.
f: Why is a full stream cut more accurate?
Where are cross cut samplers installed on this plant?
How is a pressure pipe sampler nozzle kept clear?

Code 'RB' at the crusher?.q: Why do rocks bridge in the crusher throat in the first place?
Code 'RB' at the crusher?.a:
A bridge forms when one or more oversize rocks are bigger than the throat, or wedge against each other and the concaves, so they span the opening and stop. Slabby rocks, two large rocks arriving together, and sticky fines or clay packing around them all make it more likely.

The ROM feed is designed for an F99 of about 1,000 mm, tipped directly from 250 t trucks. Any rock above that range, or poor blast fragmentation, raises the bridging rate.

It is like a log jam at a culvert: individually the logs might pass, but two arriving together lock in place.

f.q: How does blast fragmentation affect crusher bridging?
f.a:
Blasting sets the size of the rock arriving at the crusher. Poor fragmentation leaves more oversize boulders, which bridge more often and need the rock breaker. Good fragmentation keeps the feed within what the crusher can take.

The design ROM feed is F80 450 mm, F99 1,000 mm. If oversize rises, the mining team usually wants to know so they can adjust blast design.

Frequent rock breaker use is useful feedback from the plant to the pit.
f: How is ROM oversize reported back to mining?
What is F99 and why is it used for crusher feed?
Can oversize rocks be broken on the ROM pad instead?

f.q: Why do wet or clayey ores make bridging worse?
f.a:
Sticky fines pack around rocks and between them, binding them together and to the crusher walls. That turns a loose pile that would flow into a cemented plug.

Wet ore also builds up on the walls of chutes, the ROM bin and the dump pocket, narrowing the openings the rocks have to pass through.

So after rain, or with clay rich ore, expect more hang ups at the crusher and ROM bin.
f: How does wet ore affect the stockpile and reclaim feeders?
What can be done about sticky ore at the dump pocket?
Does wet ore change weightometer moisture corrections?

f.q: What happens in the crusher when a bridge forms?
f.a:
Feed stops entering the crushing chamber, so the crusher runs almost empty and draws little power. The ROM bin fills because trucks keep tipping until their lights go red, while the discharge chamber below runs low.

The truck traffic lights respond automatically to the ROM bin level, crusher state and rock breaker position, so trucks are held once the bin fills or the breaker moves out of park.

The rock breaker is then used, remotely by camera, to break or reposition the bridging rocks.
f: What does low crusher power tell the operator?
How does the rock breaker park position affect trucks?
What happens to stockpile feed while the crusher is bridged?

Code 'RB' at the crusher?.q: What handover note would flag frequent rock breaker use?
Code 'RB' at the crusher?.a:
Frequent rock breaker use means the crusher is getting more oversize or bridging than usual. The handover should note how often and for how long, any delays to trucks or crushing, and anything unusual such as slabby or wet ore or a particular pit source.

It is worth passing to the mining team, since it usually points to blast fragmentation. It also flags wear on the rock breaker hammer and boom, so the maintenance planner should know.

Any contact between the breaker and the crusher or concaves should be recorded too, since that can cause damage.

f.q: Why does heavy rock breaker use matter to maintenance?
f.a:
The rock breaker is a hydraulic boom and hammer. Heavy use wears the hammer tool and bushings, loads the boom structure and hydraulics, and increases lube and service needs.

The new unit F12-RB-401 has an automatic lubrication system and a BoomSafe smart boom automation system, but wear still scales with hours of breaking.

Recording usage lets maintenance plan tool changes and inspections.
f: What parts wear fastest on a hydraulic hammer?
How are rock breaker hours tracked?
What does BoomSafe do on the rock breaker?

f.q: Can the rock breaker damage the crusher?
f.a:
Yes, if it is used carelessly. The hammer can strike the concaves, the mantle top or the spider, causing chips or cracks. Breaking a rock against the crusher structure rather than in the clear is a common cause.

Camera views and boom automation help keep the hammer in safe zones. The equipment list mentions BoomSafe, which is designed to limit boom movement.

Any suspected strike on the crusher should be reported for inspection.
f: What is the spider on a gyratory crusher?
How are crusher components inspected after a strike?
Why is breaking against the concaves risky?

f.q: Who should hear about frequent oversize besides the plant?
f.a:
The mining team, especially the drill and blast engineers, since fragmentation is set by blast design. The crusher supervisor and plant metallurgist also care, because coarser feed affects crusher throughput and SAG performance.

The reference does not set out a feedback route, so ask your supervisor how oversize issues are reported to the pit on this site.

Photos from the crusher cameras often help make the case.
f: How does ROM size affect SAG mill throughput?
What is mine to mill optimisation?
Can crusher camera images be saved for reporting?

Code 'RB' at the crusher?.q: Is the rock breaker operated manually or automatically?
Code 'RB' at the crusher?.a:
Remotely, with automation help. The control philosophy says the rock breaker is operated remotely by camera from the crusher control room, and parks automatically. PC2 is run from the existing crusher control room with CCTV.

The equipment list describes the new unit F12-RB-401 as a Rammer XL1200R boom with a 3288E hammer, radio remote control and a BoomSafe smart boom automation system. So an operator controls the breaking, while the system handles parking and boom limits.

It reports to the DCS through its own vendor PLC. Its position is an input to the truck traffic lights.

f.q: Why must the rock breaker park before trucks can tip?
f.a:
A boom out over the crusher or ROM bin is in the path of rock tipped from a 250 t truck. Tipping onto it would damage the boom and could fling rock.

So the truck traffic lights use rock breaker position as an input. If the breaker is not parked, trucks get a red light. Auto park returns it to a safe position after use.

It is a mechanical interlock between two operations sharing the same space.
f: How does the operator know the breaker is parked?
What happens if auto park fails?
Can trucks tip on one side while the breaker works?

f.q: What does the radio remote on the rock breaker allow?
f.a:
The equipment list lists a radio remote control system on F12-RB-401. In general a radio remote lets an operator run the breaker from a nearby safe position, such as during commissioning, maintenance or if the camera system is down.

Main operation is from the crusher control room by camera.

Who may use the radio remote and where they must stand is a site rule. Ask the crusher supervisor before using it.
f: What safe zones apply around a working rock breaker?
How are radio remotes kept from interfering?
Who is trained to operate the rock breaker?

f.q: How does the rock breaker report to the DCS?
f.a:
The rock breaker is one of the vendor packages with its own PLC that reports to the DCS, along with items such as the onstream analyser, compressors and samplers.

The DCS receives status, faults and position, which feed the truck light logic and alarms. Detailed boom control stays in the vendor system.

For faults inside the package, the vendor documentation and the crusher maintenance team are the first stop.
f: What is a vendor package PLC?
What rock breaker faults appear on the OIS?
Who supports the BoomSafe system on site?

Code 'CV'?.q: Why are conveyors coded separately from control valves with a similar prefix?
Code 'CV'?.a:
CV the equipment code and CV the letters in a valve tag sit in different tagging systems. A conveyor is an equipment tag: area, dash, CV, dash, number, as in F19-CV-21 or F12-CV-402.

A control valve is an instrument tag, where the first letter is the measured variable and the letters after it give the function. So FCV13001 is a flow control valve and LCV a level control valve, with the loop number straight after and no dashes.

The dashes and the position of the letters tell you which you are looking at. CV in the middle between dashes is a conveyor; CV at the end of a letter group before digits is a control valve.

f.q: What does the equipment list say about the new crusher conveyors?
f.a:
F12-CV-401 is the primary crusher 2 discharge conveyor, 1,500 mm wide, 187.5 m long with a 24.9 m lift. F12-CV-402 is the stockpile feed conveyor, 1,500 mm wide, 196.1 m long with a 27.7 m lift.

The stockpile feed conveyor carries the weightometer F12-WD-402 that sets the crusher discharge apron feeder speed. It is interlocked to the stockpile high high switch and level alarm.

Both are F12 because they feed areas within F12, the crusher and stockpile.
f: Why do the crusher conveyors need such high lifts?
How fast do the crusher conveyors run?
What feeds the stockpile feed conveyor?

f.q: What does PCV mean on a P&ID?
f.a:
Using the letter code, P is pressure and CV is control valve, so PCV is a pressure control valve. The card's example loop PT13001, PIC13001 and PCV13001 shows it with a pressure transmitter and controller.

Some PCVs are self acting regulators with no controller, such as a pressure reducing valve, while others are positioned by a DCS loop.

Check the P&ID symbol and whether a controller with the same loop number exists to tell which kind it is.
f: What is a self acting pressure regulator?
Where would a PCV be used on a water system?
How does a back pressure valve on a ringmain work?

f.q: How are conveyor instruments tagged?
f.a:
Conveyor instruments follow the instrument rules, with letters, area digits and loop number, and the instrument list ties them to the conveyor's equipment number.

For example, the stockpile feed conveyor weightometer F12-WD-402 has instruments on loop 12557, including its tachometers and transmitter. The primary crusher 2 discharge apron feeder has pull wire switches on loop 12221.

Search the conveyor's tag in the instrument list to see its whole set: pull wires, drift switches, speed sensors and more.
f: How many pull wire switches does a long conveyor have?
What is a belt drift switch and how does it work?
What does a tachometer on a conveyor measure?

Code 'CV'?.q: What handover symptom indicates a conveyor belt tracking or slip issue?
Code 'CV'?.a:
Tracking problems show as the belt running to one side, spillage along one edge, edge damage, and alarms from the belt drift switches. The control philosophy uses inner switches to alarm and outer switches to trip.

Slip shows up on the under speed sensor. The drive pulley is turning but the belt is slower or stopped, which can trip the conveyor. Burning rubber smells, a hot pulley or a heavily loaded belt that struggles to start are other signs.

The handover should give the conveyor tag, which side or switch alarmed, whether it tripped, and what was found in the field.

f.q: What causes a conveyor belt to track off centre?
f.a:
Common causes include off centre loading at the transfer chute, misaligned idlers or pulleys, material build up on pulleys or idlers, a damaged splice or belt edge, and uneven belt tension.

Wind and spillage that jams idlers also push a belt off line.

Tracking is fixed by correcting the cause, such as cleaning, realigning or fixing the loading point. Training idlers help but do not replace the fix.
f: What is a training idler?
How is a transfer chute adjusted for central loading?
Why does build up on a pulley cause mistracking?

f.q: Why does a conveyor slip on its drive pulley?
f.a:
The drive pulley moves the belt by friction. Slip happens when the belt tension on the slack side is too low, the pulley lagging is worn, or water or fines get between belt and pulley.

Overloading and starting under heavy load make it worse. Take ups maintain tension, so a jammed take up or a lost counterweight can lead to slip.

The under speed sensor catches it before the belt burns or the pulley lagging is destroyed.
f: What is pulley lagging and why does it wear?
How does a gravity take up maintain belt tension?
Why does a wet belt slip more easily?

f.q: Can a drifting belt be adjusted while it is running?
f.a:
Not by you, and not by reaching in. Adjusting idlers on a running belt puts hands near nip points, which is one of the most common causes of serious conveyor injuries.

Tracking adjustments are done by trained maintainers under the site's procedures, normally with the conveyor isolated. Some sites allow specific adjustments with guards in place and approved tools, but only under defined rules.

If a belt is drifting, report it. Do not attempt a running adjustment unless you are trained and authorised under the site procedure.
f: What is a nip point on a conveyor?
Why are conveyor guards interlocked or fixed?
Who is authorised to track a conveyor belt?

Code 'CV'?.q: What safety devices are typically fitted along a conveyor like CV?
Code 'CV'?.a:
The control philosophy lists the standard conveyor protections. A start siren warns before starting. The LCS has an E-stop. Pull wires run along the length and are reset in the field. Belt drift switches have an inner alarm and outer trip, and there are under speed sensors, belt rip detectors, and microwave blocked chute switches with a delay.

Any trip stops the interlocked upstream equipment so material does not pile up. Tramp magnets and metal detectors on some belts protect equipment downstream.

Pull wires and E-stops are critical interlocks. They trip in every mode and cannot be bypassed.

f.q: How does a pull wire switch work?
f.a:
A steel wire runs along the conveyor at hand height and connects to switches at intervals. Pulling the wire anywhere along its length trips the switch and stops the conveyor. A slack or broken wire also trips it.

The switch latches and has to be reset at the switch itself, which forces someone to go to the spot and check why it was pulled.

The instrument list shows double sided pull wire switches, for example on the primary crusher 2 discharge apron feeder.
f: Why does a slack pull wire trip the conveyor?
How far apart are pull wire switches spaced?
What should you do after pulling a pull wire?

f.q: What does a microwave blocked chute switch detect?
f.a:
It sends a microwave beam across the chute. Flowing material passes through intermittently, but if the chute fills and blocks, the beam is blocked continuously. After a set delay the switch trips the feeding conveyor.

The delay stops it tripping on normal surges of material.

A trip then stops the interlocked upstream equipment, so the blockage does not grow while someone clears it.
f: Why use microwave rather than a mechanical tilt switch?
How long is the delay on a blocked chute switch?
How is a blocked chute cleared safely?

f.q: Why do conveyors have start sirens and flashing lights?
f.a:
Conveyors are long and people can be near them out of sight of the control room. The siren and lights warn that the belt is about to start, giving time to move clear or pull a wire.

The control philosophy fits start sirens and flashing lights to crushers, feeders, conveyors and mills. Sequences start equipment one by one, so each warning is meaningful.

Never ignore a start warning. If you are near the belt, move clear or stop it.
f: How long does a start warning sound before the belt moves?
Do conveyors restart automatically after a trip clears?
Why do sequences start conveyors from downstream?

'ROM'?.q: Why is ore hauled straight from the pit instead of being pre-screened first?
'ROM'?.a:
The primary crusher is designed to take ROM ore exactly as it comes off the truck. The design basis is a ROM feed F80 of 450 mm and F99 of 1,000 mm, and the new FLS 1300 x 1900 gyratory is sized to swallow that top size at a design rate of 3,135 t/h.

Pre-screening at the pit would mean another large handling step with its own screens, feeders and conveyors, all built to survive metre sized rocks. The gyratory already acts as its own screen: fines simply fall through the crushing chamber without being broken.

Think of it like a single stage gearbox sized for the full input torque, instead of adding a separate reduction stage in front of it. Oversize that won't enter the chamber is dealt with by the rock breaker, not by screening.

f.q: What does an F99 of 1,000 mm mean for the crusher design?
f.a:
F99 1,000 mm means 99 percent of the ROM feed by mass is smaller than one metre. So the crusher feed opening and dump pocket have to accept rocks close to a metre across without bridging.

The new gyratory is an FLS 1300 x 1900. In common gyratory naming the first number is the feed opening (gape) and the second the mantle diameter, both in millimetres, so the gape is roughly 1.3 m. That gives margin over the F99 size.

The remaining 1 percent is where the rock breaker earns its keep. Occasional slabs bigger than the gape, or rocks that wedge across the opening, are broken or repositioned by the remotely operated rock breaker rather than by people.
f: Why is gape sized well above the F99 rather than equal to it?
How often does the rock breaker typically get used in a shift?
What happens if two large rocks bridge across the crusher mouth?

f.q: Where do the fines in ROM ore go if they're never screened out?
f.a:
They go straight through the gyratory with everything else. A gyratory crushes by squeezing rock between the mantle and concave, and anything already finer than the gap just falls through the chamber with little extra work.

From there the fines join the crushed product on the apron feeder and stockpile feed conveyor to the coarse ore stockpile. The product is designed at about P80 130 mm, but it naturally contains a lot of fine material as well.

For the SAG mill this is fine, and even helpful: fines are easy to grind and the coarse rocks in the same feed act as grinding media. The main nuisance from fines is dust at tipping and transfer points, which is why the crusher has a wet scrubber and dust extraction that must run.
f: Do fines make the coarse ore stockpile segregate when it builds up?
Why do wet sticky fines cause chute blockages at the crusher?
How does feed fines content change SAG mill throughput?

f.q: Would a scalping screen ahead of the crusher ever pay off here?
f.a:
Scalping screens ahead of primary crushers are used on some plants, usually where the ore has a large proportion of fines and the crusher is the bottleneck. Removing the fines frees crusher capacity and reduces wear.

On this plant the design does not include one, and the reference gives no study of it. The likely reasons are general ones: a gyratory handles fines well, the new crusher already has spare rate over the mill (design 3,135 t/h against about 1,833 t/h of new SAG feed), and a grizzly or screen big enough for ROM would add height, cost and a maintenance point.

If you want the actual design reasoning, the process engineers or the owner's study team would know whether it was assessed during the Growth Project.
f: What is a vibrating grizzly and where is it normally installed?
Why does a gyratory tolerate fines better than a jaw crusher?
Who on site keeps the original crusher design study documents?

'ROM'?.q: What handover note flags an oversize rock in the ROM feed?
'ROM'?.a:
The reference doesn't give standard handover wording, so treat this as typical practice rather than a site rule. Common notes are along the lines of "rock bridged in the crusher, rock breaker used", "oversize at the dump pocket" or "crusher down for oversize, X minutes lost".

What the reference does say is how the plant handles it. The rock breaker at PC2 is operated remotely by camera from the existing crusher control room and auto parks when finished. The truck traffic lights take the rock breaker position as one of their inputs, so trucks are held off while it is working.

Repeated oversize notes are worth following up with the mine, because blasting fragmentation is the root cause. The crusher control room operator is the best person to ask what wording your crew uses.

f.q: Why are trucks held at a red light while the rock breaker works?
f.a:
The truck traffic lights at the new crusher are set automatically from several inputs, and rock breaker position is one of them, along with truck radar, ROM bin level, discharge chamber level and its HH switch, and whether the crusher is running.

The logic is simple protection. While the rock breaker boom is out over the dump pocket, a truck tipping 250 t of ore could hit the boom or bury it, and the operator would lose sight of the rock being broken. Holding trucks also stops more feed going onto a crusher that is already struggling with a blocked opening.

It's the same idea as a machine guard interlock: the hazardous movement and the incoming load are kept apart by logic, not by relying on someone remembering.
f: What does the truck radar actually detect at the dump pocket?
Why does the rock breaker auto park after it's used?
Who can override the crusher traffic lights if they misbehave?

f.q: What causes oversize rocks to show up in the ROM feed?
f.a:
Mostly blasting. When a blast pattern doesn't fragment the rock well, for example in harder ground, at the edge of a blast or where explosive didn't fire properly, large slabs end up in the muckpile and get loaded into trucks.

Loader and shovel operators in the pit usually try to set aside obvious oversize, which is then broken by secondary breaking or a rock breaker on the ROM pad. Some still gets through.

The crusher design allows for this with an F99 of 1,000 mm, meaning only about 1 percent of feed is expected above a metre. If oversize becomes frequent, the conversation to have is with the mine's drill and blast engineers, because fixing fragmentation at the face is far cheaper than breaking rock at the crusher.
f: How does better blast fragmentation improve SAG mill throughput?
What is secondary breaking and who does it in the pit?
Why is a misfire in a blast a safety issue for the crusher?

f.q: How do you see a rock blocking the crusher from the control room?
f.a:
At PC2 the crusher is run from the existing crusher control room using CCTV. The rock breaker is operated remotely by camera, so the operator is looking at the dump pocket and crusher mouth on screen.

Other signs come from the instruments. The discharge chamber level, ROM bin level and the crusher motor power all respond: a rock bridged across the mouth starves the crusher, so power drops and the bin level stays high while nothing flows to the apron feeder.

Feeding the crusher is like watching a pump suction: a blockage shows up as falling load downstream and a level that won't draw down upstream. The CCTV then confirms what the trends are telling you.
f: What crusher power trend shows normal choke feeding?
Why is choke feeding a gyratory better for wear and product?
What does the discharge chamber HH switch protect against?

'ROM'?.q: How is truck tipping into the dump pocket sequenced to avoid crusher overload?
'ROM'?.a:
At the new crusher (PC2) it's handled automatically by the truck traffic lights. They take inputs from truck radar, the ROM bin level, the discharge chamber level and its HH switch, whether the crusher is running, and the rock breaker position. If the bin is too full, the chamber below is backing up, the crusher has stopped or the rock breaker is out, trucks get a red light.

The dump pocket is direct tip from two sides, with about 179 m3 live from one side, sized around the CAT 793F.

Downstream protection backs this up. The apron feeder is interlocked to the discharge conveyor running, discharge chamber LL and head chute HH, and the stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to the stockpile HH switch and level alarm. It works like a series of permissives in a control loop: each stage only accepts feed if the next stage can take it.

f.q: Why is the dump pocket designed for tipping from two sides?
f.a:
The design notes say direct tip from two sides, with about 179 m3 live capacity from one side. Two tipping positions let one truck tip while the next reverses into position on the other side, which cuts truck queue time and keeps the crusher choke fed.

Choke feeding matters for a gyratory. A full crushing chamber means rock crushes rock as well as against the liners, which gives a more consistent product and more even liner wear.

It also adds resilience. If one side is out of use for maintenance or a damaged bumper block, trucks can still tip from the other side, at a lower rate. The CRO would know which side is in use on a given shift.

f.q: What does the discharge chamber LL interlock on the apron feeder do?
f.a:
The apron feeder under the crusher discharge is interlocked to three things: the discharge conveyor running, the discharge chamber low low level, and the head chute high high level.

The LL interlock stops the apron feeder when the discharge chamber is nearly empty. Keeping a bed of rock on the apron pans means falling crushed rock lands on rock, not directly on the steel pans. That protects the feeder from impact damage, much like keeping a cushion of fluid in a surge vessel so a pump never sees a slug of air.

The head chute HH interlock does the opposite job, stopping the feeder before the chute at the head of the conveyor blocks and spills. The conveyor running interlock prevents feeding onto a stopped belt.
f: Why do apron feeders handle impact better than belt feeders?

What happens upstream when the apron feeder stops on LL?

f.q: What stops the crusher overfilling the stockpile?
f.a:
The stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to a stockpile HH switch and a level HH alarm. When the pile reaches its maximum height, the conveyor stops, and because conveyor trips stop interlocked upstream equipment, the apron feeder and crushing then stop too.

The discharge apron feeder is normally speed controlled to a tonnage setpoint on the stockpile feed weightometer, so crushing rate is steady while the pile builds.

A full stockpile is actually a good position to be in, as it gives the mills their full buffer of about 11 hours of new circuit feed. The crusher simply waits until reclaim draws the pile down. It's like a pressure switch unloading a compressor once the receiver is full.

'COS'?.q: Why is stockpile buffer capacity needed between the crusher and the mills?
'COS'?.a:
Because the two ends run on very different availabilities. Crushing is designed at 65 percent availability (about 5,694 h a year), while the concentrator runs at 93.4 percent (about 8,182 h). The crusher stops for truck gaps, blockages, oversize and maintenance, but the mills need steady feed to grind efficiently.

So the crusher runs faster when it runs (2,634 t/h nominal, 3,135 t/h design) than the new SAG eats (about 1,833 t/h), and the stockpile absorbs the difference. The new COS holds about 20,460 t live, roughly 11 hours of new SAG feed.

It's the same logic as a compressor and air receiver: the compressor cycles on and off, the receiver keeps the users supplied at steady pressure.

f.q: What happens to the mill if the crusher is down for over 11 hours?
f.a:
Once live capacity is drawn down, the reclaim feeders can only pull what flows freely above them. The rest of the pile is dead stock that sits outside the drawdown cone (about 60 degrees on the new COS) and won't flow on its own.

The plant has an emergency apron feeder fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader, so the loader can push dead stock or stockpiled ore into it and keep the new SAG running. Dozing dead stock toward the draw points is the other common option.

If neither is enough, the mill feed rate is cut or the mill is stopped. Remember the 11 hour figure is a design estimate at nominal feed, not a live number; actual hours depend on current pile level and mill rate.

f.q: Why does the existing COS give longer residence at 16 hours?
f.a:
The existing FIM coarse ore stockpile holds about 21,000 t live, but it feeds the smaller existing FIM SAG, which takes about 1,313 t/h nominal. Divide one by the other and you get roughly 16 hours.

The new COS has a similar live tonnage, about 20,460 t, but feeds the new SAG at about 1,833 t/h, so it only lasts around 11 hours.

The difference is just the drain rate on the tank. Same sized receiver, bigger air consumer, shorter run time when the compressor stops. Both figures are design values from the PDC, so actual hours on shift depend on the live pile level and the feed rate the mills are running at.

How is live tonnage estimated from a stockpile level reading?

f.q: How was the 20,000 t live capacity worked out?
f.a:
The PDC gives the new crushed ore stockpile a live volume of 12,035 m3 based on a 60 degree drawdown angle. Multiply by a bulk density of 1.70 t/m3 and you get about 20,460 t live.

The drawdown angle defines the cone of material above the feeders that flows by gravity. Everything outside that cone is dead stock.

Bulk density is the uncertain part. Crushed ore with more fines packs denser, and wet or blocky ore behaves differently, so actual live tonnage varies. Treat 20,460 t as a design figure. The CRO trends stockpile level, and the metallurgist or crusher supervisor would know how that compares in practice.

'COS'?.q: What handover flag indicates the COS is running low overnight?
'COS'?.a:
The reference doesn't give standard handover wording. Typical notes are things like "new COS low, about X hours left", "crusher down, running off the stockpile" or "reclaim feeders struggling to hold tonnage".

Underlying signs come from the control system. The stockpile level trend falls, and as it gets low the reclaim feeders may not hold the SAG feed weightometer setpoint because ore isn't flowing freely onto them. You might also see the feed get finer or coarser as the pile segregates.

The design buffer is about 11 hours of new SAG feed, but that's a design value. Ask the crusher control room operator how your crew reports stockpile hours and at what level they start planning for the loader on the emergency feeder.

f.q: What is ratholing in a stockpile and how does it show up?
f.a:
Ratholing is when ore only flows down a narrow vertical channel directly above a feeder, leaving the surrounding material standing as stable walls. The pile looks full on the level reading, but the feeder is only drawing from a small hole.

It shows up as a feeder that can't hold its tonnage setpoint even though the stockpile level isn't low, often with surging flow when the walls suddenly collapse. Wet, sticky or fine ore makes it worse.

The mechanical analogy is a hopper with poor mass flow design: you get core flow and dead zones. On a coarse ore stockpile it's usually fixed by drawing from a different feeder, dozing, or waiting for the rathole to collapse.

f.q: When would the emergency apron feeder be brought into use?
f.a:
The emergency apron feeder exists so a CAT 992K or 994K loader can keep the new SAG fed when ore isn't available from the live stockpile, for example after a long crusher outage, or if the reclaim feeders are down for maintenance.

The loader fills the emergency feeder from ore stockpiled on the ground nearby, and it discharges onto the mill feed path. It's slower and more labour intensive than reclaim, so it's a fallback, not a normal operating mode.

When exactly it's called up is an operating decision. The reference doesn't give a trigger level, so ask the mill or crusher supervisor what the practice is on your site.

f.q: How does the control room see the stockpile level?
f.a:
The reference says the stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to a stockpile HH switch and a level HH alarm, which means there is a continuous level measurement on the pile as well as a hard switch at the top. On most coarse ore stockpiles that level is a radar or ultrasonic sensor mounted above the pile on the conveyor gantry.

The new crusher is run from the existing crusher control room with CCTV, so operators can also see the pile.

Be aware that a single level point only sees the peak under the feed conveyor. It doesn't show how much of that ore is live versus dead stock, or whether a feeder is ratholing, so the feeder tonnage trends tell you as much as the level itself.

'COS'?.q: How is ore reclaimed from the COS to feed the mill?
'COS'?.a:
Two reclaim apron feeders under the new stockpile draw ore from tunnels beneath the pile and discharge onto the SAG feed conveyor. Each is designed for 2,017 t/h, which is 110 percent of the new SAG's nominal feed, so either one can carry the mill alone.

The feeders are controlled to a SAG feed weightometer tonnage setpoint or a mill weight setpoint, normally set by the expert system. A deadband allows for the lag between the feeders and the weightometer.

There's also one emergency apron feeder fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader. It's a speed controlled feeder loop much like a VSD pump on flow control, with the conveyor travel time acting as dead time in the loop.

f.q: Why is there a deadband on the reclaim feeder control?
f.a:
There's a transport delay between the reclaim feeders and the SAG feed weightometer, because ore has to travel along the conveyor before it's weighed. A controller that reacts instantly to every small error would keep correcting before its last change has arrived, and the feeders would hunt up and down.

The deadband tells the controller to ignore errors within a small band around setpoint, so it only acts on real changes. That reduces feeder wear and gives the SAG steadier feed.

It's the classic dead time problem in a control loop. Like a heat exchanger outlet temperature measured far down a pipe, you either tune the loop slowly, add a deadband, or both.

f.q: What does the expert system use to choose the SAG feed rate?
f.a:
The PDC lists the expert system inputs as the SAG feed camera size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, mill load, mill speed and mill power. It uses these to set the reclaim feeder tonnage or mill weight setpoint.

The logic follows what an experienced operator would do. If the feed is getting coarser or harder, the mill load climbs, power rises and the noise drops as the charge gets cushioned, so the system backs off feed. If the load is falling, it pushes more tonnes through.

Ball addition is also automatic, to a kg/t rate or mill weight. The expert system works like a supervisory controller sitting on top of the basic feeder loops, adjusting their setpoints rather than driving the feeders directly.

f.q: Why is each reclaim feeder sized at 110 percent of nominal feed?
f.a:
The design gives each of the two reclaim feeders 2,017 t/h, which is 110 percent of the new SAG nominal feed of about 1,833 t/h. That means either feeder can carry the full mill feed with some margin on its own.

This gives redundancy: if one feeder or its drive is down, the mill doesn't have to stop. The 10 percent margin covers feed rate pushes and variable bulk density.

Running both together at part load is also common practice, because drawing from two points makes the pile draw down more evenly and reduces segregation and ratholing. It's like having two pumps each sized for full flow, giving you duty/standby flexibility or shared running.

'SABC'?.q: Why do pebble crushers matter so much for SAG mill efficiency?
'SABC'?.a:
A SAG mill breaks big rocks well and grinds fine material well, but struggles with critical size rocks, roughly 12 to 75 mm here. They're too small to act as grinding media and too big to be broken quickly by the balls, so they accumulate in the mill and soak up power.

The SAG grate has 75 mm pebble ports that let these pebbles out. The discharge screen sends them to two XL7 cone crushers running about 7 mm CSS, which crush them to about P80 12 mm before they return. The design oversize is about 375 t/h, between 16.6 and 28 percent of new feed.

Removing that bottleneck is like fixing a recirculating flow that's choking a pump: the mill can take more new feed for the same power.

f.q: Why are 12 to 75 mm rocks so hard for the SAG to break?
f.a:
Breakage in a SAG mill comes from impact and abrasion. Large rocks get lifted and dropped, so they break themselves and others. Fine particles are ground between balls and rocks. Rocks in the middle range fall between those two mechanisms.

They don't have enough mass to break when they fall, and they're too large and tough to be ground down quickly by the relatively small ball charge. So they get rounded and polished rather than broken, which is why they're called pebbles.

Left in the mill they build up as a growing load that takes power but produces little breakage. Taking them out and crushing them separately with a cone crusher is far more energy efficient.

Does a harder ore type produce more critical size material?
Why can't a bigger ball charge simply break the pebbles?

f.q: What happens to the SAG if both pebble crushers are down?
f.a:
The pebble circuit has a bypass route, so pebbles still leave the SAG but go back uncrushed. Critical size material recirculates and builds up in the mill, so mill load and power rise, and throughput usually has to be cut.

The cards describe this as a common handover situation: pebble crushers down, pebbles on bypass, SAG load building. Operators typically back off feed, watch power and bearing pressure, and may adjust mill speed.

The bypass is a designed feature, not a fault. It keeps the mill running at reduced rate instead of stopping, much like a pump recirculation line that keeps a system alive at reduced output when a downstream unit is offline.

f.q: Why are there two pebble crushers instead of one big one?
f.a:
The design has 2 XL7 SH-HD cone crushers in duty/duty, 375 kW each. At 7 mm CSS each one handles about 305 t/h, so together they can take 610 t/h.

The nominal pebble rate is about 375 t/h, but the design allows up to 610 t/h because the SAG pebble ports wear bigger over time and let more pebbles out. Pebble load also varies from 16.6 to 28 percent of new feed depending on ore and case.

Two machines also means one can be maintained while the other keeps crushing, with part of the pebbles bypassed. Each crusher has its own 65 t feed bin and feeder, which start on bin high level and stop on low level.

'SABC'?.q: What handover symptom shows the SAG mill is building up critical size material?
'SABC'?.a:
The reference doesn't fix the wording, but typical notes are "SAG load building", "bearing pressure climbing" or "pebble rate high". The classic signs are mill load and bearing pressure rising, power rising toward its limit, and the feed rate being pulled back by the expert system to hold the mill weight.

Other clues: the pebble crushers and their feed bins running hard, a bypass gate open, or the SAG noise monitor going quieter as the charge fills.

A cards example: power and bearing pressure rising with throughput unchanged usually means the load is building, often from harder or coarser feed. Ask the mill CRO which trends they watch first, because every SAG has its own habits.

f.q: Why does the SAG get quieter as the load builds?
f.a:
The SAG noise monitor is one of the expert system inputs. In a lightly loaded mill, balls and rocks thrown off the lifters fall directly onto the steel liners, which makes a loud sharp noise. As the load builds, they land on a bed of ore and slurry instead, which cushions the impact and the noise drops.

So noise is an indirect measure of how full the mill is, and also of liner protection. Too loud means balls are hitting liners, which damages them. Too quiet means the mill may be overloading.

It's similar to listening to a gearbox: the sound tells you about the load and contact conditions long before a vibration trip would.

f.q: How does bearing pressure tell you the SAG mill load?
f.a:
Large mills usually sit on hydrostatic or hydrodynamic trunnion bearings, with oil pumped in under pressure to lift the shell. The oil film pressure needed to support the mill rises directly with the weight it's carrying.

The mill shell and liners weigh roughly the same from hour to hour, so changes in bearing pressure mostly reflect changes in the charge of ore, balls and slurry inside. That makes it a useful load cell.

The reference mentions reclaim feeders controlled to a mill weight setpoint, so mill weight is a control variable here. Exactly how it's measured on this mill isn't in the reference, so check with the mill maintenance planner or CRO if you need specifics.

f.q: What can the operator change to clear a SAG overload?
f.a:
The main lever is feed rate. Cutting fresh feed lets the mill grind down its load. On this plant the reclaim feeders are normally set by the expert system to a tonnage or mill weight setpoint, so the system will usually respond first.

Mill speed is the second lever. The new SAG runs 60 to 83 percent of critical speed on its VSD, and changing speed changes how hard the charge is thrown. Water addition affects discharge density, designed around 75 percent solids, and how well slurry leaves the mill.

All of this is done within normal operating limits and interlocks. Clearing an overload never involves bypassing a trip; if a trip is stopping you, the cause needs investigating first.

'SABC'?.q: How is pebble crusher product returned to the milling circuit?
'SABC'?.a:
Pebbles leave the SAG through its 75 mm pebble ports and are screened off by the SAG discharge screen (12 x 55 mm slots), about 375 t/h of oversize. They travel by conveyor past tramp magnets and a metal detector to two 65 t pebble crusher feed bins, then through the feeders into the two XL7 cones.

The crushed product, about P80 12 mm, is returned to the SAG feed, as the cards describe.

If metal is detected or the bins get too full, the pebbles automatically bypass the crushers and go back uncrushed. The bypass gate opens if a bin is High with both feeders stopped, or at High-High. It's a closed recirculation loop, much like a pump with a filter loop on the return line.

f.q: Why does a metal detector trigger a bypass rather than a stop?
f.a:
Steel in the pebbles is normal. Broken and worn grinding balls leave the SAG through the pebble ports along with rock. Magnets remove most of it, but the metal detector is the last line of defence before a cone crusher running a 7 mm gap.

Tramp steel in a cone causes huge force spikes and can damage the mantle, bowl liner or main frame. So when metal is detected, the bypass diverts that section of belt around the crushers.

Diverting instead of stopping keeps the whole SAG circuit running. Stopping the pebble conveyor would back up the SAG discharge screen and could trip the mill. It's like a relief valve: route the problem around the vulnerable part rather than shutting everything down.

What happens to steel that reaches a cone crusher anyway?
Why do worn SAG balls break into sharp pieces in the mill?

f.q: Why do the pebble crusher feeders start and stop on bin level?
f.a:
The design says each feeder starts on bin high level and stops on bin low level. This keeps a working stock of pebbles in each 65 t bin, so the cone crusher gets a steady choke feed when it runs.

Cone crushers perform best when choke fed, meaning the crushing chamber is kept full. That gives rock on rock crushing, more consistent product and more even liner wear. Trickle feeding a cone wears the liners unevenly and gives a coarser product.

The arrangement is a simple level controlled batch, like a sump pump that starts on high level and runs until low. If the bins fill faster than the crushers can process, the bypass gate opens at High-High to protect the system.

f.q: Could crushed pebbles go to the ball mill instead of the SAG?
f.a:
On some plants they do. Sending pebble crusher product to the ball mill is a known option, used where the SAG is the bottleneck and the ball mill has spare power. It relieves the SAG further but loads the ball mill with coarser feed.

On this plant the reference and cards describe pebble crusher product returning to SAG feed, so that's the design route. With 12 mm P80 product the SAG can grind it quickly.

Whether the circuit has an alternative route to the ball mill isn't in the reference. The metallurgist or the mill PFD (F13) would show whether any diverter exists, and the process engineers would know why the design chose SAG return.

'SAG' mill?.q: Why does the SAG mill need a small ball charge if it's semi autogenous?
'SAG' mill?.a:
A fully autogenous mill relies only on the ore to grind itself, which works when the ore has enough hard, large rocks to act as media. Most ores don't supply that consistently, so throughput swings with ore type.

Adding a small steel ball charge gives the mill a steady base of grinding media. On the new SAG that's about 10.5 percent by volume, with a total load of about 27 percent. The balls are 125 mm, big enough to break rock on impact.

It's like adding a flywheel to a machine with uneven loading: the balls smooth out variation in the feed and keep breakage steady, at the cost of more power and liner wear.

f.q: Why is the SAG ball charge kept as low as 10.5 percent?
f.a:
More balls means more grinding power, but also more power draw, more liner wear and more steel consumption. The design ball charge is 10.5 percent by volume, with a structural limit of 18 percent balls and 35 percent total load.

The structural limit is about the mill itself: the shell, bearings and drive are designed for a maximum charge weight. Going above it overloads the mechanical design.

Within that limit, the ball charge is a balance set by the metallurgist. Too few balls and the mill can't break hard ore. Too many and the mill pulls a lot of power for little extra throughput, and liners take a beating. Design values aren't live; actual ball charge drifts as balls wear between additions.

f.q: How are balls added to the SAG during operation?
f.a:
The reference says ball addition is automatic, controlled to a kg per tonne rate or to mill weight. So the system adds steel to replace what's been worn away, either in proportion to tonnes milled or to hold the mill weight.

The physical equipment isn't described in the reference. On most plants a ball feeder or ball kibble meters balls onto the SAG feed conveyor or into the feed chute. Balls are delivered in bulk and stored in a bunker or bins.

Ball handling has its own hazards: dropped balls, pinch points and stored energy in the feeder. Follow the site procedure if you're working near the ball loading system, and the mill maintenance planner can show you the equipment.

How do worn balls leave the SAG once they get too small?

f.q: Why are SAG balls 125 mm when ball mill balls are smaller?
f.a:
The reference gives 125 mm balls for the SAG. The SAG's job is coarse breakage of rocks up to around 130 mm P80 feed, so it needs heavy balls that break rock on impact. Impact energy scales with ball mass, which scales with the cube of diameter, so a 125 mm ball carries a lot more energy than a smaller ball.

A ball mill grinds much finer material, where the key is the number of contact points between balls rather than impact force. Smaller balls give more surface area and more contacts for the same charge weight.

It's like choosing a sledgehammer versus a file: different tools for different stages of size reduction. The ball mill ball size isn't in the reference, so check with the metallurgist.

'SAG' mill?.q: What handover flag shows a SAG mill overload or power draw problem?
'SAG' mill?.a:
Typical notes are "SAG load high", "bearing pressure climbing", "power at limit, feed cut back" or "SAG overloading, reduced to X t/h". The reference doesn't fix wording, so ask your CRO which phrases your crew uses.

The underlying signals are load or mill weight, power, speed and noise, which are also the expert system inputs. A cards example says power and bearing pressure rising with throughput unchanged most likely means the load is building, often from harder or coarser feed.

For scale, the new SAG has 20 MW installed with a design pinion duty of about 16.8 MW. Those are design values. The actual power limit you run to on shift is set in the control system and by the metallurgist, not by the nameplate.

f.q: Why can SAG power drop even while the mill keeps filling?
f.a:
Mill power depends on the charge weight and how far its centre of gravity sits from the mill axis, like torque on a shaft. As the load rises, power rises because there's more mass being lifted.

Past a certain point, the charge fills the mill so much that it can't tumble properly. The toe and shoulder of the charge move closer together and the centre of gravity moves back toward the centre, so the torque arm shrinks. Power then flattens or falls even though weight is still increasing.

That's why operators don't rely on power alone. Bearing pressure or mill weight keeps rising as the mill fills, so the two trends diverge when the mill is overloading.

f.q: What's the difference between installed and pinion power on the SAG?
f.a:
The new SAG has 20 MW installed, meaning the motor rating. The pinion duty is about 16.8 MW, which is the design power the mill actually needs at the pinion, where the drive meets the girth gear.

The gap is design margin. Mechanical losses in the drive train, variation in ore hardness, liner wear and future duty changes all need headroom. Running a motor continuously near its rating also shortens its life.

It's the same thinking as sizing a pump motor above the duty point to cover a range of operating conditions. Remember these are design numbers. The live power on the OIS will move around with load and speed.

Why do girth gears need special lubrication and inspection?
How does liner wear change the SAG power draw over time?

f.q: What trips protect the SAG motor and drive train?
f.a:
The reference describes the general interlock classes. Critical interlocks such as E-stops, pull wires and protection relays trip in every mode and can't be bypassed. Process interlocks trip in Auto and Manual and can only be bypassed by named users. Start permissives must be healthy to start. First out detection records which trip happened first.

The specific SAG trips aren't listed in the reference. On large mills they typically include bearing temperatures, lube oil pressure and flow, motor winding temperatures, vibration and gear spray system faults.

Never try to bypass a mill trip to restart. If a trip keeps occurring, the first out record and the mill maintenance planner or electrical team are where to start.

Why do large mills need a CRO phone call before starting?
How does a mill inching drive differ from the main drive?

'SAG' mill?.q: What controls typically adjust the SAG mill's feed rate?
'SAG' mill?.a:
The reclaim apron feeders under the coarse ore stockpile set the feed rate. They're controlled to either a SAG feed weightometer tonnage setpoint or a mill weight setpoint, normally set by the expert system. A deadband allows for the lag between the feeders and the weightometer.

The expert system takes inputs from the SAG feed camera size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, mill load, mill speed and mill power. It adjusts feed to keep the mill in its sweet spot.

Ball addition is automatic as well, to a kg/t rate or mill weight. It's a cascade arrangement: the expert system or operator sets the setpoint, and the feeder speed loop chases it, like a temperature controller setting the flow setpoint on a steam valve.

f.q: Why might the controller use mill weight instead of feed tonnage?
f.a:
Controlling to tonnage holds a steady feed rate, but if the ore gets harder the mill can't break it as fast, so load builds up even though tonnage hasn't changed. Controlling to mill weight instead adjusts the feed to keep the mill load steady, so tonnage falls with harder ore and rises with softer ore.

Mill weight control keeps the mill at its best operating point regardless of ore type. Tonnage control is useful when downstream needs a steady flow or when you're testing.

It's like choosing between controlling a heat exchanger on flow or on outlet temperature: both are valid, but they protect different things. Which mode is normal on this plant is the CRO's or metallurgist's call.
f: How quickly does mill weight respond to a change in ore hardness?

f.q: How does a coarser feed from the camera change the feed rate?
f.a:
The camera size analyser on the SAG feed conveyor estimates the size distribution of the ore going in. Coarser feed usually means more large rocks that take longer to break and possibly more critical size material.

A typical expert system response is to trim feed before the load starts climbing, rather than waiting for bearing pressure to tell it. That's feedforward: acting on a disturbance as it enters rather than after it shows up in the process.

The exact rules depend on how the expert system is tuned for this ore. Some ores grind faster when there are more large rocks to act as media. The metallurgist or control engineer who maintains the expert system would know the logic.

How does fines in the feed change SAG behaviour?
Why does stockpile segregation cause feed size swings?

f.q: What happens when the CRO takes the expert system out of control?
f.a:
The reclaim feeder loop keeps running, but the setpoint is then entered by the CRO instead of written by the expert system. In loop terms, the feeder controller goes from cascade to automatic: it still controls feeder speed to hold the weightometer tonnage, but the target is fixed by the operator.

The operator then has to do what the expert system was doing: watch load, power, noise and feed size, and adjust the setpoint manually. That needs more attention and usually gives less steady performance.

Expert systems are taken off for faults, bad instrument readings, testwork or abnormal conditions. Mode changes are bumpless, so there's no sudden jump in feeder speed when switching.

'P80' of 180 µm means....q: Why use P80 as the grind target instead of an average particle size?
'P80' of 180 µm means....a:
P80 is the size that 80 percent of the product mass passes. It's a single point on the cumulative size curve that the industry has used for decades, especially because the Bond grinding energy equation is built on F80 and P80.

An average size would be skewed by large amounts of fines. The point near the coarse end matters more for recovery, because it's the coarse particles that hold unliberated sulphides and gold.

On this plant the grind target to flotation is P80 180 µm, or 220 µm in the high throughput case. It's like specifying a filter by its 80 percent retention rating rather than the average pore size: it tells you more about what gets through.

f.q: How does the Bond equation use F80 and P80?
f.a:
Bond's equation estimates grinding energy per tonne as 10 times the work index times the difference between 1 over the square root of P80 and 1 over the square root of F80, with sizes in microns. The work index is a lab measure of how hard the ore is to grind.

The square root terms mean energy rises steeply as P80 gets finer. Halving the product size takes much more than double the energy at fine sizes.

The PDC modelled ball mill specific energy at 9.68 kWh/t for P80 180 µm, and the SAG at 9.14 kWh/t. Those are design values used to size the motors, not live numbers.
f: What is the Bond work index and how is it measured?
Why does UFG to 9 µm need over 100 kWh/t of energy?
How do SAG mills use different energy models than Bond?

f.q: Why does the high throughput case accept a coarser 220 µm grind?
f.a:
The PDC high throughput case is 28.35 Mtpa at P80 220 µm, versus the nominal 25.5 Mtpa at 180 µm. Grinding coarser takes less energy per tonne, so the same mills and power can push more tonnes through.

The trade off is recovery. Coarser grind means more gold and sulphides locked inside unliberated particles, so flotation recovery tends to drop, and some of that gold is lost to tails.

The plant's economics decide which side of that trade is better at a given gold price and ore grade. The PDC gives 1.23 Moz/a for the high throughput case. It's like running a pump harder at lower efficiency because the extra flow is worth more than the energy.
f: How much flotation recovery is lost going from 180 to 220 µm?
What maximum grind does the PDC allow for flotation feed?
Who decides when the plant runs the high throughput case?

f.q: Does P80 tell you anything about the fines produced?
f.a:
Not much. P80 only fixes one point on the size curve. Two products can have the same P80 but very different amounts of very fine material, called slimes.

Fines matter for different reasons. Very fine particles float poorly and slowly, they increase slurry viscosity, consume reagents and can coat larger particles. They also make thickening harder.

That's why metallurgists also look at other points such as P20 or the percentage passing a fine size, and at the full size curve from a lab screening. The grind circuit is tuned to hit P80 without over grinding into slimes, much like a cyclone cut point needs to be sharp, not just in the right place.
f: Why do slimes reduce flotation selectivity and recovery?
What does a sharp cyclone classification curve look like?
How is a full size distribution measured in the lab?

'P80' of 180 µm means....q: What handover symptom indicates the grind is running coarser than target?
'P80' of 180 µm means....a:
A cards example reads: cyclone overflow P80 running coarse, around 230 µm. The downstream concern is poorer liberation, so flotation recovery drops and coarse sulphides can sand up in the cells.

Other signs on the trends include cyclone feed density higher than about 62 percent solids, cyclone roping, low cyclone pressure, higher throughput than normal, or scavenger tails sulphur creeping up on the OSA.

How grind is measured on shift isn't detailed in the reference. Most plants rely on regular lab sizing of overflow samples, and some have online particle size analysers. The metallurgist would know how often overflow is sized here and how the result reaches the control room.

f.q: Why do coarse particles sand up in flotation cells?
f.a:
Flotation cells rely on the agitator to keep particles in suspension. Coarse, dense particles like sulphides settle fast, and if the grind is coarser than the cell was designed for, they drop out faster than the agitator can lift them.

Over time they build up as a sand bank on the cell floor, which reduces active volume and residence time and can make the rotor work harder or bog.

The reference notes air valves interlock closed if a cell agitator stops, to prevent sanding the rotor and stator. Sanding is mechanically like a pump sump filling with settled solids when the velocity drops below what keeps solids suspended.
f: How do operators clear a sanded flotation cell safely?
Why does the air valve close when a cell agitator stops?
What agitator speed keeps coarse particles in suspension?

f.q: How does roping send coarse material to cyclone overflow?
f.a:
A healthy cyclone underflow discharges as an umbrella shaped spray. Roping is when the underflow comes out as a solid rope because the spigot can't pass all the coarse solids the cyclone is trying to reject.

When the spigot is overloaded, coarse material that should leave through the bottom gets carried up the inner vortex and out the overflow to flotation. So the grind gets coarser even though the mill hasn't changed.

Causes include too high a feed density, too much feed per cyclone, or a worn or undersized spigot. It's like a restricted drain on a separator vessel: when the outlet can't keep up, material goes where it shouldn't.
f: What spigot size changes are made to fix cyclone roping?
Why does high cyclone feed density promote roping?
Can roping be seen from the control room or only in the field?

f.q: Why does a coarser grind cut flotation recovery on this ore?
f.a:
This ore is refractory: much of the gold sits inside sulphides, mainly pyrite. Flotation recovers that gold by floating the sulphide particles. For a particle to float, enough sulphide surface has to be exposed for the collector to coat it.

If the grind is coarse, more sulphide stays locked inside gangue particles. Those composite particles are heavy and poorly hydrophobic, so they don't attach to bubbles and report to tails. The gold inside them goes to CIL4, where only about a third of the remaining gold is recovered.

So a coarse grind costs gold twice: lower flotation recovery and poor leach recovery in the tails.
f: What is liberation and how is it measured in testwork?
Why is CIL4 extraction only around 34 to 38 percent?
How much gold in the flotation tails is locked in sulphides?

'P80' of 180 µm means....q: How would operators respond to the P80 trending above target?
'P80' of 180 µm means....a:
The usual levers are feed rate, cyclone feed density and cyclone operating pressure. Cutting fresh feed reduces load on the ball mill and cyclones. Adding water at the cyclone feed hopper lowers feed density, which sharpens classification. The reference notes hopper water addition controls cyclone feed or overflow density.

Cyclone pressure is managed by the knife gate valves, which open or close cyclones as feed pressure goes high or low. Typical design pressure is about 82 kPa.

Operators also check for roping, worn spigots and the ball mill load. The changes are made within the control system's normal limits, often through the expert system, and the metallurgist decides the grind versus throughput trade off.

f.q: Why does opening another cyclone change the grind?
f.a:
For the same feed flow, more open cyclones means less flow through each, so the pressure drop across each one falls. Lower pressure gives less centrifugal force, so the cut point gets coarser.

Closing a cyclone does the opposite: more flow through each remaining cyclone, higher pressure, finer cut. The control logic here opens one cyclone when feed pressure is high for a set time and closes one when it's low, keeping pressure in a working band.

It's like nozzles on a manifold: open more nozzles and pressure drops. Too few cyclones, though, and the spigots may rope because each one gets more solids than it can reject.
f: What is the cyclone cut point, the d50, and how is it defined?
Why are there 17 cyclones installed but only about 12 running?
How does feed pump speed interact with cyclone pressure?

f.q: How does the ball charge level affect grind fineness?
f.a:
The ball mill design charge is 28.5 percent by volume, maximum 31, structural limit 38. More balls means more grinding power and more contact surfaces, so the mill can grind more cyclone underflow per hour and the grind gets finer for the same feed.

As balls wear between additions, the charge falls and mill power drops. That can let the grind drift coarser even when nothing else has changed.

The ball mill normally runs fixed speed at about 75 percent of critical speed, so the charge is a key lever. Keeping it near target is like keeping a gearbox oil level right: it isn't exciting, but performance slips when it drifts.
f: How is the ball mill charge level measured during a stop?
Why is the ball mill normally run at a fixed speed?
What happens if the ball charge goes above the structural limit?

f.q: Why not just cut throughput every time the grind goes coarse?
f.a:
Because tonnes are gold too. A coarser grind costs some recovery, but cutting feed costs production directly. The right answer depends on how far off target the grind is and what's causing it.

If the cause is a quick fix such as roping cyclones, a dense feed, or a worn spigot, fixing that restores the grind without losing tonnes. If the ore is simply harder, the metallurgist decides whether to hold tonnes and accept a coarser grind or cut tonnes.

The PDC itself shows this trade off: 25.5 Mtpa at 180 µm nominal versus 28.35 Mtpa at 220 µm in the high throughput case. It's an optimisation, not a fixed rule.

What ore properties make the grind drift without warning?
Who sets the daily throughput target for the mill?

'OSS' and 'CSS' on a crusher?.q: Why does a tighter CSS increase power draw and wear so much?
'OSS' and 'CSS' on a crusher?.a:
CSS is the narrowest gap between mantle and concave or bowl liner. Closing it means each rock has to be broken into smaller pieces before it can leave, so the crusher does more breakage per tonne and draws more power.

A tight setting also packs the chamber harder, so crushing forces rise sharply, and more rock is ground against the liners rather than broken cleanly. That accelerates liner wear and loads the bearings and frame.

The pebble cones run at about 7 mm CSS to produce P80 12 mm. It's like tightening a press tool: the closer the clearance, the higher the forces and the faster the tooling wears.

f.q: What is packing in a cone crusher and why is it bad?
f.a:
Packing is when the crushing chamber gets too full of fine material that can't escape fast enough. Instead of rocks breaking and moving down, the fines compact into a solid mass.

That compacted material transmits enormous force to the liners and frame without much useful breakage. It can trigger the crusher's overload relief, such as the hydraulic tramp release, and repeated packing can crack components.

Causes include too tight a setting for the feed, wet sticky feed, and too many fines in the feed. On this plant, steel in the pebbles is also a risk, which is why there are magnets and a metal detector ahead of the cones.
f: How does a cone crusher tramp release system work?
Why does wet feed increase the risk of packing?
How is packing detected from crusher power and pressure?

f.q: Why does the gyratory quote OSS while the cones quote CSS?
f.a:
It's largely convention. For primary gyratories, the open side setting is quoted because it best defines the largest product size and the gap the crusher opens to on each cycle. Product top size from a primary crusher is roughly related to OSS.

For secondary and pebble cone crushers, CSS is quoted because product size is closely linked to the closed side gap, and it's easier to measure and control precisely during operation.

On this plant the new gyratory runs about 165 mm OSS with a 38 mm throw, and the pebble cones about 7 mm CSS. The two numbers are linked: OSS minus throw equals CSS.
f: What is the CSS of the new gyratory given the 38 mm throw?
How is the throw of a gyratory set and can it be changed?
Why does a bigger throw increase gyratory capacity?

f.q: What does the 38 mm throw on the new gyratory mean?
f.a:
Throw is how far the mantle moves between its closest and furthest position from the concave each cycle. It's the difference between the open side and closed side settings.

The new gyratory has OSS 165 mm and a 38 mm throw, so the closed side setting works out to about 127 mm. Each gyration squeezes rock from 165 mm down to about 127 mm at that point on the circumference.

A bigger throw moves more rock per cycle and increases capacity, but it also changes product shape and loads the eccentric harder. The throw is fixed by the eccentric bushing, rather like the stroke of a crank, while the setting is adjusted by raising or lowering the mainshaft.
f: Why does raising the mainshaft close a gyratory's gap?
What is an eccentric bushing and how is it lubricated?
How does mantle wear change the gyratory setting over time?

'OSS' and 'CSS' on a crusher?.q: What would you see on the plant if the CSS drifts wider than spec?
'OSS' and 'CSS' on a crusher?.a:
A coarser product. On the gyratory that means crushed ore P80 above the design of about 130 mm. On the pebble crushers it means returned pebbles coarser than about P80 12 mm, so the SAG sees more critical size material and its load and pebble rate rise.

At PC2 the camera particle size analyser on the stockpile feed would show the size shift, and the crusher gap is auto adjusted from that analyser, so the system should compensate within its range.

Gaps drift wider as liners wear, so a slow upward creep in product size is normal between adjustments. A sudden jump usually means a hydraulic setting problem, a liner issue or a change in feed, worth raising with the crusher maintenance planner.

f.q: Why does liner wear make the crusher gap open up?
f.a:
The setting is the distance between the moving liner (mantle) and the stationary liner (concave or bowl). As both wear, material is removed from their faces, so the gap between them grows even though the machine's mechanical position hasn't changed.

On gyratories and cones, operators compensate by raising the mainshaft or lowering the bowl to close the gap back to target. Eventually there's no adjustment left and the liners must be replaced.

It's like brake pads: as they wear, the clearance grows, and the adjuster takes it up until the pads are too thin and need changing. Tracking how much adjustment is used tells maintenance when a liner change is coming.
f: How is liner wear measured on a gyratory between changes?
Why are crusher liners made from manganese steel?
What triggers a planned liner change on the pebble crushers?

f.q: How does coarser crusher product affect the SAG mill?
f.a:
It depends on the ore. Coarser feed means more large rocks, and large rocks act as grinding media in a SAG. With competent ore, a bit coarser can actually help.

More often, coarser feed means harder work for the SAG: more large rocks to break, and more material that breaks down to critical size and builds up as pebbles. The mill load rises and the expert system cuts feed to keep it stable.

That's why the SAG feed camera size analyser is an expert system input. A tight, consistent crusher setting gives the SAG a steady diet, which matters more than chasing any single size.
f: Why do some ores need a coarser feed for best SAG throughput?
How does a finer crusher setting cut SAG specific energy?
What is mine to mill optimisation and who runs it?

f.q: What does the camera size analyser on stockpile feed measure?
f.a:
It looks at the ore on the stockpile feed conveyor and uses image processing to estimate the size distribution of the rocks it can see on the belt surface. The reference says the PC2 crusher gap is auto adjusted from this analyser.

These systems see the surface of the ore stream, not the whole cross section, so they have blind spots. Fines hidden under larger rocks, dust and wet coatings can bias the estimate.

They're best used for trends rather than exact numbers. The analyser is a vendor package with its own processing that reports to the DCS. If its readings look odd, check the camera lens and lighting before trusting a gap change it requests.
