'MoL'?.q: Why does high pH specifically stop HCN gas from forming?
'MoL'?.a:
Cyanide in water exists as two forms in balance: the cyanide ion and hydrogen cyanide. At pH around 9.2 to 9.3 they're roughly half and half. Below that, HCN dominates; above about 10.5 almost all of it stays as cyanide ion.

HCN is volatile and highly toxic, so it escapes as gas. Keeping pH high holds cyanide in the ionic form, which stays dissolved and does the leaching.

That's why CIL2 runs pH 11.75 to 12.5. CIL4 runs lower, 8.8 to 9.3, because saline water makes lime expensive, so it relies on HCN gas monitoring as part of its controls. It's like keeping a refrigerant under pressure so it stays liquid.

f.q: Why does CIL4 run at only pH 8.8 to 9.3 then?
f.a:
The cards explain that the hypersaline process water buffers pH, and pushing it higher costs a lot of lime because magnesium in the water precipitates and consumes it. CIL4 treats about 3,000 t/h of tails, so lime use there is huge.

So the bulk tails leach runs at lower pH to control reagent cost. That means more of the cyanide is present as HCN, so the circuit has safety controls, including an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren.

CIL2, treating a much smaller concentrate stream, can afford high pH. It's a cost and safety balance, decided by the metallurgist and design team.
f: Why does magnesium precipitate when lime is added?
How much more cyanide is lost as HCN at pH 9?
What is the CIL4 lime consumption by design?

f.q: What HCN safety controls are fitted on CIL4?
f.a:
The reference lists an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren on CIL4. pH control runs on tank 1, with tank 2 as backup, opening the milk of lime valve at the CIL4 feed distribution box. Cyanide dosing is controlled and trimmed by a cyanide analyser.

In general, leach areas also have personal HCN monitors, safety showers, cyanide first aid, and procedures for entering the area.

If the alarm sounds, follow the site emergency response. Never silence or bypass an HCN monitor, and don't go in to investigate without the right procedure and PPE.
f: What HCN level triggers the CIL4 beacon and siren?
Why do people carry personal HCN monitors in leach areas?
What should you do when an HCN alarm sounds?

f.q: How does pH control on CIL4 tank 1 work?
f.a:
The reference says a pH controller on tank 1, with tank 2 as backup, opens the milk of lime valve at the CIL4 feed distribution box. So pH is measured in the first leach tank and lime is added upstream at the feed box.

There's a lag between adding lime and seeing the pH change in tank 1, so the loop is tuned for that dead time. Tank 2 backup gives a second measurement if the tank 1 probe fails.

It's a standard feedback loop with a transport delay, like controlling a heat exchanger outlet temperature measured downstream. The pH set point range is 8.8 to 9.3 by design.
f: Why is tank 2 used as a backup pH measurement?
How often are CIL4 pH probes cleaned and calibrated?
What happens to CIL4 pH if the lime valve sticks?

'MoL'?.q: What would a handover flag if the lime ringmain pressure dropped?
'MoL'?.a:
Something like "lime ringmain pressure low, duty pump tripped, standby started" or "lime line blocked, leach pH falling". The reference doesn't fix wording.

The ringmain distributes milk of lime with duty/standby DOL pumps. Low pressure means lime may not reach dosing points at the leach feed boxes, so leach pH can fall. In CIL2 and CIL4 that raises HCN risk and affects leaching.

Common causes are a pump trip, a blocked or scaled line, a leak, or a low milk of lime tank. The CRO watches pH trends and HCN alarms closely in that situation.

f.q: Why do lime lines scale up and block?
f.a:
Milk of lime is a suspension of calcium hydroxide. It reacts with carbon dioxide from air and with carbonates in water to form calcium carbonate scale on pipe walls. With saline water containing sulphate, gypsum can also deposit.

Low velocity areas, dead legs and valves scale fastest. Over time, scale narrows pipes and blocks valves and instruments.

That's one reason lime is pumped around a ringmain: continuous circulation keeps velocity up and reduces settling. It's like a hard water system where flow and periodic descaling keep pipes open.
f: How are lime ringmain pipes descaled?
Why does a ringmain reduce lime settling?
Which parts of a lime system scale fastest?

f.q: What happens to leach pH if lime supply stops?
f.a:
Sulphide oxidation and the saline water both consume alkalinity, so pH drifts down once lime stops. In CIL2, running pH 11.75 to 12.5, it would take a while to fall to dangerous levels. In CIL4, already at 8.8 to 9.3, any fall moves more cyanide toward HCN quickly.

Lower pH means more cyanide lost as gas, greater safety risk and poorer leaching.

So a lime supply loss is a priority. The HCN monitor on CIL4 and pH alarms warn operators. Restoring lime supply comes first; never bypass alarms or interlocks.

Why does sulphide oxidation consume alkalinity?
What emergency lime options exist if the ringmain fails?

f.q: How does the standby lime pump take over?
f.a:
The reference says the milk of lime ringmain uses duty/standby DOL pumps, and that standby changeover for pumps is defined case by case. It doesn't say whether lime pump changeover is automatic.

In general, ringmains often have pressure based auto start of the standby pump, but some sites change over manually after checks, especially with slurries that can settle in an idle pump.

Ask the CRO or reagents area supervisor how changeover works on this plant. If the standby needs flushing before starting, that's part of their procedure.
f: Why does an idle lime pump need flushing before use?
What does case by case standby changeover mean here?
How is lime ringmain pressure controlled at the return?

'MoL'?.q: What maintenance issues come with slaking and pumping lime slurry?
'MoL'?.a:
The reference says quicklime is slaked in a vendor lime plant with two parallel circuits, slaking mills, cyclones and a scrubber, then stored in a milk of lime tank and pumped round a ringmain with duty/standby DOL pumps.

In general, the main issues are scale build up in pipes, valves and instruments, abrasion from grit in pumps and cyclones, and dust from quicklime handling. Slaking is strongly exothermic, so temperatures in the slaker need watching. Lime is caustic, so skin and eye protection matter.

The reagents area maintenance planner would know the actual failure history and scale removal routines.

f.q: Why is slaking quicklime an exothermic hazard?
f.a:
Quicklime is calcium oxide. When it reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, it releases a lot of heat. In a slaker, that's used to drive the reaction, and temperature is controlled with water addition.

Too little water and the mixture can overheat, boil and steam, spraying hot caustic slurry. Too much water and slaking is incomplete, giving a poorer product.

Hot, caustic slurry causes serious burns. Follow site procedures around the lime plant, and use the specified PPE, including face and eye protection.
f: How is slaker temperature controlled during operation?
Why does too much water make slaking incomplete?
What PPE is required around the lime slaking plant?

f.q: What does the cyclone in the lime slaking circuit remove?
f.a:
The reference lists cyclones in the lime plant's slaking circuits. In general, they separate grit, unslaked lime and impurities from the fine milk of lime. The coarse underflow returns to the slaking mill for more grinding or is rejected; the fine overflow goes to the milk of lime tank.

Removing grit protects the ringmain pumps, valves and dosing points from abrasion and blockage.

It's like a strainer on a fuel system: it doesn't change the product's chemistry, but it protects everything downstream. The vendor lime plant design defines the exact setup.
f: Where does lime grit go after the cyclone?
Why does unslaked lime cause problems downstream?
How often are lime cyclone spigots changed?

f.q: Why does the lime slaker have a dust scrubber?
f.a:
The reference lists a scrubber in the vendor lime plant. Quicklime is a fine, caustic powder, and handling it, from delivery through to feeding the slaker, creates dust. The slaking reaction also produces steam carrying fine particles.

The scrubber captures dust and steam with water, protecting workers' lungs and eyes and reducing emissions.

It's like an extraction hood over a welding bench: it removes the hazard at the source. Make sure the scrubber is running when the lime plant is in operation, and report it if it's not.
f: How is quicklime delivered and unloaded on site?
What happens if the lime plant scrubber trips?
Why is quicklime dust harmful to eyes and lungs?

'TML' for concentrate?.q: Why can concentrate above its TML liquefy during shipping?
'TML' for concentrate?.a:
Fine, wet concentrate looks solid, but in a ship's hold or truck it's shaken by engine vibration and wave motion. That compacts the particles and squeezes water into the pores. Pore pressure rises, friction between particles falls and the material starts to behave like a fluid.

On a ship, liquefied cargo can shift to one side and stay there, causing the vessel to list or capsize. That's why bulk cargo rules set a Transportable Moisture Limit, below which cargo is considered safe.

The reference gives a TML of about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w for this concentrate. It's like soil liquefaction in an earthquake: same physics, same danger.

f.q: What is the flow moisture point and how does it relate to TML?
f.a:
The flow moisture point is the moisture content at which a sample of the material starts to flow in a laboratory test. The TML is set below that, typically at 90 percent of the flow moisture point, to give a safety margin.

So TML is not where the material flows; it's the safe limit below where it might start to flow. Cargo must be at or below TML to be loaded.

It's like a pressure vessel's maximum allowable working pressure, set below its burst pressure. Tests are done by accredited labs and repeated as the material changes.
f: What lab test is used to find the flow moisture point?
How often should a concentrate's TML be retested?
Why is a 10 percent margin used for TML?

f.q: Why is fine concentrate more prone to liquefaction than ore?
f.a:
Fine particles have small pores between them that hold water by capillary action and drain slowly. When vibrated, they pack more densely and the trapped water can't escape quickly, so pore pressure rises and the material loses strength.

Coarse ore has large pores that drain freely, so water runs out instead of building pressure.

Flotation concentrate is fine, and UFG product even finer. That's why moisture control matters for any concentrate that is stockpiled or transported. It's like the difference between wet sand and wet gravel.
f: Why does vibration raise pore pressure in fine material?
Does UFG ground concentrate have a lower TML?
How does particle size affect filter cake moisture?

f.q: Is concentrate actually shipped by sea from this plant?
f.a:
The reference doesn't say. It says excess concentrate beyond UFG capacity goes through vacuum belt filters to a concentrate stockpile, with a TML of 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w. In Stage 1, part of the concentrate was filtered and processed at an offsite roaster, which needed haulage.

TML applies to any bulk transport, and especially to ships. Whether stockpiled concentrate is sent anywhere by sea, or only by road, isn't stated.

The metallurgist or logistics team would know where stockpiled concentrate goes and how it's shipped.
f: Where does stockpiled concentrate go in Stage 2?
How is concentrate trucked from site safely?
Who certifies concentrate moisture before dispatch?

'TML' for concentrate?.q: What would a handover note if the filter couldn't hit the moisture target?
'TML' for concentrate?.a:
Something like "belt filter cake wet, around 12 percent, cloth needs changing" or "filter vacuum low, cake wet". The reference doesn't fix wording.

The design target is filter cake below 10 percent moisture on the existing 55 m2 vacuum belt filters. Common causes are blinded filter cloths, low vacuum from pump or seal problems, feed density off target (filter feed tanks run about 60 percent solids), cake too thick or too thin, or changes in particle size.

Wet cake makes stockpiled concentrate harder to handle and may push it above TML. The filtration operator or metallurgist would decide what to do with off specification cake.

f.q: What causes a vacuum belt filter cake to come off wet?
f.a:
The main causes are a blinded or torn filter cloth that restricts drainage or lets fines through, low vacuum from a vacuum pump problem or air leaks at seals, and a feed that's too dilute or too fine.

Cake thickness matters too: too thick and water can't drain through in the available time, too thin and air breaks through, losing vacuum. Belt speed sets how long the cake sees vacuum.

It's a bit like a vacuum system with a clogged filter or a leaking seal: the pressure difference that drives the process drops. Operators adjust belt speed, feed rate and cloth washing.
f: How does belt speed change filter cake moisture?
Why do filter cloths blind with fine concentrate?
How is vacuum measured and controlled on a belt filter?

f.q: How is filter cake moisture measured on shift?
f.a:
Usually by sampling the cake and drying it in an oven. The weight loss gives moisture content. Some plants also use online moisture meters on the cake conveyor.

The reference mentions that weightometer totals are converted from wet to dry using a moisture input, so moisture numbers matter for accounting too.

The exact sampling frequency and method for the belt filters isn't in the reference. The metallurgist or lab would know how often cake moisture is checked and reported.
f: Why does weightometer accounting need a moisture input?
How do online moisture meters work on a conveyor?
How often is filter cake sampled for moisture?

f.q: What happens to wet concentrate that's already stockpiled?
f.a:
The reference doesn't describe stockpile management. In general, concentrate above TML can't be shipped until it's dried down. On a stockpile, it may drain and dry over time, especially in a dry climate, or be blended with drier material.

Wet concentrate can also slump or flow on the stockpile, which is a handling hazard for loaders.

The metallurgist or concentrate handling supervisor would decide how wet material is managed and when it's tested again before dispatch.
f: How quickly does stockpiled concentrate dry in summer?
Why is slumping wet concentrate a loader hazard?
How is a stockpile sampled for moisture before dispatch?

'TML' for concentrate?.q: What equipment dries concentrate down to under 10% moisture?
'TML' for concentrate?.a:
The existing vacuum belt filters, 55 m2, take concentrate from the filter feed tanks and produce a cake below 10 percent moisture. That cake goes to the concentrate stockpile.

Upstream, concentrate is thickened in the concentrate thickener (existing 30-TH-61) and held in filter feed tanks A and B at about 60 percent solids, with a balance line between them.

The reference doesn't mention a thermal dryer, so filtering is the dewatering step. To get below TML, about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w, the cake may need extra drying on the stockpile. It's like a vacuum filter press rather than an oven.

f.q: How does a vacuum belt filter remove water from the cake?
f.a:
Slurry is spread onto a moving filter cloth belt. Underneath, a vacuum box pulls air and water through the cloth, leaving solids on top as a cake. As the belt moves, more water drains and air dries the cake further.

At the end, the cake is discharged over a roller, and the cloth is washed before returning to pick up more feed.

It's like a continuous version of a laboratory Buchner funnel. Performance depends on vacuum level, cloth condition, cake thickness and belt speed.
f: Why is the filter cloth washed on its return run?
What vacuum pumps are used on belt filters?
How does a belt filter's tracking system keep it straight?

f.q: Why is concentrate thickened before it reaches the filter?
f.a:
Thickening removes most of the water cheaply by settling, so the filter only has to remove what's left. The concentrate thickener feed is about 25 percent solids, while filter feed tanks run about 60 percent solids.

Filtering thin slurry would need a much larger filter area and would struggle to form a good cake. Thickened feed builds cake faster and gives a drier product.

It's like letting a tank settle before draining it through a filter: you remove the easy water first. Thickener overflow is recovered as process water.
f: Why does thin feed form a poor cake on a belt filter?
What is the concentrate thickener's testwork flux?
Where does concentrate thickener overflow water go?

f.q: Why is there a balance line between filter feed tanks A and B?
f.a:
The reference says filter feed tanks A and B have a balance line. It connects the two tanks so their levels equalise, effectively making them act as one larger tank.

That lets either tank feed the filters and smooths out level differences when one is receiving more flow. It also gives flexibility if one tank needs maintenance.

It's like connecting two fuel tanks with a crossover pipe so they drain evenly. Keep in mind that slurry can settle in a balance line if flow through it is low, so it may need flushing.
f: Why can a slurry balance line settle and block?
How are filter feed tank agitators kept running?
What happens if one filter feed tank goes offline?

'%Cs' when talking mill speed?.q: Why does running speed near critical speed risk centrifuging the charge?
'%Cs' when talking mill speed?.a:
Critical speed is the speed at which centrifugal force at the shell equals gravity. At that point, the charge sticks to the shell and rides round with it instead of tumbling, so grinding stops.

Below critical speed, the charge is lifted by the shell and lifters, then falls or cascades back down, which does the breaking. As speed approaches critical, the charge is thrown higher and further, and more of it lands directly on the liners instead of on the charge toe.

The new SAG runs 60 to 83 percent of critical speed on its VSD. It's like a spin dryer: spin fast enough and the clothes stick to the drum.

f.q: How is critical speed calculated for a mill?
f.a:
The usual formula is critical speed in rpm equals 42.3 divided by the square root of the mill's internal diameter in metres. It comes from balancing centrifugal force against gravity at the shell.

For the new SAG at 10.97 m diameter, that gives roughly 12.8 rpm, slightly higher using the smaller inside liner diameter. So 60 to 83 percent Cs is roughly 8 to 11 rpm.

This is a rough calculation for understanding, not the plant's official figure. The mill data sheet or the CRO screen will show actual speed and percent Cs.
f: Why do bigger diameter mills turn at lower rpm?
How do liners change the effective mill diameter?
What speed does the ball mill turn at in rpm?

f.q: Why does high speed damage liners at low mill load?
f.a:
At high speed, the charge is thrown further. With a full mill, it lands on the toe of the charge, cushioning impact. With a low load, there's less charge to land on, so balls fly across and hit the liners directly.

Those impacts crack and wear liners fast and can break balls. That's why the reference card says higher speed throws the charge harder but risks liner damage if the load is low.

The SAG noise monitor helps detect this, since direct liner hits are loud. Operators reduce speed or increase load to protect liners.
f: How does the noise monitor detect liner impacts?
Why do balls break more at high mill speed?
What is the charge toe and why does it cushion impact?

f.q: Why does the ball mill run fixed near 75 percent Cs?
f.a:
The reference says the ball mill has a 60 to 78 percent Cs range but normally runs at a fixed speed of about 75 percent. Ball mills grind fine material by cascading balls, and there's a well known sweet spot for that motion.

The ball mill's feed, cyclone underflow, is fairly consistent, so speed doesn't need to change much. Grind control is done with cyclones, density and ball charge instead.

The SAG sees much more variable feed, so it benefits from variable speed. It's like running a pump at fixed speed when the duty is steady and using a VSD only where duty changes.
f: Why is cascading motion best for fine grinding?
When would the ball mill speed be changed?
What does the ball mill VSD range allow for?

'%Cs' when talking mill speed?.q: What would a handover mention if the SAG mill was running low on percent Cs?
'%Cs' when talking mill speed?.a:
Something like "SAG speed backed off to protect liners, load low" or "SAG running slow after reline". The reference doesn't fix wording.

Running low percent Cs means the charge is lifted less, with less impact breakage. Mill power drops and throughput can fall.

Operators usually do this deliberately: when load is low and balls might hit liners, after a reline with new tall lifters that throw the charge further, or during start up. The expert system also uses speed as an input. Ask the CRO why speed was reduced, since it tells you about mill condition.

f.q: Why might operators slow the SAG after a reline?
f.a:
New liners have tall lifters that grip the charge and throw it further. Running at normal speed with fresh liners can throw balls onto the opposite liners, damaging them.

So many plants run slower after a reline and increase speed as lifters wear down. That keeps the charge landing on the toe.

It's like breaking in a new engine: you limit load until parts bed in. The reference doesn't specify reline speed practice here, so ask the CRO or metallurgist.
f: How quickly do SAG lifters wear after a reline?
Why do tall lifters throw the charge further?
How is the right speed after a reline decided?

f.q: How does SAG speed affect power draw?
f.a:
Power is roughly proportional to the charge weight and how high it's lifted before falling. Running faster lifts the charge higher, so power rises. Slower, less lift, less power.

Near critical speed, the relationship changes as the charge starts to centrifuge, but in the normal operating range, faster means more power.

The new SAG has a 20 MW motor with about 16.8 MW design pinion duty. Speed gives operators a way to change power, and therefore grinding, without changing feed.
f: What limits how much power the SAG can draw?
Why does power flatten near critical speed?
How does mill load interact with speed for power?

f.q: When would low speed help an overloaded SAG?
f.a:
Usually it won't. An overloaded SAG often needs more grinding to clear its load, so speeding up to increase power is a common response, along with cutting feed.

Slowing down tends to protect liners when load is low rather than clearing an overload. In some cases, when the charge is so high that it's not tumbling well, a change in speed can alter charge motion, but this is mill specific.

The CRO and metallurgist know how this SAG behaves. Follow their guidance on speed changes during overloads.
f: Why does cutting feed help clear a SAG overload?
How quickly does an overload clear after a feed cut?
What signs show a SAG overload is clearing?

'%Cs' when talking mill speed?.q: How does the VSD let operators adjust percent Cs in response to load?
'%Cs' when talking mill speed?.a:
The reference says the new SAG runs 60 to 83 percent Cs on its VSD. The VSD changes motor speed smoothly, so operators or the expert system can adjust speed in response to load, ore hardness and liner condition.

If load builds, speed can be raised to increase power and breakage. If load drops and balls risk hitting liners, speed can be lowered.

The expert system uses SAG noise, load, speed and power as inputs. It's like a VSD on a pump that adjusts flow to demand instead of throttling with a valve.

f.q: Why are large SAG VSDs worth their high cost?
f.a:
Variable speed lets the mill respond to changing ore and liner condition. Throughput can be maximised for each ore type, and liners protected when load is low. It also allows soft starts, reducing stress on the drive train.

A fixed speed mill must be set for a compromise, losing throughput in some conditions and risking liner damage in others.

For a 20 MW mill, even a small throughput gain is worth a lot of money. It's like using a VSD on a large pump: the energy and control benefits pay back the cost.
f: How does a VSD soft start protect the mill drive?
What are the downsides of a large mill VSD?
How much throughput can variable speed add?

f.q: What does the SAG noise monitor tell the speed control?
f.a:
The reference lists the SAG noise monitor as an expert system input. Noise indicates how charge impacts are landing: loud means balls hitting liners, quiet means a full, cushioned charge.

If noise is high, the system can reduce speed or increase feed to protect liners. If noise is low and load is high, it can increase speed or reduce feed to avoid overload.

It's like listening to a gearbox: noise tells you about contact conditions. The expert system uses it together with power, load and speed.
f: Where is the SAG noise monitor microphone placed?
How does liner wear change the SAG noise signal?
Can noise alone control SAG speed reliably?

f.q: Does the old FIM SAG also have variable speed?
f.a:
The reference gives the existing FIM SAG as 10.97 m by 4.27 m EGL with 12 MW, but it doesn't say whether it has a VSD or fixed speed drive.

Many older SAG mills run at fixed speed, while newer ones usually have VSDs, but you can't assume either here.

Ask the CRO or mill maintenance planner. They'll know the FIM SAG's drive arrangement and how its speed is managed.
f: How is the FIM SAG feed rate controlled?
What is the FIM SAG design throughput?
How does the FIM SAG discharge reach the cyclones?

'EGL' on a mill datasheet?.q: Why does a longer EGL nearly double grinding volume matter for throughput?
'EGL' on a mill datasheet?.a:
Mill volume is roughly proportional to diameter squared times length. Both SAG mills are 10.97 m diameter, but the new one is 8.38 m EGL versus 4.27 m on the old FIM SAG, so it has nearly twice the internal volume.

More volume holds more charge, which means more power can be drawn and more ore processed. The new SAG has 20 MW installed versus 12 MW on the old one, and takes about 1,833 t/h nominal versus 1,313 t/h.

Throughput doesn't double, because power, ore hardness and circuit limits all matter. But volume and power are what set grinding capacity, like displacement in an engine.

f.q: Why doesn't double EGL mean double the power draw?
f.a:
Power depends on charge weight and how it moves, which depends on fill level, speed, liner design and diameter. A longer mill holds more charge, but the relationship isn't perfectly linear.

The two mills also run different ball charges, fill levels and speeds, and the old mill's drive limits its power. The new SAG has 20 MW installed versus 12 MW, a ratio of about 1.7, not 2.

So EGL is a big factor, but it's one of several. It's like comparing two engines with different strokes: displacement matters, but so do other design choices.
f: How does fill level affect SAG power draw?
Why does the FIM SAG have a smaller motor?
What limits the FIM SAG's throughput today?

f.q: Why do newer SAG mills have a lower aspect ratio?
f.a:
Aspect ratio is diameter divided by length. The old FIM SAG is about 2.6, a high aspect pancake mill. The new SAG is about 1.3, much longer for its diameter.

High aspect mills give big drop heights for impact breakage, suited to competent ore. Lower aspect mills give more volume and residence time for abrasion and attrition grinding, often suited to ore that breaks down more easily or where the SAG does more of the grinding work.

The choice depends on ore testwork and circuit design. The metallurgist or process engineers could explain why this geometry was chosen.
f: What is a high aspect ratio SAG mill good for?
How does aspect ratio affect SAG residence time?
What ore testwork guides SAG mill geometry?

f.q: How does EGL affect residence time in the mill?
f.a:
A longer mill holds more slurry and charge, so for the same flow, slurry stays inside longer. More residence time means more grinding before discharge.

But SAG mills also discharge through grates and pulp lifters, which limit how fast slurry can leave. The new SAG has curved pulp lifters rated at 2,100 m3/h maximum.

So residence time depends on volume and discharge capacity. It's like a tank with a fixed outlet: a bigger tank holds fluid longer, but the outlet sets the flow.
f: What do pulp lifters do in a SAG mill?
Why does pulp lifter capacity limit throughput?
How does slurry pooling affect SAG grinding?

'EGL' on a mill datasheet?.q: What would a handover flag if liner wear was reducing effective EGL?
'EGL' on a mill datasheet?.a:
Small correction first: liner wear doesn't reduce EGL. EGL is measured inside the liners, so as liners wear thinner, the internal volume actually grows slightly.

What wear does change is the lifter height and profile. Worn lifters lift the charge less, so charge motion, power and throughput shift. Handovers might say "liners near end of life, power drifting" or "throughput down, lifters worn".

Liner wear is tracked by maintenance, often with periodic measurements. The reference gives reline scenarios but not wear rates. The mill maintenance planner would know where the liners are in their life.

f.q: How is liner wear measured inside a SAG mill?
f.a:
Common methods include laser scanning the mill interior during a stop, ultrasonic thickness testing, and physical measurement with gauges or templates. Some plants track wear by tonnes processed or operating hours too.

Scans build a profile of liner and lifter thickness, so maintenance can predict when relining is needed.

Entry to a mill for measurement needs full isolation and confined space procedures. The mill maintenance planner would know the method and schedule used here.
f: How does laser scanning build a liner wear profile?
What confined space rules apply to mill entry?
How are liner wear predictions used for planning?

f.q: Why does lifter wear change SAG grinding behaviour?
f.a:
Lifters grip the charge and lift it as the shell rotates. Tall lifters lift the charge higher before it falls, giving more impact. As they wear down, they slip more and lift less, so the charge cascades rather than cataracts.

That changes power draw, impact breakage and throughput. Some ores grind better with worn lifters; others worse.

Operators can adjust speed to compensate as lifters wear. It's like tyre tread: the same car, but grip and behaviour change as tread wears.
f: What is the difference between cascading and cataracting?
How is speed adjusted as SAG lifters wear?
When do worn lifters trigger a reline?

f.q: What happens to the plant during a new SAG reline?
f.a:
The reference lists reline scenarios. During the new SAG reline, the FIM SAG runs with the new ball mill. During an FIM SAG reline, the new SABC runs. During a ball mill reline, the new SAG runs single stage.

So the plant keeps producing at reduced rate while each mill is relined. Single stage means the SAG runs without the ball mill.

It's like having parallel trains in a process plant: one can come down for maintenance while the other keeps running.
f: What is single stage SAG operation?
How much throughput is lost during a SAG reline?
How long does a new SAG reline take?

'EGL' on a mill datasheet?.q: How does EGL factor into scheduling a liner change?
'EGL' on a mill datasheet?.a:
EGL itself doesn't drive the schedule; liner wear does. But EGL affects how big a reline job is. A longer mill has more liners, more lifters and more bolts, so a reline takes longer and needs more parts and labour.

The new SAG at 8.38 m EGL has nearly twice the liner area of the old FIM SAG at 4.27 m. That makes reline planning a significant job, coordinated with the reline scenarios: FIM SAG plus new ball mill keep running during a new SAG reline.

The mill maintenance planner sets the schedule based on wear data, tonnes and shutdown windows.

f.q: Why does a longer mill take longer to reline?
f.a:
More EGL means more shell area to cover, so more liner segments, lifters and bolts. Each one has to be removed, the shell cleaned and inspected, and new pieces fitted.

Reline crews and relining machines work segment by segment, so time scales roughly with the number of pieces.

Planning focuses on reducing critical path time, for example by prefitting parts or using larger liner segments. The mill maintenance planner would know the reline duration for each mill.
f: How does a mill relining machine work?
Why do larger liner segments shorten reline time?
What is the critical path in a mill reline?

f.q: What is a mill relining machine and how is it used?
f.a:
A mill relining machine is a powered arm mounted at the feed or discharge end, used to lift and place heavy liner segments inside the mill. It removes the need to handle very heavy parts manually.

Workers bolt liners from outside or inside, while the machine positions them. It improves safety and speed.

Mill relining is a high risk activity with confined space, heavy lifting and stored energy hazards. Follow the site reline procedure and isolations. The mill maintenance planner can show you the equipment.
f: What hazards apply during mill relining?
How are liner bolts removed from a SAG shell?
Why is the mill inched during a reline?

f.q: How do the reline scenarios keep the plant running?
f.a:
The reference gives three reline scenarios. During a ball mill reline, the new SAG runs single stage. During an FIM SAG reline, the new SABC circuit runs. During a new SAG reline, the FIM SAG runs with the new ball mill.

That works because both SAGs discharge to the shared cyclone feed hopper and ball mill. Having two SAGs gives flexibility.

It's like having parallel compressors with a shared header: one can be serviced while the others carry the load, at reduced capacity.
f: What throughput can the plant run during each reline?
How does single stage SAG affect the grind?
Why do both SAGs share one ball mill?

'Circ load' in the grinding circuit?.q: Why does a high circulating load help keep the mill grinding efficiently?
'Circ load' in the grinding circuit?.a:
The cyclones pull out finished product quickly, so the ball mill spends its energy on coarse particles that still need grinding instead of overgrinding fines. High circulating load means material passes through the mill many times in small steps, removing fines each pass.

The design is about 358 percent cyclone underflow to overflow, so for every tonne of product, about 3.6 tonnes go back to the ball mill.

As the card says, it's like a recirculating pump loop: high flow keeps the mill full of near sized material. Too high a load, though, overloads pumps, cyclones and the mill's volumetric capacity.

f.q: How is the 358 percent circulating load calculated?
f.a:
Circulating load is cyclone underflow tonnes divided by overflow tonnes. The reference gives cyclone feed about 14,400 t/h solids and overflow 3,146 t/h. So underflow is about 11,254 t/h, and 11,254 divided by 3,146 is about 358 percent.

Overflow equals new feed to the circuit at steady state, because what goes in must come out as product.

These are design values. Actual circulating load changes with ore, grind and cyclone settings.
f: How does circulating load change with ore hardness?
Why does overflow equal new feed at steady state?
How is cyclone feed tonnage measured on the plant?

f.q: Is there a limit to how high circulating load should go?
f.a:
Yes. As circulating load rises, the ball mill receives more volumetric flow, which shortens its residence time and can flush coarse material through. Cyclone feed pumps and cyclones also reach their capacity limits.

Beyond a point, efficiency gains flatten and operating problems appear, such as roping cyclones and overloaded pumps.

Designers pick a circulating load that balances efficiency with equipment limits. 358 percent is the design here. The metallurgist watches actual circulating load as part of circuit performance.
f: Why does high flow shorten ball mill residence time?
What limits cyclone feed pump capacity?
How does circulating load affect cyclone roping?

f.q: What does overgrinding cost the plant?
f.a:
Overgrinding means grinding particles finer than needed. It wastes energy, since energy rises steeply at fine sizes, and creates slimes.

Slimes float poorly, consume reagents, increase slurry viscosity and make thickening harder. They can also coat larger particles, reducing flotation selectivity.

So the grinding circuit aims to hit the P80 target without making excess fines. High circulating load helps by removing fines promptly. It's like overtightening a bolt: wasted effort and potential damage.
f: Why do slimes float poorly in flotation?
How do slimes affect thickener performance?
How is overgrinding detected in the size data?

'Circ load' in the grinding circuit?.q: What would a handover report if circulating load suddenly spiked?
'Circ load' in the grinding circuit?.a:
Something like "circ load high, cyclones roping, cut feed" or "ball mill load up, cyclone pressure high". The reference doesn't fix wording.

A spike means more material is being returned to the ball mill. Causes include harder or coarser feed, reduced ball mill grinding from a worn ball charge, cyclone changes such as worn spigots, or changes in cyclone feed density.

Consequences can include overloaded ball mill, cyclone feed pump at limits and coarser overflow. Operators typically cut feed, adjust water and check the cyclones. The CRO and metallurgist would investigate.

f.q: Why does a circulating load spike risk overloading the ball mill?
f.a:
More underflow means more slurry flowing into the ball mill. If the mill can't grind it fast enough, material builds up, power changes, and the mill can overload.

The ball mill is an overflow type, discharging through the trunnion, so excess flow can push coarse material out unground or cause spills at the trommel.

It's like overloading a pump: past its capacity, performance drops and problems appear. Cutting new feed reduces the load until the circuit stabilises.
f: What happens at the ball mill trommel when overloaded?
How does ball mill power respond to an overload?
Why does cutting new feed reduce circulating load?

f.q: How does a worn ball charge raise circulating load?
f.a:
As balls wear, the ball mill charge drops below its design of about 28.5 percent by volume. Less charge means less grinding power, so coarse particles take longer to grind down.

More coarse material then reports to cyclone underflow and returns to the mill, raising circulating load.

Ball addition is automatic on the SAG, to kg/t or mill weight, but ball mill ball addition isn't described in the reference. Keeping the charge topped up maintains grinding. It's like a worn grinding wheel taking longer to do the same job.
f: How is ball mill charge level checked?
How often are balls added to the ball mill?
What ball size is used in the ball mill?

f.q: How is circulating load measured on the plant?
f.a:
The reference says slurry mass flow is measured by mag flowmeter plus nucleonic density with operator entered solids SG. With cyclone feed flow and density, and overflow tonnage, underflow can be calculated.

Metallurgists also estimate circulating load from size distributions of feed, underflow and overflow samples, using a mass balance.

So the plant has instruments for continuous estimates, and periodic surveys give more accurate figures. It's like calculating flow in a branch from measurements on the main line.
f: How does a nucleonic density gauge work?
What is a circuit sampling survey?
Why does solids SG need to be entered by the operator?

'Circ load' in the grinding circuit?.q: How do operators control circulating load day to day?
'Circ load' in the grinding circuit?.a:
The main levers are cyclone feed density, cyclone pressure and number of cyclones, spigot sizes, ball charge and new feed rate.

Hopper water addition controls cyclone feed or overflow density; lower density sharpens classification and can lower circulating load. Knife gate valves open or close cyclones as feed pressure goes high or low. Spigot sizes are changed during shutdowns.

Feed rate is the most direct lever: less new feed means less load overall. The expert system and CRO adjust within limits set by the metallurgist.

f.q: How does hopper water addition change circulating load?
f.a:
Adding water at the cyclone feed hopper lowers feed density. Less dense feed classifies more sharply, with less hindered settling, so fewer fines are carried to underflow.

That can change circulating load in either direction depending on conditions, but generally improves cyclone efficiency.

It also changes volumetric flow to the cyclones and affects pressure. Operators balance density and pressure. It's like adjusting fluid viscosity to improve a separator's performance.
f: Why does hindered settling affect cyclone cut size?
How does feed density change cyclone pressure?
What is the design cyclone feed density?

f.q: Why are cyclone spigot sizes changed during shutdowns?
f.a:
The spigot sets how much underflow a cyclone can discharge. Larger spigots pass more underflow, raising circulating load and lowering roping risk. Smaller spigots do the opposite.

Spigots also wear, getting larger over time. Changing them restores performance.

Since spigots are inside the cyclone, changes usually need the cyclone isolated, which is easiest during shutdowns or with the cyclone closed. It's like changing a nozzle size to adjust flow.
f: How quickly do cyclone spigots wear?
Can a single cyclone be isolated while running?
Why do gravity cyclones use larger spigots?

f.q: What is the dual hopper level control on the cyclone feed?
f.a:
The reference describes dual hopper level control: loop A uses pump speed at a higher level setpoint, and loop B uses water addition at a lower setpoint to keep minimum line velocity.

On the cyclone feed hopper, hopper water addition controls cyclone feed or overflow density, with Fast and Slow level tuning. The cyclone feed is also cascaded from hopper level to pressure setpoint.

So pump speed and water work together to hold level, density and pressure. It's like two controllers sharing a tank, each with its own job.
f: What does Fast and Slow level tuning mean?
Why does the hopper level cascade to pressure?
What happens if the cyclone feed hopper runs dry?

'Mass pull' in flotation?.q: Why does too high a mass pull dilute concentrate grade?
'Mass pull' in flotation?.a:
The richest, fastest floating sulphide particles come off first. To pull more mass into the concentrate, the cell has to recover slower floating, poorer particles and more gangue carried up with the water in the froth, called entrainment. Each extra tonne is lower grade than the last, so the average grade falls.

On this plant, by design, Rougher 1 pulls about 4.4 percent of feed mass at about 15.3 percent S, Roughers 2 and 3 about 2.4 percent at 7.1 percent S, and the scavengers about 1.1 percent at 5.1 percent S. You can see grade falling as you go down the bank.

It's like opening up a filter mesh: more flow gets through, but so does more dirt.

f.q: What is entrainment and how does it differ from true flotation?
f.a:
True flotation is when a hydrophobic particle attaches to a bubble and is carried up into the froth. It's selective, because only particles coated with collector attach.

Entrainment is when fine particles, valuable or gangue, are simply carried up in the water that travels with the bubbles into the froth. It's not selective at all; it depends mainly on how much water reports to the concentrate and how fine the particles are.

High mass pull usually means more water to the concentrate, so more entrained gangue. A deeper froth lets that water drain back, improving grade. It's like spray carryover in a steam drum, carrying impurities with the moisture.
f: Why are fine particles more prone to entrainment?
How does froth depth control water recovery?
Can wash water reduce entrainment in a flotation cell?

f.q: How does the cleaner recover grade lost to high mass pull?
f.a:
All rougher and scavenger concentrate goes to the Jameson cleaner, per the PDC mass balance. The cleaner refloats it, rejecting entrained gangue and poorly floating particles to its tails, which go to the cleaner-scavenger.

Feed to the cleaner is about 15 percent S. Only cleaner concentrate reaches the final concentrate hopper, at about 35 percent S. Cleaner mass pull is 31 to 44 percent, and stage sulphur recovery is about 93 percent.

So the roughers can run for recovery, and the cleaner restores grade. It's like a two stage separator: the first stage catches everything, the second cleans it up.
f: Why does the cleaner tails go to a cleaner-scavenger?
How does cleaner tails recycle keep the Jameson stable?
What is the final concentrate grade target by design?

f.q: Why does too much concentrate overload the downstream circuit?
f.a:
Everything floated has to be thickened, ground and leached. The design concentrate rate is about 75 to 78 t/h nominal, and 104 to 107 t/h in the design grade case. The new IsaMills take about 30 t/h fresh feed each nominally, 46 t/h maximum.

If mass pull rises well above plan, concentrate can exceed UFG capacity. The Stage 2 philosophy then runs UFG 2 and 3 at maximum with excess to UFG 1, and anything beyond that goes to the vacuum belt filters and concentrate stockpile.

Extra low grade concentrate also wastes UFG energy and leach reagents on gangue. It's like oversupplying a production line: the bottleneck backs up and the extra material goes to storage.
f: How much concentrate can UFG 1, 2 and 3 handle together?
Why is grinding gangue in UFG an energy waste?
What happens to stockpiled concentrate later on?

'Mass pull' in flotation?.q: What would a handover flag if Rougher 1's mass pull jumped overnight?
'Mass pull' in flotation?.a:
Something like "R1 pulling hard, con grade down" or "R1 level control playing up, froth thin". The reference doesn't fix wording.

Common causes are a higher air rate, a lower pulp level giving a shallower froth, a frother or collector overdose, a level control valve fault, or a genuine change in feed with more sulphide. The OSA's rougher 1 concentrate stream would show grade falling if it's gangue, or steady grade if the feed simply has more sulphide.

The knock on effect is more feed to the Jameson cleaner. The flotation operator or metallurgist would check the level, air and reagent trends first.

f.q: How could a dart valve fault change rougher mass pull?
f.a:
The reference says each cell has two dart valves on split range level control, in series or parallel. The dart valves let slurry out of the cell, holding pulp level and therefore froth depth.

If a dart valve sticks open or its positioner fails, the pulp level drops, the froth gets deeper and mass pull falls. If it sticks closed, the level rises, the froth gets shallow and the cell may overflow pulp into the launder, so mass pull jumps and grade crashes.

It's like a level control valve on a separator vessel: if it fails, the interface moves and the wrong phase goes out the wrong outlet.
f: What does split range control mean for dart valves?
How is cell pulp level measured in a tank cell?
What happens when a cell overflows pulp into the launder?

f.q: Is a higher mass pull ever a good thing?
f.a:
Yes, when the feed has more sulphide. If head sulphur rises, say toward the design grade case of 1.49 percent S rather than nominal 1.02 percent, more sulphide needs to float to keep recovery up. Mass pull rising with steady concentrate grade is the plant doing its job.

The design grade case produces about 876 kt a year of concentrate, versus 637 kt in the nominal case, so higher mass pull is expected with richer ore.

The key is whether grade holds. Rising mass pull with falling grade means gangue. Rising mass pull with steady grade means more valuable mineral. It's like more flow through a pump: fine if it's demand, bad if it's a leak.
f: How does feed sulphur grade change the flotation targets?
What does the OSA flotation feed stream show?
Why is concentrate production higher in the design case?

f.q: How would a mass pull jump show up on the cleaner?
f.a:
More rougher concentrate means more feed to the Jameson cleaner. The cleaner feed is designed at about 1,998 m3/h including recycle, at 17.5 to 19.5 percent solids.

The Jameson keeps downcomer flow steady with external recycle of about half its tails, so a feed increase reduces how much is recycled, not jet flow, up to a point. Cleaner feed grade on the OSA would drop if the extra mass is gangue.

If the extra load exceeds what the recycle can absorb, cleaner performance drops and final concentrate grade suffers. It's like a pump with a minimum flow bypass: once demand exceeds the bypass margin, the system feels it.
f: Why does the Jameson need constant downcomer flow?
How does the cleaner feed pump VSD respond to load?
What does the cleaner-scavenger do with cleaner tails?

'Mass pull' in flotation?.q: How is mass pull adjusted on the plant, air rate or froth depth?
'Mass pull' in flotation?.a:
Both, plus reagents. On the FLS tank cells, air to each cell is set by a flow controller with a mass flow meter, and pulp level, which sets froth depth, is held by the dart valves on split range level control. The blowers run VSDs to hold header pressure.

More air or a shallower froth raises mass pull and lowers grade. Less air or a deeper froth does the opposite. Reagent doses, collector and frother, also shift it.

The flotation expert system uses the OSA, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set level, air and reagents automatically. It's two control knobs on one process, like flow and temperature on a heat exchanger.

f.q: Why does a deeper froth raise concentrate grade?
f.a:
A deeper froth gives more time for water to drain back down through the froth before it overflows. Entrained gangue drains with that water, and weakly attached particles drop off as bubbles coalesce.

So only strongly attached, hydrophobic particles make it to the lip. Grade rises, but recovery drops because some valuable particles also drop back.

It's like a settling tank with a longer residence time: more separation, less throughput. Froth depth is a key lever for the grade and recovery trade off.
f: Why do bubbles coalesce as they rise in the froth?
How is froth depth measured on a tank cell?
What happens if the froth gets too deep?

f.q: How is air flow to each flotation cell controlled?
f.a:
The reference says each cell's air is set by a flow controller with a mass flow meter. The LP flotation blowers run VSDs to hold air header pressure, so each cell can draw what its controller asks for.

The air valve interlocks closed if the cell agitator stops. That prevents air sanding the rotor and stator and protects the bearings.

It's a classic header with individual flow loops, like a compressed air system with flow control to each user and a pressure controlled compressor.
f: Why does air sand the rotor if the agitator stops?
How is blower header pressure setpoint chosen?
What happens to cell air if a blower trips?

f.q: Why is mass pull adjusted differently on the Jameson cells?
f.a:
The Jameson cells have no blower. Air is drawn in naturally as slurry jets down the downcomers, so the reference says Jameson air depends on total pumped flow through the downcomers, with the feed pump VSD on flow control.

So you can't simply turn up air on a Jameson as you would on a tank cell. Mass pull is managed through pulp level, froth depth, reagent dose and keeping downcomer flow steady with the external recycle.

It's like a venturi eductor: the suction depends on the motive flow, not on a separate fan. Changing the jet changes the air.
f: How does a Jameson downcomer entrain air?
Why is cleaner tails recycle set at about half?
How is froth depth controlled on a Jameson cell?

'Froth factor' in the PDC?.q: Why does froth take up more volume than plain slurry in a pipe?
'Froth factor' in the PDC?.a:
Froth is a foam of air bubbles coated with mineral particles and water. When it overflows into the launder, much of that air is still trapped. Frother and fine particles make bubbles stable, so they don't burst quickly.

So a tonne of concentrate arrives at the pump with a lot of air mixed in, taking up more volume than the same slurry would without air. The air also tends to collect at the pump eye, where low pressure lets bubbles grow.

That's why the PDC applies froth factors of 1.6 to 2.5 to concentrate lines. It's like sizing a pipe for a two phase flow rather than liquid only.

f.q: Why does stable froth resist breaking down in a launder?
f.a:
Frother reduces surface tension and strengthens bubble films, so bubbles survive longer. Fine hydrophobic particles also sit in the bubble films and stabilise them, a bit like armour.

That's good in the cell, where you want a stable froth to carry mineral. But in the launder and pump hopper, the same stability means air stays trapped.

On this plant the frother is Luprofroth 168, dosed to rougher, scavenger, cleaner and cleaner-scavenger feeds. Launder sprays help break the froth down.

f.q: Why does cleaner concentrate get the highest froth factor?
f.a:
The PDC gives froth factors of 2.0 for rougher concentrate, 1.6 for scavenger concentrate, 2.5 for cleaner concentrate and 2.0 for cleaner-scavenger concentrate.

In general, cleaner concentrate is the most heavily mineralised, with fine, high grade sulphide, about 35 percent S, and Jameson cells make very fine bubbles. Both make the froth more stable and harder to break down, so it carries more air into the pumps.

Scavenger concentrate is lightly loaded and its froth breaks more easily, hence the lowest factor. The PDC doesn't explain each number, so the process engineers could confirm the basis.

f.q: How do launder sprays help break down froth?
f.a:
The cards say screen and launder sprays use HP process water. Spray jets hit the froth in the launder, bursting bubbles and washing mineral down so the froth collapses into slurry before reaching the pump.

That reduces the air entering the pump and helps the slurry flow along the launder.

The trade off is extra water, which dilutes the concentrate and adds to downstream thickening load. It's like a defoaming spray on a tank: physical action breaks the foam.

'Froth factor' in the PDC?.q: What would you see in a handover if a concentrate line was airlocking?
'Froth factor' in the PDC?.a:
Something like "R1 con pump airlocking, hopper overflowing" or "cleaner con hopper frothing over, sprays on full". The reference doesn't fix wording.

Signs include pump discharge flow dropping or surging, motor current fluctuating, the pump hopper level rising even though the pump is running fast, and froth spilling over the hopper or launder.

Causes are usually a more stable froth than normal, from more frother or finer, richer concentrate, or launder sprays not working. The flotation operator would check reagent doses and sprays and adjust pump speed.

f.q: Why does air in a centrifugal pump cut its flow?
f.a:
A centrifugal pump adds energy by spinning liquid outward. Air collects at the eye of the impeller, where pressure is lowest, and forms a pocket the impeller can't push effectively. The pump then delivers less flow and head, or none at all.

Motor current drops because the pump is moving less mass. Flow becomes unstable as air pockets build and clear.

It's the same as a pump losing prime. In froth service, air keeps arriving, so the pump can lose flow repeatedly unless the air is released or the froth broken.

f.q: What do operators do to clear an airlocked froth pump?
f.a:
Common responses include adjusting pump speed, increasing launder or hopper sprays to break froth, reducing frother dose, and sometimes briefly stopping or slowing the pump to let air escape before restarting.

The reference doesn't give site procedures. Any field work on a pump needs the right isolation, and dump valves and interlocks must not be bypassed.

The flotation operator or CRO would know the usual approach here. If airlocking keeps recurring, it may point to a design or reagent issue worth raising with the metallurgist.

Why might a froth pump need a larger hopper?
When should a recurring airlock be escalated?

f.q: Why are froth pumps often a special design?
f.a:
Standard slurry pumps don't handle air well. Froth pumps often have larger inlets, open impellers, inducers or vertical designs that let air escape upward from the hopper rather than being dragged into the pump.

Some designs feed directly from a tall, narrow hopper so air rises out before slurry reaches the impeller.

The reference doesn't describe the concentrate pump types here. The P&IDs or maintenance planner would show which pumps are used. It's like choosing a self priming pump for a duty where air is expected.

Why do vertical pumps handle froth better?

'Froth factor' in the PDC?.q: How does froth factor influence concentrate pump sizing decisions?
'Froth factor' in the PDC?.a:
The designer calculates the concentrate slurry flow, then multiplies it by the froth factor to get the volumetric flow the pump and pipe must handle. With factors of 1.6 to 2.5, a pump may be sized for more than double the liquid flow.

That affects pump size, speed and inlet design, launder slope and width, and hopper volume so air can escape before the pump.

The aim is to stop pumps and launders airlocking or overflowing. It's like sizing a drain for peak storm flow rather than average: undersize it and it backs up.

f.q: How are concentrate hoppers sized to release air?
f.a:
The hopper needs enough volume and residence time for bubbles to rise and burst before slurry reaches the pump suction. A taller, larger hopper with a low downward velocity gives air time to escape.

Designers also position the pump suction low and away from the inlet, and sometimes add sprays above the hopper.

It's like a deaeration tank on a hydraulic system: slow the flow so entrained air can separate. The reference doesn't give concentrate hopper sizes, so check the F16 and F18 drawings.
f: Why does low downward velocity help air separate?
How is hopper level controlled on concentrate pumps?
What is the final concentrate hopper tag number?

f.q: Why does pipe slope matter for concentrate froth lines?
f.a:
Gravity launders and lines carrying froth need enough slope to keep slurry moving and avoid settling, while giving air a path to escape upward.

Too flat, and froth builds up, solids settle and the launder overflows. Too steep can cause splashing and erosion.

The PDC uses design lip loading and froth carry rates of 1.5 t/m/h and 1.5 t/m2/h for the cells, and froth factors for the lines. It's like drainage design: slope keeps things flowing.
f: What lip loading means for a flotation cell?

How are launder slopes checked during design?

f.q: What happens if a froth factor is set too low in design?
f.a:
The pumps, pipes or launders end up too small for the real froth volume. In operation, launders overflow, hoppers froth over and pumps airlock, especially when froth is stable.

Fixing it after construction is expensive: bigger pumps, modified hoppers or extra sprays. Operators may have to limit frother or mass pull to stay within capacity, costing recovery.

That's why designers use conservative factors. It's like undersizing a relief valve: fine most of the time, but it fails when you need it.

'Scats'?.q: Why do some rocks and balls resist grinding down in the ball mill?
'Scats'?.a:
Balls wear down gradually as they grind. Once they're small, they no longer grind well but are still hard steel, so they don't break up. They become part of the scats along with broken ball pieces.

Some rocks are much tougher than the rest of the ore. Particles that reach the ball mill at the coarse end of its feed, from cyclone underflow and gravity screen oversize, can round off without breaking, like pebbles in a SAG.

The ball mill trommel, with 19 x 40 mm slots, catches these, sending them to the scats bunker. It's like a strainer on a pump suction catching debris that won't pass through.

f.q: How do worn ball pieces get out of an overflow ball mill?
f.a:
An overflow ball mill has no grate. Slurry leaves by overflowing through the discharge trunnion. Worn and broken balls, once small enough, get carried out with the slurry.

The trommel on the discharge, 19 x 40 mm slotted, lets slurry through and catches the scats, sending them to the scats bunker.

It's like a weir with a screen: the liquid overflows, and anything too big is caught. Larger balls stay in the mill until they wear down.

f.q: Why can hard rock pieces survive in the ball mill?
f.a:
Ball mills grind by attrition and small impacts between balls. They're designed for fine material, not for breaking competent rocks. Tough pieces that arrive may just get rounded instead of broken.

Rock that reaches the ball mill comes from cyclone underflow, gravity screen oversize, and anything that slipped past the SAG discharge screen. Worn screen panels can let more coarse rock through.

These pieces build up unless removed, so the trommel and scats bunker take them out.

f.q: Do scats carry any gold worth recovering?
f.a:
Scats are mostly worn steel and tough rock. Gold content is typically low, so most plants dispose of them, but some test them from time to time.

The reference doesn't say what happens to scats here or whether they're assayed. If there's free gold trapped in rock pieces, it would be small.

The metallurgist would know whether scats are sampled and where they go.

'Scats'?.q: What would a handover mention if the scats bunker was filling too fast?
'Scats'?.a:
Something like "scats bunker filling fast, check trommel panels" or "high scats rate, possible ball breakage". The reference doesn't fix wording.

Possible causes include a burst of ball breakage, more coarse rock reaching the ball mill, for example through worn SAG discharge screen panels, or damaged trommel panels. A cards example notes worn SAG screen panels let pebbles report to the cyclone hopper.

The bunker needs emptying more often, and the cause should be investigated. The mill operator or maintenance planner would follow up.

f.q: How would worn SAG screen panels raise the scats rate?
f.a:
The SAG discharge screen, with 12 x 55 mm slots, keeps pebbles out of the slurry side. Worn panels let oversize through into the primary cyclone feed hopper.

That coarse material then reports to cyclone underflow and on to the ball mill, where tough pieces may survive and be rejected by the trommel as scats.

So a rising scats rate can be an early warning of SAG screen wear. It's like finding debris downstream of a damaged strainer.

f.q: Why might ball breakage suddenly increase?
f.a:
Ball breakage can rise with poor quality balls, a new ball supplier, or balls hitting liners directly when the mill load is low. Running at high speed with low load increases impact.

Broken pieces add to scats and the mill loses grinding media faster.

The metallurgist and maintenance team would check ball supply, mill load and speed. It's like a batch of brittle fasteners failing early: check the supply, then the operating conditions.

f.q: What happens if the scats bunker overflows?
f.a:
Scats spill around the trommel area, creating a housekeeping and safety hazard, and possibly backing up into the trommel discharge chute.

Steel and rock pieces on walkways are trip hazards, and cleaning up near a running mill needs care.

The reference doesn't give bunker size or alarms. The mill operator would know how often it's emptied and what alarms exist.

'Scats'?.q: How are scats removed and disposed of from the trommel?
'Scats'?.a:
The reference says the PFD shows a scats bunker by the ball mill trommel. Scats discharge from the end of the trommel by chute into the bunker.

The removal and disposal method isn't described. In general, a loader or skip lifts scats from the bunker, and they're taken to a scrap or waste area. Steel may be sold as scrap.

The mill operator or maintenance planner would know the actual process here. Working around the trommel and bunker needs care because the mill is running.

f.q: Why does the trommel use 19 by 40 mm slotted panels?
f.a:
The reference gives the ball mill trommel as 19 x 40 mm slotted. Slurry and fine particles pass through, while larger steel and rock pieces are carried along the trommel and out to the scats bunker.

The slot size is chosen to let normal mill product through while catching anything too coarse to pass on to the cyclone feed hopper and pumps.

It's like a coarse screen ahead of pumps: it protects downstream equipment from tramp material.

f.q: Is steel from the scats recycled as scrap?
f.a:
The reference doesn't say what happens to scats on this plant.

In general, worn steel balls and fragments are often separated and sold as scrap metal, especially where volumes are large. Rock content is usually dumped with other waste.

Steel recycling makes sense because the balls are high quality forged or cast steel, and scats volumes add up on a mill this size. Ask the mill maintenance planner or site environmental team for the actual disposal route.

f.q: What hazards come with emptying a scats bunker?
f.a:
Scats are heavy, sharp and irregular. Loaders and skips move them near a running mill, so traffic management and exclusion zones matter. Hand work risks cuts and crush injuries.

There's also noise, dust and slurry splash around the trommel.

Follow site procedures and PPE requirements. The reference doesn't give site specifics, so ask the area supervisor before doing any work near the scats bunker.

'EPC' in project documents?.q: Why do project documents distinguish the owner from the EPC contractor?
'EPC' in project documents?.a:
Because they carry different responsibilities. The EPC contractor engineered, procured and built the plant under contract. The owner operates it. Design documents, warranties and responsibility for defects are tied to who did what.

The project also has contract portions: SP1 and SP2, Separable Portion 1 and 2, covering Stage 1 and Stage 2 scope. DCS ownership is split into Greenfields Stage 1, Greenfields Stage 2, Brownfield modifications and Existing plant.

Knowing who's responsible tells you who to ask about a design question or defect. It's like knowing whether a machine is under the builder's warranty or your own maintenance.

f.q: What do SP1 and SP2 mean on the drawings?
f.a:
The reference says SP1 and SP2 on PFD legends mean Separable Portion 1 and Separable Portion 2, the Stage 1 and Stage 2 contract scope.

So a piece of equipment marked SP1 was part of Stage 1, and SP2 part of Stage 2. Stage 1 added the new crusher, SAG, ball mill, gravity, flotation and UFG 2. Stage 2 added CIL4, UFG 3, and repurposed CIL2 and CIL3.

That helps when tracing which contract, documents and warranties apply. It's like phases on a building project, each with its own handover.

f.q: What happens to EPC responsibility after handover?
f.a:
In general, after handover the owner takes over operation, but the EPC contractor usually stays responsible for defects during a defects liability period. Equipment warranties also apply for set periods.

During that time, defects are reported back to the contractor to fix. After it ends, the owner is fully responsible.

The reference doesn't give contract terms. The site project or engineering team would know what's still under warranty or defects liability.

The reference lists plant sections for DCS ownership: Greenfields Stage 1, Greenfields Stage 2, Brownfield, meaning modifications to the existing FIM plant, and Existing plant.

In general, splitting by ownership makes it clear who configured each part of the control system, who is responsible for changes, and which documents apply. Brownfield work touching existing systems needs careful coordination.

It's like a building with original, renovated and new wings: each has its own drawings and responsible parties.

'EPC' in project documents?.q: What would a handover reference if a drawing didn't match the built plant?
'EPC' in project documents?.a:
Something like "PFD shows different routing, redline raised" or "drawing not as built, checked in field". The reference doesn't fix wording.

When a drawing doesn't match, check its revision and status, then raise it through document control. Trust the field, but verify before acting.

f.q: What does as built mean on a drawing revision?
f.a:
As built means the drawing has been updated to show what was actually constructed, including any changes made during construction. Earlier revisions, such as issued for construction, show the design intent.

As built drawings are the reference for operations and maintenance. They're usually marked with a revision and status block.

Even as built drawings can have errors or miss later changes. Check the revision date and any later markups before relying on them.

The PDC is a design criteria document. Its older design basis uses 6 tanks x 1,685 m3, total 10,110 m3, for CIL3. Tank 62G was added in the enabling works, shown in the MEL Rev 0 Dec 2025 and the as built PFD Sep 2026.

So the PDC hasn't caught up with that change, or was written before it. The MEL and as built PFD reflect the current plant.

It's a reminder that design documents capture a point in time. Always check the most recent revision and cross check against other documents.

Most sites have a document control process. You mark up the drawing with the correction, a redline, and submit it to document control or the engineering team for review and update.

If the error affects safety or operation, also tell your supervisor immediately. Don't rely on an uncorrected drawing for isolations or work.

'EPC' in project documents?.q: How does SysCAD modelling tie into day to day plant operation?
'EPC' in project documents?.a:
SysCAD is the mass balance modelling software used in design. The PDC mass balance figures, flows, densities, mass pulls and recoveries, come from models like it.

Day to day, operators don't usually use SysCAD. They work with the DCS, PI historian and lab data. But the design numbers they compare against, such as mass pulls or flows, often originated in SysCAD.

Process engineers or metallurgists may use it for studies, such as testing new flowsheet options. It's like a design calculation for a machine: you don't run it every shift, but its numbers set the expectations.

f.q: What is a mass balance and why does the design need one?
f.a:
A mass balance tracks every tonne of solids, water and key elements, such as gold and sulphur, through the flowsheet. What goes in must come out.

It's needed to size every pump, tank, pipe and piece of equipment, and to predict recovery and reagent use.

It's like a heat and material balance for a chemical plant. The PDC figures, such as 3,146 t/h to flotation and 358 percent circulating load, come from it.

f.q: How do design mass balance numbers compare with live data?
f.a:
Design numbers are targets and sizing points, not live values. The reference stresses that PDC values are design criteria.

Live data varies with ore, operating choices and equipment condition. Mass pulls, flows, densities and recoveries move around. Comparing live data to design helps spot problems or opportunities.

It's like comparing a pump's datasheet duty point with its actual operating point: useful reference, but the real system rarely sits exactly on it.

'TQ' in project documents?.q: Why do design numbers get traced back through a formal TQ process?
'TQ' in project documents?.a:
A Technical Query is a formal question and answer between contractor and owner. It records a design decision, who made it, why, and when.

The card says many design numbers trace back to TQs, for example CIL4 carbon advance and the lime system design. That gives traceability: if someone later asks why a value was chosen, the TQ shows the reasoning.

It also protects both parties contractually. It's like keeping a change log on a machine design: you know what changed and why.

In general, a TQ records the question, who raised it, the reference documents, any proposed answer, the response from the other party, and the date and approval.

It might include attachments like calculations, data sheets or drawings. TQs are numbered and tracked in a register.

'Doré'?.q: Why does the goldroom add fluxes before smelting the sludge?
'Doré'?.a:
Cathode sludge isn't pure gold. It contains silver, copper, iron and other impurities. Fluxes such as borax, silica, soda ash and nitre combine with those impurities to form slag, a glassy layer that floats on the molten metal.

Fluxes also lower the melting point and help the metal separate cleanly. When poured, the denser gold and silver alloy sinks and the slag is removed.

The reference says electrowon sludge is dried and smelted with fluxes into doré bars. It's like using flux in soldering: it cleans the surface and carries away oxides.

f.q: What does nitre do in a gold smelting flux?
f.a:
Nitre, potassium or sodium nitrate, is an oxidiser. It oxidises base metals such as iron and copper so they move into the slag instead of staying in the metal.

Too much nitre can attack crucibles and oxidise silver. Too little leaves more impurities in the doré.

Flux recipes are set by goldroom staff based on sludge composition. The reference doesn't give the recipe here.

f.q: Why is the slag checked for gold before disposal?
f.a:
Some gold can be trapped in the slag as fine droplets or dissolved. Slag is usually crushed and assayed, and if gold content is significant, it's reprocessed, often returned to the milling circuit or resmelted.

That avoids losing gold in a waste stream. It's like checking used filter media for retained product before disposal.

The reference doesn't describe slag handling here. The goldroom supervisor would know the process.

f.q: Why is doré not pure gold?
f.a:
Doré is a gold and silver alloy, with some copper and other metals. EW plates silver and copper along with gold. ILR pregnant solution, for example, carries about 29 ppm silver and 303 ppm copper by design alongside the gold.

Smelting removes much of the base metal, but separating gold from silver needs a refinery. The reference says the refinery separates gold from silver and other metals.

So doré is an intermediate product, like a casting that still needs machining.

'Doré'?.q: What would a handover flag if a doré pour didn't match expected mass?
'Doré'?.a:
Something like "pour below expected, slag resmelt planned" or "doré mass discrepancy, reconciling with EW data". The reference doesn't fix wording.

Expected mass comes from gold in solution, EW records and sludge weights. Differences can come from moisture in the sludge, impurities, gold retained in slag or crucibles, measurement errors, or gold inventory still in the circuit.

Any discrepancy gets investigated because gold accounting and security matter. The goldroom supervisor and metallurgist would follow up.

f.q: Where can gold hide between the cells and the bar?
f.a:
Gold can stay on cathodes or in cell bottoms if harvesting isn't complete, remain in filter cloths, stay in sludge that hasn't been dried, or end up in slag and crucible linings.

There's also timing: gold in solution or on carbon may not have reached the goldroom yet.

Reconciliation checks each of these. It's like tracking inventory in a supply chain: stock can be in transit or in storage, not just lost.
f: How are crucibles checked for retained gold?
Why does incomplete harvest affect reconciliation?
How is gold in circuit inventory estimated?

f.q: How is the expected doré mass worked out?
f.a:
In general, gold accounting uses solution volumes and grades through EW, cathode sludge weights and assays, and historical recovery factors.

For gravity, ILR pregnant solution of about 14.5 m3 per batch at 1,100 to 1,800 ppm gives an estimate of gold to EW. For eluate, volumes and grades give similar estimates.

The reference doesn't detail the goldroom accounting. The metallurgist would know how expected mass is calculated.
f: How is gold in eluate measured before EW?
Why does sludge moisture affect gold estimates?
What is a monthly metallurgical reconciliation?

f.q: Who investigates a gold reconciliation difference?
f.a:
Usually the metallurgist, goldroom supervisor and site security, depending on the size and nature of the difference.

They review EW records, sludge weights, smelting logs, slag assays and security footage if needed. Most differences are explained by timing, measurement or retained gold, but security is always considered.

The reference doesn't give the site process. Ask the goldroom supervisor.
f: What security reviews follow a gold discrepancy?
How are smelting logs kept in the goldroom?
What threshold triggers a gold investigation?

'Doré'?.q: What equipment and safety controls surround the smelting furnace?
'Doré'?.a:
The reference doesn't describe the goldroom furnace. It says the goldroom is a high security area and that ores carry mercury, which loads on carbon.

In general, goldroom furnaces are induction or fuel fired, with fume extraction to capture metal fumes and mercury. Operators wear heat resistant PPE, face shields and respirators. Moisture near molten metal is a serious explosion risk, so moulds and tools must be dry.

Security controls include restricted access, CCTV and strict procedures. Ask the goldroom supervisor about the actual equipment and procedures.

f.q: Why is moisture near molten metal so dangerous?
f.a:
Water touching molten metal flashes to steam instantly, expanding about 1,700 times in volume. Trapped under or in molten metal, that steam can blow metal out violently, causing severe burns.

So moulds, tools and fluxes must be completely dry and preheated. Sludge must be fully dried before smelting.

It's one of the most serious hazards in any foundry. Follow goldroom procedures strictly.
f: How are doré moulds preheated before pouring?
Why must sludge be fully dried before smelting?
What PPE is needed for pouring molten metal?

f.q: Why does goldroom fume extraction matter for mercury?
f.a:
The cards say Goldfields ores carry mercury, which loads on carbon and comes off in the regeneration kiln, which has a mercury abatement system. Mercury can also travel with gold through elution and EW into the sludge.

When sludge is dried and smelted, mercury vaporises. Mercury vapour is toxic. Fume extraction and, often, a mercury retort before smelting capture it.

Ask the goldroom supervisor how mercury is managed here. Never bypass fume extraction.
f: What is a mercury retort and how does it work?
How is mercury exposure monitored in the goldroom?
Where does captured mercury end up?

f.q: How does an induction furnace heat the charge?
f.a:
An induction furnace uses an alternating current in a copper coil around the crucible. That creates a changing magnetic field, which induces currents in the metal, heating it from within.

It's clean, controllable and avoids combustion gases. The coil is water cooled, which is another reason to keep water and molten metal apart.

The reference doesn't say which furnace type is used here.
