Why are voids in a stockpile so dangerous?
How does the loader operator talk to the control room?

How is ore reclaimed from the new coarse.q: What would a handover flag if a reclaim tunnel feeder wasn't drawing evenly?
How is ore reclaimed from the new coarse.a:
Uneven draw usually means ore is not flowing evenly into one of the reclaim feeders. Common causes are ratholing, where a narrow channel forms above the feeder and empties while ore around it stays put, or bridging, where ore arches over the opening.

Segregation can also mean one feeder draws fines and the other coarse, so SAG feed size swings as the ratio changes. A handover would flag which feeder, symptoms such as erratic tonnage, high speed for low tonnes, or feed size changes on the SAG feed camera, and actions taken.

Note the design: each reclaim feeder is rated at 2,017 t/h, 110 percent of nominal, so one feeder can briefly cover the SAG on its own.

f.q: What is ratholing and why does it happen in stockpiles?
f.a:
Ratholing is when ore drains out through a narrow vertical channel directly above a feeder, leaving stable walls of ore around it. The feeder sees a column that empties quickly while most of the pile stays still.

It happens with cohesive ore, often wetter or clayey material, or when the pile has compacted. The live capacity you expected isn't available. It can be collapsed by changing draw rates, using the other feeder, or with a dozer, following site safety rules. Never walk on a pile over draw points, because voids can collapse.
f: How does moisture make ore more cohesive?
How would ratholing show up on the reclaim feeder trends?
Why is bridging over a feeder dangerous to clear?

f.q: Why does drawing from both feeders help with segregation?
f.a:
Each feeder draws from a different part of the pile, so each sees a somewhat different size mix. Drawing from both blends those streams on the SAG feed conveyor.

That gives a more consistent SAG feed than relying on one feeder alone. Changing the ratio between feeders can also nudge feed size coarser or finer if needed. In general, the SAG expert system and operators use the SAG feed camera size analyser to see the effect. The site practice for feeder ratios is best checked with the mill control room operator.
f: Can the expert system set the split between feeders?
What happens if one feeder trips while both are running?
Why does the SAG feed camera help feeder control?

f.q: Can one reclaim feeder supply the new SAG on its own?
f.a:
By design, yes for a while. Each reclaim apron feeder is rated at 2,017 t/h, which is 110 percent of the nominal new circuit mill feed of about 1,833 t/h.

So if one feeder is out, the other can carry the nominal rate, provided there is enough live ore above it. Running on one feeder concentrates draw on one part of the pile, making ratholing and segregation more likely and using up the live cone faster. These are design ratings, so actual capability depends on ore flow on the day.
f: How long would one feeder's live cone last on its own?
Why was 110 percent chosen as the feeder design margin?
What maintenance takes a reclaim feeder offline?

How is ore reclaimed from the new coarse.q: How does reclaim feeder speed control link to SAG mill feed rate?
How is ore reclaimed from the new coarse.a:
The reclaim feeders are controlled to a SAG feed weightometer tonnage setpoint or a mill weight setpoint, normally set by the SAG expert system. The feeders change speed to deliver the requested tonnes.

There's a delay between a speed change and the weightometer seeing it, and another before the mill load responds. The control philosophy builds in a deadband to stop the loop chasing this lag.

The expert system watches the SAG feed camera size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, load, speed and power, then adjusts the feed setpoint. It's a cascade: the expert system is the master, the tonnage loop the slave, and feeder speed the final element.

f.q: Why is a deadband used on the reclaim feeder control?
f.a:
There is transport delay between the feeders and the weightometer, and the mill responds slowly to feed changes. A controller with no deadband would see small errors, correct them, then overshoot as the delayed effect arrives.

The deadband tells the controller to ignore small deviations within a band. That avoids constant hunting of feeder speed, which wears drives and chains and upsets the mill. It's similar to tuning a slow temperature loop on a big heat exchanger: you don't react to every small wobble. The deadband value itself is set in the DCS tuning, not given in the reference.
f: How is the size of a control deadband chosen?
What is the transport delay from feeder to weightometer?
Why does the SAG mill respond slowly to feed changes?

f.q: What inputs does the SAG expert system use to set feed rate?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy: the SAG feed camera particle size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, mill load, mill speed and mill power.

The camera tells it if feed is getting coarser or finer, the noise monitor indicates whether balls and rocks are hitting liners or cushioned by charge, load shows how full the mill is, and power shows how hard it's working. It combines those to raise or lower the feed setpoint and possibly adjust speed or water. Operators can take control back if needed.
f: How does a noise monitor tell if a SAG is underloaded?
Can the expert system change SAG mill speed?
What does the CRO do when the expert system is off?

f.q: What is the difference between tonnage control and mill weight control?
f.a:
In tonnage control, the reclaim feeders hold a set tonnes per hour on the SAG feed weightometer. Feed is steady, but the mill load can drift up or down as ore hardness changes.

In mill weight control, the feeders vary their tonnage to hold the mill's load, measured through bearing pressure or load cells, at a setpoint. That keeps the mill operating in its best power region, accepting more feed when ore is soft and less when hard. The control philosophy allows either, normally with the expert system choosing.
f: How is SAG mill weight actually measured?
Why does harder ore make mill weight rise?
Which mode is better when ore hardness changes?

'Live capacity' of a stockpile is....q: Why does material outside the drawdown cone need a dozer to move?
'Live capacity' of a stockpile is....a:
Ore on a stockpile only flows by gravity into the reclaim feeders within a cone above each draw point. For the new pile the design drawdown angle is about 60 degrees.

Outside that cone, ore sits at a stable slope, held by friction between particles. Nothing pulls it toward the draw points, so it stays put even with feeders running. That is dead stock.

To use it, a dozer pushes ore into the live zone above the feeders, or a loader carries it to the emergency apron feeder. The amount of dead stock depends on pile geometry and how many draw points there are. It's similar to the unusable volume at the bottom of a tank below the suction nozzle.

f.q: What sets the drawdown angle at about 60 degrees?
f.a:
The drawdown angle depends on the ore's flow properties: particle size, shape, moisture and fines content. Coarse, dry, angular ore flows differently from wet ore with clay.

For design, engineers use testwork or typical values to choose an angle, and 60 degrees is the value in the design criteria for the new stockpile. On site, the effective angle changes with ore type and moisture, so live capacity can be bigger or smaller than design. If a particular ore type always seems to rathole, the metallurgist would want to know.
f: Why does wet ore flow worse than dry ore?
How is the drawdown angle measured on a real pile?
Does a steeper drawdown angle mean less live stock?

f.q: Why is live capacity quoted in both cubic metres and tonnes?
f.a:
Volume comes from the pile geometry: the design gives 12,035 m3 live. Tonnes depend on the bulk density of crushed ore, taken as 1.70 t/m3 for design.

So 12,035 m3 times 1.70 gives about 20,460 t, the figure usually quoted. Mill feed is in tonnes per hour, so tonnes is the useful figure for working out hours of feed. If bulk density changes with ore type or compaction, the tonnes held in the same volume change too.
f: What bulk density do different ore types have?
How does compaction change bulk density on the pile?
Why is the card's live capacity rounded to 20,000 t?

f.q: How does the existing FIM stockpile compare with the new one?
f.a:
The existing FIM coarse ore stockpile holds about 21,000 t live, roughly 16 hours of feed for the FIM SAG. The new one holds about 20,460 t live, roughly 11 hours for the new SAG.

The live tonnages are similar, but the FIM SAG draws less, about 1,313 t/h versus 1,833 t/h for the new SAG, so it gets more hours of buffer. They are separate piles fed by separate crushers, PC1 for FIM and PC2 for new. These are design values.
f: Why is the FIM SAG fed at a lower rate than the new SAG?
Can the two stockpiles share ore if one runs low?
How is the FIM stockpile reclaimed to its SAG?

'Live capacity' of a stockpile is....q: What would a handover flag if live capacity was running low on nightshift?
'Live capacity' of a stockpile is....a:
If live capacity is running low overnight, the handover should make the risk plain to the next shift. Note the estimated live stock and hours of feed left at current mill rate.

Then the reason: crusher down and why, truck shortages, or reclaim problems. Include what's been done or planned, such as calling for a loader to run the emergency feeder, dozing dead stock in, or reducing SAG feed to stretch it.

Also flag mill effects: segregation can cause SAG feed size swings as the pile empties. The design figure of about 11 hours live is an ideal value; the real buffer on a given night may be much less.

f.q: How do you estimate hours of feed left in the stockpile?
f.a:
Take the estimated live tonnes and divide by net draw: SAG feed rate minus crusher input. If the pile holds 6,000 t and the new SAG draws 1,833 t/h with the crusher stopped, that's a bit over three hours.

If the crusher is running at less than mill rate, the net draw is smaller and you get longer. The tricky part is knowing actual live tonnes, which come from level instruments and weightometer totals and can be off if the pile has ratholed. Check with the CRO how the inventory figure on screen is calculated.
f: How accurate is the stockpile tonnes figure on the OIS?
When should the crusher be restarted to avoid running out?
Why does ratholing make the estimate unreliable?

f.q: Why might the SAG feed be cut before the stockpile actually empties?
f.a:
As the pile gets low, segregation and erratic flow get worse, so SAG feed size and rate become unstable. The mill can overload or underload, and the expert system struggles.

Reducing feed earlier smooths this out and buys time for the crusher to restart. It also avoids drawing the pile so low that rock falls directly onto the reclaim feeder pans. In general, a slightly slower but steady mill gives better grind and recovery than a mill swinging from upset to upset. The metallurgist and supervisor make that call.
f: What happens to cyclone overflow grind when SAG feed drops?
How does the ball mill cope with less SAG discharge?
Why is steady feed better for flotation recovery?

f.q: What does running a SAG mill empty mean and why avoid it?
f.a:
If feed stops but the mill keeps turning, the rock in the charge grinds away and the balls are left with less cushioning. They then cascade straight onto the shell liners and lifters.

That impact damages liners and can break balls, a costly outcome in a mill of this size. The SAG noise monitor in the expert system is meant to detect this kind of liner impact. In general, if feed can't be sustained, the mill is slowed or stopped in a controlled way rather than run empty. Site procedures govern exactly how.
f: How does the SAG noise monitor detect liner impacts?
How does SAG speed affect where balls land?
What is the restart sequence for a stopped SAG?

'Live capacity' of a stockpile is....q: How do operators or crews manage dead stock buildup on the pile?
'Live capacity' of a stockpile is....a:
Dead stock builds up outside the drawdown cones over time and can compact. Common practice is to periodically use a dozer to push dead stock into the live zone, and to reclaim it through the emergency apron feeder using a loader.

Rotating which ore is drawn helps stop the edges of the pile becoming permanent. Compacted or segregated dead stock can behave differently when it finally reaches the mill.

The reference describes the emergency feeder and loader (CAT 992K or 994K) but not the routine for dead stock. Work on stockpiles carries serious risk from hidden voids over draw points, so it follows site procedures. Ask the crushing supervisor how this site manages it.

f.q: Why does dead stock tend to compact and segregate over time?
f.a:
Ore that sits still is loaded by the weight above it and by machines driving over it, so particles pack tighter. Fines fill gaps, and in wet weather moisture binds them.

Segregation happens when the pile is built: coarse rocks roll down the outside, so dead stock at the edges is often coarser. When it's finally pushed in, the SAG sees a change in feed size. Compacted ore also flows worse, increasing bridging. That's why sites try to keep ore moving rather than letting old stock sit for long periods.
f: How does rain affect a large coarse ore stockpile?
Why does coarse dead stock upset SAG mill load?
How often should dead stock be turned over?

f.q: What safety hazards come with dozing on a stockpile?
f.a:
This is general safety knowledge. The biggest hazard is voids: ratholes and bridges over draw points can be hidden by a crust of ore, and a dozer driving over one can fall in. People have been killed this way in the industry.

Other hazards are unstable slopes, poor visibility and interaction with conveyors and the feeders. Sites manage this with no go zones over draw points, isolation of feeders while working nearby, and specific procedures. Follow the site procedure and talk to the crushing supervisor before going anywhere near the pile.
f: Why are feeders isolated while a dozer works on the pile?
How do operators know where draw points are under the pile?
What training is needed to doze a stockpile?

f.q: Does dead stock ever need to be fully reclaimed?
f.a:
The reference doesn't cover this, so this is general practice. Sites sometimes reclaim dead stock fully before major tunnel or feeder maintenance, before long shutdowns, or to remove old segregated or oxidised material.

It's also done to inspect the stockpile floor, draw point openings and tunnel roof. It takes significant loader and dozer time and is normally planned well in advance. Whether and how often this site does it is a question for the crushing supervisor or area maintenance planner.
f: What inspections are done inside a reclaim tunnel?
How long does it take to empty a stockpile completely?
Why would oxidised ore be a problem for the plant?

What's the job of the wet scrubber / dus.q: Why does tipping large loads generate so much dust?
What's the job of the wet scrubber / dus.a:
A 250 t load drops several metres into the pocket in a few seconds. Two things make dust: crushed fines in the load are thrown into the air on impact, and the falling ore pushes a large volume of air out of the pocket, like a piston in a cylinder.

That displaced air carries fine particles up and out. Dry ore and windy conditions make it worse. The crusher itself also generates fines and air movement as rock is broken.

The wet scrubber and dust extraction fans pull dusty air from the pocket and crusher, wash out the particles, and discharge cleaner air. Per the control philosophy, the wet scrubber and dust extraction must run for crushing to operate.

f.q: Why does the falling ore push dusty air out of the pocket?
f.a:
The dump pocket is a confined space. A truckload of around 179 m3 suddenly takes up volume inside it, so roughly that much air has to go somewhere, fast.

It's pushed out of the top of the pocket in a gust, carrying fines with it. It's the same as a piston compressing air in a cylinder, only open topped. Dust extraction works by keeping the pocket under slight negative pressure so this air is drawn into the ducting rather than escaping. In general, extraction hoods are positioned to capture this displaced air.
f: How much air flow does a dust extraction fan need?
Why do some sites use curtains around dump pockets?
How do wind conditions affect dust escaping the pocket?

f.q: What health risks does crusher dust pose?
f.a:
In general, crushed rock dust contains fine particles that can be inhaled deep into the lungs. Respirable crystalline silica is the main concern in hard rock mining, as long term exposure can cause silicosis and other lung diseases.

Dust also reduces visibility around trucks and equipment and builds up on electrical gear. That's why there are exposure limits, monitoring and respiratory protection requirements. The specific mineralogy and exposure results for this site come from the occupational hygiene team, not the plant reference.
f: How is personal dust exposure monitored on site?
Why is respirable dust more dangerous than visible dust?
What respiratory protection is needed near the crusher?

f.q: Why is dust controlled by extraction rather than water sprays alone?
f.a:
Water sprays help by wetting the ore surface and knocking down some dust, but they can't capture the fine dust carried out by displaced air. Too much water can also make ore sticky and cause chute blockages and stockpile flow problems.

Extraction physically captures the dusty air and passes it through a scrubber, which gets much finer particles. Many sites use both. The plant reference names a wet scrubber and ventilation fans, but doesn't say whether sprays are also fitted at the pocket. Check the crushing P&IDs or ask the crusher control room operator.
f: How does a wet scrubber capture fine dust particles?
Why does extra moisture cause stockpile flow problems?
What happens to the dirty water from the scrubber?

What's the job of the wet scrubber / dus.q: What would a handover flag if the scrubber wasn't controlling dust properly?
What's the job of the wet scrubber / dus.a:
The control philosophy says the wet scrubber and dust extraction must run, so problems there affect crushing directly. A handover should flag what was seen and done.

Useful details: visible dust escaping at the pocket or crusher, scrubber or fan trips and their first out, low water flow or problems with the scrubber sump, and whether crushing was stopped as a result. Also note complaints from people working nearby or environmental alarms, and whether maintenance has been called.

It also matters for safety and environmental compliance, so supervisors need to know.

f.q: Why must the scrubber run before crushing is allowed?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, the wet scrubber and dust extraction must run with the crushing plant. In general, that's implemented as a start permissive or interlock: if dust control isn't running, crushing can't start or will stop.

The reason is health and environment. Crushing and tipping without dust control would expose people to high dust levels and breach emission limits. Treating it as a requirement rather than optional means no one is tempted to run without it. The exact interlock design is in the crushing control philosophy; it must never be bypassed.
f: What is the difference between a start permissive and an interlock?
Which process interlocks can be bypassed by named users?
How quickly does crushing stop if the scrubber trips?

f.q: What instruments would show a scrubber is underperforming?
f.a:
The reference doesn't list scrubber instruments, so this is general. Typical ones are differential pressure across the scrubber, water flow to sprays, sump level, fan motor current or speed, and duct pressure.

A falling fan current can mean a blocked duct or damper issue. Rising differential pressure can mean buildup. Low water flow means poor capture. Some sites also fit dust monitors at the discharge stack. Ask the crusher control room operator which signals appear on the OIS for this unit.
f: What does a rising pressure drop across a scrubber mean?
Why would fan motor current fall if a duct blocks?
Where are dust monitors usually located?

f.q: Who gets involved when dust emissions exceed limits?
f.a:
In general, the shift supervisor and crushing team deal with the immediate problem, maintenance fixes faulty equipment, and the site's environment and occupational hygiene people are notified because of licence and exposure limits.

Depending on severity, crushing may be stopped until dust control is restored. The reference doesn't describe the reporting chain or the licence conditions, so ask your supervisor or the environmental team what the site process is.
f: What dust limits apply under the site environmental licence?
How are dust exceedances recorded on site?
Can crushing continue with only partial dust control?

What's the job of the wet scrubber / dus.q: What maintenance keeps a wet scrubber and its fans working reliably?
What's the job of the wet scrubber / dus.a:
The reference doesn't give scrubber maintenance details, so this is general practice. Wet scrubbers mainly suffer from buildup and blockage.

Spray nozzles block with solids or scale. The scrubber sump fills with sludge that needs pumping or removing. Fan impellers can collect dust buildup, causing vibration, and bearings need lubrication and monitoring. Ducting wears through, especially at bends, which leaks air and cuts suction at the pickup hoods. Mist eliminators can blind and raise pressure drop.

Regular checks of water flow, pressure drop and fan vibration catch most issues early. Ask the crushing maintenance planner about the site routine.

f.q: Why does buildup on a fan impeller cause vibration?
f.a:
A fan impeller is balanced so its mass is evenly distributed around the shaft. When dust or sludge builds up unevenly on blades, or a chunk falls off, the centre of mass shifts.

At fan speed, that imbalance creates a rotating force that shakes the bearings and structure, just like an out of balance pump impeller. Over time it damages bearings and can crack the impeller or base. Cleaning, vibration monitoring and keeping the scrubber's mist eliminator working help prevent this.
f: How is fan vibration monitored on site?
What does a mist eliminator do in a scrubber?
Why does wet dust stick to fan blades?

f.q: Why do scrubber spray nozzles block?
f.a:
Scrubber water picks up dust and is often recirculated, so it carries solids that can lodge in small nozzle openings. Dissolved salts can also form scale, especially with saline water. This site's process water is saline, around SG 1.07, though the reference doesn't say which water feeds the scrubber.

Blocked nozzles mean poor contact between water and dusty air, so capture falls. Strainers, regular nozzle checks and controlling the solids in recirculated water help. Ask maintenance which water supply the scrubber uses here.
f: Why does saline water cause more scaling than fresh water?
How are scrubber nozzles cleaned or replaced?
What happens to the solids collected in the scrubber sump?

f.q: How does ductwork wear affect dust capture?
f.a:
Dusty air moving at speed is abrasive, especially at bends where particles hit the outer wall. Over time holes wear through.

Holes let outside air leak into the duct, so the fan pulls air through the leak instead of the pickup hoods. Suction at the dump pocket and crusher drops, and dust escapes. It's like a leak in a pump suction line reducing flow from the tank. Inspections of bends, wear liners at high wear points and prompt patching keep the system effective.
f: Why are duct bends lined with wear resistant material?
How is suction at a dust hood checked?
What air velocity keeps dust from settling in ducts?

What does 'Primary Crushing 1' vs 'Prima.q: Why does the plant run two separate primary crushing circuits at all?
What does 'Primary Crushing 1' vs 'Prima.a:
The Growth Project lifted throughput from the old FIM circuit's 10.5 Mtpa to about 25.5 Mtpa nominal. The existing PC1 crusher (F10), rated around 1,844 t/h, couldn't carry that alone, so a new PC2 gyratory (F12) was built in parallel.

The existing FIM SAG mill was retained, and PC1 still feeds its coarse ore stockpile. PC2 feeds a new stockpile for the new SAG. Keeping both made use of existing equipment rather than replacing it.

Two circuits also give some resilience: if one crusher is down, the other side keeps crushing for its own stockpile and mill.

f.q: Why was the existing crusher kept instead of replaced?
f.a:
The existing FIM SAG mill was kept as part of the new flowsheet, so it still needed its own crusher and stockpile. PC1 was already built and in service, so keeping it avoided spending on a crusher that wasn't needed.

The project added capacity where it was short: a new crusher, stockpile, SAG and pebble crushing for the new circuit. In general, brownfield expansions reuse what works and add new trains alongside. The project's actual decision papers aren't in the reference, so for detail ask the project team.
f: Why was the FIM SAG kept but the FIM ball mills retired?
What else in the old FIM plant was reused?
How old is the existing PC1 crusher?

f.q: How do the two crushers compare in size and power?
f.a:
From the design criteria: the new PC2 is an FLS 1300 x 1900 TSUV gyratory with a 165 mm open side setting, 38 mm throw and a 600 kW motor. It's designed for 3,135 t/h with a 3,436 t/h maximum.

The existing PC1 is a 54 to 75 Mk II gyratory, set at 141 mm open side setting with a 450 kW motor, crushing around 1,844 t/h. PC2 is larger in feed opening, power and throughput, matching the bigger new circuit it feeds.
f: Why does PC1 run a tighter setting than PC2?
Do both crushers take the same truck types?
What do the 54 and 75 in PC1's name refer to?

f.q: Which control room runs each crusher?
f.a:
The plant has two main control rooms: the FIM crusher control room and the main mill control building. Per the control philosophy, PC2 is run from the existing crusher control room, using CCTV to see the dump pocket, crusher and rock breaker.

The reference implies PC1 is also controlled from that crusher control room, since it is the existing crusher. The new SAG and grinding circuit are run from the main mill control building. Ask the crusher CRO how screens are split.
f: How do the crusher and mill control rooms communicate?
What CCTV views does the crusher operator have?
Can the crusher be operated from the mill control room?

What does 'Primary Crushing 1' vs 'Prima.q: What would a handover flag if PC1 was down and PC2 had to cover more feed?
What does 'Primary Crushing 1' vs 'Prima.a:
If PC1 is down, the FIM SAG relies on its own coarse ore stockpile, about 21,000 t live, around 16 hours at its design rate. PC2 feeds only the new stockpile, so it can't directly top up the FIM SAG side in the documented flowsheet.

A handover would flag PC1 status and expected return, the FIM stockpile level and hours left, any plan to reduce FIM SAG feed, and whether mine dispatch is sending more trucks to PC2 to keep the new pile full.

If PC1 is down for long, the shared ball mill and cyclones will see less total feed, which affects grind and flotation. The metallurgist will want to know.

f.q: Can PC2 product be sent to the FIM SAG stockpile?
f.a:
The reference describes PC2 feeding only the new coarse ore stockpile through its stockpile feed conveyor, and PC1 feeding the FIM stockpile. It doesn't mention any conveyor or chute link between them.

So based on the documents I have, no direct route exists. Whether there is any workaround, such as hauling crushed ore by loader, isn't covered. Ask the crushing supervisor or check the crushing PFDs for F10 and F12.
f: Which PFDs show the F10 and F12 conveyor routes?
What is area F15 Mt Charlotte stockpile used for now?
How would ore be hauled between stockpiles if needed?

f.q: How long can the FIM SAG run on its own stockpile?
f.a:
By design, the existing FIM coarse ore stockpile holds about 21,000 t live, which the design criteria give as around 16 hours at the FIM SAG's nominal 1,313 t/h.

Actual hours depend on how full the pile is and the actual FIM SAG feed rate. Beyond live stock there's dead stock that would need moving into the live zone. The reference doesn't describe an emergency feeder for the FIM stockpile, only for the new one, so check with the crushing supervisor what options exist on that side.
f: Does the FIM stockpile have its own emergency feeder?
How is the FIM stockpile reclaimed to its SAG?
What happens to the ball mill if the FIM SAG stops?

f.q: What reline scenarios change how the two SAGs run?
f.a:
The design criteria describe three: during a ball mill reline, the new SAG runs single stage, meaning without the ball mill. During a FIM SAG reline, the new SABC circuit runs on its own. During a new SAG reline, the FIM SAG runs with the new ball mill.

So each major mill can be relined while part of the plant keeps running. Feed to the crushers and stockpiles changes accordingly. Throughput is lower in each case, and grind is coarser in single stage.
f: Why does single stage SAG operation give a coarser grind?
How long does a SAG reline usually take?
Which crusher feeds the ball mill during a new SAG reline?

What does 'Primary Crushing 1' vs 'Prima.q: How do PC1 and PC2 stockpiles feed into the shared grinding circuit?
What does 'Primary Crushing 1' vs 'Prima.a:
Each primary crusher feeds its own stockpile and SAG. PC1 feeds the FIM coarse ore stockpile, reclaimed onto the FIM SAG feed conveyor to the existing FIM SAG (area F19). PC2 feeds the new stockpile, reclaimed onto the new SAG feed conveyor (area F13).

The two SAG circuits then join. The FIM SAG discharge is pumped by the duty/duty FIM mill transfer pumps from its discharge hopper to the new primary cyclone feed hopper. The new SAG discharges to the same hopper. From there, one set of cyclones and the new ball mill handle the combined feed, about 3,146 t/h nominal.

So crushing is split, grinding is partly split, and classification is shared.

f.q: Why is the FIM SAG discharge pumped rather than gravity fed?
f.a:
The FIM SAG sits in the existing plant, while the new primary cyclone feed hopper is in the new milling area. Slurry can't flow uphill or across that distance by gravity, so it's pumped.

The design uses duty/duty FIM mill transfer pumps from the FIM SAG discharge hopper, at a transfer density of about 60 percent solids. Duty/duty means both pumps normally run, sharing flow. These pumps are interlocked so they stop if the primary cyclone feed pump isn't running, protecting the hopper from overflowing.
f: Why are the transfer pumps duty/duty not duty/standby?
What happens to FIM SAG if the transfer pumps trip?
Why is transfer density lower than SAG discharge density?

f.q: What happens to the transfer pumps if the cyclone feed pump stops?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, the FIM mill transfer pumps are interlocked if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running. So they stop.

That stops slurry being pumped into a hopper that has nothing taking it out, which would overflow and cause a spill. The FIM SAG then has nowhere to send its discharge, so it would need to be stopped or fed less. It's a downstream to upstream cascade trip, just like conveyors.
f: What is the restart order after a cyclone feed pump trip?
How big is the primary cyclone feed hopper?
Why are slurry spills so costly to clean up?

f.q: How is total feed to the cyclones split between the two SAGs?
f.a:
In the nominal design case, the FIM SAG takes about 1,313 t/h and the new SAG about 1,833 t/h, giving 3,146 t/h to the cyclones and flotation. In the high throughput case it's about 3,494 t/h.

The split is set by each SAG's feed rate, which each expert system controls from its own stockpile. In practice the split changes with ore hardness, mill availability and relines. These are design values; check the OIS for current rates.
f: Why does the new SAG take more feed than the FIM SAG?
How does the cyclone circuit cope with feed swings?
Can the ball mill handle feed from only one SAG?

The plant now has two SAG mills. How do.q: Why do both SAG mills discharge to a shared cyclone feed hopper?
The plant now has two SAG mills. How do.a:
The Growth Project built one new classification and ball milling circuit for the whole plant rather than two separate ones. The FIM ball mills were made redundant, and a single new 20 MW ball mill and one Weir 800CVX cyclone cluster take discharge from both SAGs.

Sending both SAG discharges to the same primary cyclone feed hopper means the cyclones see one combined stream of about 3,146 t/h of new feed, plus the circulating load from the ball mill. The overflow goes to one set of trash screens and then flotation.

It's like two pumps discharging into a common header feeding one heat exchanger: simpler than two trains, with one set of controls, but both mills now depend on that shared equipment.

f.q: Why were the old FIM ball mills retired instead of reused?
f.a:
The reference states that the FIM ball mills, along with the Mt Charlotte plant and old FIM flotation, were made redundant in Stage 1, but it doesn't give the reasoning.

In general, one large modern ball mill tends to be more energy efficient and cheaper to maintain than several older small ones, and it lets the plant run a single classification circuit sized for the new grind target. The old mills' size, condition and location may also have played a part. For the actual decision, ask the project process team or check the study documents.

f.q: How does the primary cyclone feed hopper level control work?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, the cyclone feed pump runs in a cascade from hopper level to a cyclone pressure setpoint, and knife gate valves open or close cyclones when pressure stays high or low for a set time.

Hopper water addition controls cyclone feed or overflow density, and the level loop has Fast and Slow tuning. The general plant scheme for dual hopper level control uses pump speed at a higher level setpoint and water addition at a lower one, to keep minimum line velocity. Think of the hopper as a surge tank with two final elements: pump speed and makeup water.
f: What does Fast and Slow level tuning mean on the hopper?
Why must slurry lines keep a minimum velocity?
What happens if the cyclone feed hopper overflows?

f.q: What does the 358 percent circulating load mean?
f.a:
Circulating load is the cyclone underflow returned to the ball mill, expressed as a percentage of the new feed leaving in the overflow. The design figure is 358 percent, so for every tonne of product going to flotation, about 3.6 tonnes of coarse underflow goes back around.

That's why the cyclone feed is around 14,400 t/h of solids even though new feed is only about 3,146 t/h. A high circulating load keeps the ball mill working on coarse material and gives sharp size control. It's a design value; the real number moves with ore and cyclone settings.
f: Why does a higher circulating load help grinding efficiency?
How is circulating load calculated from plant data?
Why does gold build up in the circulating load?

The plant now has two SAG mills. How do.q: What would a handover flag if the shared ball mill circuit became overloaded?
The plant now has two SAG mills. How do.a:
When the ball mill circuit is overloaded, the classic signs are high ball mill power, rising cyclone feed pressure with more cyclones opened by the knife gate logic, a high or unstable cyclone feed hopper level, and a coarser cyclone overflow. In bad cases cyclones rope or the ball mill trommel rejects more scats.

A handover would say which signs were seen, what was done (usually reducing feed to one or both SAGs), and the cause if known, such as harder ore or a mill or cyclone problem.

Because both SAGs feed this circuit, it's important to record which SAG's feed was changed. Grind targets are design values (P80 180 um, max 250 um), so state what the grind actually did.

f.q: Which SAG feed would normally be cut to unload the ball mill?
f.a:
The reference doesn't set a rule for this. Either SAG could be cut, and the choice would depend on which mill is producing more coarse transfer, ore hardness, which SAG is closest to its own limits, and what the metallurgist wants for overall throughput.

In general, operators trim the mill that gives the quickest relief with the least loss of tonnes. The SAG expert systems and the main mill control room operator handle this day to day, so ask the CRO or metallurgist how it's normally done here.
f: How does each SAG's transfer size affect the ball mill?
Can the expert system manage both SAGs together?
What does the metallurgist look at to choose a feed cut?

f.q: How does cyclone feed pressure show the circuit is overloaded?
f.a:
More slurry going to the cyclones raises the pressure at the cluster inlet. Design feed pressure is about 82 kPa. Per the control philosophy, when pressure stays high for a set time, the knife gate logic opens another cyclone to bring it back down.

With about 12 primary cyclones operating nominally and a maximum of 14, running near the maximum with pressure still high means the cluster has no more room. It's like a pump header where all the parallel users are open and pressure keeps rising: the supply is too big for the system.
f: Why is the maximum 14 primary cyclones and not all 15?
What happens to the grind when pressure gets too high?
How does the CRO see how many cyclones are open?

f.q: Why does an overloaded ball mill produce a coarser grind?
f.a:
In an overloaded circuit, slurry passes through the ball mill faster, so each particle spends less time being ground. More coarse material comes out, the cyclone underflow grows, and the circulating load climbs.

The cyclones then struggle with the extra solids and start sending coarse particles to overflow. Ball mill power doesn't keep rising with load forever either. It's like pushing too much flow through a heat exchanger: residence time drops and outlet temperature misses target. Reducing new feed restores residence time.
f: How is ball mill residence time estimated?
What does ball mill power do when the mill overloads?
Why does a coarser grind reduce flotation recovery?

The plant now has two SAG mills. How do.q: How do the FIM mill transfer pumps affect combined feed control?
The plant now has two SAG mills. How do.a:
The FIM SAG's discharge reaches the new circuit only through the duty/duty FIM mill transfer pumps, which lift slurry from the FIM SAG discharge hopper to the new primary cyclone feed hopper at about 60 percent solids.

So any change in FIM SAG output or transfer pump flow shows up directly at the cyclone feed hopper. The hopper's level and water addition loops have to absorb it, and cyclone pressure and density swing.

The transfer pumps are also interlocked to stop if the primary cyclone feed pump isn't running. If the cyclone feed pump trips, the FIM side stops sending slurry too, which in turn affects the FIM SAG. The transfer pumps link the two circuits' control behaviour.

f.q: Why is the FIM transfer density only 60 percent solids?
f.a:
The FIM SAG discharges at a high density, but long transfer lines need slurry that pumps reliably without settling or excessive friction. Diluting to about 60 percent solids lowers viscosity and helps keep particles suspended.

In general, there's an optimum: too dilute wastes pump capacity on water, too thick risks line blockage and high pump power. The transfer density is the design value; the water is added at the FIM SAG discharge hopper, and the cyclone feed hopper water addition then sets cyclone feed density.

How does slurry viscosity change with solids density?
What causes slurry lines to block?

f.q: What happens if one transfer pump trips while both run duty/duty?
f.a:
The reference describes the FIM mill transfer pumps as duty/duty but doesn't say whether one can carry full flow alone. In general, with duty/duty pumps, losing one means the remaining pump can't carry the full flow, so the FIM SAG discharge hopper level rises.

The usual response would be reducing FIM SAG feed until both pumps are back. If a single pump can carry the flow, that just loses redundancy. Check the pump datasheets or ask the mill control room operator how this pair behaves.
f: Why choose duty/duty instead of duty/standby here?
How does the FIM SAG respond to a high discharge hopper level?
What is checked before restarting a tripped slurry pump?

f.q: Why does a cyclone feed pump trip stop the FIM transfer pumps?
f.a:
The primary cyclone feed pump is the only way slurry leaves the cyclone feed hopper. If it trips and the transfer pumps kept running, slurry from the FIM SAG would keep arriving in a hopper with no outlet and overflow it.

So the control philosophy interlocks the transfer pumps to stop when the cyclone feed pump isn't running. It's a downstream to upstream trip, just like conveyors in series. The FIM SAG then has to be slowed or stopped because its discharge has nowhere to go.

What happens to SAG discharge screen ove.q: Why are critical size rocks so hard for the SAG to grind on its own?
What happens to SAG discharge screen ove.a:
Critical size rocks sit in an awkward size range, roughly 12 to 75 mm. They are too small to act as useful grinding media because they don't have enough mass to break other rocks when they fall. But they are big and strong enough that the falling charge doesn't break them quickly either.

So they tend to accumulate in the mill. The charge fills with rocks that take up volume and power without breaking efficiently, and throughput falls.

Pulling them out through the 75 mm pebble ports and screening them off as SAG discharge screen oversize, then crushing them, breaks that bottleneck. It's a bit like removing a recirculating flow that's choking a pump.

f.q: Why do pebbles build up in the SAG if they aren't removed?
f.a:
Each pass through the charge breaks only a small fraction of critical size rock. New feed keeps adding more of it, from both the crusher product and the breakage of large rocks inside the mill.

If they couldn't leave, they would fill an increasing share of the mill volume. The mill load would rise, power would climb toward its limit, and the operator or expert system would have to cut feed. Removing them through the grate and crushing them separately keeps the charge balanced.

f.q: How do the pebble ports and discharge screen pick out pebbles?
f.a:
The SAG's discharge grate has 75 mm pebble ports, so rocks below that size can leave along with the slurry. Pulp lifters carry the discharge to the trunnion.

Discharge then goes over a horizontal vibrating screen, 4.27 x 8.54 m with 12 x 55 mm slots. Slurry and fines pass through to the cyclone feed hopper, while oversize, about 375 t/h in the design, goes to pebble crushing. The design also lists a trommel on the SAG discharge with 12 x 40 mm apertures. Together they set the pebble size range of about 12 to 75 mm.
f: Why are the screen apertures slots rather than square holes?
What happens if the SAG discharge screen deck tears?
How is screen oversize conveyed to the pebble crushers?

f.q: What size do pebbles come out of the pebble crushers?
f.a:
From the design criteria: the XL7 cone crushers take a feed F80 of about 49 mm and crush at a closed side setting of about 7 mm, giving a product P80 of about 12 mm.

At that size the crushed pebbles are no longer critical size. They break easily and pass the SAG discharge grate quickly, then report to the cyclones and ball mill. That's why returning them to SAG feed doesn't simply recreate the problem. These are design figures; actual product size depends on liner wear and setting.
f: Why is the pebble crusher feed F80 about 49 mm?
How quickly does CSS open up as the liners wear?
Why not crush pebbles even finer than 12 mm?

What happens to SAG discharge screen ove.q: What would a handover flag if pebble crushers were struggling to keep up?
What happens to SAG discharge screen ove.a:
If the pebble crushers fall behind, pebble feed bins fill. Each crusher has a 65 t bin, and the feeders start on bin high and stop on low. When a bin is High and both feeders are stopped, or reaches High High, the bypass gate opens and pebbles skip crushing.

A handover would note bypass events and duration, crusher condition (power, setting, liner wear, trips), whether metal detection was causing bypasses, and the effect on the SAG, usually rising load and lower throughput.

The design allows up to 610 t/h of pebbles across both crushers, so a bypass at lower loads suggests a crusher problem rather than simply high pebble load.

f.q: What happens to pebbles when the bypass gate opens?
f.a:
When the bypass gate opens, pebbles skip the cone crushers and return to SAG feed uncrushed. The control philosophy describes automatic bypass on metal detection and the bin level conditions; the documents describe a bypass route around the crushers.

Uncrushed pebbles are still critical size, so they add to the SAG's load without being broken. A short bypass is fine, but a long one leads to a building charge and lower throughput. The exact discharge point of the bypass is on the pebble crushing PFD.
f: Which PFD shows the pebble bypass route?
How does the gate return to the crushing route?
How long can the SAG tolerate full pebble bypass?

f.q: How do the pebble crusher feed bins and feeders work?
f.a:
There are two 65 t feed bins, one per crusher. Per the control philosophy, each feeder starts when its bin reaches high level and stops at low level, so the crusher sees batches of steady choke feed rather than a trickle.

The bins absorb short term swings in pebble flow and give a protective buffer when a crusher stops briefly. Their high and High High levels also trigger the bypass gate. It's essentially an on/off level control with hysteresis, like a sump pump starting high and stopping low.
f: Why use on/off level control rather than continuous feed?
What happens to the crusher when its feeder stops?
How is the bin level measured with rocks falling in?

f.q: Why does recycling uncrushed pebbles hurt SAG throughput?
f.a:
Uncrushed pebbles go back into the SAG as critical size material, which is exactly what the mill struggles with. They take up charge volume and power without breaking quickly.

The mill load climbs, bearing pressure and power rise, and the expert system has to reduce fresh feed to stop it overloading. It's like recirculating part of a pump's discharge back to suction: the pump works just as hard but delivers less useful flow. That's why pebble crusher availability matters so much for SABC throughput.
f: How much throughput is typically lost during pebble bypass?
Why does SAG power rise when pebbles build up?
What does the SAG noise monitor show with high load?

What happens to SAG discharge screen ove.q: How does returning crushed pebbles to SAG feed change mill throughput?
What happens to SAG discharge screen ove.a:
Crushing pebbles from about 49 mm F80 to 12 mm P80 converts them from hard to grind critical size into material that the SAG breaks and discharges quickly. That frees mill volume and power for fresh feed, so the SAG can accept more new ore.

That's the core idea of an SABC circuit: SAG, ball mill, pebble crusher. The pebble crushers take on work the SAG is poor at, using far less energy per tonne for that size range.

The cost is a higher recirculating load through the SAG. Pebble load in the design is about 16.6 to 28 percent of new feed, so the SAG handles more total tonnes, but most of that extra passes through quickly.

f.q: Why are crushed pebbles returned to the SAG and not the ball mill?
f.a:
Per the reference, crushed pebbles return to SAG feed. At about 12 mm P80 they're still coarse for a ball mill, which works best on finer material and would need larger balls to break them.

Returning them to the SAG lets the large charge finish breaking them and then pass them through the grate at transfer size. Some circuits do send crushed pebbles to the ball mill, but it depends on ball mill size and grind targets. The design team's specific reasoning isn't in the reference.

f.q: How much of the new SAG feed is recycled pebbles?
f.a:
The design criteria put pebble load at about 16.6 to 28 percent of new SAG feed, depending on the design case. The nominal SAG discharge screen oversize is about 375 t/h.

The pebble crushers are sized for 305 t/h each at a 7 mm setting, 610 t/h total, which leaves room for higher pebble loads as the 75 mm pebble ports wear larger. Actual pebble rates on site depend on ore hardness, grate condition and SAG operation.

How is pebble rate trended in PI?

f.q: What is an SABC circuit and why use it here?
f.a:
SABC stands for SAG, Ball mill, pebble Crusher. The SAG does the coarse breakage, the pebble crushers handle the critical size rocks, and the ball mill finishes grinding to the target, here P80 180 um nominal with a maximum of 250 um.

It suits competent ores where a SAG alone would build up critical size material. It also allows very high throughput with fewer machines. On this plant both SAGs feed a shared ball mill, and each SAG has its own pebble crushers.
f: Why do competent ores produce more critical size rock?
Does the FIM SAG have its own pebble crushers?
What does single stage SAG operation mean?

What type of pebble crushers are used on.q: Why run pebble crushers in a duty duty pair instead of duty standby?
What type of pebble crushers are used on.a:
Pebble load can be much higher than nominal. Each XL7 is rated at about 305 t/h at a 7 mm closed side setting, so both together give 610 t/h. The design SAG discharge screen oversize is about 375 t/h, and more as the 75 mm pebble ports wear larger.

So a single crusher couldn't handle the full range on its own, and both are needed for the design. Running both also means each runs below capacity at normal loads, which helps product size consistency.

The downside is no installed spare. If one crusher stops, the other carries part of the load and the rest is bypassed back to the SAG uncrushed.

f.q: What happens if one pebble crusher is down for maintenance?
f.a:
The remaining crusher can handle up to about 305 t/h at its design setting. With nominal pebble load around 375 t/h, the excess would need to be bypassed back to the SAG uncrushed or the SAG feed reduced.

So taking one crusher down usually costs some SAG throughput, more if pebble ports are worn. Maintenance would ideally be timed for when pebble load is lower or during a SAG stop. The site's plan for this is a question for the maintenance planner and metallurgist.
f: How long does a typical cone crusher liner change take?
Is SAG feed reduced or pebbles bypassed during maintenance?
Can pebble maintenance be done during a SAG reline?

f.q: Why is each crusher rated 305 t/h at a 7 mm setting?
f.a:
Cone crusher capacity depends strongly on the closed side setting. A tighter gap means each rock has to be broken smaller before leaving, so less material passes per hour. The design states 305 t/h each at a 7 mm setting.

Running wider would give more tonnes but coarser product; running tighter, fewer tonnes and higher power. The 375 kW motor and the liner profile also limit capacity. Vendor curves give exact figures for the XL7.
f: How does product size change if CSS opens to 10 mm?
What limits a cone crusher's power draw?
How is a cone crusher's setting adjusted?

f.q: How is pebble feed split between the two crushers?
f.a:
The design gives each crusher its own 65 t feed bin and feeder. Feeders start on bin high level and stop on low level.

How the pebble stream is divided between the two bins isn't spelled out in the reference. In general, it's done with a splitter or diverter so each bin gets a share. Check the pebble crushing PFD or ask the mill control room operator.
f: What is the pebble crusher PFD drawing number?
What happens if one bin fills faster than the other?
Can all pebbles be sent to one crusher?

What type of pebble crushers are used on.q: What would a handover flag if pebble load rose above the design range?
What type of pebble crushers are used on.a:
Pebble load above about 16.6 to 28 percent of new feed, or approaching the 610 t/h crusher limit, needs a note at handover. Common causes: worn and enlarged SAG pebble ports, harder or coarser ore, or SAG operating changes.

Symptoms to flag: pebble bins running high, bypass gate operating, SAG load building, and throughput reduction. Note when it started, whether it matches a change in ore source or SAG speed, and when the grate was last changed.

If the trend is long term, it usually points to grate wear and feeds into reline planning. Remember the design range is not a guaranteed live value.

f.q: What raises pebble load besides worn pebble ports?
f.a:
In general: harder, more competent ore that produces more critical size rock; coarser SAG feed from the crusher or stockpile segregation; changes in SAG speed or ball charge that alter breakage; and a low ball charge leaving less impact energy.

Ore blend changes are a common culprit, because a single ore type can behave very differently from the average. The metallurgist and the mill CRO look at SAG feed camera data and ore source to work out the cause.

Why does a low ball charge raise pebble load?
How is ore hardness measured for the plant?

f.q: How is pebble tonnage measured?
f.a:
The plant uses weightometers on conveyors, with calibration chains, totalised per 12 hour shift and per day from 5:00 am. The reference doesn't name a specific pebble conveyor weightometer, though it's standard practice on pebble circuits.

To find the tag, look on the pebble crushing P&ID for a weightometer, WD in the equipment list, or ask the mill control room operator where pebble tonnes show on the OIS.
f: How are weightometers calibrated on site?
Why are totals reset at 5:00 am?
How accurate are belt weightometers on pebble conveyors?

f.q: Why does high pebble load affect the ball mill?
f.a:
Crushed pebbles go back to the SAG, which then breaks them further and discharges them as fine material to the cyclone feed hopper. Higher pebble loads mean more crushed material flowing through the SAG, which can change the size of SAG transfer to the ball mill.

When pebbles are bypassed instead, the SAG slows, so less fresh feed reaches the ball mill and the overall circuit balance shifts. In general, stable pebble load helps keep the ball mill and cyclones steady.

What type of pebble crushers are used on.q: What maintenance issues are specific to a 7 mm CSS cone crusher?
What type of pebble crushers are used on.a:
This is general practice; the plant documents don't give maintenance details. A 7 mm closed side setting is very tight, so small amounts of liner wear make a large relative change in the gap. Settings need frequent checking and adjustment to hold product size.

Liners (mantle and bowl liner) wear quickly on pebbles and need regular replacement. Tramp steel is a major risk at such a tight gap, so the hydraulic tramp release and the upstream magnets and metal detector are important. Packing can occur with fine or wet feed.

Lube oil condition, hydraulic system health and dust seals are other routine items. Ask the area maintenance planner for site intervals.

f.q: Why must the setting be checked so often on a pebble crusher?
f.a:
At a 7 mm setting, a couple of millimetres of liner wear is close to a 30 percent change in gap. Product gets coarser quickly, and crushed pebbles may no longer be fine enough to leave the SAG easily.

Regular measurement and adjustment, often automatic on modern cones, keeps the setting near target. The reference doesn't describe the XL7's control system, so check the vendor manual or ask the maintenance planner how setting is controlled here.
f: How is cone crusher setting measured during operation?
What happens to crusher power as the setting opens?
Why do pebbles wear liners faster than primary ore?

f.q: What is tramp release on a cone crusher?
f.a:
Tramp release is a protective system that lets the crusher's bowl or main shaft move away when something uncrushable, like steel, enters the gap. On modern cones it's usually hydraulic, with accumulators.

When force spikes, hydraulic pressure rises and the system yields, opening the gap so the object passes, then returns to setting. It's like a relief valve on a hydraulic circuit. It limits damage but repeated events still wear the crusher, which is why steel is removed upstream.
f: Why do accumulators matter in the tramp release system?
What damage can repeated tramp events cause?
How does the metal detector stop steel reaching the crusher?

f.q: Why does choke feeding matter for cone crusher liner wear?
f.a:
When a cone crusher is choke fed, the chamber is full and rock breaks against rock as well as liners. Wear spreads along the liner and product is consistent.

When it's starved, rock drops deep into the chamber and wears a band in one area, shortening liner life and changing the crushing profile. That's why the pebble feed bins run feeders on bin level: they send pebbles to the crusher in steady batches. It's similar to keeping a pump fully primed.
f: How does the feed bin keep the crusher choke fed?
What does uneven liner wear look like?
Why does product get coarser with a starved crusher?

Why are tramp magnets and a metal detect.q: Why does steel cause such large force spikes in a cone crusher?
Why are tramp magnets and a metal detect.a:
Steel doesn't break. When a worn grinding ball or other piece of steel enters the crushing gap, the mantle keeps closing but the steel won't fracture, so force rises sharply instead of rock breaking.

At a 7 mm closed side setting, even small steel pieces can't pass. The crusher's tramp release hydraulics yield to let it through, but the shock loads the main shaft, bearings, bowl and frame and can crack liners. Repeated events cause cumulative damage.

So SAG pebbles, which include broken and worn balls from the 125 mm SAG ball charge, pass tramp magnets and a metal detector first. On detection, an automatic bypass sends pebbles around the crushers.

f.q: Why does SAG discharge contain so many broken balls?
f.a:
The SAG ball charge uses 125 mm balls. As they wear down they get smaller, and some break or spall. Once small enough, they leave through the 75 mm pebble ports with the critical size rocks.

So the pebble stream always carries steel. More balls hitting liners directly, from an underloaded or fast running mill, can raise breakage. Ball quality also matters. The magnets in the pebble circuit remove most of this steel before the crushers.
f: How does SAG speed affect ball breakage?
What makes balls spall or break?
How is steel recovered from the pebble magnets?

f.q: How do tramp magnets remove steel from the pebble stream?
f.a:
In general, magnets sit above or at the head of the pebble conveyor. Steel is lifted off the belt and carried to a reject chute or bin, often by a self cleaning belt around the magnet.

The reference says pebbles pass tramp magnets before the crushers but doesn't give their type. Magnets don't catch non magnetic metals or steel buried under rock. That's why a metal detector follows as a backup, triggering bypass if steel gets through.
f: Why can't magnets catch all steel in a pebble stream?
How is the magnet reject bin emptied?
Why would manganese steel pieces escape the magnet?

f.q: Why is a metal detector needed as well as magnets?
f.a:
Magnets miss some steel: pieces buried under pebbles on the belt, non magnetic material such as manganese steel liner fragments, and objects too heavy to be lifted. A metal detector senses metal regardless of magnetism and depth.

Per the control philosophy, detection triggers an automatic bypass, so the slug of pebbles containing the metal skips the crushers. It's belt and braces, like having a relief valve plus a high pressure trip. Together they protect the crusher.
f: How does a metal detector sense metal on a belt?
Why is manganese steel non magnetic?
How long does the bypass stay open after detection?

Why are tramp magnets and a metal detect.q: What would a handover flag if the metal detector tripped repeatedly on a shift?
Why are tramp magnets and a metal detect.a:
A metal detector tripping repeatedly means steel is reaching it often, or it's tripping falsely. Each trip sends pebbles through the automatic bypass uncrushed, so many trips have the same effect as lost crusher capacity: rising SAG load and lower throughput.

A handover would note how many trips, any pattern, whether the magnets upstream are working and clean, and whether pieces found suggest broken balls, liner bolts or other parts. A sudden rise in broken balls or liner pieces can point to a SAG problem.

Never bypass or disable the detector to keep crushers running; ask maintenance and the instrument technician to check it.

f.q: Why might a metal detector trip falsely on a pebble conveyor?
f.a:
In general, false trips come from conductive ore or wet saline slurry on the belt, metal fasteners in belt splices, interference from nearby motors or cabling, sensitivity set too high, or physical damage to the detector coil.

On this site, process water is saline, SG about 1.07, which could affect sensitivity, though the reference doesn't link them. An instrument technician can check calibration and settings. Repeated false trips are a maintenance issue, not a reason to turn the detector off.

Who maintains the metal detector on site?

f.q: What does a rise in broken balls tell you about the SAG?
f.a:
More broken balls in the pebbles can mean balls are hitting liners directly instead of landing on the charge. That happens when the mill is underloaded or running too fast for the load, so balls are thrown onto bare liner.

It can also point to poor ball quality from a new batch. Both are worth flagging to the metallurgist. The SAG noise monitor, used by the expert system, is designed to detect liner impacts, so it's worth checking alongside.

Who checks grinding ball quality?
How is the SAG noise monitor used by the expert system?

f.q: How is the slug of metal removed after a bypass?
f.a:
When the detector trips, the automatic bypass diverts that section of pebbles around the crushers, so the metal travels with them back to SAG feed. In the SAG it gets worn down and comes out again later.

The reference doesn't describe a separate reject chute for detected metal. If an object is too large or recurs, maintenance may stop and isolate the conveyor to find and remove it. Ask the mill control room operator how it's handled here.
