Why do SAG lifters wear differently?
Can composite liners be used in SAGs?

Why use Poly-Met liners in the ball mill.q: What would a handover flag if liner wear was accelerating unexpectedly?
Why use Poly-Met liners in the ball mill.a:
Accelerating liner wear should be flagged with measurements, trend, and likely cause. Possible causes: harder or more abrasive ore, changes in ball size or quality, higher mill speed, low load causing balls to hit liners, or a bad liner batch.

Note when wear started increasing and any changes in operation. It may bring a reline forward, which affects production planning.

Tell maintenance and the metallurgist.

f.q: How is liner wear measured between relines?
f.a:
In general, liner wear is measured during planned shutdowns, using thickness gauges on lifters and plates, ultrasonic thickness readings from outside, or laser scanning of the inside of the mill. Laser scans give a full 3D profile and are becoming common on large mills.

The results are trended against tonnes processed to predict when liners will reach their minimum thickness, which then sets the reline date. The reference doesn't say which method this site uses, so ask the milling maintenance planner.
f: What is laser scanning for mill liners?
How often are liners measured?
What is the wear limit?

f.q: Why does running a mill faster wear liners quicker?
f.a:
Higher speed throws balls further from the shoulder. Past a certain point they fly over the charge and land directly on the shell liners at the toe instead of on the tumbling charge, so impact energy goes into steel and rubber rather than ore.

There's also more sliding and abrasion between charge and liner. That's why the ball mill normally runs at fixed speed, about 75 percent of critical, within its 60 to 78 percent range. The SAG's speed is varied by the expert system with liner protection in mind.
f: What is the ball mill speed range?
How does speed affect ball trajectory?
Why does slip cause abrasion?

f.q: What signs suggest a liner may fail soon?
f.a:
In general, maintenance watches for cracked or very thin liners at inspections, loose or broken bolts, slurry leaking from bolt holes on the shell, and liner pieces or bolt heads turning up in the scats or on the pebble magnets.

In operation, unusual knocking noise, changes in the noise monitor pattern, or changes in power draw at steady load can also hint at a problem. Liner failure can damage the shell and cause a long unplanned stop, so anything unusual should go to maintenance promptly.
f: How are loose liner bolts detected?
What does a liner failure cost?
How are liner pieces found in scats?

Why use Poly-Met liners in the ball mill.q: How does a liner change outage get planned around production?
Why use Poly-Met liners in the ball mill.a:
Relines are planned well ahead. The design criteria describe reline scenarios: during a ball mill reline, the new SAG runs single stage; during a FIM SAG reline, the new SABC circuit runs; during a new SAG reline, the FIM SAG runs with the new ball mill.

So part of the plant keeps running at reduced throughput. Planners schedule relines around production targets, ore availability and maintenance resources, with liners and reline machine ready.

Ask the maintenance planner for the reline schedule.

f.q: What does single stage operation mean during a ball mill reline?
f.a:
Single stage means the SAG mill runs without the ball mill. While the new ball mill is being relined, the design criteria say the new SAG runs single stage, with its product classified and sent on without ball milling.

The grind to flotation is coarser and throughput lower than normal SABC operation, so recovery drops for the duration. It's still better than stopping the whole plant. The metallurgist sets the operating targets for that period, and the length of the ball mill reline sets how long it lasts.
f: How coarse is the grind in single stage?
How does single stage affect flotation?
How long does a ball mill reline take?

f.q: Why aren't the two SAGs relined together?
f.a:
If both SAGs were down together, nothing would feed the ball mill and the whole plant would stop. The design criteria lay out reline scenarios so that only one mill is down at a time: during a FIM SAG reline the new SABC circuit runs, and during a new SAG reline the FIM SAG runs with the new ball mill.

So relines are staggered and the plant keeps producing at reduced rate. It's the same thinking as never taking both pumps of a duty/standby pair out at once.

What is the throughput during a SAG reline?
Can the FIM SAG run alone?

f.q: How are spare liner sets managed on site?
f.a:
The reference doesn't cover spares or stores. In general, mill liners are long lead items made to order, so sites order sets months in advance, hold at least one full set per mill in stores, and track which set goes into which mill at each reline.

The maintenance planner usually coordinates liner orders with the reline schedule and wear measurements. Ask the milling maintenance planner or the site stores team how it works here.

What happens to the gravity scalping scr.q: Why do the Knelsons need protection from oversize material at all?
What happens to the gravity scalping scr.a:
Knelson concentrators work by trapping heavy gold particles in riffles on a spinning bowl, kept loose by fluidising water. Coarse particles can block fluidising holes, wear the bowl and pack the concentrate bed.

The scalping screens, with 3.2 mm then 2.0 mm slots, remove oversize before it reaches the Knelsons. Oversize, about 10 percent in the design, goes back to ball mill feed, while undersize feeds the Knelsons.

It's like a strainer protecting a sensitive valve.

f.q: What top size can a Knelson concentrator handle?
f.a:
The reference doesn't give a feed top size for the KC-QS70 Knelsons. What it does show is that the gravity scalping screens cut feed at 3.2 mm slots on the first half of the deck and 2.0 mm on the second half, so Knelson feed is effectively finer than about 2 mm.

In general, centrifugal concentrators are fed below a few millimetres to protect the bowl and fluidising rings. For the exact vendor limit, check the Knelson vendor data or ask the metallurgist.
f: What does the Knelson vendor recommend for feed size?
Why does top size matter?
How is Knelson feed sampled?

f.q: Why does oversize affect the Knelson concentrate bed?
f.a:
Inside the Knelson, fine dense gold works its way into the fluidised bed held in the bowl's riffles, while lighter material washes over. That depends on the bed staying loose and evenly fluidised.

Coarse particles don't behave like that. They can wedge in the riffles, disturb or compact the bed, block the small fluidising holes and erode the bowl. The bed then holds less gold and lets more wash through. That's general Knelson behaviour, and it's why the scalping screens sit ahead of the concentrators.
f: How does the concentrate bed work?
What blocks fluidising holes?
How is bed compaction detected?

f.q: Why does oversize go to the ball mill rather than back to cyclones?
f.a:
Scalping screen oversize is coarse material that still needs grinding. Sending it straight to ball mill feed gets it ground. Returning it to the cyclone feed hopper would only send it back to underflow and around again.

Per the design criteria, gravity screen oversize, about 8 to 15 percent of screen feed with a 10 percent design figure, reports to ball mill feed. The screen undersize goes to the Knelsons, and Knelson tails go back to the primary cyclone feed hopper.
f: How much oversize goes to the ball mill?
Does oversize carry gold?
How is oversize conveyed?

What happens to the gravity scalping scr.q: What would a handover flag if scalping screens passed too much oversize?
What happens to the gravity scalping scr.a:
If the scalping screens pass too much oversize, coarse particles reach the Knelsons. Likely causes are torn or worn screen panels, the wrong panels fitted, or a screen overloaded with more flow than it can handle.

Effects to watch for: blocked fluidising holes, faster bowl wear, less concentrate per cycle and lower gravity recovery. A handover should say which screen and Knelson, what was seen (coarse material in Knelson feed or concentrate, changes in oversize tonnage), and what was done.

Pass it to maintenance for panel checks under isolation, and tell the metallurgist if gravity recovery may be affected.

f.q: How is a torn screen panel found and replaced?
f.a:
In general, torn panels are found by regular inspections on planned stops, or because oversize appears where it shouldn't, such as coarse material in the Knelson feed or concentrate.

Replacement is done with the screen stopped, isolated and locked out, because vibrating screens store energy and slurry lines can still be live. Modular panels usually pin or wedge into the deck frame and are swapped individually. Follow the site's isolation procedure, and ask the area maintenance planner for the inspection routine on these screens.
f: How often are screen panels inspected?
What causes screen panels to tear?
How long does a panel change take?

f.q: What happens if a gravity screen trips while running?
f.a:
Per the design criteria, each gravity cyclone's feed valve is interlocked to its gravity scalping screen. If the screen trips, the valve closes and that gravity cyclone stops sending underflow.

That stops slurry flooding a stopped screen and spilling. The matching Knelson then loses its feed. Primary classification continues on the other cyclones, so the main circuit keeps running, but gravity recovery falls until the screen is back. It's a downstream to upstream trip, like conveyors in series.
f: What happens to the Knelson when the screen trips?
How is the screen restarted?
Does the trip affect the primary cyclones?

f.q: Why would Knelson recovery fall with coarse feed?
f.a:
Coarse particles take up space in the riffles, disturb the fluidised bed and can block fluidising holes. With the bed compacted or uneven, fine gold can't penetrate it as easily and more gets washed through to tails.

Coarse feed also wears the bowl and rings faster. So more oversize reaching the Knelsons usually shows up as less concentrate per cycle or lower gold in it. Design gravity recovery is about 14 percent of feed gold, so a drop is worth flagging to the metallurgist.
f: How is Knelson recovery measured?
What is the design gravity recovery?
How does feed density affect Knelsons?

What happens to the gravity scalping scr.q: How do the two stage screen slot sizes work together to protect the circuit?
What happens to the gravity scalping scr.a:
The scalping screens have 3.2 x 18 mm slots in the first half and 2.0 x 18 mm slots in the second half. The first half removes water and most fines with larger openings, handling the bulk flow. The second half gives a finer cut on what remains.

Oversize, 8 to 15 percent, design 10 percent, goes to ball mill feed. Undersize goes to the Knelsons.

It's two stage filtering on one deck.

f.q: Why use slotted apertures rather than square holes here?
f.a:
Slots give more open area than square holes for the same cut size, so slurry drains faster and the screen handles more flow. They also blind less, because near size particles are less likely to wedge in a long slot than in a square hole.

The trade off is that slots let some elongated particles through lengthwise. For protecting Knelsons, that's acceptable. The gravity screens use 3.2 x 18 mm and 2.0 x 18 mm slots. That's general screening practice.
f: What is screen open area?
Why do slots blind less?
How are slots oriented on the deck?

f.q: What does a design oversize of 10 percent mean for the screens?
f.a:
It means about 10 percent of the solids fed to each gravity scalping screen is expected to report to oversize, with a range of 8 to 15 percent. The other 90 percent or so passes through to the Knelsons.

Each Knelson is designed for up to 1,000 t/h, nominal 900 t/h, so the screens handle a bit more than that each. If oversize climbs well above 15 percent, either the feed is coarser or the panels are blinding. If it drops, panels may be torn and passing coarse material.
f: How is screen oversize measured?
What feed rate do the screens take?
Why is oversize range 8 to 15 percent?

f.q: Why are the gravity screens horizontal rather than inclined?
f.a:
Horizontal vibrating screens move material along by the vibration angle rather than by deck slope, so slurry stays on the deck longer. That gives more time for water and fines to pass through and a more accurate size cut.

Inclined screens move material faster and suit high capacity dry screening. For a wet slurry duty where the aim is accurate sizing and dewatering ahead of Knelsons, horizontal screens are a common choice. The gravity screens are 3.66 x 6.10 m horizontal vibrating units per the design.

What is screen retention time?
Why does dewatering matter?

What type of gravity concentrator is use.q: Why does spinning at high G let a Knelson trap heavy gold specifically?
What type of gravity concentrator is use.a:
Gravity separation works on density difference. In a still tank, fine gold settles faster than rock, but the difference in settling speed is small for fine particles, so they're hard to separate.

A Knelson spins its bowl so the slurry feels a force many times gravity. That multiplies the difference between gold, with an SG around 19, and gangue at roughly 2.7. Heavy gold pushes outward into the riffles and stays in the fluidised bed, while light particles are carried up and out with the flow.

It's the same idea as a centrifuge separating water from oil: spin it and small density differences become large forces. The plant has two KC-QS70 units, each taking up to about 1,000 t/h.

f.q: Why does gold separate from pyrite in a Knelson?
f.a:
Pyrite is dense for a mineral, around SG 5, but gold is about SG 19, nearly four times heavier. In the high G field that difference is strong enough for gold to displace pyrite in the riffle bed over time.

Some pyrite and other heavy minerals still collect in the concentrate, which is why the 150 kg flushed each cycle is mostly not gold. Gold locked inside pyrite grains behaves like pyrite, so gravity only catches free gold. The locked gold goes on to flotation and leaching.
f: How much gold is in a typical Knelson concentrate?
Why does locked gold need flotation and UFG instead?
Does the ILR leach pyrite as well as gold?

f.q: What size of gold particle does a Knelson catch best?
f.a:
In general, centrifugal concentrators recover free gold from coarse sizes down to some tens of microns well. Very fine gold, a few microns, has so little mass that drag from the fluidising and slurry flow can carry it out even in a high G field.

Very coarse particles are limited by the scalping screens upstream, which cut at 2.0 mm slots. So the Knelsons target the coarse to moderately fine free gold that would otherwise leach slowly. The ore specific size range is something the metallurgist's gravity testwork would show.
f: What is gravity recoverable gold testwork?
Why is very fine gold hard to recover by gravity?
Where does fine free gold get recovered instead?

f.q: Why is Knelson feed held at about 54 percent solids?
f.a:
The design feed to each Knelson is about 54 percent solids by weight, which comes from the gravity cyclone underflow after the scalping screens. Feed density affects how slurry flows through the bowl and how easily gold can migrate into the bed.

In general, slurry that's too thick is viscous and resists particle movement, while slurry that's too dilute wastes capacity and can upset the bed. Vendors give an operating range for each model. Ask the metallurgist whether feed density is actively controlled here or just follows the gravity cyclone underflow.
f: How does gravity cyclone underflow density vary?
Is water added to Knelson feed?
What happens to the bed if feed is too thick?

What type of gravity concentrator is use.q: What would a handover flag if a Knelson's throughput dropped off?
What type of gravity concentrator is use.a:
Knelson throughput drops when its feed supply drops or the unit itself is limited. A handover should say which Knelson, how much, for how long, and why if known.

On the feed side: the gravity cyclone feeding it may have a blocked spigot or be closed, or its gravity scalping screen may be blinding or tripped. The gravity cyclone feed valves are interlocked to their screens, so a screen trip cuts feed completely. On the unit itself: faults, a stuck valve, or extended flush cycles.

Less feed means less gold exposed to gravity, so note any expected drop in gravity recovery. Design is about 900 t/h nominal per Knelson, 1,000 t/h max.

f.q: How does a gravity cyclone problem cut Knelson feed?
f.a:
Each Knelson is fed by one of the two gravity duty cyclones on the cluster, through its scalping screen. Those cyclones use larger spigots to push about 1,000 t/h each to underflow.

If a gravity cyclone's spigot blocks or wears, or the cyclone is closed by its knife gate, less underflow reaches the screen and Knelson. A blocked spigot can also make the cyclone rope. So when a Knelson's feed falls, the gravity cyclone is one of the first things to check, along with the screen.
f: How are gravity cyclone spigots inspected?
Can a primary cyclone be swapped to gravity duty?
What happens to gravity cyclone underflow if a Knelson stops?

f.q: Why would a blinding scalping screen starve a Knelson?
f.a:
The scalping screen sits between the gravity cyclone underflow and the Knelson. If its panels blind with near size particles or trash, less slurry passes through as undersize and more reports to oversize, which goes to the ball mill feed.

So the Knelson gets less feed while the oversize stream grows. Screen oversize is designed at about 10 percent, with a range of 8 to 15 percent. A rising oversize share with falling Knelson feed points to blinding. Spray water and panel condition are the usual checks.

How are blinded panels cleaned?
How is screen oversize tonnage monitored?

f.q: How is Knelson feed rate measured?
f.a:
The reference gives design flows, about 900 t/h nominal and 1,000 t/h maximum per Knelson, but doesn't describe a flowmeter or density gauge on Knelson feed.

The plant generally measures slurry mass flow with a mag flowmeter plus a nucleonic density gauge, so one may be fitted on the gravity feed. Check the gravity circuit P&ID for an FIT or DT tag in area F14, or ask the mill control room operator what shows on the OIS.

How does a mag flowmeter measure slurry flow?
Why is solids SG entered by the operator?

What type of gravity concentrator is use.q: What maintenance keeps a Knelson bowl and riffles working properly?
What type of gravity concentrator is use.a:
The plant documents don't give Knelson maintenance details, so this is general practice. The main items are the bowl, riffle rings and fluidising water system.

Fluidising holes in the rings can block with scale or solids and need checking and cleaning. Bowl liners and riffles wear from abrasive slurry and are replaced when worn. Fluidising water strainers and valves need attention because dirty water blocks holes.

Mechanical items include the drive, bearings, rotating joint for water, and concentrate discharge valves. Vibration monitoring catches imbalance early. For the site routine and intervals, ask the gravity area maintenance planner.

f.q: Why are Knelson bowls lined with wear resistant material?
f.a:
The bowl spins at high speed with abrasive slurry sliding across it, so wear is constant. In general, bowls and riffle rings are lined with wear resistant materials, often polyurethane, that resist abrasion and can be replaced without replacing the whole bowl.

Worn riffles change the bed shape and reduce gold capture, so liner condition affects recovery as well as reliability. Replacement intervals depend on feed tonnage and abrasiveness. The vendor manual and site maintenance plan give specifics for the KC-QS70.
f: How does riffle wear affect gold recovery?
How long do Knelson liners typically last?
Who replaces Knelson bowls on site?

f.q: How does vibration monitoring help on a Knelson?
f.a:
A Knelson bowl spins with a heavy bed of concentrate, so any imbalance, such as uneven bed build up, worn bearings or liner damage, shows up as vibration.

In general, vibration sensors detect rising levels before damage occurs, letting operators stop the unit and investigate. It's the same as monitoring a large centrifugal pump or fan. The reference doesn't list the Knelson's instruments, but Knelsons are DCS controlled per the control philosophy, so trips and alarms would show on the OIS.
f: What causes uneven bed build up in a Knelson?
What vibration level trips a Knelson?
How are Knelson bearings lubricated?

f.q: Why do fluidising water strainers matter for the bowl?
f.a:
Fluidising water passes through many small holes in the riffle rings. Any solids in the water can block them, so strainers upstream catch debris before it reaches the bowl.

If strainers are clogged, water flow drops and the bed compacts. If they're damaged, debris gets through and blocks holes. On this site process water is saline, SG about 1.07, which can bring scale and solids, though the reference doesn't say which water feeds the Knelsons. Ask maintenance which supply is used.
f: Which water supply feeds the Knelson fluidising rings?
How often are the fluidising strainers cleaned?
Why does saline water cause scaling?

What is 'fluidising water' on a Knelson.q: Why does too much fluidising water wash gold back out of the bed?
What is 'fluidising water' on a Knelson.a:
Fluidising water flows inward through the bowl rings against the centrifugal force. It keeps the bed loose. But it also pushes particles inward, toward the flow leaving the bowl.

Heavy gold normally has enough centrifugal force to overcome that drag and stay in the bed. With too much water, the inward drag on fine gold becomes larger than the centrifugal force holding it, and it gets lifted out with the light material. The bed also becomes too open to trap fine particles.

It's like a fluidised bed in a boiler: too little air and the bed slumps; too much and you blow the bed out. Design is about 120 m3/h per unit, but the best setting depends on the ore.

f.q: How is fluidising water flow set for each Knelson?
f.a:
The design gives about 120 m3/h of fluidising water per Knelson. In general, flow is held by a flow control loop or a set valve, and the setpoint is tuned by the metallurgist based on concentrate grade and recovery.

The reference doesn't describe the exact control arrangement on these units. The Knelsons are DCS controlled per the control philosophy, so the flow and any alarms should be visible on the OIS. Ask the mill control room operator or metallurgist how the setpoint is chosen and changed.
f: How does the metallurgist optimise fluidising flow?
What alarms protect against low fluidising water?
Does fluidising flow change during the flush?

f.q: Why does too little fluidising water compact the bed?
f.a:
Without enough water flowing through it, the bed packs under the centrifugal force, like sand spun hard in a bucket. Particles lock together and new gold can't penetrate between them.

A compacted bed acts like a solid wall. Feed slurry slides across the surface, and gold that should be captured washes past. Compaction can also be uneven, causing imbalance. So low water flow cuts recovery even though the machine appears to run normally. It's general Knelson behaviour.
f: How do operators detect a compacted bed?
Can a compacted bed be loosened without stopping?
Why does compaction cause bowl imbalance?

f.q: Does fluidising water dilute the Knelson tails?
f.a:
Yes. About 120 m3/h of fluidising water per Knelson leaves with the tails, which go back to the primary cyclone feed hopper. That's a fair amount of water entering the grinding circuit.

The cyclone feed hopper water addition and density control have to account for it. In general, it's part of the water balance designers allow for. If fluidising flow changes, operators may notice a change in hopper water addition. Design values; actual flows vary.
f: How does Knelson water affect cyclone feed density?
What is the grinding circuit water balance?
Why do Knelson tails go back to the cyclone hopper?

What is 'fluidising water' on a Knelson.q: What would a handover flag if fluidising holes were suspected blocked?
What is 'fluidising water' on a Knelson.a:
Blocked fluidising holes cause uneven fluidising, compacted patches and lost gold, so they're worth flagging. A handover should say which Knelson and what pointed to it.

Signs: fluidising water pressure rising at the same flow, or flow falling at the same pressure; lower concentrate mass per cycle or lower gold content; vibration from uneven bed build up. Also note water quality issues, such as saline scale or solids in the water.

Note whether it was reported to maintenance and if the unit was taken out of service. Gravity recovery may be lower until cleaned.

f.q: What causes fluidising holes to block?
f.a:
In general: solids in the fluidising water passing the strainers; scale from dissolved salts building up in the holes; and slurry backflowing into the holes when water pressure drops, for example during a stop or water supply problem.

Saline water raises scaling risk, and this site's process water is saline, though the reference doesn't say which water feeds the Knelsons. Keeping water flowing whenever slurry is in the bowl and keeping strainers clean are the main preventions.
f: Why does slurry backflow when water pressure drops?
How is scale removed from fluidising rings?
Which water supply has the lowest scaling risk?

f.q: Why does fluidising water pressure rise when holes block?
f.a:
Fluidising water passes through many small holes in parallel. Blocking some reduces the total flow area, so to push the same flow through, the pressure must rise, just like closing some parallel nozzles on a pump header.

If the supply can't raise pressure, flow drops instead. Either way, trending pressure and flow together reveals blockage. In general, a gradual rise suggests scale; a sudden change suggests debris or a valve issue.
f: What pressure trend suggests scale build up?
How is fluidising water pressure measured?
What does a sudden flow drop indicate?

f.q: Why should fluidising water stay on whenever slurry is in the bowl?
f.a:
If fluidising water stops while slurry is still in the bowl, slurry can backflow into the fluidising holes and settle there, blocking them. The bed also compacts immediately.

In general, Knelson sequences keep water running through stops until the bowl is flushed. A water supply failure while feeding is serious for this reason. Ask the mill control room operator how the Knelson sequences handle water during stops on this plant.
f: What happens to the Knelson if water supply fails?
How do Knelson stop sequences handle water?
Can a Knelson restart after a water failure?

What is 'fluidising water' on a Knelson.q: How do operators check or clean blocked fluidising holes?
What is 'fluidising water' on a Knelson.a:
The reference doesn't give the procedure, so this is general. Operators usually spot blocked holes from trends: fluidising water pressure versus flow, concentrate mass per cycle, and vibration.

Cleaning is a maintenance job with the Knelson stopped and isolated. Typically the bowl is inspected, holes are cleared with water jetting or rods, and scale may be removed with an acid soak according to vendor instructions. Strainers are cleaned at the same time.

Never open a Knelson or reach into the bowl without full isolation, because it's a high speed rotating machine. Ask the gravity area maintenance planner for the site procedure and interval.

f.q: How does scale from saline water affect fluidising rings?
f.a:
Saline water carries dissolved salts that can precipitate as scale, especially where water pressure and velocity change, like small holes. Scale gradually narrows holes and reduces flow.

This site's process water is saline at SG about 1.07, but the reference doesn't say which water feeds the Knelson fluidising rings. If saline water is used, scale management matters more. Ask maintenance which water supply is used and how scale is handled.
f: What types of scale form from saline water?
How is antiscalant used on site?
Is scheme water used for any gravity duties?

f.q: What isolations apply before opening a Knelson?
f.a:
This is general safety knowledge, not a site procedure. A Knelson is a high speed rotating machine with water and slurry supplies, so isolation normally covers the drive motor, fluidising water, feed slurry, concentrate valve actuators and any air or hydraulic supply.

The bowl must be confirmed stopped, since it can coast for some time. Concentrate is gold bearing, so security rules may apply too. Follow the site's isolation procedure and ask the area supervisor.
f: Why does a Knelson bowl coast after stopping?
What security rules apply to Knelson concentrate?
Who authorises Knelson isolation?

f.q: How often are Knelson bowls inspected?
f.a:
The reference doesn't give an inspection interval. In general, sites inspect Knelson bowls during planned shutdowns, often weekly or monthly depending on wear and blockage history, and more often if trends show problems.

The vendor manual sets recommended checks for the KC-QS70. Ask the gravity area maintenance planner for this site's routine and how it fits with the 48 cycles a day the Knelsons run.
f: What does a Knelson inspection check?
How long does a Knelson inspection take?
Can one Knelson run while the other is inspected?

How does a Knelson produce concentrate?.q: Why does the concentrate bed need periodic flushing instead of running on?
How does a Knelson produce concentrate?.a:
The concentrate bed sits in the riffles. As the Knelson runs, the bed fills with heavy material: gold, but also pyrite and other dense minerals.

Once full, there's no more room for new gold to settle, and capture drops. Heavy minerals also compete with gold for the bed. So the unit stops feeding, flushes the bed out as concentrate, and starts fresh with empty riffles.

The design cycle is about 30 minutes including flush, producing about 150 kg per cycle. It's like backflushing a filter: once loaded, it must be cleaned to keep working.

f.q: What is most of the Knelson concentrate made of?
f.a:
Mostly heavy minerals, not gold. On this ore the main heavy mineral is pyrite, along with other sulphides and dense gangue. Gold, though valuable, is a small mass fraction.

That's why concentrate goes to the ILR for intensive leaching, rather than straight to smelting. In general, Knelson concentrate grade depends on fluidising water, cycle time and ore. The metallurgist tracks concentrate grade.
f: What is the typical gold grade of Knelson concentrate?
Why doesn't concentrate go straight to smelting?
How does pyrite affect ILR leaching?

f.q: How long is the flush part of the cycle?
f.a:
The reference gives a 30 minute cycle including flush but doesn't break out the flush time. In general, Knelson flushes take a short part of the cycle, a few minutes, during which feed is diverted, the bowl slows or stops and water flushes concentrate out.

Ask the mill control room operator or check the Knelson sequence in the gravity control philosophy for the exact timing.
f: Where does feed go during the flush?
Does the bowl stop fully during flushing?
Can the flush time be adjusted?

f.q: Why does cycle length affect gravity recovery?
f.a:
A short cycle flushes before the bed fills, so it keeps capturing well but produces more, lower grade concentrate for the ILR. A long cycle produces less, richer concentrate but loses gold once the bed saturates.

So cycle length is a trade off between recovery and concentrate mass. The design 30 minutes gives about 14.4 t/day, matching one ILR batch a day. The metallurgist sets cycle time.
f: How does concentrate mass affect the ILR?
Who changes the Knelson cycle time?
How is the best cycle time found?

How does a Knelson produce concentrate?.q: What would a handover flag if a Knelson cycle gave less concentrate than usual?
How does a Knelson produce concentrate?.a:
Less concentrate than usual per cycle, compared with the design 150 kg, is worth flagging. Possible causes: lower feed rate, blocked fluidising holes, coarse feed, valve faults, incomplete flushing, or changes in cycle time.

A handover should note which Knelson, how many cycles affected, and what checks were done. Lower concentrate may mean lower gravity recovery.

It could also be ore change: less heavy mineral in the feed. The metallurgist will want to know.

f.q: How is concentrate mass per cycle measured?
f.a:
The reference gives the design figure of 150 kg per cycle but doesn't describe how actual concentrate mass is measured.

In general, plants estimate it from the level or weight of the concentrate storage vessel, from the mass of each ILR batch, or from density and volume readings on the concentrate line. Some simply back calculate from the ILR feed. Because concentrate is gold rich, the number matters for metallurgical accounting. Ask the mill control room operator or the metallurgist how it's tracked on this plant.
f: How is the ILR batch weighed?
How is concentrate storage level measured?
Why is concentrate mass hard to measure?

f.q: Why would a lower feed rate give less concentrate per cycle?
f.a:
The bed fills with heavy minerals carried in by the feed. With less feed passing through the bowl, less heavy material arrives each cycle, so the bed fills more slowly and there's less to flush out at the end.

That's normal and not a fault in itself. It does mean less gold is being exposed to gravity, so gravity recovery may dip. Design feed is about 900 t/h nominal per Knelson, so a lower concentrate mass with lower feed is expected, while a lower mass at full feed points to a problem in the unit.
f: What sets Knelson feed rate?
How does feed rate affect concentrate grade?
What is design Knelson feed?

f.q: What does a Knelson's concentrate valve do?
f.a:
During the run part of the cycle the concentrate valve stays closed and the bed builds up in the bowl's riffles. At the flush step it opens so water can wash the concentrate out to the concentrate line, then closes again for the next run.

If it sticks open or leaks, gold rich material bleeds away or the bed never builds properly. If it sticks closed, the flush doesn't empty the bowl and the next cycle starts on a full bed. In general, these valves see abrasive slurry and are a regular maintenance item.
f: How is the concentrate valve actuated?
What happens if the valve leaks?
How often is the valve replaced?

How does a Knelson produce concentrate?.q: How is the flushed concentrate handled before it reaches the ILR?
How does a Knelson produce concentrate?.a:
Flushed concentrate from both Knelsons is collected and dewatered, then sent to the ILR. The design ILR batch is about 14.4 t at 90 percent solids, once a day nominally.

Each Knelson makes 150 kg per cycle, 48 cycles a day, so about 7.2 t per unit and 14.4 t/day across both, which matches one ILR batch. Concentrate is held until the batch starts.

Because it's rich in gold, it's handled securely. The reference doesn't detail the storage arrangement, so check the gravity PFD.

f.q: Why must concentrate be dewatered to about 90 percent solids?
f.a:
The ILR batch is designed at about 14.4 t at 90 percent solids. Dewatering removes excess process water so the ILR can add its own strong cyanide solution without diluting it.

Less water also means a smaller volume to leach and a richer pregnant solution, about 14.5 m3 per batch. It's like concentrating a feed before a reaction to make it more efficient.
f: How is concentrate dewatered?
What happens to the removed water?
Why is pregnant solution volume small?

f.q: Why is Knelson concentrate kept secure on its way to the ILR?
f.a:
Knelson concentrate can contain a lot of free gold in a small mass, sometimes visible to the eye, so it's an obvious theft risk. In general, sites keep gravity concentrate in locked, enclosed vessels and lines, restrict access to the gravity and ILR area, and use cameras and sealed sampling points.

The gravity circuit then feeds gravity EW in the goldroom (F66), which has its own security. The reference doesn't describe the site's security arrangements, so ask your supervisor what rules apply in the gravity area.
f: What security controls apply in the gravity area?
Who can access the ILR?
How is gravity gold tracked?

f.q: How do 48 cycles a day match one ILR batch a day?
f.a:
Each Knelson makes about 150 kg per 30 minute cycle, 48 cycles a day, so about 7.2 t per unit. Two units give about 14.4 t/day.

The ILR is designed for about 14.4 t per batch, one batch a day nominally, two max. So the two Knelsons fill one ILR batch a day. If concentrate mass rises, the ILR can run two batches.
f: When would the ILR run two batches a day?
How long is an ILR cycle?

Where do Knelson tails go?.q: Why does running gravity on a circulating stream let it catch gold repeatedly?
Where do Knelson tails go?.a:
Gravity is placed on the cyclone underflow, which circulates back to the ball mill. Knelson tails also go back to the primary cyclone feed hopper.

Gold missed on one pass doesn't leave the circuit. Being dense, it reports to cyclone underflow again and comes back around to the gravity cyclones and Knelsons. Each pass gives another chance.

Meanwhile, grinding keeps liberating more gold. So gravity recovery builds over many passes. It's like a recirculating filter loop: each pass removes some more.

f.q: Why does gold keep reporting to cyclone underflow?
f.a:
Gold is very dense, SG about 19, so even fine gold feels enough centrifugal force in the cyclone to go to underflow. It returns to the ball mill rather than overflow.

It only leaves in overflow when ground very fine or locked in light particles. So gold accumulates in the circulating load, which is why gravity taps it there. General cyclone behaviour.
f: How fine must gold be to reach overflow?
What is gold lock up in the circuit?
How does circulating load affect gold build up?

f.q: What happens to gold that never gets caught by gravity?
f.a:
Eventually it leaves the grinding circuit in cyclone overflow, either because it has been ground fine enough or because it's locked inside sulphide or other light particles.

Gold locked in sulphides mostly floats into the flotation concentrate, goes through UFG and is leached in CIL2 with adsorption in CIL3. Free or locked gold that escapes flotation goes with the tails to CIL4. Design total recovery is about 84 percent, with gravity contributing about 14 percent of feed gold and the rest coming from the leach circuits.
f: Does free gold float well?
What is the CIL4 leach extraction?
How does UFG release locked gold?

f.q: Why is only part of the circulating load sent to gravity?
f.a:
Cyclone feed is about 14,400 t/h of solids, and most of that is underflow returning to the ball mill. The two Knelsons take about 1,800 t/h nominal between them, so only a fraction of the underflow passes through gravity on each trip.

Treating it all would need many more Knelsons, screens and space. Because gold keeps circulating, treating part of the stream on every pass still catches a good share over time. It's like a side stream filter on a lube oil system: it doesn't filter all the flow, but it cleans the whole inventory over time.
f: How many passes does gold make?
Could more Knelsons be added?
What sets the gravity feed rate?

Where do Knelson tails go?.q: What would a handover flag if Knelson tails carried a lot of visible gold?
Where do Knelson tails go?.a:
Visible gold in Knelson tails means it's not capturing as it should. A handover should note which Knelson, how the gold was seen (sample, panning), and possible causes.

Causes: blocked fluidising holes, wrong fluidising water flow, bed overfilled from long cycles, a valve stuck, or feed too coarse. Also check for feed bypassing the bowl.

Report to the metallurgist. Handling gold samples follows security rules.

f.q: How would someone check Knelson tails for gold?
f.a:
In general, a sample of Knelson tails is taken from a safe sampling point and either panned to look for free gold or sent for assay. Panning gives a quick visual check on shift; assays give actual numbers but take longer.

Because coarse gold is unevenly spread, several samples tell you more than one. Sampling around gold bearing streams follows site procedures and security rules. Ask the metallurgist how and where Knelson tails are sampled on this plant.
f: How is panning done?
How often are Knelson tails sampled?
What gold content in tails is normal?

f.q: What could cause a Knelson to bypass feed straight to tails?
f.a:
In general, Knelson installations divert feed away from the bowl during the flush step, using a diverter or bypass valve, so feed goes straight to tails while concentrate is washed out.

If that valve sticks in the bypass position, leaks, or the sequence doesn't switch it back, feed skips the bowl during normal running and no gold is caught. Checking valve position feedback and the sequence state on the OIS is the first step. The Knelsons are DCS controlled, so faults should show as alarms.
f: How is the bypass valve actuated?
What does the Knelson sequence do during flushing?
How are valve faults detected?

f.q: Why is a single tails sample risky to judge from?
f.a:
Coarse gold is spread very unevenly through slurry. A single small sample might catch one particle and look rich, or miss gold completely and look clean. This is called the nugget effect.

So one result, high or low, doesn't prove much. Repeated samples, larger samples or composites over a shift give a far more reliable picture. In general, metallurgists look at trends across many samples before drawing conclusions, especially for gravity circuits where the gold is coarse.
f: What is the nugget effect?
How are composite samples taken?
How many samples give a reliable result?

Where do Knelson tails go?.q: How does gravity recovery link back into overall circuit gold balance?
Where do Knelson tails go?.a:
Gravity gold goes through the ILR and gravity EW in the goldroom (F66), separate from the CIL gold. It's counted as gravity recovery, about 14 percent of feed gold nominal, max 20 percent.

Overall recovery of about 84 percent includes gravity, flotation and leaching. The metallurgist balances gold in feed, gravity, CIL and tails to track performance.

Gravity also reduces gold held in the circuit and gives faster gold for production.

f.q: How is gravity gold measured separately from CIL gold?
f.a:
Gravity gold has its own route: Knelson concentrate goes to the ILR, its pregnant solution goes to the gravity EW cells in the goldroom (F66), and that produces its own sludge and doré.

The ILR pregnant solution volume, about 14.5 m3 per batch, times its gold assay gives gold leached, and the gravity EW output gives gold recovered. CIL gold comes through carbon, elution and separate EW. So gravity recovery can be reported on its own. The detailed accounting method is with the metallurgist.
f: How is ILR solution assayed?
How is gravity EW production measured?
What is doré?

f.q: Why can gravity recovery appear higher than 14 percent some days?
f.a:
Fourteen percent of feed gold is the nominal design figure, with a maximum case of 20 percent. Ore with more coarse free gold naturally gives more gravity gold, so some days or ore blends will be higher.

Timing also matters. The ILR runs in batches, usually one a day, and gold is counted when it's processed. A batch from a rich period can land on a day with lower feed grade, making that day look high. Weekly or monthly figures smooth this out.
f: What ore types have more coarse gold?
How does batch timing affect accounting?
What is the design max gravity recovery?

f.q: How does gravity recovery reduce gold lock up in the circuit?
f.a:
Coarse gold circulates many times between the cyclones and ball mill, so a stock of gold builds up in the grinding circuit. That gold is in the plant but not yet produced.

Each pass through the Knelsons pulls some out, so the inventory stays smaller and gold reaches the goldroom sooner. Less gold held in the mill circuit also means less at risk during relines and shutdowns. The reference notes gravity reduces circuit gold inventory and gives fast gold for production.
f: How much gold is held in the circuit?
Why does inventory matter during shutdowns?
How is circuit gold inventory estimated?

What does the ILR do with the Knelson co.q: Why does the ILR achieve such high leach recovery compared to normal CIL?
What does the ILR do with the Knelson co.a:
The ILR is built for one job: leaching a small mass of gold rich concentrate quickly and completely. It treats about 14.4 t per batch over a 12 hour cycle, with strong cyanide and an oxidant, in a small enclosed vessel.

CIL is the opposite. It treats thousands of tonnes per hour with much weaker cyanide, so each particle gets limited time and chemistry. Coarse gold, which is what gravity captures, dissolves slowly because it has little surface area for its mass, so in CIL some of it may not fully dissolve before the slurry leaves.

The ILR's intense conditions dissolve even coarse gold, giving 92 to 98 percent leach recovery, with 98 percent used for design.

f.q: Why can the ILR use far stronger cyanide than CIL?
f.a:
Scale. The ILR treats about 14.4 t of concentrate per batch in a small closed reactor. Strong cyanide on that small volume costs little and stays contained, and the pregnant solution volume is only about 14.5 m3.

Using the same strength on CIL feed of thousands of tonnes per hour would cost a fortune in reagent and leave far more cyanide to detoxify before tails reach the TSF. So the plant concentrates the coarse gold first, then hits it with intense chemistry where it's cheap to do so.
f: How is cyanide added to the ILR batch?
What happens to cyanide left in ILR residue?
Why is cyanide dosed in g/t in the CIL circuits?

f.q: How does the Acacia reactor keep concentrate in contact with solution?
f.a:
The reference only names the unit, an Acacia CS10000. In general, Acacia reactors work as an upflow fluidised bed: leach solution is pumped up through the concentrate bed in a conical vessel, lifting and loosening it so every particle is bathed in solution, then the solution is recirculated through a tank.

That avoids heavy mechanical agitation of very abrasive, dense concentrate. It's similar in principle to the fluidising water in the Knelson. For the exact internals and cycle steps on this unit, check the vendor manual or ask the metallurgist.
f: Why is fluidising gentler than mechanical agitation?
How is the ILR solution heated or cooled?
What steps make up the 12 hour ILR cycle?

f.q: What happens to the ILR leach residue?
f.a:
The design criteria give the ILR residue at about 40 percent solids, but the summary doesn't say where it goes.

In general, intensive leach residue is returned to the grinding circuit so any unleached gold gets another chance through gravity, flotation and CIL. Because it carries cyanide, the route has to be designed for that. Check the gravity and ILR PFD for area F14, or ask the metallurgist, to confirm the residue destination on this plant.
f: Which PFD covers the F14 gravity and ILR area?
How much gold is usually left in ILR residue?
Why must cyanide bearing residue be routed carefully?

What does the ILR do with the Knelson co.q: What would a handover flag if an ILR batch didn't reach 98% recovery?
What does the ILR do with the Knelson co.a:
If a batch falls below the 98 percent design figure (design range 92 to 98 percent), more gold stays in the residue. A handover should name the batch, the recovery or residue assay if known, and any suspected cause.

Possible causes: cyanide or oxidant running low during the cycle, a short or interrupted cycle, coarser or more locked gold in the concentrate, high copper or other cyanide consumers (the design pregnant solution carries about 303 ppm Cu), or poor solution flow through the bed.

Note any equipment issues such as pump or valve faults, and pass it to the metallurgist. A single low batch may be ore related; a trend points to the reactor or reagents.

f.q: Why does copper in the concentrate consume cyanide in the ILR?
f.a:
Some copper minerals dissolve readily in cyanide, forming copper cyanide complexes. Each unit of copper ties up several units of cyanide, so free cyanide available for gold falls.

The design pregnant solution carries about 303 ppm Cu alongside 1,100 to 1,800 ppm Au, so copper is a real competitor. If copper in the concentrate rises, the batch can run short of free cyanide and gold leaching slows. Copper also follows through to electrowinning, where it competes with gold for current.
f: How is free cyanide measured during a batch?
Which copper minerals dissolve fastest in cyanide?
How does copper end up in the doré?

f.q: How is ILR recovery worked out for each batch?
f.a:
In general, recovery is a mass balance. Gold leached equals the pregnant solution volume times its gold assay. Gold fed equals the concentrate mass times its assay, or gold leached plus gold left in the residue.

Recovery is gold leached divided by gold fed. With about 14.5 m3 of solution at roughly 1,100 to 1,800 ppm Au, the solution side is fairly precise; concentrate sampling is harder because coarse gold is uneven. The metallurgist owns this calculation and its sampling method.
f: Why is concentrate hard to sample accurately?
How is pregnant solution volume measured?
What residue assay suggests a poor batch?

f.q: Where does gold not leached in the ILR end up?
f.a:
It stays in the ILR residue, which the design gives at about 40 percent solids. The summary doesn't state the residue destination.

In general, residue goes back to the grinding circuit, so the unleached gold rejoins the circulating load and gets another chance in the Knelsons, or reports to flotation and CIL. That means a poor batch delays gold rather than losing it outright, though some will end up in tails. Confirm the route on the F14 PFD or with the metallurgist.
f: How quickly does recycled gold reach the goldroom?
Does recycled residue affect Knelson performance?
Can a poor ILR batch be re leached?

What does the ILR do with the Knelson co.q: How does oxygen supply to the ILR tie into the PSA plant?
What does the ILR do with the Knelson co.a:
The reference doesn't say how the ILR gets its oxidant. It lists oxygen from the new PSA oxygen plant, backed by liquid oxygen, going to CIL2/3 and CIL4, but it doesn't mention the ILR.

In general, intensive leach reactors use either oxygen gas or a chemical oxidant such as hydrogen peroxide, sometimes with a leach aid. Whether this unit draws from the PSA header, a separate supply or uses peroxide isn't covered in the documents I have.

Check the F14 gravity and ILR P&ID, or ask the metallurgist or the mill control room operator.

f.q: What other oxidants are used in intensive leach reactors?
f.a:
In general, the common choices are oxygen gas, hydrogen peroxide, and proprietary leach aids that release oxygen in solution. All of them do the same job: supply dissolved oxygen at the gold surface so cyanide can dissolve it quickly.

Peroxide is easy to dose into a small batch but adds reagent cost and handling hazards. Oxygen gas is cheap where a supply exists. The choice depends on vendor design and site services. Which one this ILR uses isn't in the reference, so ask the metallurgist.
f: Why is hydrogen peroxide a handling hazard?
How is dissolved oxygen measured in a leach?
Does extra oxidant ever slow gold leaching?

f.q: Why does gold leaching need oxygen at all?
f.a:
Gold doesn't dissolve in cyanide by itself. The reaction needs an oxidant at the gold surface: oxygen accepts electrons while gold combines with cyanide to form a soluble gold cyanide complex. Chemists summarise this as the Elsner equation.

If dissolved oxygen runs low, leaching slows sharply even with plenty of cyanide. That's why the CIL circuits here have oxygen injection and DO analysers, and why intensive leach reactors add oxidant. It's like combustion: fuel alone won't burn without air.
f: What dissolved oxygen levels do the CIL tanks target?
Why does high sulphide content consume oxygen?
How do DO analysers work in slurry?

f.q: What does the PSA plant supply on this site?
f.a:
Per the reference, the new oxygen plant uses pressure swing adsorption, with liquid oxygen as well, and supplies oxygen to CIL2/3 and CIL4.

In CIL2, oxygen goes in through side lances on the tanks plus new VSD oxygen injection pumps on the first two tanks. In CIL4, VSD injection pumps with flow control valves serve both leach tanks, with side lances on the leach tanks and the first two adsorption tanks, and DO analysers alarm high and low. The ILR isn't listed as a PSA user in the summary.

When does the liquid oxygen supply get used?
Why are oxygen injection pumps on VSDs?

Where does the ILR pregnant solution go?.q: Why does gravity EW use separate cells instead of sharing the main EW cells?
Where does the ILR pregnant solution go?.a:
The ILR makes a small, very rich batch of solution, about 14.5 m3 at roughly 1,100 to 1,800 ppm Au, once or twice a day. The gravity EW is sized for exactly that: a clean in place split cell with two compartments of 11 cathodes, about 10 hours of electrowinning per batch, driving barren solution below 5 ppm Au.

Keeping it separate means gravity gold is accounted for on its own, the batch timing doesn't disrupt the CIL eluate electrowinning, and the high gold, copper and silver content can be handled in cells set up for it.

It's like having a dedicated small heat exchanger for one hot process stream instead of mixing it into the main plant cooling system.

f.q: Why does very rich ILR solution suit a small dedicated EW cell?
f.a:
Electrowinning rate depends on how much gold is in solution and the current applied. A small volume of very rich solution can be stripped quickly in a compact cell, with flow of about 24 m3/h per compartment recirculating the 14.5 m3 batch many times.

Mixing it into the much larger CIL eluate flows would dilute it and tie up main EW capacity. A dedicated cell finishes each batch in about 10 hours, ready for the next ILR batch. The two rectifiers of 2,500 A give the current needed.
f: How many times is the batch recirculated in 10 hours?
Why does EW slow down as gold concentration falls?
What are the 2,500 A rectifiers for?

f.q: What does clean in place mean for an EW cell?
f.a:
In a conventional EW cell, cathodes loaded with gold sludge are lifted out and washed down in a separate area. In a clean in place cell, the sludge is washed off the cathodes inside the cell, usually with high pressure water sprays, and collects in the cell's bottom for draining to a filter.

That saves handling heavy cathodes, reduces spillage and exposure, and improves security because gold stays enclosed. The gravity EW cell here is a clean in place split cell, model 1000x1000 22D per the design.
f: How is the sludge drained from the cell bottom?
Why is handling loaded cathodes a security risk?
What are EW cathodes usually made of?

f.q: How does gravity EW keep gold accounting separate?
f.a:
Gravity gold has its own route from Knelson to ILR to gravity EW in the goldroom (F66). The gravity cells produce their own sludge, which can be smelted and weighed as a separate gravity lot.

That lets the metallurgist report gravity recovery, about 14 percent of feed gold in the design, separately from the CIL circuits. It also helps spot problems: a drop in gravity gold points to the Knelsons or ILR rather than flotation or leaching. Detailed accounting rules sit with the metallurgist.
f: How is gravity sludge kept apart in the goldroom?
How is gravity doré weighed and assayed?
What does the monthly gold reconciliation compare?

Where does the ILR pregnant solution go?.q: What would a handover flag if gravity EW barren solution tested above 5 ppm Au?
Where does the ILR pregnant solution go?.a:
Barren above 5 ppm Au means the cell didn't strip the batch fully, so gold is left in solution. A handover should note the batch, the barren assay and what was checked.

Likely causes: the cycle cut short of the design 10 hours, low current from a rectifier fault (2 x 2,500 A, design current density 15 to 25 A/m2), low recirculation flow (design 24 m3/h per compartment), shorted or poorly connected cathodes, or high copper in the solution competing for current (design about 303 ppm Cu).

Flag it to the metallurgist, who may extend the cycle or recycle the solution.

f.q: Why does copper in the solution slow gold electrowinning?
f.a:
Copper plates onto the cathodes alongside gold. Every amp spent depositing copper is an amp not depositing gold, so gold recovery per hour falls.

With about 303 ppm Cu in the design pregnant solution, copper is a meaningful share of what plates out. High copper also lowers the purity of the sludge and the doré. In general, if copper rises, the cycle may need more time or current to get gold below the 5 ppm barren target.
f: How does copper affect doré purity?
Can copper be removed before electrowinning?
Why does silver also plate in the cell?

f.q: What does current density tell you about an EW cell?
f.a:
Current density is the current divided by the cathode area, here a design range of 15 to 25 A/m2. It's a measure of how hard each square metre of cathode is being driven.

Too low and plating is slow, so the batch takes longer. Too high and the deposit becomes loose and poorly attached, side reactions like hydrogen gas increase, and current efficiency falls. It's similar to heat flux in an exchanger: push too hard and you get fouling and boiling issues rather than more useful duty.
f: How is current shared across 11 cathodes?
What is current efficiency in EW?
Why does hydrogen gas form at high current?

f.q: Where does gravity EW barren solution go?
f.a:
The reference gives the barren target of below 5 ppm Au but doesn't say where barren solution goes afterwards.

In general, gravity EW barren still carries cyanide and some gold, so it's usually returned to the process, for example to the grinding circuit or a leach circuit, rather than discarded. Check the gravity EW part of the F66 PFD, or ask the goldroom supervisor or metallurgist for the route on this plant.
f: Which PFD shows the F66 gravity EW circuit?
Why can't barren solution go straight to tails?
How is barren solution sampled for gold?

Where does the ILR pregnant solution go?.q: How is the gravity EW circuit cleaned between batches?
Where does the ILR pregnant solution go?.a:
The gravity EW cells are clean in place, so cleaning means washing the gold sludge off the cathodes inside the cell rather than lifting them out. In general, after a batch finishes, the solution is drained, cathodes are sprayed with high pressure water, and the sludge collects in the cell bottom.

The sludge is then drained to a filter, dried and taken for smelting into doré in the goldroom. The cell is rinsed and ready for the next ILR batch.

The reference doesn't give the step by step procedure or its frequency, and goldroom work runs under strict security. Ask the goldroom supervisor for the site procedure.

f.q: What happens to gold sludge after it's washed off cathodes?
f.a:
In general, the sludge is filtered to remove water, dried in an oven, mixed with fluxes, and smelted in a furnace. The molten metal is poured into moulds to make doré bars, while the flux carries impurities off as slag.

The doré, a gold and silver alloy, is weighed and sampled for assay before dispatch to the refinery. Gravity sludge may be smelted separately so gravity gold can be accounted for. The goldroom procedure for this site isn't in the reference.
f: Why are fluxes added when smelting gold sludge?
How is doré sampled for assay?
What happens to the smelting slag?

f.q: Why is goldroom work done under strict security?
f.a:
The goldroom holds concentrated gold in sludge, bars and filter cake, so the theft risk is high. In general, sites restrict access to named people, require at least two people for gold handling, use cameras, searches and logged entry, and keep gold in secure storage.

Security rules also apply to sampling and to any maintenance in the goldroom. The specific site rules aren't in the reference, so ask your supervisor or the goldroom supervisor before going in.
f: Who is authorised to enter the goldroom?
Why does gold handling need two people?
How is gold stored before dispatch?

f.q: How are EW cathodes checked for shorting?
f.a:
A short happens when a cathode touches an anode, often because sludge build up or a bent cathode bridges the gap. Current then flows through the short instead of plating gold.

In general, operators watch cell voltage and current, since a short lowers cell voltage, and check for hot spots by hand held thermal camera or by feeling bus bar connections where safe. Visual checks at cleaning catch bent or misaligned cathodes. Shorts waste current and can damage cathodes and anodes.

What does a thermal camera show on bus bars?

Why keep gravity gold separate rather th.q: Why does coarse gold leach more slowly than fine gold in cyanide?
Why keep gravity gold separate rather th.a:
Gold dissolves only at its surface. A coarse particle has far less surface area per gram than fine particles, so the same cyanide and oxygen take much longer to dissolve it completely. Doubling particle size roughly doubles the time to dissolve it.

CIL residence is fixed by tank volume and flow. In CIL4 total residence is about 12.8 hours, below the 14 hours considered ideal. Coarse gold that hasn't dissolved by the last tank leaves with the tails.

Gravity plus the ILR pulls coarse gold out early and leaches it under intense conditions, so it doesn't depend on CIL time. It also reduces gold held in the circuit and gives fast gold for production. Gravity recovery is about 14 percent of feed gold nominal.

f.q: How long would a coarse gold particle take to dissolve in CIL?
f.a:
The reference doesn't give leach times by particle size. In general, dissolution proceeds inward from the surface at a roughly steady rate under fixed conditions, so time to fully dissolve grows roughly in proportion to particle size.

A particle several times larger than typical fine gold can therefore need many times longer, potentially more than the 12.8 hour CIL4 residence. Gravity recoverable gold testwork and leach kinetics tests on this ore would give real figures; the metallurgist would have them.
f: What is leach kinetics testwork?
Why is CIL4 residence below the 14 hour ideal?
Does higher cyanide strength shorten leach time?

f.q: Why does coarse gold get trapped in the grinding circuit?
f.a:
Gold is extremely dense and also malleable. In the mill it tends to flatten and fold rather than break, so it stays coarse. In the cyclones its density sends it to underflow, back to the ball mill, again and again.

So coarse gold builds up as an inventory in the circulating load. Without gravity, it would only leave once ground fine enough or by slowly escaping to overflow. The Knelsons on the gravity cyclone underflow tap that inventory every pass, reducing gold held in the circuit.
f: Why does gold flatten instead of breaking in a mill?
How large can the gold inventory in a mill circuit get?
What happens to circuit gold during a mill reline?

f.q: What happens to coarse gold that reaches flotation?
f.a:
Coarse free gold is heavy for its size and tends to drop off bubbles, so it floats poorly compared with fine sulphide particles. Some may float, but a share goes with the scavenger tails to the flotation tails thickener and on to CIL4.

CIL4 runs a leach pH of 8.8 to 9.3 with about 3.2 hours of leach and 12.8 hours total residence, designed for fine gold in tails, with design extraction of 38 percent. Coarse gold there has a poor chance of dissolving fully, which is exactly the loss gravity is meant to prevent.
f: Why does CIL4 run a lower pH than CIL2?
How is gold in CIL4 tails sampled?
What sets the 38 percent CIL4 extraction figure?

Why keep gravity gold separate rather th.q: What would a handover flag if coarse gold losses to tails increased?
Why keep gravity gold separate rather th.a:
Rising coarse gold losses show up as higher or more erratic tails assays, often alongside a drop in gravity gold. A handover should note the evidence: tails assay trend, gravity concentrate or ILR batch results, and any visible gold in samples.

Then possible causes: Knelson problems (fluidising water, valves, cycle settings), blinding or torn gravity scalping screens, gravity cyclone issues reducing gravity feed, a coarser grind, or ore with more coarse gold than usual.

Note actions taken and pass it to the metallurgist, who can compare against the gravity recovery design of about 14 percent.

f.q: How are gold losses to tails measured on this plant?
f.a:
Per the reference, a three stage sampler takes a shift composite of CIL4 tails, and a carbon detection meter with a reference probe monitors carbon in the tails. The final tails tank then sends CIL4 tails, acid wash waste and fine carbon waste to the TSF.

The shift composite is assayed for gold, giving the main measure of what's being lost. The OSA also measures gold on flotation final tails. Together they show whether losses are coming from flotation, leaching or both.
f: How does a three stage sampler build a composite?
Why is carbon in the tails monitored?
What does the OSA measure on final tails?

f.q: Why do coarse gold losses make tails assays jumpy?
f.a:
Coarse gold particles are few and heavy, so whether a sample contains one or not changes the assay a lot. Two samples from the same stream can give very different results. This is the nugget effect.

That's why tails results with coarse gold present swing from shift to shift. Larger samples, more increments in the composite, and looking at trends over several days give a truer picture. A single high assay is a prompt to look closer, not proof of a problem.
f: How do larger samples reduce the nugget effect?
What is a sample increment in a composite?
How many shifts make a reliable trend?

f.q: Which equipment would you check first if gravity gold drops?
f.a:
Start at the feed and work forward. Check the two gravity duty cyclones are open and not blocked, then the gravity scalping screens for blinding, torn panels or trips, since their feed valves are interlocked to the screens.

Next the Knelsons: feed rate, fluidising water flow and pressure, cycle timing, and concentrate and bypass valve positions. Then the ILR batch results and gravity EW barren. Trends for each on the OIS or PI usually show which step changed first.
f: Which PI trends show Knelson health?
How do you tell a screen trip from a Knelson fault?
How often should gravity cyclones be checked?

Why keep gravity gold separate rather th.q: How does gravity recovery performance get tracked against its 14% target?
Why keep gravity gold separate rather th.a:
Gravity recovery compares gold recovered through the gravity route, from Knelson concentrate through the ILR and gravity EW, with gold in plant feed over the same period. The design figure is about 14 percent of feed gold nominal, with 20 percent as the maximum case.

In general, the metallurgist tracks this daily and reconciles it monthly as part of metallurgical accounting, using ILR pregnant solution assays and volumes, gravity EW output and head grade from feed sampling.

The reference doesn't describe this site's accounting method or reports, so ask the metallurgist how gravity recovery is reported here.

f.q: Why is the gravity recovery design ceiling 20 percent?
f.a:
The design criteria give gravity recovery of 14 percent of feed gold nominal and a maximum of 20 percent. The maximum is a design case for ore carrying more coarse free gold, used to size the Knelsons, ILR and gravity EW so they can handle that extra load.

It isn't a physical limit; actual gravity recovery depends on how much gold in the ore is free and coarse enough for the Knelsons to catch. Ask the metallurgist how actual figures compare with the design range.
f: How was the gravity recoverable gold measured?
Could the ILR handle more than 20 percent recovery?
Which ore sources carry the most coarse gold?

f.q: How does head grade affect gravity recovery figures?
f.a:
Gravity recovery is a percentage of feed gold, so it depends on how much gold is free and coarse, not just how much gold there is. Higher grade ore often carries more coarse gold, which can lift gravity recovery, but not always.

Head grade also comes from sampling plant feed, which carries its own error, especially with coarse gold. So a day with an unusual head grade can make gravity recovery look odd. The design nominal head grade is 1.58 g/t Au.
f: How is plant head grade sampled?
Why does coarse gold make head grade uncertain?
What is the design grade case head grade?

f.q: Who reports gravity recovery and how often?
f.a:
The reference doesn't say. In general, the plant metallurgist or metallurgical team calculates gravity recovery, often daily for operations and monthly as part of the formal gold reconciliation between mill, goldroom and refinery.

Shift supervisors and control room operators usually see the related figures, like concentrate mass and ILR batch results, on daily reports. Ask the metallurgist which reports include gravity recovery on this site and where to find them.

Where are daily metallurgical reports kept?

How are the rougher and scavenger cells.q: Why run tank cells in series instead of parallel through flotation?
How are the rougher and scavenger cells.a:
Flotation is a rate process. In any single well mixed tank, some particles leave almost as soon as they arrive, while others stay far longer than needed. Running seven tank cells in series (3 roughers, 4 scavengers) makes the bank behave much closer to plug flow, so nearly every particle gets close to the full 36.5 min design residence time.

Series also gives a grade profile. Fast floating, well liberated sulphide comes off Rougher 1 (design 4.4 percent mass pull at about 15 percent S), slower material comes off Rougher 2 and 3 and the scavengers at lower grade. Think of it like multistage heat exchangers in series getting closer to the target temperature than one big shell.

f.q: Why does a single big mixed tank let particles short circuit?
f.a:
In a perfectly mixed tank the outlet has the same composition as the tank contents, so a fresh particle has the same chance of leaving in the next second as one that has been there for twenty minutes. The residence time distribution is exponential: a big fraction leaves well before the average time.

For slow floating particles that is lost recovery. Splitting the same volume into several cells in series narrows that distribution, the same way several CSTRs in series approach a plug flow reactor in chemical engineering.
f: How many cells in series are enough to get close to plug flow?
Does short circuiting get worse when throughput goes up?
How is residence time distribution measured in a real plant?

f.q: Why is Rougher 1 concentrate higher grade than Rougher 2 and 3?
f.a:
The first cell sees the freshest feed, full of well liberated, fast floating sulphide. That material loads the bubbles quickly and gives a rich froth. By Rougher 2 and 3 the easy sulphide is gone and what is left floats slowly: finer or coarser particles and composites with gangue attached.

The PDC reflects this: Rougher 1 at 4.4 percent mass pull and about 15.3 percent S, Rougher 2 and 3 at 2.4 percent mass pull and about 7.1 percent S, scavengers at about 5.1 percent S. These are design values, not live readings.
f: What makes a sulphide particle fast floating or slow floating?
Could Rougher 1 concentrate ever bypass the cleaner?
How does a change in head grade shift the rougher grade profile?

f.q: How does slurry move from cell to cell without pumps?
f.a:
The cells are set out so slurry flows by gravity from one cell to the next and on to the scavenger tails. Each cell's pulp level is held by its own level control, which the control philosophy describes as two dart valves per cell on split range level control, arranged in series or parallel.

Think of it like a cascade of weirs with control valves: each cell's discharge valve throttles to hold its own level, and whatever it passes becomes the next cell's feed. The bank is only as steady as its level loops.
f: Why are there two dart valves per cell instead of one?
What happens downstream if a dart valve sticks open?
How do the level loops on neighbouring cells interact with each other?

How are the rougher and scavenger cells.q: What would a handover flag if slurry level was backing up between cells?
How are the rougher and scavenger cells.a:
A good handover would say which cell was backing up, when it started, and what the level controller and dart valves were doing. A level rising while its dart valves are already near fully open points to a restriction: a worn or stuck dart valve, a blockage, or the next cell running high. A level rising with valves part closed suggests a control problem, such as a loop left in manual.

It should also note consequences: lost froth depth, pulp spilling into the concentrate launders and diluting grade, and any throughput change at the time. Two dart valves per cell on split range control is from the control philosophy; actual causes on the day need the CRO and area maintenance to confirm.

f.q: Why does pulp spilling into the launder hurt concentrate grade?
f.a:
The froth is meant to carry hydrophobic sulphide while letting water and gangue drain back. If the pulp level rises to the lip, raw slurry, which is mostly gangue at about 34 percent solids feed density, flows straight into the concentrate launder.

That slug dilutes the concentrate and adds mass and water to the cleaner feed. The cleaner then has to reject that gangue, and the extra flow can upset its feed hopper and downcomer flow. It is like bypassing a filter: the downstream equipment gets the dirt.
f: How does the Jameson cleaner cope with a sudden dilute feed slug?
Where do the rougher and scavenger launders actually discharge?
Can operators see pulp carry over on the froth cameras?

f.q: How would you tell a stuck dart valve from a blockage downstream?
f.a:
Compare commanded output, valve position feedback and the levels either side. If the controller output is high but position feedback has not moved, the valve or actuator is the suspect. If the valve shows open but the cell still backs up, look at the next cell: if its level is also high, the restriction is further down.

A trend of level, controller output and position on the PI historian usually tells the story faster than a field walk. Any field work on a dart valve needs proper isolation through the area's permit process.
f: What does a dart valve watchdog alarm tell the operator?
How is a dart valve isolated for maintenance on a running bank?
Why do flotation dart valves wear so quickly in slurry service?

f.q: Does air to a cell change automatically when its level is upset?
f.a:
Not from the level itself, based on the reference. Air to each cell is on its own flow controller with a mass flow meter, and the documented interlock closes a cell's air valve if its agitator stops, to stop the rotor and stator sanding up and protect the bearings.

During a level upset, operators or the flotation expert system may trim air or level setpoints, since the expert system uses OSA data, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set froth depth, air and reagents. Exact logic is a question for the process control engineer.
f: Why does air keep flowing if the agitator is still running?
What does the flotation expert system do when a level loop is in manual?
How quickly does froth depth change when pulp level rises?

How are the rougher and scavenger cells.q: How do the blowers and air rate get adjusted across the cell bank?
How are the rougher and scavenger cells.a:
Air comes from LP flotation blowers fitted with VSDs. The blowers do not set each cell's air; they hold the air header at a pressure setpoint. Each cell then has its own air flow controller with a mass flow meter and control valve, so air is set cell by cell.

The setpoints come from operators or the flotation expert system, which uses the onstream analyser, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set froth depth, air and reagent addition. A cell's air valve closes automatically if its agitator stops. It is the same idea as a compressed air ring main on pressure control with individual flow regulators at each user.

f.q: Why hold header pressure instead of running blowers at fixed speed?
f.a:
If the blowers ran at fixed speed, every time one cell's air valve opened or closed the header pressure would move, and all the other cells' flows would shift with it. Their flow controllers would then fight each other.

Holding header pressure with the blower VSDs decouples the loops. Each cell's flow controller sees a steady supply pressure, just like users on a constant pressure water system fed by a VSD pump. It also saves power because the blowers only make the air actually demanded.
f: What happens to the cells if one blower trips?
How is the header pressure setpoint chosen?
Why use a mass flow meter for air rather than a simple orifice plate?

f.q: What does the flotation expert system use to set air rates?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, the flotation expert system takes in onstream analyser results (Au and Fe, with S inferred from Fe), froth camera data and launder velocity cameras, and uses them to set froth depth (level), air and reagents.

In plain terms, it watches grade and how fast the froth is moving over the lip, then nudges air and level to hold a target grade and recovery. The detailed rules and limits are not in the reference; the process control engineer or metallurgist would know how it is tuned.
f: What does a froth camera actually measure?
When should operators take the expert system out of control?
How often does the onstream analyser update each stream?

f.q: Why does a cell's air valve close if its agitator stops?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the air valve is interlocked closed when the agitator stops, to prevent sanding of the rotor and stator and to protect the bearings.

Without agitation, solids settle around the mechanism. Blowing air into a settled bed channels through it and can pack solids into the rotor and stator. Restarting a rotor buried in sand means very high starting torque, a bit like trying to start a pump full of settled solids. Agitators are kept running whenever a cell has slurry or water in it.
f: How long can a cell sit with no agitation before it sands up?
Why are the agitator drives reversible?
What checks are needed before restarting a flotation agitator?

What is the significance of the scavenge.q: Why is locked gold largely unrecoverable once it reaches CIL4?
What is the significance of the scavenge.a:
Much of the gold in this ore is locked inside sulphides, mainly pyrite, and in tellurides. At the plant grind of P80 180 µm, cyanide can only reach gold that is exposed on a particle surface or cracked open. Gold sealed inside a solid pyrite grain never sees the solution.
