That is why the design leach extraction for CIL4 is only about 38 percent, against about 90 percent for the concentrate leach, where the sulphide has been ground to about 9 µm in the IsaMills. Flotation is the step that sorts locked gold into the stream that gets that fine grinding. Once it slips past the scavengers it gets no second chance.

f.q: Why can't CIL4 just leach longer to get at the locked gold?
f.a:
Time does not help if the solution physically cannot reach the gold. Cyanide and oxygen dissolve gold at its surface; a gold grain fully enclosed in pyrite has no surface exposed to the slurry, so the leach rate for that gold is essentially zero.

CIL4 already has about 12.8 h total residence by design, so it extracts the free and partly exposed gold. Extra tanks would give diminishing returns. Unlocking the rest needs size reduction (UFG) or oxidation, which is why the flowsheet splits concentrate from tails.
f: Why does the concentrate leach need extra oxygen and lead nitrate?
What is the future extra CIL4 tank space intended for?
How fast does free gold leach compared with partly exposed gold?

f.q: What makes telluride gold hard to leach?
f.a:
Gold tellurides, such as calaverite, dissolve in cyanide much more slowly than native gold. Their surfaces tend to passivate, forming tellurium rich layers that slow further reaction, and they are often finely associated with sulphides.

General practice for telluride ores is fine grinding, high oxygen, strong cyanide and additives such as lead nitrate, or oxidation ahead of leaching. That lines up with how this plant treats concentrate. The detailed mineralogy of this ore body is something the site metallurgist or geologist would know.
f: What share of the gold here sits in tellurides?
Does lead nitrate help telluride leaching as well as sulphides?
Why did the old roaster suit telluride ores?

f.q: What is one percent more flotation recovery worth in ounces?
f.a:
Rough arithmetic on design values: 25.5 Mtpa at 1.58 g/t is about 40 t, or about 1.3 Moz, of gold in feed a year. One percent of that is about 13,000 oz.

If that gold went to tails, CIL4 would recover roughly a third. Sent to concentrate instead, it would be recovered at roughly 84 to 90 percent. The net gain is therefore in the order of 6,000 to 7,000 oz a year per percent. These are design numbers, not live operating figures; the metallurgist can give current values.
f: How does gold price change the value of scavenger recovery?
What does the extra concentrate mass cost in UFG power?
How is recovery reconciled each month against the gold poured?

What is the significance of the scavenge.q: What would a handover flag if scavenger tail grades were creeping up?
What is the significance of the scavenge.a:
The handover should flag the trend, not just the last number: how long the scavenger tails grade has been rising, which source showed it (onstream analyser scavenger tails stream or shift samples), and whether head grade or throughput changed at the same time.

It should list likely causes checked: reagent dosing pumps and flows, air and froth depth settings on the scavengers, grind size from the cyclones, and any blower or agitator problems. And it should say what was done and what is still pending, such as a sample sent to the lab. Rising scavenger tails grade means gold heading to CIL4, where only about a third is recovered, so it deserves early attention.

f.q: Why would a coarser grind push scavenger tail grades up?
f.a:
Flotation needs the sulphide surface exposed and particles light enough for a bubble to lift. If the grind drifts coarser than the P80 180 µm target, more sulphide stays locked in composite particles with gangue, and coarse particles are more easily knocked off bubbles in the turbulent cell.

Both effects lower recovery in the roughers and scavengers, and the losses show up in the tails. A cyclone problem, such as roping or too few cyclones open, is a common cause of a coarser grind.
f: How would roping cyclones show up in flotation performance?
What grind size does the high throughput case allow?
How quickly does a grind change reach the scavenger tails?

f.q: How far can you trust the OSA scavenger tails reading?
f.a:
The onstream analyser measures Au and Fe, with sulphur inferred from Fe, on several streams including scavenger tails. Tails are the lowest grade stream in flotation, so the readings sit nearest the analyser's limits and are the most sensitive to calibration drift and sampling issues.

Treat a single reading with caution and look at the trend. Compare against shift composite assays from the lab. If they diverge, the OSA may need recalibrating; the metallurgist or instrument technician would confirm.
f: How is the onstream analyser calibrated against lab assays?
What happens to OSA data if a sample line blocks?
Why is sulphur inferred from iron instead of measured directly?

f.q: Which reagent faults most often show up as tail losses?
f.a:
Collector is the first suspect. If PAX dosing drops, from a pump fault, blocked line or empty tank, sulphides lose their hydrophobic coating and simply stay in the pulp. Frother loss gives weak froth that cannot hold its load. Copper sulphate problems reduce pyrite activation.

The reagent pumps are VSD dosing pumps on flow control with g/t or flow setpoints, so compare actual flow against setpoint first, then check the tank level and line. A flow meter reading normal with a blocked dosing point is also worth ruling out in the field.
f: How quickly does a PAX dosing failure show on the OSA?
Why is copper sulphate added at SAG discharge?
What does overdosing collector do to the cleaner?

What is the significance of the scavenge.q: How do froth depth and air rate on scavengers get tuned to limit losses?
What is the significance of the scavenge.a:
Two main handles: froth depth (set by pulp level) and air rate. A shallow froth with more air lifts more mass and recovers more slow floating sulphide, but carries more gangue. A deep froth with less air drains better and gives higher grade but lower recovery.

Scavengers are a recovery duty, because their concentrate goes to the cleaner rather than to final concentrate. So they generally run shallower froth and higher air than the roughers, within limits: froth carry rate (design about 1.5 t/m2/h), cleaner capacity and avoiding a turbulent, boiling froth. Setpoints come from operators or the expert system; the actual targets are with the metallurgist.

f.q: What limits how hard you can push air on the scavengers?
f.a:
Beyond a point, extra air stops helping. Bubbles coalesce into large ones that carry less mineral, the pulp surface gets turbulent and the froth can boil or collapse, and entrained gangue climbs.

There are also plant limits: blower and header capacity, and the cleaner, since all scavenger concentrate goes to the Jameson cleaner circuit. Overloading the cleaner with low grade mass can cost final concentrate grade. Like overdriving a pump past its best efficiency point, you get more flow but less useful work per unit.
f: How do you recognise a boiling froth from the control room?
What happens to the cleaner if scavenger pull doubles?
Is air distributed evenly across all four scavenger cells?

f.q: How is froth depth actually measured and controlled?
f.a:
Froth depth is the distance from the pulp and froth interface up to the launder lip. Since the lip is fixed, controlling pulp level controls froth depth. Each cell's level is held by its own level controller driving two dart valves on split range control.

The flotation expert system can adjust the level setpoints using OSA and froth camera data. The type of level sensor used on these cells is not stated in the reference; the instrument technician for the area would know.
f: Why does froth depth drift when slurry density changes?
How is froth depth set differently in Rougher 1 and Scavenger 4?
What is a typical froth depth range for scavenger cells?

f.q: What is froth carry rate and why does it matter?
f.a:
Froth carry rate is the tonnes of concentrate solids removed per square metre of froth surface per hour. Lip loading is similar but per metre of launder lip. The design uses 1.5 t/m2/h and 1.5 t/m/h.

If carry rate is too high the froth cannot drain, so it carries water and gangue with the sulphide, and recovery drops because loaded bubbles burst before reaching the lip. It is a capacity limit, like a heat exchanger's maximum heat flux: push past it and performance falls off.
f: How are froth crowders used to manage carry rate?
Why do scavenger and rougher froth factors differ in the design?
Which flotation cell is closest to its carry rate limit?

Where does Rougher 1 concentrate go?.q: Why is 15% S Rougher 1 concentrate still cleaned up to 35% S?
Where does Rougher 1 concentrate go?.a:
Because everything after flotation is paid for per tonne of concentrate. UFG uses about 116 kWh/t, and the concentrate leach uses very high cyanide additions. Every tonne of gangue removed in the cleaner is a tonne that does not have to be ground to 9 µm and leached.

Rougher 1 concentrate at about 15 percent S is still largely non sulphide by mass. The cleaner lifts final concentrate to about 35 percent S, which roughly halves the mass while keeping most of the sulphur (design cleaner stage S recovery about 93 percent). The PDC mass balance and the as built PFD both route Rougher 1 concentrate to the cleaner. Think of it as a pre filter that shrinks the load on expensive downstream equipment.

f.q: How much does cleaning cut the mass going to UFG?
f.a:
As a rough mass balance, if sulphur stayed constant, going from about 15 percent S to about 35 percent S would cut the mass by more than half. In practice the combined cleaner feed is lower grade than Rougher 1 alone, and the cleaner's design mass pull is 31 to 44 percent of its feed.

The design result is about 637 kt/a of final concentrate in the nominal case (about 75 to 78 t/h), which is what sizes the UFG mills. These are design values; the metallurgist has the current figures.
f: How many IsaMills would be needed with no cleaning stage?
Why does the design grade case make more concentrate?
How is concentrate mass measured on its way to the thickener?

f.q: Doesn't cleaning lose some gold along the way?
f.a:
A little, which is why the cleaner is backed up. Cleaner tails go to the cleaner-scavenger Jameson cell, whose concentrate returns to cleaner feed. Only cleaner-scavenger tails leave the loop, going to the flotation tails thickener and then CIL4.

So sulphide rejected once still gets another chance. The design cleaner stage sulphur recovery is about 93 percent, and the cleaner-scavenger recovers much of what the cleaner rejects. Whatever finally escapes is leached in CIL4 at the lower tails extraction.
f: How much gold leaves in cleaner-scavenger tails by design?
Why does the cleaner tails recycle not count as a loss?
How do metallurgists measure gold losses in the cleaner loop?

f.q: When would the dashed bypass to the final hopper be used?
f.a:
The as built PFD (Rev 1, Sep 2026) shows a dashed line from Rougher 1 concentrate straight to the final concentrate hopper, but the reference does not say when it is used.

In general, a bypass like this gives flexibility, for example if the cleaner circuit is down for maintenance or if Rougher 1 concentrate is already high enough grade. Using it would raise concentrate mass to UFG. The metallurgist or a senior control room operator would know whether and when it is actually used.
f: What happens to final concentrate grade when the bypass is open?
Is the Rougher 1 bypass manual or actuated?
How is the cleaner circuit isolated for a shutdown?

Where does Rougher 1 concentrate go?.q: What would a handover flag if Rougher 1 grade dropped below expectations?
Where does Rougher 1 concentrate go?.a:
It should note how far the Rougher 1 grade fell and how it was seen, usually the onstream analyser's Rougher 1 concentrate stream backed by shift samples. Then the likely causes checked: a lower head grade in the flotation feed, froth too shallow or air too high on Rougher 1 pulling gangue, frother overdosing, a change in grind, or a reagent fault.

It should also say what it did downstream. A lower grade Rougher 1 concentrate puts more mass and less sulphide into the cleaner feed, which can cut final concentrate grade. Any setpoint changes made and their effect should be written down so the next shift doesn't undo or repeat them.

f.q: Could a lower head grade alone explain a Rougher 1 grade drop?
f.a:
Yes. Rougher concentrate grade tracks feed grade. Design nominal head grade is 1.02 percent S and the design grade case is 1.49 percent S, so ore variation over that range moves concentrate grade without anything being wrong in the cells.

Check the onstream analyser flotation feed stream first. If feed grade fell by a similar proportion, the cells are probably doing their job. If feed grade held but Rougher 1 grade fell, look at air, froth depth and reagents instead.
f: How does the mine schedule warn the plant of grade changes?
Why does a high sulphur ore still sometimes float poorly?
How do blends from the two SAG mills affect flotation feed?

f.q: How does too much frother pull gangue into the froth?
f.a:
Frother makes small, stable bubbles and a persistent froth. In excess, the froth becomes too stable and wet. It holds more water between the bubbles and does not drain, and that water carries fine gangue with it by entrainment rather than true flotation.

The result is higher mass pull at lower grade. It is a common reason for a grade drop when everything else looks normal. Frother here is Luprofroth 168, dosed to the rougher, scavenger, cleaner and cleaner-scavenger feeds.
f: How can you tell an overdosed frother froth by eye?
Does saline process water change how much frother is needed?
How long does excess frother take to clear the circuit?

f.q: What does a lower Rougher 1 grade do to the cleaner?
f.a:
The cleaner gets more mass with less sulphide per tonne. Its froth has to reject more gangue, so either it holds grade by pulling less (and passing more to the cleaner-scavenger) or it pulls the same mass at lower grade.

More cleaner tails means more load on the cleaner-scavenger and more recirculation back to cleaner feed. The Jameson feed pumps are on flow control, so the external recycle shrinks as new feed rises. The final result can be lower final concentrate grade and more tonnes to UFG.
f: How does the cleaner-scavenger respond to extra cleaner tails?
At what point does the cleaner run out of froth area?
Why does lower final concentrate grade matter for UFG energy?

Where does Rougher 1 concentrate go?.q: How does the cleaner cope when Rougher 1 mass pull rises?
Where does Rougher 1 concentrate go?.a:
The Jameson cleaner is designed around a constant total flow through its downcomers. The feed pump runs on flow control via its VSD, and about half of the cleaner tails are normally recycled back to the cleaner feed hopper. When Rougher 1 pull rises, more new feed arrives and less recycle is needed, so the downcomer flow and jet stay steady.

The real limits come when new feed alone approaches the downcomer design flow, or when the froth area (22.2 m2) cannot carry the extra concentrate. Then grade falls or the feed hopper level climbs. Operators usually respond upstream by trimming Rougher 1 air or deepening its froth.

f.q: What happens when new feed exceeds what the recycle can absorb?
f.a:
The recycle acts as a buffer only while there is recycle left to cut back. Once new feed alone fills the design downcomer flow, the recycle is effectively zero and any more feed pushes total flow up.

Higher downcomer flow means higher jet pressure, a different air to slurry ratio and less time in the tank. The feed hopper level also rises if the pump cannot keep up. At that point the upstream cells need to pull less, or the circuit is simply above design capacity.
f: What hopper level alarms exist on the cleaner feed hopper?
Can the cleaner run with some downcomers shut to suit low flow?
How does the cleaner-scavenger share load with the cleaner?

f.q: Why does froth area limit the cleaner's capacity?
f.a:
Froth can only carry so much concentrate per square metre per hour before it stops draining and loaded bubbles start bursting. The cleaner has a froth area of 22.2 m2 and a design froth factor of 2.5 for cleaner concentrate.

With a high grade, heavy concentrate (design SG 3.93), the froth gets loaded quickly. If carry rate is exceeded, gangue is entrained and sulphide drops back, so grade and recovery both suffer. Like a heat exchanger at maximum flux, extra feed does not make extra output.
f: What is a froth factor in the flotation design criteria?
How do launder velocity cameras help spot an overloaded froth?
Why is concentrate SG important for froth handling?

f.q: How do operators trim rougher pull to protect the cleaner?
f.a:
The usual levers on Rougher 1 are less air and a deeper froth, both of which cut mass pull and lift grade. Reagent trims are slower and affect the whole bank, so air and level are usually adjusted first.

The flotation expert system can make these changes automatically using OSA grades and froth camera data. Operators should note any manual changes and the reason in the handover, since rougher pull, cleaner load and final grade all interact and the effect takes time to show.
f: How long after a rougher air change does cleaner grade respond?
Why trim Rougher 1 rather than the scavengers first?
What does the expert system do if an operator overrides it?

Where do Rougher 2 & 3 concentrate and S.q: Why does lower grade concentrate need extra upgrading before final concentrate?
Where do Rougher 2 & 3 concentrate and S.a:
Rougher 2 and 3 concentrate (about 7 percent S) and scavenger concentrate (about 5 percent S) are mostly gangue by mass. Final concentrate runs at about 35 percent S. Sending low grade concentrate straight on would load the UFG mills and concentrate leach with rock.

That matters because UFG grinds at about 116 kWh/t, and the concentrate leach doses cyanide in thousands of ppm. Grinding and leaching gangue costs power, media, reagents and tank residence time while recovering almost no gold. The cleaner rejects that gangue first. It is like filtering a fluid before a fine bore heat exchanger: you only pay to treat what matters.

f.q: What is the gangue in this ore mostly made of?
f.a:
The reference describes the valuable minerals, mainly pyrite and tellurides carrying refractory gold, but it does not give a gangue mineralogy.

In general, gangue in sulphide gold ores is mostly silicates such as quartz and feldspars, plus carbonates and clay or talc type minerals in some ore types. Its makeup affects entrainment, froth behaviour and grinding. The site geologist or metallurgist would have the mineralogy reports for this ore.
f: Why do clay minerals cause trouble in flotation?
Does gangue type change how hard UFG grinding is?
How is mineralogy checked on plant samples?

f.q: Why is entrainment worse for fine gangue particles?
f.a:
Gangue mostly reaches the froth by riding up with water, not by sticking to bubbles. Fine particles settle slowly, so they follow the water closely. Coarse gangue tends to drop back out of the froth as it drains.

So the finer the gangue, the more it behaves like dissolved material in the water carried into the froth. Recovery of fine gangue rises roughly in step with water recovery. That is why froth drainage and avoiding a wet froth matter so much in cleaning.
f: How does froth wash water reduce entrainment?
Why does more water in the froth mean more gangue?
How does grind size change the amount of fine gangue?

f.q: Why not send scavenger concentrate straight to CIL4 instead?
f.a:
Because its gold is mostly locked in sulphide. CIL4 leaches at about 180 µm and has a design extraction of only about 38 percent. Scavenger concentrate is exactly the slow floating, sulphide bearing material whose gold needs UFG to be released.

Sending it through the cleaner lets its sulphide reach final concentrate, get ground to about 9 µm and leached in CIL2 at about 90 percent extraction. The low grade concentrate is worth the extra cleaning step.
f: How much gold does the scavenger concentrate carry by design?
What would happen to CIL4 cyanide use if it got more sulphide?
Could scavenger concentrate ever be reground before cleaning?

Where do Rougher 2 & 3 concentrate and S.q: What would a handover flag if cleaner feed grade was unusually low?
Where do Rougher 2 & 3 concentrate and S.a:
The handover should say which stream showed it, usually the onstream analyser's cleaner feed stream, and compare it with the streams that make it up: Rougher 2 and 3 concentrate, scavenger concentrate and cleaner-scavenger concentrate (and Rougher 1 concentrate, which also reports to the cleaner).

Likely causes: roughers or scavengers pulling too much mass at low grade from high air or shallow froth, a lower head grade, or a cleaner-scavenger loop building up. It should also note the effect on final concentrate grade and any changes made to air, level or reagents, so the next shift knows what has already been tried.

f.q: Which upstream stream would you check first?
f.a:
Look at the onstream analyser streams feeding the cleaner: Rougher 1 concentrate, Rougher 2 and 3 concentrate and scavenger concentrate, and also the flotation feed.

If feed grade dropped, everything downstream drops with it. If feed is steady, find the concentrate stream that changed most, as it points to the cells pulling too much. The scavengers are a common suspect, since they make the lowest grade concentrate and any air increase there adds a lot of gangue.
f: How does cleaner-scavenger concentrate affect cleaner feed grade?
Can froth camera data point to the cell pulling too much?
Why is sampling a low grade stream less reliable?

f.q: Can a low grade cleaner feed still make target final grade?
f.a:
Often yes, but at a cost. The cleaner can reject more by lowering its mass pull (design range 31 to 44 percent), which holds grade but sends more to the cleaner-scavenger and around the loop. Recovery can suffer if the loop overloads.

If feed is too low grade, the cleaner can't make grade without losing too much sulphide, and the better fix is upstream: get the roughers and scavengers to pull cleaner concentrate. The metallurgist sets the target grade and recovery trade off.
f: What sets the target final concentrate grade on site?
How does the cleaner's pull change with froth depth?
What happens to the cleaner-scavenger when cleaner pull drops?

f.q: How does final concentrate grade affect UFG throughput?
f.a:
UFG is sized in tonnes per hour. Lower grade concentrate means more tonnes for the same gold and sulphide, so the mills fill up sooner. UFG 2 and 3 take about 30 t/h fresh feed each nominally, up to 46 t/h.

When concentrate exceeds UFG 2 and 3, the excess goes to UFG 1, and beyond that to the vacuum belt filters and concentrate stockpile. Every tonne of gangue in concentrate also uses about 116 kWh of grinding energy for no gold.
f: What decides when excess concentrate goes to the stockpile?
How does finer grinding of low grade concentrate affect leach?
Why does UFG power draw track feed rate?

Where do Rougher 2 & 3 concentrate and S.q: How does the cleaner circuit separate sulphide from gangue?
Where do Rougher 2 & 3 concentrate and S.a:
The cleaner is a Jameson cell. Feed is pumped through downcomers as a high velocity jet that sucks in air and shears it into very fine bubbles. Hydrophobic sulphide particles, coated with PAX, attach to those bubbles in the intense mixing zone.

In the tank the bubble and particle clusters rise into the froth, while hydrophilic gangue stays in the pulp and leaves as tails. The froth then drains, letting water and entrained gangue fall back. Fine bubbles give fast, selective attachment, and froth drainage gives the upgrade. Design cleaner mass pull is 31 to 44 percent and stage S recovery about 93 percent.

f.q: Why does froth drainage reject entrained gangue?
f.a:
Gangue that is not attached to bubbles only sits in the froth because it is carried in the water between bubbles. As the froth rises, that water drains back down through the channels between bubbles, taking the loose gangue with it.

Attached sulphide stays stuck to the bubble surfaces. So a froth with time to drain, deep enough and not overloaded, ends up richer in sulphide than the pulp below. It is a gravity separation happening inside the froth layer.
f: What makes a froth too wet to drain properly?
Why does froth depth affect drainage time?
How do bubbles bursting in the froth affect grade?

f.q: Why is a Jameson better than a tank cell for cleaning duty?
f.a:
Jameson cells give very fine bubbles and intense contact in the downcomer without a mechanical agitator, and they are compact. The plant uses Glencore Jameson B6500/24 cells for both cleaner and cleaner-scavenger duty.

Fine bubbles suit the fine, already concentrated feed, and the short, intense contact suits a cleaning duty where the goal is selectivity, not long residence. A tank cell of similar capacity would need much more volume and agitator power. Jamesons are also commonly fitted with froth washing to further reduce entrainment.
f: Do the Jameson cells here use froth wash water?
Why are there no agitators in a Jameson cell?
How does the B6500/24 designation describe the cell?

f.q: How is the cleaner's froth depth controlled?
f.a:
Froth depth depends on the pulp level in the cell. The control philosophy describes level control on flotation cells using two dart valves per cell on split range control, and the flotation expert system can set level (froth depth) along with air and reagents.

On the Jameson cells, air is not separately blown; it depends on total pumped flow through the downcomers, with the feed pump VSD on flow control. The exact level control arrangement on the Jameson tails is best confirmed on the P&ID or with the CRO.
f: Why does Jameson air depend on pumped flow?
What happens to grade if the cleaner froth gets too shallow?
How quickly does the Jameson level loop respond?

Where do cleaner tails go?.q: Why do cleaner tails still need a second pass through a scavenger cell?
Where do cleaner tails go?.a:
The cleaner is run for grade, so it deliberately rejects anything that floats slowly. That reject still holds slower floating sulphide, including composite particles with gold locked inside. Throwing it away would send that gold to CIL4, where only about a third is recovered.

The cleaner-scavenger is another Jameson cell that gives cleaner tails a second, recovery focused pass. Its concentrate, about 13.1 percent S by design, is not good enough for final concentrate, so it goes back to cleaner feed for another try. Only cleaner-scavenger tails leave the loop. It is like a two stage separator with the second stage returning its catch to the first.

f.q: Why is the cleaner run for grade rather than recovery?
f.a:
Because its concentrate is the final concentrate. Everything it sends to the hopper gets ground at about 116 kWh/t in UFG and leached with high cyanide, so gangue there is expensive.

Recovery is protected elsewhere: the roughers and scavengers pull hard for recovery, and the cleaner-scavenger catches sulphide the cleaner rejects. Splitting the job lets each cell be tuned for one target, much like a two stage pump arrangement where each stage is optimised for a different duty.
f: What final concentrate grade is the cleaner aiming for?
What would happen if the cleaner was tuned for recovery instead?
How does froth depth differ between cleaner and cleaner-scavenger?

f.q: Why does cleaner-scavenger concentrate go back to the cleaner?
f.a:
At about 13.1 percent S by design it is well below final concentrate grade of about 35 percent S. Sending it to the final hopper would dilute the concentrate and add gangue to UFG.

Back in the cleaner feed, it mixes with the rougher and scavenger concentrate and gets another cleaning pass. The sulphide eventually reports to final concentrate and the gangue is rejected. The trade off is a circulating load between the two Jameson cells, which needs watching.
f: How large is the circulating load in the cleaner loop?
Can the cleaner-scavenger concentrate overload the cleaner?
How is cleaner-scavenger concentrate pumped back to the cleaner?

f.q: Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?
f.a:
About half of the cleaner-scavenger tails are recycled to its own feed hopper (the external recycle that keeps downcomer flow constant). The rest go to the flotation tailings thickener, where they join the scavenger tails.

Thickener underflow then feeds CIL4. In Stage 2 all flotation tails thickener underflow goes to CIL4, which leaches the remaining gold at the lower tails extraction of about 38 percent by design. Thickener overflow mostly goes to the process water tank.
f: Why does the cleaner-scavenger recycle its own tails?
How do cleaner-scavenger tails change thickener feed density?
How much gold is lost in cleaner-scavenger tails by design?

Where do cleaner tails go?.q: What would a handover flag if cleaner-scavenger concentrate volume spiked?
Where do cleaner tails go?.a:
A spike in cleaner-scavenger concentrate usually means the cleaner is rejecting more sulphide than normal, so more is getting caught on the second pass and sent back. The handover should flag it because it can build into a growing circulating load in the cleaner loop.

It should note likely causes checked: a cleaner downcomer problem cutting air and recovery, cleaner froth too deep, reagent changes, or rougher and scavenger cells sending more mass. It should also note effects seen: cleaner feed hopper level, cleaner feed pump speed, final concentrate grade. And any actions taken, so the next shift doesn't make the opposite change.

f.q: Why can a recycle loop build up a circulating load?
f.a:
Whatever the cleaner fails to float goes to the cleaner-scavenger, which floats much of it back to cleaner feed. If the cleaner keeps rejecting that material, it keeps going round. More recycle in means even more going round, until something limits it.

It behaves like positive feedback in a control loop. A small drop in cleaner recovery can produce a large rise in loop flow. Cleaner-scavenger tails are the only exit, so the loop settles only when enough leaves that way or the cleaner recovers.
f: How long does it take for a cleaner loop buildup to settle?
What limits the maximum circulating load in the loop?
How can operators spot a building loop on the PI trends?

f.q: What does cleaner feed hopper level tell you here?
f.a:
A rising cleaner feed hopper level means more is arriving than the feed pump is sending to the downcomers. With the pump on flow control and the recycle normally shrinking as new feed rises, a sustained high level suggests the new feed, including returning cleaner-scavenger concentrate, has outgrown the downcomer flow.

The general hopper philosophy uses pump speed and water addition loops on level. Exact loops on the cleaner feed hopper are best confirmed on the P&ID or with the CRO.
f: What happens if the cleaner feed hopper overflows?
Why do slurry hoppers need a minimum level?
How does water addition affect cleaner feed density?

f.q: How would cleaner downcomer problems cause this spike?
f.a:
Jameson air comes from the jet in each downcomer. A blocked or worn downcomer or nozzle gives less air and coarser bubbles, so the cleaner floats less sulphide and more reports to its tails.

The cleaner-scavenger then recovers that sulphide and sends it back, so its concentrate flow rises. Fix the cleaner and the loop calms down. Check downcomer pressures, air flow indications and froth appearance, and involve maintenance for any downcomer work under proper isolation.
f: How are downcomer air flows checked on the Jameson cells?
Can a single blocked downcomer be seen from the control room?
Why does nozzle wear lower the jet's air intake?

Where do cleaner tails go?.q: How does recycling cleaner-scavenger concentrate affect circuit stability?
Where do cleaner tails go?.a:
The recycle closes a loop between the cleaner and cleaner-scavenger. That adds buffering, because sulphide is not lost on its first rejection, but also lag and interaction. A disturbance in the cleaner goes to the cleaner-scavenger, then comes back as changed cleaner feed some minutes later, and can circulate a few times before settling.

The design manages this with the external recycle on each Jameson, which keeps downcomer flow steady regardless of new feed rate, and feed pumps on flow control. For operators the lesson is patience: make one change, wait for the loop to settle, then judge. It is like tuning a loop with a long dead time; aggressive moves cause oscillation.

f.q: Why does a recycle loop add lag to the circuit's response?
f.a:
Material rejected now returns later. After a change in the cleaner, the effect on cleaner-scavenger concentrate takes time to show, then that concentrate has to travel back and pass through the cleaner again.

So the full response to a change is spread over several passes around the loop rather than happening at once. In control terms the loop adds dead time and a slow tail to the response, which makes it easy to overcorrect if you judge too soon.
f: How long is the residence time in each Jameson cell?
Why do fast reagent changes make cleaner loops oscillate?
How do metallurgists test the loop's response time?

f.q: How do operators avoid chasing the loop with changes?
f.a:
Make one change at a time and give it time to work through the loop before making another. Use trends of grade and flow rather than single OSA readings, and look at the cleaner, cleaner-scavenger and final concentrate streams together.

The flotation expert system is designed to manage froth depth, air and reagents using OSA and camera data, so manual overrides should be deliberate and recorded in the handover. The detailed tuning and settling times are a question for the process control engineer.
f: When should the flotation expert system be switched off?
How is a manual setpoint change logged for the next shift?
Which stream best shows the whole cleaner loop's health?

f.q: Can the loop be bled to break a buildup?
f.a:
The reference does not describe a dedicated bleed. In the documented flowsheet, cleaner-scavenger tails to the flotation tails thickener are the only normal exit from the cleaner loop, and the as built PFD shows a dashed bypass of Rougher 1 concentrate to the final hopper, not a loop bleed.

In general, a buildup is broken by restoring cleaner recovery or reducing upstream pull. Whether any extra routing exists for upsets is a question for the metallurgist or a senior CRO.
f: What upstream changes reduce load on the cleaner loop?
Is there an emergency dump route for the cleaner circuit?
How long do the Jameson cells take to drain for a shutdown?

Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?.q: Why does combining these tails with scavenger tails make sense before CIL4?
Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?.a:
Both streams are what flotation has finished with: scavenger tails from the end of the rougher and scavenger bank, and cleaner-scavenger tails from the end of the cleaner loop. Both carry low grade sulphide and some free gold, and both need leaching in CIL4 to recover what is left.

Combining them in one thickener means one feed system, one density control point and one water recovery step. The thickener raises solids from about 33 percent to about 56 percent, giving CIL4 more residence time and sending clear water back to the process water tank. Running two separate thickeners for streams headed to the same place would add cost without benefit.

f.q: How much of the thickener feed is cleaner-scavenger tails?
f.a:
By the PDC design mass balance, thickener feed is about 3,071 t/h and scavenger tails about 2,914 t/h. The difference, roughly 150 to 160 t/h, comes from the cleaner-scavenger tails.

So the cleaner-scavenger stream is only about 5 percent of thickener solids. It is small, but it has been through the cleaner circuit and may carry a different sulphide content per tonne. These are design values; actual flows come from the plant's mass flow meters and the metallurgist's balance.
f: Why is scavenger tails so much bigger than cleaner-scavenger tails?
Does the small stream affect flocculant demand much?
How is thickener feed tonnage measured?

f.q: Why does thickener overflow go to the process water tank?
f.a:
The thickener recovers water. The overflow is relatively clear process water, so it goes mainly to the Process Water Tank, which feeds the plant. Top up comes from Bore Water Dam 2 using saline pumps.

Process water here is saline bore water, SG about 1.07. Recycling it reduces demand on borefields and scheme water. It is like a closed cooling water circuit: reuse what you can, top up the losses.
f: What happens if thickener overflow carries too many solids?
Why is process water saline at this plant?
How does recycled water affect flotation reagent behaviour?

f.q: Do cleaner-scavenger tails carry more gold than scavenger tails?
f.a:
The reference doesn't give separate gold grades for the two tails streams. In general, cleaner-scavenger tails can carry more sulphide per tonne than scavenger tails, since they come from material that was already floated once, but they are only a small share of total tails mass.

The onstream analyser does include a cleaner-scavenger tails stream (Au and Fe), so the data exists. The metallurgist would have the actual grades and how much each stream contributes to gold losses.
f: How do metallurgists split gold losses by stream?
Why would composite particles end up in cleaner-scavenger tails?
Could cleaner-scavenger tails be reground instead of leached?

Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?.q: What would a handover flag if thickener feed density suddenly changed?
Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?.a:
Thickener feed density is set by upstream flotation: throughput, flotation feed density and water additions in the circuit. A sudden change usually means something moved upstream, so the handover should say what was found, such as a throughput change, mill water addition change or a flotation upset.

It should also flag the thickener's response: flocculant dosing (in Stage 2 ratioed to feed solids), bed level, bed pressure, rake torque, underflow density and overflow clarity. A big drop in feed solids can dilute floc and cloud the overflow; a big rise can build the bed quickly and raise rake torque. Actions taken and any alarms should be recorded.

f.q: How does flocculant dosing respond to a feed density change?
f.a:
In Stage 2, flocculant is dosed to a feed solids ratio setpoint, so dosing follows the solids tonnage coming in, worked out from flow and density. An inline mixer provides secondary dilution. In Stage 1 dosing was cascaded from bed level using the Manta sub.

If the density measurement is wrong, the floc ratio will be wrong too. So a sudden density change is worth checking against the flowmeter and the actual thickener behaviour before trusting it.
f: What is a Manta sub and how does it measure bed level?
Why is flocculant diluted before it reaches the feed?
What does overdosing flocculant do to the underflow?

f.q: What would rising rake torque tell you?
f.a:
Rake torque shows how hard the rakes are working to move the settled bed. Rising torque usually means bed mass or underflow density is building, from more solids arriving, less being pumped out, or the bed compacting.

The vendor panel also gives bed level, rake height and bed pressure, so look at them together. If torque keeps climbing the rakes can lift or the thickener can bog. Pumping more underflow, within downstream limits, is the normal response. Rake trips and lifts are protective and must not be bypassed.
f: Why do thickener rakes lift automatically under high torque?
What does bogging a thickener mean in practice?
How is bed pressure used to estimate bed mass?

f.q: Why does thickener overflow clarity matter downstream?
f.a:
Overflow mainly feeds the Process Water Tank, which supplies water across the plant. Solids in the overflow end up back in the circuit, in sprays, dilution water and pump gland systems, causing wear and blockages, and the fine solids can carry gold.

The vendor panel reports overflow clarity, so poor clarity usually prompts a floc dosing check and a look at feed conditions. It is like having a filter bypass in a cooling water system: dirt circulates everywhere.
f: What causes a sudden loss of thickener overflow clarity?
How is overflow clarity measured on the vendor panel?
Which users are most sensitive to dirty process water?

Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?.q: How does the flotation tailings thickener prepare this stream for CIL4?
Where do cleaner-scavenger tails go?.a:
The flotation tails thickener takes scavenger and cleaner-scavenger tails at about 33 percent solids (about 3,071 t/h, 6,871 m3/h by design) and raises them to about 56 percent solids underflow (range 50 to 62) for CIL4. It is about 60 m across, 2,827 m2 area, with flocculant to speed settling.

Thicker feed means more leach residence time in CIL4's fixed tank volume and less reagent diluted in water. Underflow pumps are duty/standby, in cascade from bed pressure or density to flow control on the VSD, with recycle to feed on start up or low flow. Overflow is recovered as process water.

f.q: Why does thicker CIL4 feed give more leach residence time?
f.a:
Residence time is tank volume divided by slurry volume flow. For the same tonnes of solids, a higher percent solids means less water and so fewer cubic metres per hour.

CIL4 has fixed tanks, 5,600 m3 live each, and design total residence is about 12.8 h, already below the ideal 14 h. Any loss of underflow density cuts that further. It also means cyanide and lime are dosed into less water, keeping concentrations up for less reagent.
f: What happens to CIL4 if underflow density drops to 50 percent?
Why is 14 h the ideal CIL4 residence time?
Can underflow density be too high for CIL4?

f.q: How are the thickener underflow pumps controlled?
f.a:
Duty/standby underflow pumps, total about 3,329 m3/h by design, are run in cascade. The master loop is bed pressure or density, and it sets the setpoint of a flow loop that drives the pump VSD.

If the bed gets heavy, the master asks for more flow; if it gets light, flow is cut back so the bed can rebuild. It is a standard master and slave arrangement, like a level loop setting a flow controller's setpoint.
f: Why use bed pressure rather than bed level as the master?
How is changeover to the standby underflow pump handled?
What limits underflow pump speed on the high side?

f.q: What happens on start up or at low underflow flow?
f.a:
The underflow can be recycled back to the thickener feed on start up or low flow. That keeps the pumps and lines running above a safe minimum velocity while the bed builds, instead of sending thin slurry to CIL4 or letting the line settle and block.

It is like a pump minimum flow bypass. Pump protection and line velocity are kept safe, and CIL4 only gets underflow once the thickener is producing proper density.
f: How long does a thickener take to build a proper bed?
Why do slurry lines block at low velocity?
How does the CRO switch from recycle to forward flow?

What type of cells are the cleaner and c.q: Why does a plunging jet in a downcomer create finer bubbles than blown air?
What type of cells are the cleaner and c.a:
In a Jameson cell the feed is pumped through a nozzle at the top of each downcomer, forming a high velocity jet. The jet drags air in at the top, then plunges into the liquid column inside the downcomer. In that small, very turbulent mixing zone the air is torn into very fine bubbles, and particles are forced into contact with them.

In a forced air tank cell, air from the blowers is broken up by the rotor and stator in a large volume, which gives bigger bubbles and lower energy per unit volume. A good mechanical analogy is a jet pump or eductor: the motive jet creates suction and violent mixing in a short throat.

f.q: Why do finer bubbles help recover fine particles?
f.a:
Fine particles have little momentum, so they follow the water around a bubble instead of hitting it. Smaller bubbles give more bubble surface per litre of air, and a smaller bubble disturbs less water, so fine particles are more likely to collide and attach.

That makes fine bubbles valuable in cleaning, where the feed is already a fine sulphide concentrate. The trade off is that very fine bubbles rise slowly and can carry less load each, which the Jameson's tank and froth design take into account.
f: Why do coarse particles fall off bubbles more easily?
How is bubble size measured in a flotation cell?
Does saline water change bubble size?

f.q: Is a Jameson downcomer really like a jet pump?
f.a:
Yes, quite closely. A jet pump uses a high velocity motive fluid through a nozzle to create low pressure that draws in a second fluid, then mixes them in a throat. In a Jameson the motive fluid is the slurry jet, the drawn fluid is air, and the downcomer is the throat.

As with a jet pump, performance depends on nozzle pressure and velocity. Drop the motive flow and suction and mixing fall off. That is why steady pumped flow through the downcomers matters.
f: What jet velocity do Jameson nozzles typically run at?
Why does nozzle wear reduce air suction?
How is air drawn into each downcomer metered?

f.q: What sets the air rate in a Jameson cell?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, Jameson air depends on the total pumped flow through the downcomers. There is no blower; the jet draws the air in. The feed pump is on a VSD under flow control, and the external recycle of about half the tails keeps that flow steady when new feed changes.

So controlling the pump flow is, in effect, controlling the air. It's a different mindset from the tank cells, where each cell has its own air flow controller fed from the blower header.
f: Why don't the Jameson cells have their own air flow controllers?
What happens to Jameson air when slurry density changes?
How many downcomers does a B6500/24 cell have?

What type of cells are the cleaner and c.q: What would a handover flag if a Jameson cell's downcomers were blocking?
What type of cells are the cleaner and c.a:
The handover should name which cell (cleaner or cleaner-scavenger) and which downcomers are suspect, and how it was seen. Typical signs are a change in froth appearance, lower air draw, higher pressure at the distributor, falling recovery, or rising cleaner-scavenger concentrate.

It should also say what was done: whether the cell was still running at reduced capacity, whether a downcomer had been taken out of service by maintenance under isolation, and what follow up is booked. Blockage often traces back to trash or oversize getting into the feed, so any upstream screen problems should be noted too. Specific downcomer instrumentation on this plant is not described in the reference.

f.q: What usually causes Jameson downcomers or nozzles to block?
f.a:
Most often trash and oversize. Wood fibre, plastic, rags or coarse particles that get past upstream screening can lodge in a nozzle orifice. Scale build up and settled solids after a stop can also restrict flow.

This plant has linear trash screens on the mill circuit with 1.0 mm apertures, so blockage often hints at a screen problem upstream, such as a torn panel or a screen bypassed during maintenance. Good screening protects nozzles the way a suction strainer protects a pump.
f: How do you check whether a trash screen panel is torn?
Does saline process water cause scale in the downcomers?
How do settled solids after a stop affect restart?

f.q: How does losing a few downcomers change the rest of the cell?
f.a:
With some downcomers blocked, the same pumped flow is shared by fewer nozzles, so pressure and velocity in the rest rise, and air draw and bubble size change. If the feed pump flow controller holds total flow, the remaining downcomers run harder; if the pressure limit is reached, total flow falls.

Either way, contact is less even around the cell and recovery usually drops. It is like a manifold of spray nozzles with some blocked: the others run off design.
f: Can the feed pump flow setpoint be lowered to suit fewer downcomers?
How does nozzle pressure relate to air entrainment?
What recovery loss does one blocked downcomer cause?

f.q: Why does upstream trash removal matter so much for Jamesons?
f.a:
The Jameson relies on small nozzle orifices to make its jet. Anything stringy or oversize that reaches them restricts or blocks flow and kills air entrainment in that downcomer.

Trash removal starts on the mill circuit, with four linear trash screens (three operating, one standby) at 1.0 by 1.0 mm aperture, removing about 27 t/day of wood, grit and trash by design. If those screens are not working well, the Jamesons are among the first places it shows.
f: How is trash screen undersize routed to flotation?
What happens when a trash screen is on standby or down?
Why is wood fibre especially troublesome in slurry circuits?

What type of cells are the cleaner and c.q: What maintenance is specific to Jameson cell downcomers and nozzles?
What type of cells are the cleaner and c.a:
The reference does not list maintenance tasks for the Jameson cells, so this is general practice. The parts that matter most are the nozzles (often ceramic or hard wearing inserts), which wear and enlarge, lowering jet velocity and air draw. Downcomers and their air lines can scale or block and need inspecting and cleaning.

The slurry distributor that feeds the downcomers and the feed pump also wear. Typical work includes measuring nozzle wear against limits, swapping worn nozzles, clearing blockages and checking air entry points. Frequencies and wear limits come from the Glencore vendor manuals and the site maintenance strategy; the area maintenance planner would have them.

f.q: Why does nozzle wear change Jameson performance?
f.a:
As the nozzle orifice wears larger, the same flow passes at lower velocity and pressure. The jet then pulls in less air and mixes less violently, so bubbles get bigger and contact weaker.

Worn nozzles also take more flow for the same pressure, which can push the feed pump harder. Recovery and grade drift off slowly rather than failing suddenly, which is why wear is managed by measurement and scheduled change out. It is like a worn pump impeller wear ring: performance fades quietly.
f: How is nozzle wear measured during a shutdown?
Why are ceramic nozzles used in slurry jets?
Does feed density change nozzle wear rate?

f.q: Can a single downcomer be isolated while the cell runs?
f.a:
The reference does not say. Jameson designs generally allow individual downcomers to be taken out of service, but whether that is done here with the cell running, and how, depends on the isolation design and site procedures.

Any work on a downcomer must follow the area's isolation and permit process, and must never involve bypassing an isolation or interlock. The area maintenance planner or the flotation area supervisor would know the approved method.
f: Who approves isolations for work on the flotation cells?
How many downcomers can be out before performance suffers?
What checks are done before returning a downcomer to service?

f.q: How does feed pump wear affect the Jameson jet?
f.a:
The feed pump is on a VSD under flow control. As the impeller wears, the pump makes less head at a given speed, so the controller speeds it up to hold flow. The jet stays steady while there is speed in hand.

Once the pump reaches maximum speed, flow and nozzle pressure fall, and air entrainment drops with them. A slowly rising pump speed trend for the same flow is an early sign of wear, much like any centrifugal pump on flow control.
f: What does a rising pump speed trend for the same flow tell you?
How is the Jameson feed pump changed out for maintenance?
Why does slurry pump wear accelerate at high speed?

The Jameson cells have an 'external recy.q: Why is steady downcomer flow so important to Jameson cell performance?
The Jameson cells have an 'external recy.a:
A Jameson cell has no blower. Air is drawn in by the jet in each downcomer, and the amount of air and the bubble size both depend on the jet's velocity and pressure. Those depend directly on the flow pumped through the nozzles.

If flow drops, the jet weakens, less air is drawn in, bubbles get coarser and contact suffers. Recovery falls. If flow rises too far, pressure and wear increase. The control philosophy says Jameson air depends on total pumped flow through the downcomers, with the feed pump VSD on flow control. It is like a pump that only performs well near its best efficiency point.

f.q: What happens to air intake if downcomer flow drops?
f.a:
Less flow through the nozzle means lower jet velocity, so the jet creates less suction and drags in less air. The air that does enter is broken up less violently, so bubbles are bigger.

At very low flow the downcomer can lose its proper liquid column and the mixing zone can collapse. Recovery then falls off quickly, not gradually. That is why the design keeps downcomer flow steady with an external recycle rather than letting it follow new feed.
f: Can a Jameson cell flood its downcomers?
How does air to slurry ratio affect recovery?
What does a weak Jameson froth look like?

f.q: Why compare the recycle to a pump minimum flow bypass?
f.a:
A centrifugal pump needs a minimum flow to avoid overheating, recirculation damage and instability, so a bypass returns some discharge to suction when demand is low. Total pump flow stays above the minimum whatever the process takes.

The Jameson external recycle does the same job for the downcomers. When new feed is low, more tails are recycled; when new feed is high, less. The downcomers always see roughly the same total flow, so the jet and air entrainment stay steady.
f: What happens to a centrifugal pump below minimum flow?
Does the recycle split change automatically or by hand?
Why recycle tails rather than adding water?

f.q: How is the Jameson feed pump controlled?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, the Jameson feed pump runs on a VSD under flow control. The flow controller holds the setpoint for total pumped flow through the downcomers, and since air depends on that flow, it also holds the air.

Recycled tails from the external recycle and new feed both enter the feed hopper, and the pump draws from there. Design total cleaner feed including recycle is about 1,998 m3/h, and about 2,048 m3/h for the cleaner-scavenger.
f: What does the operator see if the feed pump hits maximum speed?
How is feed pump flow measured on slurry service?
Why use a VSD rather than a control valve here?

The Jameson cells have an 'external recy.q: What would a handover flag if the recycle pump on a Jameson cell tripped?
The Jameson cells have an 'external recy.a:
The reference describes the external recycle as about half of the cleaner tails going back to the cleaner feed hopper, with the rest going forward. It doesn't describe a separate recycle pump, so check the P&ID for how the split is made on this plant.

If the recycle stream were lost, the feed hopper would receive only new feed. At low new feed rates the hopper level would fall and the feed pump could not keep total downcomer flow, so jet pressure and air would drop and recovery would suffer. A handover should flag when it happened, what alarms showed, how the cell performed and what was done to restore it.

f.q: What happens to a Jameson if its feed pump trips?
f.a:
With no pumped flow there is no jet, so no air is drawn in and the cell stops floating. Slurry in the tank and downcomers can start to settle. New feed arriving at the hopper has nowhere to go but up, so hopper level rises.

The cleaner loop and upstream cells are affected, since rougher and scavenger concentrate keeps arriving. The CRO would see the trip with first out detection. Restart follows the normal sequence and permissives; trips and interlocks must never be bypassed to restart faster.
f: What does first out detection show the CRO after a trip?
Where does cleaner feed go if the Jameson is stopped?
How is the cleaner restarted after a feed pump trip?

f.q: How might the plant's hopper level philosophy apply here?
f.a:
The general control philosophy describes dual hopper level control: loop A uses pump speed at a higher level setpoint, and loop B uses water addition at a lower setpoint to keep minimum line velocity.

On the Jameson feed hoppers the pump is described as on flow control instead, so the arrangement may differ. Whether water addition backs up a falling feed hopper level on the Jameson cells should be confirmed on the P&ID or with the CRO.
f: Why keep a minimum velocity in slurry lines?
What happens if water addition dilutes the cleaner feed too far?
How do the two hopper level loops avoid fighting each other?

f.q: Why is the tails split roughly half recycle, half forward?
f.a:
The split is a result of the design flows rather than a fixed rule. The downcomers are sized for a total flow (about 1,998 m3/h for the cleaner, including recycle), and at nominal new feed about half of the tails need to come back to fill that flow.

When new feed is higher than nominal, less recycle is needed, and when lower, more. About half at design gives room to absorb feed swings both ways, like sizing a buffer for the middle of its range.
f: What new feed rate would leave no recycle at all?
Does the cleaner-scavenger have a similar split?
How is the recycle flow actually measured?

The Jameson cells have an 'external recy.q: How is the recycle rate set relative to new feed rate?
The Jameson cells have an 'external recy.a:
The design basis sets the total downcomer flow, not the recycle. The feed pump holds total flow on its VSD flow controller, and the recycle effectively makes up the difference between that total and the new feed arriving, so the recycle rate falls as new feed rises and rises as new feed falls.

At design, the cleaner feed including recycle is about 1,998 m3/h at 17.5 to 19.5 percent solids, with about half of cleaner tails recycled. The cleaner-scavenger is about 2,048 m3/h. These are design values; actual setpoints are set during commissioning and tuning, and the CRO or process control engineer can show you the live ones.

f.q: What does recycling tails do to cleaner feed density?
f.a:
Recycled tails are thinner and lower grade than the new concentrate feed, so they dilute the feed going into the downcomers. The design cleaner feed, including recycle, is about 17.5 to 19.5 percent solids.

Lower density helps the jet and gives better selectivity, since there is less crowding and entrainment. But at low new feed rates, when recycle dominates, the downcomer feed becomes even more dilute and lower grade, which changes froth loading. Operators should keep that in mind when judging froth appearance at low throughput.
f: Why does dilute feed help Jameson selectivity?
How is cleaner feed density measured?
What happens to grade when recycle dominates at low feed?

f.q: What happens to recycle when new feed rises above design?
f.a:
The recycle shrinks as new feed takes up more of the fixed total downcomer flow. Once new feed alone matches the design total, there is nothing left to cut.

Beyond that, total flow and nozzle pressure rise, or the hopper level climbs if the pump is at its limit. Residence time in the cell falls and the froth can overload. So a sustained high new feed is a signal to look upstream at rougher and scavenger mass pull, not just at the Jameson.
f: How does high mass pull upstream overload the Jamesons?
What happens to Jameson residence time at high flow?
Which alarms warn the CRO of cleaner overload?

f.q: Why is the design flow higher for the cleaner-scavenger?
f.a:
The PDC gives about 2,048 m3/h total feed for the cleaner-scavenger against about 1,998 m3/h for the cleaner, both including recycle. Both are the same Jameson B6500/24 size.

The reference does not explain the difference. In general, the cleaner-scavenger's feed is the cleaner tails, which carry most of the cleaner's water, plus its own recycle, so its volume can be a little higher. The process engineer or metallurgist can confirm the mass balance reasoning.
f: Why are both Jameson cells the same size?
How much water reports to cleaner tails versus concentrate?
Could the two Jameson cells ever swap duties?

Name the flotation collector, activator.q: Why does flotation need three different reagent types working together?
Name the flotation collector, activator.a:
Each reagent does a different job, and flotation needs all three.

The collector, PAX (potassium amyl xanthate), coats sulphide surfaces with a water repellent layer so bubbles can grab them. The activator, copper sulphate, conditions the pyrite surface so the collector attaches more strongly. The frother, Luprofroth 168, does nothing to the minerals; it makes small, stable bubbles and a froth that holds together long enough to carry the sulphide over the lip.

A mechanical analogy is welding: the activator is surface prep, the collector is the bond, and the frother is the fixture that holds everything in place while it sets. Miss any one and the joint fails.

f.q: How does PAX actually stick to a sulphide surface?
f.a:
Xanthate molecules have a polar head that reacts with the sulphide surface and a hydrocarbon tail that points outwards. On pyrite, xanthate is generally thought to adsorb partly as dixanthogen, an oxidised form, and partly as metal xanthate at activated sites.

The result is a surface covered in oily tails that repel water, so a passing air bubble can displace the water film and attach. Amyl xanthate has a fairly long tail, which makes it a strong, less selective collector suited to recovering pyrite with locked gold.
f: Why does xanthate break down if stored or mixed too long?
Is a longer chain xanthate always a stronger collector?
Does saline process water affect how PAX adsorbs?

f.q: Why does pyrite need copper sulphate to float well?
f.a:
Pyrite surfaces oxidise easily and in alkaline or calcium rich water can be partly depressed, so xanthate does not bond strongly. Copper ions from copper sulphate adsorb onto the pyrite surface and create sites where xanthate attaches readily, forming a copper xanthate layer.

The effect is faster, more robust flotation of pyrite, especially slow floating or partly oxidised particles, which is where much of this ore's locked gold sits. The dose has to be right: too much copper can activate unwanted minerals and waste collector.
f: What happens if copper sulphate is overdosed?
How long does copper activation need before flotation starts?
Why is lime pH control important for pyrite flotation?

f.q: Why can't the collector alone make a stable froth?
f.a:
Collector makes particles hydrophobic but does little for the bubbles. In plain water, bubbles coalesce into big ones quickly and the froth bursts as soon as it forms, dropping its load back into the pulp.

Frother molecules gather at the air and water surface, slowing coalescence and making smaller bubbles and a froth that lasts long enough to drain and reach the lip. Loaded mineral particles also help stabilise the froth, so frother and collector work together. Saline water also affects bubble behaviour.
f: Why does saline water make bubbles smaller on its own?
What makes one frother stronger than another?
How long should a good froth last before it collapses?

Name the flotation collector, activator.q: What would a handover flag if froth stability changed despite steady dosing?
Name the flotation collector, activator.a:
Steady dosing setpoints don't guarantee steady chemistry. Common reasons froth changes anyway: ore changes (sulphide content, oxidised or clay rich ore), water chemistry (saline process water and residual reagents returning from thickener overflow), pulp density changes, and changes in air or froth depth.

The reagent itself can also be the problem: a new batch mixed at the wrong strength, an aged PAX solution that has partly decomposed, or a blocked dosing point while the flowmeter still reads normal.

The handover should say when it changed, which cells, what was checked (feed grade, density, air, reagent tank and flows) and what was ruled out, so the next shift doesn't start from scratch.

f.q: How can ore type change the froth with no reagent change?
f.a:
The froth is stabilised partly by the mineral particles riding on it. If feed sulphide grade falls, there is less mineral to load the bubbles and the froth goes thin and watery. Oxidised ore floats poorly with xanthate, so it gives the same symptom.

Clay rich ore does the opposite: fine clays raise pulp viscosity and can make a sticky, overstable froth that carries gangue. So when froth changes suddenly, check the flotation feed OSA grade and ask what the mine is sending before blaming reagents.
f: How does the mine warn the plant about clay rich ore?
What does oxidised pyrite look like in flotation tails?
Why does a low sulphide feed need less collector?

f.q: Can recycled process water bring reagents back into flotation?
f.a:
Yes. The flotation tails thickener overflow mainly feeds the Process Water Tank, and that water goes back around the plant. It can carry residual frother and collector and dissolved salts, on top of the saline bore water itself (SG about 1.07).

So the effective dose at the cells is the fresh reagent plus whatever is in the recycled water. When the water balance changes, such as more top up from Bore Water Dam 2 or poorer thickener clarity, froth behaviour can shift with no change in dosing setpoints.
f: How much fresh top up water does the process water tank get?
Does residual frother in process water build up over time?
Why is scheme water used for some duties instead?

f.q: How would you check the reagent strength actually dosed?
f.a:
Start at the mixing and storage. By the PDC design, PAX is made up at 20 percent w/v, copper sulphate at 25 percent w/v as the pentahydrate, and frother is used neat. A batch mixed at the wrong strength changes the actual g/t even though the pump flow is right.

The dosing pumps are VSD pumps on flow control with g/t or flow setpoints, so compare flow against setpoint, then check the line delivers at the dosing point. Solution strength checks are normally done by the lab or the reagents operator.
f: How long can mixed PAX solution be stored before it degrades?
How are reagent dosing pumps calibrated?
What safety precautions apply to handling PAX?

Name the flotation collector, activator.q: Where along the circuit is each reagent dosed?
Name the flotation collector, activator.a:
From the PDC design basis (nominal doses, design is double for pump sizing):

Copper sulphate is added at SAG mill discharge, actually at the cyclone feed hopper, about 35 g/t of fresh feed, plus a small dose in the cleaner circuit (the PDC lists about 10 g/t of fresh cleaner-scavenger feed).

PAX is staged: rougher feed about 40 g/t, scavenger feed about 35 g/t, cleaner conditioning about 16 g/t and cleaner-scavenger about 16 g/t, all per tonne of fresh mill feed.

Frother, Luprofroth 168, goes to rougher feed (about 12 g/t), scavenger, cleaner and cleaner-scavenger feeds (about 6 g/t each). Actual operating doses are set by the metallurgist and can differ.

f.q: Why is copper sulphate added so far upstream at the cyclones?
f.a:
Activation needs time and mixing. Adding copper sulphate at the cyclone feed hopper means it passes through the cyclones and ball mill circuit before reaching flotation, giving it plenty of contact time with freshly broken pyrite surfaces.

Fresh surfaces made by grinding activate well before they oxidise. By the time slurry reaches the roughers, the pyrite has had its copper treatment and is ready for xanthate. It is like applying primer early in a production line so it has cured by the painting stage.
f: Does copper sulphate affect the gravity circuit on the way?
Why is a little copper sulphate also added in the cleaner circuit?
How is copper sulphate stored and delivered on site?

f.q: Why stage PAX down the circuit instead of one big dose?
f.a:
Xanthate is consumed as it adsorbs on sulphides and slowly decomposes in solution. If it was all added at the rougher feed, the fast floating sulphide would take most of it and the slow floaters in the scavengers would see too little.

Staging keeps fresh collector available along the bank: rougher feed, scavenger feed, then the cleaner and cleaner-scavenger. It also avoids a huge excess at the front end, which would hurt selectivity and waste reagent. It is like injecting fuel at several points rather than all at the inlet.
f: Why is the scavenger PAX dose nearly as large as the rougher's?
What does cleaner conditioning mean in practice?
How does excess PAX affect concentrate grade?

f.q: How do the dosing pumps hit their g/t setpoints?
f.a:
Per the reagent control philosophy, copper sulphate, PAX and frother are dosed by VSD dosing pumps on flow control, with either a g/t or a direct flow setpoint.

In g/t mode the DCS multiplies the dose by the relevant tonnage signal, such as the mill feed weightometer, to work out a flow setpoint, so dosing follows throughput automatically. In flow mode the operator sets litres per hour directly. If the tonnage signal is wrong, the g/t dose will be wrong too.
f: Which tonnage signal does the flotation reagent g/t use?
What happens to dosing if the weightometer fails?
When would an operator choose flow mode over g/t mode?

Froth in the rougher looks flat, watery.q: Why does poor mineral loading make froth watery rather than stable?
Froth in the rougher looks flat, watery.a:
A stable froth is held together partly by the mineral particles on it. Hydrophobic particles sit in the bubble films and armour them, slowing the drainage of the liquid film between bubbles and stopping bubbles from merging and bursting.

With little mineral on the bubbles, the films are bare liquid. They drain fast, thin out and pop, and bubbles coalesce into large ones that collapse. What is left is mostly water and frother, so the froth looks flat, glassy and watery, and carries little sulphide. It is a bit like a foam made with soap alone compared with one stiffened by fine solids.

f.q: What does a healthy, well loaded froth look like?
f.a:
A good rougher froth is fairly fine and even textured, with bubbles that look matt and dark with mineral rather than clear and glassy. It moves steadily over the lip without boiling or collapsing, and drains so it is not dripping with water.

Operators learn the look of each cell, and the froth cameras measure bubble size, colour and speed so the expert system can track it. Exact appearance varies with ore, so ask experienced CROs to show you good and bad froth on the cameras.
f: What do froth cameras measure besides froth speed?
Why does froth colour change with sulphide content?
How does froth look different in Rougher 1 and the scavengers?

f.q: Why do attached particles stop bubbles from bursting?
f.a:
Particles that are partly wetted sit across the thin liquid film between bubbles, like posts in a fence. They resist the film thinning and stop neighbouring bubbles from touching and merging.

They also slow the drainage of liquid through the froth. Too few particles and the films thin and rupture; a well loaded froth is more stable. Very hydrophobic or very large particles can puncture films, so the effect depends on particle size and how strongly collected they are.
f: Can a froth be too stable to handle in the launders?
Why do very fine particles overstabilise froth?
How does froth stability affect concentrate pumping?

f.q: Can too much frother also make the froth look watery?
f.a:
It looks different. Too little frother gives a flat froth that collapses. Too much frother gives a tall, very stable froth of small bubbles that is wet and carries lots of water and entrained gangue. It can look watery in the launder, but it does not collapse in the cell.

So collapsing points to too little frother, collector or mineral, while wet but overstable and tall points to excess frother. Frother dose on this plant is from Luprofroth 168, set by g/t at each feed point.
f: How long does it take an overdose of frother to clear?
Why does excess frother lower concentrate grade?
Can process water carry enough frother to cause overdosing?

Froth in the rougher looks flat, watery.q: What would a handover flag about corrective actions taken on watery froth?
Froth in the rougher looks flat, watery.a:
The handover should list each change made, its time, the size of the change and its effect. For example: frother g/t raised on rougher feed at 0300, froth firmer within about 20 minutes, grade steady. Include air and froth depth changes too, and whether the expert system was in control or overridden.

It should also say whether a root cause was found, such as a dosing pump fault, low feed grade or extra water addition, or whether changes were only treating the symptom. Note any reagent increases that should be reversed once the cause clears, and any samples or lab results pending. That stops the next shift from stacking more changes on top or undoing a fix that worked.

f.q: Why record the time of every setpoint change?
f.a:
Flotation responds with a delay. A reagent change can take several minutes to reach the cells and longer to show in OSA grades and recovery. Without times it is hard to tell which change caused which effect.

Times also let the next shift and the metallurgist line up changes against PI historian trends. It is the same reason a maintenance log records when a valve was adjusted: cause and effect are only clear when you can see the sequence.
f: How long does a reagent change take to reach the scavengers?
Does the DCS log operator setpoint changes automatically?
How are handover notes recorded on site?

f.q: Should temporary reagent increases be reversed later?
f.a:
Usually, once the cause has cleared. If frother or collector was raised to rescue a froth upset caused by low feed grade or a pump problem, leaving the higher dose on afterwards wastes reagent and can hurt grade through over frothing or less selective collection.

That is why the handover should flag them as temporary with the reason. The decision on when to reverse belongs to the shift supervisor or metallurgist, based on froth, OSA and assays.
f: How much does excess PAX cost per day at design rates?
Who signs off on reagent setpoint changes on shift?
What are the signs that a reagent increase is no longer needed?

f.q: Where would the next shift verify those changes?
f.a:
On the OIS screens for the flotation area, which show reagent flows and setpoints, air flows, cell levels and expert system status. The PI historian trends show the history: when setpoints changed and how froth, OSA grades and flows responded.

Comparing the handover notes with the trends is a good habit. If they don't match, ask before assuming. Froth cameras give a quick check of what the froth looks like now compared with the description handed over.
f: How do you pull up a PI trend for a flotation cell?
What does expert system status look like on the OIS?
Which flotation trends are most useful at shift start?

Froth in the rougher looks flat, watery.q: How do operators tell apart a reagent problem from a mechanical air problem?
Froth in the rougher looks flat, watery.a:
Start by asking whether one cell or the whole bank is affected. Reagents and ore act on the whole bank, often starting at the front and moving down. A mechanical air problem is usually local: one cell with its air flow off setpoint, its air valve not responding, or its agitator running poorly.

Then check the air side: each cell's air flow controller (setpoint against actual, valve position) and blower header pressure. Check agitator status and power draw. Then check the reagent side: dosing flows against setpoint, tank levels and feed grade.

If air and agitation look normal in every cell, the cause is probably chemistry or ore. It is like fault finding a multi pump system: a fault on one unit points to that unit, a fault on all points to the common supply.

f.q: Why does a problem in one cell point to a mechanical cause?
f.a:
Reagents and feed changes reach all cells, because slurry flows through them in series. If only one cell is struggling while its neighbours look fine, the common inputs are probably not the problem.

The usual suspects are that cell's own equipment: air flow controller, air valve, agitator, rotor and stator, dart valves or level loop. A partly blocked air line or a sticking air valve can starve one cell while the header pressure looks normal.
f: How can a cell show normal air flow but still be starved of air?
What does a failed level transmitter do to one cell's froth?
How are individual cell air valves tested?

f.q: What does a worn rotor and stator do to the froth?
f.a:
The rotor and stator disperse air into fine bubbles and keep solids suspended. As they wear, the bubbles get coarser and less evenly spread, and suspension can suffer.

The froth then gets patchy and coarser, with areas boiling where big bubbles break through, and recovery drops, especially of fine particles. Agitator power draw can drift too. The agitators here have reversible drives to even out rotor wear. Wear inspections are a planned maintenance task.
f: Why do reversible drives even out rotor wear?
How is agitator power draw used to spot problems?
How often are flotation rotors and stators replaced?

f.q: How do you confirm a dosing pump is really delivering?
f.a:
The flowmeter reading against setpoint is the first check, but a meter can read normally while a line downstream is blocked or leaking. A drawdown test, timing the fall in a calibration column or tank level, confirms the actual rate.

In the field, check the dosing point is not blocked and the line is intact. Reagent work involves hazardous chemicals such as PAX, so it must follow the area's procedures and PPE requirements. Instrument or reagent area techs normally do calibration checks.
f: What PPE is needed around the PAX dosing system?
Why can a blocked dosing point still show normal flow?
How often are reagent flowmeters checked?

Raising the air rate on the scavengers g.q: Why does more air lift gangue along with the wanted sulphides?
Raising the air rate on the scavengers g.a:
More air means more bubbles and faster froth removal, and three things pull gangue up with it.

First, entrainment: a faster, wetter froth carries more water from the pulp, and fine gangue rides up suspended in that water. Second, weakly floating particles, such as composites with a small sulphide patch, get more chances to meet a bubble and get lifted. Third, the froth spends less time draining, so less gangue falls back.

The result is higher mass pull and recovery but lower grade. That is why scavenger concentrate goes to the cleaner rather than straight to final concentrate. It is like opening a filter's bypass: more flow, less clean.

f.q: Why does a faster moving froth carry more water?
f.a:
Water reaches the froth in the films around bubbles. More air means more bubbles and so more water carried up per minute. A faster moving froth also gets to the lip sooner, giving that water less time to drain back down.
