What happens to concentrate in excess of.q: Why does filter cake need to stay under 10% moisture?
What happens to concentrate in excess of.a:
The design target for filter cake from the existing vacuum belt filters is below 10 percent moisture. Lower moisture means less water to carry, cake that handles and stacks properly rather than slumping, and a stockpile that is easier to reclaim.

There is also a transport angle. Stockpiled concentrate must be under its Transportable Moisture Limit, about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w, if it is to be moved in bulk. The 10 percent cake target is above that range, so cake straight off the filter may still be too wet to ship. The reference doesn't explain how that gap is closed; the metallurgist would know whether further drying on the stockpile is relied on.

f.q: What is the Transportable Moisture Limit in plain terms?
f.a:
TML is the highest moisture content at which a bulk material can be safely shipped without risk of liquefying. Under the international bulk cargo code it is set from lab testing at a margin below the flow moisture point, the moisture at which the material starts to behave like a fluid under vibration.

For this concentrate the reference gives a TML of about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w. Above it, the material is not considered safe to transport in bulk.

How is TML tested in the lab?
Why does the TML range vary for this concentrate?

f.q: How does a horizontal vacuum belt filter dewater cake?
f.a:
Slurry is spread onto a moving filter cloth supported on a rubber belt running over vacuum boxes. Vacuum draws water through the cloth, leaving a cake that dries as it travels along. At the end the cake drops off the belt and the cloth is washed.

The equipment list shows two 55 m2 Delkor horizontal belt filters with filtrate pumps, wash pumps and blowback fans. Cake moisture depends on vacuum level, belt speed, cake thickness and particle size.

What does a filter blowback fan do?

f.q: Why is the cake target higher than the TML?
f.a:
The reference gives both figures, cake below 10 percent moisture and TML of about 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w, but not how they relate. They serve different purposes: 10 percent is a design target for filter performance, while TML is a transport safety limit.

In general, cake can drain or dry further on a stockpile, and material only needs to meet TML when loaded for bulk transport. Whether that happens here, and how moisture is checked before dispatch, is a question for the metallurgist.

What happens to concentrate in excess of.q: What happens if concentrate exceeds its Transportable Moisture Limit?
What happens to concentrate in excess of.a:
Above its Transportable Moisture Limit, concentrate can liquefy during transport. Vibration and motion in a truck or ship push water out of the pores, the particles lose contact, and the cargo suddenly behaves like a slurry. In a ship hold it can shift to one side and capsize the vessel; in trucks it slops and spills.

So concentrate above TML must not be moved in bulk until its moisture is brought down, by drying, draining or blending, depending on site practice. Stage 2 removes regular concentrate haulage to the offsite roaster, but the stockpile limit still applies whenever concentrate is moved. The metallurgist or logistics coordinator would know the local rules.

f.q: Why does wet concentrate liquefy under vibration?
f.a:
In a moist granular material, particles hold each other up through contact, with water in the gaps. Vibration compacts the particles, shrinking the gaps and squeezing the water. If there's too much water, pore pressure rises until particles are effectively floating and the contacts are lost.

The material then flows like a liquid even though it looked solid. It's the same mechanism as soil liquefaction in earthquakes. Below TML there isn't enough water for this to happen.
f: Why does fine concentrate liquefy more easily than coarse ore?
How fast can liquefaction happen in a ship's hold?
Does compaction on a stockpile cause liquefaction?

f.q: How is concentrate moisture tested?
f.a:
Routine moisture is measured by weighing a sample, drying it in an oven, and weighing again; the loss is the moisture percentage. It's simple and reliable if the sample is representative.

TML itself is set by specialised lab tests, such as a flow table or penetration test, on the specific concentrate. Routine moisture results are then compared against that limit before dispatch. The site lab and metallurgist would run and interpret these.

f.q: What happens to stockpiled concentrate in Stage 2?
f.a:
The reference only says excess concentrate beyond UFG capacity goes through the vacuum belt filters to the concentrate stockpile. It doesn't say whether it is later reclaimed into UFG, sold, or held.

Since Stage 2 is meant to remove concentrate haulage to the offsite roaster, the stockpile is likely a buffer for peaks. The metallurgist or plant superintendent would know the actual plan and any limits on stockpile size.

What happens to concentrate in excess of.q: What equipment moves filtered concentrate onto the stockpile?
What happens to concentrate in excess of.a:
Per the equipment list, cake from the two 55 m2 Delkor horizontal belt filters (F35-FI-01 and F35-FI-21) goes onto the concentrate stockpile feed conveyors, F35-CV-17 and F35-CV-18. Both are 650 mm wide belts, and CV-17 is listed at about 114 t/h and 0.6 m/s.

CV-17 feeds through a transfer chute (F35-CH-01, lined with UHMWPE to stop sticky cake building up) and CV-18 lifts the cake to the stockpile. Like all plant conveyors, they have start sirens, pull wires, belt drift switches, under speed sensors and blocked chute detection. How the stockpile is reclaimed isn't stated in the reference.

f.q: Why do the stockpile conveyors run so slowly?
f.a:
At about 0.6 m/s, CV-17 runs slowly compared with ore conveyors. Filter cake is fine, damp and sticky, and the tonnage is small, so a slow, narrow belt has plenty of capacity.

Slow speed also reduces spillage, carryback and dust, and is gentler at transfer points where sticky cake can build up. The UHMWPE lined chute helps for the same reason. It's a good example of sizing a conveyor for material behaviour rather than just tonnes.
f: What causes carryback on conveyors handling sticky cake?
How are belt scrapers set up for fine concentrate?
Why is UHMWPE used to line sticky material chutes?

f.q: What protections apply on these conveyors?
f.a:
The plant conveyor philosophy applies: start siren, LCS E stop, pull wires reset in the field, inner (alarm) and outer (trip) belt drift switches, under speed sensor, belt rip detector, and microwave blocked chute switch with delay. A trip stops interlocked upstream equipment.

So if CV-18 trips, CV-17 and the filter discharge upstream stop too. These are safety and process protections; pull wires and E stops are critical interlocks and must never be bypassed.
f: Why must pull wires be reset in the field?
What does a belt drift switch protect against?
How does a microwave blocked chute switch work?

f.q: How is filtrate from the belt filters recovered?
f.a:
The equipment list shows filtrate pumps and final filtrate pumps on each filter, plus wash pumps and blowback fans. Vacuum draws filtrate through the cloth into a receiver, and the pumps move it on.

The reference doesn't say where filtrate is sent. In general it's returned to a thickener or process water system so fine solids and dissolved values aren't lost. The UFG and filtration operators or the P&IDs for area F35 would show the routing.
f: Why is filtrate pumped from a vacuum receiver?
What causes cloudy filtrate on a belt filter?
How is filter vacuum generated?

After UFG, where does the ground concent.q: Why does more residence time in leach improve gold extraction?
After UFG, where does the ground concent.a:
Gold dissolution in cyanide takes time, especially for gold that is only partly exposed after UFG, or held in tellurides that leach slowly. The longer the slurry stays in contact with cyanide and oxygen, the more of that slow leaching gold dissolves, up to a plateau.

CIL2 has a fixed volume: seven tanks of 1,685 m3. Thickening UFG product from the very dilute cyclone overflow (about 17 to 18 percent solids) to about 52 to 58 percent solids cuts the slurry volume flow sharply, so the same tonnes stay much longer. It also concentrates reagents in less water and recovers water. It is the same logic as slowing flow through a heat exchanger to get more heat transfer.

f.q: How long does concentrate spend in the CIL2 leach train?
f.a:
The PDC works it out directly. Seven tanks of 1,685 m3 give 11,795 m3. At the design grade feed of about 104 t/h solids (about 137 m3/h of slurry including reagents), leach residence is about 86 hours. At the nominal 75 t/h it is about 119 hours. The design minimum is 80 hours.

That is a very long leach compared with CIL4's design 12.8 h, reflecting how slowly refractory concentrate gold dissolves. CIL3 adds roughly another 74 to 102 hours of adsorption. Live residence depends on actual flow, density and tank levels.
f: Why does refractory concentrate need such a long leach?
How do tank levels affect actual residence time?
What is CIL4's leach residence time by design?

f.q: Why does UFG product need thickening at all?
f.a:
UFG cyclone overflow is only about 17 to 18 percent solids by design, so most of the stream is water. Feeding that straight to CIL2 would cut residence time to a fraction and dilute cyanide, lime and lead nitrate, raising reagent use.

The pre-leach thickener (existing 30-TH-31, repurposed) brings it up to about 52 to 58 percent solids and returns the water to the circuit. It makes the leach work properly in tanks that were already there.
f: Why is UFG cyclone overflow so dilute?
Where does pre-leach thickener overflow go?
How does flocculant affect fine UFG product settling?

f.q: Does longer residence ever stop paying off?
f.a:
Yes. Leach curves flatten: after the easily reached gold has dissolved, each extra hour recovers less. Meanwhile the slurry keeps consuming cyanide and oxygen, and reactive sulphides can tie up cyanide.

The design balances residence, reagent use and extraction at about 90 percent. Beyond that point, more residence costs more than the gold it recovers. Leach testwork, which the metallurgist holds, defines where the curve flattens.
f: What does a typical leach kinetics curve look like?
Why do sulphides keep consuming cyanide over time?
How is the CIL2 leach profile sampled along the train?

After UFG, where does the ground concent.q: What would low pre-leach thickener underflow density do to CIL2?
After UFG, where does the ground concent.a:
Low underflow density means more water going to CIL2 with the same solids. Residence time falls, since there are more cubic metres per hour through fixed tanks, and reagent concentrations drop: cyanide on CIL2 is ratioed to solids mass flow, so the same kilograms end up in more water, giving lower ppm.

The combined effect is slower, less complete leaching and a risk of extraction falling below the design 90 percent. Extra water also flows on through CIL3 to CIL4, cutting its residence too. The handover should flag the density drop, its cause, such as a thickener upset, floc problem or pumping too hard, and any effect on CIL2 cyanide levels.

f.q: Why does extra water dilute cyanide if dosing follows solids?
f.a:
On CIL2, cyanide is ratioed to the solids mass flow on the feed: so many kilograms per tonne of solids. That keeps the dose matched to the concentrate's cyanide demand.

But cyanide concentration in ppm is about kilograms per volume of solution. If density falls and water rises, the same kilograms spread through more solution, so ppm falls. Leach rate depends on concentration, so it slows. Operators may need to raise the dose or fix density to restore it.
f: How is free cyanide measured in CIL2?
What cyanide levels does CIL2 target along the train?
Why are later CIL2 tanks run at higher cyanide?

f.q: Can underflow density be too high for CIL2?
f.a:
Yes. Very dense slurry gets viscous, especially with fine UFG product. That makes agitation and oxygen transfer harder, since bubbles don't disperse well, it raises pumping and agitator loads, and it risks sanding in tanks and lines.

The design range of about 52 to 58 percent solids balances residence against those limits. Pushing above it to gain residence can backfire through poor oxygen and mixing. The metallurgist sets the target.
f: How does viscosity affect oxygen transfer in a leach tank?
What happens if a CIL2 agitator trips with dense slurry?
How is slurry viscosity checked on plant?

f.q: Where does extra leach water end up?
f.a:
Water fed to CIL2 flows on through CIL3, then CIL3 tails go to the CIL4 feed distribution box, joining thickened flotation tails. So extra water upstream also adds volume to CIL4, where residence is already tight at about 12.8 h by design.

From CIL4, slurry goes to the final tails tank and to the tailings storage facility. Water comes back as cyanide water from decant return, treated with hydrogen peroxide. Holding density at the pre-leach thickener protects both leach circuits.
f: Why is CIL4 residence below the 14 h ideal?
How is decant water treated before reuse?
What does CIL3 tails add to CIL4 feed?

After UFG, where does the ground concent.q: How is this thickener's underflow density controlled and checked?
After UFG, where does the ground concent.a:
Per the control philosophy, the concentrate pre-leach thickener (existing 30-TH-31) has duty and standby VSD underflow pumps in a cascade: the master loop is bed pressure or underflow density, and it sets the speed or flow of the pumps. If the bed gets heavy, the pumps speed up; if it gets light, they slow down so the bed can build. Underflow can also be recycled to the feed box.

Density is normally measured by a nucleonic density gauge with a magnetic flowmeter, giving slurry mass flow using an operator entered solids SG. Flocculant on existing thickeners is pumped by VSD floc pumps cascaded from bed level. The design target is about 52 to 58 percent solids underflow.

f.q: Why recycle underflow back to the feed box?
f.a:
Recycling lets the underflow pumps keep running at a safe minimum flow when the bed is thin, such as at start up or after an upset, without sending dilute slurry to CIL2. It also keeps the underflow line moving so it doesn't settle and block.

Once the bed builds and density reaches target, flow goes forward to CIL2. It's like a pump minimum flow bypass that also protects the downstream process from off spec feed.
f: How long does 30-TH-31 take to build a bed after a stop?
Why do slurry lines block at low velocity?
Who switches the underflow from recycle to forward?

f.q: How does a nucleonic density gauge work?
f.a:
A small sealed radioactive source on one side of the pipe sends gamma rays through the slurry to a detector on the other side. Denser slurry absorbs more radiation, so fewer counts reach the detector. The gauge is calibrated to convert counts into density.

It's non contacting, so it suits abrasive slurry. Combined with a mag flowmeter and the operator entered solids SG, the DCS calculates dry solids mass flow. Radiation sources are controlled items; only licensed people may work on them.
f: What safety rules apply around nucleonic gauges?
Why does solids SG have to be entered by the operator?
How is a density gauge recalibrated?

f.q: What does bed pressure tell you that bed level doesn't?
f.a:
Bed level shows where the interface between settled solids and clear liquid sits. Bed pressure, from a pressure sensor near the thickener floor, shows the mass of solids sitting above it.

Two beds at the same level can hold different masses if one is more compacted, so bed pressure is a better guide to inventory and to the underflow density you'll get. That's why it is used as the master for underflow pump control on these thickeners.
f: How does compaction change underflow density?
Can bed pressure readings drift over time?
What happens if the bed pressure sensor fails?

In Stage 2, what are CIL2 and CIL3 used.q: Why split leaching and adsorption into two separate tank trains here?
In Stage 2, what are CIL2 and CIL3 used.a:
Concentrate leaching needs harsh conditions: cyanide targets rising to thousands of ppm, pH about 11.75 to 12.5, oxygen injection and lead nitrate, over a long residence of about 86 to 119 hours by design. Splitting the job lets CIL2 be run purely for dissolution, with oxygen injection pumps and side lances, while CIL3 holds the carbon in calmer tanks with no oxygen added.

Keeping carbon out of the leach tanks also protects it from the high shear oxygen pumps, which would grind it into fines that carry gold to tails. And it suited the existing plant: two trains of 1,685 m3 tanks were already there. The design adsorption efficiency in CIL3 is about 99 percent. It's like separating a reactor from its product recovery column.

f.q: Why is no oxygen added in the CIL3 adsorption tanks?
f.a:
By the time slurry reaches CIL3, the leach is meant to be essentially finished in CIL2, so CIL3's job is just to load dissolved gold onto carbon. Carbon adsorption doesn't need oxygen.

The reference simply states CIL3 has no oxygen. In general, leaving it out saves oxygen and avoids extra shear and turbulence that would wear the carbon. Any small amount of further leaching in CIL3 relies on oxygen and cyanide already in solution.
f: Does any gold still leach inside CIL3?
Why does turbulence wear activated carbon?
How long does slurry spend in CIL3 by design?

f.q: What is the difference between CIL and CIP?
f.a:
In carbon in leach (CIL), carbon sits in the same tanks where leaching happens, so gold is adsorbed as soon as it dissolves. In carbon in pulp (CIP), leaching is done first in separate tanks, then the slurry passes through a separate train of adsorption tanks containing carbon.

Stage 2 runs the concentrate circuit like a leach then adsorption, CIP style, train: CIL2 leach, CIL3 adsorption. The names CIL2 and CIL3 are kept from their history. CIL4 is a true leach plus CIL arrangement with 2 leach and 6 adsorption tanks.
f: Why is CIL used for preg robbing ores?
Why does CIL4 have leach only tanks at the front?
Which arrangement needs less carbon inventory?

f.q: Why would carbon in the leach tanks be a problem here?
f.a:
Several reasons, in general terms. The oxygen injection pumps on the first CIL2 tanks shear slurry hard, which would grind carbon into fines, and fine loaded carbon escaping through screens takes gold with it. High lime and reactive sulphide slurry can also foul carbon, lowering its activity.

Carbon in the leach also means moving carbon through more tanks and screens. The reference doesn't give the design reasoning; the process engineer could confirm what drove the split.
f: How does carbon fouling reduce gold adsorption?
What size are carbon fines that escape intertank screens?
How is fine carbon recovered from tails?

In Stage 2, what are CIL2 and CIL3 used.q: What would you see if CIL2 leach tanks weren't dissolving gold fast enough?
In Stage 2, what are CIL2 and CIL3 used.a:
You'd see it first in the leach profile: gold in solution along the CIL2 tanks rising more slowly than normal, and solid residue assays in the CIL2 discharge and CIL3 tails staying high. CIL3 carbon would load less, and extraction would fall below the design 90 percent.

The usual suspects are low dissolved oxygen (PDC target about 10 ppm), free cyanide below the tank targets, pH out of range, lead nitrate dosing problems, coarse UFG product, and short residence from low feed density or high throughput. The handover should flag which of these were checked, what was out, and what was done.

f.q: How does dissolved oxygen limit gold dissolution?
f.a:
Gold dissolution in cyanide needs both cyanide and oxygen: the classic reaction uses oxygen as the oxidant. At the high cyanide levels in CIL2, oxygen usually becomes the limiting reagent, so the rate of gold dissolution follows the dissolved oxygen level.

Fine sulphide concentrate also consumes oxygen quickly. That is why the PDC sets a dissolved oxygen target of about 10 ppm in CIL2 and adds oxygen through side lances and injection pumps rather than relying on air.
f: Why is pure oxygen used instead of air?
How quickly does fine sulphide consume dissolved oxygen?
What DO target does CIL4 run at by design?

f.q: How is the leach profile sampled along the train?
f.a:
In general, samples are taken from each tank for solution gold, free cyanide, pH, dissolved oxygen and solids residue. Plotting solution gold and residue down the train shows where dissolution is happening and where it stalls.

On CIL4 the Gekko Carbon Scout samples leach tanks for DO, pH and solids. The reference doesn't describe an automatic sampler on CIL2, so CIL2 profiles may rely on manual samples. The metallurgist or CIL operators can show the routine.
f: What is a solids residue assay?
How often is a CIL2 leach profile run?
Why might solution gold fall in later leach tanks?

f.q: Why can coarse UFG product look like a leach problem?
f.a:
If UFG product drifts coarser than about 9 to 12 µm, more gold stays locked in sulphide and simply can't dissolve, however good the leach chemistry is. The symptoms match a slow leach: low solution gold and high residue.

So before changing cyanide or oxygen, check the UFG particle size analyser trend and power draw per tonne. If grind moved first, fix the mills, not the leach. It's like blaming a heat exchanger when the inlet temperature changed.
f: How long does a UFG grind change take to reach CIL2 tails?
What residue grade signals a grind problem?
How do metallurgists separate grind from chemistry effects?

In Stage 2, what are CIL2 and CIL3 used.q: How is loaded carbon moved out of CIL3 to elution?
In Stage 2, what are CIL2 and CIL3 used.a:
Carbon moves countercurrent to the slurry. Barren carbon is added at the last tank and pumped forward tank by tank against the slurry flow, using recessed impeller pumps, with Kemix MPSP intertank screens (1.0 mm) keeping carbon in each tank.

Loaded carbon is pumped from the first adsorption tank (Tank A, or Tank B) by a new single loaded carbon pump to a new Derrick linear motion screen (0.8 x 12.8 mm), which separates carbon from slurry. Carbon goes to a transfer hopper, then is pumped to the existing acid wash columns ahead of elution. By design, each carbon transfer cycle takes about 4 h, based on 11 t batches.

f.q: Why does carbon move against the slurry flow?
f.a:
Countercurrent flow keeps the driving force high. Fresh barren carbon meets the leanest solution at the tail end, so it scavenges the last traces of gold. The most loaded carbon meets the richest solution at the front, so it can load up to a high grade.

It's the same principle as a counterflow heat exchanger: running the streams opposite ways gets the most transfer from the least area. Here it gets the most gold onto the least carbon.
f: Why does fresh carbon go into the last tank?
What happens if carbon is moved too quickly?
How is carbon concentration checked in each tank?

f.q: What does the loaded carbon screen do?
f.a:
Loaded carbon is pumped out as a carbon and slurry mix. The Derrick linear motion screen, with 0.8 x 12.8 mm openings, holds the carbon granules on its deck and lets slurry pass through to return to the circuit.

The drained carbon then goes to a transfer hopper and on to the acid wash columns. Without the screen, slurry would go to elution with the carbon and upset the acid wash and strip. It's a coarse strainer that keeps the elution feed clean.
f: Where does the screen undersize slurry return to?
Why are slotted openings used on carbon screens?
What happens if the carbon screen panels wear?

f.q: Why are recessed impeller pumps used to move carbon?
f.a:
A recessed impeller sits back in the casing, so most of the flow moves by vortex action rather than passing through the impeller vanes. Carbon granules don't get struck hard, which limits attrition.

Carbon breakage makes fines that pass the screens and leave with tails, taking loaded gold with them. The PDC specifies recessed impeller pumps for CIL3 carbon transfer. It's the same reason gentle pumps are used for food solids: protect the product, accept lower efficiency.
f: How much carbon is lost to attrition each year?
What is the efficiency penalty of a recessed impeller?
How does the carbon detection meter on CIL3 tails work?

Why is the concentrate leach run at high.q: Why does sulphide passivation slow gold dissolution without lead nitrate?
Why is the concentrate leach run at high.a:
Sulphide minerals partly dissolve in an alkaline cyanide leach, releasing sulphide ions. Those react at the gold surface to form thin sulphur rich films that block cyanide and oxygen, so gold dissolution slows or stalls. This is passivation. Very fine UFG product has a lot of fresh sulphide surface, so the effect is strong.

Lead nitrate counters it in two ways. Lead ions precipitate dissolved sulphide as insoluble lead sulphide, removing it from solution. And lead deposits on the gold surface in a way that keeps it electrochemically active. The result is faster gold dissolution and lower cyanide and oxygen use. On this plant, lead nitrate is added at the CIL2 leach feed box.

f.q: Where do the sulphide ions in the leach come from?
f.a:
From the sulphide minerals themselves. Pyrite is fairly stable, but more reactive sulphides such as pyrrhotite, and fresh fractured pyrite surfaces made in UFG, partly dissolve in alkaline cyanide and oxygen, releasing sulphide and other sulphur species.

Those also consume cyanide, forming thiocyanate, and oxygen. The finer the grind, the more surface is exposed, so the more sulphide is released. That's the downside of grinding to about 9 µm.
f: Does this ore contain pyrrhotite?
What is thiocyanate and where does it go?
Why does fresh fracture surface react faster?

f.q: Can too much lead nitrate harm the leach?
f.a:
Yes, in general. Excess lead at high pH can form lead hydroxide layers that themselves passivate gold, and it adds cost and heavy metal load to tails. There's usually an optimum dose found in testwork.

The PDC sets a nominal dose of about 10,000 g/t of CIL feed, with 15,000 g/t design capacity for the pumps. Actual operating doses are set by the metallurgist based on leach performance.
f: How was the lead nitrate dose chosen in testwork?
Does lead in tails create environmental limits?
How quickly does lead nitrate act after dosing?

f.q: Why add lead nitrate at the leach feed box?
f.a:
The leach feed box is where thickener underflow meets reagents before tank 32A. Adding lead nitrate there, along with milk of lime, means it is mixed in before the slurry sees the high cyanide and oxygen of the first tanks, where fresh sulphide is most reactive.

Getting the lead in early removes released sulphide and conditions gold surfaces before passivation sets in. It's like adding a corrosion inhibitor at the inlet of a system rather than partway along.
f: What else is added at the CIL2 leach feed box?
Why is milk of lime added with lead nitrate?
How is mixing ensured in the leach feed box?

Why is the concentrate leach run at high.q: What would a falling pH and rising HCN risk look like in a handover?
Why is the concentrate leach run at high.a:
Cyanide in solution exists as free cyanide ions or as hydrogen cyanide (HCN), depending on pH. Above about pH 11 almost all is cyanide ions; as pH falls toward about 9, a large share becomes HCN, which can come out of solution as a toxic gas.

The handover should flag pH trending below the targets (11.75 to 12.5 in the early CIL2 tanks, 11 to 12.5 later), the likely cause, such as milk of lime supply, a pH probe fault or high sulphide acid generation, what was done to restore it, and any gas alarms. Low pH also wastes cyanide. This is a safety issue first: follow the site's cyanide and HCN procedures, and never bypass alarms or interlocks.

f.q: Why does HCN form as pH drops?
f.a:
Hydrogen cyanide is a weak acid with a pKa around 9.2 to 9.3. At that pH, half the cyanide is HCN and half is free cyanide ions. Each pH unit higher reduces the HCN share about tenfold.

At pH 11 or above, HCN is a small fraction; at pH 10 it's noticeable; at pH 9 it's about half. HCN is volatile and very toxic, so keeping pH high both protects people and keeps cyanide in solution where it leaches gold.
f: Why does CIL4 run at a lower pH than CIL2?
How is HCN gas detected around leach tanks?
What makes the pH fall in a sulphide leach?

f.q: How is milk of lime supplied to the leach feed box?
f.a:
Quicklime is slaked in the vendor lime plant (two parallel circuits with slaking mills, cyclones and a scrubber) and sent to the milk of lime tank. A ringmain with duty and standby DOL pumps circulates it around the plant.

At CIL2, milk of lime is added at the leach feed box. A lime problem anywhere in that chain, such as a slaker trip, a blocked ringmain or a pump fault, can starve the leach of lime and let pH fall.
f: Why does milk of lime block lines so easily?
How is the lime ringmain pressure held?
What alarms warn of low milk of lime supply?

f.q: What should you do if an HCN alarm sounds?
f.a:
Follow the site emergency response for cyanide: move away from the area, upwind if possible, raise the alarm, and don't go back in to investigate unless you are trained, authorised and equipped with the right gas detection and breathing protection.

The reference notes HCN gas monitors with beacon and siren on CIL4; the arrangement on CIL2 isn't described. Your area induction will cover the local muster points and procedures. Never silence or bypass a gas alarm to keep running.
f: Where are the muster points near the leach tanks?
What cyanide first aid is kept on site?
Who is trained to respond to cyanide exposures?

Why is the concentrate leach run at high.q: How is lead nitrate dosing controlled at the leach feed box?
Why is the concentrate leach run at high.a:
Per the reagent control philosophy, lead nitrate is dosed by VSD pumps on flow control with a g/t setpoint, so dose follows feed tonnage. It is added at the CIL2 leach feed box.

The PDC design basis has lead nitrate delivered as bulk liquid, made up at 40 percent w/v, stored in one 283 m3 tank, and dosed at about 10,000 g/t of CIL feed nominal (15,000 g/t design margin), with dosing pumps sized for about 5,000 L/h. At the design feed of about 104 t/h that is roughly 2,600 L/h of solution nominal. These are design values; the metallurgist sets the live dose.

f.q: Why is the lead nitrate dose so large?
f.a:
It's per tonne of concentrate, not ore, and concentrate is very reactive. At about 10,000 g/t of CIL feed, that's about 10 kg per tonne of concentrate. Since concentrate is only about 2.5 percent of ore tonnage, that works out to roughly 0.25 kg per tonne of ore.

The high dose reflects the large exposed sulphide surface after UFG. Testwork set it; the metallurgist would know whether operation has trimmed it.
f: How much does lead nitrate cost per ounce recovered?
Has the operating dose been trimmed from design?
What testwork supports the lead nitrate dose?

f.q: What happens to the leach if lead nitrate dosing stops?
f.a:
In general, passivation builds up again: sulphide released from the fine concentrate coats the gold surfaces and gold dissolution slows. Cyanide and oxygen consumption can rise because sulphide reactions continue.

The effect isn't instant because the leach is long, about 86 hours at design, but extraction would drift down. A stopped lead nitrate pump should be flagged in the handover and restored quickly. The metallurgist can say how sensitive this ore is.
f: How quickly does extraction drop without lead nitrate?
Is there a standby lead nitrate dosing pump?
How is lead nitrate flow verified at the feed box?

f.q: How is lead nitrate handled safely?
f.a:
Lead nitrate is toxic, a heavy metal compound that can be absorbed if swallowed or inhaled, and it's an oxidiser that shouldn't contact combustible material. In general it calls for gloves, eye protection and good hygiene, with spill containment in the storage area.

The site's safety data sheet and reagent area procedures give the exact PPE and handling rules. Delivery is by compressed air displacement from bulk tankers per the PDC; unloading follows site procedures.
f: What PPE is required in the lead nitrate area?
How are lead nitrate spills cleaned up?
Why is compressed air used to unload reagent tankers?

The concentrate leach uses very high cya.q: Why do cyanide consuming sulphides need such aggressive dosing?
The concentrate leach uses very high cya.a:
Reactive sulphides, especially freshly ground ones, eat cyanide. Cyanide reacts with sulphur species to form thiocyanate and with metals such as copper and iron to form cyanide complexes. None of that cyanide leaches gold. To keep enough free cyanide to drive gold dissolution through the whole train, much more has to be added than for a low sulphide ore.

The PDC targets rise along CIL2: about 500 ppm in tank 32A, 1,000 in 32B, 2,200 in 32C, 5,000 in 32D and 6,500 in 32E, with about 21.5 kg/t of concentrate dosed nominal. Tellurides and partly exposed gold also leach slowly and benefit from strong cyanide. It's like a pump with a big recirculation loss: you have to oversupply to deliver the flow you need.

f.q: Why do cyanide targets rise along the CIL2 train?
f.a:
The PDC sets increasing targets from about 500 ppm in 32A to 6,500 ppm in 32E but doesn't explain why.

In general, the slow leaching refractory and telluride gold left in later tanks benefits from a stronger driving force, while keeping early tank cyanide lower limits waste where fresh sulphide surfaces react most. It also means slurry leaving CIL2 carries plenty of cyanide forward to CIL3 and CIL4. The metallurgist can explain the testwork behind the profile.
f: How is cyanide split between the seven CIL2 tanks?
Does high cyanide in late tanks raise losses to tails?
Why are cyanide targets set by tank rather than overall?

f.q: What is thiocyanate and why does it matter?
f.a:
Thiocyanate (SCN) forms when cyanide reacts with sulphur species released from sulphide minerals. It doesn't leach gold, so every bit formed is cyanide lost from the leach.

Thiocyanate stays in solution and builds up in recycled water, and it is an environmental consideration in tailings. Monitoring it helps metallurgists understand cyanide consumption. Its levels on this plant aren't in the reference; the metallurgist or environmental team would track them.
f: How is thiocyanate measured in leach solution?
Does peroxide destruct remove thiocyanate?
How does thiocyanate build up in recycled water?

f.q: How much cyanide does the concentrate leach use by design?
f.a:
The reference gives about 21.5 kg of sodium cyanide per tonne of concentrate nominal, dosed across the leach tanks, delivered as about 29 percent solution. At the nominal 75 t/h concentrate, that's roughly 1.6 t/h of sodium cyanide.

Cyanide on CIL2 is ratioed to the solids mass flow on the feed. These are design values; actual use depends on ore, grind and leach conditions, and the metallurgist tracks it closely because it's a major cost.
f: How is cyanide consumption reported each day?
Why is cyanide delivered as a 29 percent solution?
How does spent eluate return affect cyanide demand?

The concentrate leach uses very high cya.q: What would falling extraction below 90% suggest is going wrong?
The concentrate leach uses very high cya.a:
Falling below the design 90 percent extraction means gold is staying in the solids. The usual causes are coarser UFG product, so more gold stays locked; low dissolved oxygen (PDC target about 10 ppm); free cyanide below the tank targets; pH out of range; lead nitrate dosing problems; or short residence from low feed density or high tonnage (design minimum 80 h).

Ore changes matter too: more gold in solid solution or tellurides can cap extraction whatever the conditions. And check it really is extraction: high gold in solution leaving CIL3 is an adsorption problem, not a leach one. The metallurgist confirms with residue and solution assays.

f.q: How do you tell a leach problem from an adsorption problem?
f.a:
Look at where the gold is in CIL3 tails. If gold in the solids residue is high, it never dissolved: a leach or grind problem. If gold in solution is high, it dissolved but wasn't caught by carbon: an adsorption problem.

CIL3 is designed for about 99 percent adsorption efficiency. Low carbon concentration, fouled carbon or carbon moved too fast can cause solution losses. Residue and solution assays of CIL3 tails, from the lab, separate the two.
f: What solution gold in CIL3 tails is acceptable?
How is carbon activity tested?
Does CIL4 recover dissolved gold from CIL3 tails?

f.q: What is the minimum CIL2 leach residence in the design?
f.a:
The PDC sets a minimum leach residence of 80 hours. At the design grade feed of about 104 t/h, CIL2 gives about 86 hours; at the nominal 75 t/h, about 119 hours. That's with seven tanks of 1,685 m3, 11,795 m3 in total.

So at design grade the circuit runs close to the minimum, and any loss of volume from low density, a tank offline or sanded tanks, or higher tonnage, pushes it below. That's a common hidden cause of falling extraction.
f: What happens if one CIL2 tank is bypassed?
How does tank sanding reduce live volume?
Why was tank 32G added to CIL2?

f.q: Can ore mineralogy cap extraction no matter what?
f.a:
Yes. Some gold is held inside the pyrite crystal structure itself, often called solid solution or invisible gold. No amount of grinding exposes it, and cyanide can't reach it without destroying the sulphide by oxidation, for example roasting or pressure oxidation.

If the share of that gold rises in the ore, concentrate extraction falls even with perfect leach conditions. Gold deportment studies on the ore, held by the metallurgist or geology team, show how much gold is in that form.
f: How is solid solution gold measured?
Why did the offsite roaster recover more refractory gold?
Does ore source change gold deportment much?

The concentrate leach uses very high cya.q: How is free cyanide concentration measured and controlled in CIL2?
The concentrate leach uses very high cya.a:
Control: per the reference, cyanide on CIL2 is ratioed to the solids mass flow on the CIL2 feed, with addition points on all tanks. Cyanide comes from a pressurised ringmain with flowmeters at each dosing point, so each tank's addition can be set against its target concentration, which the PDC sets from about 500 ppm in 32A to 6,500 ppm in 32E.

Measurement: the reference describes an online cyanide analyser on CIL4 tanks 1 and 2, but doesn't mention one on CIL2. In general, free cyanide is measured by silver nitrate titration on tank samples, either in the field or the lab. Ask the CIL operators how often CIL2 is titrated and who adjusts the additions.

f.q: How does silver nitrate titration measure free cyanide?
f.a:
A filtered solution sample is titrated with silver nitrate solution using an indicator such as rhodanine or potassium iodide. Silver ions combine with free cyanide to form a soluble silver cyanide complex. Once all the free cyanide is used up, extra silver gives a colour change or cloudiness. The volume used gives the free cyanide concentration.

It's quick and cheap, but sensitive to technique and interferences such as copper. At thousands of ppm, samples are usually diluted first.
f: Why does copper interfere with cyanide titration?
How often should leach tanks be titrated?
What does WAD cyanide measure compared with free cyanide?

f.q: Why ratio cyanide to solids rather than slurry flow?
f.a:
Cyanide demand comes from the concentrate: its gold and its reactive sulphides. A tonne of solids needs roughly the same cyanide whether it arrives at 50 or 58 percent solids, so dosing per tonne of solids matches the real demand.

The solids mass flow comes from the feed flowmeter and density gauge. The catch is that concentration in ppm then depends on how much water comes with it, so density changes still need watching.
f: How is solids mass flow calculated on the CIL2 feed?
What happens to the ratio if the density gauge drifts?
Why does the operator enter solids SG for mass flow?

f.q: How is cyanide delivered around the plant?
f.a:
Per the reagent philosophy, cyanide and caustic go through pressurised ringmains with DOL pumps and a mechanical back pressure valve on the return, so pressure at every take off stays steady. Flowmeters at each dosing point measure what each user takes.

Sodium cyanide is about 29 percent solution. It's a closed loop like a compressed air ring main: constant header pressure, individual users drawing what they need. Any work on cyanide lines needs strict isolation and PPE under site procedures.
f: Why use a back pressure valve on the ringmain return?
What happens to dosing if a ringmain pump trips?
What PPE is required for cyanide line work?

Where do CIL3 tails go?.q: Why is residual cyanide from CIL3 tails still useful in CIL4?
Where do CIL3 tails go?.a:
CIL3 tails still carry dissolved cyanide from the strong concentrate leach, and cyanide water is also added at the CIL3 tails hopper. CIL4 needs cyanide to leach its own feed, with the PDC targeting about 175 ppm in the first CIL4 tank.

Sending CIL3 tails to the CIL4 feed distribution box puts that cyanide to work leaching flotation tails instead of sending it straight to final tails. It reduces fresh cyanide demand in CIL4, and any gold still in solution gets another pass over CIL4 carbon. CIL4's cyanide controller is trimmed by an analyser, so it sees the extra cyanide and adds less. It's like using exhaust heat from one process to preheat another.

f.q: What cyanide level does CIL4 aim for?
f.a:
The PDC targets about 175 ppm in the first CIL4 tank, F21-TK-411, with cyanide added at the feed box and tank 2. That's far below CIL2's thousands of ppm, because flotation tails have much less gold and sulphide per tonne.

The control philosophy sets cyanide flow at the front end by an operator setpoint or g/t on thickener underflow tonnes, trimmed by a cyanide analyser on tanks 1 and 2. These are design targets; the live setpoint is set by the metallurgist.
f: Why does CIL4 need so much less cyanide than CIL2?
How does the CIL4 cyanide analyser trim dosing?
Where are the extra cyanide addition lines on CIL4?

f.q: Does CIL4 cyanide control account for CIL3 cyanide?
f.a:
Indirectly, yes. CIL4 cyanide flow is set by operator setpoint or g/t on thickener underflow tonnes, then trimmed by the online cyanide analyser on tanks 1 and 2. Since the analyser measures actual cyanide in the tanks, cyanide arriving with CIL3 tails shows up and the trim reduces fresh addition.

If the CIL3 tails flow stops suddenly, the analyser would see cyanide drop and add more, with some lag. Big changes in CIL3 flow are worth flagging so the CRO watches CIL4 cyanide.
f: How fast does the CIL4 cyanide analyser respond?
What happens to CIL4 if the analyser fails?
Why trim on analyser rather than dose purely by g/t?

f.q: Why is cyanide water added to the CIL3 tails hopper?
f.a:
The reference states that cyanide water is added to the CIL3 tails hopper but doesn't give the reason. Cyanide water here is TSF decant return, treated with hydrogen peroxide.

In general, adding water at a pump hopper helps hold level and minimum line velocity, and using cyanide water rather than fresh water avoids wasting clean water and keeps some cyanide in the stream. The process engineer or CIL operators can confirm the purpose and control.
f: What is cyanide water and where does it come from?
How is the CIL3 tails hopper level controlled?
Why use decant water rather than process water here?

Where do CIL3 tails go?.q: What would you check if gold recovery from concentrate seemed low?
Where do CIL3 tails go?.a:
Work along the chain. Grind first: UFG product size and power draw per tonne. Then leach conditions in CIL2: dissolved oxygen (PDC target about 10 ppm), free cyanide against tank targets, pH, lead nitrate dosing, and residence, which falls with low density or high tonnage.

Then adsorption in CIL3: carbon concentration (design about 20 g/L), carbon activity, carbon transfer rate, and solution gold in CIL3 tails. Also check the carbon detection meter on CIL3 tails for loaded carbon escaping, and elution performance. Finally, check the data itself: sampling and assays. Residue and solution assays from the metallurgist tell you which link is weak.

f.q: Why is loaded carbon in CIL3 tails a gold loss?
f.a:
CIL3 carbon is designed to load to about 4,490 g/t. A small amount of carbon fines or broken granules slipping through the Kemix 1.0 mm intertank screens carries a lot of gold with it. Once in CIL4 or final tails, that carbon is hard to get back.

That's why there's a carbon detection meter on CIL3 tails with a reference probe. A screen failure or worn screen can release carbon quickly, so a carbon alarm deserves prompt attention.
f: How does the carbon detection meter work?
How are intertank screens inspected?
Can CIL4 carbon screens catch carbon from CIL3?

f.q: What does solution gold in CIL3 tails tell you?
f.a:
It shows how well CIL3 carbon is catching dissolved gold. The design adsorption efficiency is about 99 percent, so solution gold in CIL3 tails should be very low compared with the CIL2 discharge.

If it rises, look at carbon concentration in the tanks, carbon activity (fouled or poorly regenerated carbon), carbon moved too fast, or short residence. Some of that gold may still be picked up by CIL4 carbon, but at much lower efficiency.
f: How is solution gold measured in the lab?
What makes carbon activity fall over time?
How often is CIL3 carbon concentration checked?

f.q: How does carbon activity affect adsorption?
f.a:
Activated carbon adsorbs gold cyanide onto its internal pore surfaces. Over time, the pores get fouled by calcium carbonate scale (from high lime), organics such as flotation reagents and oils, and other metal complexes. Fouled carbon loads more slowly and to lower grades.

Acid washing with dilute HCl removes carbonate scale, and thermal regeneration in the kilns burns off organics and restores activity. If regeneration is skipped or poor, carbon activity falls and solution losses rise.
f: How is carbon activity measured in the lab?
What temperature does carbon regeneration run at?
Why do flotation reagents foul carbon?

Where do CIL3 tails go?.q: How does CIL3 tails flow combine with the main tails stream at CIL4?
Where do CIL3 tails go?.a:
CIL3 tails go to a CIL3 tails hopper, where cyanide water is added, and duty and standby VSD pumps send them to the CIL4 feed distribution box. There they join thickened flotation tails underflow and a portion of spent eluate, and milk of lime is added under pH control from the tank 1 pH controller.

The CIL3 stream is small, about 75 to 104 t/h of solids by design against about 3,164 t/h of total CIL4 feed solids, roughly 2 to 3 percent. But it brings high cyanide and high pH, which reduces CIL4's fresh cyanide and lime demand. From the feed box, combined slurry goes to CIL4's 2 leach and 6 adsorption tanks.

f.q: How big is the CIL3 stream compared with CIL4 feed?
f.a:
By design, CIL2 and CIL3 handle about 75 t/h of concentrate solids nominal and about 104 t/h in the design grade case. CIL4 feed is about 3,164 t/h solids in total.

So CIL3 tails are about 2 to 3 percent of CIL4 solids. Small by mass, but rich in cyanide, high in pH and with some residual gold, so they have an outsized effect on CIL4 chemistry compared with their tonnage.
f: How much cyanide does CIL3 tails bring to CIL4?
Does CIL3 tails raise CIL4 feed grade noticeably?
Why is spent eluate also returned to CIL4?

f.q: Why does high pH CIL3 tails matter for CIL4 pH control?
f.a:
CIL4 runs a leach pH of about 8.8 to 9.3, much lower than CIL2's 11 to 12.5. CIL3 tails arriving at high pH reduce the lime CIL4 needs. The tank 1 pH controller opens the milk of lime valve at the feed distribution box as needed.

If CIL3 tails stop, CIL4 pH could drift down until the controller catches up. Since HCN forms more readily near pH 9, CIL4 has an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren. Big changes in CIL3 flow are worth a heads up to the CRO.
f: Why does CIL4 run at such a low pH?
Where is the CIL4 HCN gas monitor located?
How does tank 2 back up the tank 1 pH controller?

f.q: What happens if the CIL3 tails pumps trip?
f.a:
The pumps are duty and standby on VSDs. The plant philosophy treats standby changeover case by case, so the standby may start automatically or need operator action. If both are unavailable, the CIL3 tails hopper fills and the CIL2 and CIL3 trains would need feed reduced or stopped to avoid spills.

The CRO would see the trip with first out detection and hopper level alarms. Restart follows the normal sequence. Trips and interlocks must never be bypassed to keep slurry moving.
f: How long can the CIL3 tails hopper hold before overflowing?
Is CIL3 tails pump changeover automatic?
Where does a CIL3 tails hopper overflow report?

Typical loaded carbon grade in CIL3 vs C.q: Why does richer pregnant solution produce higher carbon loading?
Typical loaded carbon grade in CIL3 vs C.a:
Carbon adsorption is an equilibrium process. For any gold concentration in solution, carbon will load toward a matching gold level, described by an adsorption isotherm. The richer the solution, the higher the loading carbon can reach.

Concentrate holds much more gold per tonne than flotation tails, and after leaching in CIL2 its solution is far richer than CIL4's. So CIL3 carbon loads to about 4,490 g/t by design, against about 332 to 579 g/t in CIL4. It's like a sponge in a strong dye bath picking up more colour than one in a weak bath. Contact time and carbon activity also matter, but solution tenor sets the ceiling.

f.q: What is an adsorption isotherm?
f.a:
An isotherm is a curve showing how much gold the carbon holds at equilibrium for each gold concentration in solution, at a fixed temperature. It's usually measured by shaking carbon in solutions of different strengths until loading stops changing.

Metallurgists use it to estimate how much carbon is needed and what loading is achievable. It's commonly fitted with a Freundlich type equation. Real plant carbon rarely reaches full equilibrium because of limited contact time.
f: Why does temperature change carbon adsorption?
How is carbon loading capacity tested in the lab?
Why does real carbon not reach equilibrium?

f.q: Is there a maximum gold loading on carbon?
f.a:
Yes. Carbon has a finite capacity, and at very high solution tenors it can hold tens of kilograms of gold per tonne in theory. In practice, plant loadings are limited by contact time, competing species such as silver and copper cyanide complexes, and fouling.

The design loading of about 4,490 g/t for CIL3 is well within capacity but reflects realistic kinetics. Higher loading means fewer elution strips per ounce, so there's a balance between loading and gold held in the circuit.
f: How do copper cyanide complexes compete with gold?
What is the risk of holding too much gold on carbon?
Why does silver load alongside gold?

f.q: How is loaded carbon grade measured?
f.a:
Carbon samples are taken from tanks or the loaded carbon screen, dried, then ashed or digested and assayed for gold, usually by the site lab. The result is grams of gold per tonne of carbon.

On CIL4, the Gekko Carbon Scout measures carbon concentration in g/L in each adsorption tank, which is carbon quantity, not grade. The reference doesn't describe an automatic sampler on CIL3; the metallurgist or lab can show how CIL3 carbon is sampled.
f: How representative are carbon samples from a tank?
How often is CIL3 carbon sampled for grade?
What is the difference between g/L and g/t for carbon?

Typical loaded carbon grade in CIL3 vs C.q: What would falling CIL3 carbon grade tell you about the leach circuit?
Typical loaded carbon grade in CIL3 vs C.a:
A falling CIL3 carbon grade has a few possible causes. Less gold dissolving in CIL2, from a grind, oxygen, cyanide or lead nitrate problem, means less gold to load. Carbon moved faster than usual means each tonne has less time to load. Fouled or poorly regenerated carbon loads more slowly. And lower concentrate grade or tonnage simply brings less gold.

Check the CIL2 leach profile, solution gold in the CIL3 tanks and tails, the carbon transfer rate and recent regeneration. If solution gold in CIL3 tails is rising while carbon grade falls, suspect carbon activity. If both are low, suspect the leach. The metallurgist interprets the full picture.

f.q: How does carbon transfer rate change loaded grade?
f.a:
Gold loading depends on how long carbon sits in the circuit contacting rich solution. Moving carbon faster means each tonne spends less time loading, so it leaves at a lower grade; moving it slower raises the grade but holds more gold in the circuit.

The PDC sets maximum carbon movements of about 33 t/day and a maximum carbon residence of 14 days for CIL3, with about 202 t of carbon in circuit. Transfer rate is a key lever the metallurgist uses to balance loading and elution capacity.
f: How is the CIL3 carbon transfer rate set?
What gold inventory does CIL3 carbon hold?
Why does slower transfer raise loaded grade?

f.q: What fouls activated carbon in a leach circuit?
f.a:
Common foulants are calcium carbonate scale from high lime slurry, organics like flotation reagents, oils, grease and frother, and some base metal and silica deposits. They block the pores where gold adsorbs.

The circuit deals with these through acid washing with dilute HCl, which removes carbonates, and thermal regeneration in the kilns, which burns off organics. Concentrate leach slurry at pH 11.75 to 12.5 with lots of lime is prone to carbonate scaling.
f: How does acid washing remove carbonate scale?
How often is CIL3 carbon regenerated?
Can antiscalant reduce carbon fouling?

f.q: Why does high carbon grade matter for elution?
f.a:
Elution strips a set mass of carbon per batch. The higher the gold loading, the more gold comes out per strip. The existing elution has two circuits of about 11 t each, averaging about 1.5 strips per column per day by design, with a weekly range of about 8 to 24 strips.

If CIL3 carbon grade falls, more strips are needed for the same gold, which can push elution toward its capacity. High grade carbon also needs a good strip to avoid leaving gold behind.
f: What barren carbon grade does elution achieve?
How long does one elution strip take?
What limits strips per day on the existing columns?

Typical loaded carbon grade in CIL3 vs C.q: How often is CIL3 carbon pulled for elution compared with CIL4?
Typical loaded carbon grade in CIL3 vs C.a:
Carbon movement is set by gold loading and production, so actual frequency varies. By design, CIL3 runs about 20 g/L carbon with about 202 t in circuit, allows up to about 33 t/day of carbon movement and a maximum carbon residence of 14 days. Each transfer cycle is about 4 h, based on 11 t batches matching the existing 11 t elution columns.

CIL4 runs about 12.5 g/L carbon with a maximum of about 30 t/day of movement and the same 14 day maximum residence, eluted in its own CIL4 elution column. Because CIL4 carbon loads to only about 332 to 579 g/t, it needs far more tonnes of carbon stripped per ounce than CIL3. Live transfer schedules come from the metallurgist.

f.q: Why limit carbon residence to 14 days?
f.a:
The PDC sets a maximum carbon residence of 14 days for both CIL3 and CIL4 but doesn't explain why.

In general, carbon held too long loses activity through fouling, keeps a lot of gold locked up as inventory, and suffers more attrition into fines that can escape. Moving carbon at least every 14 days keeps it active and limits gold at risk. The metallurgist can explain the site's reasoning.
f: How much gold sits on carbon in CIL3 at any time?
How does attrition increase with carbon age?
What happens to old carbon in the regeneration kiln?

f.q: How long does one CIL4 elution strip take?
f.a:
The PDC sets out the CIL4 split AARL sequence at about 10.2 hours in total: about 0.5 h carbon transfer in, about 3.3 h acid wash including rinsing, about 5.5 h elution including cooling, and about 0.9 h carbon transfer out.

The sequence runs acid wash, water rinse, pre soak with caustic and cyanide, elution with lean eluate then scheme water, and cooling. Timing for the existing CIL2/3 elution circuits isn't given in the reference.
f: Why does the elution column need pressurising?
What is a split AARL sequence?
How is the LPG elution heater controlled?

f.q: What does the acid wash step remove from carbon?
f.a:
Acid washing soaks carbon in dilute hydrochloric acid to dissolve calcium carbonate scale and some base metals that build up during leaching. Removing scale opens the pores so carbon strips better and re adsorbs well when returned.

The reference describes acid wash with HCl in the existing elution circuits, and a single SAF2205 duplex column for both acid wash and elution on CIL4. Acid waste goes to the final tails tank. HCl handling requires full PPE and site procedures.
f: Why does scale stop carbon stripping properly?
What PPE is needed around the acid wash columns?
Why use duplex stainless steel for the CIL4 column?

How is oxygen added in the CIL2 leach?.q: Why use injection pumps to shear oxygen instead of just sparging?
How is oxygen added in the CIL2 leach?.a:
Sparging through side lances releases oxygen as fairly large bubbles. They rise quickly, and much of the oxygen escapes from the slurry surface before dissolving. That's acceptable in later tanks with lower demand, but fine sulphide concentrate in the first tanks consumes oxygen fast.

Oxygen injection pumps take slurry from the tank and inject oxygen into it under pressure and high shear, breaking it into very fine bubbles with a large surface area. More oxygen dissolves, more quickly, so dissolved oxygen can be held high (PDC target about 10 ppm) with less wasted gas. The PDC has side lances on tanks A to F and oxygen circulating pumps on tanks A and B. It's like a pressurised mixer versus bubbling gas through a tank.

f.q: Why does the first part of the leach need the most oxygen?
f.a:
Freshly ground UFG product has the most reactive sulphide surface when it first meets cyanide and oxygen. Those surfaces oxidise rapidly, consuming oxygen, and gold dissolution is also fastest at the start, which needs oxygen too.

As slurry moves down the train, the most reactive surfaces are used up and demand falls. That's why injection pumps are on the first two tanks, with side lances on the rest. It's matching supply to the demand profile, like sizing cooling for a reactor's hottest zone.
f: How does oxygen demand change along the CIL2 train?
Why are only tanks A and B fitted with pumps?
Can oxygen pumps be added to later tanks if needed?

f.q: Where does the leach oxygen come from?
f.a:
From the new oxygen plant, a pressure swing adsorption (PSA) unit, backed by liquid oxygen. It supplies CIL2/3 and CIL4.

A PSA plant passes compressed air through beds of adsorbent that hold nitrogen and let oxygen through, giving high purity oxygen. Liquid oxygen storage covers outages and peaks. If oxygen supply is interrupted, DO in the leach tanks falls and extraction can suffer, so supply status is worth knowing at shift start.
f: How does a PSA oxygen plant separate oxygen from air?
How long can liquid oxygen backup supply the leach?
What alarms show low oxygen supply pressure?

f.q: What DO target does the CIL2 leach run at?
f.a:
The PDC sets a dissolved oxygen target of about 10 ppm for CIL2. For comparison, the CIL4 leach target is about 15 ppm.

Air saturated water holds only about 8 ppm or less, depending on temperature and salinity, so reaching 10 ppm or more needs pure oxygen, not air. These are design targets; live setpoints come from the metallurgist, and actual DO is checked with DO probes or samples.
f: Why does salinity lower oxygen solubility?
How is DO measured in a slurry tank?
Why is the CIL4 DO target higher than CIL2's?

How is oxygen added in the CIL2 leach?.q: What would a handover mean if oxygen injection pumps tripped?
How is oxygen added in the CIL2 leach?.a:
It means the first two CIL2 tanks lose their main oxygen supply. The side lances keep working, but they transfer oxygen less efficiently, so dissolved oxygen in tanks A and B would likely fall below target, slowing gold dissolution right where demand is highest.

The handover should flag which pump tripped, when, the first out cause, DO trends in tanks A and B, whether the standby or restart worked, any maintenance called, and how long DO was low. A long outage can drag down extraction, so the metallurgist should know. Don't reset or restart around a trip without understanding its cause, and never bypass interlocks.

f.q: Can the side lances alone hold dissolved oxygen up?
f.a:
Partly. Side lances still inject oxygen, but as coarser bubbles that rise and escape faster, so less dissolves. In the high demand first tanks they may not hold the target on their own, especially with fresh, reactive concentrate.

Operators may raise lance flow to compensate, at the cost of more oxygen use. Whether lances alone can hold target on this plant depends on feed conditions; the CIL operators and metallurgist would know from experience.
f: How is side lance oxygen flow controlled?
Why do coarse bubbles transfer less oxygen?
What oxygen flow do the side lances use by design?

f.q: How does low DO affect the leach chemistry?
f.a:
Gold dissolution needs oxygen, so low DO directly slows the gold leach. In general, low oxygen also changes how sulphides react: more reduced sulphur species can remain in solution, which raises passivation of gold surfaces and can increase cyanide consumption through thiocyanate formation.

So a DO drop can hurt twice: slower leaching now, and worse conditions for the rest of the train. That's why DO is one of the first things checked when extraction falls.
f: How quickly does extraction fall when DO drops?
Does lead nitrate help when DO is low?
How is DO trended on the leach tanks?

f.q: How is dissolved oxygen measured in the leach tanks?
f.a:
In general, DO is measured by probes, either optical (luminescent) or electrochemical, mounted in the tank or a sample stream. They need regular cleaning and calibration because slurry and lime scale coat the sensor.

The reference describes DO analysers with high and low alarms on CIL4, and the Carbon Scout sampling DO on CIL4 leach tanks. The DO measurement arrangement for CIL2 isn't described; the instrument technicians or CRO can show it.
f: How often are DO probes cleaned and calibrated?
Why do optical DO probes suit slurry service?
What does a fouled DO probe reading look like?

How is oxygen added in the CIL2 leach?.q: What maintenance issues are common on leach tank oxygen pumps?
How is oxygen added in the CIL2 leach?.a:
The reference doesn't describe maintenance for the CIL2 oxygen injection pumps, so this is general practice. They're slurry pumps in abrasive, high pH, cyanide service, so impeller, liner and casing wear is the main issue, along with gland or seal wear; the plant supplies gland water to slurry pump glands.

The oxygen injection point or nozzle can wear or block, and VSDs and motors need normal checks. Oxygen adds its own rules: components in oxygen service must be kept clean and free of oil and grease, and oxygen supply must be isolated and vented before work. Cyanide exposure adds PPE and decontamination needs. The area maintenance planner has the actual tasks and intervals.

f.q: Why must oxygen lines be kept free of oil and grease?
f.a:
Pure oxygen makes materials burn far more readily than air. Oil and grease can ignite spontaneously in high pressure oxygen, from heat of compression or friction, and a fire in an oxygen line can burn through metal fittings.

So parts in oxygen service are cleaned to a standard, use oxygen compatible lubricants and seals, and are handled with clean gloves. This applies to valves, lances and injection points on the leach tanks as much as to the oxygen plant itself.
f: What lubricants are approved for oxygen service?
How are oxygen lines cleaned after maintenance?
Why does a valve opening fast in oxygen cause ignition?

f.q: How are oxygen pumps isolated for maintenance?
f.a:
The reference doesn't describe the isolation procedure. In general, work on an oxygen injection pump means electrical isolation of the motor and VSD, process isolation of slurry suction and discharge, and isolation and venting of the oxygen supply, all under the site permit system.

Cyanide in the slurry adds draining, flushing and decontamination before the pump is opened. The area maintenance planner and the permit issuer have the approved isolation points.
f: Who issues permits for work in the leach area?
How is a slurry pump drained in cyanide service?
What gas tests are needed before opening leach equipment?

f.q: Why do slurry pumps in leach service wear quickly?
f.a:
Slurry is abrasive: even fine sulphide concentrate wears impellers and liners over time, and higher speed raises wear sharply, roughly with velocity cubed in general. High pH and cyanide are corrosive to some materials, and oxygen speeds corrosion.

Oxygen injection pumps may also run hard to create shear, which adds wear. Good practice is matching materials to the duty, running near best efficiency point, and condition monitoring such as vibration and performance trends.
f: What impeller materials suit cyanide slurry service?
How does vibration monitoring catch pump wear early?
Why does wear rise so sharply with pump speed?

What feeds the flotation tailings thicke.q: Why does scavenger tails still carry so much solid mass at that rate?
What feeds the flotation tailings thicke.a:
Because flotation only pulls a small slice of the mass into concentrate. On the design mass balance, rougher 1 pulls about 4.4 percent, roughers 2 and 3 about 2.4 percent and the scavengers about 1.1 percent. So of roughly 3,146 t/h fed to flotation, about 2,914 t/h leaves as scavenger tail.

Flotation is selective: it targets the sulphides (mainly pyrite) that carry the gold. The quartz, silicates and carbonates that make up most of the ore are never meant to float, so they all report to tails.

Think of it as a filter that pulls a few percent of contaminant out of a big flow. The bulk passes straight through, which is why the thickener sees about 3,071 t/h of solids on design figures.

f.q: What fraction of the plant feed ends up as flotation concentrate?
f.a:
On the PDC nominal case, flotation concentrate is about 637 kt/a, roughly 75 to 78 t/h, against about 3,146 t/h of flotation feed. That is only about 2.5 percent of the mass. In the design grade case concentrate rises to about 876 kt/a, roughly 104 to 107 t/h, still only around 3.4 percent.

So about 96 to 97 percent of the mass carries on as flotation tails to the thickener and then CIL4. That's why the card says CIL4 treats the bulk of the tonnage even though it recovers a modest share of the gold.

These are design figures from the mass balance. The live split depends on head grade, sulphur content and how the flotation expert system is running.
f: Why does the design grade case make so much more concentrate?
How is mass pull measured on the plant in real time?
What sets the target mass pull in the roughers?

f.q: Why doesn't the plant just float harder to pull more gold out?
f.a:
It's a grade versus recovery trade off. Pulling more mass into the froth catches some extra gold, but it also drags in gangue, which dilutes the concentrate and loads up everything downstream.

Downstream capacity is finite. UFG 2 and 3 are designed for about 30 t/h fresh feed each nominal, up to 46 t/h maximum, and concentrate beyond UFG capacity has to go to the belt filters and stockpile. CIL2 leach capacity is also sized around design concentrate tonnes.

The PDC puts flotation gold recovery at about 71.8 percent nominal, with a ceiling of about 75 percent. The gold that doesn't float is not written off: it goes on to CIL4, which is the second chance. Like sizing a pump for its best efficiency point, you run flotation where the whole system performs best, not where one stage is maxed.
f: What limits UFG capacity when concentrate tonnage rises?
How does the flotation expert system choose air and froth depth?
What happens to concentrate in excess of UFG capacity?

f.q: Does the cleaner-scavenger tail add much mass to the thickener feed?
f.a:
Not much by mass. On design numbers the scavenger tail is about 2,914 t/h and total thickener feed about 3,071 t/h, so the cleaner-scavenger tail is roughly 150 t/h by difference.

It matters more for gold than for tonnes. It's the reject stream from the cleaning circuit, so it can carry sulphide and gold that the Jameson cells chose not to upgrade. About half the cleaner-scavenger tail is recycled internally and the rest goes to the thickener.

The onstream analyser (OSA) measures cleaner-scavenger tails for gold and iron, so the control room can see if that stream is running rich. A rich cleaner-scavenger tail is a hint the cleaning circuit is losing performance, and the metallurgist would want to know.
f: Why is about half the cleaner-scavenger tail recycled?
What does the OSA show on the cleaner-scavenger tails stream?
How would a rich cleaner-scavenger tail be corrected?

What feeds the flotation tailings thicke.q: What would you check if flotation tailings thickener feed suddenly spiked?
What feeds the flotation tailings thicke.a:
First ask what changed upstream, because the thickener only receives what flotation sends it. Typical causes are a mill throughput increase, flotation cells dumping level (dart valves opening wide), or an upset in the cleaner circuit pushing more to cleaner-scavenger tails. PI trends of mill feed tonnes and cell levels usually show it.

Then check how the thickener is coping: bed level (SmartDiver), bed pressure, rake torque, rake height and overflow clarity from the vendor panel. In Stage 2 flocculant is ratioed to feed solids, so the dose should rise with the load.

Underflow pumps run in cascade from bed pressure or density to a flow setpoint on the VSD. Like a surge tank with a level loop, a short spike gets absorbed; a sustained one needs more underflow withdrawal. Talk to the control room operator before changing anything.

f.q: Why does rake torque matter during a feed surge?
f.a:
More solids arriving means the bed builds and gets heavier, and the rakes have to drag through denser, deeper mud. Torque rises, a bit like load on a gearbox climbing as the conveyor it drives gets heavier.

The thickener vendor panel reports rake torque and rake height. In general, rising torque is handled by pulling more underflow and checking flocculation, and many thickeners lift the rakes automatically to ride over a heavy bed. If torque keeps climbing, protective alarms and trips act to stop the drive before something breaks.

A bogged thickener is a long, messy recovery job, so torque is the number to watch closely in any upset. The exact torque alarm and trip settings are in the vendor package, so ask the control room operator for the live limits.

f.q: How does flocculant dosing respond automatically to more feed?
f.a:
In Stage 2 the flocculant is dosed to a feed solids ratio setpoint, so it works in grams per tonne. When feed tonnes go up, the floc flow goes up with it. In Stage 1 it was cascaded from bed level measured by the Manta sub.

The floc is diluted again just before the thickener at an inline mixer (F17-XM-413), with flow transmitters on both the process water and the flocculant lines.

Getting the dose right matters both ways. Too little and fines don't settle, so overflow goes dirty and that water feeds the Process Water Tank. Too much and the bed can become sticky and hard to rake, and you waste an expensive reagent. Like feedforward on a heat exchanger, ratio control gets you close and the operator trims.
f: Why does overdosing flocculant cause problems too?
What does dirty thickener overflow do to process water users?
How is flocculant made up in the floc plant?

f.q: What happens to CIL4 if the thickener underflow density drops?
f.a:
Underflow is designed for about 56 percent solids (range 50 to 62), and CIL4 feed targets about 55 percent after dilution. If density drops, every tonne of ore comes with more water, so the slurry flow in cubic metres per hour rises.

Tank volume is fixed, so residence time falls. The design total is already only about 12.8 h against a 14 h ideal, so there isn't much margin. More water also dilutes the cyanide and lime, and more volume passes through the intertank screens.

It's like pushing more flow through a fixed size heat exchanger: less time in the tubes, less duty done. The thickener underflow density transmitter and the Carbon Scout solids readings on the leach tanks are where the control room would spot it.
f: How much residence time is lost per point of density drop?
Can CIL4 feed density be raised again after the thickener?
What alarms flag low underflow density to the operator?

What feeds the flotation tailings thicke.q: What instrument measures the feed rate into this thickener?
What feeds the flotation tailings thicke.a:
In the instrument list I couldn't find a dedicated flowmeter on the thickener feed line itself. The feed has a large knife gate feed valve (XV17009) and a two stage launder feed sampler (F17-SA-416) that takes samples for metallurgical accounting.

The flow and density measurement sits on the underflow: FIT17121 (a magnetic flowmeter) and DIT17121 (a nucleonic density gauge) on the underflow pump discharge. Together with an operator entered solids SG, these give dry tonnes per hour.

Feed tonnes are normally inferred from upstream: the mill feed weightometers and the flotation mass balance. If you need the definitive answer for the as built plant, check the F17 P&IDs or ask the area instrument technician.

f.q: How does a mag flowmeter plus nucleonic density give solids tonnes?
f.a:
The mag flowmeter measures volumetric flow. A conductive slurry moving through a magnetic field generates a voltage proportional to velocity, so you get cubic metres per hour. Saline water is very conductive, which suits mag meters.

The nucleonic gauge fires gamma radiation across the pipe and measures how much gets through; denser slurry absorbs more, giving slurry SG. The plant control philosophy then uses the operator entered solids SG to work out percent solids and dry tonnes per hour.

Errors creep in if the solids SG entered is wrong, if scale builds on the pipe, or if air is entrained. It's like calculating heat duty from flow and temperature difference: both inputs need to be right for the answer to be right.
f: Why must the operator enter a solids SG value?
What makes a nucleonic density gauge drift over time?
Who calibrates these meters, and how often?

f.q: Why is the feed sampled rather than just measured for flow?
f.a:
Flow alone tells you tonnes, not gold. To know how much gold flotation lost to tails, you need an assay of the stream. The F17-SA-416 sampler cuts a representative slice of the thickener feed so the lab can assay it for gold and sulphur.

That assay, together with feed and concentrate assays, lets the metallurgists calculate flotation recovery and track how much gold is heading to CIL4. The onstream analyser also measures final flotation tails in near real time, which helps the expert system respond faster.

In mechanical terms it's like oil analysis on a gearbox: the flow rate tells you it's running, the sample tells you what's actually in it.
f: How does a two stage launder sampler take a fair sample?
What does the OSA report on the final flotation tails?
Why do bad samples upset metallurgical accounting?

f.q: What controls the underflow pumps if feed rate isn't measured directly?
f.a:
The thickener is run on inventory rather than on feed. The underflow pumps (duty/standby, F17-PP-455 and 456) are controlled in cascade: bed pressure or underflow density is the master loop, and it sets the flow setpoint for the slave loop on the pump VSD.

If the bed gets heavier, the master asks for more underflow; if it thins, it asks for less. On start up or at low flow, underflow is recycled back to the feed so the line keeps moving and doesn't sand up.

It's the same idea as level control on a tank with an unmeasured inflow: you don't need to know exactly what's coming in, as long as you control what's held inside.

What is bed pressure actually telling the operator?
