Why thicken flotation tails before CIL4?.q: Why does halving slurry volume roughly double leach residence time?
Why thicken flotation tails before CIL4?.a:
Residence time is simply tank live volume divided by volumetric flow. The CIL4 tanks are fixed: 8 tanks at about 5,600 m3 live, roughly 44,800 m3 in total.

On design figures the thickener feed is about 6,871 m3/h at 33 percent solids, while CIL4 receives about 3,511 m3/h at about 55 percent. If the unthickened tails went straight to CIL4, the same tanks would give only about 6.5 h instead of about 12.8 h.

The solids tonnes don't change; only the water is removed. It's like a heat exchanger: halve the flow through the same tubes and the fluid spends twice as long inside. These are design values, not live readings.

f.q: Why does leach residence time matter so much for gold extraction?
f.a:
Gold leaching is slow. Cyanide and dissolved oxygen have to diffuse to the gold surface, react, and the gold cyanide complex has to diffuse back out. In flotation tails at a grind of about 180 microns, much of the remaining gold is only partly exposed, so it takes time.

Extraction rises quickly at first then flattens off, so each extra hour gives less than the one before. The carbon also needs time to adsorb the dissolved gold in the adsorption tanks.

The design aimed for 14 h total but accepted about 12.8 h. Like a heat exchanger approaching its outlet temperature, the last few degrees take the most area, and here the last few percent of extraction take the most tank volume.
f: What does a typical leach extraction curve look like?
Why is oxygen added to speed up leaching?
Does finer grinding reduce the residence time needed?

f.q: Does water removal change the cyanide concentration in CIL4?
f.a:
Yes. Cyanide concentration is mass per volume of solution, so with less water the same cyanide addition gives a higher ppm. Put the other way, thickening means you need less cyanide to hit the target concentration.

CIL4 cyanide is dosed at the front end with the setpoint either from the operator or as grams per tonne on thickener underflow tonnes, then trimmed by a cyanide analyser on tanks 1 and 2. The design target is about 175 ppm in the first leach tank. CIL3 tails also arrive carrying residual cyanide (about 750 ppm design), which helps.

So thickening saves reagent as well as tank volume, which matters when you're treating around 3,000 t/h.
f: Why is cyanide dosed per tonne rather than per cubic metre?
How does the cyanide analyser trim the dose?
What happens to cyanide left in the CIL4 tails?

f.q: Why not thicken even higher than 56% solids?
f.a:
Because thicker slurry gets viscous fast, and CIL relies on good mixing. At high density the agitators struggle to keep solids and carbon suspended, oxygen transfers into the slurry more slowly, and carbon has a harder time contacting solution.

Intertank screens and pumps also work harder with viscous slurry. The design underflow range is 50 to 62 percent, and the PDC sets a maximum CIL4 feed density of about 60 percent after dilution, with a target of about 55.

It's a classic optimum: like oil viscosity in a gearbox, too thin and you lose film strength, too thick and you lose efficiency and run hot. The design target sits where residence time gains still outweigh the mixing penalty.
f: How does slurry viscosity affect oxygen transfer in the leach?
What limits how dense the thickener can make the underflow?
Why is the CIL4 maximum feed density about 60%?

Why thicken flotation tails before CIL4?.q: What would low thickener underflow density do to CIL4 retention?
Why thicken flotation tails before CIL4?.a:
It would cut it. For the same solids tonnes, a lower percent solids means more water and so more cubic metres per hour into fixed tanks. Residence time drops roughly in proportion to the extra volume.

The design is already tight: about 12.8 h total at nominal against a 14 h ideal. Losing time reduces leach extraction and gives carbon less chance to capture dissolved gold, so more gold leaves in tails.

Side effects follow too: reagents get diluted, and the intertank screens pass more flow. It's like increasing the flow through a fixed size heat exchanger: the fluid spends less time inside, so less work gets done. The live residence also depends on actual tank levels and any tank bypassed, which design figures don't show.

f.q: How would the control room spot low underflow density?
f.a:
The most direct signal is the nucleonic density transmitter on the thickener underflow pump discharge (DIT17121), which the operator sees on the OIS with alarms. The underflow pumps also run in cascade from bed pressure or density, so a thinning underflow shows up in the controller output.

Further downstream, the Gekko Carbon Scout reports solids along with DO and pH on the leach tanks, so a drop in tank density is visible there too.

On the thickener itself, falling bed pressure or bed level from the vendor panel usually comes first. Like a falling suction pressure warning you before a pump cavitates, the bed tells you before the underflow goes thin.
f: What alarm limits apply to underflow density?
How does bed pressure relate to underflow density?
How reliable are the Carbon Scout density readings?

f.q: What causes underflow density to drop in the first place?
f.a:
Usually one of a few things. Pumping harder than the solids arriving pulls the bed down until clearer liquor is drawn through. Poor flocculation, from wrong dose, bad floc make up or a change in water quality, leaves fines in suspension. A change in ore, especially clays or very fine material, settles more slowly.

Mechanical causes count as well: rat holing, where the pump draws a channel of thin slurry through the bed, or a sudden feed surge the thickener can't absorb.

And sometimes it's the instrument, so a drifting density gauge should be ruled out. Check bed level and bed pressure trends alongside the density reading before acting.
f: What is rat holing in a thickener underflow?
How do clays in the ore hurt thickener settling?
Why does pumping too hard thin out the underflow?

f.q: Does lower density also affect intertank screen loading?
f.a:
Yes. The intertank screens pass all the slurry flowing from tank to tank, so more water means more cubic metres per hour across the same screen area.

CIL4 has two Kemix MPS2535(P) screens per tank, each about 25 m2. On design figures the peak flow is about 1,756 m3/h per screen without carbon advance, a flux of about 69 m3/m2/h, rising to about 81 in the high throughput case.

Push more flow through and the screens run closer to their limit, with a higher risk of the tank level rising and slurry overflowing, which can carry carbon downstream the wrong way. Like a strainer on a pump suction, the same open area handles only so much flow before it backs up.

How are the bypass gates used if a screen floods?
What is the flux limit for the CIL4 intertank screens?

Why thicken flotation tails before CIL4?.q: How is recycled thickener overflow water reused elsewhere?
Why thicken flotation tails before CIL4?.a:
The flotation tails thickener overflow mainly feeds the new Process Water Tank (about 2,080 m3 live, duty/standby pumps). The process water demand is very large, about 5,355 m3/h on design figures, so this overflow is the backbone of the water circuit.

Process water then goes back to grinding dilution, flotation, sprays and hose points. When overflow isn't enough, the tank is topped up with saline bore water from Bore Water Dam 2 (South Dam).

The water is hypersaline (SG about 1.07) and carries some residual flotation reagents, so it suits duties that tolerate salt, not gland seals or reagent make up. Think of it as a closed cooling circuit: reuse most of the water and top up the losses.

f.q: Why does overflow clarity matter for the process water users?
f.a:
Solids in recycled water cause wear and blockages. Fine particles erode spray nozzles, settle in tanks and pipes, and can block small orifices in hose points and screen sprays. They also go back into grinding and flotation, which adds unwanted fines.

That's why the thickener vendor panel sends an overflow clarity signal to the DCS. Dirty overflow is usually a flocculation problem or a thickener being pushed beyond its flux.

From a mechanical view, it's like running a hydraulic system with dirty oil: everything still works for a while, but wear accelerates and small passages clog first.
f: What is done when overflow clarity alarms?
Which users are most sensitive to dirty process water?
How is settled sludge removed from the process water tank?

f.q: Can residual flotation reagents in the water cause problems?
f.a:
They can. Overflow water carries traces of frother, xanthate collector and copper sulphate back into the circuit. Usually that's harmless or even mildly helpful, since some reagent is recycled. But frother building up can make froth too stable or change bubble behaviour, and residual collectors can float things you didn't intend.

The reference doesn't give process water chemistry limits for this plant. In general it's a metallurgist's call: they watch reagent consumption and flotation performance and adjust dosing if recycled water is changing behaviour.

Like a cooling water treatment programme, the chemistry in recirculated water drifts over time, so someone has to keep an eye on it.
f: Why might recycled frother upset froth stability?
Does recycled copper sulphate affect pyrite flotation?
Who monitors process water chemistry on site?

f.q: What tops up process water when overflow isn't enough?
f.a:
Saline bore water. The Process Water Tank is topped up from Bore Water Dam 2 (South Dam) by three DOL saline pumps, which trip on a low low dam level to protect them from running dry.

The wider saline supply includes the Kaltails borefield (WBS N02), the Eastern Borefield and the offsite roaster saline transfer dam, feeding the plant's storage dams.

Water is lost mainly with the tailings: the final tails leave at about 54.5 percent solids on design figures, so a lot of water goes to the TSF. Some comes back as decant (cyanide water). Like a closed loop with a known leak, the bore water makes up the difference.

What is the CIL4 tank layout on the PFD?.q: Why is 14 hours considered the ideal residence time for CIL4?
What is the CIL4 tank layout on the PFD?.a:
The 14 h figure comes from the design basis supplied for the project. The PDC notes that 2 leach tanks plus 6 adsorption tanks will not achieve the 14 h total, that the client is aware, and that the decision was to keep 8 tanks with a 9th as a future addition.

The reference doesn't show the testwork behind the 14 h. In general, a target like that comes from leach and adsorption kinetics tests: it's the time at which extraction and gold capture on carbon reach the expected values before the curve flattens.

So treat 14 h as the metallurgical sweet spot and 12.8 h as the accepted compromise. The project metallurgist can explain the testwork if you want the detail.

f.q: How much residence time does each part of the train give?
f.a:
On PDC design figures, the 2 leach tanks (11,200 m3 live) give about 3.2 h and the 6 adsorption tanks (33,600 m3) about 9.6 h, for a total of about 12.8 h in the nominal case.

The reduced throughput case gives about 13.6 h and the high throughput case (28.35 Mtpa) only about 11.5 h, because more slurry flows through the same tanks.

These are calculated from live volume and design flow. Real residence also depends on actual tank levels, any sanding in the tanks and whether a tank is bypassed. Like a heat exchanger rating, it's a design number you compare the plant against, not a measurement.
f: Why is the leach section only two tanks long?
How does the high throughput case cut residence to 11.5 h?
Does gold keep leaching in the adsorption tanks?

f.q: Does leaching continue in the adsorption tanks too?
f.a:
Yes, that's the point of carbon in leach. The adsorption tanks still contain cyanide and oxygen, so gold keeps dissolving while carbon pulls it out of solution.

On CIL4 the design adds oxygen by side lances on the first two adsorption tanks as well as the leach tanks, and there's an extra cyanide addition point on adsorption tank 3. That only makes sense if leaching is still going on there.

Carbon helps too: by removing dissolved gold it keeps solution gold low, which keeps the driving force for dissolution up. It's like continuously removing product from a reaction so it keeps running forward.
f: Why is extra cyanide added at adsorption tank 3?
How does carbon pull dissolved gold out of solution?
What is preg robbing, and does it matter here?

f.q: Who decided to accept less than 14 hours?
f.a:
The PDC records that the client (the owner) was aware that 2 leach plus 6 adsorption tanks would fall short of 14 h, and advised to keep 8 tanks with the 9th as a future. So it was an owner decision recorded in the design criteria, with a layout provision for the extra tank.

The reasoning isn't spelled out in the reference. In general, it's a capital versus recovery trade off: each 5,600 m3 tank with agitator, screens and foundations is expensive, and the extra recovery from the last hour or so may not justify it up front.

Leaving space means the option stays open if plant data later shows the lost recovery is worth chasing.
f: How much recovery is lost by running 12.8 h instead of 14 h?
What would adding the ninth tank mean for plant downtime?
Where is the future tank located on the layout?

What is the CIL4 tank layout on the PFD?.q: What problem shows up if residence time stays under 12.8 h at full rate?
What is the CIL4 tank layout on the PFD?.a:
Less time means less gold dissolved and less dissolved gold captured. Leach extraction drops a little, and more gold leaves in tails, either still locked in the solids or dissolved but not adsorbed (soluble loss).

In the high throughput case the design residence is only about 11.5 h, so pushing tonnes through the mill has a cost at CIL4. Metallurgists would watch tails solid and solution assays and the Carbon Scout gold in solution readings per tank.

These are design numbers. The real effect depends on the ore and on how well DO, cyanide and carbon are held on target, which can partly compensate. The metallurgist is the person who quantifies the trade off between throughput and recovery.

f.q: What are soluble gold losses and why do they matter?
f.a:
Soluble losses are gold that has been dissolved by cyanide but not captured on carbon, so it leaves in the tails solution. It's the most annoying loss because the hard work (dissolving it) has been done.

The CIL4 design adsorption efficiency is about 88 percent, in a range of 84 to 92. With short residence or poorly performing carbon, the efficiency can slip toward the bottom of that range.

Some dissolved gold may come back with the TSF decant water, but you can't count on it. Like heat lost from an uninsulated pipe after you've paid to generate it, soluble losses are energy and reagent spent for no return.

How is gold in the tails solution measured?
What raises adsorption efficiency in CIL4?

f.q: How would operators claw back performance at short residence?
f.a:
By keeping everything else on target. That means holding dissolved oxygen near the design target (about 15 ppm in the leach), keeping cyanide at setpoint using the analyser trim, holding carbon near 12.5 g/L in every adsorption tank, and making sure carbon is active, since freshly regenerated carbon adsorbs faster.

Keeping feed density near the upper end of the acceptable range also helps, as fewer cubic metres per hour means more residence, but too dense hurts mixing.

None of this involves bypassing screens or tanks. Like running a heat exchanger with clean tubes when you can't add area, you get the best out of what's installed. The metallurgist would set the priorities.
f: Why does higher carbon activity help at short residence?
What DO target is set for the CIL4 leach tanks?
How does feed density trade off against agitation?

f.q: Is the 12.8 hours an actual measured value?
f.a:
No. It's a design value calculated in the PDC from the live tank volume (5,600 m3 each) and the design slurry flow (about 3,511 m3/h). It assumes all tanks are online and full to their live level.

Real residence varies. Sanded tanks lose live volume, a tank on bypass drops out of the train, and changes in throughput or feed density change the flow. Dead zones from poor mixing also mean some slurry short circuits faster than average.

So use 12.8 h as a reference point. Live residence can be estimated from current flow and tank levels on the DCS, but it's always an approximation, a bit like a nameplate rating versus actual duty.

What happens to residence when a tank is bypassed?

What is the CIL4 tank layout on the PFD?.q: What would trigger the plant to actually build the future extra tank?
What is the CIL4 tank layout on the PFD?.a:
The reference only says the layout includes provision for a future 7th adsorption tank (the 9th tank in the train). It doesn't define a trigger.

In general, a decision like that comes from economics backed by plant data. If metallurgical surveys show meaningful gold being lost because of short residence, if throughput is pushed toward the high case where residence falls to about 11.5 h, or if gold price makes the extra ounces worth the capital, the owner would build a business case.

That's an owner decision driven by the site metallurgy and projects teams, not something operations does on its own. Ask the senior metallurgist if a study is under way.

f.q: Where does the future tank sit in the CIL4 train?
f.a:
The PDC describes it as provision in the layout for a future 7th adsorption tank, and the card notes space for a future tank on the PFD. The reference doesn't give its exact position or tag.

In general, an extra adsorption tank goes at the end of the train so the slurry passes through one more stage of carbon contact before tails, and the carbon flow simply starts one tank further back.

To see the actual footprint, check the CIL4 general arrangement and layout drawings, or ask the area engineer. Don't assume a tag number until you've seen it on a drawing.
f: Would the future tank go at the start or the end of the train?
How would carbon flow change with a seventh adsorption tank?
Which drawings show the future tank footprint?

f.q: How much extra residence would one more tank add?
f.a:
Using the design figures: one more tank at about 5,600 m3 live, divided by the CIL4 slurry flow of about 3,511 m3/h, gives roughly 1.6 h. That would take the nominal total from about 12.8 h to about 14.4 h, just over the 14 h ideal.

In the high throughput case the gain is a bit smaller per tank because flow is higher, so the total would go from about 11.5 h to about 13 h.

That's my arithmetic on design values, not a number from a study. Actual benefit depends on how much extra extraction and adsorption the ore gives for the extra time, which only testwork or plant trials can tell you.
f: Would 14.4 hours fully meet the design residence target?
Why might extra adsorption help more than extra leach time?
What would one more tank do at high throughput?

f.q: What data would metallurgists use to justify the tank?
f.a:
Mainly evidence of recoverable gold leaving in tails. They'd run leach profile surveys, sampling each tank for solid and solution gold, to see whether gold is still dissolving and being captured at the end of the train. If the curve is still climbing at the last tank, more time would help.

They'd combine that with tails assays from the shift composite sampler, Carbon Scout gold in solution trends, bottle roll tests on tails at longer times, and throughput plans.

Then it becomes a business case: extra ounces per year times gold price, against capital and installation downtime. That's general practice; the reference doesn't describe a specific study for this plant.

How does carbon move in CIL4?.q: Why does counter current flow work like a counterflow heat exchanger?
How does carbon move in CIL4?.a:
Both keep the driving force high along the whole length. In a counterflow heat exchanger, the coolest incoming fluid meets the already cooled outgoing fluid, so there's always a temperature difference to push heat.

In CIL4, the freshest barren carbon enters the last tank, where solution gold is lowest, so even weak solution can still load onto it. As carbon is advanced upstream it meets richer and richer solution and keeps loading. The most loaded carbon is pulled from the first adsorption tank, where solution gold is highest.

That keeps a concentration difference in every tank, like a healthy log mean temperature difference, which lets carbon load to roughly 332 to 579 g/t while tails solution stays low.

f.q: What sets how much gold carbon can hold at equilibrium?
f.a:
The adsorption isotherm. For a given gold concentration in solution, carbon will load up to an equilibrium value; richer solution allows higher loading. That's why CIL3 carbon (concentrate solution) loads to about 4,490 g/t but CIL4 only to about 332 to 579 g/t.

Other things reduce capacity: competing metals such as silver, copper and mercury that also adsorb, organic fouling from oils or reagents, carbonate scale blocking pores, and loss of activity as carbon ages. Acid washing and kiln regeneration restore much of it.

It's similar to a filter element: rated capacity drops as it fouls, so you clean or replace it.
f: Why do copper and mercury compete with gold on carbon?
How does organic fouling reduce carbon activity?
What is a carbon activity test?

f.q: What would co-current carbon flow do instead?
f.a:
If carbon moved with the slurry, the most loaded carbon would end up in the last tank, meeting the leanest solution. There it would have almost no driving force to load more, and some gold could even desorb back into solution.

You'd also have to pull loaded carbon off the tail end of the circuit, right where you want the lowest gold losses. Tails solution gold would be higher and carbon loading lower, so you'd strip more carbon for the same gold.

It's the same reason parallel flow heat exchangers are less effective: the outlet temperatures converge and the last part of the exchanger does very little.
f: Can gold come off carbon and go back into solution?
Why is barren carbon added at the last tank?
How low does tails solution gold need to be?

f.q: How often is carbon moved along the CIL4 train?
f.a:
The PDC design basis allows up to about 30 t/day of carbon movement, with a maximum carbon residence of 14 days and about 420 t of carbon in circuit at 12.5 g/L. The CIL4 elution column holds 15 t and is designed for 2 strips per day, 6 days a week.

A carbon transfer between tanks is calculated at about 5.5 h at about 220 m3/h of carbon and pulp, and the loaded carbon pull to the screen about 4.3 h.

Those are design numbers. The actual schedule is set by operations using Carbon Scout readings and loading targets, and the CIL operator or metallurgist will know the current routine.
f: Why is carbon residence capped at 14 days?
How is a 15 t carbon batch measured out?
What happens to the schedule if elution is down?

How does carbon move in CIL4?.q: What would the Carbon Scout show if carbon advance stalled mid train?
How does carbon move in CIL4?.a:
A carbon imbalance. Carbon moves upstream tank by tank. If the transfer from one tank stalls, that tank keeps receiving carbon from the tank downstream of it but stops sending any on, so its carbon g/L climbs. The tank it normally feeds keeps sending carbon forward without getting any back, so its g/L falls.

The Carbon Scout, which samples carbon concentration in every adsorption tank, would show a high reading at the stalled tank and a low one just upstream, while total inventory stays about the same.

Likely causes are the recessed impeller transfer pump, a blocked line or a spool piece set wrong. It's like a blocked stage in a multistage process: material piles up behind the restriction.

f.q: What problems come from too much carbon in one tank?
f.a:
Several. A high carbon concentration loads up the intertank screens, so they're more likely to blind or overflow. More carbon also means more carbon to carbon and carbon to impeller contact, which breaks carbon into fines that slip through the 1.0 mm screens and carry gold to tails.

Meanwhile the starved tank upstream has too little carbon to capture gold, so solution gold rises there and adsorption efficiency drops.

The target is about 12.5 g/L in each tank. Like an overloaded bearing on one shaft while its neighbour runs light, uneven loading wears the system faster and gets less done.

How much carbon is too much for an intertank screen?
Can a high carbon g/L cause a screen to overflow?

f.q: How do the removable spool pieces affect carbon routing?
f.a:
According to the control philosophy, loaded carbon routing between CIL4 tanks is set by removable spool pieces rather than automated valves. Changing where carbon goes is therefore a mechanical job, not a click on the OIS.

The practical upshot is that a wrong route stays wrong until someone physically changes it, so after maintenance or a reroute, it's worth checking the spool configuration matches the intended carbon path.

Any spool change means breaking into a slurry line that may contain cyanide, so it's done under the site isolation and permit system. The reference doesn't give the procedure; the area supervisor or maintenance planner will.

f.q: What else does the Carbon Scout measure besides carbon?
f.a:
On CIL4 the Gekko Carbon Scout MK6 samples all adsorption tanks for carbon concentration and the leach tanks for dissolved oxygen, pH and solids.

The instrument list shows soft tags for eight tanks (AI21140 to AI21147), each with DO, pH, density and gold ppm channels, plus a fault signal. So it also gives an indication of gold in solution along the train, which is useful for spotting where adsorption is falling off.

It's a vendor package with its own PLC that reports to the DCS. Think of it as a condition monitoring system that walks round every tank on a cycle, much like a route based vibration survey.

Why is the Carbon Scout run on its own vendor PLC?
How often does it cycle through all eight tanks?

How does carbon move in CIL4?.q: What pumps physically advance carbon upstream between tanks?
How does carbon move in CIL4?.a:
Recessed impeller pumps. The PDC lists carbon transfer by recessed impeller pump at about 220 m3/h of carbon and pulp, and the loaded carbon pump forwarding from the first adsorption tank at about 280 m3/h.

A recessed (vortex) impeller sits back in the casing, out of the main flow path. It spins up a vortex that drags the slurry and carbon through the pump, so most carbon particles never touch the vanes.

That's the key: carbon is fragile, and a normal closed impeller would chop it into fines that pass the screens and take gold to tails. It's the same reason vortex pumps are used for sewage or food solids: gentle handling and resistance to clogging, at the cost of efficiency.

f.q: Why does carbon breakage matter so much?
f.a:
Broken carbon becomes fines. Anything under about 1 mm passes the 1.0 mm intertank screens and keeps moving downstream with the slurry, eventually to tails. That carbon carries whatever gold it has loaded, so it's a direct gold loss.

You also lose the carbon itself, which has to be replaced with fresh carbon added through the hoist, bag splitter and quench hopper.

The design fights breakage in several places: recessed impeller pumps, a sizing screen after the regeneration kiln to remove fines before they go back, and a carbon detection meter on CIL4 tails. Like bearing wear particles, fines tell you something is grinding where it shouldn't.
f: How much carbon is typically lost per tonne treated?
How are carbon fines recovered from the circuit?
Does the regeneration kiln also break carbon?

f.q: What's the tradeoff with a recessed impeller pump?
f.a:
Efficiency and head. Because most of the fluid never passes through the impeller vanes, a recessed impeller pump is noticeably less efficient than a closed impeller slurry pump and develops less head for the same size and speed.

For carbon transfer that's acceptable. The duty is intermittent, distances between tanks are short, and protecting carbon is worth far more than a few kilowatts. They also handle large solids and stringy trash without blocking.

It's like choosing a slow, oversized gearbox for a shock loaded drive: you give up some efficiency to protect what matters.
f: Why is pump efficiency less important for carbon transfer?
What wear parts fail first on recessed impeller pumps?
How are carbon transfer pumps started and stopped?

f.q: How is slurry moved along while carbon moves the other way?
f.a:
Slurry flows downstream by gravity, tank to tank, through the intertank screens, which hold carbon back. The tanks are set so each one overflows to the next.

Carbon goes upstream by pumping: a transfer pump lifts carbon with a lot of slurry into the previous tank. That slurry then simply flows back down through the screens with the main stream, while the carbon stays behind. That's why the screen feed rate is quoted with and without carbon advance.

There are pneumatic slurry bypass gates that are operated locally only, for when a screen has to be taken out of the flow path. It's a bit like a recirculation line around a pump: some flow goes round in a loop, but the net flow still goes forward.
f: Why are the slurry bypass gates local operation only?
What happens to the slurry pumped back with the carbon?
How much extra screen load does a carbon advance add?

What do intertank screens do in CIL4?.q: Why is 1.0 mm wedge wire the right cut point between carbon and slurry?
What do intertank screens do in CIL4?.a:
It sits in the gap between the two size ranges. Carbon granules are roughly 1 to 3 mm, while CIL4 slurry is ground to a P80 of about 180 microns (maximum about 250). So the ore passes easily and carbon stays, with a comfortable margin either side.

Wedge wire has a V shaped profile: the slot is narrowest at the surface and widens underneath. A particle that gets through the top doesn't wedge in the slot, so the screen resists pegging.

Going finer would retain more worn carbon but blind more easily with near size ore and trash. Going coarser would let smaller carbon escape. The 1.0 mm trash screens upstream also mean nothing much bigger than that should arrive.

f.q: What happens to carbon once it wears below 1 mm?
f.a:
It starts passing through the intertank screens and moving downstream with the slurry. Eventually it can reach the final tank and leave in tails, taking its gold with it.

Several design features are aimed at this. After regeneration, carbon goes over the CIL4 carbon sizing screen (1.25 x 18.5 mm polyurethane apertures) before going back to the last tank, which removes fines before they enter the train. There's a carbon detection meter on CIL4 tails with a reference probe at the front end, and carbon safety screens on the tails (0.85 x 18.5 mm) are shown as future equipment.

Fine carbon waste also goes to the final tails tank by design.
f: How does the carbon detection meter on tails work?
Why is the sizing screen aperture larger than 1 mm?
Where do carbon fines removed by the sizing screen go?

f.q: Why do trash screens upstream protect the intertank screens?
f.a:
Trash like wood chips, fibres and plastic would otherwise reach CIL4, where it blinds intertank screens, mats onto carbon and ends up in elution and the kiln. Wood fibre is especially bad because it wraps around wedge wire and slowly closes the open area.

The milling circuit has four linear trash screens (3 operating, 1 standby) with 1.0 x 1.0 mm apertures, removing about 27 t/day of wood, grit and trash on design figures. Spillage returned from the event pond and silt traps goes through the CIL4 static screen for the same reason.

It's the same logic as a suction strainer ahead of a pump: catch the debris early where it's easy to deal with.
f: What trash gets past the trash screens anyway?
How does wood fibre blind a wedge wire screen?
What happens if a trash screen panel tears?

f.q: Why are the screens mechanically swept rather than static?
f.a:
A static screen in a tank full of carbon would quickly get covered: carbon pins against the wire and near size particles pile up, cutting the open area. The Kemix design uses sweeping blades that continually wipe the screen surface, keeping it clear so slurry can pass.

They're also pumped screens, meaning an impeller draws slurry through the screen basket and moves it on, rather than relying only on head difference. CIL4 has two Kemix MPS2535(P) screens per tank, each about 25 m2.

A good mechanical comparison is a self cleaning strainer with a rotating wiper: it costs a drive and some wear parts, but avoids constant manual cleaning.
f: What drives the sweeper on a Kemix screen?
Why are there two screens per CIL4 tank?
What wears out first on a swept pumped screen?

What do intertank screens do in CIL4?.q: What would a blinded intertank screen do to carbon distribution?
What do intertank screens do in CIL4?.a:
Blinding cuts the open area, so slurry can't leave the tank as fast as it arrives. The level in that tank rises, and if it gets high enough, slurry spills over a launder or has to be sent through the bypass. Either way some carbon goes downstream with it, the wrong way.

The tank downstream then gains carbon and the blinded tank loses it, and the Carbon Scout readings show the imbalance. Moving loaded carbon downstream also means it meets leaner solution, and some gold can come back off.

The fix is to get the screen clean and working again under the site procedure, then rebalance carbon with the transfer pumps. The CIL operator handles this routinely.

f.q: How do operators know a screen is blinding before it overflows?
f.a:
Mostly from rising tank level. As the screen loses open area, the level in that tank climbs relative to the next, and level alarms on the DCS give warning before slurry spills. A change in carbon concentration on the Carbon Scout can also hint at carbon moving where it shouldn't.

Field checks matter too. Operators doing rounds look at the screen and the head difference between tanks, and listen for changes in the sweeper drive.

The reference doesn't list the CIL4 tank level instruments or alarm settings, so check the F21 P&IDs or ask the control room operator for the live alarm limits.
f: What level instruments are fitted on the CIL4 tanks?
How fast can a screen go from blinding to overflowing?
Who on shift inspects the intertank screens?

f.q: What is done with carbon that has migrated downstream?
f.a:
Generally it gets moved back upstream by the normal carbon transfer pumps. Since carbon is always being advanced upstream anyway, operators can run extra transfers from the tank that gained carbon to rebalance the train, guided by Carbon Scout readings.

If carbon has moved several tanks, rebalancing takes a while, and carbon that reached the last tank is at risk of leaving in tails. That's where the carbon detection meter on CIL4 tails is useful as a check.

The reference doesn't describe a specific rebalancing procedure, so the CIL operator or metallurgist would set the plan.
f: How is a carbon imbalance corrected across the train?
Can migrated carbon reach the final tails?
How is carbon inventory reconciled each month?

f.q: Why does carbon moving the wrong way hurt gold recovery?
f.a:
Because loaded carbon is in balance with the richer solution near the front of the train. If it gets carried downstream into leaner solution, the driving force can reverse and some gold desorbs back into solution, which then has less carbon and less time left to recapture it.

Worse, carbon that keeps moving downstream can reach the final tank and leave to the TSF with all its gold. At 332 to 579 g/t design loading, every tonne lost carries hundreds of grams of gold.

It's like a heat exchanger with a bypass leaking hot fluid into the cold outlet: you undo some of the work you've already done.
f: How much gold can loaded carbon release in lean solution?
What does a tonne of carbon lost to tails cost in gold?
Why are carbon safety screens planned for the tails?

What do intertank screens do in CIL4?.q: How are these Kemix screens cleaned or maintained on shift?
What do intertank screens do in CIL4?.a:
The reference doesn't give the cleaning procedure. What it does say is that CIL4 has pneumatic slurry bypass gates operated locally only, which is how a screen is taken out of the flow path.

In general, shift care means checking the sweeper is running, looking for blinding or trash build up, hosing the screen surface with HP process water from hose points, and checking for damaged wedge wire. Basket or panel changes are planned jobs done during shutdowns with proper isolation.

Never reach into or stand over a running screen, and work only under the site permit and isolation system. The CIL area operator and the area maintenance planner know the actual routines.

f.q: Why are the CIL4 slurry bypass gates operated locally only?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the pneumatic slurry bypass gates on CIL4 are operated locally only, but doesn't give the reason.

In general, the logic is that a bypass sends slurry round a screen, which can also carry carbon downstream. Making it a local action means someone is standing at the tank, can see the level and screen condition, and knows why they're opening it. It avoids an accidental remote click sending carbon the wrong way.

It's similar to keeping some isolation valves manual only on a hydraulic system: the person operating it has to be there and look first.
f: What does opening a bypass gate do to carbon distribution?
How long can a screen safely stay bypassed?
Who authorises opening a bypass gate?

f.q: What isolation is needed before working on an intertank screen?
f.a:
The reference doesn't give the procedure. In general, before any hands on work you'd need the screen drive electrically isolated and locked out, pneumatic supplies isolated, and the screen taken out of the flow using the bypass. Personal locks go on under the site permit system, and stored energy such as a raised basket must be secured.

CIL tanks also bring chemical hazards: cyanide in the slurry and the possibility of HCN gas, which is why CIL4 has an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren. Cyanide PPE and gas awareness apply.

Never bypass an interlock or work on a screen that is still running. Your supervisor and the permit issuer set the exact requirements.
f: Why is HCN a risk when working above CIL tanks?
What PPE is standard around cyanide tanks?
How is a screen basket lifted out for repair?

f.q: What typical faults do swept pumped screens develop?
f.a:
In general: worn or torn wedge wire, which lets carbon through; broken or worn sweeper blades, which let the screen blind; bearing and gearbox failures on the drive; impeller wear on the pumping element; and trash wrapped around the basket.

Many show up first as process symptoms: rising tank level for blinding, or carbon appearing downstream for a torn screen. Others show up as mechanical symptoms like noise, vibration or drive current changes.

The reference doesn't give the maintenance strategy for these screens. The area maintenance planner will have the vendor recommended inspection intervals and spares.
f: How is wedge wire damage spotted during an inspection?
What gearbox checks apply to the screen drives?
How are spare screen baskets managed on site?

What's the 'Carbon Scout'?.q: Why does even carbon distribution matter for adsorption efficiency?
What's the 'Carbon Scout'?.a:
Each adsorption tank acts as one stage in the counter current train. For the staging to work, every tank needs enough carbon to capture the gold in its solution. The design target is about 12.5 g/L in every adsorption tank.

If one tank is short of carbon, gold passes through that stage without being captured, and the next tank has to do extra work with carbon that's already loaded. If a tank has too much, its screens are overloaded and carbon breakage increases.

Design adsorption efficiency is about 88 percent, so there isn't a lot of slack. It's like a multistage pump with one weak impeller: the whole machine underperforms even if the others are fine.

f.q: Why was 12.5 g/L chosen as the carbon concentration?
f.a:
The PDC sets 12.5 g/L as the duty carbon concentration per tank, from an owner source, and also uses it for carbon transfer. At that concentration CIL4 holds about 420 t of carbon.

The reference doesn't explain the choice. In general, more carbon adsorbs faster and gives lower tails solution gold, but it ties up more gold on carbon inventory, increases carbon breakage, and loads the screens harder. Less carbon is cheaper and gentler but lets more gold escape.

CIL3 runs about 20 g/L because concentrate solution is far richer. For CIL4's lean solution and huge flow, 12.5 g/L is the agreed balance.
f: How much gold is tied up in the CIL4 carbon inventory?
What happens if carbon concentration drops to 8 g/L?
Why does CIL3 run 20 g/L but CIL4 only 12.5?

f.q: What is adsorption efficiency and how is it measured?
f.a:
It's the share of the dissolved gold that ends up on carbon instead of leaving in tails solution. If 100 units of gold dissolve and 88 get captured, efficiency is 88 percent. The CIL4 design figure is 88 percent, range 84 to 92.

It's worked out from solution assays: gold in solution entering and leaving, combined with how much gold was dissolved. The Carbon Scout gives an indication of solution gold per tank, and lab assays of tails solution confirm it.

In mechanical terms it's like the effectiveness of a heat exchanger: actual duty divided by the best duty possible.
f: How are CIL4 tails solution samples taken?
What lowers adsorption efficiency in saline water?
How does carbon fouling show up in the numbers?

f.q: Does carbon quality matter as much as quantity?
f.a:
Yes. Carbon activity, how fast and how much gold it adsorbs, drops as pores get blocked by carbonate scale, organic fouling and fine slimes. Fouled carbon at 12.5 g/L can perform worse than clean carbon at a lower concentration.

The plant restores carbon in two ways: acid washing with dilute HCl removes carbonate scale before elution, and thermal regeneration in the kiln burns off organics. Flotation tails can carry residual reagents such as frother and xanthate, which in general can foul carbon, so regeneration matters here.

Like a filter element, quantity on paper means little if the media is clogged.
f: Can flotation reagents in the tails foul CIL4 carbon?
How often is carbon activity tested on site?
What does acid washing remove from the carbon?

What's the 'Carbon Scout'?.q: What would an uneven Carbon Scout reading across tanks suggest?
What's the 'Carbon Scout'?.a:
Look at the pattern. One tank high with its upstream neighbour low usually means a carbon transfer has stalled: a recessed impeller pump problem, a blocked line or a spool piece set the wrong way. Carbon showing up in tanks further downstream than expected suggests a screen has overflowed or been bypassed, sending carbon the wrong way.

A general drift low across all tanks can mean carbon is being lost, through fines to tails or carbon held up in elution and regeneration and not returned.

A single odd reading might just be the sampler, so confirm before acting. Check PI trends, recent carbon movements and screen status, and talk to the CIL operator.

f.q: How would you tell a sampler fault from a real carbon imbalance?
f.a:
Cross check. A manual sample, a known volume of slurry screened to recover and weigh the carbon, gives an independent carbon concentration. If it agrees with the Carbon Scout, the imbalance is real.

Also check whether the readings make physical sense. Total carbon inventory shouldn't change suddenly; if one tank jumps without a matching drop elsewhere, suspect the instrument. The Carbon Scout reports a fault signal to the DCS (XA21140), so check that too.

It's like a single high vibration reading: confirm with a second instrument before pulling the machine apart.
f: How is a manual carbon concentration sample taken?
What does the Carbon Scout fault alarm cover?
Who maintains the Carbon Scout on site?

f.q: What does low carbon in the last tank risk?
f.a:
The last tank is the final polishing stage before tails. It should hold fresh, active, barren carbon to grab the last of the dissolved gold. If carbon is low there, solution gold leaving CIL4 rises and soluble losses go up.

Regenerated carbon returns to the last tank through the CIL4 carbon sizing screen, so if the elution and regeneration cycle falls behind, or carbon is being lost, the last tank is often the first to run short.

It's like the last filter stage in a cleaning system: if it's missing, everything upstream can be working and you still lose product.
f: How is regenerated carbon returned to the last tank?
What happens if the regen kiln falls behind on carbon?
How low can the last tank go before losses rise?

f.q: Can a carbon imbalance be fixed without stopping the plant?
f.a:
Usually yes. Carbon is moved with transfer pumps while the circuit runs, so operators can run extra transfers out of the tank holding too much and let the starved tank refill from downstream. That's routine CIL operation, guided by the Carbon Scout.

Bigger problems take longer: a failed transfer pump has to be repaired or swapped, and a wrong spool piece arrangement needs a mechanical change under isolation. Those may need that part of the circuit isolated, though the whole plant keeps running.

The reference doesn't describe the procedure for this plant. The CIL operator or metallurgist will set the plan.
f: Which tank transfer pump would you run first to rebalance?
How long does a full train rebalance usually take?
What records are kept for carbon movements?

What's the 'Carbon Scout'?.q: How often does Carbon Scout data trigger a carbon advance?
What's the 'Carbon Scout'?.a:
The reference doesn't give a set frequency. It says the Carbon Scout tells operators when to advance carbon and whether it's evenly distributed, so it informs the decision rather than setting a fixed timer.

The design gives the bounds: the CIL4 elution column takes 15 t per strip, designed for 2 strips per day, 6 days a week, and maximum carbon movement is about 30 t/day. A carbon transfer between tanks is calculated at about 5.5 h.

So carbon advance is broadly paced by elution capacity and loading targets, with Carbon Scout readings used to keep the tanks balanced. The CIL operator can tell you the current routine.

f.q: Is the carbon advance automatic or operator initiated?
f.a:
The reference doesn't say. It shows the Carbon Scout as a vendor package with its own PLC reporting to the DCS, and carbon routing set by removable spool pieces, but not whether advances are triggered by a DCS sequence, a timer or an operator.

In general, many plants run carbon advance as an operator decision using sampler data, sometimes with a DCS sequence once started. Because the routing here is set mechanically by spool pieces, there's likely an operator element.

Don't assume either way. Ask the control room operator or check the CIL4 control philosophy section for carbon advance.
f: Which DCS screen shows carbon advance status?
Can a carbon advance be paused partway through?
Who signs off the daily carbon movement plan?

f.q: Why is elution capacity tied to the carbon advance rate?
f.a:
Carbon only leaves CIL4 when it's pulled from the first adsorption tank and sent to elution. If carbon can't leave, there's no room to advance more carbon forward. The design matches these: the 15 t column, 2 strips per day, gives about 30 t/day, the same as the maximum carbon movement, and the CIL4 transfer vessel holds 30 t.

If elution stops, loaded carbon stays in the first tank, loading creeps up, and the whole train slows. Regenerated carbon also stops coming back to the last tank.

It's like a conveyor feeding a bin: the upstream rate can't run ahead of what the downstream can take away.
f: What happens to CIL4 if the elution column is offline?
Why does the transfer vessel hold 30 tonnes?
How high can carbon loading go before losses rise?

f.q: How does carbon loading tell you to pull carbon faster?
f.a:
The PDC design carbon loading is about 461 g/t nominal, with a range of about 332 to 579 g/t. If loaded carbon assays run toward or above the top of that range, carbon is getting close to equilibrium with the solution, so it adsorbs more slowly and more gold escapes downstream.

Pulling and stripping carbon more often brings fresh carbon back sooner and lowers loading. If loading runs low, you're stripping more carbon than needed, which costs reagents, LPG and carbon wear.

Like changing a filter on pressure drop rather than on a calendar, loading tells you when the carbon has done its job.
f: How is loaded carbon grade assayed?
Why does high loading slow adsorption?
What barren carbon grade comes back from elution?

CIL4 leach pH is about 8.8 to 9.3, much.q: Why does magnesium in the water consume so much lime at higher pH?
CIL4 leach pH is about 8.8 to 9.3, much.a:
Saline bore water carries a lot of dissolved magnesium. When you add lime, you're adding hydroxide to lift pH. Once pH climbs toward about 9 to 10, magnesium starts to precipitate as magnesium hydroxide, and every bit of that precipitate locks up hydroxide that would otherwise have raised the pH.

So the water acts as a buffer: you keep adding lime, but much of it goes into dropping out magnesium instead of moving the pH. It's like trying to heat water that's already boiling, where the energy goes into the phase change, not the temperature.

The reference doesn't give the magnesium concentration, but the process water design data shows TDS of about 140,000 mg/L and pH about 4.6, so lime has a lot of work to do.

f.q: Why is the process water pH as low as 4.6?
f.a:
The PDC process water quality data lists pH 4.6 with about 140,000 mg/L dissolved solids and very high chlorides. It doesn't explain why.

In general, hypersaline groundwater in the Goldfields is often naturally acidic. Iron and sulphide minerals in the aquifer oxidise and release acidity, and the water has very little natural alkalinity to neutralise it.

The practical effect is that some lime is spent just neutralising the water before pH even reaches neutral, then more fights the magnesium buffer above about pH 9. Acidic, salty water is also hard on carbon steel, which is part of why material selection matters on this plant.
f: Does acidic water attack pumps and pipework faster?
How much lime goes just to neutralising the water?
Does the process water pH change much over time?

f.q: Does magnesium hydroxide precipitate cause other problems?
f.a:
It can. Magnesium hydroxide forms a fine, gelatinous solid. In general it can coat pH probes, scale tank walls, pipes and valves, and add to slurry viscosity. Coated pH probes respond slowly or read wrong, which makes lime control harder.

There's also a general concern that fine precipitates and scale can coat carbon and block pores, reducing activity. The CIL4 elution includes acid washing, which removes calcium and magnesium carbonate scale from carbon before stripping.

Running CIL4 at a lower pH limits how much magnesium drops out in the first place. The reference doesn't quantify scaling on this plant, so the metallurgist or area maintenance planner would know how bad it is in practice.
f: How does scale on pH probes affect lime control?
Can magnesium scale foul carbon pores?
How is scale removed from CIL4 pipework?

f.q: How much lime does CIL4 use compared to the concentrate leach?
f.a:
Per tonne, far less. The PDC gives dry lime consumption of about 3.2 kg/t nominal (4.5 design) for the flotation tails CIL, against about 51.2 kg/t nominal (120.1 design) for the concentrate CIL.

But CIL4 treats about 3,164 t/h against about 75 to 78 t/h of concentrate. Multiplying out on nominal figures, CIL4 uses around 10 t/h of lime and the concentrate leach around 4 t/h, which matches the PDC total of about 13.9 t/h. So CIL4 is the biggest lime user by far, even at its low pH.

That's my arithmetic on design figures. It shows why a few tenths of a pH unit on CIL4 matter so much for the lime bill.
f: Why does concentrate need so much more lime per tonne?
How big is the lime slaking plant?
What happens to CIL4 if the lime ringmain fails?

CIL4 leach pH is about 8.8 to 9.3, much.q: What HCN safety symptom would you watch for at this lower pH?
CIL4 leach pH is about 8.8 to 9.3, much.a:
Hydrogen cyanide gas. In solution, cyanide exists as both free cyanide ions and dissolved HCN, and the split depends on pH. Around pH 9.2 to 9.3 it's roughly half and half, and below that HCN dominates. So at CIL4's 8.8 to 9.3, much more HCN can come off the slurry than in CIL2 at above 11.

CIL4 has an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren. Treat any HCN alarm, beacon or siren as real, and respect a falling pH trend on the OIS. Don't rely on smell; many people can't detect the bitter almond odour.

If the alarm goes, follow the site cyanide emergency procedure: move upwind to the muster point and don't go back to investigate.

f.q: Why is HCN release so sensitive to pH?
f.a:
Because it's a chemical equilibrium: HCN in solution splits into a hydrogen ion and a cyanide ion. The balance point (pKa) is about 9.2 at room temperature. Each pH unit below that shifts the balance about tenfold toward HCN.

Dissolved HCN is volatile, so agitation, air or oxygen sparging and warm temperatures strip it out of the slurry as gas. At pH 11 almost all cyanide is safely held as ions; at pH 9 a lot is present as HCN.

That's why concentrate leaching runs at high pH, and why CIL4 needs gas monitoring. In general, very high salinity can shift the balance slightly, but the reference doesn't give site data on that.
f: Does high salinity change the HCN balance point?
Why does agitation increase HCN off gassing?
How much cyanide is lost to air as HCN?

f.q: What happens on site when the HCN monitor alarms?
f.a:
The plant reference only says CIL4 has an HCN gas monitor with a beacon and siren. The response procedure is site specific.

In general: stop work, move upwind and away from the tanks to the designated muster point, and report in. Don't investigate the source yourself. Only trained responders with gas detection and breathing apparatus re enter. Meanwhile the control room checks pH, lime supply and cyanide dosing.

Make sure you've done the site cyanide induction and know where the muster points and cyanide first aid kits are near CIL4. Never mute or bypass a gas alarm.
f: Where are the CIL4 HCN detectors located?
What personal gas monitor should I carry near CIL4?
Who is trained to respond to a cyanide alarm?

f.q: What would cause CIL4 pH to drop suddenly?
f.a:
Usually a lime supply problem. Milk of lime comes round a ringmain from the lime plant, so a ringmain pump trip, slaker outage, blocked line or a milk of lime valve stuck shut at the CIL4 feed distribution box would all cut lime.

Instrument faults are next: the pH controller uses tank 1 with tank 2 as backup, so a fouled or failed probe can make the loop act on a false reading.

Process changes count too: a change in water quality or ore that consumes more lime. In control terms, compare the controller output with the PV. If output is at maximum and pH is still falling, the problem is supply, not tuning.
f: How does the tank 2 pH probe back up tank 1?
What alarms if the milk of lime valve stops responding?
How quickly does CIL4 pH respond to lime changes?

CIL4 leach pH is about 8.8 to 9.3, much.q: How is lime dosing balanced against reagent cost here?
CIL4 leach pH is about 8.8 to 9.3, much.a:
Through the pH setpoint. The control philosophy has a pH controller on tank 1 (tank 2 as backup) opening the milk of lime valve at the CIL4 feed distribution box. The design range is pH 8.8 to 9.3.

Running higher costs a lot more lime because of the magnesium buffer, and CIL4 is already the plant's biggest lime user by tonnage. Running lower saves lime but increases HCN gas risk and cyanide lost to air.

The chosen setpoint sits where both are acceptable, with HCN gas monitoring as a safety layer. It's like choosing boiler pressure: higher gives margin but costs fuel. The metallurgist owns the setpoint, not the control room on its own.

f.q: How does the CIL4 pH control loop actually work?
f.a:
It's a feedback loop. The pH analyser in tank 1 is the process variable. The controller compares it with the setpoint and drives the milk of lime valve at the CIL4 feed distribution box. Tank 2's pH measurement is the backup if tank 1's is unavailable.

The difficulty is lag. Lime added at the feed box takes time to mix and react before tank 1 sees it, so the loop has dead time. Tuned too aggressively, it overshoots and cycles; too gently, it drifts.

Think of a large tank temperature loop with a long pipe between heater and sensor: you tune slow and steady. The Carbon Scout pH readings on the leach tanks give a useful cross check.
f: Why is the pH probe in tank 1 rather than the feed box?
How is a slow pH loop tuned to avoid cycling?
How often are CIL4 pH probes cleaned and calibrated?

f.q: Does lower pH also increase cyanide consumption?
f.a:
In general, yes. At lower pH more cyanide is present as HCN, which can volatilise off the tank surface. That cyanide is lost: you pay for it and it does no leaching.

So the pH choice trades lime cost against cyanide cost and safety. The PDC gives CIL4 nominal cyanide at about 0.22 kg/t, with dosing at the feed box, the leach tanks and adsorption tank 3, trimmed by a cyanide analyser on tanks 1 and 2.

The reference doesn't give a lime versus cyanide cost comparison for this plant. That optimisation is a metallurgist's job, using plant trials and reagent prices.
f: Which costs more per tonne here, lime or cyanide?
How is cyanide loss to air estimated?
Can covering tanks reduce HCN losses?

f.q: Where does the milk of lime for CIL4 come from?
f.a:
From the Stage 2 lime plant. Quicklime is delivered in bulk to two silos (about 1,132 t each), then slaked in a vendor package with two parallel circuits, each with a slaking mill, cyclones and a scrubber. The milk of lime (about 20 percent w/w) goes to a storage tank of about 524 m3 live.

From there, duty/standby DOL pumps circulate it round a ringmain past the dosing points, including the CIL4 feed distribution box. Make up water for slaking is raw water.

A ringmain keeps the slurry moving so it doesn't settle, a bit like a recirculating lube system that keeps oil moving past every take off.
f: Why is milk of lime made with raw water?
What keeps milk of lime from settling in the ringmain?
How long can CIL4 run if the slaker stops?

CIL4 leach gold extraction is quite low.q: Why is most tails gold locked in unfloated sulphides rather than free gold?
CIL4 leach gold extraction is quite low.a:
Because the ore is refractory, and the free gold has mostly been taken out earlier. Much of the gold is locked inside sulphides, mainly pyrite, and in tellurides. Coarse free gold is grabbed by the gravity circuit (about 14 percent of feed gold) and free or sulphide gold that liberates well floats into concentrate.

What escapes flotation is mostly gold in sulphide particles that didn't float: fine particles, composites still stuck to gangue at a 180 micron grind, or slow floating grains. Cyanide can't reach gold sealed inside pyrite.

That's why concentrate is ground to about 9 microns before leaching, and why CIL4 only manages about 34 to 38 percent extraction on design figures.

f.q: Why does the concentrate get ultra fine ground but the tails don't?
f.a:
Cost. UFG to a P80 of about 9 microns takes about 116.5 kWh/t on design figures. That's affordable on concentrate at roughly 75 to 105 t/h, using IsaMills drawing about 3.5 MW each.

The tails are about 3,000 t/h. Grinding that to 9 microns would need roughly forty times the concentrate tonnage at the same energy per tonne, which is completely uneconomic.

So the flowsheet concentrates the gold first, then spends energy only on the small mass that holds most of it. Like sizing a heat exchanger for the stream that carries the heat, you put the expensive kit where it does the most good.
f: How much energy would grinding all tails to 9 microns take?
Why does UFG liberate gold locked in pyrite?
What happened to the offsite roaster route?

f.q: What role do tellurides play in the refractory gold?
f.a:
The reference says the ore is refractory with gold locked in sulphides and tellurides. In general, gold telluride minerals dissolve much more slowly in cyanide than native gold, so some of the gold associated with them won't leach well in normal CIL residence times.

Fine grinding, high pH, extra oxygen and lead nitrate are general ways to improve telluride leaching, which fits the CIL2 design with lead nitrate at the leach feed box and high cyanide.

The reference doesn't say how much of the tails gold is in tellurides. The site metallurgist or mineralogy reports would have the gold deportment.
f: Why do gold tellurides leach slowly in cyanide?
Does lead nitrate help with tellurides?
Are tellurides recovered by flotation here?

f.q: How does gravity recovery affect what's left for CIL4?
f.a:
Gravity takes the coarse free gold out early. Two Knelson concentrators on the gravity cyclone underflow recover about 14 percent of feed gold nominal (up to 20 percent), and that concentrate goes to the intensive leach reactor and gravity electrowinning.

Coarse free gold is exactly the kind that leaches slowly in a big CIL tank, so removing it early means less coarse gold drifting through flotation into tails.

What's left for CIL4 is mostly fine, locked or sulphide associated gold, which explains the modest leach extraction. It's like pulling the big debris out with a coarse strainer before the fine filter.
f: Why is gravity placed on the cyclone underflow?
What happens to gravity concentrate after the Knelsons?
Does gravity recovery vary with ore type?

CIL4 leach gold extraction is quite low.q: What would a handover note if CIL4 extraction dropped even lower?
CIL4 leach gold extraction is quite low.a:
Facts first: what dropped, by how much, and from which data, such as tails shift composite assays, Carbon Scout gold in solution and pH and DO trends. Extraction comes from lab assays, so note the time lag.

Then what was checked: dissolved oxygen against target and oxygen plant status, cyanide analyser readings and dosing, pH excursions, throughput and feed density (residence), any tanks bypassed, carbon distribution and loading, and any change in ore or flotation performance.

Finish with actions taken and open items for the metallurgist. A good handover reads like a fault report on a machine: symptom, evidence, checks done, what's next. Remember design extraction is 38 percent; live performance can differ.

f.q: How is CIL4 extraction actually calculated each shift?
f.a:
From assays. The gold going into CIL4 (thickener underflow plus CIL3 tails) is compared with the gold leaving in the CIL4 tails solids. The difference, divided by the feed gold, is leach extraction. Solution assays tell you how much dissolved gold escaped carbon.

The CIL4 tails sample comes from a three stage sampler that takes a shift composite. Samples go to the lab, so the figure is always several hours behind the plant.

It's like calculating efficiency from fuel used and output over a shift: an averaged, after the fact number, not a live gauge.
f: Where is the CIL4 feed sample taken?
Why does lab turnaround delay the extraction figure?
How is the three stage tails sampler maintained?

f.q: Could low dissolved oxygen explain falling extraction?
f.a:
Yes, it's one of the first things to check. Gold leaching needs oxygen as well as cyanide, and sulphides in the tails consume oxygen. The CIL4 design DO target is about 15 ppm in the leach tanks.

Oxygen comes from the new PSA oxygen plant with liquid oxygen backup, and is injected by VSD oxygen pumps with flow control on both leach tanks, plus side lances on the leach tanks and first two adsorption tanks. DO analysers alarm high and low.

So check DO trends, oxygen flows and oxygen plant status. A dip in DO is like a fuel starved engine: everything else can be right and it still won't perform.
f: What happens to CIL4 if the oxygen plant trips?
How do oxygen injection pumps shear gas into slurry?
Why do sulphides consume dissolved oxygen?

f.q: Could a change in flotation explain lower CIL4 extraction?
f.a:
Yes, and it's not always bad news. If flotation starts recovering more of the easier gold, what's left in the tails is more refractory, so CIL4 extraction as a percentage falls even though overall plant recovery rises.

The reverse can happen too: a flotation upset sends more leachable gold to tails, and CIL4 extraction looks better while total recovery drops.

So judge CIL4 extraction alongside flotation recovery and tails grade, not on its own. The onstream analyser on final tails and the shift assays help. It's like judging a second stage filter by its own efficiency without looking at what the first stage let through.
f: Why can CIL4 extraction fall while plant recovery rises?
Which OSA stream shows gold lost to flotation tails?
How does ore blend change gold in the tails?

CIL4 leach gold extraction is quite low.q: How could better upstream flotation reduce the gold load into CIL4?
CIL4 leach gold extraction is quite low.a:
By moving more gold onto the high recovery route. Gold that floats goes to UFG and CIL2, where design leach extraction is about 90 percent. Gold that doesn't float goes to CIL4 at about 38 percent. So every extra percent of flotation recovery shifts gold from a poor route to a good one.

The levers are grind size (P80 about 180 microns), reagents (copper sulphate activator, PAX collector, frother), air rates, froth depth and residence time, all managed by the flotation expert system using the onstream analyser and froth cameras.

There are limits: the PDC puts maximum flotation gold recovery at about 75 percent, and more mass pull loads UFG and CIL2.

f.q: Why does finer primary grind improve flotation recovery?
f.a:
Liberation. At a finer grind, more sulphide grains break free of the gangue or are exposed enough for collector to attach and bubbles to lift them. Composite particles stuck to quartz float poorly or not at all.

The design target is P80 180 microns, with 220 microns in the high throughput case. Coarser grind lets more ore through the mills but leaves more sulphide locked up, so some gold slides to tails.

Grinding finer isn't free: it costs mill energy and throughput, and very fine particles float poorly too. Like most design choices, there's an optimum, and the metallurgist and mill operators balance it.
f: What does coarser grind at high throughput cost in recovery?
Why do very fine particles float poorly?
How is grind size measured online?

f.q: How does copper sulphate help float more pyrite carrying gold?
f.a:
Copper sulphate is an activator. In general, copper ions adsorb onto the pyrite surface and make it far more receptive to the xanthate collector (PAX), so the pyrite becomes water repellent and attaches to bubbles more reliably.

On this plant it's dosed at the SAG discharge (via the cyclone feed hopper, about 35 g/t nominal) and to the cleaner-scavenger (about 10 g/t). Dosing early gives it time to condition the pyrite before flotation.

Too much can hurt selectivity and waste reagent. Dosing is on VSD pumps with flow control to a grams per tonne or flow setpoint, and the metallurgist sets the rates.
f: Why is copper sulphate added as early as the SAG discharge?
Can too much copper sulphate hurt selectivity?
How is PAX dosing split between rougher and scavenger?

f.q: Is there a downside to pushing flotation recovery higher?
f.a:
Yes. To recover the last slow floating gold, you pull more mass, which drags more gangue into concentrate. Grade falls, and the extra tonnes load the cleaners, the concentrate thickener, the UFG mills and CIL2.

UFG 2 and 3 are designed for about 30 t/h fresh feed each, up to 46 t/h, and anything beyond UFG capacity goes to filters and stockpile. Lower grade concentrate also means more cyanide and lime per ounce in CIL2.

Recovery gains also get smaller as you push: the PDC caps flotation gold recovery at about 75 percent. The metallurgist balances this; operators run to the targets set.
f: What happens to UFG when concentrate tonnes jump?
How does lower concentrate grade affect CIL2 leaching?
Who sets the flotation grade and recovery targets?

Where does loaded carbon from CIL4 go?.q: Why is a separate loaded carbon screen needed before the transfer vessel?
Where does loaded carbon from CIL4 go?.a:
Because the loaded carbon pump moves far more slurry than carbon. It pulls about 280 m3/h of carbon and pulp from the first adsorption tank. Most of that is CIL slurry that belongs back in the tank.

The CIL4 loaded carbon screen is a horizontal vibrating screen, about 1.83 x 4.88 m, with polyurethane non pegging 0.8 x 18.5 mm slots and spray water. Carbon stays on top and leaves at about 40 percent moisture; slurry drops through and returns to CIL4.

Without it, ore solids would go into the elution column, filling the voids between carbon particles, blocking flow and contaminating the eluate. It's a strainer that separates the valuable solids from the carrier fluid.

f.q: Why does the loaded carbon screen have spray water?
f.a:
To wash adhering slurry off the carbon. Carbon coming off the tank is coated in fine ore particles and solution. Sprays rinse that off so the carbon reaching the transfer vessel is clean.

The PDC gives about 13 m3/h of spray water for this screen. The instrument list shows the spray water valve on the hypersaline water line, so process water is used here.

Clean carbon means fewer fines in the elution column, better flow through the bed and cleaner eluate. Like washing a part before inspection, a quick rinse at the right point saves trouble downstream.
f: Why is hypersaline water acceptable for these sprays?
What happens if the screen sprays block?
How is spray water flow checked on the screen?

f.q: Why does the screen deck use 0.8 mm slots?
f.a:
It's a bit finer than the 1.0 mm intertank screens. Carbon in the circuit has mostly survived 1.0 mm screens, so a 0.8 mm slot holds it back with margin while slurry at about 180 microns passes easily.

The 0.8 x 18.5 mm slotted polyurethane panels are non pegging: long, narrow slots and flexible polyurethane make it hard for near size particles to jam. Carbon finer than 0.8 mm goes back to CIL4 with the slurry rather than into elution.

On a vibrating screen, polyurethane panels also wear well and are quick to change, a bit like modular wear liners on a chute.
f: Why use polyurethane decks instead of wedge wire here?
What happens to carbon finer than 0.8 mm?
How often are screen deck panels replaced?

f.q: Why is the loaded carbon screen fitted with fire protection?
f.a:
The instrument list shows a sprinkler deluge system, a linear heat cable flame detector and a fire panel for the CIL4 loaded carbon screen (F22-SC-421), with a safety shower in the area. The reference doesn't say why.

In general, fire protection is set by the site fire risk assessment. Equipment with polyurethane panels, rubber, lubricants and motors in an enclosed building can be a fire load, and dry activated carbon is combustible.

For the actual reasoning, ask the fire systems engineer or check the fire protection basis of design. Never isolate fire detection or deluge without the proper permit.
f: Can activated carbon catch fire in a plant?
How does a linear heat cable detect a fire?
What happens to the screen area when the deluge fires?

Where does loaded carbon from CIL4 go?.q: What would happen if the loaded carbon screen blinded or failed?
Where does loaded carbon from CIL4 go?.a:
It depends on how it fails. If the deck blinds, slurry can't drain through, so wet slurry carries over with the carbon into the transfer vessel. That puts ore solids into the elution column, which slows flow, causes poor stripping and contaminates the eluate.

If the deck tears, carbon falls through with the undersize and goes back into CIL4. That's less harmful, since the carbon isn't lost, but the transfer takes longer and less carbon reaches elution.

Either way the fix is to stop the transfer, isolate the screen and repair it under the site permit system. Like a failed strainer on a hydraulic return line, you don't keep running and hope.

f.q: What happens if slurry gets into the elution column?
f.a:
In general, fine ore particles fill the gaps between carbon granules, increasing resistance to flow. Pressure drop rises, flow channels through the easier paths, and parts of the bed don't get properly washed or stripped. Gold stripping drops and barren carbon leaves with more gold.

Fines also travel with the eluate into heat exchangers and electrowinning cells, fouling surfaces and contaminating the cathode product.

It's like running a packed filter with dirty feed: pressure climbs and performance drops. Operators would treat a dirty carbon batch as something to investigate before the next strip.
f: How would high column pressure drop show on the DCS?
Can slurry fines foul the elution heat exchangers?
How is a contaminated carbon batch cleaned up?

f.q: How would a torn screen deck show up?
f.a:
Mostly by what doesn't arrive. With a torn panel, carbon falls through with the undersize and returns to CIL4, so the transfer vessel fills more slowly and the batch for elution comes up short.

Other signs are carbon visible in the undersize returning to the tank and an unexpected change in carbon concentration in the first adsorption tank on the Carbon Scout.

A visual inspection of the deck usually confirms it. The reference doesn't describe instrumentation for this, so it relies on operators doing their rounds and noticing a slow transfer.
f: How is the carbon quantity in the transfer vessel measured?
Where does the screen undersize return to?
What spares are kept for this screen?

f.q: Is the loaded carbon pump stopped if the screen trips?
f.a:
The reference doesn't spell out the interlocks for this pair. In general, plants interlock a screen's feed pump to the screen running, so if the screen stops the pump stops too and slurry doesn't flood a stationary deck. This kind of protection would be a process interlock under the site control philosophy.

To confirm for CIL4, check the interlock list or functional description for F22, or ask the control room operator.

Process interlocks can only be bypassed by named users under the site procedure, and that's not something to do to keep a transfer going.
f: Where can I find the CIL4 interlock list?
What is a process interlock compared with a critical one?
Who is allowed to bypass a process interlock?

Where does loaded carbon from CIL4 go?.q: What does the transfer vessel do between screen and elution column?
Where does loaded carbon from CIL4 go?.a:
It's a buffer and batching vessel. Carbon comes off the loaded carbon screen over several hours, but elution works in batches of a fixed size. The transfer vessel collects screened carbon until a batch is ready, then sends it to the column in one go.

The PDC gives a carbon transfer vessel capacity of about 30 t, a 15 t elution column, a transfer time of about 30 minutes and scheme water for the transfer. Carbon leaves the vessel at about 55 percent moisture.

So it decouples the continuous CIL side from the batch elution side, like an accumulator in a hydraulic circuit that lets a steady pump feed an intermittent load.

f.q: Why is the transfer vessel twice the column size?
f.a:
The PDC lists the carbon transfer vessel at 30 t against a 15 t column. It doesn't give the reasoning.

In general, extra buffer lets operators pull the next batch of loaded carbon while the current strip is still running, so CIL carbon movements don't have to wait for the column. With 2 strips per day designed, holding up to two batches gives flexibility if a strip runs long or is delayed.

It's like sizing a surge bin bigger than one load so the upstream feeder never has to stop for the downstream one. Operations can confirm how the vessel is actually used.
f: What happens if the transfer vessel fills before the column is free?
How is the carbon level in the vessel measured?
Can the column be fed without using the transfer vessel?

f.q: How is carbon moved from the vessel into the column?
f.a:
It's slurried with water and pumped or educted across. The PDC gives a transfer time of about 30 minutes, a combined carbon and water transfer flow of about 50 m3/h, and scheme water as the transfer water.

Using fresh scheme water rather than hypersaline process water keeps salt and chlorides out of the elution circuit, where they would cause corrosion and interfere with stripping.

Once carbon is in the column, excess water drains and the sequence starts with the acid wash. It's like hydraulic conveying of solids: water is the carrier and is separated once the solids arrive.
f: Why use scheme water instead of process water for transfer?
What happens to the transfer water once in the column?
How do operators confirm the full batch arrived?

f.q: Why is elution done in batches rather than continuously?
f.a:
Because split AARL is a fixed bed process with distinct steps. The carbon sits in the column while different solutions pass through in order: acid wash, rinse, caustic cyanide pre soak, elution with lean eluate, elution with scheme water, then cooling. Each step needs the whole bed to see the right solution at the right temperature.

That's naturally a batch job. The CIL4 design is 15 t per strip, 2 strips per day, 6 days a week.

Continuous elution designs exist elsewhere but are less common. Batch elution is like a heat treatment furnace cycle: load, run the programme, unload.
f: How long does a full CIL4 elution cycle take?
What limits the number of strips per day?
Are continuous elution designs used elsewhere?

Where do CIL4 tails go?.q: Why are acid wash waste and fine carbon waste routed to the same tank?
Where do CIL4 tails go?.a:
The final tails tank is the plant's single exit to the TSF, so it makes sense to collect all solid and liquid wastes there and send them out with the tailings pumps. The PDC lists its feeds as CIL4 tails, acid wash waste and fine carbon waste, about 3,164 t/h at 54.5 percent solids.

The acid wash waste is dilute HCl and rinse water. Mixed into an enormous alkaline, lime treated tails stream, it gets neutralised and diluted almost instantly.

Fine carbon is too small to stay in the CIL circuit, so it leaves with tails. Think of the tank as the main drain header: every waste stream joins the largest flow, where it's least concentrated.

f.q: Is it safe to mix acid waste with cyanide tails?
f.a:
Acid and cyanide together can release HCN gas, so it's a real hazard in general. The design manages it by sending a small, dilute acid stream into a huge alkaline tails flow, where the acid is neutralised immediately.

For scale, the PDC gives about 18 m3 of dilute acid per CIL4 acid wash (3 percent HCl) plus about 128 m3 of rinse water, against final tails of over 3,500 m3/h.
