Who on site manages pressure vessel compliance?
How does corrosion affect a pressure vessel's rating?

What acid is used for acid washing carbo.q: Why do calcium and magnesium carbonates build up as scale on carbon?
What acid is used for acid washing carbo.a:
Because the CIL slurry is full of the ingredients. Calcium comes from the lime added for pH control, and magnesium from the hypersaline process water. CIL runs alkaline, and carbonate is supplied by carbon dioxide from the air and carbonate minerals in the ore.

Under these conditions, calcium and magnesium carbonate precipitate, and the huge internal surface of activated carbon gives them plenty of places to deposit, blocking pores.

Hot elution makes it worse, since calcium carbonate becomes less soluble as temperature rises. It's exactly like scale in a kettle or on hot heat exchanger tubes. That's why every CIL4 strip starts with a dilute hydrochloric acid wash.

f.q: Why does hot alkaline elution make scaling worse?
f.a:
In general, calcium carbonate has inverse solubility: it's less soluble in hot water than cold. Heating also drives dissolved carbon dioxide out of solution, which pushes more carbonate to precipitate.

So the hot steps of elution are prime scaling conditions, both on the carbon and in the heater and heat exchangers. That's why the PDC includes antiscalant dosing into the CIL4 elution circuit and the CIL4 elution heat exchanger.

It's the same reason domestic hot water systems scale up at the heating element first.
f: Which antiscalant is dosed into the CIL4 elution circuit?
How does scale reduce heat exchanger performance?
How are elution heat exchangers descaled?

f.q: Does the saline water make carbonate scaling worse here?
f.a:
It adds to it. The hypersaline process water carries a lot of magnesium, and in alkaline conditions magnesium compounds precipitate readily. So CIL4 carbon sees more scaling potential than carbon in a fresh water plant.

The plant limits this inside elution by using scheme (fresh) water for the transfer, rinse, elution and cooling steps, so salty water isn't heated in the column.

The reference doesn't quantify scale on CIL4 carbon. The metallurgist would know from carbon assays how much calcium and magnesium the carbon typically carries.
f: Why is scheme water used throughout the elution circuit?
Does magnesium scale behave differently from calcium scale?
How much scale does typical CIL4 carbon carry?

f.q: Why is the acid wash done at ambient temperature?
f.a:
The PDC lists the CIL4 acid wash temperature as ambient. It doesn't explain why.

In general, dilute hydrochloric acid removes carbonate scale well enough at ambient temperature. Heating it would speed things up slightly but would make the acid far more corrosive to the column and pipework, and would drive off more acid fumes.

So ambient is the practical choice. Like cleaning with a cold descaler rather than a boiling one: slower, but kinder to the equipment and the operator.
f: Why is hot hydrochloric acid more corrosive?
How long does the acid soak take?
What fumes come off during acid washing?

What acid is used for acid washing carbo.q: What would you notice if acid wash concentration was too weak?
What acid is used for acid washing carbo.a:
Probably nothing on the first strip. Weak acid removes less scale, so the effect builds up slowly over many strips: carbon activity drifts down, barren carbon grade drifts up, and CIL adsorption efficiency slowly suffers.

The design is about 3 percent w/v HCl, diluted from 32 percent supply acid. CIL4 has its own dilute acid tank (about 25 m3), with acid dosing pumps started by the elution sequence.

If you suspect weak acid, check the dilution ratio and dosing flows, the dilute acid strength, and whether the spent acid leaving the column is still acidic. Like a weak coolant mix, the symptoms show up slowly.

f.q: How is 32% HCl diluted down to about 3% for the wash?
f.a:
The reference gives the pieces but not the mixing detail. HCl arrives at 32 percent, CIL4 has a separate dilute acid tank of about 25 m3, and the PDC lists about 1.5 m3 of neat acid making about 18 m3 of dilute solution per wash, pumped at about 64 m3/h.

In general, neat acid is metered into water to a set ratio, either in the tank or inline, and strength is checked by titration or a conductivity type measurement.

A golden rule for any acid dilution: acid goes into water, never water into acid, because the heat released can make it spit.
f: Why does acid always go into water, never the reverse?
How is dilute acid strength checked before a wash?
What PPE is needed around the HCl tanks?

f.q: Could the acid be too strong instead?
f.a:
Yes. In general, stronger acid doesn't clean much better but costs more, adds more chloride to the system, increases corrosion on the column and pipework, and gives off more fumes. It also raises the stakes if any cyanide is left in the bed, since more acid means more potential HCN.

The duplex stainless column is chosen to resist this service, but it still has limits.

So the target is right strength, not maximum strength. Like a cleaning solvent, more concentrated isn't always better.
f: How does duplex stainless handle stronger acid?
Does stronger acid damage the carbon itself?
What checks confirm the acid dosing ratio?

f.q: How would you check if acid washing is working?
f.a:
In general, a few ways. Compare carbon activity tests before and after acid washing. Assay carbon for calcium and magnesium over time. Watch the pH of the spent acid leaving the column: if it comes out neutral, the acid was all used up and probably didn't remove all the scale.

Trends in barren carbon grade and CIL4 adsorption efficiency also help, though many things affect those.

The reference doesn't describe the site's carbon testing routine. The metallurgist or lab would have the carbon activity data.
f: What does the pH of spent acid tell you?
How is calcium on carbon measured?
How often is carbon activity tested?

What acid is used for acid washing carbo.q: How is the acid waste stream handled safely afterward?
What acid is used for acid washing carbo.a:
Per the PDC, acid wash waste and the acid rinse water go to the final tails tank. There they mix into a very large alkaline, lime treated tailings stream, so the acid is neutralised and diluted almost instantly and leaves with the tails to the TSF.

The safety principle is that acid never meets concentrated cyanide in a confined space. Routing is controlled by the elution sequence, which starts the HCl dosing pumps and aligns the valves only during the acid steps.

Don't reroute acid waste or open drains during an acid wash without authorisation. Acid and cyanide meeting in the wrong place can release HCN gas.

f.q: Why does the acid waste go to final tails and not CIL4?
f.a:
The reference doesn't explain it, but the logic is sound in general. CIL4 tanks hold cyanide at around pH 9. Dumping acid into a tank would locally drop pH and release HCN right where people work, and would waste lime.

The final tails tank takes the whole tailings flow on its way out of the plant. Acid added there is diluted into thousands of cubic metres per hour of alkaline slurry and is gone within minutes.

It's the same logic as discharging a small hot stream into a large cold one rather than into a sensitive process tank.
f: How far is the final tails tank from the elution area?
What lines carry acid waste to the tails tank?
Could acid waste upset tails pipeline pH?

f.q: What hazards does hydrochloric acid bring to the elution area?
f.a:
In general: it's corrosive to skin and eyes, gives off irritating HCl fumes, and reacts with cyanide to release HCN gas. It also reacts with caustic, releasing heat. Concentrated acid at 32 percent is far more hazardous than the 3 percent dilute wash.

That's why there are safety showers and eyewash stations, bunded storage, and procedures for deliveries and handling. The instrument list shows safety showers with flow switches around the elution area.

Wear the PPE the site specifies for acid handling, and know where the nearest safety shower is before you start.
f: Where are the safety showers near the acid tanks?
Why must acid and cyanide lines never be cross connected?
How are HCl spills cleaned up?

f.q: Why does the elution sequence start the acid pumps?
f.a:
The control philosophy says the HCl dosing pumps (DOL) are started by the elution sequences. The reference doesn't spell out why, but in general it ties acid flow to the right step with the right valves confirmed in position.

That means acid only flows when the column is lined up for the acid wash and the waste path is open to final tails. Sequence steps confirm valve feedback within a transition time or the sequence pauses.

It's an engineered way of preventing human error, like a machine that won't start until its guards are confirmed closed.
f: Can the acid pumps be run manually outside a sequence?
What happens if the acid pump fails mid wash?
How does the sequence confirm the valves are aligned?

The CIL4 elution uses a single column fo.q: Why is duplex stainless steel needed for this combined duty?
The CIL4 elution uses a single column fo.a:
Because the column sees two very different aggressive environments. During the acid wash it's filled with dilute hydrochloric acid, which is full of chlorides. During elution it holds hot caustic cyanide solution at about 130 degrees C under about 340 kPa. Salt carryover from the hypersaline circuit adds more chlorides.

Ordinary austenitic stainless like 316 is vulnerable to chloride pitting and chloride stress corrosion cracking, especially when hot. Duplex SAF2205, with a mixed ferrite and austenite structure plus molybdenum, resists both far better and is stronger, so walls can be thinner.

It's the same reason duplex is common in seawater heat exchangers: it's the step up for hot, salty service.

f.q: What is chloride stress corrosion cracking?
f.a:
In general, it's cracking that happens when three things combine: tensile stress (from pressure or welding), chlorides, and elevated temperature, typically above about 60 degrees C. Austenitic stainless steels like 304 and 316 are particularly prone.

Cracks are fine, branching and can grow through the wall with little visible corrosion, so failure can be sudden.

Duplex grades like 2205 resist it much better thanks to their ferrite content. It's a key consideration for any hot, pressurised stainless equipment on a plant running hypersaline water.
f: Why does temperature make chloride cracking worse?
How is stress corrosion cracking detected in service?
Is 2205 completely immune to chloride cracking?

f.q: What do the existing acid wash columns use instead?
f.a:
The reference says the existing concentrate elution circuits have separate acid wash columns but doesn't give their material of construction.

In general, separate acid wash columns that never see hot cyanide are often made from rubber lined or plastic lined steel or fibreglass, since they only need to resist ambient dilute acid. The elution columns that run hot can then be ordinary stainless.

Combining both duties in one vessel removes that option, which is why CIL4 needed a material that handles both. Check the existing elution drawings or ask the area maintenance planner for the actual materials.
f: Why do older circuits use separate acid wash columns?
How long do rubber linings last in acid service?
Which elution circuits strip CIL3 carbon?

f.q: Why is welding duplex stainless more demanding?
f.a:
In general, duplex depends on keeping roughly equal amounts of ferrite and austenite. Too much or too little heat input during welding upsets that balance, and the weld or heat affected zone can lose corrosion resistance or toughness. Specific filler metals, controlled heat input and qualified procedures are needed.

So repairs to a duplex column aren't a job for any welder with any rod. They need a qualified procedure, a qualified welder and usually inspection afterwards.

The area maintenance planner would arrange specialist welding if the column ever needs repair.
f: Who is qualified to weld repairs on the column?
What inspections follow a weld repair?
Can duplex be welded to ordinary stainless?

The CIL4 elution uses a single column fo.q: What risk does combining both duties in one column create versus two?
The CIL4 elution uses a single column fo.a:
The main one is that acid and cyanide now share a vessel. The acid must be thoroughly rinsed out before the caustic cyanide pre soak, or HCN can form in the column. A valve or sequence error has bigger consequences than with separate columns.

There's also a single point of failure. With one column, if it's down for repair, CIL4 has neither acid washing nor elution.

And the column is tied up for the acid steps (about 3.3 hours on design) as well as elution, lengthening each strip. The benefits are lower capital cost, a smaller footprint and fewer carbon transfers, meaning less carbon breakage.

f.q: How does the sequence prevent acid meeting cyanide in the column?
f.a:
By order and confirmation. The design sequence runs acid wash, then a water rinse of about 4 bed volumes over 120 minutes, and only then the caustic cyanide pre soak. The general sequence philosophy has each step confirm feedback, such as valve positions, within a transition time, or the sequence pauses.

The reference doesn't list the specific CIL4 elution interlocks or rinse end point checks, so check the F22 functional description.

The principle is like a purge cycle on a burner: you prove the previous step finished before allowing the next.
f: What valve feedback does the elution sequence check?
What happens if a valve fails to close mid sequence?
How is the rinse end point confirmed?

f.q: What happens to CIL4 if the single column is out of service?
f.a:
Stripping stops. Loaded carbon can still be pulled into the 30 t transfer vessel for a while, but once that's full, carbon can't leave CIL4. Loading on carbon in the first adsorption tank climbs, adsorption slows, and regenerated carbon stops returning to the last tank.

The reference doesn't say whether CIL4 carbon could be stripped in the existing concentrate elution circuits as a contingency.

A short outage is manageable; a long one hits adsorption efficiency. It's like losing the only filter press on a circuit: upstream can buffer for a while, then performance drops.
f: Could CIL4 carbon be stripped in the existing elution circuits?
How long can CIL4 run without elution?
What maintenance is planned on the column?

f.q: Why did the design choose one combined column?
f.a:
The PDC records the owner's choice of a single column for acid wash and elution but doesn't give reasons.

In general, the benefits are lower capital cost (one vessel, one set of valves and structure), a smaller footprint, and fewer carbon transfers. Every transfer between vessels breaks some carbon into fines, so cutting one out reduces carbon loss.

The cost is the special material, duplex SAF2205, and a longer cycle per strip. The project team that made the decision could explain the trade off in detail.
f: Do fewer carbon transfers really reduce carbon breakage?
How does footprint affect the elution building layout?
Was a separate acid column ever considered for CIL4?

The CIL4 elution uses a single column fo.q: How does using one column instead of two change strip cycle time?
The CIL4 elution uses a single column fo.a:
It makes each strip longer. With a separate acid wash column, the next batch can be acid washed while the current batch is being eluted, so the steps overlap. With one combined column, the acid steps and elution happen one after the other in the same vessel.

On CIL4 design figures, the acid steps take about 197 minutes (3.3 hours) and the elution steps about 330 minutes (5.5 hours). With transfers in and out, the total is about 10.2 hours per strip.

The design still achieves 2 strips per day, but with less spare time. It's like a single station machine doing two operations back to back instead of two machines working in parallel.

f.q: How much of the 10.2 hour cycle is acid washing?
f.a:
About a third. On PDC figures, the acid steps add up to about 197 minutes: acid injection about 17 minutes, acid soak about 60 minutes, and the acid water rinse about 120 minutes. That's about 3.3 hours of the roughly 10.2 hour cycle.

The rinse is the biggest chunk, because enough water must pass to clear the acid before the caustic cyanide pre soak.

These are design times. Any change to them is a metallurgist's decision, since a shorter rinse risks acid meeting cyanide.
f: Could the acid soak be shortened without losing performance?
Why is the acid injection only 17 minutes?
How long does carbon transfer out take?

f.q: Is there spare capacity for more strips per day?
f.a:
Not much. Two strips at about 10.2 hours is about 20.4 hours, leaving about 3.6 hours a day on design figures. That's for delays, not for a third strip.

The design schedule is 6 days a week, so the seventh day is the main reserve to catch up lost strips.

If CIL4 ever needs more carbon stripped, it would need changes such as longer operating weeks, shorter steps proven by testwork, or more equipment. That's a metallurgy and projects question, not something operations can just turn up.
f: Could elution run seven days a week if needed?
What would a third strip per day require?
How does strip timing affect carbon loading?

f.q: How do the existing concentrate circuits schedule acid wash and elution?
f.a:
The existing concentrate elution has two circuits, each with its own acid wash column and elution column, at about 11 t of carbon per strip. The PDC says they can average about 1.5 strips per column per day, within an operating envelope of 8 to 24 strips per week.

With separate acid wash columns, the next batch can be acid washed while elution runs, so the steps overlap.

These circuits strip the CIL3 carbon, which loads far higher (about 4,490 g/t design) than CIL4 carbon.
f: Why are the existing columns 11 t versus 15 t for CIL4?
How is carbon moved between acid and elution columns?
How long does CIL3 carbon stay in circuit before stripping?

How is the CIL4 elution solution heated?.q: Why is LPG chosen over electric heating for elution?
How is the CIL4 elution solution heated?.a:
The reference doesn't state the reason. What it does show is that LPG is already used widely on site: the existing elution burners, the existing regeneration kilns, the regenerative thermal oxidiser and the goldroom smelting furnace all run on it, and the main LPG storage vessel was upgraded to about 161 kL for Stage 2.

In general, elution heating is a large, intermittent thermal load. The CIL4 heater uses about 708 L/h of LPG at steady state, roughly 5 MW of heat. Doing that electrically would need a lot of extra electrical capacity, and the site already manages large electrical loads carefully.

Interestingly, the new CIL4 regeneration kiln is electric, so the choice was made case by case.

f.q: How much heat does the CIL4 elution heater put in?
f.a:
The PDC gives vendor LPG consumption of about 823 L/h during preheat and about 708 L/h at steady state. Using a general figure of roughly 25 MJ per litre for propane, steady state is about 17,700 MJ/h, or roughly 5 MW of heat input.

Preheat uses more because the circuit, column and solution all start cold.

That's my estimate from design figures. Actual consumption depends on heat exchanger condition, flows and ambient temperature. Like a boiler, fuel per strip is a good health indicator over time.
f: How much heat do the elution heat exchangers recover?
Why is preheat LPG use higher than steady state?
How is LPG consumption tracked per strip?

f.q: How long can the plant run on the LPG storage?
f.a:
The PDC gives one upgraded LPG storage vessel of about 161 kL, with a calculated residence of about 5.3 days. It notes the owner confirmed and accepted that this doesn't achieve 7 days.

That storage serves the existing elution burners, the CIL4 elution heater, the existing regeneration kilns and the regenerative thermal oxidiser. The goldroom smelting furnace has its own dedicated LPG storage.

So LPG deliveries need to keep coming regularly. A delay of a few days would start to affect elution and regeneration.
f: What uses LPG besides the CIL4 elution heater?
What happens if LPG deliveries are delayed?
Who orders LPG deliveries for site?

f.q: Why is the CIL4 regen kiln electric if elution uses LPG?
f.a:
The PDC lists the CIL4 carbon regeneration kiln as horizontal, indirect fired, electric, while the existing kilns are LPG fired. It doesn't explain the choice.

In general, an indirect electric kiln gives precise zone temperature control and no combustion gases mixing with the off gas from the carbon. That keeps the off gas volume small, which makes mercury capture easier and cheaper, and that's important here because mercury abatement must run with the kiln.

The elution heater is a different duty: heating a liquid stream, which LPG does well.
f: Why does an indirect kiln make mercury capture easier?
What do the existing regen kilns burn?
How much power does the CIL4 kiln draw?

How is the CIL4 elution solution heated?.q: What would you check first if eluate temperature wasn't reaching target?
How is the CIL4 elution solution heated?.a:
Start with the heater. Is the burner actually firing, or has the burner management system tripped or locked out? Is LPG supply pressure and storage level normal? Is the temperature controller in automatic with a sensible output?

Then the heat transfer: scale in the elution heat exchangers cuts duty, which is why antiscalant is dosed there. Check eluate flow too, because more flow than the design 2 bed volumes per hour means less temperature rise for the same heat.

Finally, check the temperature transmitter against another reading. Don't keep resetting a BMS lockout; it's a safety system, and repeated trips need investigation by a qualified person.

f.q: What does a burner management system do on the heater?
f.a:
In general, a burner management system runs the burner safely through its whole cycle. It purges the combustion chamber before ignition, proves the pilot and main flame, supervises the flame continuously, and shuts the gas valves if the flame fails or a limit is exceeded, such as gas pressure or high temperature.

After certain trips it locks out and needs a manual reset once the cause is found.

The control philosophy shows the CIL4 heater with a burner management system and a vendor PLC for the critical gas train safety functions. Treat it like a boiler's safety controls: never bypass it.
f: Why must a burner be purged before ignition?
What causes a burner flame failure trip?
Who can reset a BMS lockout?

f.q: How does scale in the heat exchangers show up?
f.a:
In general, scale acts as insulation on the heat transfer surface. Symptoms are a rising gap between heating medium and eluate temperatures, longer heat up times, more LPG burned for the same eluate temperature, and sometimes higher pressure drop.

The PDC includes antiscalant dosing to both the CIL4 elution circuit and its heat exchanger to slow this down.

It's exactly like a fouled cooler on a gearbox lube system: it still works, just less well each week, until it's cleaned.
f: How is antiscalant dosing checked on the elution circuit?
How often are elution heat exchangers cleaned?
Can scale cause hot spots in the heater coil?

f.q: Why does flow rate affect the eluate temperature?
f.a:
Heat balance. In general, the temperature rise equals the heat input divided by mass flow times specific heat. If the heater is near its maximum firing, pushing more flow through means each litre gets less heat, so the outlet temperature falls.

The CIL4 design flow is about 2 bed volumes per hour, around 63.8 m3/h. If flow drifts above that, the heater may not keep up.

It's the same as a shower water heater: turn the flow up and the water runs cooler.
f: What sets the 2 BV/h elution flow?
How is elution flow measured and controlled?
What happens to stripping at higher flow?

How is the CIL4 elution solution heated?.q: What safety systems protect an LPG heater package on site?
How is the CIL4 elution solution heated?.a:
The plant reference mentions a burner management system on the CIL4 LPG heater, and the Stage 2 control philosophy lists vendor PLC control for the critical safety systems relating to the gas train.

In general, an LPG fired heater package also includes flame detection, a gas train with double block and bleed shutoff valves, low and high gas pressure switches, high temperature limits, a purge before ignition, and an emergency shutdown. The surrounding area is usually hazardous area rated, often with gas detection.

The details are in the vendor manual and P&IDs. Never bypass a heater safety function, and leave fault finding on the gas train to qualified gas fitters.

f.q: What is a double block and bleed valve arrangement?
f.a:
In general, it's two shutoff valves in series on the gas line, with a small vent valve between them. When the burner is off, both shutoff valves close and the vent opens, so any gas leaking past the first valve is vented safely instead of building up against the second.

It's a standard safety arrangement on gas trains, because a single valve can leak.

Think of it like two isolations with a proven zero energy point between them, the same principle you use when isolating a hydraulic system for work.
f: Why vent the space between two shutoff valves?
How are gas train valves leak tested?
Who maintains the gas train?

f.q: Why is the gas train on its own vendor PLC?
f.a:
The Stage 2 control philosophy lists the elution heater with vendor PLC control for the critical safety systems relating to the gas train. It doesn't give the reasoning.

In general, burner safety functions are kept on a dedicated, certified controller so they're independent of the main DCS. A DCS fault, change or software error can't then stop the burner shutting down safely.

The DCS still sees status and alarms and can start or stop the heater within the sequence. It's like a machine safety relay that works no matter what the main PLC is doing.
f: What does the DCS see from the heater PLC?
Can the DCS override the heater safety system?
How are heater safety functions proof tested?

f.q: Why is an LPG leak treated so seriously?
f.a:
In general, LPG is heavier than air, so a leak doesn't disperse upward like natural gas. It flows along the ground and collects in low points: pits, trenches, drains and sumps. A small leak can build into a large explosive cloud.

LPG is odorised so leaks can be smelled, but you shouldn't rely on smell alone. Areas around LPG equipment are classified as hazardous areas, which controls what electrical equipment and ignition sources are allowed.

If you smell gas, move away, don't operate switches, and raise the alarm under the site procedure.
f: Where would leaking LPG collect around the heater?
What gas detection is fitted near the LPG systems?
What is hazardous area zoning?

What happens to barren (stripped) carbon.q: Why does a low oxygen atmosphere matter during thermal reactivation?
What happens to barren (stripped) carbon.a:
Because carbon burns. At regeneration temperatures of about 650 to 750 degrees C, activated carbon exposed to air would simply combust, and you'd lose the carbon you're trying to restore.

The goal is to drive off and break down organic foulants, like oils, flotation reagents and other organics, and reopen the pores, without burning the carbon itself. Wet carbon generates steam inside the kiln, which helps gasify the foulants while keeping oxygen low.

The CIL4 kiln is indirect fired and electric, so heat comes through the tube wall and no combustion gases contact the carbon. It's like heat treating steel in a controlled atmosphere furnace to stop it scaling.

f.q: What role does steam play inside the regen kiln?
f.a:
In general, carbon goes into the kiln wet, and that moisture turns to steam as it heats up. The steam displaces air, keeping oxygen low, and at high temperature it reacts with the organic deposits and char, gasifying them and reopening pores.

The PDC gives CIL4 kiln dewatering screen oversize moisture of about 40 percent nominal, up to 60 percent maximum.

Too much water costs energy and increases off gas volume. Like steam cleaning, the right amount does the job; too much floods it.
f: Why does carbon enter the kiln wet?
Can too much moisture overload the kiln?
How is kiln feed moisture controlled?

f.q: What does indirect firing mean for the CIL4 kiln?
f.a:
The PDC lists the CIL4 kiln as horizontal, indirect fired and electric. In general, that means the carbon travels through a rotating tube heated from outside, here by electric elements. Heat passes through the tube wall to the carbon.

The carbon never contacts flames or combustion gases, so the atmosphere inside is just steam and gases from the carbon. That makes temperature and atmosphere easier to control and keeps off gas volume small for mercury capture.

It's like an electric oven versus a wood fire: cleaner, more controllable heat.
f: How long do electric heating elements last in a kiln?
How is heat transferred through the kiln tube?
What happens if one heating zone fails?

f.q: What happens if air leaks into the kiln?
f.a:
In general, extra oxygen lets some carbon burn. You lose carbon, the burning carbon can overheat locally, and carbon weakened by partial burning breaks more easily into fines later.

Air leaks usually come in at the seals where the rotating tube meets the fixed feed and discharge ends, or through worn feeders.

The reference doesn't describe kiln seal arrangements for the Lochhead package. The area maintenance planner and vendor manual would cover seal inspection and replacement.
f: Where do air leaks typically occur on a rotary kiln?
How would carbon burning show on kiln trends?
How are kiln seals inspected?

What happens to barren (stripped) carbon.q: What would happen if the sizing screen after the kiln was bypassed?
What happens to barren (stripped) carbon.a:
Fine carbon would go straight back into CIL4. Regenerated carbon returns to the last tank, and any pieces small enough to pass the 1.0 mm intertank screens would leave with the slurry, straight to final tails.

Those fines adsorb gold while they're in the tank, so they take gold to the TSF as well as being lost carbon. Near size pieces just above 1 mm would soon wear down and escape too.

The CIL4 carbon sizing screen uses 1.25 x 18.5 mm polyurethane apertures to remove this material before it re enters the circuit. Bypassing it is like skipping the final filter on a lube system: dirt goes where you least want it.

f.q: Why is the sizing screen aperture 1.25 mm?
f.a:
The PDC gives the CIL4 carbon sizing screen apertures as 1.25 x 18.5 mm. It doesn't explain the choice, but in general it makes sense to size slightly coarser than the 1.0 mm intertank screens.

Carbon just above 1 mm would wear below 1 mm within a few transfers and slip through the intertank screens. Removing it at 1.25 mm gives a margin, so what goes back into CIL4 is robust enough to stay in the circuit for a while.

It's like replacing a part slightly before it reaches its wear limit rather than letting it fail in service.
f: What fraction of carbon reports to sizing screen undersize?
Where does the sizing screen undersize go?
How is the sizing screen deck inspected?

f.q: Where does the regenerated carbon go after the sizing screen?
f.a:
Back to the last CIL4 tank. The control philosophy says barren carbon returns to the last tank via the CIL4 carbon sizing screen, completing the loop.

Before that, carbon from the kiln drops into a quench tank (at least about 20 m3, filled with scheme water) and is pumped by the barren carbon pump to the sizing screen. The PDC notes carbon transfer from the quench is completed with raw water.

It enters the tank with the leanest solution, which suits fresh, active carbon best, just like counterflow in a heat exchanger.
f: Why is carbon quenched before screening?
How is regenerated carbon pumped back to CIL4?
What is the quench tank filled with?

f.q: Do fine carbon particles still load gold?
f.a:
Yes, and quickly. In general, small particles have short diffusion paths and lots of outer surface relative to their mass, so fine carbon picks up gold fast.

The problem is that fines don't stay put. They move with the slurry through the screens and leave CIL4 loaded with gold. In effect they act as a gold leak to tails.

That's why the design removes fines at the sizing screen and why carbon handling aims to minimise breakage. Fine carbon waste that is collected goes to the final tails tank.
f: Why do fine carbon particles load gold so quickly?
Can fine carbon carry gold out through the tails?
How is fine carbon measured in CIL4 tails?

What happens to barren (stripped) carbon.q: How is kiln temperature controlled to avoid damaging the carbon?
What happens to barren (stripped) carbon.a:
The reference gives the targets but not the loop details. The CIL4 kiln is a Lochhead package, horizontal and indirect electric fired, with a screw feeder and its own vendor PLC working within an overall regeneration sequence. The PDC gives an operating temperature of about 650 to 750 degrees C (750 design), a nominal capacity of about 1,500 kg/h, and about 20 hours per batch of 30 t.

In general, kilns like this control zone temperatures with thermocouples adjusting heating power, and control residence by feed rate and tube rotation speed.

Too hot and the carbon burns and weakens; too cool and organics aren't removed. The vendor manual and kiln operator have the details.

f.q: Why is the target temperature range 650 to 750 C?
f.a:
The PDC gives a CIL4 kiln operating range of about 650 to 750 degrees C with 750 as the design temperature. It doesn't explain the range.

In general, below about 650 degrees C organic foulants aren't fully removed and activity isn't restored. Much above the range, carbon starts to burn and its structure weakens, so it loses mass and breaks into fines more easily.

The existing kilns also run at about 750 degrees C. It's like a tempering range for steel: a window where the job gets done without damaging the part.
f: What happens to carbon activity if the kiln runs too hot?
How is regenerated carbon activity tested?
Does kiln temperature affect mercury removal?

f.q: How does the screw feeder rate affect regeneration?
f.a:
The screw feeder sets how fast carbon enters the kiln, and so how long each particle spends at temperature. The PDC gives a nominal capacity of about 1,500 kg/h, which works out to about 20 hours for a 30 t batch.

In general, feeding too fast means carbon passes through before it's fully heated and cleaned; too slow wastes energy and risks over burning. The kiln feed hopper holds about 30 t, two strips' worth.

It's like feed rate on a heat treatment conveyor furnace: the speed is part of the recipe, not just throughput.
f: What sets the kiln feed rate setpoint?
What happens if the kiln feed hopper runs empty?
How long does carbon stay in the hot zone?

f.q: What does the regeneration sequence coordinate?
f.a:
According to the control philosophy, barren carbon is educted from the column to the regeneration kiln dewatering screen and kiln feed hopper. The kiln package, with its screw feeder and vendor PLC, runs within an overall regeneration sequence along with the quench tank and the barren carbon pump. The mercury abatement system must run with the kiln.

So the sequence links feed, kiln, quench and return so carbon flows smoothly and nothing runs that shouldn't.

It's like a group start on a conveyor line: downstream equipment proves it's running before upstream equipment feeds it.
f: Why must mercury abatement run whenever the kiln runs?
What happens if the barren carbon pump trips?
How is the kiln shut down safely?

Why does the carbon regeneration kiln of.q: Why does mercury preferentially load onto activated carbon?
Why does the carbon regeneration kiln of.a:
Because it behaves a lot like gold in cyanide solution. In general, mercury dissolves in the leach as mercury cyanide complexes, and activated carbon adsorbs those complexes along with the gold cyanide complex. Carbon's huge internal surface area holds a lot of them.

Elution strips some of the mercury, but some stays on the carbon. The PDC gives CIL4 barren carbon mercury of about 37 g/t nominal (range 20 to 72) going to the kiln. At regeneration temperatures mercury is volatile, so it leaves the carbon as vapour in the kiln off gas, and regenerated carbon comes out at about 1.3 ppm.

So the kiln is where the mercury ends up, and that's why its off gas needs treating.

f.q: Where does the mercury on carbon come from in the first place?
f.a:
From the ore. Goldfields ores carry trace mercury, which dissolves in cyanide leaching and travels with the gold through adsorption and elution.

The reference doesn't give the mercury grade of the plant feed. It does give mercury levels on carbon: about 124 ppm on CIL3 loaded carbon and 79 ppm on CIL3 barren carbon for the existing circuit, and about 37 g/t nominal on CIL4 barren carbon.

So even tiny amounts in the ore concentrate onto the carbon, much like contaminants concentrating in a lube oil filter over time.
f: Does mercury also report to the gravity concentrate?
How much mercury is in the plant feed?
Does mercury leave the plant in the tails too?

f.q: Does mercury come off during elution as well as in the kiln?
f.a:
Yes, partly. In general, some mercury strips off the carbon with the gold, travels in the pregnant eluate to electrowinning, and deposits on the cathodes with the gold.

That's why the goldroom has a mercury retort oven. The PDC lists an electric retort used about two days a week, which heats the gold sludge to distil off mercury before smelting.

The mercury left on carbon after elution then comes off in the kiln. So mercury has two exits: the goldroom retort and the kiln off gas system.
f: What does the goldroom mercury retort do?
Why must mercury be removed before smelting?
How is recovered mercury stored and disposed of?

f.q: How much mercury does the CIL4 kiln abatement have to capture?
f.a:
The PDC sets a design mercury load of about 108 g/h, based on 72 g/t mercury on barren carbon at 1,500 kg/h of carbon through the kiln. The mercury recovery target is above 92 percent.

The stack emission limit is 0.20 ppmv mercury, with the vendor system calculated at about 0.027 ppmv. VOC is limited to 3.2 ppmv. The stack is about 35 m high.

These are design and permit values. Actual emissions are monitored, and the environmental team tracks compliance.
f: How is stack mercury emission measured?
What happens if the stack limit is exceeded?
Why is the kiln stack 35 m tall?

Why does the carbon regeneration kiln of.q: What would an alarm on the mercury abatement system mean for the kiln?
Why does the carbon regeneration kiln of.a:
The control philosophy says the mercury abatement system must run with the kiln. So an abatement fault is expected to stop or prevent kiln operation. The exact interlocks are in the regeneration functional description.

If the kiln stops, regeneration stops. Barren carbon builds up in the kiln feed hopper, and regenerated carbon stops returning to the last CIL4 tank. Elution can continue for a while until the hopper fills.

The response is to fix the abatement fault, not to run the kiln without it, which would release mercury vapour. Report it to the control room and follow the alarm response.

f.q: What equipment makes up the CIL4 mercury abatement train?
f.a:
The PDC lists, in order: a carbon fines knock out box, a kiln off gas condenser (shell and tube, cooled with scheme water), a kiln mist eliminator, a small kiln duct heater (about 7.5 kW), a kiln adsorption vessel with a bed of 3 mm Mersorb HT carbon, a kiln exhaust fan (about 3,003 Am3/h, 12.5 kW) and a discharge stack about 35 m high.

Antiscalant is dosed into the mercury abatement system at about 61 ml/min.

The logic is to remove dust, condense and drop out moisture, reheat slightly so the gas is dry, then capture mercury on the adsorbent bed.
f: Why is the off gas reheated before the adsorption vessel?
How often is the adsorption bed carbon replaced?
What does the condenser do with captured mercury?

f.q: What happens to CIL4 while the kiln is stopped?
f.a:
Barren carbon from elution goes to the kiln feed hopper, which the PDC sizes at about 30 t, 200 percent of a full column. So it can hold about two strips' worth before elution has to stop too.

Meanwhile regenerated carbon stops returning to the last CIL4 tank, so carbon there gradually runs short. Fresh carbon can be added through the hoist, bag splitter and quench hopper.

The reference doesn't say whether unregenerated barren carbon can be returned to CIL4 as a contingency. That's an operations and metallurgy decision.
f: How many strips can the kiln feed hopper hold?
Can unregenerated carbon go straight back to CIL4?
How is fresh carbon added if the kiln is down?

f.q: Why is mercury exposure such a concern for people?
f.a:
In general, mercury vapour is invisible and odourless, and it's absorbed through the lungs. Long term exposure damages the nervous system and kidneys, and effects can build up over time.

Around kilns, retorts, the goldroom and their off gas systems, exposure is controlled by engineering (enclosure, extraction, abatement), monitoring, PPE and hygiene, and often health monitoring.

Opening mercury contaminated equipment needs special precautions. Follow the site mercury management procedure and ask the hygienist or area supervisor before working on these systems.
f: How is mercury vapour monitored in the work area?
What PPE protects against mercury vapour?
Are workers tested for mercury exposure?

Why does the carbon regeneration kiln of.q: How is the regenerative thermal oxidiser kept effective over time?
Why does the carbon regeneration kiln of.a:
First a clarification: in the PDC, the regenerative thermal oxidiser belongs to the existing brownfields kiln off gas train, along with a venturi scrubber, packed bed scrubber, mist eliminator and duty/standby carbon filters. It's LPG fired at about 1,580 MJ/h. The new CIL4 kiln train uses a condenser and adsorption vessel and doesn't list an RTO.

The reference doesn't describe RTO maintenance. In general, effectiveness depends on keeping the ceramic heat storage media clean (dust and salts can plug it), the flow switching valves sealing properly, and the burner holding temperature.

The upstream scrubbers protect the RTO by removing dust and droplets. The area maintenance planner has the actual routine.

f.q: How does a regenerative thermal oxidiser destroy organics?
f.a:
In general, it heats the off gas to a high temperature, typically around 800 degrees C or more, where organic compounds oxidise to carbon dioxide and water.

To save fuel, it has beds of ceramic media. Hot gas leaving the combustion chamber heats one bed, while incoming cold gas is preheated by another bed that was heated in the previous cycle. Valves switch the flow direction every few minutes, so heat is recycled and fuel use is low.

It's like a regenerative heat exchanger on a glass furnace, swapping hot and cold sides to store and return heat.
f: Why does an RTO switch flow direction?
What temperature does an RTO operate at?
How much LPG does the RTO use?

f.q: Why does the off gas pass a scrubber before the RTO?
f.a:
The PDC lists the existing train as a venturi scrubber, a packed bed wet scrubber and a mist eliminator, then the RTO and duty/standby carbon filters. The venturi is designed for a dust load of about 375 mg/Nm3 and uses process water.

In general, dust and droplets would foul the RTO's ceramic media and valves, so scrubbing first protects it. The scrubbers also capture some mercury and cool the gas, and the carbon filters at the end catch remaining mercury.

It's like putting a pre filter ahead of an expensive fine filter to make it last.
f: What water does the venturi scrubber use?
Why are the existing carbon filters duty/standby?
What happens to the dust caught in the venturi scrubber?

f.q: What are the stack emission limits for the kiln off gas?
f.a:
The PDC gives stack emission limits of 0.20 ppmv for mercury and 3.2 ppmv for VOC, for both the existing kiln off gas system and the new CIL4 kiln system. For CIL4 the mercury limit is also stated as about 1,800 micrograms per cubic metre at standard conditions.

These are permit style limits that the abatement equipment is designed to meet with margin.

Actual stack testing and reporting are handled by the site environmental team. If an alarm suggests the limits are at risk, follow the alarm response and report it.
f: Who reports stack emissions to the regulator?
How is VOC in the stack measured?
What happens to the kiln if emissions exceed limits?

What happens in the goldroom?.q: Why does electrowinning deposit gold onto cathodes rather than in solution?
What happens in the goldroom?.a:
Because electricity drives the reaction. In general, a DC current passes between anodes and cathodes in the cell. At the cathode, gold cyanide ions pick up electrons and turn back into metallic gold, which deposits on the cathode surface. At the anode, oxygen is given off.

The CIL4 design uses two split clean in place cells with 1 x 1 m stainless steel 316 mesh cathodes, 11 per cell, four 2,500 A rectifiers and about 10 hours of electrowinning, aiming for barren solution below 5 ppm gold from pregnant eluate of about 52.6 g/m3.

It's electroplating in reverse thinking: instead of coating a part, you're harvesting the metal from solution.

f.q: Why are the cathodes made of stainless steel mesh?
f.a:
In general, mesh gives a lot of surface area for its size and lets solution flow through rather than just past it, so gold ions reach a cathode surface quickly. Stainless steel conducts well, resists the caustic cyanide solution and is reusable.

Gold deposits as a loose sludge on the mesh that can be washed off. The PDC specifies stainless steel 316 mesh cathodes for CIL4 EW.

It's like a fin tube heat exchanger: more surface in the same space means more transfer per pass.
f: How does clean in place remove gold from the cathodes?
Why is high cathode surface area important?
How often are cathodes washed down?

f.q: What does a clean in place electrowinning cell mean?
f.a:
The PDC specifies clean in place cells for CIL4. In general, that means gold sludge is washed off the cathodes inside the cell with sprays, rather than lifting cathodes out and washing them elsewhere. The sludge drains to a collection point and goes on to filtering.

It saves labour, reduces handling of gold, which helps security, and keeps operators away from caustic cyanide solution.

It's like a self cleaning filter that backwashes in place instead of being removed for cleaning.
f: Where does the washed off gold sludge go?
Why is clean in place more secure than pulling cathodes?
How long does a cell wash take?

f.q: Why does eluate recirculate through the cells many times?
f.a:
Because each pass only takes out part of the gold. The PDC gives about 5.6 passes of the 160 m3 pregnant eluate volume over about 10 hours, at about 90 m3/h total through the cells.

In general, the deposition rate falls as gold concentration drops, so recirculating lets the cells keep pulling gold until the solution is barren, targeting below 5 ppm.

Barren eluate is then pumped back to the leach. It's like recirculating oil through a filter cart until it reaches the target cleanliness.
f: What happens to barren eluate after electrowinning?
Why is the target barren grade below 5 ppm?
How is eluate gold grade monitored during EW?

What happens in the goldroom?.q: What would you check if cathode gold deposits looked unusually thin?
What happens in the goldroom?.a:
Start with whether the gold was there to deposit. A thin deposit often means a weak pregnant eluate from a poor strip: check eluate temperature, flows and the pre soak. Design pregnant eluate is about 52.6 g/m3.

Then check the electrowinning itself: rectifier current and voltage, electrical connections to anodes and cathodes, solution flow through each cell, eluate temperature and conductivity, and any shorts between anodes and cathodes.

Finally compare barren solution grade with the target of below 5 ppm. If barren is high, the cells aren't pulling gold out; if it's low, there just wasn't much gold. Like diagnosing low output from a pump, check supply before blaming the pump.

f.q: How does eluate temperature affect electrowinning?
f.a:
In general, warmer solution conducts electricity better and lets ions move faster, so deposition is more efficient and the cell voltage needed is lower. Eluate coming from a hot strip is warm, which helps.

Too cold and the cells work harder for less gold. Very hot solution can increase evaporation and side reactions.

The reference doesn't give an electrowinning temperature target for CIL4. The elution operator or metallurgist would know the normal range.
f: Why does conductivity matter in an electrowinning cell?
What caustic level keeps eluate conductive?
Can eluate be too hot for the EW cells?

f.q: What does a shorted cathode look like?
f.a:
In general, if a cathode touches an anode, current takes the easy path through the short instead of through the solution. That cathode gets little deposition, the contact point can overheat, and the rectifier may show high current at low voltage.

Visual signs include burnt or discoloured spots, uneven deposits and a cathode out of alignment.

Shorts are cleared under the site procedure with the rectifier isolated, since the cells carry high current and caustic cyanide solution. Never reach into a live cell.
f: How are anodes and cathodes kept apart?
What alarms show a rectifier problem?
How is a short safely cleared?

f.q: How would poor elution show up in the electrowinning results?
f.a:
As a weak pregnant eluate. If gold stays on the carbon, there's less gold in solution to plate, so deposits are thin even with healthy cells. The design pregnant eluate grade is about 52.6 g/m3.

The giveaway is in the barren carbon. A poor strip leaves barren carbon above the design range of about 15 to 60 g/t, and the barren solution leaving EW is low because there wasn't much gold to start with.

So check elution and EW together. It's like low output from a heat exchanger: you need to know whether the hot side was hot enough before blaming the tubes.
f: How is pregnant eluate grade sampled?
What barren carbon grade suggests a poor strip?
Can EW recover gold efficiently from a weak eluate?

What happens in the goldroom?.q: How is doré bar purity checked before it's dispatched?
What happens in the goldroom?.a:
The reference doesn't describe the doré sampling or assay process for this site.

In general, goldrooms weigh each bar, take samples by drilling or from the melt, and assay them, usually by fire assay, for gold and silver. Bars are numbered, sealed and recorded under strict security. Final payment is based on the refinery's own assay, and the site's numbers are checked against it.

Ask the goldroom supervisor or metallurgist for the local procedure. The goldroom is a high security area, so access is controlled.

f.q: What else is in a doré bar besides gold?
f.a:
Mostly silver, plus small amounts of base metals such as copper, and other impurities depending on the ore. The reference gives intensive leach pregnant solution at about 29 ppm silver and 303 ppm copper alongside 1,100 to 1,800 ppm gold, which shows other metals travel with the gold.

In general, flux in the smelting furnace takes up much of the base metal and other impurities into the slag, but silver stays with the gold.

The refinery separates gold and silver later. Doré purity is site specific, and the goldroom keeps the records.
f: Why does copper end up in the doré?
How does flux remove impurities during smelting?
What purity does the refinery expect?

f.q: What happens in the goldroom before smelting?
f.a:
The PDC describes the existing goldroom: gold sludge from electrowinning goes through a sludge filter (TEFSA HPLE plate filter), then a mercury retort oven (electric, about 20 ft3) to distil off mercury, before smelting in a Westofen LPG fired furnace.

The goldroom handles product from both the concentrate EW (CIL2/3) and the CIL4 EW. The PDC lists about 6 smelts per week, with two downloads per week and three pours per day.

The retort step matters: mercury must be removed before the high temperature furnace, both for safety and product quality.
f: Why must mercury be retorted before smelting?
What flux is used in the smelting furnace?
How is slag handled after a pour?

f.q: Why is the goldroom such a high security area?
f.a:
Because it's where the plant's value becomes portable. In general, goldrooms hold concentrated sludge and finished bars that are worth a lot in a small volume, so access is tightly controlled, often with CCTV, logged entry, two person rules and searches.

The reference only notes the goldroom is a high security area.

As a new engineer, expect not to enter without specific authorisation and an escort. If maintenance is needed there, it's arranged through the goldroom supervisor.
f: What access controls apply to the goldroom?
Who can enter the goldroom during a pour?
How are gold movements recorded?

What is 'lean eluate'?.q: Why does reusing lean eluate save both reagents and water?
What is 'lean eluate'?.a:
Lean eluate is the second half of the previous strip's solution. It still contains caustic and cyanide from the pre soak, low levels of gold and some residual heat. Reusing it for the next strip's pre soak and first elution step means you don't have to make up all that solution from fresh scheme water and new chemicals.

In the CIL4 design, the pre soak uses about 1 bed volume of lean eluate topped up to about 1.7 percent cyanide and 2 percent caustic, then about 5 bed volumes of lean eluate elute the carbon. The later scheme water elution and cooling, about 5 bed volumes, becomes the next strip's lean eluate.

It's like a counterflow rinse: the cleanest water does the final step, then gets reused for the dirtier one.

f.q: What's in the lean eluate when it's reused?
f.a:
In general, residual sodium cyanide and caustic from the previous strip, a small amount of gold, and whatever else came off the carbon late in the strip.

For the pre soak it's topped up with fresh reagents. The PDC gives about 543 kg of sodium cyanide and 638 kg of caustic per pre treatment, made up into about 29.5 m3 per mix.

The low level of gold isn't lost. It ends up in the next strip's pregnant eluate and goes to electrowinning.
f: How much fresh cyanide goes into each pre soak mix?
Does gold in lean eluate get recovered later?
How is lean eluate strength checked?

f.q: Where does the scheme water elution end up?
f.a:
According to the PDC, solution leaving the column during the scheme water elution goes first to the CIL4 eluate circulation tanks. When those are full, discharge switches to the lean eluate tank.

So the early, gold rich solution goes to electrowinning, and the later, leaner solution is saved as lean eluate for the next strip. The PDC calls for 5 bed volumes of pregnant eluate, about 160 m3.

It's like a diverter valve on a process that sends first runnings one way and last runnings another.
f: Why does the discharge switch when the circulation tanks fill?
How big are the CIL4 eluate circulation tanks?
What happens to eluate after electrowinning?

f.q: How much scheme water does a CIL4 strip use?
f.a:
The PDC totals about 432 m3 of scheme water per strip: carbon transfer about 8 m3, acid wash about 17, water rinse about 128, water elution and cooling about 160, carbon eduction from elution to regeneration about 60, and carbon quench to the sizing screen about 60.

At 12 strips a week, that's over 5,000 m3 of scheme water weekly just for CIL4 elution, which is why reuse matters given scheme water's cost.

These are design figures; actual use depends on how closely operators follow the recipe.
f: Why is so much water used just for the acid rinse?
Where does the carbon eduction water end up?
Could any of this water be recycled further?

What is 'lean eluate'?.q: What would you flag if lean eluate volume didn't match the next strip's needs?
What is 'lean eluate'?.a:
The volume, the timing and the likely cause. The CIL4 lean eluate tank is designed for at least about 160 m3 live, matched to the 5 bed volume elution step. If it's short, the next strip can't run its pre soak and lean eluate elution as designed. If it's over, solution is coming from somewhere unexpected.

Possible causes: the switch from circulation tanks to lean eluate happening at the wrong time, a strip cut short, a leak or passing valve, water ingress, or a level instrument fault.

Note it in the handover with levels and strip numbers, and tell the elution operator and metallurgist before the next strip starts.

f.q: Why would lean eluate run short after a strip?
f.a:
In general, the most likely reasons are routing: more solution sent to the eluate circulation tanks than expected, so less ends up in the lean eluate tank; a strip that stopped early; or a leak or passing drain valve.

The PDC says discharge switches to the lean eluate tank when the CIL4 eluate circulation tank is full, so anything affecting that tank's level or level reading changes the split.

Check PI trends for both tanks through the last strip. It's like a mass balance on any two tank system: where did the volume go?
f: How does the sequence decide when to divert to lean eluate?
Can lean eluate be made up from scheme water?
What tank level alarms protect the lean eluate tank?

f.q: What happens if the lean eluate tank overflows?
f.a:
In general, caustic cyanide solution spills into the bund and drains to a sump, from where it's pumped back to the process. It's a cyanide spill, so it needs the site's cyanide spill response, even if it stays within the bund.

Overflow usually means a level instrument failure, a stuck valve or wrong routing.

Don't walk into a spill area without the right PPE and gas monitoring. Report it to the control room and follow the spill procedure.
f: Where does lean eluate tank overflow drain to?
What PPE is needed to clean up eluate spills?
How is a cyanide solution spill reported?

f.q: Does lean eluate gold content affect the next strip?
f.a:
Only slightly. In general, lean eluate is the tail end of the strip, so it carries little gold. When it's reused, that gold goes into the next strip's pregnant eluate and on to electrowinning, so it isn't lost.

If lean eluate gold was unusually high, it would suggest the previous strip was diverting to the lean eluate tank too early, sending gold rich solution there instead of to electrowinning.

The reference doesn't give a lean eluate gold grade. The metallurgist would watch it as a strip health check.
f: How much gold is typical in lean eluate?
Why is the last elution water lowest in gold?
Can lean eluate be sent to electrowinning directly?

What is 'lean eluate'?.q: How is lean eluate stored and tracked between strips?
What is 'lean eluate'?.a:
The PDC gives one lean eluate tank of at least about 160 m3 live. During the scheme water elution, discharge goes to the CIL4 eluate circulation tanks and switches to the lean eluate tank when they're full. The next strip draws lean eluate for its pre soak and lean eluate elution.

The reference doesn't describe how lean eluate is tracked, such as level alarms, sampling or strength checks.

In general, plants track it by tank level on the DCS and sometimes by sampling for cyanide strength before the pre soak make up. Ask the elution operator how it's done here.

f.q: Is the lean eluate tank heated or insulated?
f.a:
The reference doesn't say. It gives the lean eluate tank's minimum live volume but nothing about heating or insulation.

In general, some plants insulate lean eluate tanks to keep some heat for the next strip, which shortens heat up and saves fuel. Others don't, especially if strips run back to back so the solution doesn't sit long.

Check the F22 P&ID or ask the elution operator. With 2 strips a day designed, lean eluate shouldn't wait long either way.
f: How much heat does lean eluate lose between strips?
Does cold lean eluate slow the next strip?
Is the elution water tank used for anything else?

f.q: What is the elution water tank for?
f.a:
The PDC lists one elution water tank of about 160 m3 live volume. It doesn't describe its role in detail.

In general, an elution water tank holds the clean water used for the water elution and cooling steps. Here that's scheme water, about 5 bed volumes or 160 m3 per strip, which matches the tank size. Having it stored means the strip can draw water at the design rate without depending on scheme water supply pressure at that moment.

It's like a header tank that decouples a variable supply from a steady demand.
f: Why is the elution water tank sized at 160 cubic metres?
Where does the elution water tank get its water from?
Is the elution water heated before use?

f.q: How is cyanide made up into the pre-soak solution?
f.a:
Cyanide and caustic are distributed round the plant on pressurised ringmains with DOL pumps and a back pressure valve on the return, with flowmeters at each dosing point. For CIL4, the PDC gives about 1.51 m3 of 29 percent cyanide solution and about 0.85 m3 of 50 percent caustic per pre treatment, made up with lean eluate into about 29.5 m3 per mix at about 1.7 percent cyanide and 2 percent caustic.

The caustic tank has an immersion heater that switches on below about 20 degrees C to stop the 50 percent solution freezing.

Dosing is handled within the elution sequence, so operators aren't hand mixing cyanide.
f: Why is caustic added along with cyanide in the pre soak?
Why does 50 percent caustic need heating to avoid freezing?
What happens if the cyanide ringmain pressure drops?

Process water on this plant has an SG of.q: Why does high salinity affect corrosion and reagent chemistry so much?
Process water on this plant has an SG of.a:
Because the water is extreme. The PDC process water quality data shows TDS of about 140,000 mg/L, chlorides of roughly 20,000 to 86,000 mg/L and pH about 4.6. Seawater is around 35,000 mg/L, so this is several times saltier.

For corrosion, chlorides break down the protective film on stainless steel, causing pitting, crevice corrosion and, when hot, stress corrosion cracking. Highly conductive water also speeds up general and galvanic corrosion of carbon steel.

For chemistry, magnesium in the water consumes lime, which is why CIL4 runs at pH 8.8 to 9.3. In general, salt also lowers oxygen solubility and changes froth behaviour. It's like designing for a marine environment, only harsher.

f.q: Why does salt water reduce dissolved oxygen in the leach?
f.a:
In general, gases dissolve less in salty water than in fresh water, an effect called salting out. The more dissolved salt, the less oxygen the water can hold at a given temperature and pressure.

That makes it harder to reach high dissolved oxygen in hypersaline slurry. The CIL4 design targets about 15 ppm DO, which is well above what air alone could give, so the plant uses pure oxygen from the PSA oxygen plant, injected by VSD oxygen pumps and side lances.

It's like trying to dissolve more gas in a fluid that's already crowded: you need higher partial pressure to push it in.
f: Why does CIL4 use pure oxygen instead of air?
How do DO analysers cope with saline slurry?
Does temperature also limit oxygen solubility?

f.q: How does saline water change flotation behaviour?
f.a:
In general, dissolved salts stop small bubbles merging into bigger ones, so saline water produces finer bubbles and a more stable froth than fresh water, even with less frother. That can help recovery of fine particles.

The downside is that a very stable froth can carry more entrained gangue, lowering concentrate grade, and stiff froth can be hard to move in launders, which is one reason for launder sprays.

The reference doesn't quantify these effects for this plant. The flotation metallurgist tunes frother dosing to suit.
f: Why do salts stop bubbles from merging?
Does saline water change frother dosing?
Can a too stable froth hurt concentrate grade?

f.q: Which materials resist hypersaline water best?
f.a:
In general, the main options are non metallic or lined materials (rubber lined steel, HDPE, fibreglass) and higher alloy stainless steels (duplex and super duplex) where metal is needed.

The plant shows both approaches. The equipment list has thickener feed and overflow boxes in mild steel with 10 mm rubber or EPDM lining, the flotation tails thickener overflow launder in SAF2507 super duplex, and the CIL4 elution column in SAF2205 duplex.

Ordinary 304 and 316 stainless are risky in hot chloride service. It's the same logic as choosing materials for seawater cooling systems.
f: Why is super duplex used for the thickener overflow launder?
When is HDPE pipe preferred over steel?
How long does rubber lining last in slurry service?

Process water on this plant has an SG of.q: What would you check if process water SG suddenly changed?
Process water on this plant has an SG of.a:
First whether it's real. Check the density instrument against a manual measurement.

If it's real, look at the water sources. Process water is mainly flotation tails thickener overflow, topped up with saline bore water from Dam 2. A rise in SG often means solids in the water, for example dirty thickener overflow from poor flocculation or overloading. A fall suggests fresher water getting in, such as rainfall in the dams or a scheme or raw water connection passing into the process water system.

It matters because the site metallurgical accounting assumes water SG of about 1.07 when converting slurry density to percent solids. Report it to the control room and metallurgist.

f.q: Why does water SG matter for density based measurements?
f.a:
Nucleonic density gauges measure slurry SG. To turn that into percent solids and dry tonnes, the calculation needs both the solids SG and the liquid SG. The PDC notes water SG of 1.07 as a site metallurgical accounting assumption.

If the actual water SG differs from the assumed value, every percent solids and tonnage calculated from density is slightly wrong. At thousands of tonnes per hour, small errors add up in the mass balance.

It's like calibrating a flowmeter for the wrong fluid density: it reads consistently, but consistently off.
f: Where is the water SG value entered in the DCS?
How much error does a wrong water SG cause?
Who updates the metallurgical accounting assumptions?

f.q: Could dirty thickener overflow raise process water SG?
f.a:
Yes. Suspended solids in the water raise its measured density, so a thickener sending cloudy overflow to the Process Water Tank would push apparent process water SG up.

The thickener vendor panel sends an overflow clarity signal to the DCS for exactly this kind of problem. Poor flocculation, overloading or a disturbed bed are the usual causes.

Solids in process water also wear sprays and nozzles and settle in tanks. Like dirt in a hydraulic reservoir, it's a symptom to fix at the source, not just clean up downstream.
f: What overflow clarity is normal for this thickener?
How fast can solids build up in the process water tank?
Which users suffer first from solids in process water?

f.q: What would lower SG suggest about the water supply?
f.a:
In general, fresher water getting into the system. Possible causes are heavy rain diluting the saline storage dams, a change in which borefield or dam is supplying top up, or a cross connection where raw or scheme water is passing into the process water system through a valve left open.

A falling SG isn't harmful in itself, but it may change reagent consumption and means expensive scheme water could be leaking away.

Check recent rainfall, which dams are supplying, and any valves recently operated on water headers.
f: Can heavy rain dilute the saline dams noticeably?
Where could scheme water leak into process water?

Process water on this plant has an SG of.q: What materials selection choices respond to this salinity on plant?
Process water on this plant has an SG of.a:
The equipment list shows a consistent pattern. Many boxes and tanks are mild steel with rubber linings, for example the flotation tails thickener boxes with 10 mm rubber or EPDM lining and painted exteriors. Where metal is in contact with salty water and lining isn't practical, higher alloys appear: the thickener overflow launder is SAF2507 super duplex and the CIL4 elution column is SAF2205 duplex.

In general, other common choices are HDPE or lined pipe for water and slurry, fibreglass for some tanks and launders, and corrosion resistant fasteners and paint systems.

It's like marine engineering: assume ordinary steel will rust and ordinary stainless will pit, and choose accordingly.

f.q: Why are many tanks and boxes rubber lined?
f.a:
In general, mild steel is cheap and strong but corrodes rapidly in hypersaline water and wears under slurry. A rubber lining separates the steel from the water and absorbs impact from particles, so you get a steel structure with a corrosion and wear resistant surface.

The equipment list shows examples like the flotation tails thickener recirculation feed box with 10 mm Reglin rubber lining.

Linings do need inspection: a small tear lets salt water reach the steel behind it, and corrosion can spread unseen. It's like paint on a car: fine until it's chipped.
f: How is rubber lining damage found during inspections?
What causes rubber linings to come away from the steel?
Can rubber linings be repaired in place?

f.q: What's the difference between duplex 2205 and super duplex 2507?
f.a:
In general, both have a mixed ferrite and austenite structure. Super duplex 2507 has more chromium, molybdenum and nitrogen than 2205, giving it a higher pitting resistance number (roughly in the low 40s versus mid 30s). That means it resists chloride pitting and crevice corrosion better, but costs more.

The plant uses both: SAF2205 for the CIL4 elution column, and SAF2507 for the flotation tails thickener overflow launder, which is in constant contact with hypersaline water.

It's like choosing between two grades of bearing steel: both work, one handles harsher conditions.
f: What does the pitting resistance number tell you?
Why not use super duplex everywhere?
How is duplex identified on site?

f.q: Why do pump impellers and casings wear faster here?
f.a:
In general, because of erosion corrosion. Abrasive slurry scrubs away the thin protective oxide film on the metal, and the salty, acidic water immediately attacks the fresh surface. Each process speeds up the other, so wear is faster than either would cause alone.

That's why slurry pumps typically use high chrome white iron or rubber liners, chosen by particle size and duty.

The reference doesn't give pump material specifications. The area maintenance planner and pump vendor data would show what's fitted and expected wear life.
f: What is erosion corrosion and how does it look?
Why are high chrome iron impellers common in slurry pumps?
How do you choose between rubber and metal pump liners?

What is 'scheme water' used for?.q: Why can't hypersaline process water be used for gland seals or reagents?
What is 'scheme water' used for?.a:
Because salt and solids cause problems wherever clean water is needed. Process water carries about 140,000 mg/L of dissolved solids and some fine suspended solids. Scheme water is about 454 mg/L.

In a gland, salty water can crystallise as it evaporates, leaving abrasive deposits, and chlorides attack shaft sleeves. In reagent make up, magnesium and calcium in salty water react with caustic and lime, precipitating out, wasting reagent and scaling tanks and lines.

In elution, salt interferes with stripping and adds chloride to hot equipment. So scheme water is saved for duties where quality matters. It's like using distilled water in a battery or cooling system: tap water works for washing, not there.

f.q: How different is scheme water from process water chemically?
f.a:
Very. The PDC gives scheme water as SG 1.00, TDS about 454 mg/L, pH about 8.0 and chlorides about 232 mg/L. Process water is SG 1.07, TDS about 140,000 mg/L, pH about 4.6 and chlorides roughly 20,000 to 86,000 mg/L.

So process water has around 300 times the dissolved solids, up to a few hundred times the chlorides, and is distinctly acidic.

These are design basis values. Actual water quality varies with the sources in use, and the metallurgy or environmental team would have current analyses.
f: Why is process water so much more acidic than scheme water?
How is scheme water quality monitored on site?
Does scheme water quality vary over time?

f.q: Do all gland water pumps on the plant use scheme water?
f.a:
Not necessarily. The reference says the new gland water comes from the lower part of the Raw Water Tank, with LP and HP gland water pumps (duty/standby each), and that the Raw Water Tank is fed from bore water and saline dam storage via booster pumps. The existing gland water system draws from Dam 2 (South).

It also says the new UFG mills use scheme water for their gland seals.

So gland water quality may differ by area. The card's general point holds, that glands need clean water, but check the actual source for the pump you're looking at on the P&ID.
f: What is the Raw Water Tank fed from?
Why do the UFG mills need scheme water for glands?
How is gland water quality checked?

f.q: Why is scheme water used for elution and carbon transfer?
f.a:
The PDC specifies scheme water for CIL4 loaded carbon transfer, the acid rinse, and the water elution and cooling steps, about 432 m3 per strip in total.

In general, AARL elution works best with low salt water: salt in the solution reduces how readily gold comes off the carbon. Salt in hot circuits also adds chlorides that attack stainless steel and adds scaling.

So keeping hypersaline water out of the column improves stripping and protects the equipment. It's like using clean oil in a precision gearbox, even if the rest of the machine runs on something cheaper.
f: How does salt interfere with AARL stripping?
How much scheme water does elution use weekly?
Could treated process water replace scheme water?

What is 'scheme water' used for?.q: What would happen if scheme water supply pressure dropped mid shift?
What is 'scheme water' used for?.a:
It depends on which users are affected and whether they have storage. The UFG mills use scheme water for gland seals, and the control philosophy says low gland flow blocks a pump start and trips a running pump after a delay. Other scheme water users include elution, the Carbon Scout (about 200 L/h), reagent make up and the CIL4 kiln off gas condenser cooling.

Elution has some buffer in its elution water tank, but continuous users don't.

Report it to the control room straight away. Don't defeat gland flow trips to keep pumps running; they're there to protect the seals. Supply restoration is a matter for whoever manages the scheme water connection.

f.q: Why do pumps trip on low gland water flow?
f.a:
To protect the seal. The control philosophy says low gland water flow blocks a pump start and, if the pump is running, trips it after a delay. Without gland water, packing runs dry and overheats, and slurry gets into the stuffing box and grinds the shaft sleeve.

The delay lets a brief dip pass without nuisance trips. Gland water has a flow switch, and some critical pumps have mag flowmeters on gland water instead.

It's like a low oil pressure trip on an engine: annoying when it happens, but far cheaper than the damage it prevents.
f: How long is the delay before a gland water trip?
What flow switch monitors gland water?
Can operators restart straight after a gland trip?

f.q: Which scheme water users have storage to ride through an outage?
f.a:
The reference shows an elution water tank of about 160 m3 for CIL4, roughly one strip's water elution and cooling, so elution has some buffer. The goldroom and some other users may have their own arrangements.

The PDC gives total scheme water demand of about 172 m3/h, but doesn't list a main scheme water storage tank or which users are fed directly from the supply.

Ask the utilities or area engineer how scheme water is distributed and stored. That would tell you which users stop first in an outage.
f: How long would the elution water tank last?
Is there a scheme water storage tank on site?
Which scheme water users are most critical?

f.q: Does the kiln off gas system rely on scheme water?
f.a:
Yes. The PDC lists the CIL4 kiln off gas condenser as shell and tube, cooled with scheme water, and the knock out box and mist eliminator sprays also use scheme water, though those sprays are for maintenance only.

The condenser cools the off gas so moisture and some mercury condense out before the adsorption vessel. If cooling water is lost, the condenser runs hot and the abatement system works less well. Since mercury abatement must run with the kiln, a cooling problem can mean stopping the kiln.

The specific interlocks are in the regeneration control description.
f: What happens to mercury capture if the condenser runs hot?
Is the condenser cooling water recirculated?
What alarms flag low cooling water flow?

What is 'scheme water' used for?.q: How is scheme water usage minimised given its cost?
What is 'scheme water' used for?.a:
Mostly by using it only where it's truly needed and reusing it where possible. Process water handles sprays, dilution and most slurry duties; the instrument list shows even the CIL4 loaded carbon screen sprays on hypersaline water. Raw water is used for lime slaking.

Within elution, split AARL reuses lean eluate, so the scheme water from one strip's later steps becomes the next strip's first elution solution. Gland water lines use Maric constant flow valves, which stop excess flow.

The PDC gives total scheme water demand of about 172 m3/h, against process water demand of about 5,355 m3/h. Like compressed air, it's an expensive utility, so it's metered and used deliberately.

f.q: What does a Maric constant flow valve do?
f.a:
In general, a Maric valve uses a flexible rubber orifice ring that deforms as upstream pressure changes. Higher pressure squeezes the orifice smaller, so flow stays roughly constant across a wide pressure range.

On gland water, that means each pump gets the set flow regardless of header pressure fluctuations. It avoids starving a gland when pressure dips and wasting water, or diluting slurry, when pressure is high.

The control philosophy lists a Maric constant flow valve in the standard gland water arrangement. It's a simple, passive flow regulator, like a pressure compensated flow control valve in hydraulics.
f: How does a flexible orifice keep flow constant?
What happens when a Maric valve wears out?
Why does too much gland water dilute the slurry?

f.q: Why is lime slaked with raw water instead of scheme water?
f.a:
The PDC specifies raw water as the make up water for the lime slaking mills. It doesn't explain why.
