In general, lime slaking tolerates water quality that would be unacceptable in elution or reagent make up for cyanide, and milk of lime is used in large volumes (about 56 m3/h nominal). Using scheme water there would consume a lot of expensive water for little benefit.

Very salty water can affect slaking and scaling, which may be why raw water is used rather than process water. The lime plant vendor would know the water quality limits.
f: Does salty water affect lime slaking?
What is raw water used for besides slaking?
Where does raw water come from on this plant?

f.q: How much scheme water does the plant use overall?
f.a:
The PDC gives a calculated scheme water demand of about 172 m3/h in the nominal case, rising slightly to about 175 m3/h in the high throughput case. Process water demand is about 5,355 m3/h, so scheme water is only about 3 percent of the plant's water use.

Within that, CIL4 elution alone uses about 432 m3 per strip, or roughly 36 m3/h averaged over 2 strips per day.

These are design figures. Actual use is metered, and the site would track it closely because scheme water comes from the Goldfields pipeline at a real cost.
f: Which area is the largest scheme water user?
How is scheme water metered and billed?
What would cut scheme water use further?

What is 'cyanide water'?.q: Why is it worth treating decant water instead of just using fresh water?
What is 'cyanide water'?.a:
Because there's a lot of it, and fresh water is scarce. The PDC assumes about 49 percent of tailings water is recovered as decant, with total decant flow to the cyanide water tank of about 1,940 m3/h nominal. Replacing that with scheme water is out of the question; the plant's whole scheme water demand is only about 172 m3/h.

The decant carries residual cyanide. The plant doses hydrogen peroxide through inline mixers on the three decant lines, controlled by an online WAD cyanide analyser, to a residual WAD target of about 1.5.

In general, controlling cyanide in returned water protects people and downstream processes. It's like a coolant reclamation system: clean and reuse rather than buy new.

f.q: Why would cyanide in recycled water hurt flotation?
f.a:
In general, cyanide is a well known depressant for pyrite. It stops pyrite floating, which is exactly the mineral this plant needs to float because it carries the gold. Even modest cyanide levels in water reaching grinding and flotation can reduce sulphide recovery.

The reference doesn't spell out where treated decant water is used or whether flotation protection is a design reason for the peroxide treatment.

So keeping cyanide low in any water that might reach flotation makes sense. The metallurgist would know how cyanide water is routed on this plant.
f: Where does cyanide water enter the plant circuit?
How much cyanide depresses pyrite noticeably?
Does treated decant go into the process water tank?

f.q: How does hydrogen peroxide destroy cyanide?
f.a:
In general, hydrogen peroxide oxidises free cyanide and weakly complexed cyanide to cyanate, which is far less toxic and breaks down further over time. Copper in solution often acts as a catalyst and speeds it up.

On this plant, peroxide is supplied at about 70 percent strength and dosed through three inline mixers, one per decant line, at about 140 L/h each nominal. The dose is controlled by an online WAD cyanide analyser.

Strong peroxide is a hazardous oxidiser in its own right: it can cause burns and fires with organic materials, so it has its own handling rules.
f: Why does copper speed up peroxide cyanide destruction?
What hazards does 70 percent hydrogen peroxide bring?
How is peroxide dosing adjusted to the analyser?

f.q: How much water comes back from the TSF as decant?
f.a:
The PDC assumes decant recovery of about 49 percent of total tailings water. Decant from Kaltails is about 728 m3/h, and total flow to the cyanide water tank is about 1,940 m3/h in the nominal case.

There are three decant streams: Kaltails decant; offsite roaster and FIM I decant; and Decant Dams 3 and 4. Each line has its own peroxide inline mixer. The existing cyanide water tank is about 1,115 m3 live.

These are design figures marked for confirmation with updated drawings in places. Actual decant recovery varies with weather, evaporation and how the TSF is operated.
f: Why do three separate decant lines come back?
What affects how much decant water is recovered?
How big is the cyanide water tank?

What is 'cyanide water'?.q: What would rising WAD cyanide in the decant line suggest is failing?
What is 'cyanide water'?.a:
If WAD cyanide rises after the peroxide dosing point, the treatment isn't keeping up. Likely causes are on the dosing side: a peroxide pump tripped or not delivering, a blocked dosing line or mixer, low peroxide in the storage tank, or the analyser or control loop misbehaving.

It could also be a bigger cyanide load coming back: more cyanide going to tails from CIL4, more decant flow than the dosing can handle, or less natural cyanide breakdown in the TSF.

The design has duty/duty/duty/standby peroxide pumps, with the standby acting as a lag pump on high demand. Check pump status, peroxide tank level and analyser health, and report it.

f.q: What does WAD cyanide measure that free cyanide doesn't?
f.a:
In general, WAD (weak acid dissociable) cyanide includes free cyanide plus cyanide held in weaker metal complexes, such as those of zinc, copper, nickel and cadmium, which release cyanide under mildly acidic conditions. It excludes very stable complexes like iron cyanides.

WAD is used because it represents the cyanide that's biologically available and could become toxic in the environment, which is why tailings and decant targets are usually set as WAD.

The plant's Stage 2 residual WAD target on decant is below about 1.5.
f: Why are iron cyanide complexes excluded from WAD?
What limit applies to WAD at the TSF?
How does an online WAD analyser work?

f.q: How are the peroxide dosing pumps arranged?
f.a:
The PDC gives three dosing points, one inline mixer per decant line, with duty/duty/duty/standby pumps, one duty pump per mixer. The standby pump acts as a lag pump to the duty pumps when peroxide demand is high.

Nominal dosing is about 140 L/h per mixer (420 L/h total), with design up to about 280 L/h per mixer. Control is from the online WAD cyanide analyser. Peroxide is stored in a 316 stainless tank of about 84 m3, roughly 8 days at nominal use.

It's a classic duty and lag arrangement, like extra compressors that cut in when demand outruns the duty units.
f: How does the lag pump know when to start?
What happens if peroxide storage runs low?
How is a peroxide pump safely isolated?

f.q: Could high cyanide in CIL4 tails cause rising decant WAD?
f.a:
Yes. Whatever cyanide leaves CIL4 goes to the TSF with the tails, and some returns in the decant. CIL4 cyanide is dosed as grams per tonne or by operator setpoint, trimmed by an analyser on tanks 1 and 2. CIL3 tails also arrive carrying residual cyanide (about 750 ppm design).

If CIL4 is overdosed, or the analyser trim fails, more cyanide goes to tails, and decant cyanide rises after a delay.

In general, some cyanide breaks down naturally in the TSF through sunlight and volatilisation, but that can't be relied on to absorb big swings.
f: How is CIL4 cyanide dosing kept from overshooting?
Does cyanide break down naturally in the TSF?
How long does tailings water take to return as decant?

What is 'cyanide water'?.q: Where in the plant is treated cyanide water reused?
What is 'cyanide water'?.a:
The reference gives some of the picture. Decant water goes to the existing cyanide water tank (about 1,115 m3 live), with duty/standby cyanide water pumps and duty/standby cyanide transfer pumps. The control philosophy says cyanide water is added to the CIL3 tails hopper, which pumps to the CIL4 feed distribution box.

The reference doesn't list every cyanide water user. In general, it would be sensible to use it where residual cyanide is harmless or useful, such as the leach circuits, and avoid sending it where cyanide hurts, like flotation.

Check the water services P&IDs or ask the metallurgist for the full list of destinations.

f.q: Why is cyanide water added to the CIL3 tails hopper?
f.a:
The control philosophy states cyanide water is added to the CIL3 tails hopper, whose duty/standby VSD pumps send CIL3 tails to the CIL4 feed box. It doesn't give the reason.

In general, adding water to a pump hopper helps control density and level so the pumps run smoothly. Using cyanide water there makes sense because the stream is headed to CIL4, where residual cyanide is useful rather than a problem, and it saves using process or scheme water.

The metallurgist or area engineer could confirm how much is added and why.
f: How does CIL3 tails reach the CIL4 feed box?
Does cyanide water help CIL4 leaching?
What controls the cyanide water addition rate?

f.q: Is cyanide water safe to handle like process water?
f.a:
No. Even after peroxide treatment it still contains residual cyanide (target WAD below about 1.5), and untreated or poorly treated decant can carry more. In general, it should be treated as cyanide bearing: avoid skin contact and spray, and never let it meet acid, which could release HCN.

Leaks and spills from cyanide water lines are handled under the site cyanide procedures, not just hosed away.

Know which lines carry cyanide water in your area; the line list and field labelling identify them. Ask your supervisor if you're not sure.
f: What labels identify cyanide water lines on site?
What PPE applies to cyanide water leaks?
Why must cyanide water never meet acid?

f.q: What's the cyanide water tank and pump arrangement?
f.a:
The PDC describes the existing cyanide water system: a cyanide water tank of about 1,115 m3 live fed by decant return, duty/standby cyanide water pumps (TKL 200x200 500HT) and duty/standby cyanide transfer pumps (TKL 100x65 315HT).

The PDC doesn't say exactly which users each pump set supplies. The larger pumps are presumably the main distribution, and the smaller ones a transfer duty, but check the water services P&IDs.

Total feed to the cyanide water tank is about 1,940 m3/h nominal, so the tank gives under an hour of buffer.
f: What do the cyanide transfer pumps supply?
How is the cyanide water tank level controlled?
What happens if both cyanide water pumps trip?

What is 'gland water'?.q: Why does packing overheat so quickly once it runs dry?
What is 'gland water'?.a:
Because packing is a friction seal that relies on a small flow of liquid for cooling and lubrication. The packing rings are pressed against the rotating shaft sleeve, and a thin film of gland water between them carries heat away and keeps friction down.

Take that water away and the packing rubs dry on a sleeve moving at several metres per second. Friction heat builds within minutes, the packing hardens and glazes, and the sleeve can score. Once the seal is damaged, slurry gets in and the abrasive particles finish the job.

It's exactly like a plain bearing losing its oil supply: fine one minute, smoking the next.

f.q: What does slurry do once it gets into the stuffing box?
f.a:
In general, abrasive particles get trapped between the packing and the shaft sleeve and act like grinding paste. They cut grooves into the sleeve, chew up the packing, and leakage increases, which lets even more slurry in.

Slurry leaking past the gland can also reach the bearing housing, contaminating the bearings, and makes a mess around the pump base.

That's why the gland water must be at a higher pressure than the slurry in the stuffing box, so the flow always goes from clean side to dirty side.
f: How is a grooved shaft sleeve repaired?
Why does slurry leakage damage pump bearings?
How do you tell gland wear from sleeve wear?

f.q: Why do slurry pumps use packing rather than mechanical seals?
f.a:
In general, packing is cheap, tolerant of abrasive slurry and shaft movement, and easy to replace in the field. Mechanical seals can work in slurry service but are more expensive and sensitive to dry running and solids.

Many slurry pumps also use expeller or centrifugal seals that keep slurry away from the gland while running, sometimes with little or no gland water.

The reference doesn't list seal types for each pump, but the control philosophy assumes gland water on the main slurry pumps. The pump datasheets or area maintenance planner would show what's fitted.
f: When would a mechanical seal be chosen instead?
What is an expeller or dry gland seal?
How often is gland packing replaced?

f.q: How much gland water should a pump use?
f.a:
The reference doesn't give per pump gland flows. It gives a total design gland water demand of about 92 m3/h for the new plant, and says gland water lines have Maric constant flow valves to hold a set flow.

In general, each pump's gland flow comes from the pump vendor, sized for the shaft size and seal type, and pressure must be above the stuffing box pressure.

Too little and the packing runs hot; too much wastes water and dilutes the slurry. The pump datasheets or the area maintenance planner will have the set points.
f: What happens if gland water flow is set too high?
How is gland water pressure set above pump pressure?
Where are gland flow rates documented?

What is 'gland water'?.q: What would a low gland water pressure note mean for pump seals?
What is 'gland water'?.a:
It means the seals are at risk. Gland water has to be at a higher pressure than the slurry in the stuffing box, so clean water flows in and slurry stays out. If gland pressure falls, flow drops, and on high pressure pumps slurry can push back into the gland.

The control philosophy says low gland flow blocks a pump start and trips a running pump after a delay. So a plant wide low pressure problem can stop several pumps at once.

Check the gland water pumps (LP and HP, duty/standby from the Raw Water Tank), tank level, strainers and header valves, and report it. Don't bypass gland trips to keep pumps running.

f.q: Why are there separate LP and HP gland water systems?
f.a:
The PDC lists low pressure and high pressure gland water pumps, each duty/standby, drawing from the Raw Water Tank. It doesn't say which pumps go on which system.

In general, gland water must be a margin above the pump's stuffing box pressure. High head slurry pumps, like cyclone feed or tailings pumps, need high pressure gland water, while low head pumps don't. Running everything at high pressure would waste energy and water.

It's like having separate low and high pressure hydraulic circuits instead of throttling one high pressure supply everywhere.
f: Which pumps are on the HP gland water system?
What pressure margin over pump pressure is needed?
What happens if the HP gland pump trips?

f.q: What instruments watch gland water on the pumps?
f.a:
The control philosophy gives the standard gland water arrangement: a manual isolation valve, an actuated valve opened in the pump's start sequence, a Maric constant flow valve, and a flow switch. Cyclone feed, thickener underflow and final tails pumps get a mag flowmeter instead of a simple switch.

The instrument list shows examples like FIT17105 on the flotation tails thickener underflow pump 1 gland water.

Low flow blocks a start and trips a running pump after a delay. It's a small instrument protecting a very expensive pump.
f: Why do only some pumps get gland mag flowmeters?
How is a gland flow switch tested?
What does the actuated gland valve do when the pump stops?

f.q: What's the right response to a gland water trip on a running pump?
f.a:
Find out why before restarting. Check the gland water supply to that pump: is the header pressure normal, is the manual isolation open, is the actuated valve working, is the Maric valve or line blocked? If many pumps are affected, the problem is likely the gland water pumps or tank.

The standby pump, if there is one, also needs gland water, so changing over may not help.

Tell the control room operator. Process interlocks can only be bypassed by named users under the site procedure, and running a slurry pump without gland water just converts a trip into a seal failure.
f: Can a standby pump start if gland water is low?
Who is allowed to bypass a gland water interlock?
How do you confirm gland flow is restored?

What is 'gland water'?.q: How do fitters check gland water flow during routine rounds?
What is 'gland water'?.a:
The reference doesn't describe the round. In general, a fitter or operator looks for a steady flow of clean water at the gland and checks local flow indicators or gauges where fitted. They feel or use an infrared gun to check the gland isn't running hot, and look for slurry at the gland, worn hoses, closed valves or leaks.

On pumps with mag flowmeters on gland water, the flow is also visible on the OIS.

Don't adjust packing on a running pump unless the site procedure allows it and the guarding is in place. The area maintenance planner and senior fitters will know the local checks.

f.q: What should a healthy gland look like on a slurry pump?
f.a:
In general, a steady, small flow of clean water, warm at most, with no slurry, no steam and no grinding noise. The surrounding area should be fairly clean, without slurry build up on the pump base or bearing housing.

Warning signs are a hot gland, steam, a dry gland, slurry weeping out, or a drip that suddenly becomes a stream.

What's normal varies by pump and seal type, so learn the good baseline for each pump on your rounds. Like knowing the normal sound of a gearbox, the baseline is what lets you spot change.
f: How much drip from a gland is normal?
Why does a hot gland mean trouble?
What does slurry at the gland tell you?

f.q: Is it safe to adjust gland packing on a running pump?
f.a:
In general, it depends on site rules and pump design. Adjusting gland followers on a running pump puts hands close to a rotating shaft, so many sites restrict it to specific pumps with suitable guarding, or prohibit it entirely and require isolation.

The reference doesn't give the site rule. Ask your supervisor before touching a running gland, and never remove guards from a running machine.

Repacking always requires isolation under the site permit system, with the pump locked out and drained.
f: What guarding covers the gland area?
How is packing replaced under isolation?
What tools are used to tighten gland followers?

f.q: How would gland water problems show up in maintenance records?
f.a:
In general, as repeated packing replacements, shaft sleeve changes and bearing failures on the same pumps, often with notes about leaking glands or slurry contamination. Gland water faults also show in the DCS alarm history as low gland flow trips.

Reliability engineers use the maintenance system to spot bad actors: pumps with far more seal work orders than their peers. Root causes are often gland water supply, wrong flow, or poor packing practice.

The area maintenance planner can show you the history in the site maintenance system.
f: How do I pull pump failure history from the maintenance system?
Which pumps on site use the most packing?
How is a bad actor pump list kept?

What's the difference between 'HP proces.q: Why do sprays and hose points need higher pressure than mill dilution?
What's the difference between 'HP proces.a:
Because sprays and hoses need velocity, while dilution only needs volume. A spray nozzle turns pressure into velocity to wash fines off screen decks, break down froth or scour a floor. Flow velocity scales with the square root of pressure drop across the nozzle, so you need real pressure for a useful jet.

Mill dilution water just has to arrive in a hopper or mill feed chute at atmospheric pressure. Low pressure and big flow suit that.

The trash screens alone use about 60 m3/h of spray each on design figures. It's like the difference between a pressure washer and a garden hose filling a bucket: both deliver water, for different jobs.

f.q: How much spray water do the trash screens use?
f.a:
The PDC gives about 60 m3/h of spray water per trash screen. There are four linear trash screens, 3 operating and 1 standby, so about 180 m3/h when three are running.

Other screens use less: the CIL4 loaded carbon screen and the CIL4 carbon sizing screen are each about 13 m3/h. The future carbon safety screens would need about 263 m3/h each, a big extra HP water demand if they're ever installed.

Spray water is part of what makes the screens work, not an extra. Low spray pressure means poor washing and more trash or fines carried over.
f: What happens to trash removal if spray pressure drops?
Why does the standby trash screen need sprays too?
How are spray nozzles checked for blockage?

f.q: Why does spray nozzle wear matter with process water?
f.a:
In general, process water carries some fine suspended solids and a lot of dissolved salt. Solids erode nozzle orifices, making them bigger, so they pass more water at lower pressure with a poor spray pattern. Salt can crystallise and block small nozzles, especially when sprays sit idle.

Either way the screen gets poorer washing. On screens that matters for trash removal and fines carryover.

Nozzle material choice and regular checks keep this under control. Like injector nozzles on an engine, small changes in the orifice have a big effect on performance.
f: What nozzle materials last longest in saline water?
How do blocked nozzles show on a screen?
How often are spray bars cleaned?

f.q: What is mill circuit water and where does it come from?
f.a:
The PDC describes the existing mill circuit water system: it's sourced from the concentrate pre leach thickener overflow and the concentrate thickener overflow, stored in a circuit water tank of about 1,500 m3 live, and pumped by duty/standby pumps with design flow about 1,800 m3/h.

It's used as lower pressure dilution water in grinding and classification, such as hopper water addition, where density control needs a reliable flow.

Reusing thickener overflow keeps water in the circuit. The reference doesn't list every circuit water user, so check the water services PFDs.
f: Why reuse concentrate thickener overflow as mill water?
How big is the circuit water tank?
Which mills and hoppers receive circuit water?

What's the difference between 'HP proces.q: What would you notice plant wide if HP process water pressure dropped?
What's the difference between 'HP proces.a:
Cleaning and washing jobs would suffer first. Trash screens would wash poorly, so more fines go to oversize and more trash may get through. Flotation launder sprays would weaken, and stiff froth could build up and overflow launders. Hose points would be weak for clean up, and other screen sprays would lose effect.

None of these are instant trips, so the signs are gradual: messier screens, launder alarms, complaints from field operators about hoses.

Check the HP water pumps and whether the standby has started, process water tank level, burst hoses or pipes, and valves left open. Report it to the control room.

f.q: Why do launder sprays matter in flotation?
f.a:
In general, froth carrying sulphides can be stiff and stable, and saline water tends to make froth even more stable. In the launder, that froth may not collapse and flow away, so it builds up and can overflow back into the cell or onto the floor.

Launder sprays knock the froth down so it flows as slurry to the concentrate hopper. The reference notes that launder sprays are on HP process water.

Too much spray water dilutes the concentrate, which the cleaners and thickener then have to handle. It's a balance the operators manage by eye.
f: What happens when a concentrate launder overflows?
Why is saline froth harder to break down?
Can launder sprays dilute concentrate too much?

f.q: How would poor screen spraying affect downstream equipment?
f.a:
In general, sprays rinse fine material off the oversize. With weak sprays, fines stay with the oversize and good ore or slurry goes where it shouldn't. On trash screens, mats of material can carry trash past, which ends up in flotation, UFG trash screens and CIL4 intertank screens.

On carbon screens, poor washing sends slurry with carbon into the transfer vessel and elution column.

So a utility problem becomes a process problem a few hours later. It's like a weak coolant pump: no alarm at first, then overheating somewhere downstream.
f: How does trash carryover reach the CIL tanks?
What happens to carbon if the loaded screen sprays fail?
How is screen spray pressure monitored?

f.q: What could cause HP process water pressure to drop?
f.a:
In general: the duty HP pump tripping with the standby not starting; low level in the process water tank starving the pumps; a burst pipe or hose; too many hose points open at once during clean up; a valve left in the wrong position; or a blocked suction strainer.

The process water tank itself is topped up from Dam 2 by saline pumps that trip on low low dam level, so a water supply problem can show up as HP water pressure loss.

Check PI trends of pump status, header pressure and tank level to narrow it down.
f: Does the HP water pump have an automatic standby start?
How does process water tank level affect the HP pumps?
Where are the strainers on the HP water system?

What's the difference between 'HP proces.q: How are these two water distributions kept separate and metered?
What's the difference between 'HP proces.a:
The reference says the PFDs show both distributions but doesn't describe how they're separated or metered.

In general, they're separate systems with their own pumps and headers at different pressures, sized for their duties, with line numbers in the line list and pipe marking in the field. Main headers usually have flowmeters, and many individual users have flow measurement where water is part of a control loop, such as hopper dilution for density control or the flocculant mixer water (FIT17001 on the flotation tails thickener floc mixer).

For the detail on a specific area, check the water services P&IDs and the line list.

f.q: How are water lines identified in the field?
f.a:
In general, pipes are marked with colour bands and labels showing the fluid and flow direction, following the site standard, and each line has a line number tied to the line list and P&IDs.

The plant numbering spec covers equipment, instruments and cables; the line list gives each pipeline's number, service and size. Field labels let you match a pipe to its drawing.

Before working on any pipe, confirm its service from the label and the drawing, not just its position. Unlabelled lines should be reported.
f: Where can I find the line list for water services?
What colour marks process water pipes on site?
How are cyanide water lines labelled?

f.q: Why does it matter if HP water and mill water get cross connected?
f.a:
In general, connecting a high pressure system to a lower pressure one can over pressurise the low pressure piping, hoses and fittings, which may not be rated for it. It also upsets both systems' control: header pressures and flows go wrong, and dilution control loops behave oddly.

If water of different quality is involved, cross connections can also contaminate a cleaner system, such as process water getting into raw or scheme water.

Changes to water piping should go through the site management of change process, not be done as a quick fix.
f: What protects a low pressure header from overpressure?
How would a cross connection show on trends?
Who approves changes to water piping?

f.q: Which water flows are measured on the DCS?
f.a:
The reference gives examples rather than a full list. Hopper water addition controls cyclone feed or overflow density in milling; dual hopper level control uses water addition at a lower setpoint; UFG feed hopper water addition holds solids or cools the mill. Flocculant dilution water at the flotation tails thickener has FIT17001, and key pumps have gland water flowmeters.

In general, any water flow used in a control loop is measured, and main headers are metered for water balances.

The instrument list for each area shows exactly which water flows have transmitters.
f: How does hopper water addition control cyclone feed density?
Why is dilution water flow controlled rather than just opened?
How are water flowmeters checked for accuracy?

What supplies air to the rougher and sca.q: Why do Jameson cells avoid needing a blower at all?
What supplies air to the rougher and sca.a:
Because the slurry does the work. In a Jameson cell, feed is pumped at pressure through an orifice into the top of a vertical pipe called the downcomer. The high velocity jet creates suction, drawing air in naturally, and plunges into the liquid below, shearing that air into fine bubbles in intense contact with the particles.

The plant reference says Jameson air depends on total pumped flow through the downcomers, and the feed pump runs on a VSD in flow control. About 50 percent of cleaner tails is recycled to the feed hopper to keep downcomer flow constant.

It's like a venturi eductor: the motive fluid's velocity entrains the second fluid, with no separate compressor.

f.q: Why does the Jameson cell recycle tails to keep downcomer flow constant?
f.a:
Air entrainment depends on jet velocity, which depends on flow through each downcomer orifice. If feed to the cleaner varies, downcomer flow and air rate would swing with it, and flotation performance would wander.

So the design recycles roughly half of the cleaner tails back to the cleaner feed hopper, topping up flow when fresh feed is low. That keeps the jet and air rate stable. The cleaner-scavenger works the same way.

It's like a minimum flow recirculation line on a centrifugal pump: it keeps the machine at its design point regardless of process demand.
f: What happens to air entrainment if downcomer flow drops?
How is the recycle split controlled?
Does recycling tails reduce cleaner capacity?

f.q: How does a plunging jet create such fine bubbles?
f.a:
In general, the jet hits the liquid in the downcomer at high speed and creates a zone of intense turbulence and shear. Entrained air is torn into very small bubbles, and particles collide with bubbles in a confined space at high frequency.

Fine bubbles give a large bubble surface area per unit of air, which suits fine particles that are hard to catch with big bubbles. That's why Jameson cells are popular for cleaning duties on fine concentrate.

It's similar to how a high pressure atomising nozzle produces finer droplets than a low pressure one.
f: Why do fine bubbles suit fine particles?
What wears out in a Jameson downcomer?
How is the downcomer orifice size chosen?

f.q: What's the trade off of using pumps instead of blowers for air?
f.a:
In general, the energy for aeration moves from a blower to the feed pump, which has to deliver enough pressure at the orifice to form the jet. You need a stable, controlled flow, hence the VSD and the tails recycle.

Orifices and downcomers wear and can block, so they need inspection and replacement. But there are no blowers, air valves or agitators in the cell itself, which simplifies the mechanical side.

So it's a trade: fewer machines, but the feed pump becomes critical. If it stops, the cell gets neither feed nor air.
f: How often are Jameson orifice plates replaced?
What happens if a downcomer blocks?
How is Jameson air rate measured?

What supplies air to the rougher and sca.q: What would falling froth quality suggest if a blower tripped?
What supplies air to the rougher and sca.a:
That the remaining blowers can't fully cover the air demand. The PDC gives four low pressure blowers, duty/duty/duty/standby, each about 8,688 m3/h free air delivery. The control philosophy has the blowers on VSDs holding header pressure, with each cell's air set by a flow controller and mass flow meter.

When one trips, header pressure dips, the remaining blowers speed up, and the standby should be brought in. If air can't be restored, cell air flow controllers run out of valve, cells get less air, froth thins and mass pull drops, so more gold goes to tails and on to CIL4.

Check blower status and header pressure, and tell the control room.

f.q: How do the blower VSDs respond when one blower trips?
f.a:
The blowers run on VSDs in a header pressure loop. When a blower trips, header pressure drops, and the controller speeds up the running blowers to bring pressure back to setpoint, within their capacity.

Downstream, each cell's air flow controller opens its valve further to hold its own air setpoint. As long as the remaining blowers can supply total demand, the cells barely notice.

The reference doesn't say whether the standby blower starts automatically. It's like a multi pump booster set: the pressure loop shares load, but you need to know if the spare cuts in by itself.
f: Does the standby blower start automatically?
How much spare capacity do three duty blowers have?
What sets the blower header pressure setpoint?

f.q: Why does less air lower flotation recovery?
f.a:
In general, air provides the bubbles that carry hydrophobic particles up into the froth. Less air means less bubble surface area for particles to attach to, so fewer particles get collected and the froth layer thins. Mass pull drops, and slower floating sulphides stay in the pulp and go to tails.

Too much air isn't good either: it can make the froth unstable or carry more gangue. That's why air is a key lever for the flotation expert system, which uses the onstream analyser and froth cameras.

It's like fuel to a burner: too little and output drops, too much and it runs dirty.
f: Can too much air also hurt recovery?
How does froth depth interact with air rate?
What does the froth camera measure?

f.q: Why does each cell's air valve close if its agitator stops?
f.a:
The control philosophy says each cell's air valve is interlocked closed if its agitator stops, to prevent sanding of the rotor and stator and to protect the bearings.

In general, with the agitator stopped, solids settle around the rotor. Air blowing up through settled solids can pack them around the mechanism, so restarting means breaking out a buried rotor under load, which is hard on the drive and bearings.

The philosophy also says agitators should keep running whenever a cell has slurry or water in it.
f: How does air cause sanding of a stopped rotor?
What restarts air after the agitator restarts?
Why must agitators keep running with slurry in the cell?

What supplies air to the rougher and sca.q: How many blowers run duty and standby for these cell banks?
What supplies air to the rougher and sca.a:
Four. The PDC lists four low pressure flotation blowers in a duty/duty/duty/standby arrangement. They're oil free screw blowers with sound enclosures, each with a design capacity of about 8,688 m3/h free air delivery, giving about 26,064 m3/h from the three duty units, at a design pressure of about 119.7 kPa gauge.

They supply the FLS forced air tank cells: three roughers and four scavengers. The Jameson cleaner and cleaner-scavenger don't use blower air.

Control is by VSDs holding header pressure, with air to each cell set by its own flow controller. These are design values; check the OIS for what's actually running.

f.q: Why are the flotation blowers oil free?
f.a:
In general, any oil carried into the air would end up in the flotation pulp. Oil acts like a collector or froth modifier and can upset flotation chemistry, float unwanted material or destabilise the froth. Oil free blowers avoid that risk.

The PDC specifies low pressure, oil free screw blowers for flotation air.

It's the same reason food and pharmaceutical plants use oil free compressors: when the air touches the product, the air quality matters.
f: How would oil in the air upset flotation?
What maintenance do oil free screw blowers need?
Why do the blowers have sound enclosures?

f.q: How does blower capacity compare with the cells' air demand?
f.a:
The PDC gives about 26,064 m3/h of duty blower capacity, but doesn't give the air demand per cell in the condensed reference, so I can't confirm the margin.

In general, blower capacity is sized for the maximum air rate the cells might need, plus allowance for losses and future flexibility, with the standby providing redundancy rather than extra capacity.

The flotation design section of the PDC or the FLS cell data would have the per cell air rates. The flotation metallurgist would also know the typical operating air flows.
f: What air flow does each tank cell use?
How is air split between roughers and scavengers?
Does air demand rise in the high throughput case?

f.q: What's the difference between plant air and flotation air?
f.a:
Very different duties. Flotation air comes from the low pressure blowers: large volumes (about 8,688 m3/h each) at about 120 kPa gauge, just enough to push air down into the cells against the slurry head.

High pressure air comes from three oil injected rotary screw compressors (duty/duty/standby), each about 750 L/s at about 980 kPa gauge, for the new facilities. That supplies plant air for tools and actuators and, after drying and filtering, instrument air.

It's like the difference between a fan and a compressor: one moves lots of air gently, the other delivers less air at high pressure.
f: Why is instrument air dried and filtered?
What uses plant air on the plant?
Why are the compressors oil injected but the blowers oil free?

Why is instrument air kept separate from.q: Why does wet or dirty air specifically foul positioners and solenoids?
Why is instrument air kept separate from.a:
Positioners and solenoid pilot valves are precision pneumatic devices. They have tiny nozzles, orifices, spool clearances and diaphragms, often a fraction of a millimetre across. Think of them like the servo valve on a hydraulic press: a little dirt makes them stick or leak.

Water condenses when compressed air cools in field piping, and it carries rust and pipe scale with it. The plant's high pressure air comes from oil injected rotary screw compressors (per the PDC), so oil carryover is another risk, leaving a varnish that gums up spools.

The result is valves that hunt, stick, respond late or fail to stroke, which shows up as poor loop control and nuisance alarms.

f.q: Where does the moisture in compressed air actually come from?
f.a:
It comes from the humidity in the air drawn into the compressor. Compressing air to around 1,000 kPa squeezes the same water vapour into a much smaller volume, so the air becomes saturated and the dew point rises sharply.

The aftercooler condenses a lot of it out, much like a condenser on a refrigeration plant, and drains remove the liquid. The air leaving the aftercooler is still saturated though, so any further cooling in field lines drops more water out.

The dryer's job is to lower the pressure dew point well below the coldest temperature the pipework will see, so nothing condenses downstream.
f: What is the difference between a refrigerated and a desiccant dryer?
Why do condensate drains need regular checking?
What dew point should instrument air be dried to?

f.q: What does a sticking positioner look like on a control loop trend?
f.a:
Sticking, or stiction, gives a very recognisable pattern. The controller output (CV) ramps slowly as integral action builds up, but the valve does not move. Then friction breaks free, the valve jumps, and the process variable (PV) overshoots. The controller winds back the other way and the cycle repeats.

On a trend this looks like a sawtooth on the CV and a square or stepped wave on the PV, cycling steadily around setpoint. It is a limit cycle, similar to a slip stick vibration in a machine slide.

Retuning the loop will not fix it. The valve or positioner needs attention, so raise it with instrument maintenance.
f: How do instrument techs test a valve for stiction?
Can dirty air cause valve limit switch alarms on the OIS?
Why does integral action make stiction cycles worse?

f.q: How is oil removed if the compressors are oil injected?
f.a:
The PDC lists three oil injected rotary screw compressors, duty/duty/standby, about 750 L/s each at about 980 kPa(g), serving the new facilities. Oil injection seals and cools the screw rotors, so some oil always leaves with the air.

In general practice the package has an oil separator vessel that removes most of it. Downstream, coalescing filters capture fine oil mist and particulate filters catch dust and desiccant fines, sometimes with an activated carbon stage for oil vapour.

The reference does not give the exact filter arrangement for this plant, so check the air system P&ID or ask the utilities maintenance planner. Filter differential pressure gauges show when elements need changing.
f: How often are coalescing filter elements usually replaced?
What happens if the compressor oil separator fails?
Do plant air and instrument air share the same compressors?

Why is instrument air kept separate from.q: What would you see across the plant if the instrument air dryer failed?
Why is instrument air kept separate from.a:
The reference does not describe a specific dryer failure case, so this is general engineering reasoning applied to the plant.

Wet air would reach every pneumatic device fed from that header. Expect sluggish or erratic control valves, loops cycling, and an increase in valve alarms on the OIS. The DCS valve logic includes watchdog timers for fail to open or fail to close, and flags both limit switches on or both off, so many of those alarms appearing together is a strong clue.

You may also see water at low point drains and filter bowls. Problems are often worse on cold early mornings when more water condenses. Raise it quickly with the control room and utilities maintenance.

f.q: Why would a dryer fault show up worse on cold mornings?
f.a:
Air that leaves a failed dryer is saturated at compressor discharge temperature. Any pipe colder than that air condenses water, just as a cold glass sweats on a humid day.

Overnight, outdoor pipe racks and field tubing cool down a lot, so the temperature difference is biggest early in the morning. More water drops out, collects in low points and gets pushed into valve positioners as demand picks up.

In very cold conditions water can even freeze in small tubing or vent ports. That is why instrument air is dried to a dew point below the lowest expected ambient temperature, not just below room temperature.
f: How is a dryer's dew point monitored on site?
Why do low point drains matter on air headers?
Can a dryer be bypassed safely for maintenance?

f.q: Which DCS alarms would flag many valves misbehaving at once?
f.a:
The control philosophy gives every automated valve a watchdog timer. If a valve is commanded open or closed and its limit switch does not confirm within the set time, a fail to open or fail to close alarm is raised. A valve showing both limit switches made, or neither, is also flagged.

Control loops would show deviation alarms where the PV cannot follow setpoint. Interlocks may trip equipment if a permissive valve fails to reach position.

One or two of these alarms is normal maintenance. A burst of them across different areas at the same time points to a common cause, and the air supply is a prime suspect.
f: What is first out detection and how would it help here?
How do alarm priorities work under ISA 18.2 on this plant?
Why are alarms masked when equipment is not running?

f.q: Do fail safe valves move to a safe position if air is lost?
f.a:
Most pneumatic control valves are spring return. The designer chooses the fail position, open, closed or last position, based on what is safest for the process, and it is shown on the P&ID as fail open (FO), fail closed (FC) or fail last (FL).

When air pressure collapses, the spring drives each valve to its fail position. That is safe by design but it is still a plant upset, because many valves moving at once will stop flows, dump hoppers or isolate reagents.

The reference does not list the fail positions for individual valves, so check the P&ID for any valve you care about.
f: How do I read the fail position symbol on a P&ID?
Why might a dump valve be designed to fail open?
What does fail last position mean for a valve?

Why is instrument air kept separate from.q: What backup does the instrument air receiver give during a compressor trip?
Why is instrument air kept separate from.a:
An air receiver is a pressure vessel that stores compressed air, like an accumulator in a hydraulic circuit. When a compressor trips, the receiver keeps supplying the header while pressure falls, buying time for the standby compressor to start or for operators to respond.

How long it lasts depends on its volume, the pressure drop the instruments can tolerate and the air demand. The reference does not give the receiver size or ride through time, so do not assume a number.

The PDC shows three high pressure compressors in duty/duty/standby, so losing one should not starve the plant if the standby starts. The receiver also smooths pressure swings from compressor load and unload cycling.

f.q: How do you estimate how long a receiver lasts with no compressor?
f.a:
A quick estimate uses the volume and allowable pressure drop. Time in minutes is roughly the receiver volume in cubic metres, times the pressure drop in bar, divided by atmospheric pressure (about 1 bar) and the free air demand in cubic metres per minute.

For example, a 10 m3 receiver allowed to fall from 9 to 6 bar holds about 30 m3 of free air. At a demand of 10 m3 per minute that is only about three minutes.

These are illustration numbers, not plant values. The real answer depends on the actual receiver size and demand, which you would get from the air system data sheet or utilities engineer.
f: What is the minimum pressure instruments need to work properly?
Why is compressor capacity quoted as free air delivery?
Can leaks in the air system shorten receiver ride through?

f.q: What happens to valves when instrument air pressure falls too low?
f.a:
As header pressure drops, positioners lose the force they need to hold valves against process forces and spring loads. Valves first respond slowly and drift off position, then, below a certain pressure, springs win and the valves move to their designed fail positions.

On a big plant this means many loops lose control together: hopper levels, densities, reagent dosing and flotation cell levels can all swing. Interlocks may then trip pumps and mills.

That is why low instrument air pressure is normally an alarm well before it becomes critical, giving operators time to act. Exact alarm setpoints for this plant are not in the reference.
f: Why do flotation cell levels upset so fast when air drops?
Which loops on this plant would hurt most on air loss?
How do operators recover a plant after an air failure?

f.q: Does the standby compressor start automatically on a trip?
f.a:
The PDC configures the high pressure compressors as duty/duty/standby, which implies the standby is there to cover a trip or maintenance. The control philosophy lists the air compressor package as a vendor package with its own PLC, monitored by the DCS rather than controlled by it.

So the start logic lives in the vendor controller. Typically such packages auto start the standby on low header pressure or a duty unit fault, but the reference does not confirm how this plant's package is set up.

To be sure, ask the utilities maintenance planner or the control systems engineer, or check the compressor vendor manual.
f: What compressor alarms does the DCS actually see?
How is duty rotated between the air compressors?
Who looks after vendor package PLCs on site?

What's lime used for, and how is it deli.q: Why does low pH in leach risk releasing HCN gas?
What's lime used for, and how is it deli.a:
Cyanide exists in two forms in solution: the cyanide ion (CN) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). Which form dominates depends on pH. Around pH 9.2 to 9.3 they are present in equal amounts. Below that, more cyanide becomes HCN, which is volatile, boils at about 26 C and readily escapes as a toxic gas.

At pH 10.5 and above nearly all cyanide stays as the ion, which also keeps it available to dissolve gold.

On this plant CIL2 runs at pH 11.75 to 12.5 in the early tanks. CIL4's design leach pH is 8.8 to 9.3, much closer to the danger zone, which is one reason CIL4 has an HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren.

f.q: Why does CIL4 run at a much lower pH than CIL2?
f.a:
The reference gives the CIL4 design pH of 8.8 to 9.3 but does not explain why, so treat this as general reasoning to check with a metallurgist.

CIL4 treats over 3,000 t/h of flotation tails in saline process water. Saline bore water usually carries a lot of magnesium, and adding lime precipitates magnesium hydroxide, which buffers pH and consumes lime heavily. Pushing a huge tonnage of low grade slurry to pH 11 would cost a lot of lime for a modest benefit.

Running lower accepts more cyanide loss as HCN and more gas risk, so gas monitoring and good ventilation become more important.
f: How much lime does saline water typically consume?
Does lower pH change cyanide consumption in CIL4?
What other gases could form in a cyanide leach tank?

f.q: What does the HCN gas monitor do when it detects gas?
f.a:
The control philosophy says CIL4 has an HCN gas monitor with a beacon and siren. When gas exceeds the alarm level, the beacon and siren warn people nearby, and the alarm reports to the control room.

Your response is to follow the site emergency procedure: move away, upwind, and do not enter the area to investigate. Re-entry is controlled by trained responders with gas detection and breathing apparatus.

The CRO will look at pH and cyanide dosing on the leach tanks, because low pH or a cyanide overdose are the usual process causes. Exact alarm setpoints are not in the reference, so check the area procedure.
f: Where are HCN monitors usually placed around leach tanks?
What personal gas detectors are used around cyanide?
How is cyanide exposure first aid handled on site?

f.q: How does the pH controller on CIL4 tank 1 dose lime?
f.a:
Per the control philosophy, a pH analyser on CIL4 tank 1 drives a controller that opens the milk of lime valve at the CIL4 feed distribution box. Tank 2's pH probe is the backup if tank 1's probe is out.

It is a feedback loop with a long dead time: lime added at the feed box takes time to mix through a 5,600 m3 tank before the probe sees it. That is like controlling a shower temperature with a long pipe between mixer and head. Tuning has to be gentle or the loop will overshoot and cycle.

pH probes foul in lime slurry, so they need regular cleaning and calibration.
f: Why are pH probes in lime slurry so prone to fouling?
What happens to pH control if the lime valve sticks?
How does Carbon Scout pH data back up the tank probes?

What's lime used for, and how is it deli.q: What would you check if lime ringmain pressure dropped?
What's lime used for, and how is it deli.a:
The lime system is a ringmain with duty/standby DOL pumps from the milk of lime tank, per the reference. A pressure drop is like losing pressure in a hydraulic header: either supply has weakened or demand has jumped.

Check, in rough order: is the duty pump running or did it trip, and did the standby take over? Is the milk of lime tank level low? Is a dosing valve wide open or a line leaking or burst? Is the line or a valve scaled up or blocked?

Lime lines are notorious for scaling and settling, so a slow decline suggests buildup, while a sudden drop points to a trip, leak or burst.

f.q: Why do milk of lime lines scale up and block so often?
f.a:
Milk of lime is a slurry of calcium hydroxide particles in water. Two things cause trouble.

First, settling: if velocity falls too low, particles drop out in low points, dead legs and partly closed valves, like sand in a slow pipe. Second, scaling: dissolved calcium reacts with carbon dioxide and with carbonates in the water to form hard calcite scale on pipe walls, valve seats and instruments.

Ringmains help by keeping slurry moving continuously. Plants also flush lines, design for minimum velocities, use pinch or full bore valves and replace scaled sections periodically.
f: How are scaled lime lines cleaned or descaled?
Why are pinch valves popular in lime service?
What velocity keeps milk of lime solids in suspension?

f.q: What happens to leach pH if the ringmain stops entirely?
f.a:
With no lime flowing, pH in the leach tanks starts to drift down. Ore and saline water consume alkalinity continuously, so the drop is gradual but steady.

The CIL4 pH controller will open the lime valve fully with no effect, and low pH alarms should follow. As pH falls, more cyanide converts to HCN gas, cyanide consumption rises and gas alarms become more likely.

CIL2 runs at a higher design pH (11.75 to 12.5), which gives some margin but not unlimited time. Restoring lime is a priority, and the metallurgist and CRO may reduce cyanide addition or feed until it is back.
f: How long can a leach tank hold pH without lime addition?
Why might cyanide dosing be cut back during a lime outage?
Is there a backup lime supply if the ringmain fails?

f.q: Why use a ringmain instead of a pump per dosing point?
f.a:
A ringmain is a loop that runs continuously from the tank, past every dosing point and back to the tank. It works like a hydronic heating loop: the pumps keep a steady header pressure and each user simply opens its own valve.

For slurry like milk of lime, constant circulation keeps the solids in suspension so lines do not settle out between dosing demands. One pump set (duty/standby here) serves many users, which is simpler than a pump at every point.

The downside is that a single ringmain fault affects every dosing point at once, which is why pump redundancy and line maintenance matter.
f: How is ringmain pressure held constant as users open valves?
What happens to a dosing point at the end of a long ringmain?
Why are cyanide and caustic also on ringmains here?

What's lime used for, and how is it deli.q: How is the slaking package maintained to keep milk of lime consistent?
What's lime used for, and how is it deli.a:
The reference describes the Stage 2 lime plant as a vendor package with two parallel circuits, slaking mills, cyclones and a scrubber, feeding the milk of lime tank. It does not give the maintenance routine, so for the actual procedure ask the area maintenance planner or check the vendor manual.

In general, consistent milk of lime depends on stable quicklime feed rate, correct water to lime ratio and slaking temperature, removal of grit and unslaked lumps by the cyclones, and keeping the mill and pumps in good condition.

Typical maintenance includes checking slaking mill wear parts and liners, cyclone wear, clearing grit, servicing the scrubber that captures lime dust, and calibrating feeders and density measurements.

f.q: Why does slaking water ratio and temperature matter so much?
f.a:
Slaking is the reaction of quicklime (calcium oxide) with water to form calcium hydroxide. It releases a lot of heat.

If the water ratio and temperature are right, the reaction produces very fine, reactive particles that stay suspended and dissolve quickly in the leach. Too much water cools the reaction and gives coarser, slower reacting particles. Too little water can overheat and even boil, producing poor quality lime and steam.

So the slaker is controlled a bit like a reactor with a heat balance. Consistent particle size gives consistent dosing response in the pH loops downstream.
f: What does poor quality lime do to pH control loops?
How is milk of lime strength measured?
Why does quicklime need dust control when handled?

f.q: What are the cyclones in the lime plant actually removing?
f.a:
The reference lists cyclones in the vendor lime plant but does not describe their exact duty, so this is the usual arrangement.

Quicklime contains impurities like sand, unburnt limestone and lumps that do not slake. These are coarse and dense compared with fine calcium hydroxide. The cyclones split them out: the coarse grit reports to underflow, often returning to the slaking mill for more grinding or being rejected, while the fine slurry goes to the milk of lime tank.

Removing grit protects the ringmain pumps, valves and pipes from wear and blockage, much like a strainer protects a hydraulic system.
f: What happens if grit gets into the lime ringmain?
Why does the slaking mill grind quicklime at all?
How often do lime cyclones wear out?

f.q: Why does the lime plant have two parallel circuits?
f.a:
The reference states the Stage 2 vendor lime plant has two parallel circuits but does not say why. The usual reasons are reliability and maintainability.

With two circuits, one can be stopped for maintenance, liner changes or blockage clearing while the other keeps the milk of lime tank supplied. It also lets the plant run one circuit at lower demand and both at high demand, like running two pumps in parallel only when flow requires it.

Since leach pH control and HCN safety depend on lime, keeping supply going during maintenance is important.
f: Can one lime circuit meet full plant demand alone?
How big is the milk of lime tank buffer?
What triggers switching between the two lime circuits?

Why is flocculant added to thickeners?.q: Why do fine particles settle so much faster once flocculated?
Why is flocculant added to thickeners?.a:
Settling speed of a small particle follows Stokes' law: it rises with the square of the particle diameter. Double the size and it settles roughly four times faster. Make it ten times bigger and it can settle around a hundred times faster.

Fine particles from grinding, especially slimes of a few microns, settle so slowly that they would stay in the overflow. Flocculant is a long chain polymer that adsorbs onto many particles at once and bridges them into large, loose flocs.

The flocs are less dense than solid particles, which slows them a little, but the size increase wins by a big margin. The result is clear overflow and a thicker underflow.

f.q: Why does saline process water affect how flocculant works?
f.a:
This plant's process water is saline bore water with an SG of about 1.07. Water chemistry changes how polymers behave.

High salt content compresses the electrical charge layer around particles, which actually helps them approach each other and coagulate. But it can also make the polymer chains coil up rather than stretch out, which weakens their bridging reach. Calcium and magnesium ions can interact with anionic polymers too.

That is why flocculant type is chosen from testwork with the actual water and ore. The reference does not name the specific flocculant product used here.
f: What is the difference between a coagulant and a flocculant?
How is flocculant chosen from thickener testwork?
Does water temperature affect flocculant performance?

f.q: Why is flocculant dosed dilute rather than neat?
f.a:
Flocculant solution is very viscous, a bit like thin honey. If added strong, it does not spread through the slurry fast enough. Some particles get far too much polymer and others none, giving poor flocs and wasted reagent.

Diluting it lets it disperse quickly and evenly in the feed well. The reference notes an inline mixer for secondary dilution on the flotation tails thickener floc line, which mixes in extra water just before dosing.

The polymer is first made up at higher strength in the flocculant plant, then aged and diluted. Dilution is like atomising fuel in a burner: better mixing gives better reaction.
f: Why does made up flocculant need ageing time?
What water is used to dilute flocculant here?
What are fish eyes in flocculant make up?

f.q: Why is the feed well the right place to add flocculant?
f.a:
The feed well is a cylinder at the thickener centre where feed enters and slows down. It is designed to dissipate the feed's energy and give a short, gentle mixing zone before slurry spreads out into the tank.

Flocculant needs some mixing to contact particles, but too much shear tears the flocs apart again. The feed well gives the right balance: enough turbulence to spread polymer, then calm conditions for flocs to grow.

Adding it too far upstream in a pipe or pump would shear the flocs. Adding it out in the tank would give poor contact. Feed dilution in the feed well also helps flocculation.
f: Why does feed dilution improve flocculation?
What happens if the feed well is damaged or blocked?
How do flocs behave once they settle into the bed?

Why is flocculant added to thickeners?.q: What would overdosed flocculant look like in the underflow?
Why is flocculant added to thickeners?.a:
Overdosed underflow tends to be sticky, gluey and high in yield stress, almost like wet clay. The bed compacts into a thick mass that resists flow.

Signs include rising rake torque, higher underflow pump discharge pressure or lower flow for the same pump speed, and possibly ratholing where the pump draws a channel through the bed instead of pulling evenly. Overflow is often very clear, which can fool people into thinking all is well.

Overdosing also wastes expensive reagent. The thickener vendor panel signals listed in the reference (rake torque, bed level, bed pressure, overflow clarity) are the main tools to spot it.

f.q: Why does sticky underflow push rake torque up?
f.a:
The rake arms plough through the settled bed to move solids toward the central discharge cone. The force they need depends on the bed's resistance, which is set by its yield stress and depth.

Overdosed flocs bind into a strong network, so the bed resists shearing much more. The rake drive has to deliver more torque to push through it, just as a mixer motor draws more current in thick dough.

If torque keeps rising the rakes may lift automatically or trip on high torque. That is why rake torque is a key signal on the vendor panel and why sticky underflow is a mechanical risk, not just a process issue.
f: How do rake lifting systems respond to high torque?
What torque level trips a thickener rake drive?
Why can rake damage be so expensive to repair?

f.q: Can excess flocculant cause problems downstream in CIL4?
f.a:
The reference does not cover this directly, so this is general experience from other plants.

Residual polymer carried in thickener underflow can coat carbon particles, which can reduce gold adsorption rates. It can also contribute to sticky slurry that makes intertank screens blind more easily, and may affect slurry rheology so agitators and pumps work harder.

The effect is usually modest at normal doses but grows with overdosing. If CIL4 screens or adsorption performance worsen at the same time as high floc use, it is worth raising with the metallurgist as a possible link.
f: How would the metallurgist test for carbon fouling?
What causes intertank screens to blind in CIL tanks?
How does slurry rheology affect agitator power?

f.q: How would you tell overdosing from simple overloading?
f.a:
Both give high rake torque, but other signals differ.

Overloading means more solids are arriving than the thickener can discharge. The bed level rises, bed pressure climbs and overflow often becomes dirty as solids escape upward.

Overdosing gives a very clear overflow with a sticky bed. Torque rises but bed level may not rise much; underflow flow becomes hard to pull even at higher pump speed.

So compare overflow clarity, bed level, bed pressure and floc dose rate together on the trends. One signal alone can mislead, which is why the vendor panel provides several.
f: What does a rising bed level alone tell you?
How is bed pressure related to bed mass?
What is overflow clarity measured with?

Why is flocculant added to thickeners?.q: How is flocculant dosage tuned across different thickeners on site?
Why is flocculant added to thickeners?.a:
The reference gives the control method rather than set doses.

On the flotation tails thickener, Stage 1 flocculant dosing was cascaded from bed level measured by a Manta sub. In Stage 2 it changes to a ratio of flocculant to feed solids, a grams per tonne setpoint, with an inline mixer for secondary dilution.

The existing thickeners use flocculant pumps on VSDs cascaded from bed level. The flocculant plant makes up solution with a screw feeder, heated cone, blower and wetting head.

Actual operating doses are set by metallurgists from testwork and plant experience, so ask them for current targets.

f.q: What does a g/t ratio setpoint do when feed tonnage changes?
f.a:
A ratio setpoint is a feedforward control. The controller measures feed solids mass flow and multiplies it by the g/t setpoint to give the flocculant flow target. If tonnage rises 10 percent, floc flow rises 10 percent straight away, before the thickener bed has even responded.

It is like the fuel to air ratio control on a burner: you do not wait for oxygen to drop before adding air.

The weakness is that it assumes ore behaves the same. If ore gets finer or clay rich, the right dose changes, so operators or the expert layer still need to adjust the ratio.
f: How is feed solids mass flow measured on the thickener?
Can ratio control be trimmed by a feedback signal?
What happens if the feed density meter fails?

f.q: Why switch from bed level control to a feed ratio in Stage 2?
f.a:
The reference states the change but not the reason, so this is general reasoning.

Bed level control is feedback with a very slow response: a dose change takes a long time to show in bed level, so the loop is sluggish and can overshoot. In Stage 2 all flotation tails thickener underflow goes to CIL4, so stable underflow density matters more for leach residence time and reagent use.

A feed ratio responds immediately to tonnage changes, which suits a high, varying feed rate. Bed level and bed pressure are still watched and used for underflow pump control.
f: How does underflow density affect CIL4 residence time?
Why are thickener loops so slow to respond?
Is bed level still used for any control in Stage 2?

f.q: What do the heated cone and wetting head do in the floc plant?
f.a:
Powdered flocculant absorbs moisture readily. If it gets damp in the hopper or feed cone, it forms lumps and blocks the screw feeder. A heated cone keeps the powder dry and free flowing at that point.

The blower conveys the metered powder to the wetting head, which sprays water to wet each particle individually as it enters the make up tank. If powder lumps hit water together, they form gel balls called fish eyes, with dry powder trapped inside, which waste reagent and block strainers.

The reference lists these parts. The function described is general practice for polymer make up systems.
f: How long does flocculant need to age after mixing?
What happens if the floc screw feeder blocks?
How is flocculant make up strength controlled?

What is hydrogen peroxide used for?.q: Why does oxidising cyanide with peroxide make water safe to reuse?
What is hydrogen peroxide used for?.a:
Hydrogen peroxide oxidises cyanide to cyanate. Cyanate is far less toxic than cyanide, and over time it breaks down further into ammonia and carbonate.

Peroxide works on free cyanide and on the weak acid dissociable (WAD) complexes, mainly copper, zinc and nickel cyanides, which release cyanide easily and are the forms that matter for wildlife and people. Copper in the water actually catalyses the reaction.

On this plant peroxide is dosed through inline mixers on the 3 decant water lines, controlled by an online WAD cyanide analyser, to a residual WAD target below 1.5 in the PDC. Lower WAD reduces the risk wherever that water is handled or exposed. It is reduced risk, not zero.

f.q: What happens to the cyanate formed after peroxide treatment?
f.a:
Cyanate (OCN) is much less toxic than cyanide. In water it slowly hydrolyses to ammonia and carbonate, especially in acidic or warm conditions.

Ammonia can be a concern in its own right in some environments, so overall water quality still matters, but it is a far smaller hazard than the cyanide it replaced.

In a closed water circuit returning to the plant, cyanate generally does not interfere much with leaching. The reference does not cover cyanate monitoring on this site, so the environmental team would know if it is tracked.
f: Does ammonia from cyanate affect flotation or leach?
How is cyanate measured in plant water?
Does cyanate break down faster in hot weather?

f.q: Why does copper in the water matter for peroxide destruction?
f.a:
Copper plays two roles. First, copper cyanide complexes form part of WAD cyanide, so they must be destroyed too. Second, copper ions act as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction between peroxide and cyanide considerably.

Without enough copper, peroxide reacts slowly and more of it decomposes to water and oxygen before it finds cyanide, which wastes reagent. Some plants add copper sulphate for this reason. This plant uses copper sulphate as a flotation activator, though the reference does not say it is added to the destruct.

When destroyed, copper typically precipitates as a hydroxide.
f: Does flotation copper sulphate end up in decant water?
What other metals form WAD cyanide complexes?
Why does peroxide decompose without doing useful work?

f.q: What is the difference between WAD and total cyanide?
f.a:
Total cyanide includes every form: free cyanide, weak complexes and strong complexes. WAD, weak acid dissociable, cyanide covers only the free cyanide plus the weak metal complexes, mainly zinc, copper, nickel and cadmium, that release cyanide in mildly acidic conditions.

The strong iron complexes (ferrocyanide and ferricyanide) are very stable and not counted in WAD.

WAD is what regulators, environmental codes and wildlife protection focus on, because it represents the cyanide that can become biologically available. That is why this plant's destruct targets residual WAD rather than total cyanide.
f: Why are iron cyanide complexes considered low risk?
What WAD level is considered safe for wildlife?
How does sunlight affect cyanide in ponds?

What is hydrogen peroxide used for?.q: What would a handover flag if the online WAD analyser failed?
What is hydrogen peroxide used for?.a:
The reference says peroxide dosing is controlled by the online WAD analyser and flowmeters, but does not describe a fallback mode, so this answer is general practice.

A good handover would flag that the analyser is down, what mode peroxide dosing is now in (typically a fixed manual rate or flow ratio set conservatively), and when the last valid reading and last lab sample were taken.

It would also note increased manual sampling for WAD, who has been told (instrument technician, metallurgist, environmental team), and whether peroxide stock and pump status are healthy. Without feedback there is a real risk of under or over dosing, so it needs active attention.

f.q: Why is overdosing peroxide also a problem, not just underdosing?
f.a:
Underdosing leaves WAD cyanide above target, which is the obvious risk. But overdosing has costs too.

Peroxide is expensive, so overdosing wastes money quickly at plant water flows. Excess peroxide decomposes to oxygen and water, which can release gas in pipes and tanks. Strong oxidiser residuals may also affect equipment or downstream processes where the water is reused.

So the aim is to dose just enough to hit the residual WAD target, like a fuel trim that keeps a boiler slightly lean rather than wasting fuel. Analyser feedback is what makes that precision possible.
f: How much peroxide per kilogram of cyanide is typical?
Can residual peroxide affect leaching if water returns?
What does the PDC say about peroxide supply strength?

f.q: How would grab samples back up a failed WAD analyser?
f.a:
Operators or lab technicians take grab samples from the decant lines and test them for WAD cyanide, usually by titration or a picric acid or colorimetric method in the site lab.

The drawback is time delay. A result may take an hour or more, so control is slower and dosing is usually set more conservatively to cover the gap.

Sample frequency during an outage is normally set by the metallurgist or environmental team. The reference does not specify this site's procedure, so check with the control room or lab supervisor.
f: How is the online WAD analyser calibrated against the lab?
Why does sample delay make dosing control harder?
Who decides when the analyser is back in service?

f.q: Why is 70% hydrogen peroxide handled so carefully?
f.a:
The PDC lists peroxide supplied at 70 percent w/v (SG 1.29), delivered in bulk isotainers and unloaded by compressed air displacement.

At this strength it is a powerful oxidiser. Contact with organic material, rust, metals or dirt can make it decompose rapidly, releasing heat and oxygen. In a closed space that can build pressure or start a fire. It also causes serious skin and eye burns.

So storage is vented, kept clean and compatible in material, and spills are flushed with lots of water. Never trap peroxide between closed valves in a line, because decomposition can pressurise it.
f: Why is peroxide unloaded by air displacement here?
What materials are compatible with strong peroxide?
What is the spill response for hydrogen peroxide?

What is hydrogen peroxide used for?.q: How is peroxide dosing rate set relative to WAD cyanide readings?
What is hydrogen peroxide used for?.a:
The reference says peroxide is dosed through inline mixers on each of the 3 decant water lines, controlled by the online WAD analyser and flowmeters, to a residual WAD target below 1.5. The PDC lists duty/duty/duty/standby dosing pumps, with the standby acting as a lag pump when peroxide demand is high.

The detailed algorithm is not in the reference. In general practice the controller works out the cyanide load from water flow times WAD concentration, applies a peroxide to cyanide ratio, then trims with feedback from the residual reading.

Theoretical peroxide demand is about 1.3 kg per kg of cyanide, but real plants usually need more because of side reactions and decomposition.

f.q: Why does each decant line need its own inline mixer?
f.a:
Peroxide has to mix thoroughly with the water to react before the water reaches its destination. An inline static mixer creates turbulence over a short pipe length, like baffles in a heat exchanger, so the dose spreads evenly across the flow.

Each of the 3 decant lines carries its own flow and possibly its own cyanide load, so each gets its own dosing point and mixer. That lets dosing match each line rather than overdosing one and underdosing another.

The reference confirms 3 inline mixers, one per line. Contact time after the mixer also matters for the reaction to finish.
f: How much contact time does peroxide need to react?
Do the three decant lines carry different WAD levels?
What is a static mixer's pressure drop cost?

f.q: What does a lag pump do when peroxide demand is high?
f.a:
The PDC configures the peroxide dosing pumps as duty/duty/duty/standby, noting that the standby acts as a lag pump to the duty pumps when peroxide demand is high.

So normally three pumps run, likely one per decant line, with the fourth on standby for a failure. If demand rises beyond what the duty pumps can deliver, the fourth starts to add capacity, like lead/lag control of compressors where a second machine starts only when header pressure falls.

It gives both redundancy and extra capacity from the same spare unit. The exact start logic is not in the reference.
f: How is duty rotated among the peroxide pumps?
What happens if two peroxide pumps fail at once?
Why use metering pumps rather than control valves here?

f.q: Where is the WAD analyser sampling, before or after dosing?
f.a:
The reference does not say where the analyser draws its sample, so this cannot be answered reliably from the documents. Check the cyanide destruct P&ID, or ask the control room operator or instrument technician.

In general, designs vary. A sample before dosing gives a feedforward signal of incoming cyanide load. A sample after dosing and adequate contact time measures the residual, which is the actual target. Some plants use one analyser switching between several points.

Since the PDC mentions a residual WAD target, a downstream measurement is likely involved, but confirm on the drawings.
f: How do multi stream analysers switch between sample points?
Why does analyser sample line length matter?
How is the residual WAD reading checked against lab results?

What is caustic (NaOH) mainly used for?.q: Why does elution pre-soak need an alkaline cyanide solution?
What is caustic (NaOH) mainly used for?.a:
Split AARL elution works by changing the chemistry so carbon lets go of gold. Gold sits on carbon as the gold cyanide complex.

The pre-soak floods the carbon with a hot, strong caustic and cyanide solution. Cyanide competes for the adsorption sites and the high pH conditions loosen the gold complex. Caustic also keeps the solution alkaline so cyanide stays as cyanide and does not form HCN gas at elution temperatures.

Then elution with low salt water strips the loosened gold. The PDC gives about 638 kg of caustic per pre-treat and elution at 130 C for the CIL4 column. The acid wash before the pre-soak removes scale that would otherwise block the pores.

f.q: Why is acid wash done before the caustic pre-soak, not after?
f.a:
Carbon picks up calcium carbonate and other scale in the leach, especially with saline water and lime. This scale clogs pores and covers adsorption sites.

Dilute hydrochloric acid dissolves the scale and some base metals. If you did it after elution, scale would hinder the strip and gold recovery would suffer. Acid wash first cleans the surface so the pre-soak can reach the gold.

A water rinse follows the acid wash to remove acid before caustic goes in, otherwise acid and caustic would neutralise each other and waste reagent. That sequence is shown in the reference.
f: Where does acid wash waste go on this plant?
What happens if the rinse after acid wash is too short?
Why does saline water make carbon scaling worse?

f.q: Why does elution then switch to low salt water after pre-soak?
f.a:
Gold cyanide adsorbs best onto carbon in high ionic strength solutions, which is why loading works well in saline leach slurry. The reverse is also true: low ionic strength water encourages gold to come off.

So after the pre-soak, hot clean water flows through the column and the loosened gold desorbs into it. The reference shows elution first with lean eluate then with scheme water, the fresh pipeline water at SG 1.00, rather than saline process water.

Using saline water here would hold gold on the carbon and reduce the strip, which is why fresh water matters.
f: What is lean eluate and why reuse it in the next strip?
How many bed volumes of eluate pass through the column?
How is elution temperature controlled on CIL4?

f.q: Why is the elution column pressurised during the strip?
f.a:
The PDC gives an elution temperature of 130 C. At atmospheric pressure water boils at 100 C, so to keep the solution liquid at 130 C the column must be held above saturation pressure, as a boiler or pressurised hot water system is.

The reference says the column is pressurised to stop flashing. If solution flashed to steam, it would create vapour pockets, poor contact with the carbon, erratic flow and possible mechanical damage.

Higher temperature speeds up desorption, so pressurising gives a faster, more complete strip in the same column.
f: What material is the CIL4 elution column made from?
What protects the column from overpressure?
How does the LPG heater control eluate temperature?
