What is caustic (NaOH) mainly used for?.q: What would low caustic dosing do to electrowinning solution stability?
What is caustic (NaOH) mainly used for?.a:
The reference says caustic keeps electrowinning solution alkaline but does not describe failure effects, so this is general reasoning.

If caustic is low, pH and conductivity fall. Lower conductivity raises cell voltage for the same current, wasting power and heating the solution, much like resistance in a long cable. Lower pH also lets cyanide break down faster at the anode and increases the risk of HCN gas forming in the cells.

Gold plating efficiency can drop and anodes may corrode faster. That shows up as higher barren gold and higher cell voltages. Ventilation over the cells matters even more if solution chemistry drifts.

f.q: Why does electrowinning generate gases at the cells?
f.a:
Electrowinning passes current through the solution between anodes and cathodes. At the cathode, gold plates out, but some current also splits water to make hydrogen gas. At the anode, water is oxidised to oxygen, and some cyanide is oxidised too, which can produce ammonia and other by products.

If the solution pH falls, HCN can also be released. These gases are why EW cells sit under extraction hoods with good ventilation.

The reference gives gravity EW current density of 15 to 25 A/m2, but does not describe the gas extraction system, so check the goldroom procedures.
f: Why does hydrogen in EW cells need ventilation?
What current efficiency do gold EW cells usually reach?
How is gold removed from EW cathodes?

f.q: What does solution conductivity do to cell voltage and power?
f.a:
An EW cell behaves partly like a resistor. Part of the voltage drives the chemical reactions and part simply pushes current through the solution. That second part equals current times solution resistance.

Low conductivity means higher resistance, so the rectifier must supply more voltage for the same current. Power is voltage times current, so energy use rises and the extra appears as heat in the solution.

The gravity EW has two 2,500 A rectifiers per the reference. Keeping caustic up keeps conductivity high, which keeps voltage and heat down.
f: What limits how much current an EW cell can take?
Why does solution temperature affect EW efficiency?
How is rectifier current controlled during a batch?

f.q: How is caustic strength checked in eluate or EW solution?
f.a:
The reference does not describe the testing method or frequency, so this is general practice.

Caustic strength is normally checked by acid titration in the site lab, giving a result as percent sodium hydroxide or grams per litre. Operators may also use pH and conductivity readings as quick indications, though pH is less useful at very high alkalinity.

Free cyanide is usually titrated at the same time with silver nitrate. Check with the elution operators or the lab for this site's sampling routine and targets.
f: Why is pH less useful at very high alkalinity?
How is free cyanide measured in elution solutions?
Who sets the target caustic strength for elution?

What is caustic (NaOH) mainly used for?.q: How is caustic delivered and stored safely on site?
What is caustic (NaOH) mainly used for?.a:
The PDC lists caustic as 50 percent w/w bulk liquid (SG 1.50), delivered in 20,000 L trailers, up to three per delivery, by pumped transfer from the truck.

From storage it goes round a pressurised ringmain with DOL pumps and a mechanical back pressure valve on the return, with flowmeters at each dosing point. The storage tank has an immersion heater that switches on below about 20 C and off above about 25 C to stop the caustic freezing.

Safety relies on bunding, safety showers and eyewash stations, proper PPE including face shield and chemical gloves, and controlled unloading procedures. Check the area procedure before working near caustic lines.

f.q: Why does 50% caustic freeze at temperatures that aren't very cold?
f.a:
Sodium hydroxide at 50 percent strength has a surprisingly high freezing point, around 12 C. Below that it begins to crystallise into a solid, which can block lines, pumps and valves and is hard to clear.

On a desert site with cold winter nights, that is a real risk. So the tank immersion heater, switched on below about 20 C and off above about 25 C per the reference, keeps a margin above freezing.

Lines may also be trace heated or insulated. Diluting caustic lowers its freezing point, which is why some plants store a weaker solution.
f: Are the caustic lines trace heated as well as the tank?
How do you clear a line blocked by frozen caustic?
Why not just buy weaker caustic to avoid freezing?

f.q: What does the back pressure valve on the ringmain return do?
f.a:
A mechanical back pressure valve on the return holds the ringmain pressure at a set value. It opens more when pressure rises and closes when it falls, like a pressure sustaining or relief valve in a hydraulic circuit.

This keeps a steady header pressure for every dosing point, regardless of how many users are drawing. Without it, pressure would vary with demand and the dosing control valves would struggle.

The reference notes this arrangement for both cyanide and caustic ringmains, with DOL pumps rather than VSDs, so the back pressure valve does the pressure regulation.
f: What happens if the back pressure valve sticks closed?
Why are DOL pumps used rather than VSDs here?
How is each caustic dosing point flow controlled?

f.q: Why is caustic so hazardous to skin and eyes?
f.a:
Caustic soda reacts with fats and proteins in tissue, turning them into soap (saponification). Unlike acids, which tend to form a barrier as they burn, alkalis keep penetrating deeper, so burns can be severe and painless at first.

In the eyes this can cause permanent damage within seconds. That is why the immediate response is to flush with plenty of water for a long time, at least 15 to 20 minutes, and get medical help.

Always use a face shield, goggles and chemical gloves near caustic, and know where the nearest safety shower is before starting work.
f: How far apart are safety showers on reagent areas?
What PPE is needed to break into a caustic line?
How is a caustic spill neutralised and cleaned up?

Why is oxygen a key 'reagent' on this pl.q: Why do sulphide rich slurries consume oxygen so quickly?
Why is oxygen a key 'reagent' on this pl.a:
Sulphide minerals, mainly pyrite on this ore, react with oxygen and alkaline solution. Pyrite oxidises slowly, but more reactive sulphides like pyrrhotite oxidise quickly. Freshly broken sulphide surfaces are especially reactive.

Dissolved iron and sulphur species also consume oxygen as they oxidise further, and sulphides react with cyanide to make thiocyanate, a side reaction that uses both oxygen and cyanide.

On this plant the concentrate is ultra fine ground to about 9 microns P80, creating enormous fresh surface area, so CIL2 leach demand is high. The PDC uses about 13 Nm3 of oxygen per tonne of concentrate as the nominal consumption rate.

f.q: Why does ultra fine grinding make oxygen demand even higher?
f.a:
Surface area rises sharply as particle size falls. Grinding concentrate to about 9 microns gives many times more surface than flotation concentrate at normal grind size.

Reactions with oxygen happen at that surface, so the slurry consumes oxygen much faster. The fresh surfaces from the IsaMill are also more reactive than old, weathered ones.

That is the point of UFG: exposing locked gold for cyanide. The trade off is a hungry leach, which is why CIL2 has side lances plus VSD oxygen injection pumps on the first two tanks.

f.q: Why use pure oxygen rather than just blowing air?
f.a:
Air is only about 21 percent oxygen. The amount of oxygen that dissolves in water is proportional to its partial pressure, so near pure oxygen gives roughly five times higher dissolved oxygen potential than air.

Saline water like this plant's process water dissolves less oxygen than fresh water, which makes the gap even more important. High oxygen demand from sulphide concentrate could not be met with air alone without huge air volumes.

The PDC specifies a new VPSA oxygen plant with minimum purity around 90 to 92 percent and 70 t/d capacity selected.

What DO level do leach tanks usually target?

f.q: What is the Elsner equation and why does oxygen appear in it?
f.a:
The Elsner equation describes gold dissolution in cyanide: four gold atoms plus eight cyanide ions plus one oxygen molecule plus two water molecules give four gold cyanide complexes plus four hydroxide ions.

Gold does not dissolve in cyanide on its own. It needs an oxidant to remove electrons from the gold, and dissolved oxygen does that. Cyanide then holds the gold in solution.

It is an electrochemical cell on the gold surface: gold oxidises at one site while oxygen is reduced at another. Without enough oxygen, dissolution slows no matter how much cyanide is present.

Why is oxygen a key 'reagent' on this pl.q: What would a handover mean if the PSA oxygen plant went offline?
Why is oxygen a key 'reagent' on this pl.a:
It means the leach is running on the liquid oxygen backup, or short of oxygen if backup is not keeping up.

The PDC gives a liquid oxygen capacity of 60 t, at about 850 kPa, against a calculated nominal oxygen demand of about 53 t/d and a maximum of about 71 t/d. As a rough design estimate, that is around a day of backup at nominal demand. These are design values, not live stock levels.

So a handover should cover LOX level, deliveries arranged, DO readings in CIL2 and CIL4 leach tanks, and the expected time for the PSA to return. The metallurgist will want to know early.

f.q: What DO readings would show the leach is getting short of oxygen?
f.a:
The reference says CIL4 leach tanks have DO analysers with high and low alarms, and the Carbon Scout also samples leach tanks for DO, pH and solids. CIL2 has oxygen addition but the reference gives no DO setpoints.

A falling DO trend in the first leach tanks, with oxygen flow control valves opening wider, is the classic sign. Low DO alarms would follow.

The actual target values are not in the reference, so check with the metallurgist or CRO for current DO setpoints in each circuit.
f: How quickly does DO drop when oxygen supply stops?
Why are DO probes difficult to maintain in slurry?
Does low DO show up in cyanide analyser readings?

f.q: How much liquid oxygen storage is there compared to demand?
f.a:
The PDC lists the new LOX plant at 60 t capacity. It gives Stage 2 oxygen consumption of about 53.2 t/d nominal and 70.8 t/d maximum, and a VPSA capacity selected at 70 t/d.

So at nominal demand, full storage covers a bit over a day. At maximum demand, a little under a day. That is the design picture only; actual tank level and demand on the day can be very different.

Delivery logistics then become the limit, which is why a prolonged PSA outage is a significant event.
f: How is liquid oxygen delivered and refilled on site?
Can oxygen addition be prioritised to certain tanks?
What does VPSA availability look like in the design?

f.q: Which tanks would be prioritised if oxygen ran short?
f.a:
The reference does not cover a priority scheme for oxygen shortage, so this needs to come from the metallurgist or the area procedure.

As general reasoning, concentrate leach in CIL2 handles the richest, most refractory material with the highest oxygen demand, and front tanks do most of the dissolution, so they would usually matter most per tonne. CIL4 handles far more tonnes but lower grade.

Decisions like reducing oxygen to some tanks or cutting feed are metallurgical calls weighing gold loss. Ask the shift metallurgist rather than adjusting oxygen distribution yourself.

How does reduced feed rate help oxygen supply?
Can peroxide be used as an emergency oxygen source?

Why is oxygen a key 'reagent' on this pl.q: How does liquid oxygen backup kick in if PSA output falls short?
Why is oxygen a key 'reagent' on this pl.a:
The reference only says oxygen comes from a PSA plant with liquid oxygen backup. The PDC lists the LOX plant as an owner supplied package with 60 t capacity at about 850 kPa, matching the existing oxygen plant. It does not describe the changeover logic.

In general practice, liquid oxygen passes through an ambient air vaporiser into the same header as the PSA product. A pressure regulator on the backup line is set slightly below the normal header pressure. If PSA output falls, header pressure drops and the backup valve opens automatically, like a pressure reducing valve feeding a second supply.

Confirm the actual arrangement with the utilities engineer or the vendor manual.

f.q: How does a VPSA plant separate oxygen from air?
f.a:
A vacuum pressure swing adsorption plant blows air through vessels filled with zeolite. Under pressure, zeolite adsorbs nitrogen more strongly than oxygen, so oxygen rich gas passes through as product.

When the zeolite is loaded, the vessel switches to vacuum, releasing the nitrogen, while another vessel takes over production. Cycling between vessels gives near continuous supply, like a twin tower desiccant dryer.

The PDC lists a 70 t/d VPSA with minimum purity around 90 to 92 percent. Purity is limited mainly by argon, which passes through with oxygen.
f: What maintenance does a VPSA plant need?
Why is VPSA purity lower than liquid oxygen?
What does the VPSA blower and vacuum pump consume?

f.q: Why does liquid oxygen need a vaporiser before use?
f.a:
Liquid oxygen is stored at about minus 183 C. The plant needs it as a gas at ambient temperature, so it must be boiled and warmed.

Ambient vaporisers are banks of finned aluminium tubes. Heat from the surrounding air warms the liquid through the fins, like a radiator working in reverse. They need no power but can ice up heavily under sustained high flow, reducing capacity, so large demands may need duty switching between banks.

Getting cold gas or liquid into the header could damage carbon steel pipework, which becomes brittle at low temperatures.
f: Why do vaporisers ice up and how is it managed?
What pipe materials are used for cold oxygen service?
How is liquid oxygen tank pressure maintained?

f.q: What safety hazards come with oxygen rich areas?
f.a:
Oxygen does not burn, but it makes everything else burn much faster and hotter. Clothing, grease and even metal can ignite more easily in oxygen enriched air.

Key rules: never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings, keep ignition sources away, and do not let oxygen vent into enclosed spaces. Clothing exposed to oxygen can stay enriched for some time.

Oxygen depletion is the opposite risk around the nitrogen vent of a PSA plant or confined spaces. Follow site permits and gas testing rules near oxygen equipment.

Nominal Stage 2 plant throughput?.q: Why does the high throughput case rely on a coarser P80 of 220 microns?
Nominal Stage 2 plant throughput?.a:
Grinding is limited by mill power. The SAG and ball mill each have 20 MW installed, so the tonnes per hour they can handle equals the available power divided by the energy each tonne needs.

Energy per tonne climbs steeply as you grind finer. Bond's grinding law makes energy roughly proportional to one over the square root of product size, so grinding to 180 microns needs noticeably more kWh per tonne than 220 microns.

Accepting a coarser 220 micron P80 cuts the energy per tonne, so the same motors push about 3,494 t/h instead of 3,146 t/h, giving the 28.35 Mtpa high case. The price is poorer liberation and some lost flotation recovery. These are design values.

f.q: How much does grinding energy change between 180 and 220 microns?
f.a:
Using Bond's law and ignoring the feed size term, energy scales with one over the square root of P80. One over root 180 is about 0.075 and one over root 220 is about 0.067, so the finer grind needs roughly 10 percent more energy in the final grinding step.

The PDC shows the effect in the SAG modelling: about 9.14 kWh/t at nominal versus 7.68 kWh/t in the high throughput case. The ball mill is modelled at 9.68 kWh/t for 180 microns.

So a modest change in target size shifts throughput noticeably, which is why grind is the main lever between tonnes and recovery.
f: What is the Bond work index and how is it measured?
Why does the SAG specific energy also fall in the high case?
How is cyclone overflow P80 measured online?

f.q: Does a coarser grind change flotation recovery much?
f.a:
Usually yes. Gold and sulphides locked inside larger particles are not exposed to collector, so they do not float. Very coarse particles also tend to drop out of the froth even when they are liberated.

The PDC grind target is P80 180 microns with a maximum of 250, and the flotation design conservatively assumes 220 microns. The exact recovery penalty between those sizes for this ore is not given in the reference.

Metallurgists set the grind target from testwork that maps recovery against size. Ask them how much recovery the site loses per 10 microns of coarser grind.
f: Why do coarse particles fall out of the froth?
How is grind versus recovery testwork carried out?
What does sanding in a flotation cell look like?

f.q: Why isn't the plant just run at the high throughput case all the time?
f.a:
It is an economic trade off. More tonnes means more gold processed, but coarser grind means a lower percentage recovered and more gold to tails.

Downstream equipment also matters. Flotation residence time shortens with more flow, the flotation tails thickener sees more load, and CIL4 total residence is already 12.8 h at nominal, below the 14 h ideal in the PDC. More tonnes would shorten it further.

So the best rate depends on ore hardness, grade, gold price and plant constraints on the day. The metallurgy and production team set the target, not the design document.
f: How does CIL4 residence time change with higher feed?
Why is 14 hours called ideal for CIL4 leach?
Who sets the daily throughput target on site?

Nominal Stage 2 plant throughput?.q: What would it mean if instantaneous throughput ran well under 3,146 t/h?
Nominal Stage 2 plant throughput?.a:
3,146 t/h is the nominal design mill feed rate while running: about 1,313 t/h through the old FIM SAG plus 1,833 t/h through the new SAG. It is a design value, not a live target.

Running well under it means a constraint somewhere. Common causes: harder or coarser ore limiting SAG throughput, one SAG down or relining, pebble crushers down so critical size builds up, low stockpile, a high ball mill or cyclone load, or a downstream limit like flotation, the tails thickener or tailings pumping.

Annual tonnage also assumes 93.4 percent availability, so a low running rate stacks on top of any downtime. Check which unit is at its limit first.

f.q: What split of the 3,146 t/h comes from each SAG mill?
f.a:
Per the PDC, the existing FIM SAG supplies about 1,313 t/h and the new SAG about 1,833 t/h at nominal. Both discharge to the same new primary cyclone feed hopper, the old SAG via the FIM mill transfer pumps.

So the new SAG carries roughly 58 percent of the feed and the old SAG about 42 percent. The new SAG has a 20 MW motor, against 12 MW on the old one, which roughly matches the split.

Losing either SAG therefore cuts feed sharply, though the reline scenarios in the reference show how the circuit keeps running in reduced configurations.
f: What happens to throughput during a new SAG reline?
Why is the old FIM SAG shorter than the new SAG?
What limits the FIM mill transfer pump capacity?

f.q: How does ore hardness limit SAG throughput?
f.a:
A SAG mill relies on the ore itself plus a modest steel ball charge to break rock. Harder ore takes more energy per tonne to break and wears down more slowly, so it accumulates in the mill.

As the load builds, power and bearing pressure rise. Once power reaches the motor or charge limit, the only way to stop overloading is to cut feed. Coarse, competent ore is the worst case.

The expert system uses SAG power, load, noise, speed and the feed camera size analyser to adjust feed to stay just below these limits. Softer ore lets it push feed higher.
f: How does SAG feed size from the stockpile affect throughput?
Why does the SAG noise monitor help detect overloads?
What role do pebble crushers play with hard ore?

f.q: What downstream bottlenecks could cap mill feed rate?
f.a:
Several. The cyclone cluster runs about 12 primary cyclones at nominal, maximum 14, so very high circulating loads can limit it. Ball mill power is another limit.

Beyond grinding, flotation cell residence time falls as flow rises, the flotation tails thickener has a design flux, CIL4 residence time is already tight, and tailings pumping to the TSF must keep up with the final tails tank. If any of those stops, the mills must slow.

That is why a low mill rate is not always a mill problem. Check the trends for whichever unit is pinned at its limit.

How does the flotation tails thickener flux limit work?
What happens to the mills if tails pumping stops?

Nominal Stage 2 plant throughput?.q: How is mill availability of 93.4% actually tracked and reported?
Nominal Stage 2 plant throughput?.a:
93.4 percent availability equals about 8,182 running hours out of 8,760 in a year, per the PDC. It is a design assumption covering planned and unplanned downtime.

The reference says weightometer totals are logged per 12 hour shift and per day starting at 5:00 am, and the PI historian records equipment running status. Those give run hours and tonnes.

How downtime is categorised and reported, for example planned shutdown versus breakdown, comes from the site reporting system, which the reference does not describe. The production or maintenance reliability team would explain the site method.

f.q: What counts as downtime against availability versus utilisation?
f.a:
Definitions vary by company, but a common split is:

Availability is the share of total time the equipment is mechanically able to run. Planned maintenance and breakdowns reduce it.

Utilisation is the share of available time the equipment actually runs. It drops for things like no feed, downstream stoppages or waiting on power approval.

The PDC uses a single concentrator figure of 93.4 percent as an overall planning number. The site's exact definitions come from its reporting standard, so check with the reliability or production team.
f: How is a breakdown classified versus a planned stop?
What is OEE and is it used for mills?
How do relines fit into the annual availability figure?

f.q: Why do planned relines count against the 93.4%?
f.a:
Availability in design terms is about how many hours a year the plant processes ore. A reline stops part of the circuit just as surely as a breakdown, so it reduces the hours available.

The reference lists reline scenarios that soften the impact: the new SAG runs single stage during a ball mill reline, the new SABC runs during a FIM SAG reline, and the FIM SAG plus new ball mill run during a new SAG reline.

So throughput falls but does not stop completely during most relines. That partial running is part of how the design reaches its annual tonnage.

How long does a typical SAG reline take?
How are relines scheduled across the year?

f.q: How do the weightometer shift totals feed production reports?
f.a:
Per the reference, weightometers keep totals for each 12 hour shift and each day, with the day starting at 5:00 am. Wet tonnes are converted to dry using a moisture input, and the weightometers are checked with calibration chains.

These totals give the official tonnes milled, which combine with assays to calculate gold in feed and recovery. Errors in calibration or moisture flow straight into the reported numbers.

Typically the shift totals land in a daily production report reviewed by metallurgy and production. The reporting format itself is not in the reference.

Nominal head grade the design is based o.q: Why does the design case use a higher grade than the nominal case?
Nominal head grade the design is based o.a:
Equipment has to cope with the toughest realistic feed, not the average. The PDC design grade case of 1.81 g/t Au and 1.49 percent S carries more gold and much more sulphur than the nominal 1.58 g/t and 1.02 percent S.

More sulphur means more flotation concentrate: about 876 kt/a in the design case versus 637 kt/a nominal. That drives the size of the concentrate thickener, UFG mills, filters, CIL2 leach, oxygen supply, carbon loading, elution and electrowinning.

It is like sizing a cooling system for the hottest day rather than an average day. If the plant were sized only for nominal, high sulphur ore would overwhelm the concentrate side.

f.q: Which equipment is sized off the design grade case?
f.a:
The reference says the design grade concentrate rate, about 876 kt/a or around 104 t/h into the thickener, is what UFG 1, 2 and 3 plus the filters are sized for. CIL2 is designed for a feed of about 104 t/h of solids, which matches that case.

Downstream of that, carbon handling, elution and electrowinning capacity on the concentrate side also follow from higher gold in solution.

The milling circuit is sized more around throughput and ore hardness than grade, so its key cases are the nominal and high throughput cases.
f: How does CIL2 residence time change at design grade?
Why is the concentrate thickener existing equipment?
How much more oxygen does the design grade case need?

f.q: Why is the design grade case run at a lower 24.0 Mtpa?
f.a:
The reference gives the reduced 24.0 Mtpa for the design grade case but does not explain why, so this is reasoning to confirm with the process engineer.

The likely reason is that the concentrate side becomes the bottleneck. At 1.49 percent sulphur each tonne of ore makes much more concentrate. Pushing 25.5 Mtpa of that ore would exceed UFG, CIL2 and elution capacity, so the case assumes fewer tonnes.

The design grade ore may also differ in hardness. Either way, the plant's maximum rate depends on ore type, not just mill power.

What sets the concentrate side capacity limit?

f.q: What is the achievable grade case in the PDC?
f.a:
The PDC includes an achievable grade case of 1.70 g/t Au and 1.40 percent S. It sits between nominal (1.58 g/t, 1.02 percent S) and design grade (1.81 g/t, 1.49 percent S).

In that case gold production is about 1.20 Moz/a, and flotation concentrate is about 876 kt/a, around 104 to 107 t/h, the same concentrate tonnage as the design grade case.

So it represents a realistic higher grade operating case that still loads the concentrate circuit to its design rate. All of these are design cases, not forecasts of daily grade.
f: Why do achievable and design cases give similar concentrate?
How was the achievable grade case chosen?
What gold production does the nominal case give?

Nominal head grade the design is based o.q: What would you expect downstream if head grade ran below nominal for a shift?
Nominal head grade the design is based o.a:
The reference does not describe a low grade shift scenario, so this is general reasoning with plant figures.

Less gold goes into the plant, so gold production falls in proportion, even if recovery holds. If sulphur is also low, flotation mass pull and concentrate tonnes drop, which lightens the load on UFG, CIL2 and elution.

Recovery percentage often slips a little at lower grade, because tails grade tends not to fall as fast as head grade. The OSA on flotation feed would show lower gold readings, and carbon loadings would trend down. Reagent use per tonne of ore changes less, so cost per ounce goes up.

f.q: Why can recovery percentage fall when head grade drops?
f.a:
Some gold is very hard to recover, for example extremely fine or locked particles. That loss tends to behave like a floor in the tails grade that does not drop much when the feed grade falls.

Recovery equals one minus tails gold over feed gold. If feed falls from 1.6 to 1.2 g/t but tails only fall a little, the loss becomes a bigger share of the feed, so recovery percentage drops.

It is like a fixed leakage in a pipe: the lower the flow, the bigger the percentage lost. The actual behaviour for this ore comes from metallurgical records.
f: How is a recovery versus grade curve built?
What tails grade does CIL4 typically achieve?
Why does locked gold resist both flotation and leach?

f.q: Does a lower sulphur grade change flotation mass pull?
f.a:
Usually yes. Flotation here mainly recovers sulphides, especially pyrite, because gold is locked in them. Less sulphide in the feed means less mass floats, so mass pull falls if the circuit is run to the same concentrate grade.

The PDC shows the link: nominal 1.02 percent S gives about 637 kt/a of concentrate, while design 1.49 percent S gives about 876 kt/a.

Operators and the expert system may adjust air, froth depth and reagents in response. Low mass pull lightens the UFG load, while high sulphur pushes it toward capacity.
f: How do operators control mass pull in the roughers?
What does the OSA show when sulphur feed drops?
Can mass pull be too low for good gold recovery?

f.q: Would low grade change cyanide or oxygen use downstream?
f.a:
Cyanide in CIL2 is ratioed to the solids mass flow of concentrate, per the reference. Less concentrate means less cyanide flow, though the dose per tonne stays similar.

Oxygen demand comes mainly from sulphides, so lower sulphur generally lowers oxygen demand. The PDC rate is about 13 Nm3 per tonne of concentrate nominal.

In CIL4, cyanide is set by the operator or ratio to thickener underflow tonnes, so it follows ore tonnes more than grade. Overall reagent use per tonne of ore changes less than gold output, so cost per ounce rises at low grade.

What drives cyanide consumption apart from gold?
How is oxygen flow adjusted to demand?

Nominal head grade the design is based o.q: How is head grade measured or estimated before ore reaches the mills?
Nominal head grade the design is based o.a:
The reference covers the plant side only. On the mine side, grade control drilling and the block model estimate grade before ore is blasted and hauled, but those systems are not described here.

In the plant, the onstream analyser (OSA) measures gold and iron on the flotation feed stream, with sulphur inferred from iron. That gives a near real time indication of head grade.

The official head grade is usually confirmed from samplers and lab assays, or back calculated from gold produced plus gold in tails. Ask the plant metallurgist how the site reports head grade.

f.q: How accurate is the OSA gold reading on flotation feed?
f.a:
The reference says the OSA measures Au and Fe, but gives no accuracy figures.

In general, measuring gold at around 1.6 g/t online is challenging because it is a trace level. Online readings are best treated as a trend that tells you grade is rising or falling, rather than as an accounting number. The analyser is calibrated against lab assays of samples cut from the same stream.

Iron, and sulphur inferred from it, are usually much more reliable because they are present at percent levels. Ask the metallurgist how far to trust the gold signal.
f: How is an OSA calibrated against lab assays?
Why is sulphur inferred from iron on this OSA?
What streams does the OSA sample on this plant?

f.q: Why is head grade often back calculated rather than measured?
f.a:
Mill feed is coarse rock, up to hundreds of millimetres, so taking a truly representative sample of it is very hard. Gold is also unevenly distributed, the so called nugget effect.

Product streams are easier to measure: gold poured is weighed exactly, and tails slurry is fine and sampled continuously. So many plants calculate head grade as gold recovered plus gold in tails, divided by tonnes milled.

The catch is that any error in tails sampling flows straight into the head grade and recovery figures, which is why samplers matter so much.

How does gold in circuit inventory affect back calculation?
Why must tails samplers cut the full stream?

f.q: How does grade control in the pit feed into plant planning?
f.a:
This is outside the plant reference, so general practice only.

Mine geologists drill and assay blast holes to mark ore and waste boundaries and estimate grade for each block. Ore is hauled to the crusher or to stockpiles grouped by grade or ore type. Planners then blend feed to keep grade and hardness steady.

The plant uses that information to anticipate changes in throughput, reagent demand and gold output. For details on how this site links mine and mill planning, ask the mine geology or planning team.

Nominal overall gold recovery?.q: Why does combining gravity, concentrate leach and tails leach lift recovery?
Nominal overall gold recovery?.a:
Each stage catches gold the others would miss, a bit like staged filtration where each filter removes a different size range.

Gravity on cyclone underflow takes out coarse free gold early, about 14 percent of feed gold at nominal. Flotation then recovers sulphide bound gold into a small concentrate, about 71.8 percent of the gold in its feed. The concentrate is ultra fine ground and leached hard, with the CIL2/3 design using 90 percent extraction. The flotation tails, which still carry a meaningful amount of gold, are leached in CIL4 at about 34 to 38 percent extraction.

Added together these give the nominal 84 percent overall. These are PDC design values.

f.q: Why is coarse free gold removed by gravity before flotation?
f.a:
Coarse gold is very dense, so it gets caught in the cyclone underflow and recirculates to the ball mill again and again. It can build up in the circulating load instead of reaching flotation.

Coarse gold also floats poorly and leaches slowly because of its size. Recovering it early with Knelson concentrators, then dissolving it quickly in the intensive leach reactor, avoids those problems.

That is why the Knelsons sit on cyclone underflow, where the coarse heavy particles concentrate, rather than on the final product.
f: Why does gold concentrate in cyclone underflow?
How does the intensive leach reactor treat Knelson concentrate?
What gravity recovery does the PDC allow as a maximum?

f.q: How much gold is left in flotation tails before CIL4?
f.a:
The PDC gives nominal flotation gold recovery of 71.8 percent, so roughly 28 percent of the gold entering flotation reports to tails. That is gold locked in non sulphide minerals, very fine particles, or sulphides that did not float.

CIL4 then leaches that tail at a design extraction of about 38 percent, with about 34 percent used in the nominal overall recovery figure. So roughly a third of the tails gold is recovered there.

The rest goes to the TSF. That remaining loss is why scavenger tails sulphur and flotation performance matter so much.
f: Why does CIL4 recover only about a third of tails gold?
What is the flotation sulphur recovery in the PDC?
How does scavenger flotation reduce tails losses?

f.q: Why is tails leach extraction so much lower than concentrate leach?
f.a:
Concentrate is ultra fine ground to about 9 microns, which exposes gold locked in sulphides, and it is leached with high cyanide and plenty of oxygen over a long residence time.

Flotation tails are at the primary grind of about 180 microns, so much of their remaining gold is still locked away. Their grade is low and the tonnage is huge, about 3,164 t/h, so leach residence is short, about 3.2 h of leach and 12.8 h total, and reagent doses must stay economic.

So CIL4 catches the easily leached gold in the tails but cannot reach the locked portion. The PDC uses 34 to 38 percent extraction.
f: Why can't flotation tails be ultra fine ground too?
How does CIL4 cyanide dosing compare with CIL2?
What would an extra CIL4 tank add to recovery?

Nominal overall gold recovery?.q: What would falling overall recovery on a shift report suggest to check first?
Nominal overall gold recovery?.a:
First, check the numbers are real: confirm tails samplers and assays are valid, because a sampler fault can make recovery look wrong.

Then find which stage lost gold. Look at grind: a coarse cyclone overflow P80 cuts flotation recovery. Check flotation: rising scavenger tails sulphur on the OSA shows sulphides escaping. Check gravity: Knelson cycles and ILR batches running normally. Check leach: DO, pH and cyanide in CIL2 and CIL4, and carbon concentrations from the Carbon Scout. Compare solution and solid tails assays to see whether gold is undissolved or dissolved but not adsorbed.

Head grade also matters: a low grade shift can lower recovery percentage on its own.

f.q: How do you tell soluble gold loss from undissolved gold loss?
f.a:
Tails samples are split into solids and solution. Gold in the solid residue was never dissolved, pointing to leach conditions, liberation or grind. Gold in the solution was dissolved but not captured by carbon, pointing to the adsorption side.

Soluble losses suggest low carbon concentration, poor carbon activity, fouled carbon, short residence or carbon distribution problems. Solid losses suggest low DO, low cyanide, coarse grind or locked gold.

The reference notes a three stage sampler taking a shift composite of CIL4 tails, which supplies this kind of data.
f: What carbon activity tests do metallurgists run?
How does fouled carbon reduce adsorption?
Why is CIL4 tails sampled in three stages?

f.q: Why might a sampler fault make recovery look worse than it is?
f.a:
Many plants calculate recovery from feed, concentrate and tails assays. If a tails sampler is cutting unrepresentative material, for example only part of the stream or a coarse segregated layer, the tails assay can come out higher or lower than reality.

A biased high tails grade makes recovery look worse; a biased low one hides real losses. A blocked or stuck cutter might also give no sample at all.

So before chasing a process problem, metallurgists check that samplers are running, cutters are moving across the full stream and samples look normal.

How does a stuck sampler cutter show on the OIS?
How do metallurgists handle missing sample data?

f.q: Which OSA streams help locate a flotation recovery problem?
f.a:
The reference lists OSA streams: flotation feed, rougher 1 concentrate, rougher 2/3 concentrate, scavenger concentrate, scavenger tails, cleaner feed, cleaner scavenger tails, final concentrate and final tails. Gold and iron are measured, with sulphur inferred from iron.

Scavenger tails sulphur shows what is escaping the rougher scavenger bank. Cleaner scavenger tails show losses in the cleaning circuit. Feed readings show whether the problem is simply a grade change.

Comparing these lets you narrow down whether losses come from roughing, scavenging or cleaning.
f: How does the flotation expert system use OSA data?
Why are cleaner scavenger tails sent to the thickener?
What does rising final concentrate iron indicate?

Nominal overall gold recovery?.q: How is the 1 to 2% Stage 2 recovery uplift actually achieved technically?
Nominal overall gold recovery?.a:
The reference gives three main reasons.

In Stage 1 only part of the flotation tails thickener underflow went through CIL2 and CIL3, limited to their capacity, with the rest going straight to final tails unleached. In Stage 2 the new CIL4 leaches all of the flotation tails, recovering gold that previously went to the TSF.

The new UFG 3 mill lets all concentrate be ground and leached on site, with CIL2 repurposed for concentrate leaching and CIL3 for adsorption. That replaces sending concentrate to the offsite roaster.

CIL3 tails also pass through CIL4, giving another chance to capture residual gold. The PDC expects a 1 to 2 percent uplift overall.

f.q: Why did Stage 1 send part of the flotation tails straight to final tails?
f.a:
In Stage 1, existing CIL2 and CIL3 were the only leach capacity available for flotation tails. They were much smaller than the full tails stream, so their feed was flow controlled to their capacity, and the balance of the thickener underflow went to final tails, per the reference.

That unleached portion still contained recoverable gold. Building CIL4, with 8 large tanks of 5,600 m3 each, gives enough volume to leach the whole stream.

It was a staged approach: get the new grinding and flotation running first, then add the leach capacity in Stage 2.
f: How large is CIL4 compared with CIL2 and CIL3?
Why was CIL4 built with space for a future tank?
What happened to concentrate in Stage 1?

f.q: What happens to CIL3 tails in Stage 2?
f.a:
Per the reference, CIL3 tails go to a CIL3 tails hopper and are pumped by duty/standby VSD pumps to the CIL4 feed box. Cyanide water is added to the hopper.

So the concentrate leach residue gets a second pass through CIL4 alongside the flotation tails. Any dissolved gold not adsorbed in CIL3, and any slowly leaching gold, has another opportunity to be captured on CIL4 carbon.

A carbon detection meter on CIL3 tails watches for carbon escaping, so carbon is not lost into CIL4 unnoticed.
f: Why is cyanide water added to the CIL3 tails hopper?
How does the CIL3 carbon detection meter work?
What does CIL3 do now that it is adsorption only?

f.q: Why was the offsite roaster decommissioned in Stage 2?
f.a:
The reference states that the additional UFG mill (UFG 3) lets the offsite roaster be decommissioned, and that Stage 2 removes concentrate haulage to the roaster.

In general terms, roasting burns the sulphides to release gold, which is effective but involves high energy use, sulphur dioxide emissions control and operating cost. Trucking concentrate adds cost and handling risk.

Ultra fine grinding plus intensive cyanide leaching achieves a similar goal by exposing locked gold mechanically. Doing it on site simplifies logistics and keeps all value in one plant.
f: How does ultra fine grinding compare with roasting?
What happens to concentrate if UFG capacity is short?
Why does roasting create sulphur dioxide?

Approximate annual gold production in th.q: Why is annual production quoted per year rather than per tonne processed?
Approximate annual gold production in th.a:
Gold is sold, budgeted and reported over time, so annual ounces are the figure that matters for revenue, mine planning and company guidance. Per tonne figures describe the ore, not the business output.

Annual production combines tonnes, grade and recovery: 25.5 Mt at 1.58 g/t and 84 percent recovery gives roughly 34 tonnes of gold, around 1.1 million ounces. The PDC quotes 1.11 Moz/a from its detailed mass balance.

Annual numbers also average out short term swings: shutdowns, grade variation and relines. They assume the design 93.4 percent concentrator availability, so they are targets for the design case, not guarantees.

f.q: How many grams is a troy ounce, and why use ounces?
f.a:
A troy ounce is about 31.1 grams, heavier than the everyday ounce of about 28.3 grams. Precious metals have been traded in troy ounces for centuries, and gold prices are quoted per troy ounce worldwide.

So 1.11 million ounces is about 34.5 tonnes of gold. A 25.5 Mtpa plant at 1.58 g/t is feeding about 40 tonnes of gold a year, and recovers about 84 percent of it.

Plant operators often think in grams per tonne and kilograms, while finance and markets think in ounces.
f: How much gold does the plant recover per day at nominal?
What is in a doré bar besides gold?
How is gold weighed in the goldroom?

f.q: Why does the high throughput case make the most gold?
f.a:
The PDC gives 1.23 Moz/a for the high throughput case, compared with 1.11 Moz/a at nominal. That case processes 28.35 Mtpa at a coarser P80 of 220 microns.

The coarser grind costs some recovery percentage, but 11 percent more tonnes outweighs that loss in the design model. It is like running a pump at a less efficient point on its curve because you need more flow.

Whether that holds in practice depends on ore hardness, grade and downstream limits such as CIL4 residence time. Metallurgists weigh that trade off.
f: What recovery penalty does the high throughput case assume?
Can downstream circuits handle 3,494 t/h?
How is the throughput versus grind trade off reviewed?

f.q: How would a week of SAG downtime affect annual ounces?
f.a:
As a rough illustration only: 1.11 Moz/a is about 3,000 ounces a day at design. The new SAG carries about 58 percent of mill feed, so a week with it stopped and nothing else compensating could cost in the order of 12,000 ounces.

In reality the reference shows the FIM SAG plus new ball mill keep running during a new SAG reline, and the old SAG may run harder, so the loss is smaller. Planned relines are already within the 93.4 percent availability.

Unplanned stops are the ones that eat into the annual target. Real impacts come from the metallurgy and planning team.
f: How much feed can the FIM SAG take with the new ball mill?
How are unplanned stops tracked against plan?
Why do relines get scheduled long in advance?

Approximate annual gold production in th.q: What would a shortfall against 1.11 Moz/a suggest to metallurgists?
Approximate annual gold production in th.a:
Production is tonnes times grade times recovery, so a shortfall means one or more of those fell short. Metallurgists will break it down: were tonnes milled low (availability or running rate), was head grade below plan, or did recovery slip?

They will also look at timing. Gold can be sitting in circuit, on carbon, in eluate or in the goldroom, so poured gold can lag behind gold recovered.

Then they drill into whichever factor dropped: mill trends for tonnes, mine reconciliation for grade, and stage by stage recovery for losses. The PDC figures are design targets; actual budgets may differ.

f.q: Why can gold locked up in circuit hide true production?
f.a:
A lot of gold sits on carbon and in solutions at any moment. As a design illustration, CIL3 holds about 202 t of carbon at a design loading of about 4,490 g/t, which is roughly 900 kg, near 29,000 ounces. CIL4 at 12.5 g/L holds about 420 t of carbon at a nominal 461 g/t, roughly 6,000 ounces more.

If carbon loadings build up because elution falls behind, gold is recovered but not yet poured. Production looks low until the inventory is stripped.

So month end reports adjust for changes in gold in circuit.
f: How is gold in circuit estimated each month?
What limits how fast loaded carbon can be eluted?
Why does inventory build up after a shutdown?

f.q: Which of tonnes, grade or recovery usually drives a shortfall?
f.a:
It varies, but in general grade and tonnes often swing more than recovery. Grade depends on which part of the pit is mined, and tonnes depend on availability and ore hardness. Recovery tends to be steadier unless something goes wrong in the circuit.

A drop in all three at once often points to a single cause, for example hard, low grade ore that slows the mills and floats poorly.

The useful approach is a variance analysis: calculate how many ounces each factor cost against plan, then focus on the biggest. Metallurgists do this monthly.
f: What is a production variance analysis?
How does hard ore affect both tonnes and recovery?
Why can recovery improve when throughput drops?

f.q: How does grade variability from the mine affect annual production?
f.a:
Gold output scales directly with head grade. A 10 percent lower grade at the same tonnes and recovery means about 10 percent fewer ounces.

Mines plan to an average grade, but actual grade varies block by block. Short periods of low grade can often be offset later, but sustained shortfalls show up in annual numbers.

The PDC considers several grade cases, nominal 1.58 g/t, achievable 1.70 g/t and design 1.81 g/t, to make sure the plant can handle the range. Actual mine grade forecasts come from the mine planning team.
f: How do mine plans account for grade uncertainty?
Can the plant raise throughput to offset low grade?
What happens to recovery at higher than design grade?

Approximate annual gold production in th.q: How is daily gold production reconciled against this annual target?
Approximate annual gold production in th.a:
The reference covers the measurements, not the full reconciliation method.

Daily, weightometer totals give tonnes milled for each shift and day from 5:00 am. Samplers and the OSA give feed and tails grades. Metallurgists use these to calculate gold in feed, gold recovered and recovery for the day.

That calculated gold is compared over longer periods with gold actually poured as doré, adjusted for changes in gold in circuit. Monthly reconciliation then compares plant results with the mine's predicted tonnes and grade, and with the annual plan. The site's metallurgical accounting team owns the exact process.

f.q: Why does poured gold lag behind calculated gold produced?
f.a:
Gold passes through several stages before it becomes a bar: dissolved in leach, adsorbed on carbon, held on carbon for days, stripped in elution, plated in electrowinning, then smelted in the goldroom.

Carbon may spend up to about 14 days in the circuit at design, per the PDC carbon residence limits. Elution and EW run in batches, and smelting happens on a schedule.

So gold recovered today may be poured a week or two later. That is why monthly figures include a change in gold in circuit adjustment.
f: How often is doré poured in the goldroom?
How is cathode sludge recovered after EW?
What is the maximum carbon residence time in CIL4?

f.q: What is the difference between calculated and actual recovery?
f.a:
Calculated recovery comes from sampling and assays: head grade, tails grade and tonnes. It is available quickly but relies on sampling accuracy.

Actual recovery uses gold really poured, adjusted for gold in circuit. It is the true answer but only becomes clear over weeks or months.

The two should agree over time. A persistent gap points to sampling bias, weightometer errors, gold inventory estimates being wrong, or, rarely, losses or security issues. Metallurgical accountants track this closely.
f: How are weightometer errors detected in reconciliation?
What causes sampling bias in tails samplers?
How often is gold in circuit physically surveyed?

f.q: Who owns metallurgical accounting on site?
f.a:
The reference does not cover site roles for metallurgical accounting, so ask the processing manager or senior metallurgist.

In general, a plant metallurgist or dedicated metallurgical accountant compiles daily and monthly figures from weightometers, samplers, assays and goldroom records. Results are reviewed by the processing manager and reported to the company.

Many sites follow formal standards for metallurgical accounting, which set how samples are taken, how data are checked and how gold in circuit is valued.
f: What standards guide metallurgical accounting?
How do daily reports reach the processing manager?
Where can I see the daily production report?

How much flotation concentrate is produc.q: Why is concentrate mass so much smaller than total ore throughput?
How much flotation concentrate is produc.a:
Flotation is designed to pull out the sulphide minerals that carry the gold, and sulphides are only a small part of the ore, about 1 to 1.5 percent sulphur.

The rougher and scavenger cells take a few percent of the feed as concentrate: about 4.4 percent from rougher 1, 2.4 percent from roughers 2 and 3, and 1.1 percent from scavengers. The cleaners then reject more gangue. The final concentrate is about 75 to 78 t/h against 3,146 t/h of feed, roughly 2.5 percent.

That small stream still holds about 72 percent of the flotation feed gold, so it is very concentrated. It is like a centrifuge separating a small dense fraction from a large stream.

f.q: What is upgrade ratio and how does it apply here?
f.a:
Upgrade ratio is the concentrate grade divided by the feed grade. If feed sulphur is 1 percent and concentrate is 15 percent, the upgrade ratio is 15.

The PDC uses upgrade ratios to set concentrate grades: roughers 2 and 3 at an upgrade ratio of 7 and scavengers at 5, for example. Rougher 1 runs at about 15.3 percent sulphur.

High upgrade means a small, rich concentrate that is cheaper to treat downstream. Too high and recovery suffers because marginal particles are rejected.
f: Why does rougher 1 make a higher grade concentrate?
How does the Jameson cleaner raise concentrate grade?
What concentrate sulphur grade does the plant target?

f.q: Why does concentrate mass track sulphur grade in the ore?
f.a:
Gold here sits mainly in sulphides, especially pyrite, so flotation chases sulphur. More sulphide in the ore means more mass floats to keep sulphur and gold recovery up.

The PDC shows it clearly: nominal 1.02 percent S gives about 637 kt/a of concentrate, while design grade at 1.49 percent S gives about 876 kt/a, about 104 t/h.

That is why sulphur grade, not just gold grade, drives the size of the UFG mills, CIL2 and oxygen supply. Operators watch sulphur on the OSA closely for this reason.
f: What happens to UFG load on a high sulphur shift?
Does high sulphur ore always carry more gold?
How is sulphur inferred on the OSA?

f.q: Why does a smaller concentrate stream justify UFG and intense leach?
f.a:
Ultra fine grinding is very energy intensive: the PDC gives about 116.5 kWh/t for UFG. On 78 t/h of concentrate that is roughly 9 MW, which the IsaMills can supply.

Grinding the whole 3,146 t/h feed that fine would need hundreds of megawatts, which is impossible. Similarly, high cyanide leaching with lots of oxygen is affordable on 100 t/h but not on 3,000 t/h.

So flotation acts like a pre concentrator, letting the expensive treatment focus only on the gold rich fraction.
f: What are IsaMills and how do they grind so fine?
What cyanide levels does CIL2 run compared with CIL4?
Why is UFG media ceramic rather than steel?

How much flotation concentrate is produc.q: What would you expect if concentrate production ran well above 100 t/h?
How much flotation concentrate is produc.a:
Above 100 t/h you are in the PDC design grade territory of about 104 to 107 t/h. Expect the concentrate circuit to be near or at capacity.

Per the reference, UFG 2 and 3 run at maximum, up to about 46 t/h each at a coarser P80 of 12 microns, with excess sent to UFG 1 at about 10 t/h. Anything beyond UFG capacity goes to the vacuum belt filters and concentrate stockpile. CIL2 is designed around 104 t/h of solids.

Possible causes are high sulphur ore or a high mass pull from flotation, which may mean lower concentrate grade. Watch UFG power, thickener loading and CIL2 residence.

f.q: Why might high mass pull mean lower concentrate grade?
f.a:
Concentrate grade and recovery trade off against each other. Pushing more mass into the froth recovers more marginal sulphide but also drags in non sulphide gangue, either by entrainment with water or as partly liberated particles.

So concentrate tonnes rise faster than the gold and sulphur in them, and grade drops. Downstream circuits then grind and leach more waste per ounce.

Operators control this with froth depth, air rate and reagents. The cleaner circuit with Jameson cells is there to reject much of the entrained gangue.
f: What is entrainment in flotation?
How does froth depth affect concentrate grade?
How does the Jameson wash water reduce entrainment?

f.q: What is the UFG capacity with all three mills running?
f.a:
Per the reference, UFG 2 and 3 are IsaMill M15000 units at 30 t/h fresh feed nominal each, up to 46 t/h maximum each at a coarser P80 of 12 microns. UFG 1 is an IsaMill M3000 at about 10 t/h, 13 t/h design, when used.

So nominal capacity is about 60 t/h from UFG 2 and 3, and maximum is around 105 t/h with all three running at their limit and a coarser product.

That roughly matches the design grade concentrate rate, with filters and the stockpile as relief for anything more.
f: Why does UFG product coarsen at higher feed rates?
How is UFG mill power draw controlled?
What does a coarser UFG product do to CIL2 extraction?

f.q: What is the TML and why does it matter for the stockpile?
f.a:
TML is the transportable moisture limit. Fine wet materials like concentrate can liquefy when vibrated during transport, behaving like a slurry and shifting suddenly. Keeping moisture below the TML prevents that.

The reference gives the concentrate TML as 6.1 to 8.3 percent w/w, and the vacuum belt filters produce cake below 10 percent moisture. So filter cake moisture and TML need watching if concentrate is to be hauled or rehandled.

For handling rules on site, ask the metallurgist or the concentrate handling supervisor.
f: How do vacuum belt filters dewater concentrate?
How is stockpiled concentrate fed back to UFG?
Why does fine concentrate liquefy when vibrated?

How much flotation concentrate is produc.q: How is concentrate tonnage measured before it reaches UFG?
How much flotation concentrate is produc.a:
The reference describes the general method for slurry streams: mass flow is calculated from a magnetic flowmeter giving volume flow and a nucleonic density gauge giving slurry density, with the solids SG entered by the operator.

From flow, density and solids SG the DCS calculates percent solids and dry tonnes per hour. For concentrate, the solids SG is much higher than ore, around 3.9 for cleaner concentrate in the PDC, so that entry matters.

The final concentrate stream is also sampled for the OSA and accounting. The exact meter tags are on the P&IDs for the concentrate thickener feed.

f.q: Why does the operator entered solids SG matter so much?
f.a:
A density gauge measures slurry density only. To work out how much of that is solids, the DCS needs the density of the solids and the density of the water.

If the solids SG entered is wrong, the percent solids and dry tonnes are wrong. Concentrate SG of about 3.9 is far higher than typical ore, so using an ore value would badly overstate the water fraction and understate tonnes.

Process water here is saline at SG about 1.07, which also matters in the calculation.
f: How is concentrate SG measured in the lab?
What happens to tonnage if the water SG is wrong?
Who updates solids SG values on the DCS?

f.q: How does a nucleonic density gauge work?
f.a:
A small sealed radioactive source sits on one side of the pipe and a detector on the other. Gamma rays pass through the slurry, and denser slurry absorbs more of them, so fewer reach the detector.

The count rate is converted to density. It is non contact, so it suits abrasive slurries, but needs calibration and periodic checks.

Because there is a radioactive source, only licensed, trained people can work on these gauges. Never remove or shield one yourself, and follow the site radiation safety rules.
f: How are nucleonic density gauges calibrated?
What radiation safety rules apply near these gauges?
Can pipe scale affect density gauge readings?

f.q: Can thickener underflow measurement cross check concentrate tonnes?
f.a:
Yes, in principle. The concentrate thickener underflow goes to the filter feed tanks and UFG at around 60 percent solids, and that stream will normally have its own flow and density measurement.

Over a shift, solids in should equal solids out, allowing for changes in thickener inventory. A persistent gap between feed and underflow tonnes suggests an instrument problem or solids lost to overflow.

The reference does not list the exact meters on each stream, so check the concentrate handling P&IDs.
f: What does dirty concentrate thickener overflow indicate?
How does thickener bed inventory affect mass balance?
How are filter feed tanks A and B balanced?

Concentrator availability vs crushing av.q: Why would crushing availability be so much lower than the concentrator's?
Concentrator availability vs crushing av.a:
Primary crushing depends on trucks arriving with ore, so anything that affects the mine fleet affects the crusher: shift changes, blasting, weather, haul road issues and fleet availability.

The crusher itself also stops for rock breaker work on oversize, chokes, liner changes on the gyratory and conveyor faults such as belt drift, rips or blocked chutes. It is a single line with no standby.

Designing to 65 percent, about 5,694 h/a, accepts this reality. Rather than make the crusher more reliable, the design adds a stockpile between crusher and mills, like a receiver smoothing a reciprocating compressor's pulsing supply.

f.q: What typical events stop a primary crusher?
f.a:
Common ones are oversize rocks bridging the crusher throat, needing the rock breaker; the discharge chamber filling because the apron feeder or conveyor stopped; conveyor trips from pull wires, belt drift, rip detection or blocked chutes; and planned liner or mantle changes.

The reference notes the rock breaker is operated remotely by camera with auto park, and truck traffic lights respond to ROM bin level, discharge chamber level and crusher status, so trucks are held when the crusher cannot accept ore.

Mining side delays, such as no trucks, also count as crusher downtime in practice.
f: How is the rock breaker operated from the control room?
What does a discharge chamber high level do to trucks?
How often are gyratory mantles changed?

f.q: How do truck deliveries limit crusher run time?
f.a:
The crusher can only crush what arrives. Trucks cycle from the pit, and their arrival is uneven: bunching after shift change, gaps during blasting or refuelling, slowdowns in wet weather.

The dump pocket and ROM bin give a little buffer, but a gyratory with no trucks simply runs empty. The reference describes automatic truck traffic lights driven by radar, bin level and crusher status, which manage queuing safely.

So crushing availability reflects the mine as well as the crusher's mechanical reliability.
f: What payload do the CAT 793F trucks carry?
How do the truck traffic lights decide red or green?
Why can trucks tip on both sides of the dump pocket?

f.q: Why is designing to 65% cheaper than a more reliable crusher?
f.a:
Raising crusher availability would need a second crusher line or major redundancy, which is very expensive. A stockpile with reclaim feeders is comparatively cheap and also decouples the mills from mine disruptions.

The trade off is a crusher sized for a higher instantaneous rate, so it can refill the stockpile when it runs. It is the same logic as a water tower: a smaller pump runs intermittently while storage meets steady demand.

The Growth Project also kept the existing gyratory, PC1, running in parallel, which adds overall crushing capacity.
f: How does the existing PC1 crusher share the load?
How big is the new crushed ore stockpile?
What happens to the mills if both crushers stop?

Concentrator availability vs crushing av.q: What would you see if the stockpile ran low during a crushing outage?
Concentrator availability vs crushing av.a:
The new crushed ore stockpile holds about 20,460 t live, roughly 11 hours of residence at design rates, per the PDC. As it runs low, the reclaim apron feeders start drawing from the edges of the live zone and eventually cannot keep up.

You would see SAG feed rate falling below setpoint, the feeder speeds at maximum, and possibly a change in SAG behaviour because feed size changes as the stockpile is drawn down.

The reference lists an emergency apron feeder fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader, which lets the mill keep running from dead stockpile ore for a while. Operators may also cut feed rate to stretch the stockpile.

f.q: Why does stockpile drawdown change SAG feed size?
f.a:
When ore drops onto a conical stockpile, coarse rocks roll to the outside and fines stay near the centre under the drop point. This is segregation.

Reclaim feeders under the centre draw finer material first when the pile is full. As it is drawn down, the coarse material from the sides slides in, so feed suddenly coarsens.

SAG mills are sensitive to feed size: coarser feed can help grinding media but too much coarse, competent rock can overload the mill. The SAG feed camera size analyser helps the expert system respond.
f: How does the SAG feed camera size analyser work?
Why do SAG mills need some coarse rock as media?
Can stockpile segregation be reduced?

f.q: How is the emergency apron feeder used during low stockpile?
f.a:
The reference says there is one emergency apron feeder, fed by a CAT 992K or 994K front end loader. It lets operators reclaim ore from the dead zone of the stockpile, or from a separate pile, and feed it to the SAG feed conveyor when the main reclaim feeders cannot.

It is a manual, labour intensive way to keep the mill turning, used during long crushing outages.

Loader operation near feeders and conveyors needs a clear safe system of work. Follow the site procedure for emergency feeding.
f: How much feed can the emergency apron feeder supply?
What isolations apply when loaders work near feeders?
How is dead stockpile ore recovered afterwards?

f.q: What does live versus dead stockpile capacity mean?
f.a:
A conical stockpile sits over reclaim feeders. Only ore that can flow by gravity into the feeders is live capacity. The rest, sitting outside the drawdown cone, is dead and needs a dozer or loader to move.

The PDC gives the new stockpile live capacity as about 12,035 m3, roughly 20,460 t at 1.70 t/m3, based on a 60 degree drawdown angle. The total pile is much bigger.

So the useful buffer for the mills is the live capacity, about 11 hours at design rates.
f: What is the drawdown angle and why 60 degrees?
How big is the existing coarse ore stockpile?
How do dozers push dead ore into reclaim?

Concentrator availability vs crushing av.q: How is the crusher's higher instantaneous rate designed to compensate?
Concentrator availability vs crushing av.a:
The crusher must deliver the mills' annual tonnes in fewer running hours. The numbers in the PDC line up neatly: the new SAG takes about 1,833 t/h for 8,182 h/a. Delivering that in only 5,694 crushing hours needs 1,833 times 8,182 divided by 5,694, which is about 2,634 t/h.

That is exactly the nominal new crushing rate in the PDC. The design rate is higher again at 3,135 t/h, and the crusher maximum is about 3,436 t/h, giving margin for catch up after stoppages.

The discharge apron feeder is sized for the same 3,135 t/h design rate.

f.q: Why is the crusher design rate higher again than nominal?
f.a:
Nominal rate assumes average conditions. Real operation includes harder or blockier ore, surges from trucks arriving in bunches, and the need to refill the stockpile after outages.

Designing to 3,135 t/h, about 19 percent above nominal, gives margin for those conditions. The crusher's maximum of about 3,436 t/h adds a little more headroom.

Downstream conveyors and feeders are sized to match the design rate, so the whole crushing line can catch up without one item becoming a bottleneck.
f: How is crusher throughput measured?
What limits a gyratory crusher's maximum capacity?
Why are conveyors sized to the crusher design rate?

f.q: How does the crusher gap control affect crushing rate?
f.a:
The open side setting, OSS, sets the largest product size. The new gyratory runs at an OSS of 165 mm per the PDC.

A tighter gap makes finer product, which helps the SAG, but lowers crusher capacity and increases liner wear and power. A wider gap boosts capacity but coarsens product.

The reference says the crusher gap is adjusted automatically from a camera particle size analyser on the stockpile feed conveyor. That closes the loop on product size as liners wear, like automatic tool wear compensation on a CNC machine.
f: How does liner wear change the crusher gap?
What crusher product P80 does the PDC target?
How is crusher power related to throughput?

f.q: What happens if the stockpile reaches its high level?
f.a:
Per the reference, the stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to a stockpile high high switch and a high high level alarm. When the pile is full, the conveyor stops, which stops the discharge apron feeder through its interlocks.

The discharge chamber under the crusher then fills, and the truck traffic lights, driven by discharge chamber and ROM bin levels, hold trucks.

So a full stockpile pauses crushing rather than overfilling. That is a normal, controlled stop, not a fault.
f: How are stockpile levels measured?
What interlocks stop the discharge apron feeder?
Why must the wet scrubber run with the crusher?

The new SAG mill motor is rated....q: Why does a bigger motor allow higher throughput on the same mill duty?
The new SAG mill motor is rated....a:
For a SAG mill, throughput is mostly limited by how much power it can put into the ore. Tonnes per hour roughly equals power divided by the specific energy the ore needs, in kWh per tonne.

The new SAG's pinion duty is about 16.8 MW per the PDC, and its modelled specific energy is about 9.14 kWh/t. 16,800 divided by 9.14 gives about 1,840 t/h, which matches the 1,833 t/h nominal new SAG feed.

The old FIM SAG has 12 MW and runs about 1,313 t/h. More motor power means more tonnes on the same ore, like a bigger engine pulling a heavier load up the same hill.

f.q: Why is pinion power lower than installed motor power?
f.a:
Installed power is the motor nameplate rating, 20 MW for the new SAG. Pinion power is what actually reaches the mill gear, about 16.8 MW at the design duty point per the PDC.

The gap covers drive losses and, more importantly, design margin for harder ore, liner wear changing charge behaviour and operating at the top of the speed range. A motor run continuously at nameplate has no headroom.

It is like specifying a pump motor with margin above the duty point power on the pump curve.
f: What drive type does the new SAG use?
How does liner wear change SAG power draw?
Why does the ball mill pinion power differ from the SAG?

f.q: What is specific energy and why is 9.14 kWh/t important?
f.a:
Specific energy is the energy needed to grind one tonne of ore from feed to product size, in kWh/t. It depends on ore hardness and the size reduction asked for.

The PDC models the new SAG at about 9.14 kWh/t at nominal and about 7.68 kWh/t in the high throughput case, and the ball mill at about 9.68 kWh/t for a 180 micron grind.

Dividing mill power by specific energy gives throughput, so if ore becomes harder and needs more kWh/t, throughput falls for the same power.
f: How is ore hardness tested for SAG design?
Why does the high case have lower SAG specific energy?
How do operators see specific energy in real time?

f.q: Does the SAG use a VSD to vary speed?
f.a:
The PDC gives the new SAG a speed range of 60 to 83 percent of critical speed, which means it is variable speed. The reference does not specify the drive type, but a variable speed drive of some form is implied.

Speed is a powerful lever: faster speed lifts the charge higher and adds impact energy, while slower speed reduces impact and liner damage.

The ball mill, by contrast, normally runs at a fixed speed of about 75 percent, per the reference. Check the mill drive data sheet for the actual arrangement.
f: What is critical speed in a mill?
Why would operators slow the SAG down?
How does speed affect liner wear?

The new SAG mill motor is rated....q: What would it mean if SAG motor power was running well below normal?
The new SAG mill motor is rated....a:
Low SAG power has two very different meanings, so check before acting.

The mill may be underloaded: low feed, softer or finer ore, or a low ball charge means less material to lift, so power drops. Bearing pressure or mill weight will also be low.

Or the mill may be overloaded past its power peak. As charge builds beyond a point, the load shape changes and its centre of gravity moves toward the mill centre, so power falls even as weight rises. Rising bearing pressure with falling power is the warning sign.

The responses are opposite: more feed for underload, less feed for overload. The expert system watches both.

f.q: Why can an overloaded SAG show falling power?
f.a:
Mill power comes from lifting the charge on one side of the shell. Power is roughly the charge weight times how far its centre of gravity sits from the mill centre line.

As the mill fills beyond its optimum, the charge expands toward the centre and the cascading toe and shoulder move closer together. The centre of gravity shifts toward the axis, so the torque arm shrinks and power drops even though weight is rising.

It is like a full washing machine drum spinning more easily than a part full one with a heavy lump.
f: What is the optimum SAG load percentage?
How long does it take to recover an overloaded SAG?
Why does slurry pooling also reduce SAG power?

f.q: How does bearing pressure show the mill's load?
f.a:
SAG mills sit on hydrostatic or hydrodynamic bearings at the trunnions or shell. The oil pressure needed to support the mill rises with total mill weight, including the ore and ball charge.

So bearing pressure works as a scale, showing how much is inside. The reference lists mill load as an input to the expert system, and feed can be controlled to a mill weight setpoint.

Rising bearing pressure with flat or falling power is the classic overload signature.
f: How does the expert system respond to rising load?
What is a mill weight setpoint?
Why are load cells sometimes used instead of pressure?

f.q: What does the SAG noise monitor tell operators?
f.a:
The reference lists a SAG noise monitor as an input to the expert system. It measures sound from the mill shell.

In general, a loud, ringing mill means balls are hitting bare liners, often because the mill is underloaded or running too fast. That damages liners and breaks balls. A quiet mill can mean it is well loaded or, if very quiet, overloaded.

Operators combine noise with power and bearing pressure to judge charge condition, much like listening to a gearbox while watching its load.
f: What causes balls to hit liners directly?
How are acoustic sensors mounted on mills?
Can noise data detect liner damage early?

The new SAG mill motor is rated....q: How does SAG motor power draw get used to control feed rate?
The new SAG mill motor is rated....a:
Per the reference, reclaim feeders are controlled to a SAG feed weightometer tonnage setpoint or a mill weight setpoint, normally from the expert system. A deadband is used to allow for the lag between feeder change and mill response.

The expert system takes SAG power, load, speed, the SAG noise monitor and the feed camera size analyser, and adjusts feed to keep the mill near its best operating point without overloading.

Power is one of several inputs rather than a direct loop. When power is near the limit and load rising, feed is reduced; when power has headroom and load is low, feed is increased.

f.q: What does the expert system do that a PID loop cannot?
f.a:
A PID loop controls one variable with one output, like holding a flow at setpoint. A SAG mill has many interacting variables: power, load, speed, noise and feed size, plus constraints such as maximum power or bearing pressure.

An expert system uses rules, models or optimisation to balance all of these at once and respect limits. It behaves like an experienced operator who watches several gauges and makes small, measured adjustments.

It still writes setpoints down to normal PID loops, such as feeder tonnage, which do the fast control.
f: Who maintains the expert system rules on site?
What happens when the expert system is switched off?
How does the expert system handle sensor faults?

f.q: Why is there a deadband in the feeder control?
f.a:
Changing feeder speed does not affect the mill instantly. Ore takes time to travel along the conveyor and the mill takes minutes to respond in power and load.

If the controller reacted to every small deviation, it would keep correcting before the previous change showed up, causing hunting. A deadband tells it to ignore small errors inside a band, like a thermostat that waits for a degree or two before switching.

The reference mentions this deadband for lag on the reclaim feeder control.
f: How long does ore take from feeder to mill?
What is integral windup in slow loops?
How is the deadband size chosen?

f.q: How does SAG speed change interact with feed rate control?
f.a:
Raising SAG speed lifts the charge higher, increasing power and breakage, so the mill can handle more feed. Lowering speed reduces power and impact.

The PDC range for the new SAG is 60 to 83 percent of critical speed. Within this range speed and feed are two levers the expert system can use together: if load builds with feed already cut, raising speed can help grind it down.

But too high a speed with low load throws balls onto bare liners, which the noise monitor will flag.
f: What speed does the SAG usually run at?
How does speed affect pebble generation?
Why does the ball mill not vary its speed?

Gravity cyclone underflow aims to send h.q: Why does the vendor recommend running below the 1,000 t/h max?
Gravity cyclone underflow aims to send h.a:
The PDC gives each Knelson KC-QS70 a maximum feed of about 1,000 t/h, with an operating range of about 300 to 1,000 t/h per unit, and the vendor recommended running at about 90 percent of maximum.

Running right at the limit leaves no room for normal swings in flow and density, so short surges push the unit over capacity. Overfeeding thins and erodes the concentrate bed and lets fine gold wash through, reducing recovery.

There is also a volumetric limit of about 910 m3/h per unit in the PDC, so water as well as solids counts. It is like running a pump comfortably left of its maximum flow.

f.q: Why is the volumetric limit as important as the solids tonnage?
f.a:
The Knelson relies on slurry flowing over a spinning bowl with fluidised rings. The flow velocity across the bowl determines how much time heavy gold particles have to settle into the rings.

If volume flow is too high, slurry passes too quickly and fine gold is carried out with tails, even if solids tonnage is within limits. Dilute feed increases volume for the same tonnes.

So both the 1,000 t/h solids limit and the 910 m3/h volumetric limit in the PDC must be respected, and feed density around 54 percent solids matters.
f: How is Knelson feed density controlled?
What happens if Knelson feed is too dense?
How is Knelson feed flow measured?

f.q: What happens to recovery when a Knelson is overfed?
f.a:
Gold capture depends on centrifugal force and retention time in the concentrate bed. Overfeeding increases flow, shortens retention and can scour the bed.

Fine gold is lost first because it settles slowest. The bed may also pack with heavy minerals such as pyrite, crowding out gold.

The result is lower gravity recovery. Since gravity contributes about 14 percent of feed gold at nominal per the PDC, losses here push more gold into flotation and leach, where it may be recovered less efficiently.
f: Does gold lost from gravity get recovered later?
Why does pyrite compete for space in the Knelson bed?
How is gravity recovery measured on site?

f.q: Why feed only 1,800 t/h out of 14,400 t/h of cyclone feed?
f.a:
The cyclone cluster handles about 14,400 t/h of solids, mostly circulating load. Only two cyclones in the cluster are on gravity duty, feeding about 1,800 t/h to the two Knelsons.

Because coarse gold keeps circulating between ball mill and cyclones, it passes the gravity circuit many times. Treating a fraction of the stream each pass still captures much of it over time, like a side stream filter on a lube oil system.

Treating the full stream would need many more concentrators for diminishing returns.
f: How many times does gold circulate before recovery?
Why are Knelsons on cyclone underflow not overflow?
Could a third Knelson be added in future?
