Gravity cyclone underflow aims to send h.q: What would you check if flow to one Knelson dropped well below 900 t/h?
Gravity cyclone underflow aims to send h.a:
Each Knelson is fed from its own gravity cyclone through its own scalping screen, so look along that path.

Check the gravity cyclone feed valve and whether the cyclone is blocked, roping or has a worn or plugged apex. Check the gravity scalping screen: blinding, overflow or a tripped screen will stop feed, and the reference notes the cyclone feed valves are interlocked to their gravity screens. Check feed density and primary cyclone pressure.

Also confirm it is not just the normal Knelson cycle: each unit runs a 30 minute cycle including a flush, so flow drops briefly during rinse.

f.q: Why is the gravity cyclone valve interlocked to its scalping screen?
f.a:
The reference says the gravity cyclone feed valves are interlocked to their gravity screens. If the screen stops, slurry from the cyclone would pile up on a stationary deck, overflow and spill, and oversize could get into the Knelson.

So the interlock closes the cyclone valve when its screen is not running, stopping flow to that gravity circuit.

It is a process interlock, the kind that protects equipment and prevents spills. It must not be bypassed except under the site rules for named users.
f: How do process interlocks differ from critical interlocks?
What happens to slurry when the gravity valve closes?
Who can bypass a process interlock on this plant?

f.q: What does the scalping screen remove before the Knelson?
f.a:
Per the PDC, each gravity scalping screen is a horizontal vibrating screen with 3.2 x 18 mm slots on the first half and 2.0 x 18 mm on the second. About 8 to 15 percent of the feed reports to oversize, with 10 percent used for design, and oversize returns to the ball mill feed.

The screen removes coarse particles and tramp material that would damage the Knelson bowl, block fluidising rings or overload it.

It works like a strainer upstream of a precision pump.
f: Why do the scalping screen slots change along the deck?
What happens if scalping screen panels wear through?
Why does oversize go back to the ball mill?

f.q: Does flow dip during the Knelson flush part of each cycle?
f.a:
The PDC gives each Knelson a 30 minute cycle including flush, 48 cycles a day, producing about 150 kg of concentrate per cycle.

At the end of each cycle feed is diverted, the bowl slows, and concentrate is rinsed out. In general practice, feed bypasses to tails during this short period, so flow to the unit drops briefly then returns.

A regular, short, repeating dip every 30 minutes is normal. A sustained low flow is a real problem worth investigating.
f: Where does Knelson concentrate go after flushing?
How much gravity concentrate is made per day?
Why does a Knelson need to stop to discharge?

Gravity cyclone underflow aims to send h.q: How is flow split evenly between the two Knelson units?
Gravity cyclone underflow aims to send h.a:
There is no splitter box. Per the reference, two cyclones in the main Weir cluster are on gravity duty, each feeding its own gravity scalping screen and its own Knelson.

So the split comes from the cyclone arrangement. Both gravity cyclones see the same cluster feed pressure, about 82 kPa nominal, so they deliver similar underflow if their apexes and wear are similar.

Differences arise from worn or blocked apexes, valve problems or one screen blinding. Knelson tails return to the primary cyclone feed hopper.

f.q: Why use dedicated cyclones in the cluster for gravity feed?
f.a:
Cyclone underflow is rich in dense, coarse particles, including free gold. Using two cyclones from the main cluster gives a gravity feed stream without separate pumps.

Sharing the cluster's feed pressure keeps their performance tied to the main classification. The 18 outlet cluster has 17 cyclones installed, 15 for primary duty and 2 for gravity, per the reference.

It is a neat way to tap a side stream from a high flow circuit, similar to taking a sample stream from a header.
f: How many primary cyclones normally run?
What happens if a gravity cyclone is taken offline?
How are cyclones opened and closed automatically?

f.q: How does cyclone apex wear change gravity feed flow?
f.a:
The apex, or spigot, is the underflow outlet at the bottom of the cyclone. As it wears, it gets larger, so more slurry and more water report to underflow.

A worn apex sends more flow, at lower density, to the gravity screen and Knelson. A blocked or undersized apex starves it and can cause roping, where coarse solids escape to overflow.

So mismatched apex wear between the two gravity cyclones gives an uneven Knelson feed. Regular apex inspection and replacement keeps them balanced.
f: What is cyclone roping and how is it spotted?
How often are cyclone apexes replaced?
How does feed pressure affect cyclone underflow?

f.q: What happens to Knelson tails after concentration?
f.a:
Per the PDC, Knelson tails go back to the primary cyclone feed hopper. They rejoin the main grinding circuit and are reclassified by the cyclones.

Gold the Knelson missed gets another chance in later passes or reports to flotation. Scalping screen oversize also returns to ball mill feed.

So the gravity circuit is a loop within the grinding loop, taking concentrate out while everything else goes back.
f: Why don't Knelson tails go straight to flotation?
How does gravity water affect cyclone feed density?
What is the intensive leach reactor cycle time?

CIL4 carbon concentration target per tan.q: Why does CIL3 need a higher carbon concentration than CIL4?
CIL4 carbon concentration target per tan.a:
CIL3 receives leached concentrate from CIL2, a small tonnage with a lot of dissolved gold, so its solution is rich. More gold in solution needs more carbon capacity to capture it.

The PDC sets CIL3 at about 20 g/L carbon, about 202 t in circuit, with a design carbon loading of about 4,490 g/t. CIL4 treats a huge volume of low grade tails, so 12.5 g/L is enough and its loading range is only about 332 to 579 g/t.

Higher carbon also keeps loading from getting so high that adsorption slows down and gold passes through as soluble loss.

f.q: Why can't carbon loading just keep rising in CIL3?
f.a:
Carbon adsorbs gold until it approaches equilibrium with the solution. The higher the loading, the more gold must be in solution to keep driving adsorption, so capture slows down.

If loading gets too high, gold in solution leaving the last tank rises, which is soluble loss. More carbon and more frequent carbon movement keep loading in the efficient range.

It is like a heat exchanger approaching its temperature limit: the closer you get to equilibrium, the less transfer you get per unit area.
f: What is a carbon adsorption isotherm?
How often is carbon moved through CIL3?
What happens to carbon activity over many cycles?

f.q: How much gold is held on carbon in CIL3 at design?
f.a:
Using PDC figures, about 202 t of carbon at a design loading of about 4,490 g/t is roughly 900 kg of gold, near 29,000 ounces.

That is a significant inventory sitting in the tanks at any time. If elution falls behind, that number grows; if carbon is lost through a damaged screen, gold is lost with it.

It is why intertank screens, carbon detection on tails and carbon movement records get serious attention. Real inventory depends on actual loading.
f: How is carbon inventory measured in each tank?
What happens if an intertank screen fails?
How is lost carbon detected on CIL3 tails?

f.q: Why is CIL4 carbon loading so much lower than CIL3?
f.a:
CIL4 leaches flotation tails, which are low grade, so solution gold is low. Carbon can only load in proportion to the gold available.

The PDC gives CIL4 a nominal loading of about 461 g/t, range 332 to 579 g/t, against about 4,490 g/t design for CIL3. CIL4 also holds more carbon, about 420 t at 12.5 g/L across its larger tanks.

Lower loading means more carbon must be eluted per ounce in CIL4, which is why it has its own elution column and kiln.
f: How much carbon does CIL4 move per day?
Why does CIL4 have its own elution circuit?
What carbon residence time does CIL4 allow?

CIL4 carbon concentration target per tan.q: What would a low carbon concentration reading mean for gold adsorption?
CIL4 carbon concentration target per tan.a:
Low carbon concentration means less surface area to capture gold and slower adsorption. More dissolved gold passes through to the next tank and, if the shortfall is widespread, out to tails as soluble loss.

Loading per tonne on the remaining carbon rises, which also slows adsorption.

The Carbon Scout reading tells operators which tanks are low. One low tank with a high neighbour points to a distribution problem; low readings across the train suggest not enough carbon in circuit or carbon losses. The PDC targets are 12.5 g/L for CIL4 and about 20 g/L for CIL3.

f.q: How is soluble gold loss measured in CIL tails?
f.a:
Tails samples are filtered and the solution assayed for gold, usually in parts per billion. That is soluble loss: gold dissolved but not captured.

The reference notes a three stage sampler takes a shift composite of CIL4 tails. In general, metallurgists also take spot solution samples down the tank train to build a profile of solution gold falling from tank to tank.

A flattening profile or high final solution gold points to carbon problems.
f: What is a solution gold profile down a CIL train?
How fast can solution samples be assayed?
Why does solution gold matter more than solid gold here?

f.q: Can too much carbon in a tank also be a problem?
f.a:
Yes. Very high carbon concentration loads intertank screens more, increasing blinding risk and carbon attrition into fines. It also ties up gold inventory and lengthens carbon residence time.

Carbon also has a maximum residence time in the PDC, 14 days, beyond which it can foul and lose activity.

So both too little and too much are undesirable. The Carbon Scout helps keep each tank near target.
f: Why does carbon lose activity over time?
How does carbon attrition create fines?
What happens to carbon fines in CIL4?

f.q: What is carbon fines loss and why does it matter?
f.a:
Carbon granules wear as they are agitated and pumped, creating fines that pass through intertank screens and leave with tails. Fine carbon still carries gold, so lost fines are lost gold.

The reference notes a carbon detection meter on CIL4 tails, and fine carbon waste going to the final tails tank. Recessed impeller pumps move carbon gently to limit breakage.

Watching carbon additions over time shows how much is being lost.
f: How does a carbon detection meter work on tails?
How much fresh carbon is added each week?
Why do recessed impeller pumps reduce carbon breakage?

CIL4 carbon concentration target per tan.q: How is carbon concentration adjusted when it drifts from target?
CIL4 carbon concentration target per tan.a:
Per the reference, carbon moves counter current to slurry, using recessed impeller pumps between tanks. Loaded carbon is removed from the first adsorption tank and sent to the loaded carbon screen and elution. Barren, regenerated carbon returns to the last tank via the carbon sizing screen. Fresh carbon is added through a hoist, bag splitter and quench hopper.

If a tank is low, operators adjust carbon advance pumping from the next tank, or add regenerated or fresh carbon at the end. The PDC allows up to about 30 t/d carbon movements on CIL4 and about 33 t/d on CIL3.

f.q: Why are recessed impeller pumps used to move carbon?
f.a:
A recessed impeller pump has the impeller set back from the flow path. It creates a vortex that moves the slurry without most particles touching the impeller vanes.

That greatly reduces carbon breakage compared with a normal centrifugal pump, so less carbon becomes fines and less gold is lost.

They are less efficient hydraulically, but for carbon transfer, gentle handling matters more than efficiency. The PDC specifies recessed impeller pumps for carbon transfer.
f: How long does a carbon transfer take between tanks?
What happens if a carbon advance pump blocks?
How is carbon transfer flow monitored?

f.q: What limits how much carbon can be moved each day?
f.a:
Elution capacity is the main limit. Loaded carbon must be stripped before it can come back, so you cannot remove carbon faster than the elution column and kiln can handle.

For the CIL4 column, the PDC gives a 15 t column capacity and about 12 elutions a week. The max carbon movement rate is about 30 t/d.

Transfer pump capacity and screen capacity also matter. If elution falls behind, loadings rise and inventory builds.
f: How long does a CIL4 elution cycle take?
What happens to carbon loadings if elution stops?
Why is carbon screened before elution?

f.q: Why is barren carbon returned to the last tank?
f.a:
It is counter current flow, like a counterflow heat exchanger. Slurry flows from the first tank to the last, losing gold as it goes. Carbon moves the other way.

Fresh, barren carbon meets the leanest solution in the last tank, where it can still pick up the final traces of gold. As it moves forward it meets richer solution and loads further. Loaded carbon is removed from the first adsorption tank where solution gold is highest.

This gives maximum loading and minimum soluble loss.
f: Why are leach tanks before the adsorption tanks?
How does carbon sizing screen remove fines?
What does counter current mean for gold profile?

Tailings disposal pumps arrangement?.q: Why is redundancy on tails pumps considered so critical here?
Tailings disposal pumps arrangement?.a:
The final tails tank is the last stop before the TSF. It receives about 3,164 t/h of CIL4 tails, plus acid wash waste and fine carbon, at about 54.5 percent solids, per the PDC.

The PDC calculates actual tank residence at only about 6.9 minutes. If tails pumping stops, the tank fills in minutes, and the whole plant upstream must stop or slow because there is nowhere else for slurry to go.

That is why four pumps are installed with three running and one standby. It is like the discharge pump on a sewage lift station: if it fails, everything upstream backs up.

f.q: How long can the final tails tank absorb a pump trip?
f.a:
The PDC gives the final tails tank an actual residence time of about 6.9 minutes at nominal flow. That is the total buffer if outflow stopped completely.

If only one pump trips, outflow drops but does not stop, so the tank level rises more slowly. The standby pump starting, or upstream feed cutting back, has to happen quickly.

The reference says tank level sets the tails pump flow setpoints, so level rising will push the running pumps harder until a limit is reached.
f: How quickly can the standby tails pump start?
What alarms warn of high final tails tank level?
What upstream equipment stops first on high level?

f.q: What happens to slurry left in a stopped tails line?
f.a:
Slurry at 54.5 percent solids settles quickly when flow stops. Solids drop to the bottom of the pipe, especially in low points, and can form a plug that is hard to clear.

So when a tails line stops, it is normally flushed with water or drained through dump valves. The reference notes dump valves on pumps fail open on power loss.

Long tailings lines are at particular risk of sanding, so restarting after an unplanned stop must follow procedure.
f: How are long tailings lines flushed after a stop?
Why do dump valves fail open on power loss?
What is the critical deposition velocity in a slurry line?

f.q: Why does tank level set the tails pump flow setpoints?
f.a:
The tank has little buffer, so its level must be held steady. Level control sets the flow setpoints for the running pumps: if level rises, flow setpoint increases; if level falls, it decreases. This is a cascade from level to flow, per the reference.

That keeps outflow matching inflow and avoids running the tank dry, which would let air into pumps, or overflowing.

Each line has flow, density and pressure measurement, so operators can see how each pump is performing.
f: Why must slurry pumps avoid drawing air?
How are flow setpoints shared between three pumps?
What does high pressure on a tails line indicate?

Tailings disposal pumps arrangement?.q: What would it mean if the standby tails pump was already out of service?
Tailings disposal pumps arrangement?.a:
It means there is no redundancy. One more failure would cut tailings pumping capacity, and with only about 7 minutes of tank residence, the plant would have to slow or stop quickly.

Operators would watch the running pumps closely: pressure, flow, density and gland water. Maintenance would treat the standby repair as a priority.

The production team may also plan reduced feed rate or other contingencies. It is the kind of item a handover should always flag clearly.

f.q: Could the plant run at reduced feed on two tails pumps?
f.a:
The reference gives the duty/duty/duty/standby arrangement but not whether the pumps are in parallel lines or in series stages, so this cannot be answered reliably from the documents.

If they are parallel, losing one duty pump could mean running at about two thirds capacity, so reduced feed might work. If they are in series as booster stages on one line, losing one could stop the whole line.

Check the tailings P&ID or ask the control room operator or tailings area engineer.
f: How do series and parallel pumps behave differently?
Where is the tailings pump P&ID?
Who is responsible for the tailings system?

f.q: What early warning signs point to a tails pump failing?
f.a:
Watch for rising motor current for the same flow, falling discharge pressure, falling flow at the same speed, increasing vibration and noise, and bearing temperatures creeping up.

The reference says each tails line has flow, density and pressure measurement. Gland water flow is monitored too: low gland flow blocks starting and trips the pump after a delay.

Slurry pumps wear impellers and liners, so performance often declines gradually before a failure.
f: How do slurry pump impellers wear?
Why does gland water matter for slurry pumps?
How is pump vibration monitored here?

f.q: Who decides priority for repairing the standby pump?
f.a:
The reference does not cover maintenance prioritisation, so this is general practice.

Typically the area maintenance planner and supervisor set priority based on risk, with input from production. A standby on a critical system like tails usually gets high priority because losing it puts the whole plant at risk.

Raise the concern through the normal work order or handover process. Ask the area maintenance planner for the actual priority and expected completion time.
f: How are work order priorities set on site?
How is critical equipment identified on site?
What spare parts are held for tails pumps?

Tailings disposal pumps arrangement?.q: How often are these pumps rotated between duty and standby?
Tailings disposal pumps arrangement?.a:
The reference does not give a rotation schedule. The control philosophy only says standby changeover is decided case by case.

In general practice, duty and standby pumps are rotated regularly to equalise wear and make sure the standby is proven to work. Some plants rotate weekly, others by run hours.

Ask the area maintenance planner or control room operator for the site rotation practice.

f.q: Why does a standby pump need to be run regularly?
f.a:
A standby pump left idle for long periods can develop problems: seals dry out, bearings can be damaged by vibration from nearby running equipment, and slurry can settle in the casing.

Running it regularly proves it will start when needed and keeps components in good condition. It also spreads wear so all pumps age similarly.

It is like starting a backup generator weekly.
f: What is false brinelling in idle bearings?
How do you check a standby pump is ready to run?
Why does settled slurry damage pump casings?

f.q: How is a slurry pump changeover done safely?
f.a:
The reference describes duty and standby pumps with actuated suction, discharge and dump valves. Changeovers follow a sequence that opens valves, starts the new pump and stops the old one with flushing.

Before any maintenance, the pump must be properly isolated and locked out under the site isolation procedure. Never bypass interlocks or isolations.

Follow the site procedure and check with the control room before starting.
f: What isolations are needed for a slurry pump?
Why are dump valves used on slurry pumps?
How is a pump flushed after stopping?

f.q: What is the leak detection flowmeter on the tails line for?
f.a:
Per the reference, each tails line has a flowmeter near the plant and a second near the deposition end. Comparing them detects leaks.

If flow at the far end is lower than at the plant end, slurry is being lost somewhere, possibly through a burst pipe.

That matters because tailings contain residual cyanide and a spill is a serious environmental issue. A flow mismatch alarm lets the control room stop pumping and send someone to inspect the line quickly. The reference does not give the mismatch alarm setting, so check the tailings control narrative.
f: What alarms trigger on a flow mismatch?
How long is the line to the TSF?
What is the spill response for tailings?

Handover: 'Pebble crushers both down, pe.q: Why does critical size material build up instead of passing through?
Handover: 'Pebble crushers both down, pe.a:
A SAG mill breaks large rocks well and fine particles reasonably, but rocks of an in between size, roughly 25 to 75 mm, break slowly. They are too small to act as grinding media and too big to be ground quickly by the balls. This is the critical size.

The SAG grate has 75 mm pebble ports to let these out, and normally the pebble crushers (two XL7 cones, CSS 7 mm) crush them to about 12 mm. On bypass, uncrushed pebbles go straight back into the SAG, so they recirculate and accumulate.

It is like a recirculation loop with no sink: the load keeps rising until feed is reduced.

f.q: Why is the 25 to 75 mm range so hard for a SAG to break?
f.a:
Breakage in a SAG comes from impact when rocks and balls fall from the shoulder of the charge, and from abrasion as the charge tumbles.

Large rocks have enough mass to break themselves and others on impact. Fine particles get crushed between balls. Mid size pebbles are too light to break by their own impact, and too large and tough to be broken by the 125 mm balls efficiently.

So they wear down slowly, building up in the mill. Pebble crushing removes that bottleneck mechanically.
f: Why does a higher ball charge help critical size breakage?
How does ore competency affect pebble build up?
What size are the SAG grinding balls?

f.q: How much pebble tonnage is normally recycled?
f.a:
The PDC gives the SAG discharge screen oversize, the pebble stream, as about 375 t/h at nominal, and pebbles at about 16.6 to 28 percent of new feed. The two pebble crushers are rated about 305 t/h each, 610 t/h total, allowing for worn pebble ports.

So with both crushers down, several hundred tonnes per hour of uncrushed rock returns to the SAG. That is a large extra load, which is why feed usually has to be cut back significantly.

Actual tonnage depends on ore hardness and grate wear on the day.
f: Why does worn pebble port size increase pebble flow?
Where does the pebble bypass send the pebbles?
How is pebble tonnage measured?

f.q: Can the SAG speed change help when pebble crushers are down?
f.a:
The new SAG runs between 60 and 83 percent of critical speed per the PDC. Raising speed lifts the charge higher and increases impact energy, which can help break critical size material a little faster.

But too much speed with a light charge throws balls onto bare liners, damaging them, so operators balance speed against noise monitor and load readings.

The card notes operators may adjust speed alongside backing off feed and watching power and bearing pressure. It helps but does not replace the crushers.
f: How does the noise monitor protect SAG liners?
What is the risk of running the SAG too fast?
How long can the SAG run with pebbles on bypass?

Handover: 'Pebble crushers both down, pe.q: What SAG power or bearing trend would confirm pebbles are building up?
Handover: 'Pebble crushers both down, pe.a:
Expect SAG bearing pressure, or mill weight, to rise steadily as pebbles accumulate. Power may rise at first as the load grows.

If the mill continues to fill, power can level off or even fall while bearing pressure keeps rising, because the charge moves past its power peak. That combination is the classic overload warning.

You may also see the SAG noise monitor reading quieter as the charge cushions impacts, and the pebble conveyor tonnage stay high. Watch these on the PI trends against feed rate.

f.q: How does the expert system respond to rising SAG load?
f.a:
Per the reference, the expert system takes inputs from the SAG feed size camera, noise monitor, load, speed and power, and normally sets the reclaim feeder tonnage or mill weight setpoint.

When load rises toward its limit, the expert system reduces feed. It may also adjust speed within the allowed range.

With pebble crushers down, operators may need to lower the expert system's targets or take manual control if it struggles to keep up. Feed reductions are the main tool.
f: When would operators take the SAG out of expert control?
What load limit does the SAG run to?
How fast does SAG load respond to feed changes?

f.q: Why does power fall when the SAG is overloaded?
f.a:
Mill power comes from lifting the charge against gravity. Power roughly equals charge weight times the distance from its centre of gravity to the mill centre line.

As the mill overfills, the charge spreads toward the centre and the cascading toe climbs. The centre of gravity moves toward the axis, so even though weight rises, the torque arm shrinks and power falls.

So falling power with rising weight means overload, not underload. Feeding more in that situation makes it worse.
f: How can an operator tell underload from overload?
What is slurry pooling in a SAG?
How is an overloaded SAG recovered?

f.q: What does the pebble conveyor tonnage show during bypass?
f.a:
The pebble stream from the SAG discharge screen passes along conveyors to the pebble crusher bins, or on bypass back to SAG feed. With both crushers down, all pebbles go round the bypass.

Rising pebble tonnage shows critical size material building up in the SAG and recirculating faster. Once it stabilises, the SAG has reached a new balance at the reduced feed.

Comparing pebble tonnage with fresh feed tonnage tells operators how much of the SAG's capacity is going to recirculating pebbles.
f: How is pebble conveyor tonnage measured?
What is the pebble crusher bypass gate logic?
Why do pebble ports wear larger over time?

Handover: 'Pebble crushers both down, pe.q: What maintenance issue commonly takes both pebble crushers down at once?
Handover: 'Pebble crushers both down, pe.a:
The reference does not describe common failure causes, so this is general experience plus the plant's bypass logic.

Shared systems are the usual suspects: the common pebble feed conveyor, the tramp metal magnet and metal detector, a shared lube or hydraulic system, or a common power supply or MCC.

Per the reference, pebbles automatically bypass on metal detection, and the bypass gate opens if the bin is High and both feeders are stopped, or the bin is High High. So a blocked feed chute, a metal detection event or feeders tripping can push both crushers onto bypass at once. Ask the area maintenance planner for the site history.

f.q: Why does metal detection send pebbles to bypass?
f.a:
Steel from broken balls and liner bolts ends up in the pebble stream. A cone crusher cannot crush steel, and tramp metal can damage the mantle, bowl liner or main shaft and cause dangerous overpressure in the hydraulic system.

So when the metal detector senses metal, the bypass diverts that portion of pebbles around the crusher, per the reference. A tramp magnet upstream removes most steel first.

Repeated metal detection events can keep the crushers on bypass for long periods.
f: How does a tramp magnet remove steel from pebbles?
Why do broken balls appear in the pebble stream?
How long does the bypass stay open after detection?

f.q: What is the closed side setting on a cone crusher?
f.a:
The closed side setting, CSS, is the smallest gap between the mantle and the bowl liner during each gyration. It controls product size.

The PDC gives the pebble crushers a CSS of 7 mm, producing a product P80 of about 12 mm from feed of about 49 mm F80.

A tighter CSS makes finer product, which helps the SAG, but increases power, liner wear and the risk of overload. Liner wear opens the CSS, so it is adjusted periodically.
f: How is cone crusher CSS checked and adjusted?
What happens if CSS is set too tight?
How long do pebble crusher liners last?

f.q: How are pebble crusher feed bins controlled?
f.a:
Per the reference, there are two feed bins of about 65 t each. Feeders start on bin high level and stop on low level. The bypass gate opens if the bin reaches High with both feeders stopped, or if it reaches High High.

So the bins buffer pebbles and protect against overfilling. If crushers are unavailable, rising bin level automatically sends pebbles to bypass.

This keeps the SAG running even when pebble crushing is offline.
f: Why do feeders start on high level not low?
What does a bin high high alarm mean?
How is bin level measured?

Handover: 'Cyclone overflow P80 running.q: Why does coarser grind leave more gold locked in unliberated particles?
Handover: 'Cyclone overflow P80 running.a:
Gold and sulphides are often fine grains embedded in larger particles of waste rock. Grinding breaks particles until those grains are exposed, liberated, so collectors can attach and flotation can recover them.

At a coarser P80 of about 230 microns, more particles still have their sulphide grains locked inside or only partly exposed. These may not float, or they float poorly, so more gold reports to flotation tails.

The PDC target is P80 180 microns, with a maximum of 250 microns. Coarse particles are also harder to lift in the froth, so even liberated ones can be lost. It is a trade off: coarser grind gives more tonnes but more losses.

f.q: What is liberation and how is it measured?
f.a:
Liberation is the degree to which a mineral particle is free from other minerals. A fully liberated pyrite particle is pure pyrite; a locked one has pyrite inside quartz or other gangue.

It is measured in the lab using automated mineralogy, which uses electron microscopes to scan polished particles and identify minerals and their associations.

Metallurgists use liberation data to choose grind size targets. For this ore the PDC sets 180 microns as the target.
f: What is automated mineralogy and how is it done?
Why is gold often locked in pyrite?
How does UFG improve gold liberation?

f.q: How does coarse grind affect flotation cells?
f.a:
Coarse particles are heavy, so they settle more easily in flotation cells. If agitation is not strong enough, they can drop to the bottom of the cell and sand up, building deposits that reduce effective volume and can block dart valves.

The card notes coarse sulphides can sand up in the cells. Air valves are interlocked closed if the agitator stops, which helps prevent sanding of the rotor and stator.

Coarser grind also loads the froth with heavier particles that drop back more easily.
f: How do flotation agitators keep coarse particles suspended?
What happens if a flotation cell sands up?
Why are dart valves used for cell level control?

f.q: Why does coarse grind matter for CIL4?
f.a:
CIL4 leaches flotation tails at the primary grind size. Coarser tails mean gold in them is less exposed to cyanide, so CIL4 extraction drops too.

Coarse particles also settle more in tanks and can stress agitators and intertank screens.

So a coarse grind costs recovery twice: once in flotation and again in tails leach. The PDC CIL4 design extraction is about 38 percent at design grind.
f: How does CIL4 agitation handle coarse particles?
What is the CIL4 design leach residence time?
Why does tails leach recovery depend on grind?

Handover: 'Cyclone overflow P80 running.q: What would you check on the cyclones if overflow suddenly ran coarse?
Handover: 'Cyclone overflow P80 running.a:
Start with the cyclone cluster's operating conditions on the OIS.

Check feed pressure, nominally about 82 kPa: low pressure gives a coarser cut. Check the number of cyclones open: the reference says cyclones open when pressure is high and close when low, but too few open raises pressure, too many lowers it. Check feed density: higher density gives coarser overflow. Look for roping, where overloaded underflow sends coarse material to overflow, and for worn or blocked apexes.

Also check whether ball mill power or circulating load changed, and whether feed rate increased.

f.q: What is cyclone roping and how do you spot it?
f.a:
Roping happens when the underflow can't discharge solids fast enough, often because the apex is too small or the feed too dense. The underflow changes from a spray cone to a dense rope, and coarse solids are forced up into overflow.

Signs are a rope like discharge at the apex, coarse particles in overflow, a sudden coarsening of P80 and higher overflow density.

Fixes include reducing feed density by adding hopper water, opening more cyclones or replacing the apex.
f: What causes a cyclone apex to block?
How does cyclone feed density affect the cut size?
How often are cyclone apexes inspected?

f.q: How does feed density affect cyclone cut size?
f.a:
Cyclones separate by settling velocity in a spinning flow. Denser slurry is more viscous and crowded, so particles settle less easily, and the cut size coarsens.

The PDC gives cyclone feed at about 62 percent solids. The reference says hopper water addition controls cyclone feed or overflow density.

So adding water to the cyclone feed hopper dilutes the feed and gives a finer overflow, at the cost of more water downstream.
f: What overflow density does the PDC target?
How is hopper water addition controlled?
What happens to flotation if overflow is too dilute?

f.q: How does circulating load affect grind size?
f.a:
Circulating load is the cyclone underflow returned to the ball mill as a percentage of new feed. The PDC gives about 358 percent at nominal.

Higher circulating load means more material recycled for further grinding, but it can overload the ball mill and cyclones, making the cut coarser.

If circulating load rises sharply, it often means feed got harder, the ball charge dropped or the cyclones changed. It is a key indicator alongside P80.
f: How is circulating load calculated on site?
What ball charge does the ball mill run?
How does ball mill power relate to grind?

Handover: 'Cyclone overflow P80 running.q: How would operators adjust the circuit to bring P80 back down?
Handover: 'Cyclone overflow P80 running.a:
Operators have several levers, usually used together.

Reduce fresh feed rate to the SAG so the ball mill and cyclones have more capacity per tonne. Adjust cyclone feed density by adding water to the hopper, which sharpens the cut. Check the number of cyclones open to bring pressure back to target. Increase ball mill ball addition if the charge is low.

The expert system may make some of these changes automatically. Changes take time to show in the P80 reading, so avoid overcorrecting.

f.q: How quickly does P80 respond to circuit changes?
f.a:
Grinding circuits have long residence times. Changes to feed rate or density take several minutes to affect the ball mill and cyclones, and the particle size analyser itself has a sample and measurement delay.

So operators should make one change, wait, and watch the trend, rather than stacking several changes quickly. It is like tuning a slow temperature loop.

The reference notes an online particle size analyser on the UFG; the main grind measurement method is not detailed for the primary circuit.
f: How does the particle size analyser measure P80?
Why do grinding circuits respond slowly?
What is overcorrection in slow processes?

f.q: Why add balls to the ball mill to fix coarse grind?
f.a:
Ball mill grinding power depends on the ball charge. As balls wear, the charge drops and power falls, so less grinding is done and grind coarsens.

Per the reference, ball addition is automatic to a kg/t or mill weight setpoint, with the ball charge around 28.5 percent of mill volume, max 31.

Topping up restores power. It is like topping up oil in a gearbox: run low and performance drops.
f: How much do grinding balls wear per tonne?
What ball size does the ball mill use?
How is ball mill charge level measured?

f.q: Can reducing feed always fix coarse grind?
f.a:
Reducing feed usually helps because each tonne gets more grinding energy. But it costs throughput, and if the problem is a cyclone fault such as a blocked apex, cutting feed only partly helps.

So operators check the cyclones first. If they are fine, feed reduction or density changes are the next step.

The goal is the best balance of tonnes and recovery, which the metallurgist sets.
f: When is a coarse grind worth accepting?
How do metallurgists set grind targets?
What causes cyclone faults most often?

Handover: 'Scavenger tails sulphur is cr.q: Why does rising sulphur in tails directly indicate lost gold?
Handover: 'Scavenger tails sulphur is cr.a:
On this ore, much of the gold is locked in sulphides, mainly pyrite. Flotation is designed to recover those sulphides, and gold goes with them.

So sulphur in the scavenger tails is a proxy for gold escaping flotation. If tails sulphur rises, more pyrite, and therefore more gold, is heading to the flotation tails thickener and on to CIL4, where only about 34 to 38 percent of gold is recovered at design.

The OSA measures iron and gold on the scavenger tails, with sulphur inferred from iron. Gold itself is hard to measure online at tails levels, so sulphur is the more reliable early warning.

f.q: Why is sulphur inferred from iron on the OSA?
f.a:
Pyrite is iron sulphide, FeS2. Since most sulphur on this ore is in pyrite, iron and sulphur go together in a predictable ratio.

The OSA measures iron directly by X ray fluorescence, which works well at percent levels. Sulphur is harder to measure online, so it is calculated from iron, per the reference.

This works as long as the iron and sulphur ratio is stable. Iron from non sulphide minerals can throw it off.
f: What other minerals contain iron in this ore?
How does X ray fluorescence measure iron?
When might the iron to sulphur ratio change?

f.q: What sulphur recovery does flotation aim for?
f.a:
The PDC gives nominal flotation sulphur recovery of about 85.1 percent, with a maximum of 90 percent. Gold recovery is about 71.8 percent nominal, max 75 percent.

So about 15 percent of the sulphur entering flotation goes to tails at design. A rising trend above normal means flotation is losing more than that.

Metallurgists set targets, so check current scavenger tails sulphur norms with them.
f: Why is gold recovery lower than sulphur recovery?
What scavenger tails sulphur is normal?
How do scavengers improve sulphur recovery?

f.q: Does tails sulphur affect CIL4 performance?
f.a:
Higher sulphides in CIL4 feed consume more oxygen and cyanide, because sulphides react with both. That can lower dissolved oxygen in CIL4 and raise cyanide consumption.

So a flotation problem shows up downstream too. Watch DO alarms and cyanide analyser readings in CIL4 if tails sulphur rises.

The gold locked in those sulphides mostly will not leach at the primary grind, so it is still lost.
f: How does CIL4 control oxygen in the leach tanks?
Why do sulphides consume cyanide?
What is thiocyanate and why does it form?

Handover: 'Scavenger tails sulphur is cr.q: What reagent or air rate change would you check first on this trend?
Handover: 'Scavenger tails sulphur is cr.a:
Start with things that changed recently, and check in a logical order.

Check feed: has grind coarsened, has feed rate risen, or has ore type changed? Then check air: are cell air flows at setpoint, and are blowers holding header pressure? Then reagents: are PAX, copper sulphate and frother pumps running at the right dose and flow? Then levels: are froth depths and dart valves working?

The flotation expert system uses OSA data and froth cameras, so check whether it is in control and whether any inputs are faulty.

f.q: What does PAX do in flotation?
f.a:
PAX, potassium amyl xanthate, is a collector. It adsorbs on sulphide mineral surfaces, making them water repellent so they attach to air bubbles and float.

Too little PAX means sulphides stay wet and don't float, so recovery drops. Too much wastes money and can reduce selectivity.

Per the reference, PAX is dosed by VSD pumps on flow control, with g/t or flow setpoint.
f: How is PAX dosage set on this plant?
Why does PAX need to be fresh?
What is a collector versus an activator?

f.q: What does copper sulphate do in flotation?
f.a:
Copper sulphate is an activator. Copper ions adsorb on sulphide surfaces such as pyrite and sphalerite, making them more receptive to the collector.

Per the reference, it is dosed at SAG discharge and at the cleaner. Low copper sulphate can mean poor sulphide activation and lower recovery.

Overdosing can also activate unwanted minerals and waste reagent. Copper sulphate solution is corrosive to carbon steel, so its lines and pumps use suitable materials.
f: Why dose copper sulphate at SAG discharge?
How is copper sulphate stored and mixed?
What happens if copper sulphate is overdosed?

f.q: How does cell air rate affect recovery?
f.a:
Air creates the bubbles that carry sulphides to the froth. More air generally means more bubbles and more recovery, up to a point. Too much air makes the froth unstable, increases entrainment of gangue and can lower grade.

Per the reference, each cell has an air flow controller with a mass flow meter, and blowers have VSDs holding header pressure. Air valves close if the agitator stops.

Check that air flow is at setpoint and the valve is responding.
f: Why are air valves interlocked to agitators?
How are flotation blowers controlled?
What is froth stability and why does it matter?

Handover: 'Scavenger tails sulphur is cr.q: How is the OSA sulphur reading used to trigger operator response?
Handover: 'Scavenger tails sulphur is cr.a:
Per the reference, the flotation expert system uses OSA data, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set level (froth depth), air and reagents. So OSA sulphur readings feed straight into automatic adjustments.

Operators also see OSA trends on the OIS. A rising scavenger tails sulphur trend would be flagged by alarms or noticed on the trend, prompting checks of air, reagents and levels.

The exact alarm limits and response rules are not in the reference, so ask the metallurgist or control room operator.

f.q: How do froth cameras help control flotation?
f.a:
Froth cameras look down on the froth surface and measure bubble size, froth speed and colour. Launder velocity cameras measure how fast froth flows into the launder.

These indicate how much mass is being recovered. The expert system uses them alongside OSA data to adjust froth depth, air and reagents.

It is like watching the flame in a burner to tune fuel and air.
f: What does froth colour tell operators?
How does froth depth control mass pull?
Why are launder velocity cameras used?

f.q: How often does the OSA analyse each stream?
f.a:
The reference lists the OSA streams but does not give cycle time. In general, an OSA with many streams rotates through them, with each stream measured every few minutes to every quarter hour.

That makes OSA data suitable for trend control rather than instant response.

Ask the instrument technician or metallurgist for this OSA's cycle time. Knowing it helps you judge how stale a reading on the OIS might be when you see a sudden change.
f: How does a multi stream OSA switch samples?
Why are OSA results delayed?
How is OSA availability tracked?

f.q: What happens if the OSA goes offline?
f.a:
Without OSA data, the expert system loses a key input and may revert to manual or fixed setpoints. Operators must rely on froth appearance, shift samples and lab assays.

Response to changes becomes slower and less precise, increasing the chance of losses.

Flag it at handover and get the instrument team to restore it quickly. Lab assays of shift composite samples remain the official record, but they arrive hours later.
f: Who maintains the OSA on site?
How do operators control flotation without OSA?
What lab assays back up the OSA?

Handover: 'Trash screen 2 is blinding, r.q: Why does losing open area on a trash screen risk downstream equipment?
Handover: 'Trash screen 2 is blinding, r.a:
Trash screens remove wood, plastic, grit and other debris from cyclone overflow before it goes to flotation. Per the PDC, there are four linear screens with 1.0 mm apertures, three operating and one standby.

If a screen loses open area through blinding, less slurry passes through the mesh. The excess either overflows with the trash, losing slurry, or bypasses untreated depending on design.

Trash that gets past can block flotation dart valves, air spargers, OSA sample lines, CIL intertank screens and, critically, the UFG mills and their 1.0 mm trash screens. It is like a strainer blocking upstream of precision equipment.

f.q: What causes trash screens to blind?
f.a:
Blinding happens when particles or fibres lodge in apertures and block them. Near size particles, wood fibres, plastic and grease are common causes.

Sticky material and fine clays can also coat the mesh. Per the PDC, each screen has spray water of about 60 m3/h to help keep the deck clean.

Regular wash down and panel replacement are needed to restore open area.
f: How are spray bars set on trash screens?
How often are trash screen panels replaced?
What happens to wood removed by the trash screens?

f.q: How much trash do the screens remove?
f.a:
The PDC estimates about 27 t/day of wood, grit and trash removed. The trash goes to a dewatering screen, 1.83 x 3.66 m with 1 x 15 mm apertures, before disposal.

That is a significant amount of material that would otherwise end up in downstream equipment.

Trash comes from mining activity, timber supports, plastic liners and other debris mixed with ore.
f: Where does trash come from in mined ore?
How is trash disposed of from site?
What does the trash dewatering screen do?

f.q: What is screen flux and why does it matter?
f.a:
Flux is flow per unit screen area, here in m3 per m2 per hour. The PDC gives a maximum flux of 75 m3/m2/h for the trash screens.

If flow exceeds that limit, slurry can't pass through the mesh fast enough and overflows with trash. Losing one of three screens increases flux on the remaining two.

So flux is the capacity limit, like flow per tube in a heat exchanger.
f: What flux do the trash screens run at nominally?
How does blinding change effective flux?
Why are there four trash screens?

Handover: 'Trash screen 2 is blinding, r.q: What would happen to UFG feed if this screen failed completely?
Handover: 'Trash screen 2 is blinding, r.a:
The reference does not describe this failure mode directly, so this is general reasoning with plant details.

If a trash screen fails completely while no standby is available, the plant loses a quarter of its installed screen capacity, and the remaining two screens must handle the flow. Flux would exceed design and more trash would get through or overflow.

Trash would travel with flotation feed and concentrate. UFG 2 and 3 have inclined static wedge wire trash screens of 1.0 mm ahead of them, per the reference, which would catch some, but they could become overloaded. Trash inside an IsaMill can damage media separators and block flows.

f.q: What does an IsaMill trash screen protect?
f.a:
Per the reference, UFG 2 and 3 have inclined static wedge wire trash screens of 1.0 mm ahead of them, and UFG 1 has a vibrating 1.0 mm mesh screen.

These protect the IsaMill from debris that could block the product separator, which keeps grinding media inside the mill. Debris could also damage internal discs.

So the IsaMill trash screen is the last line of defence.
f: How does an IsaMill product separator work?
What is the grinding media in an IsaMill?
How often are UFG trash screens cleaned?

f.q: Can trash reach CIL4 if the screens fail?
f.a:
Yes. Trash passing the main trash screens goes to flotation, and much of it ends up in flotation tails, which go via the thickener to CIL4.

In CIL4, trash can blind intertank screens and get mixed with carbon, complicating carbon handling and screening.

The reference notes future carbon safety screens and a CIL4 static screen, but primary trash removal relies on the trash screens.
f: How do intertank screens get blinded?
What does the CIL4 static screen do?
What are carbon safety screens for?

f.q: How does losing a trash screen affect flotation?
f.a:
Losing a screen raises flux on the others and can cause overflow or trash bypass. Trash in flotation can block dart valves, clog air spargers and coat cell surfaces.

It can also block OSA sample lines, reducing control quality.

So trash screen problems quickly become flotation problems. Debris in cell launders or repeatedly blocked dart valves is often the first visible sign that trash is getting past the screens upstream.
f: How do dart valves get blocked?
What is a flotation air sparger?
How do OSA sample lines get blocked?

Handover: 'Trash screen 2 is blinding, r.q: How quickly can screen panels be changed out during a running shift?
Handover: 'Trash screen 2 is blinding, r.a:
The reference does not give panel change times, so ask the area maintenance planner or screen fitter crew.

In general, modular polyurethane panels can be replaced quickly, but the screen must be stopped, isolated and locked out first. Working on or near a running screen is not safe.

The time depends on how many panels need changing and whether spares and crews are ready. With no standby, the plant may need to reduce feed during the change.

f.q: What isolations are needed before working on a screen?
f.a:
A vibrating screen must be electrically isolated and locked out under the site isolation procedure. The feed must be stopped or diverted, and any spray water isolated.

Stored energy, such as springs and drive belts, must be secured.

Never work on a running screen or bypass interlocks to save time. Follow the site permit system. If you are unsure who holds the isolation or whether it is complete, ask the area supervisor before starting.
f: What is stored energy on a vibrating screen?
How is a screen feed diverted for maintenance?
Who issues isolation permits on site?

f.q: What material are the trash screen panels made from?
f.a:
The PDC lists the trash dewatering screen deck as polyurethane. The main trash screen panel material is not specified in the reference.

Polyurethane panels are common because they resist abrasion and are easy to replace. Some screens use wedge wire or woven mesh.

Check the screen data sheet for the main trash screens, or ask the area maintenance planner, who will know which spare panels are held in the store.
f: Why is polyurethane good for screen panels?
What is a modular screen panel system?
How are screen panels fixed to the deck?

f.q: How does the standby trash screen come into service?
f.a:
The reference says four screens are installed with three operating and one standby. It does not describe the changeover process.

In general, flow distribution to each screen is set by valves or a distribution box. Bringing the standby on line means opening its feed and starting it.

Ask the control room operator for the specific procedure. The operator will also know whether the standby screen is actually serviceable before anyone relies on it.
f: How is flow distributed between trash screens?
Can all four trash screens run together?
What causes a trash screen to trip?

Handover: 'Flotation tails thickener und.q: Why does lower underflow density directly cut leach residence time?
Handover: 'Flotation tails thickener und.a:
CIL4 tanks have a fixed volume, about 5,600 m3 live each. Residence time is tank volume divided by slurry volume flow, so if the same tonnes of solids arrive carrying more water, the slurry moves through faster.

At 56 percent solids each tonne of solids carries about 0.79 t of water. At 48 percent it carries about 1.08 t, nearly 40 percent more. Assuming a typical ore SG of about 2.8, slurry volume per tonne rises by roughly 25 percent.

So the PDC's 3.2 h leach residence could fall toward about 2.6 h, with total CIL4 time dropping from 12.8 h in proportion. Less time in the leach means less gold dissolved. These are design based estimates, not live values.

f.q: How is CIL4 residence time calculated?
f.a:
Residence time is live tank volume divided by slurry volume flow. CIL4 has 8 tanks of about 5,600 m3 live each, per the PDC: 2 leach tanks give about 11,200 m3 and the whole train about 44,800 m3.

At the design flow of about 3,511 m3/h, that gives about 3.2 h of leach and about 12.8 h total. The PDC notes 12.8 h is already below the 14 h ideal.

Any increase in volume flow, whether from more solids or more water, shortens residence. It is the same as a heat exchanger: push more flow through and each litre spends less time in it.
f: Why is CIL4 residence below the 14 h ideal?
Where would the future extra CIL4 tank fit?
Does short circuiting reduce real residence time?

f.q: Does diluted slurry affect reagent concentrations?
f.a:
Yes. Cyanide and lime are dissolved in the slurry water, so extra water dilutes them unless dosing increases.

Per the reference, CIL4 cyanide flow is set by the operator or as a g/t ratio on thickener underflow tonnes, then trimmed by the cyanide analyser on tanks 1 and 2. A g/t setting adds cyanide per tonne of solids, so with more water the solution concentration falls until the analyser trim catches up.

pH is controlled by the tank 1 pH controller opening the lime valve, so it should recover, but lime use rises. Overall, dilution costs reagent and leach performance.
f: How does the cyanide analyser trim the CIL4 dose?
Why does cyanide concentration matter more than dose?
How does extra lime demand show on the OIS?

f.q: What happens to the extra water in CIL4?
f.a:
The extra water passes through CIL4 with the slurry and goes to the final tails tank and on to the TSF. It adds to the volume the tailings pumps must move and to the water stored at the TSF.

It also carries dissolved cyanide, so more cyanide goes to tails with it, which increases cyanide use and the load on the decant water destruct system when water returns.

Meanwhile, that water was not returned through thickener overflow to the Process Water Tank, so the plant water balance shifts too. Low underflow density has effects well beyond the leach.
f: How does thickener overflow feed the process water tank?
How does decant water come back from the TSF?
What sets the final tails tank density?

Handover: 'Flotation tails thickener und.q: What rake or flocculant symptom would you look for causing this drop?
Handover: 'Flotation tails thickener und.a:
Start with the thickener vendor panel signals listed in the reference: rake torque, bed level from the SmartDiver, rake height, bed pressure (bed mass) and overflow clarity.

A low bed level and low bed pressure mean the bed has thinned, often because underflow is being pumped faster than solids settle or because flocculation is poor. Dirty overflow points to poor flocculation or overloading. Unusually low rake torque also suggests a thin bed.

Then check flocculant: in Stage 2 it is dosed to a feed solids ratio setpoint. Confirm the floc plant is running, make up is normal and the dilution and dose rates are right.

f.q: How does the SmartDiver measure bed level?
f.a:
The SmartDiver is a vendor bed level instrument listed in the reference. In general, devices of this type lower a sensor down through the thickener and detect the change in density or turbidity where clear liquor turns into settling slurry and then compacted bed.

That gives a direct reading of bed depth, which operators trend alongside bed pressure.

A falling bed level with steady feed suggests underflow is being withdrawn faster than solids arrive. Stage 1 used a Manta sub for bed level, which the floc dosing was cascaded from. Check the vendor manual for this unit's exact principle.
f: What is the difference between bed level and bed mass?
Why did Stage 1 dose floc from bed level?
How often should bed level sensors be cleaned?

f.q: How does bed pressure relate to underflow density?
f.a:
Bed pressure is measured near the bottom of the thickener and reflects the weight of solids in the bed above. More bed mass means more compaction and a denser underflow, a bit like the head of material in a hopper.

The reference says underflow pumps run in cascade from bed pressure or density to a flow controller driving the VSD. If bed pressure falls, the controller should slow the pumps so the bed can rebuild.

If that loop is in manual, its setpoint is wrong or the density meter is faulty, underflow density can drop. Check the loop mode first.
f: What is cascade control in thickener underflow?
How do you tell a faulty density meter from a real drop?
Why are underflow pumps on duty/standby VSDs?

f.q: What flocculant problems lower underflow density?
f.a:
Underdosing is the most common. Too little polymer gives small, weak flocs that settle slowly and pack loosely, so the bed is less dense and overflow gets cloudy.

Other causes include a blocked screw feeder or wetting head in the floc plant, a make up tank running low, old or degraded solution, wrong dilution at the inline mixer, or a floc pump or flowmeter fault.

A change in ore, such as more clay or finer grind, can also need a higher dose than the ratio setpoint provides. Check pump status, make up level and dose trends against feed tonnes.
f: How does clay in the ore affect thickening?
How is a blocked floc screw feeder detected?
How fast does a floc change show in the bed?

Handover: 'Flotation tails thickener und.q: How would operators recover underflow density back to target?
Handover: 'Flotation tails thickener und.a:
Operators usually take these steps, watching trends between each one.

First, check the underflow pump loop is in automatic cascade from bed pressure or density, and let it slow the pumps so the bed rebuilds. Second, fix flocculation: confirm dosing is running and raise the ratio setpoint if underdosed. Third, if the thickener is overloaded, reduce feed or ask whether upstream conditions changed.

The reference notes underflow can be recycled to the feed box on start up or low flow, which keeps lines moving without sending dilute slurry to CIL4. Thickeners respond slowly, so changes may take hours to show fully.

f.q: Why recycle underflow back to the thickener feed?
f.a:
Per the reference, underflow can be recycled to the feed on start up or low flow. The pumps keep running and the line keeps moving, but dilute slurry goes back into the thickener instead of on to CIL4.

That avoids settling in the underflow line, which could block it, and gives the bed time to build up density.

It is like a minimum flow recirculation line on a pump: flow keeps going for the equipment's sake while the process is not ready to take it.
f: What line velocity stops slurry settling?
How is the recycle valve controlled?
Does recycling affect thickener capacity?

f.q: How long does a thickener take to recover density?
f.a:
It depends on how much bed has been lost and how fast new solids arrive. The flotation tails thickener receives about 3,071 t/h of solids at design, so it can rebuild bed fairly quickly once withdrawal is cut back, but full recovery of a stable dense bed often takes several hours.

The reference gives a 60 m diameter thickener with an area of about 2,827 m2.

Slowing the pumps too much can overshoot and raise bed mass and torque, so operators watch bed pressure and density trends and adjust gradually.
f: What is the design flux of this thickener?
How can overshooting density raise torque?
Why does a large thickener respond slowly?

f.q: Can underflow density be too high?
f.a:
Yes. The PDC range is 50 to 62 percent solids, with 56 percent nominal. Above the range, the slurry becomes very viscous and its yield stress climbs steeply.

That makes it hard to pump, raises underflow pump pressure, increases rake torque and raises the risk of the thickener bogging. In CIL4, very thick slurry is harder to agitate and mix with oxygen and reagents.

So operators aim for the target band, not the maximum. It is like tightening a bolt to a specified torque rather than as tight as possible.
f: What rake torque level should worry an operator?
How does slurry yield stress affect pumping?
Why is mixing harder in thick CIL slurry?

Handover: 'Thickener rake torque high an.q: Why does a bogged thickener become such a major outage to recover from?
Handover: 'Thickener rake torque high an.a:
A bogged thickener has a bed so dense and deep that the rakes stall and cannot move it. The solids set up like wet concrete around the rake arms.

Recovering usually means stopping feed, pumping out what will flow, then breaking up and removing thousands of tonnes of settled solids, often with water lances and sometimes excavation. That can take days or longer.

Because this thickener takes all the flotation tails, the plant may have to run at reduced rate or stop while it is down. The rake mechanism itself can be damaged by the overload. That is why rake torque gets so much attention.

f.q: How is a bogged thickener recovered?
f.a:
The reference does not describe a recovery procedure, so this is general practice.

Feed is stopped, and the underflow pumps are used to draw out as much as will flow. Water is added through lances or nozzles to break up the bed and re-slurry it so it can be pumped. In bad cases the thickener is drained and solids are dug out with machinery.

It is slow and hazardous work with engulfment and confined space risks. Any entry is under strict permits and isolation. Prevention is far cheaper than recovery.
f: What confined space controls apply to thickeners?
How are water lances used to break a bed?
How long did past thickener recoveries take?

f.q: Can the plant run without the flotation tails thickener?
f.a:
The reference does not describe a bypass for this thickener, so this cannot be answered reliably from the documents.

In Stage 2 all flotation tails thickener underflow goes to CIL4, and the overflow is the main feed to the Process Water Tank. Losing it affects both the leach feed and the process water supply.

Whether there is an emergency route to final tails and what rate the plant could sustain is a question for the metallurgist or production superintendent. Ask them about the contingency plan.
f: What tops up the process water tank if overflow stops?
Is there a contingency route for flotation tails?
Who decides plant rate during a thickener outage?

f.q: Why are rake mechanisms expensive to repair?
f.a:
A thickener rake drive is a large, slow speed, very high torque gearbox, often a planetary or slewing ring design, turning arms that span about 60 m on this thickener.

Overloads can crack gear teeth, twist the drive shaft or bend rake arms. Parts are large, custom and often long lead, and repairs need the thickener drained and a crane on site.

So torque protection, rake lifting and early operator response are designed to stop the mechanism ever reaching that point.
f: How does rake drive torque protection work?
What inspections are done on rake drives?
How are rake arms checked for damage?

Handover: 'Thickener rake torque high an.q: What early warning signs would precede a rake torque trip?
Handover: 'Thickener rake torque high an.a:
Watch for a steady upward trend in rake torque rather than a single spike. It usually comes with rising bed pressure (bed mass) and bed level, and often rising underflow density.

Underflow pump discharge pressure may climb as slurry thickens, or flow may fall at the same pump speed. Rake height changing, if the rakes are lifting automatically, is another sign the drive is under load.

Overflow clarity can go either way: overloading tends to dirty it, overdosing keeps it very clear. All of these are vendor panel signals listed in the reference.

f.q: How quickly can rake torque rise to a trip?
f.a:
It depends on the cause. A gradual overload from too much feed, too little underflow or flocculant overdose may build over hours, giving time to respond. A sudden slump of material, a large object falling into the tank or a bed collapse can spike torque within minutes.

The trip and alarm settings sit in the vendor panel and are not given in the reference.

The safest habit is to act on the trend early, while there is still margin, rather than waiting for a high alarm.
f: What causes a sudden thickener torque spike?
Where are rake torque alarm settings found?
How is rake torque actually measured?

f.q: What does raising the rakes actually do?
f.a:
Raising the rakes lifts the arms up out of the densest, deepest part of the bed. They then plough through softer material, so the drive needs less torque.

The reference lists rake height as a vendor panel signal, which means the rakes can be raised and lowered. In many designs this happens automatically when torque gets high, and operators can also raise them manually.

The downside is that solids under the raised rakes are not being moved to the cone, so the bed can build further. Rakes need to come back down once the bed is brought under control.
f: How are rakes lowered back safely after lifting?
Why can a raised rake let the bed build further?
Is rake lifting automatic on this thickener?

f.q: What does high underflow pump pressure mean?
f.a:
Rising discharge pressure at the same flow usually means the slurry is getting thicker and more viscous, so friction in the line goes up. That is a sign of rising underflow density and a heavier bed.

It can also mean a partial blockage, such as a valve not fully open or material building up in the line.

Compare pump pressure with density and flow readings. If density is rising too, the bed is thickening. If density is steady, look for a restriction.
f: How does slurry density change pipe friction?
What causes underflow line blockages?
Where are underflow density and flow measured?

Handover: 'Thickener rake torque high an.q: What's the typical operator response sequence to rising rake torque?
Handover: 'Thickener rake torque high an.a:
The card lists the usual responses: increase underflow pumping, raise the rakes, and reduce feed or flocculant.

A typical sequence is to confirm the torque reading is real, then increase underflow withdrawal to take solids out, while watching density so it does not become unpumpable. If torque keeps climbing, raise the rakes. Check flocculant dose: if it is high, reduce it, because overdosing makes the bed sticky. If torque still rises, reduce feed to the thickener.

The exact steps and limits come from the site procedure, so check it with the CRO. Never bypass rake torque protection.

f.q: Why can increasing underflow pumping backfire?
f.a:
If the bed is very stiff, a pump can pull a channel straight through it, called ratholing, and draw thin slurry or water from above instead of the thick bed. Density then drops while the stiff bed stays put and torque remains high.

Pumping very dense slurry can also overload or block the underflow pumps and line.

So operators watch underflow density and pump pressure as they increase flow. If density falls sharply, ratholing is likely and other steps are needed.
f: How do you spot ratholing on the trends?
What density limit do the underflow pumps handle?
How is a blocked underflow line cleared?

f.q: Why does reducing flocculant help with high torque?
f.a:
Excess flocculant binds the bed into a strong, sticky network with a high yield stress. The rakes have to push through that, so torque rises.

Reducing the dose lets newly settled solids form a softer bed that flows to the cone more easily. It takes time, because the existing bed was already formed with the higher dose.

It only helps if flocculant was actually high. If the cause is overloading, reducing floc could make overflow dirty without fixing torque.
f: How do you know if flocculant is overdosed?
How long does a dose change take to reach the bed?
What does dirty overflow cost the plant?

f.q: What happens if the rake drive actually trips?
f.a:
A rake trip on high torque protects the mechanism, but a stopped rake in a dense bed is a serious situation. Solids keep settling around the arms, and the longer it stays stopped, the harder it is to restart.

Typically operators stop or reduce feed, keep withdrawing underflow if possible, raise the rakes, and restart as soon as torque allows. The reference does not give the restart procedure.

Do not try to force a restart by bypassing protection. Get the supervisor and follow the site procedure.
f: How is a tripped rake restarted safely?
Why does a stopped rake get harder to restart?
Who must be called when a rake trips?

Handover: 'Carbon Scout shows Tank 6 low.q: Why would an intertank screen fault cause carbon to pile up unevenly?
Handover: 'Carbon Scout shows Tank 6 low.a:
Each CIL4 tank has an intertank screen, Kemix MPS2535(P) with 1.0 mm wedge wire per the reference, at its outlet. Slurry passes through to the next tank, but carbon granules are too big and stay behind.

Carbon is supposed to move the other way, counter current, by recessed impeller pumps advancing it from each tank to the one upstream.

If tank 6's screen is worn or holed, carbon leaks forward with the slurry into tank 7, so tank 6 runs low and tank 7 builds up. The same pattern appears if the carbon advance pump from tank 7 back to tank 6 is not moving carbon. Either way the counter current flow is broken.

f.q: How do intertank screens keep carbon in each tank?
f.a:
An intertank screen is a cylindrical wedge wire screen at the tank outlet, with mechanical sweeping or pumping action to keep the surface clear. The 1.0 mm slots on CIL4 let slurry particles, ground to around 180 microns, pass, while carbon granules of a couple of millimetres are held back.

It works like a strainer basket in a pipeline: fluid passes, larger solids stay.

If the screen blinds, slurry backs up and the tank level rises. If it is damaged, carbon escapes to the next tank. Both show up on Carbon Scout and level trends.
f: What makes CIL intertank screens blind?
How is tank level used to spot a blinded screen?
How are intertank screens cleaned in service?

f.q: How would you confirm a screen is damaged?
f.a:
Look at the Carbon Scout trend over several cycles. A steady fall in one tank with a matching rise in the next, with no change to carbon advance pumping, points to a leaking screen.

Check the carbon advance pump from the downstream tank is running and actually moving carbon, to rule it out.

Physical confirmation needs the screen inspected, which requires the area isolated under permit. Carbon appearing further down the train, or on the carbon detection meter at tails, means the problem is worse.
f: How is an intertank screen removed for inspection?
How often does Carbon Scout sample each tank?
What does carbon at the tails meter signal?

f.q: What does the carbon detection meter on tails tell you?
f.a:
Per the reference, CIL4 has a carbon detection meter on the tails with a reference probe at the front end. It detects carbon particles leaving the last tank in the tails.

Carbon in tails means carbon, carrying gold, is being lost to the TSF. That usually signals a damaged screen on the last tanks or carbon overflowing.

The reference probe at the front end gives a baseline for comparison, so the meter responds to carbon rather than to changes in slurry.
f: How much gold is lost with each tonne of carbon?
What are the future carbon safety screens for?
Where does fine carbon waste go?

Handover: 'Carbon Scout shows Tank 6 low.q: What downstream gold loss would you expect from this imbalance?
Handover: 'Carbon Scout shows Tank 6 low.a:
In CIL4, tanks 3 to 8 are adsorption tanks. Uneven carbon means tank 6 has less capacity to capture gold, so more dissolved gold passes into tank 7. Tank 7 has extra carbon and can pick up some of it, so the immediate loss is usually modest.

The bigger risks are that adsorption efficiency drops, more soluble gold reaches the last tanks and tails, and if carbon is leaking through a damaged screen it may keep moving down the train and eventually out with tails.

The PDC design adsorption efficiency for CIL4 is about 88 percent, range 84 to 92. A distribution problem pushes toward the low end.

f.q: Why does uneven carbon matter if total carbon is unchanged?
f.a:
Counter current adsorption works in stages. Each tank removes a share of the gold still in solution, and carbon loading builds step by step as it moves forward.

If one tank is short of carbon, that stage does less work. The tank with too much carbon cannot fully make up for it, because it sees solution that is already leaner. It is like a multi pass heat exchanger with one pass partly bypassed.

So the same total carbon gives lower overall recovery when it is badly distributed.
f: How many adsorption stages does CIL4 have?
How is soluble gold profiled down the train?
What happens to loading in the overloaded tank?

f.q: How much gold could escape on carbon through a failed screen?
f.a:
The PDC gives CIL4 carbon a nominal loading of about 461 g/t, range 332 to 579 g/t. So each tonne of loaded carbon lost carries roughly half a kilogram of gold, around 15 ounces.

Carbon leaking forward one tank is not lost yet. It becomes a loss when it leaves the final tank with tails.

On CIL3, design loading is about 4,490 g/t, so carbon losses there would be ten times more costly per tonne. That is why screen condition matters.
f: How is lost carbon tracked over time?
Why is CIL3 carbon much higher in gold?
How quickly could a failed screen lose a tonne?

f.q: What is CIL4's design adsorption efficiency?
f.a:
The PDC gives CIL4 adsorption efficiency of about 88 percent, with a range of 84 to 92 percent. That means about 88 percent of the gold dissolved in CIL4 is captured on carbon.

Combined with a design leach extraction of about 38 percent, that is what drives the tails leach contribution to overall recovery.

Carbon distribution, carbon activity, concentration and residence time all affect where in that range the plant runs.
f: What affects carbon activity in CIL4?
How is adsorption efficiency calculated on site?
What CIL4 leach extraction does the PDC use?

Handover: 'Carbon Scout shows Tank 6 low.q: How would operators correct carbon distribution once it's identified?
Handover: 'Carbon Scout shows Tank 6 low.a:
First, find the cause. Check that the carbon advance pump from tank 7 to tank 6 is running and moving carbon. If it is, suspect tank 6's intertank screen and arrange inspection.

To rebalance, operators adjust carbon advance pumping. The reference notes loaded carbon routing between tanks can be changed using removable spool pieces, which allows flexibility when a pump or route is out.

Pneumatic slurry bypass gates, operated locally only, let a tank be bypassed for maintenance. After changes, the Carbon Scout readings confirm whether distribution is back to target, about 12.5 g/L in each adsorption tank.

f.q: What are removable spool pieces used for in CIL4?
f.a:
Per the reference, loaded carbon routing between CIL4 tanks is set by removable spool pieces. A spool piece is a short flanged length of pipe that can be removed and reinstalled in a different position to connect a different route.

It is a simple, positive way to change a flow path, more reliable than valves in abrasive carbon slurry, which can wear or jam valve seats.

Changing a spool piece is a mechanical job that needs the line isolated and drained under permit.
f: Why avoid valves in carbon slurry lines?
How is a carbon line isolated to change a spool?
How are carbon transfer routes recorded?

f.q: How is a tank bypassed to repair an intertank screen?
f.a:
The reference says CIL4 has pneumatic slurry bypass gates that are operated locally only. These let slurry flow around a tank so it can be taken out of service.

The exact bypass and drain procedure is not in the reference. In general, the tank is bypassed, carbon is pumped out or retained, the tank is drained and the screen is isolated before anyone works on it.

Local only operation means someone must be at the gate, which helps avoid accidental remote operation while people are working.
f: Why are bypass gates local only operation?
Where does carbon go when a tank is drained?
How long does an intertank screen change take?

f.q: How long until Carbon Scout confirms the fix?
f.a:
The reference does not give the Carbon Scout sampling cycle. In general, these units sample each tank in turn over a cycle of some hours, so a change in carbon distribution may take a few cycles to show clearly.

Carbon transfers also take time to rebalance a 5,600 m3 tank.

Watch the trend over a shift or two rather than reacting to a single reading. Ask the CRO for the current cycle time.
f: What else does Carbon Scout measure in CIL4?
How accurate are Carbon Scout readings?
What water does Carbon Scout use?

Handover: 'DO low in CIL2 leach tanks.'.q: Why does low dissolved oxygen slow gold dissolution specifically?
Handover: 'DO low in CIL2 leach tanks.'.a:
Gold dissolution in cyanide needs an oxidant, described by the Elsner equation. Dissolved oxygen takes electrons from the gold surface while cyanide holds the gold in solution as the gold cyanide complex.

The reaction happens at the gold surface, and both cyanide and oxygen must diffuse there through the solution. When DO is low, oxygen supply becomes the limiting step, so the rate falls no matter how much cyanide is present.

CIL2 leaches ultra fine sulphide concentrate, which consumes oxygen quickly, so DO falls fast if supply drops. It is like a combustion process starved of air.

f.q: What cyanide to oxygen ratio gives the fastest leach?
f.a:
In general, research shows dissolution is fastest when cyanide and dissolved oxygen are in balance, often quoted as a molar ratio of cyanide to oxygen of around 6. Too little oxygen relative to cyanide and oxygen limits the rate; too little cyanide and cyanide limits it.

That is why simply adding cyanide when DO is low does not help much.

CIL2 runs high cyanide concentrations, 1,000 to 6,500 ppm in later tanks per the reference, so it needs high oxygen to stay balanced. Actual targets come from the metallurgist.
f: Why does CIL2 run such high cyanide levels?
How is the cyanide to oxygen balance monitored?
What DO targets does CIL2 use?

f.q: Why does saline water make DO harder to maintain?
f.a:
Oxygen dissolves less in salty water than in fresh water, a salting out effect. Process water here has an SG of about 1.07, so its oxygen solubility is noticeably lower.

Higher temperature also reduces solubility, which matters in summer.

So reaching a given DO target takes more oxygen and better mass transfer, which is why CIL2 uses side lances plus VSD oxygen injection pumps on the first two tanks.
