What is chain of custody for samples?
How are lab results reported?

Handover: 'FIM SAG transfer pump tripped.q: Why does the old SAG rely on the new cyclone cluster instead of its own?
Handover: 'FIM SAG transfer pump tripped.a:
In Stage 1 the Growth Project made the old FIM ball mills redundant and built one new ball mill fed by both SAG mills, per the reference. So the old FIM SAG no longer has its own downstream ball mill and classification circuit.

Its discharge is collected in the FIM SAG discharge hopper and pumped by duty/duty FIM mill transfer pumps to the new primary cyclone feed hopper, at about 60 percent solids. From there it is classified in the new cyclone cluster along with new SAG discharge.

So the old SAG is effectively a feeder to the new circuit. Without the transfer pumps it has nowhere to send its product.

f.q: Why were the old FIM ball mills made redundant?
f.a:
The reference lists it as part of Stage 1 scope, along with Mt Charlotte processing and the old FIM flotation, but does not explain the reasons.

In general, one large modern ball mill and cyclone cluster is simpler and more efficient to run than several older, smaller mills. It also lets both SAG mills feed a single classification and flotation train, which simplifies control and maintenance.

Ask the process engineer if you want the project rationale.
f: How big is the new ball mill motor?
What happened to the old FIM flotation cells?
Is any old FIM equipment still running?

f.q: What transfer density do the FIM mill transfer pumps run at?
f.a:
The reference gives a transfer density of about 60 percent solids. That is a fairly dense slurry for pumping over distance.

Density matters because too dense risks settling and blockage, while too dilute wastes pump capacity and adds water to the cyclone feed hopper.

The FIM SAG discharge rate is about 1,313 t/h at nominal, so the pumps move a large flow.
f: How is transfer line density controlled?
What happens if transfer density rises too high?
How is the transfer line flushed?

f.q: How far is the FIM SAG from the new cyclone hopper?
f.a:
The reference does not give the distance or pipe route between the FIM SAG discharge hopper and the new primary cyclone feed hopper, so this cannot be answered from the documents.

The plant layout drawings or the transfer line P&ID would show the route, length and elevation change. Those matter because they set the pump head, the risk of slurry settling if flow stops and how much flush water is needed after a trip.

Ask the control room operator, or check the layout drawings in the document system.
f: Where are the plant layout drawings?
How is transfer pump head calculated?
What flush water is used on the transfer line?

Handover: 'FIM SAG transfer pump tripped.q: What would the CRO see on the OIS when this pump trips?
Handover: 'FIM SAG transfer pump tripped.a:
The CRO would see a pump trip alarm, with first out detection showing the cause, per the reference. Transfer line flow would drop and the FIM SAG discharge hopper level would start rising quickly.

At the new cyclone feed hopper, level would fall as the old SAG's contribution stops, and the cyclone feed pump control would respond.

Depending on interlocks and how many transfer pumps are still running, the FIM SAG feed may need to be cut or stopped. The reference notes the transfer pumps are interlocked if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running.

f.q: What happens to the FIM SAG if its discharge hopper fills?
f.a:
The reference does not give the interlock details for the FIM SAG discharge hopper, so this cannot be confirmed from the documents.

In general, a high high hopper level would trip or stop the SAG feed to prevent the hopper overflowing and flooding the area. The SAG itself might keep turning briefly to empty, then stop.

Check the FIM SAG interlock list or ask the CRO for the specific actions.
f: What is the FIM SAG discharge hopper volume?
How does a hopper high high level trip work?
How is a FIM SAG restart sequenced?

f.q: How does first out detection help diagnose this trip?
f.a:
Per the reference, the DCS records which trip happened first. When a pump trips, several alarms may follow, such as low flow, high hopper level and interlocked equipment stopping.

First out shows the original cause, for example motor overload, low gland water flow or an interlock, so operators fix the right problem.

It is like reading the first fault code on a machine controller rather than all the later ones.
f: What trip causes are most common on slurry pumps?
How is first out shown on the OIS?
Who resets a pump trip?

f.q: Why are transfer pumps interlocked to the cyclone feed pump?
f.a:
Per the reference, the FIM mill transfer pumps are interlocked to stop if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running.

The transfer pumps deliver into the primary cyclone feed hopper. If the cyclone feed pump stops, nothing is leaving that hopper, so continued transfer flow would overfill it and spill slurry across the area. The interlock stops the transfer pumps first.

It is a process interlock, active in Auto and Manual, designed to prevent spills. Bypassing it is limited to named users under site rules, and it should never be bypassed just to keep the old SAG running.
f: What happens to the old SAG if the cyclone feed pump trips?
How fast does the cyclone feed hopper fill?
Can this interlock be bypassed?

Handover: 'FIM SAG transfer pump tripped.q: Is there a standby transfer pump, or is this a single point of failure?
Handover: 'FIM SAG transfer pump tripped.a:
Per the reference, the FIM mill transfer pumps are duty/duty, meaning both normally run together, rather than duty/standby. So there is no installed standby that sits idle waiting.

If one trips, transfer capacity drops, likely to about half if they share the flow, and the FIM SAG feed must be reduced or stopped until it is restored. The reference does not say whether one pump alone can carry a reduced flow.

So the transfer pumps are a significant point of vulnerability for the old SAG. Ask the CRO or area maintenance planner how the site manages a single pump trip.

f.q: Can one transfer pump carry the FIM SAG at reduced feed?
f.a:
The reference does not say, so this cannot be answered reliably from the documents.

It depends on each pump's size and curve, the line hydraulics and whether one pump can keep enough velocity in the transfer line to hold the solids in suspension. Running a slurry line too slowly risks settling and a blockage, which would be worse than a controlled stop.

Check the transfer pump data sheet and line design, or ask the process engineer or CRO what reduced rate, if any, the site allows on one pump.
f: What minimum velocity keeps slurry suspended?
How are transfer pump curves used?
What happens if a slurry line settles?

f.q: Why choose duty/duty rather than duty/standby here?
f.a:
The reference gives the duty/duty arrangement but not the reason, so this is general reasoning.

Duty/duty is usually chosen when the full flow needs both pumps, either because a single pump that size is not available or is impractical, or to share wear. It gives the required capacity but no installed spare.

Duty/standby gives redundancy but needs each pump sized for the full duty. With the FIM SAG producing about 1,313 t/h at nominal, sharing the flow between two running pumps is a plausible design choice. Ask the process engineer for the actual rationale.
f: How much flow do the transfer pumps move?
What is the cost of adding a standby pump?
How is duty/duty load shared?

f.q: What maintenance keeps the transfer pumps reliable?
f.a:
The reference does not give the maintenance plan, so this is general practice for slurry pumps.

Key items are regular inspection and replacement of wear parts such as impellers, liners and throat bushes, healthy gland water supply (the reference notes low gland flow blocks starting and trips running pumps), bearing lubrication and condition monitoring with vibration and temperature checks.

Wear parts are often changed on run hours or when performance drops. Ask the area maintenance planner for the actual schedule and critical spares held for these pumps.
f: How often are slurry pump wear parts changed?
How is pump vibration monitored?
What spares are kept for transfer pumps?

What control system runs the FIM plant?.q: Why did site standardise both plants on one DCS platform?
What control system runs the FIM plant?.a:
The reference says the new and old plant are configured to the same site templates so they look and operate as one plant, all on the Yokogawa Centum VP DCS.

The practical reasons are the ones you would expect from standardising any fleet of machines. One CRO can move between screens for the new SAG and the existing FIM SAG without relearning symbols, faceplates or alarm behaviour. Maintenance holds one set of spares and one skill set for Field Control Stations. Interlocks and sequences that cross the old and new plant, such as the FIM mill transfer pumps tripping if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running, are simpler when both ends live in the same system.

Think of it like standardising on one gearbox family across a plant: fewer surprises, faster fault finding, cheaper support.

f.q: What are the site templates that make old and new plant look the same?
f.a:
The reference only says the new and old plant are configured to the same site templates; it does not list them.

In a Centum VP system, templates usually mean standard function blocks and faceplates for each equipment type: a drive block with Auto, Manual and Local modes, a valve block with watchdog and limit switch checks, a PID block with Manual, Auto and Cascade, and a standard alarm set. Every pump or valve is then built from the same block, so it behaves and displays the same way wherever it sits.

The drive modes, interlock types and valve watchdog described in the control philosophy are exactly the behaviour those templates encode. For the actual template library, ask the site control systems engineer.
f: Who maintains the DCS template library on site?
What happens to old plant logic that doesn't fit the new templates?
Are vendor PLC packages built on the same templates?

f.q: Which equipment runs on vendor PLCs instead of the DCS?
f.a:
The reference lists vendor packages with their own PLC that report to the DCS: the rock breaker, OSA, particle size analysers, compressors, chillers, samplers, the IsaMill liquid resistance starters and the regen kiln.

By contrast the SAG, ball mill, flotation cells, thickener, Knelsons, ILR, EW cells and Jameson cells are DCS controlled directly.

The split is usual practice. A vendor who supplies a self contained machine with tight internal logic, like a kiln burner or a compressor, keeps that logic in their own PLC and guarantees it. The DCS then sees status, alarms and a few commands over a network link, rather than owning every internal step.
f: How does a vendor PLC send its alarms up to the DCS?
Can the CRO change setpoints inside a vendor PLC package?
Who fault finds a vendor package when its PLC trips?

f.q: What is a Field Control Station and where does it sit?
f.a:
A Field Control Station (FCS) is the Yokogawa controller that actually runs the control logic: the PID loops, drive blocks, interlocks and sequences. The OIS screens in the control room are only the window onto it.

The reference says FCSs are spread around the plant. That is the distributed part of a distributed control system: each controller sits close to its area, usually in a switchroom, and connects to local remote I/O, which keeps field cabling short.

The reference also says the DCS and RIO have UPS backup, so a short power dip should not drop the controllers. The exact FCS locations would be on the control system architecture drawings, which the control systems engineer can show you.
f: What does RIO mean and how does it link to an FCS?
Is each Field Control Station duplicated for redundancy?
Which area's FCS covers the new SAG mill?

What control system runs the FIM plant?.q: What would you see on the OIS if a Field Control Station lost comms?
What control system runs the FIM plant?.a:
The reference does not describe the OIS display for an FCS comms failure, so this is general Centum VP behaviour rather than site specific.

Typically the system alarm screen raises a station or communication fault, and the graphics for that area stop updating. Values may show as bad quality, often with a changed colour or marker, and faceplates for that area stop accepting commands.

An important point: losing comms between the OIS and an FCS does not mean the plant stops. The FCS keeps running its loops and interlocks with the last setpoints, and hardwired critical trips stay active. You just lose visibility and control from the screen.

For exactly what this site's screens show, ask a control room operator or the control systems engineer.

f.q: Does the plant keep running if the OIS goes blank?
f.a:
Generally yes, for a short time. In a DCS the control logic lives in the Field Control Stations, not the operator screens. If an OIS fails, the FCS keeps executing PID loops, interlocks and sequences on the last setpoints.

The risk is that nobody can see what is happening or respond to upsets, so operators would normally move to another OIS or, if all screens are lost, follow a site procedure that may involve bringing the plant down in a controlled way.

Critical interlocks such as E-stops, pull wires and protection relays act regardless of the screen. The reference does not give the site response to OIS loss, so check the control room procedures with a senior CRO.
f: Are there spare OIS screens in each control room?
What procedure do CROs follow if all OIS screens fail?
Can field operators see any DCS data locally?

f.q: Are the Field Control Stations redundant?
f.a:
The reference does not say whether the FCSs or their networks are redundant. It only says the DCS and remote I/O have UPS backup.

In general, Centum VP FCSs in a plant this size are commonly specified with duplex CPUs, duplex power supplies and dual control networks, so one failure switches to the backup without a bump. Think of it like a duty and hot standby pump that changes over automatically.

Whether that was done here, and which stations are duplex, would be in the DCS architecture and hardware specification. The site control systems engineer is the person to ask.
f: What does the UPS on the DCS actually keep alive?
How long can the UPS hold the DCS on battery?
Where is the DCS architecture drawing kept?

f.q: How would field operators know a comms fault had happened?
f.a:
The reference does not cover this. In practice, the CRO sees the system alarm first and radios the field operators, because the field has no screen showing DCS health.

In the field, equipment would keep running on its last state, so nothing obvious happens at first. The field operator's role would be to check local indications, stay alert to anything drifting, and be ready to use the LCS stop, which works in every mode.

Never treat a comms fault as permission to bypass anything. Hardwired E-stops and protection relays still act. For the site procedure, ask the control room operator or shift supervisor.
f: Does the LCS stop button rely on DCS comms to work?
Who decides to shut the area down after a comms fault?
How is a comms fault logged for the maintenance team?

What control system runs the FIM plant?.q: How far back can you pull trend data from the PI historian?
What control system runs the FIM plant?.a:
The reference says data is logged to a PI historian and that is where trends come from, but it does not state the retention period or the logging resolution.

PI historians generally keep data for many years because they store compressed data, recording a new point only when the value moves by more than a set deviation. That makes long term trends cheap to keep, though the very short spikes may be smoothed out.

For the actual retention, and whether older data has been archived elsewhere, ask the site process control engineer or whoever administers PI. A metallurgist will also know how far back they routinely pull data for monthly reporting.

f.q: Why is PI better for trends than the DCS itself?
f.a:
The DCS trend function is built for the CRO watching the last few hours of a loop. It usually keeps a limited window at fixed resolution.

A PI historian is built to store years of data from thousands of tags and serve it to engineers on office PCs without loading the control system. It also lets metallurgists combine tags, for example SAG power against feed tonnage, and export to spreadsheets.

The reference only says PI is where the trends come from. Keeping the historian separate is like logging vibration data to a condition monitoring server rather than reading it off the machine's local gauge: the control system keeps controlling, and analysis happens elsewhere.
f: Can PI data be pulled into Excel for analysis?
Does PI record operator actions or just process values?
Who gives access to PI for a new engineer?

f.q: What is data compression in a historian and why does it matter?
f.a:
This is general historian knowledge, not covered in the plant reference.

PI typically stores a new value only when the signal changes by more than a set deviation, or after a maximum time. A flat signal costs almost no storage, while a busy one is stored in detail.

It matters when you investigate a trip. A very short spike might not have been stored if the compression deviation is wide, so the PI trend can look smoother than what the DCS actually saw. The first out record in the DCS and the alarm log are better for exact trip sequences, while PI is ideal for longer patterns like slow pump wear or creeping SAG power.
f: How do I check the compression settings on a PI tag?
Is the DCS alarm log stored in PI as well?
What resolution is best for investigating a pump trip?

f.q: Which tags would I trend to understand a slurry pump's health?
f.a:
Trends are pulled from PI, per the reference. For a slurry pump, useful tags generally include: VSD speed and motor current or power, discharge flow from the mag flowmeter, density from the nucleonic gauge, the hopper level feeding it, and the gland water flow switch or flowmeter.

The tag names follow the numbering spec, for example FIT plus area plus loop for flow, DT for density and LT for level.

As pump wear increases, you usually see speed creeping up to hold the same flow, much like a worn centrifugal water pump needing more speed for the same duty point. A falling gland flow trend is also worth watching because low gland flow blocks starts and trips running pumps after a delay.
f: How do I find the right tag number for a given pump?
What does rising speed for the same flow say about the impeller?
Can PI show pump hours run for maintenance planning?

What are the two main control rooms?.q: Why keep the new crusher run by camera instead of a local control room?
What are the two main control rooms?.a:
The reference says the new primary crusher PC2 is run remotely from the existing crusher control room using CCTV. It does not give the reasons, so the following is general reasoning.

One control room means one crew can watch both gyratories, PC1 and PC2, and coordinate trucks, stockpile levels and feeders without extra staff. It avoids building and staffing a second control room in a dusty, noisy location. Much of PC2 is already automated: truck traffic lights work from radar and level signals, the crusher gap adjusts from a camera particle size analyser, and the rock breaker runs remotely by camera with auto park.

It is a bit like monitoring several compressors from one central panel rather than standing a person at each.

f.q: How do truck traffic lights at PC2 decide when to let trucks tip?
f.a:
The reference says the truck traffic lights are automatic, based on truck radar, ROM bin level, the discharge chamber level and its High-High switch, crusher running status and the rock breaker position.

In effect it is a set of permissives. A truck gets a green light only when the crusher is running, there is room in the dump pocket, the discharge chamber below the crusher is not overfull and the rock breaker is parked clear of the tipping area. Radar confirms a truck is in position.

It works like a start permissive on a drive: all conditions must be healthy before the action is allowed. The detailed logic and timing would be in the crusher control philosophy.
f: What happens if a truck tips on a red light?
Why does rock breaker position matter to the traffic lights?
Who overrides the traffic lights if a sensor fails?

f.q: How does the rock breaker work if nobody is beside it?
f.a:
The reference says the rock breaker is remote operated by camera with an auto park function, and it is a vendor package with its own PLC reporting to the DCS.

The operator in the crusher control room uses the CCTV view and a joystick to break oversize rocks bridging the crusher throat. When finished, auto park returns the boom to a safe position, which also feeds into the truck traffic light logic so trucks are not allowed to tip while the boom is in the way.

Generally, remote rock breakers keep people away from the crusher throat, which is one of the highest risk spots in a crushing plant.
f: What size rocks typically need breaking at the crusher?
How does the operator judge depth with only a camera view?
Is the rock breaker locked out during crusher maintenance?

f.q: How is the PC2 crusher gap adjusted automatically?
f.a:
The reference says the crusher gap is auto adjusted from a camera particle size analyser on the stockpile feed conveyor.

The design product size is P80 130 mm (145 mm in the high throughput case), with a new gyratory OSS of 165 mm. The camera estimates the size distribution of ore on the belt, and the control adjusts the gyratory setting to hold the product size as the mantle and concaves wear.

It is a closed loop, much like a feedback controller trimming a valve: as wear opens the gap and the product coarsens, the system closes the setting back. These are design figures; the actual target is set by operations.
f: Why does liner wear make crusher product coarser?
What happens to the SAG if crusher product goes too coarse?
How often are the gyratory mantle and concaves replaced?

What are the two main control rooms?.q: What happens to the crusher if the CCTV link to the CrCR drops?
What are the two main control rooms?.a:
The reference does not describe what happens on a CCTV failure, so I cannot give the site procedure.

It is worth separating control from vision. The crusher, apron feeder and conveyors are controlled through the DCS and their interlocks, not through the cameras. Losing CCTV would not by itself trip the crusher. What it removes is the operator's eyes on the dump pocket and rock breaker, which matters most for remote rock breaking and spotting blockages.

A sensible general expectation is that remote rock breaking stops and operations may need a person in the field or a controlled stop. Ask the crusher control room operator or crushing supervisor what the site procedure says.

f.q: Can the crusher keep running without anyone watching it?
f.a:
Partly, by design. The reference describes automatic truck traffic lights, crusher gap control from the particle size analyser, and interlocks on the apron feeder (discharge conveyor running, discharge chamber Low-Low, head chute High-High) and the stockpile feed conveyor (stockpile High-High).

Those interlocks protect against the common failure modes like overfilling a chute or running a feeder into a stopped belt. But they do not see oversize rocks bridging the throat or people in the area. That is what the cameras and operators are for.

Whether the site allows unattended running and for how long is an operating rule, not in the reference. Ask the crushing supervisor.
f: Why does the apron feeder stop on discharge chamber Low-Low?
What does a head chute High-High switch protect against?
Who monitors the crusher area cameras at night?

f.q: Why is the apron feeder interlocked to the discharge chamber Low-Low level?
f.a:
The reference lists the apron feeder interlocked to discharge conveyor running, discharge chamber Low-Low and head chute High-High.

The Low-Low interlock is most likely there to keep a bed of ore in the discharge chamber under the crusher. Without that buffer, rocks falling from the crusher land straight on the apron feeder pans, causing impact damage, a bit like running a gear pump dry so the teeth take the shock instead of the fluid.

So the feeder stops drawing ore out until the chamber has rebuilt its bed. The exact reason and setpoint are not stated, so confirm with the crushing maintenance planner or metallurgist.
f: How is the discharge chamber level measured?
What damage does impact cause to apron feeder pans?
What sets the apron feeder speed during normal running?

f.q: What dust controls must run with the crusher?
f.a:
The reference says the wet scrubber and dust extraction must run with the new crusher circuit.

That suggests an interlock or permissive tying the crushing plant to its dust system, so crushing does not continue without dust control. Crushing large rocks generates a lot of fine dust, which is a health hazard and can contain silica.

In mechanical terms the dust extraction is like a ventilation fan on an enclosure: it holds the hood and transfer points under slight negative pressure so dust is drawn into the scrubber instead of escaping. The exact interlock arrangement is not given, so check the crushing control philosophy or ask the crushing supervisor.
f: How does a wet scrubber actually remove dust?
What happens to the crusher if the dust fan trips?
Where does scrubber slurry go after it collects dust?

What are the two main control rooms?.q: How do CRO and CrCR operators coordinate during a crusher stoppage?
What are the two main control rooms?.a:
The reference does not describe the coordination procedure, so this is general.

The key buffer is the crushed ore stockpile. The new stockpile has about 20,460 t live, roughly 11 hours of residence at design, and the existing COS about 21,000 t live, around 16 hours. So a crusher stop does not immediately starve the mills.

The crusher operator would tell the mill CRO the expected duration, and the mill CRO watches stockpile levels and reclaim feeder performance. If the stop runs long, the mill operator may reduce SAG feed rate to stretch the stockpile. These are design figures; live levels decide.

For the actual protocol, radio channels and who has authority, ask a senior CRO or the shift supervisor.

f.q: What happens to the mills if the stockpile runs empty?
f.a:
The reference does not describe an empty stockpile event, so this is general.

The reclaim apron feeders draw from the live portion of the stockpile, which on the new stockpile is defined by a 60 degree drawdown. As it empties, rat holing may form and feed becomes erratic, so the SAG feed weightometer cannot hold its tonnage setpoint.

The SAG then loses load, power drops, and if feed is lost entirely the mill must be stopped to avoid running an empty mill, where balls hit liners directly. There is also an emergency apron feeder fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader, which is how ore from the dead stockpile can still be fed.
f: When is the emergency apron feeder used?
Why is running a SAG empty so damaging to liners?
What is rat holing in a stockpile?

f.q: Why does the new stockpile have less residence time than the old one?
f.a:
From the reference: the new crushed ore stockpile holds about 20,460 t live with roughly 11 hours residence, while the existing COS holds about 21,000 t live and about 16 hours.

The live tonnes are similar, but the new SAG draws faster. New SAG feed is 1,833 t/h nominal versus 1,313 t/h for the existing FIM SAG. The same tonnage drains faster at a higher draw rate, much like two identical tanks drained by pumps of different capacity.

The residence figures are design values, so in practice they depend on how full the stockpiles are kept and the actual mill throughput.
f: What limits how big the live stockpile can be?
How is stockpile level measured from the control room?
Can the crushers feed either stockpile?

f.q: Does the crusher run at the same availability as the mills?
f.a:
No. The reference gives crushing availability as 65 percent, about 5,694 hours a year, while the concentrator is 93.4 percent, about 8,182 hours a year.

That difference is why the crushers are sized above the mill rate. The new crusher nominal is 2,634 t/h with design at 3,135 t/h, while the new SAG draws about 1,833 t/h. The crusher runs harder for fewer hours, and the stockpile buffers the gap.

It is the same idea as sizing a compressor larger than average demand so it can fill a receiver and then rest. These are design numbers, not actual operating availability.
f: Why is crushing availability planned so low?
What maintenance does the gyratory crusher need most often?
How is crusher downtime planned around the mills?

A drive has three modes. Name them..q: Why give drives three separate modes instead of just on and off?
A drive has three modes. Name them..a:
On and off is the command; the mode is who is allowed to give that command and which protections apply.

Per the reference: in Automatic, the DCS starts and stops the drive from sequences or process conditions, and the field LCS cannot start it, though its stop always works. In Manual, the CRO starts and stops from the OIS or LCS, and all interlocks still apply but there is no automatic starting. In Local, the drive starts from the LCS only, bypasses process interlocks and start permissives but keeps critical interlocks, and is for fault finding and maintenance only under supervision.

It is like a machine tool with automatic cycle, operator jog and maintenance setup modes, each giving a different level of control and protection.

f.q: When would a CRO choose Manual instead of Automatic?
f.a:
The reference says Manual means the CRO starts and stops the drive from the OIS, and it will not start or stop automatically with sequences or process conditions. All interlocks still apply.

Typical reasons in general practice: running one pump outside its normal sequence, testing a drive after maintenance before handing it back, controlling something by hand while its level switch or sequence logic is faulty, or holding a drive steady during an upset.

Note that when a group start sequence runs, any Manual drives in it get switched to Auto, per the sequence rules. That is a good reason to check the mode of drives before starting a sequence.
f: Does a drive stay in Manual after a power dip?
Can a Manual drive be stopped by a sequence stop?
How do I see a drive's current mode on the OIS?

f.q: Why does the LCS have no mode selector switch?
f.a:
The reference says the mode is selected from the OIS only, and the field LCS has start and latch off stop buttons but no mode selector switch.

Keeping mode selection in the control room means the CRO always knows and controls who has authority over the drive. A field selector would let someone change the mode without the CRO knowing, which is exactly the situation that leads to equipment starting or not starting unexpectedly.

It also means putting a drive into Local is a deliberate two person act: the field technician asks, the CRO selects it. The latch off stop button still works in every mode, so field stopping is never lost.
f: What is a latch off stop button and how is it reset?
How does a fitter ask the CRO for Local mode?
Does the LCS show which mode the drive is in?

f.q: Is Local mode the same as isolating a drive for maintenance?
f.a:
No. Local is a control mode, not an isolation. The drive is still energised and can be started from the LCS. The reference says Local is for fault finding and maintenance only, must be supervised, and keeps critical interlocks active.

Isolation means positively removing energy, typically through the site lockout and tagout process at the switchroom and on mechanical energy sources, so the drive cannot start at all. Work inside a machine requires isolation, not Local.

Think of Local as the jog button on a lathe, useful for testing rotation, and isolation as the main switch locked off with your personal lock. Follow the site isolation procedure; never rely on a DCS mode for personal safety.
f: What is the site lockout and tagout process for a pump?
Can a drive in Local start if someone is working on it?
Who signs off that a drive is safe to test in Local?

A drive has three modes. Name them..q: What would a handover note mean by 'left it in Local overnight'?
A drive has three modes. Name them..a:
It means a drive was left in Local mode, so it is out of the control of the DCS sequences and process interlocks. That is usually a flag for a problem.

The reference says Local is for fault finding and maintenance only, must be supervised, and a configurable timer drops the drive back to its target mode. So if the note says it stayed in Local overnight, either the timer was set long, the drive was stopped and simply sitting in Local, or something is not working as designed.

Practical points: a drive in Local will not start with a group sequence, which can stall a plant start. It also has process interlocks bypassed if running. Ask the outgoing shift why, and get it returned to Auto or Manual.

f.q: Why would a drive in Local stop a plant start sequence?
f.a:
The reference says sequences require all drives, valves and PIDs in the sequence to be in Auto or Manual. A drive in Local or faulted will not start, and the sequence will not proceed.

Each step must also confirm feedback, such as run status, within a set transition time, or the sequence pauses and alerts the operator.

It is a deliberate check, like a pre start checklist. The sequence refuses to run if anyone has field control of one of its drives, because starting the whole train while someone is testing one machine could hurt them or damage equipment.
f: How does the OIS highlight which drive is holding a sequence?
Can a CRO force a drive out of Local from the OIS?
What other states block a sequence from starting?

f.q: What does the Local mode timer actually do?
f.a:
The reference says a configurable timer drops the drive out of Local back to its target mode. It does not give the timer value.

The idea is to stop drives being forgotten in Local, where process interlocks and permissives are bypassed. After the timer runs out, the drive returns to Auto or Manual, whichever it is meant to be in, and normal protection is back.

Mode changes are bumpless, so the return itself should not stop or start the drive; only a new command or an interlock changes the drive state. The actual timer setting would be in the DCS configuration, and a control systems engineer or senior CRO can tell you.
f: Does the Local timer restart if the field operator presses start?
What is the drive's target mode and who sets it?
Is the Local timer the same for every drive?

f.q: What should I check before asking for a drive back to Auto?
f.a:
General good practice, as the reference does not give a checklist: confirm the maintenance or fault finding is finished and all people and tools are clear, that any isolations have been properly removed under the site permit system, and that guards are back on.

Then check the drive's process conditions: for a slurry pump, valves in the right positions, gland water available and the hopper level suitable. In Auto the DCS may start it straight away if its process condition is already met, such as a sump pump on high level.

That last point is the main trap. Tell the CRO you are clear and let them make the change.
f: Can a sump pump start immediately when switched to Auto?
Who removes the isolation locks after the job is done?
How do I confirm guards and valves are ready to run?

A drive has three modes. Name them..q: Who is allowed to change a drive's mode, and is it logged?
A drive has three modes. Name them..a:
The reference says mode is selected from the OIS only, so in practice the CRO makes mode changes. It does not say whether particular users are restricted, or how changes are logged.

It does say process interlocks can be bypassed only by named users, one at a time, which shows the DCS uses user based access for some actions.

In general, Centum VP records operator actions such as mode changes and setpoint changes in an operation history, with the user and time. That is what you would check after an incident to see who changed what. For the site's access levels and where the history is kept, ask the control systems engineer or a senior CRO.

f.q: What is an operator action log and how is it used?
f.a:
This is general DCS knowledge, not in the plant reference.

Most DCS platforms, Centum VP included, keep a record of operator actions: mode changes, setpoint changes, manual outputs, acknowledgements and bypasses, each with a time stamp and the logged in user.

After a trip or upset, engineers line this up against the alarm log, first out record and PI trends to rebuild the sequence of events. It is like a flight data recorder for the control room. It is not a blame tool so much as a way of understanding what happened. Ask the control systems engineer how to view it on site.
f: Can I see operator actions alongside PI trends?
How long is the operator action history kept?
Do field LCS button presses appear in the log?

f.q: Why should field staff not ask for mode changes over the radio casually?
f.a:
The reference says Local is for fault finding and maintenance only and must be supervised, and that mode selection is from the OIS only.

A mode change changes which protections apply. In Local, process interlocks and start permissives are bypassed. If the CRO switches the wrong drive, or the field person is not where they think, a drive can be started without the protection the operator expects.

Good practice is a clear exchange: state the exact tag number, the mode wanted and why, and have the CRO repeat it back. Tag numbers like F13-PP-401 follow the numbering spec, which removes ambiguity between similar pumps.
f: How do I read a drive tag number like F13-PP-401?
What is a closed loop radio call in plant operations?
Should mode changes be noted in the shift log?

f.q: Can a mode change bypass a critical interlock?
f.a:
No. The reference is clear that critical interlocks, such as E-stops, pull wires and protection relays, trip in every mode and cannot be bypassed. Hardwired devices and protection relays always stay active even in Local.

What Local does bypass is process interlocks and start permissives. Separately, process interlocks can be bypassed individually by named users.

That layering is deliberate. The protections that keep people safe and stop equipment destroying itself are outside the reach of any mode change, much like a pressure relief valve that works no matter what the controller is doing.
f: Where are critical interlocks wired if not through the DCS?
What does a protection relay protect on a large motor?
How is a pull wire tripped and reset?

In Automatic mode, can you start the dri.q: Why block a field start in Automatic mode?
In Automatic mode, can you start the dri.a:
In Automatic the DCS owns the start and stop decision. Per the reference, it starts and stops the drive from a sequence or process condition, for example a sump pump starting on its high level switch.

If a field start were also allowed, two masters would be giving commands, and the sequence logic could be upset. A pump started out of order might run against a closed valve, or feed into a downstream unit that is not running.

The field stop always works, because stopping is the safe direction. It is like a conveyor control where anyone can hit stop but starting goes through one controller that checks everything downstream first.

f.q: Why is stopping always allowed when starting is restricted?
f.a:
Stopping is almost always the safe state for a person in danger, so the reference says the field stop works in every mode, and the LCS has a latch off stop button.

Starting is where the risk lies: someone may be near the equipment, valves may be wrong, or downstream may not be ready. So starts are controlled by mode, permissives and sequences.

There are exceptions in process terms, such as flotation agitators that should keep running to avoid sanding, but even there the stop is available. It mirrors a basic machine safety principle: any operator can stop, only an authorised one can start.
f: What does latch off mean on a stop button?
Are there drives where stopping causes process damage?
Does the latch off stop need resetting at the LCS?

f.q: What is a process condition start, beyond the sump pump example?
f.a:
The reference gives the sump pump starting on its high level switch as the example of Auto starting from a process condition. Other examples in the reference include pebble crusher feeders starting on bin high level and stopping on low level.

In general, Auto drives respond to levels, pressures, flows or the state of other equipment without the CRO pressing anything. A sequence is a related case, where a group of drives start in a set order, each step confirmed before the next.

It is just like a float switch on a water tank turning a pump on and off, with the DCS adding time delays and alarms around it.
f: How do pebble crusher feeders start and stop in Auto?
Can a CRO override a process condition start?
What alarms if a sump high level does not clear?

f.q: How does the DCS know the drive is actually running?
f.a:
The reference says sequence steps must confirm feedback, such as run feedback, within a set transition time or the sequence pauses and alerts the operator.

In general, the run feedback comes from an auxiliary contact on the motor starter, or from the VSD status over the field network. The reference notes LV DOL starters have electronic overloads on Modbus TCP and VSDs sit on a field network. Some drives also have a speed or motion sensor, such as conveyor under-speed sensors, to confirm the machine is turning and not just the motor energised.

It is the difference between knowing the contactor closed and knowing the shaft is turning.
f: What does a fail to start alarm look like on the OIS?
Why can a motor run but the belt still not move?
How long is the transition time for a pump start?

In Automatic mode, can you start the dri.q: What would happen if someone tried to start it locally while in Auto?
In Automatic mode, can you start the dri.a:
Nothing would start. The reference says in Automatic the field start is blocked, while the field stop always works.

The reference does not say whether the attempted start is alarmed or logged. In general, the press may simply be ignored by the DCS logic.

If a field person genuinely needs to start the drive, they would ask the CRO to change the mode. Manual allows an LCS start with all interlocks active. Local allows LCS start with process interlocks and permissives bypassed, but only for fault finding or maintenance under supervision. The CRO selects the mode from the OIS.

f.q: If a drive won't start from the LCS, how do I tell why?
f.a:
Several possible causes, from the reference: the drive is in Automatic, which blocks field start; a start permissive is not healthy, such as low gland water on a slurry pump; a process interlock is active in Auto or Manual; or a critical interlock like an E-stop or pull wire is tripped.

The quickest route is to radio the CRO, who can see the drive's mode, the active interlocks and the first out on the OIS faceplate. Also check the LCS stop button is not still latched off.

Do not try to work around it. A drive refusing to start is usually telling you something real.
f: How does the CRO see which permissive is unhealthy?
How do I reset a latched off LCS stop button?
What does a protection relay trip look like on the OIS?

f.q: Why not just let the DCS start drives that fieldies request?
f.a:
Because the DCS is checking more than the field person can see. In Auto, the start decision depends on sequences and process conditions across the whole circuit.

For example, the reference says FIM mill transfer pumps are interlocked if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running, and slurry pumps cannot run against closed valves except briefly on start or changeover. A field operator at one pump does not see all those conditions.

Routing starts through the CRO with the right mode keeps one person who can see the whole picture in charge of starting equipment. It is a coordination safeguard as much as a technical one.
f: Why are mill transfer pumps tied to the cyclone feed pump?
What is the CRO's view of a pump faceplate like?
How do field operators and CROs share the start decision?

f.q: Is an attempted field start in Auto alarmed in the control room?
f.a:
The reference does not say. It only states that in Automatic the field start is blocked and the field stop always works.

Some DCS configurations raise a low priority or logging alarm when a field start is pressed while the drive is not in a mode that accepts it, to help the CRO understand what is happening. Others simply ignore it.

The alarm system follows ISA-18.2 with priorities Logging, Low, High and Urgent, so if it is configured, it would probably be at the Logging or Low level. For certainty, ask a control room operator or the control systems engineer.
f: What do the four alarm priority levels mean in practice?
What is ISA-18.2 and why does the site follow it?
How do I see Logging priority alarms on the OIS?

In Automatic mode, can you start the dri.q: Does the field stop button trip the DCS sequence too, or just that drive?
In Automatic mode, can you start the dri.a:
The reference does not say directly how a field stop affects the rest of a sequence. It does describe related behaviour.

It says a conveyor trip stops any upstream interlocked equipment so material does not pile up, and that sequence steps must confirm feedback or the sequence pauses. So stopping one drive is likely to stop anything upstream that is interlocked to it, and a sequence that loses run feedback would pause or alarm.

In general, think of it like a series of conveyors: stopping one stops everything feeding it, while downstream equipment may keep running. For the specific behaviour on a given sequence, ask a senior CRO or check the control philosophy for that area.

f.q: Why stop upstream equipment and not downstream?
f.a:
The reference says a conveyor trip stops upstream interlocked equipment so material does not pile up.

If a downstream conveyor stops, everything feeding it must also stop or ore will spill and bury the transfer chute. Equipment downstream can keep running, emptying itself, which is usually what you want for a restart.

The same logic applies to slurry. A stopped pump means its feed hopper fills, so whatever feeds that hopper may need to stop or divert. Think of it like a production line: if a station stops, the stations feeding it must stop, but the ones after it can clear their work.
f: How do restart sequences work from downstream back?
What happens to slurry in a stopped pump hopper?
Which interlocks protect a chute from overfilling?

f.q: What does a restart sequence check before starting up again?
f.a:
The reference says restart sequences work backwards from downstream with checks, listing flocculant, thickener rakes, mill inching, pumps and dump valves.

Starting from downstream means each piece of equipment has somewhere to send its product before it begins. For example, thickener rakes must be running and floc available before tails arrive, and pumps need their dump valves closed and lines primed before slurry is sent.

Mill inching is used when a mill has stopped with a load; turning it slowly helps check the charge is not frozen. Exact steps for each area are in the control philosophies.
f: What is a frozen charge in a SAG mill?
Why must thickener rakes run before feed starts?
How does mill inching work mechanically?

f.q: Can a field stop be used to stop a whole circuit in an emergency?
f.a:
The LCS stop stops that one drive, plus anything interlocked upstream of it per the reference. For an emergency, the protection devices in the reference are E-stops on LCSs and pull wires along conveyors, which are critical interlocks acting in every mode.

Whether a single E-stop stops a whole circuit or only its machine depends on how it is wired, which is not in the reference.

If there is an emergency, use the nearest E-stop or pull wire and call the control room immediately, so the CRO can bring the rest of the circuit down in a controlled way. Learn where the E-stops are in your area on your first walk round.
f: What is the difference between a stop and an E-stop?
How is a conveyor pull wire tripped and reset?
Who resets an E-stop after an incident?

What does Manual mode mean for a drive?.q: Why does Manual still respect all interlocks if the CRO is in control?
What does Manual mode mean for a drive?.a:
Because the interlocks protect things the CRO cannot react to fast enough or may not see. Per the reference, in Manual all process interlocks, critical interlocks and permissives still apply; the only difference from Auto is that the drive will not start or stop automatically.

A CRO might be watching 30 screens. If a pump's discharge valve closes or a hopper runs dry, the interlock trips the pump in seconds, which no human could guarantee.

It is like driving a car in manual gears: you choose the gear, but the ABS and rev limiter still protect you. Only Local bypasses process interlocks, and that is for supervised maintenance work.

f.q: What kind of thing does a process interlock protect against?
f.a:
The reference says process interlocks stop a drive to prevent spills or poor performance, and trip in Auto and Manual.

Typical examples from the reference: slurry pumps interlocked so they cannot run against a closed valve except briefly on start or changeover; FIM mill transfer pumps interlocked if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running; low gland water flow tripping a running slurry pump after a delay; and the stockpile feed conveyor interlocked to the stockpile High-High switch.

They are about protecting the process and equipment, while critical interlocks are about people and catastrophic damage.
f: What is the difference between process and critical interlocks?
Who can bypass a process interlock and how?
Why trip a slurry pump that runs against a closed valve?

f.q: Can a CRO bypass an interlock to keep a drive running?
f.a:
Only process interlocks, and only by named users one at a time, per the reference. Critical interlocks, such as E-stops, pull wires and protection relays, cannot be bypassed.

The one at a time rule stops someone bypassing a whole group, which would remove protection without anyone fully understanding the combined risk.

In practice a bypass is usually used for a failed instrument giving false trips while it is repaired, under a site authorisation process. The reference does not describe that process; ask the shift supervisor or control systems engineer about the bypass register and approvals.
f: What paperwork goes with a process interlock bypass?
How does the OIS show that an interlock is bypassed?
How long can a bypass stay in place?

f.q: Does Manual mode change how loops behave as well as drives?
f.a:
Drive modes and loop modes are separate, per the reference. Drives have Automatic, Manual and Local. Loops have Manual, Automatic and Cascade.

A drive in Manual means the CRO starts and stops it. A loop in Manual means the CRO sets the controller output directly, such as VSD speed or valve position, and the PID is not acting.

A pump can be in drive Auto while its speed loop is in loop Manual, or the reverse. Watch for this when reading the OIS; it is like a car with separate choices for gearbox mode and cruise control.
f: What happens to a PID loop's output when switched to Manual?
Can a loop in Cascade drive a pump that is in Manual?
How does the OIS show drive mode and loop mode?

What does Manual mode mean for a drive?.q: What would you see if a Manual drive tripped on a process interlock?
What does Manual mode mean for a drive?.a:
The reference says the DCS records first out on trips, so the CRO can find which condition tripped the drive first. Alarms follow ISA-18.2 with Logging, Low, High and Urgent priorities.

So you would expect the drive to show as stopped or tripped on its faceplate, an alarm for the trip, and a first out indication naming the interlock, such as low gland flow or a closed valve.

In Manual the drive will not restart by itself once the condition clears. The CRO has to reset and restart it. Exact symbols and colours are site specific; ask a CRO to show you a tripped faceplate.

f.q: Does a tripped drive need resetting before it can restart?
f.a:
The reference does not describe the reset requirements in detail, beyond saying pull wires and rip detectors must be reset in the field and that the LCS has latch off stop buttons.

In general, a DCS drive that trips on an interlock latches the trip so it does not restart unexpectedly when the condition clears. The CRO acknowledges and resets it before starting again. Some trips, particularly field devices like pull wires, also need a physical reset where the device is.

Latching trips is basic machine safety: a machine should not restart on its own after a fault.
f: Why must pull wires be reset in the field?
What is the difference between acknowledging and resetting?
What else needs a field reset besides pull wires?

f.q: How does first out help if several interlocks show at once?
f.a:
The reference says the DCS records which condition tripped the drive first, so you can find the root cause.

When a pump stops, other conditions quickly follow: low flow, falling discharge pressure, rising hopper level. All of them alarm, but they are consequences. First out marks the one that actually caused the trip.

It is like diagnosing a car breakdown: the oil light, temperature light and stall all come on, but the first one tells you where it started. Without first out, you might chase the symptoms.
f: Where is first out shown on the OIS?
Can first out be wrong if two trips happen at once?
Is first out stored in PI or only in the DCS?

f.q: Would the trip alarm be masked once the drive stops?
f.a:
Partly. The reference says alarms are masked when equipment is not running. That generally refers to alarms that only make sense while running, such as low flow or low pressure on a stopped pump, so the CRO is not flooded with meaningless alarms.

The trip itself and the first out are not the kind of alarm that gets masked, because they tell you why the drive stopped.

Alarm masking like this is a core part of ISA-18.2 alarm management, which the site follows. It keeps the alarm list meaningful, much like a car dashboard not warning about low oil pressure while the engine is off.
f: What is an alarm flood and why is it dangerous?
How does ISA-18.2 decide alarm priority?
Can a CRO see masked alarms if needed?

What does Manual mode mean for a drive?.q: Why do some pumps need the isolation valve opened before starting in Manual?
What does Manual mode mean for a drive?.a:
The reference says some pumps with manual isolation valves are field start only, so you open the valve before starting and do not run against a closed valve.

A centrifugal slurry pump running against a closed valve is deadheading. All the energy goes into heating and churning the slurry in the casing, which damages the seals, wears the impeller and can overheat the pump. Without position feedback on a manual valve, the DCS cannot know it is closed, so the start is done locally by someone who can see and open it.

Actuated valves have limit switches that the DCS can check, which is why pumps with them can start from the OIS.

f.q: Why can't the DCS check a manual valve's position?
f.a:
Most manual valves have no position switch or transmitter, so there is no signal to the DCS. The reference describes actuated valves with proximity or limit switches, and the watchdog that faults if the limit switch does not confirm in time. Manual valves have none of that.

So the only way to know the valve is open is a person looking at it. That is why those pumps are field start only, with the operator confirming the valve and pump together.

Some sites add position switches to critical manual valves, but the reference does not say whether that has been done here.
f: What are proximity switches and how do they sense valves?
When is it worth fitting a switch on a manual valve?
How does the valve watchdog detect a stuck valve?

f.q: How long can a slurry pump survive running deadheaded?
f.a:
The reference does not give a figure, and it depends on the pump.

In general, a centrifugal pump at zero flow turns nearly all of its input power into heat in a small trapped volume. Temperature rises quickly, and with slurry you also get local abrasion. Seals and gland packing suffer first, then bearings from vibration. Damage can begin within minutes for large pumps.

That is why the reference says pumps are interlocked so they cannot run against a closed valve except briefly on start or changeover. Treat any deadhead as an urgent stop.
f: What signs show a pump is running deadheaded?
Why does zero flow cause vibration in centrifugal pumps?
How is a minimum flow line used to protect pumps?

f.q: What is the safe start order for a pump with manual valves?
f.a:
The reference does not give a start procedure for specific pumps, only that you open the isolation valve before starting so the pump does not run against a closed valve.

In general practice for a slurry pump: confirm gland water is on and flowing, open the suction valve so the pump floods, check the discharge path is open, then start. The site's standard work instructions will set the exact order, and the gland water permissive will block a start if seal water is low.

Use the area work instruction or ask the area supervisor for the exact steps on a given pump.
f: Why must gland water be on before a slurry pump starts?
What is pump priming and when is it needed?
Where are area work instructions kept?

What does Local mode bypass, and what do.q: Why is Local allowed to bypass process interlocks at all?
What does Local mode bypass, and what do.a:
Because fault finding sometimes needs to run a drive when its process conditions are not normal. The reference says Local is for fault finding and maintenance only, started from the LCS, and must be supervised.

For example, a fitter might need to bump a pump to check rotation after a motor change, while the hopper is empty and the permissive for level is not met. Or an electrician might need to run a motor to test a starter when an instrument interlock is faulty.

Critical interlocks, hardwired devices and protection relays stay active, so the protections for people and catastrophic damage remain. It is like a maintenance jog mode on a machine: limited, supervised and still guarded.

f.q: Why are critical interlocks hardwired rather than in DCS logic?
f.a:
The reference says critical interlocks include E-stops, pull wires and protection relays, and that hardwired devices always stay active. It also says VSD E-stops act on Safe Torque Off.

Hardwiring takes the safety function out of software. A software bug, a configuration change or an FCS failure cannot defeat it. A pull wire opens a contact in the motor control circuit and the motor stops, regardless of the DCS.

It is the same reason pressure relief valves are mechanical: the last line of protection should not depend on a controller that could fail or be changed.
f: What is Safe Torque Off on a VSD?
What does a motor protection relay detect?
Are hardwired trips tested regularly on site?

f.q: What does supervised mean for Local mode?
f.a:
The reference says Local must be supervised but does not define it.

In general, it means a competent person is physically at the equipment and in control of it while in Local, with the CRO aware. Because process interlocks and permissives are bypassed, a person must be there to stop it if something goes wrong, such as a pump deadheading or a hopper overflowing.

It also means not leaving the drive in Local when the job is done. The configurable timer is a backstop for that. Check the site procedure for the exact rules, as it may also tie in with the permit system.
f: Who counts as a competent person for Local operation?
What should a supervisor watch for when testing in Local?
How is the CRO told that Local testing is finished?

f.q: What is a start permissive bypassed in Local likely to be?
f.a:
The reference gives gland water low flow as a start permissive example: it stops a slurry pump starting. Other permissives in general practice include valve positions, level conditions and lubrication status.

In Local, the permissive does not stop the start. So a pump could be started without gland water flow, for example. That is why Local is for short, supervised tests, not for running production.

It is worth asking what the permissive protects before testing in Local, and making sure that risk is covered by the person at the machine.
f: How long can a slurry pump run safely without gland water?
What permissives are typical on a conveyor start?
Can lube oil pressure be a start permissive on a mill?

What does Local mode bypass, and what do.q: What could go wrong if Local mode wasn't supervised on site?
What does Local mode bypass, and what do.a:
In Local, process interlocks and start permissives are bypassed, per the reference. If nobody is at the machine, the things those interlocks prevent can happen.

For a slurry pump: running against a closed valve, running dry with an empty hopper, or running without gland water and wrecking the seal. For a conveyor or feeder: running onto a stopped downstream belt and spilling ore. For a tank or hopper: overflowing.

The critical interlocks remain active, so E-stops, pull wires and protection relays still protect people and motors. But equipment damage, spills and production loss are all possible. That is why the reference says Local is for fault finding and maintenance only and must be supervised.

f.q: Does a spill from Local running count as an environmental incident?
f.a:
The reference does not cover site incident classification. In general, slurry spills are reportable on most sites, and spills in cyanide areas such as the CIL tanks are taken very seriously because of the toxicity.

The reference notes cyanide areas have HCN gas monitors with beacons and sirens, which shows the level of hazard involved.

The site's environmental and HSE procedures would define what is reportable. Ask the area supervisor or site HSE advisor. As a rule, report any spill rather than trying to judge its significance yourself.
f: Why is a cyanide area spill treated differently?
Who is the site HSE advisor for the processing plant?
How is slurry cleaned up after a spill?

f.q: Why not just disable Local mode to remove the risk?
f.a:
Because maintenance and fault finding would then be harder and, ironically, riskier. Without Local, technicians might be tempted to force signals, jump out interlocks or bypass permissives in less controlled ways to test equipment.

The reference's design keeps a controlled path: mode selected from the OIS by the CRO, start only from the LCS, critical interlocks still active, supervision required and a timer to drop out of Local.

It is like having a proper jog button on a machine rather than forcing someone to hold a contactor in by hand. A defined path with limits is safer than an informal workaround.
f: What is the risk of forcing a signal in the DCS?
How are interlock jumpers controlled on site?
When is a force in the DCS ever acceptable?

f.q: Who is accountable if a drive is damaged in Local?
f.a:
The reference does not cover accountability. In general, the person supervising the drive in Local and the CRO who selected the mode share responsibility for it being used properly, within the site's permit and work control system.

Most sites focus investigations on what went wrong with the system rather than blaming individuals, using tools such as the operator action log, first out records and PI trends.

For the site's rules on who may request and supervise Local, ask the maintenance superintendent or shift supervisor.
f: How does the site investigate equipment damage incidents?
What is the permit to work system on site?
Who can request Local mode for a drive?

What does Local mode bypass, and what do.q: How long is the configurable timer usually set for before it drops out?
What does Local mode bypass, and what do.a:
The reference does not give the timer value. It only says a configurable timer drops the drive out of Local back to its target mode.

It is likely to be set during commissioning and may differ by drive type. A short timer reduces the chance of forgetting a drive in Local; a longer one avoids interrupting genuine fault finding.

For the actual value on a particular drive, ask a senior CRO or the control systems engineer, who can read it from the DCS configuration. Do not assume all drives have the same value.

f.q: What happens to a running drive when the Local timer expires?
f.a:
The reference says the timer drops the drive out of Local back to its target mode, and that mode changes are bumpless: only a new command or an interlock changes the drive state.

So the switch itself should not stop the drive. But once back in Auto or Manual, the process interlocks and permissives apply again. If a process interlock condition is true at that moment, such as a closed discharge valve, the drive will trip.

In Auto, the DCS logic may also decide the drive should be stopped or started. So be ready for a change in state as the timer runs out.
f: Can the field operator extend the Local timer?
Does the OIS show how long a drive has left in Local?
What happens if the target mode is Auto and no start is needed?

f.q: Why might different drives have different timer values?
f.a:
The reference does not say whether timer values differ, so this is general reasoning.

Some tests are quick, such as bumping a motor to check rotation, while others take longer, such as running a conveyor to check belt tracking after maintenance. A single short timer would interrupt the longer jobs and tempt people to work around it.

Higher risk drives might have shorter timers. The values are a DCS configuration choice, made during commissioning. Ask the control systems engineer for the actual list.
f: Where are DCS configuration settings documented?
Who can change a Local timer value?
How are DCS configuration changes approved?

f.q: Is the timer reset each time the field start is pressed?
f.a:
The reference does not say. Whether pressing start in Local restarts the timer is a detail of the DCS template configuration.

Both designs are common. A timer from the time Local was selected limits total time out of normal control. A timer from the last field action lets a long fault finding job continue as long as someone is actively working.

For this site, ask the control systems engineer or check the drive template description in the DCS functional specification.
f: What is a DCS functional specification?
Can I watch the Local timer count down on the OIS?
Is the timer also used for valves in Local?

Does switching a running drive between A.q: Why design mode changes to be bumpless rather than resetting the drive?
Does switching a running drive between A.a:
The reference says mode changes are bumpless: only a new command or an interlock changes the drive state.

If switching modes stopped or restarted the drive, a simple act like moving a pump from Auto to Manual for a few minutes would cause a process upset. Stopping a slurry pump can let the line settle and bog. Stopping a flotation agitator can sand the rotor. Restarting a large motor adds wear and can need power supplier approval for the mills.

It is the same principle as bumpless transfer on a PID loop: you change who is in control without kicking the output.

f.q: What is bumpless transfer on a PID loop?
f.a:
This is general control knowledge; the reference only mentions loop modes Manual, Automatic and Cascade.

Bumpless transfer means switching a controller between modes without a jump in its output. When going from Manual to Auto, the PID starts from the output the operator had set and the integral term is preset so there is no step. Many controllers also set the setpoint to the current process value on the switch, which is called setpoint tracking.

Without it, switching modes could slam a valve open or shut. Think of taking over cruise control in a car smoothly at the current speed rather than jerking.

f.q: Why does stopping a slurry pump risk bogging the line?
f.a:
When flow stops, solids in the slurry settle to the bottom of the pipe. Coarse heavy particles go first. If they compact, the line can block, and the pump may not be able to restart against it.

The reference says slurry pump dump valves fail open on power loss to drain the line so slurry does not settle and bog the pump and pipe. Dual level controllers on some hoppers also add water to keep line velocity above the settling velocity.

It is a key difference from clean water systems, where a stopped pump just means stopped flow.
f: What is settling velocity in a slurry line?
How is a bogged slurry line cleared?
Why do dump valves fail open on power loss?

f.q: Do mode changes on loops also avoid bumping the output?
f.a:
The reference says drive mode changes are bumpless, but it does not specifically say the same for loops. In general, Centum VP PID blocks are configured for bumpless transfer between Manual, Automatic and Cascade, and that is standard practice.

For example, when a CRO switches the cyclone feed hopper level loop from Manual to Auto, the pump speed should not jump. The PID begins from the current output.

If you ever see a bump on a mode change in PI trends, it is worth reporting, as it may indicate a configuration problem. A process control engineer can confirm the loop settings.
f: How do I check for a bump in PI after a mode change?
Who tunes the PID loops on site?
What does a bad mode change look like on a trend?

Does switching a running drive between A.q: What would happen if a mode change did knock the drive offline?
Does switching a running drive between A.a:
The reference says mode changes are bumpless, so by design this should not happen. If it did, it would be treated as a fault in the configuration.

The consequences depend on the drive. For a slurry pump, stopping could cause line settling and, if the dump valve opens, a drain cycle. For a conveyor, upstream interlocked equipment would stop. For a flotation agitator, the air valve interlocks closed and solids could start to settle. For a large mill, an unplanned stop may need power supplier approval to restart.

In short, small mode changes could cause significant upsets, which is why bumpless behaviour matters.

f.q: What would you do if you saw a mode change trip a drive?
f.a:
First, make the plant safe and let the CRO manage the upset. Then report it, as it should not happen per the reference.

Useful information to collect: the drive tag, the time, which modes it changed between, who made the change, and the first out record. PI trends and the operator action log help reconstruct it.

The control systems engineer would then check the drive template configuration. A fault like this can affect every drive built from the same template, so it is worth investigating properly rather than just restarting and moving on.
f: How do I raise a fault report for a DCS issue?
Who owns DCS template changes on site?
How do I find the operator action log entry?

f.q: Why does restarting a big mill need extra care after a trip?
f.a:
The reference says there is no DCS link to the Parkeston Power Station, so the CRO phones for approval before starting large loads, and sequences pause for confirmation. The mill motors are 20 MW.

In general, after a stop the mill charge can settle and compact, sometimes called a frozen charge, and restart sequences may include mill inching to check it. Large mill starts also stress the drive train and the power system.

So a spurious trip on a mill is costly: lost throughput, a restart procedure, and a call to the power supplier.

f.q: Could a mode change ever be expected to stop a drive?
f.a:
Not by itself. But the reference notes that only a new command or an interlock changes drive state, and switching modes can change which interlocks and logic apply.

For example, if a drive running in Local with a process interlock condition active is switched back to Manual, the process interlock now applies and the drive will trip. Or if a drive is switched to Auto, the DCS logic may issue a stop command because its process condition is not met.

So the mode change is bumpless, but what follows may not be. Check the conditions before asking for a mode change.
f: How do I check active interlocks before a mode change?
Can an Auto drive stop immediately on mode change?
What does the OIS show about pending interlocks?

Does switching a running drive between A.q: Would you ask the CRO to switch to Local while the drive is still running?
Does switching a running drive between A.a:
You can, technically: the reference says mode changes are bumpless, so the drive keeps running. But think about what Local means before asking.

In Local, process interlocks and start permissives are bypassed, and the drive must be supervised. A running drive moved to Local loses the process protections the CRO relies on. You also lose DCS starts and stops from sequences.

Only ask if you have a genuine fault finding or maintenance reason, you are at the machine to supervise it, and you have told the CRO why. If you do not need Local, Manual keeps all interlocks active while still allowing an LCS start.

f.q: When is Manual a better choice than Local for testing?
f.a:
Most of the time. The reference says in Manual the CRO can start and stop from the OIS, or the LCS start and stop works, and all process interlocks, critical interlocks and permissives still apply.

So if you only need to start and stop a drive to check it, and its process conditions are normal, Manual gives you that with full protection.

Local is for the narrower case where a process interlock or permissive would stop you testing, such as a level permissive not being met during commissioning. Ask yourself first whether you really need the bypass.
f: Can I start from the LCS in Manual without the CRO?
What is a permissive that commonly blocks testing?
Why would Local be needed during commissioning?

f.q: What should I tell the CRO when asking for Local?
f.a:
General good practice, as the reference does not give a script: the exact tag number, the reason, who will supervise at the drive, how long you expect it to take and how you will tell them it is finished.

The CRO needs to know because, in Local, process interlocks and permissives are bypassed and the drive will not follow its sequence. They may need to adjust other parts of the circuit while it is out of normal control.

The reference also notes a timer drops the drive back to its target mode, so let the CRO know if your job might run longer than that.
f: How does the CRO record that a drive is in Local?
What if the Local timer runs out mid test?
Should Local requests go through the shift supervisor?

f.q: Is it safe to switch a running mill drive into Local?
f.a:
The reference does not give a specific rule for the mills. General principles still apply: Local bypasses process interlocks and permissives, keeps critical interlocks, and is for supervised fault finding and maintenance only.

A SAG or ball mill relies on many process interlocks, such as lube oil and bearing protections, some of which may be handled by the mill's own protection system. Bypassing process protections on a 20 MW mill carries a big consequence if something goes wrong.

This is a question for the mill maintenance planner or process control engineer before anyone tries it. Do not assume what is fine for a sump pump is fine for a mill.
f: What protections does a SAG mill's lube system have?
Who supervises maintenance testing on the mills?
How are mill interlocks different from pump interlocks?

Name the three interlock types in the DC.q: Why split interlocks into three types instead of one universal trip?
Name the three interlock types in the DC.a:
Because they protect different things, and need different rules. From the reference:

Critical interlocks protect people and prevent catastrophic damage: E-stops, pull wires and protection relays. They trip in every mode and cannot be bypassed.

Process interlocks stop a drive to prevent spills or poor performance. They trip in Auto and Manual, and named users can bypass them one at a time.

Start permissives only prevent a start; they do not stop a running drive.

One universal trip would either be too strict, stopping production for minor conditions, or too lax, letting safety trips be bypassed. It is like a car having a seatbelt warning, a rev limiter and airbags: each has its own job and rules.

f.q: What makes a protection relay a critical interlock?
f.a:
The reference lists protection relays among critical interlocks, along with E-stops and pull wires.

A motor protection relay watches electrical quantities such as current, voltage, earth faults and sometimes temperature. It trips the motor if it detects overload, a short circuit, an earth fault or other electrical damage, faster than any operator could. Failure to trip can mean a burnt out motor or a cable fire.

Because the consequence is serious and the action has to be fast, it acts directly on the switchgear and cannot be bypassed through the DCS.
f: What does an earth fault trip mean on a motor?
How are protection relays tested on site?
Who resets a protection relay trip?

f.q: Can a process interlock ever be more important than a critical one?
f.a:
In terms of rules, no: critical interlocks are always active and cannot be bypassed, while process interlocks can be bypassed by named users.

In terms of consequence, some process interlocks protect expensive equipment from serious damage. A slurry pump running against a closed valve is a process interlock case, but it can wreck the pump.

That is why process interlock bypasses are restricted to named users, one at a time, per the reference. The bypass should only happen with a clear understanding of what the interlock protects and what replaces it during the bypass.
f: What extra controls apply during an interlock bypass?
Why are bypasses limited to one at a time?
How does the CRO track active bypasses?

f.q: Which interlock type covers equipment like HCN gas monitors?
f.a:
The reference says cyanide areas have HCN gas monitors with beacons and sirens. It does not say which interlock type, if any, they feed.

In general, gas detection systems are primarily alarm systems that warn people to evacuate. Some sites also use them to trigger actions, such as starting ventilation or stopping cyanide dosing. Those actions could be configured as process or critical functions depending on the risk assessment.

For how HCN monitors are tied into the plant here, ask the area metallurgist or site HSE advisor.
