Where are HCN monitors located in the CIL area?
How is HCN formed in a cyanide leach circuit?

Name the three interlock types in the DC.q: How would you tell from an alarm screen which interlock type has tripped?
Name the three interlock types in the DC.a:
The reference does not describe the alarm screen layout, so this mixes the reference with general practice.

The reference says the DCS records first out on trips and uses ISA-18.2 priorities: Logging, Low, High and Urgent. The tag and description of the first out usually tell you the type. A pull wire, E-stop or protection relay is critical. Low gland flow on a running pump, or a closed valve, is process. A blocked start, such as low gland flow before starting, is a permissive.

On many DCS faceplates the interlock list is grouped by type. Ask a CRO to walk you through a drive faceplate on this site.

f.q: What do the alarm priorities Logging, Low, High and Urgent mean?
f.a:
The reference lists the priorities but does not define them, so this is general ISA-18.2 practice.

Logging alarms are recorded but not presented as needing action, useful for history. Low priority means action is needed but there is time. High priority needs prompt action to avoid a significant consequence. Urgent needs immediate action to avoid serious consequences.

Priority is set from how severe the consequence is and how quickly the operator must respond. The goal is that the CRO always deals with the most important alarm first, like triage in an emergency room.
f: How many alarms per hour can a CRO handle?
Who decides an alarm's priority on site?
What is alarm rationalisation?

f.q: Why are analogue alarms set as LL, L, H and HH?
f.a:
The reference lists analogue alarms as LL, L, H and HH.

The outer alarms, L and H, are early warnings that a value is drifting so the CRO can correct it. The inner ones, LL and HH, mean it has gone further and usually trigger an interlock or stronger response.

Examples from the reference include the stockpile High-High switch stopping the stockpile feed conveyor, and the pebble bin bypass gate opening on bin High-High. It is like a tank with a high level warning and a separate overflow trip.
f: Which HH alarms trip equipment in the milling area?
Is an HH alarm always tied to an interlock?
How are alarm setpoints chosen for a hopper?

f.q: Can an alarm screen show a trip that has already cleared?
f.a:
In general yes. Most DCS alarm systems keep an alarm on the list until it has been acknowledged, even if the condition has returned to normal. The alarm history also records when it came in and cleared.

The reference says first out records which condition tripped the drive first, which helps when the original cause has cleared by the time someone looks.

That is common with short spikes. It is one reason interlocks have adjustable time delays, so momentary spikes do not trip the plant.
f: How do I view alarm history on the OIS?
What is the difference between acknowledged and cleared?
Why do interlocks need time delays?

Name the three interlock types in the DC.q: Who is authorised to bypass a process interlock on shift?
Name the three interlock types in the DC.a:
The reference says process interlocks can be bypassed by named users, one at a time. It does not name the roles.

In general, named users are typically senior CROs, shift supervisors or control systems staff with specific DCS access rights, and the bypass is managed through a site process such as an interlock bypass register with a risk assessment and approval.

Critical interlocks cannot be bypassed by anyone. For who holds bypass rights on site and what paperwork applies, ask the shift supervisor or control systems engineer.

f.q: Why must process interlock bypasses be one at a time?
f.a:
The reference says process interlocks can be bypassed only individually by named users. It does not give the reason, so this is general reasoning.

Each bypass removes one layer of protection. Allowing several at once makes it easy to lose track of the combined risk, especially if they interact. A pump with both its closed valve interlock and gland flow interlock bypassed is far less protected than with just one.

The one at a time rule forces each bypass to be a deliberate decision, and keeps the list short enough to manage.
f: What is an interlock bypass register?
How often are active bypasses reviewed?
Is there a time limit on a process interlock bypass?

f.q: What should be in place before a process interlock is bypassed?
f.a:
The reference does not describe the procedure, so this is general good practice.

Usually: a clear reason, such as a failed instrument giving false trips; a risk assessment; an alternative protection while bypassed, such as a person watching the equipment or a portable instrument; approval from the right person; a record in a bypass register; and a plan and time limit to remove it.

The bypass is only part of the job. The fault that made it necessary must be fixed. Ask the shift supervisor for the site procedure.
f: Who approves interlock bypasses on site?
What counts as an alternative protection?
How is a bypass removed and recorded?

f.q: How does the OIS show that an interlock is currently bypassed?
f.a:
The reference does not describe this. In general, DCS faceplates show a bypass indicator on the interlock, often a symbol or colour change, and many sites keep a bypass list or summary page so the CRO can see all active bypasses in one place.

That visibility matters at shift handover. An outgoing CRO should hand over active bypasses explicitly, as the incoming operator may otherwise assume the drive is fully protected.

Ask a CRO to show you how bypasses appear on this site's screens.
f: How are bypasses handed over between shifts?
Is there a bypass summary page on the OIS?
Can a bypass remain after the drive is restarted?

Difference between a start permissive an.q: Why can't a start permissive trip a drive once it's already running?
Difference between a start permissive an.a:
By definition, per the reference, a start permissive stops a drive starting but will not stop it once running.

It is a design choice. Some conditions matter at the moment of starting but are tolerable briefly while running. The reference example is gland water: low flow stops a slurry pump starting, but once running, low gland flow must persist for a set time before it trips.

So the same signal acts as a permissive at start and as a delayed process interlock while running. That avoids tripping a pump for a momentary dip while still protecting it from a sustained loss.

It is like checking oil level before starting an engine, but relying on the oil pressure switch while it runs.

f.q: Why is a gland water dip tolerated briefly on a running pump?
f.a:
The reference says once running, low gland flow must persist for a set time before it trips.

Short dips in gland water flow are common: another pump starting on the same header, a pressure fluctuation, or a flow switch flicker. Tripping a slurry pump for that would cause unnecessary upsets, including line settling and dump valve cycles.

The gland packing can tolerate a short interruption without damage. A sustained loss lets slurry get into the gland and wear the shaft sleeve. The time delay balances those two risks.
f: What does gland water actually do in a slurry pump?
What causes gland water header pressure dips?
How is the gland water trip delay chosen?

f.q: What other conditions are commonly start permissives?
f.a:
The reference gives gland water low flow as the example. Other permissives that appear in the reference include a minimum number of cyclones open before the cyclone feed pump starts, and valves in the correct position for a pump start.

In general practice, permissives also include lube oil pressure on large machines, guards and doors closed, downstream equipment running, and tank levels above a minimum for pump suction.

They are all conditions that should be right before you commit to a start.
f: Why must cyclones be open before the feed pump starts?
Is downstream equipment running a permissive or an interlock?
What permissives does a SAG mill start need?

f.q: Is a permissive bypassed in Local mode?
f.a:
Yes. The reference says Local bypasses process interlocks and start permissives, while critical interlocks, hardwired devices and protection relays stay active.

So in Local, a slurry pump could be started without gland water flow. That is why Local is for supervised fault finding and maintenance only, and why the person supervising should understand what each bypassed permissive normally prevents.

In Auto and Manual, permissives always apply.
f: What risks come from starting a pump without gland water?
How long can a drive stay in Local?
Who can request Local for testing a pump?

Difference between a start permissive an.q: What would a handover mean by 'gland flow permissive was bypassed'?
Difference between a start permissive an.a:
It means the gland water low flow check that normally stops a slurry pump starting has been bypassed. The pump can be started even if the gland water flow switch or flowmeter shows low.

Per the reference, process interlocks can be bypassed by named users individually, and Local mode bypasses permissives. Either could be what the note means.

Common reasons: a faulty flow switch giving a false low. Important follow ups: is the gland water actually flowing, has the fault been raised for repair, and is someone checking the gland visually? The bypass should be removed as soon as the instrument is fixed.

f.q: How would you check gland water is actually flowing?
f.a:
General practice, as the reference does not give a field check: look at the gland area for a steady drip or flow from the packing, check any local flow indicator or the mag flowmeter reading for the large pumps, and confirm the manual isolation valves are open and the actuated valve has opened.

The reference says the gland water arrangement includes manual isolation valves, an actuated on/off valve, a Maric constant flow valve and a flow switch or flowmeter. A blocked Maric valve or closed isolation valve would cause low flow even with a healthy supply.

If in doubt, ask the area operator to show you.
f: What does a healthy gland look like on a slurry pump?
How does a Maric valve block or fail?
Which pumps have gland water mag flowmeters?

f.q: How long can a gland flow bypass safely stay in place?
f.a:
The reference does not give a time limit. In general, a bypass should stay only as long as needed to fix the instrument, and the site's bypass procedure would set the review period.

The longer it stays, the more likely it is forgotten, and a real gland water loss could then go undetected and damage the pump.

A sensible practice is to make sure there is a work order for the faulty instrument, the bypass is in the register and handover, and a field check is done each shift. Ask the shift supervisor for the site rule.
f: How do I raise a work order for a faulty flow switch?
What does the shift field check for a bypass include?
Who reviews the bypass register?

f.q: What damage happens if gland water is lost for a long time?
f.a:
General pump knowledge, not in the reference: gland water flushes the packing or seal with clean water at higher pressure than the pump casing, so slurry does not get into the gland.

Without it, abrasive slurry enters the packing, rapidly wearing the shaft sleeve and packing. The packing can also overheat from friction without the water's cooling. Leakage increases, and slurry may spray out of the gland, which is a housekeeping and safety issue. Eventually the shaft sleeve needs replacing.

It is like running a mechanical seal dry on a water pump.
f: How often are slurry pump shaft sleeves replaced?
What is the difference between packing and a mechanical seal?
Why is gland water pressure kept above casing pressure?

Difference between a start permissive an.q: What's the mechanical risk if a pump keeps running on low gland flow?
Difference between a start permissive an.a:
The reference says low gland flow blocks a start and, while running, trips after a delay. It does not detail the damage, so this is general.

Gland water keeps abrasive slurry out of the packing and cools it. With low flow, slurry particles get into the packing, scoring the shaft sleeve. Friction heats the packing, which can harden and lose its seal. Leakage increases and may spray slurry.

The result is shorter sleeve and packing life, unplanned maintenance and possible downtime. For a large pump like cyclone feed, that can stop the mill circuit. That is why the big pumps have mag flowmeters rather than simple flow switches, giving a real flow value to watch.

f.q: Why do the big pumps get mag flowmeters for gland water?
f.a:
The reference says the big pumps, cyclone feed, tails thickener underflow and final tails, get mag flowmeters instead of flow switches.

A flow switch only tells you above or below a set point. A flowmeter gives a continuous value, so you can see gradual drift, such as a slowly blocking Maric valve or packing wear, before it trips.

These pumps are the most critical. Losing cyclone feed stops the grinding circuit; losing final tails stops the whole plant discharge. Better instrumentation is worth it on equipment where downtime is so costly.
f: What makes cyclone feed pumps so critical to the plant?
How does a mag flowmeter measure water flow?
Can PI show gland water flow trends for the big pumps?

f.q: How would you spot low gland flow before it trips the pump?
f.a:
For the big pumps with mag flowmeters, trend the gland water flow in PI and look for a slow decline. For pumps with flow switches, you only get an alarm when the switch trips, so field checks matter more.

In the field, look at the gland: a steady clean water drip is normal; slurry coming out, steam or a dry hot gland is not.

The reference says the Maric valve gives a set flow regardless of supply pressure, so low flow usually means a blocked Maric, a closed isolation valve, a failed actuated valve or a supply header problem.
f: What is the usual cause of a blocked Maric valve?
How do I trend a tag in PI?
What does slurry leaking from a gland indicate?

f.q: Does low gland water affect pump performance or just the seal?
f.a:
Mostly the seal and shaft sleeve. Hydraulic performance, the flow and head the pump delivers, is set by the impeller, casing and speed.

But it can affect performance indirectly. A badly worn gland lets air in on the suction side of some pumps, which can reduce performance. And a gland failure can force an unplanned stop, which matters far more than any efficiency change.

This is general pump knowledge; the reference covers the gland water arrangement and its interlocks but not the failure effects.

What signs show a slurry pump impeller is worn?
How is pump performance monitored on site?

Why do DCS interlocks have an adjustable.q: Why not just trip instantly the moment the instrument reads bad?
Why do DCS interlocks have an adjustable.a:
Instruments in a plant are noisy. Slurry sloshes in a hopper, a level radar sees splashes, a flow switch flickers, a pressure transmitter catches a water hammer spike. If every reading past a limit tripped a drive, the plant would trip constantly for nothing.

The reference says DCS interlocks have adjustable time delays so a momentary spike does not trip the plant; the condition must be true continuously for a set time. Delays are set during commissioning.

It is like a motor overload relay with an inverse time curve: a brief overcurrent on start is allowed, but a sustained one trips. Hardwired critical trips like E-stops act immediately because their purpose is to stop now.

f.q: Why do hardwired critical trips act immediately?
f.a:
The reference says hardwired critical trips like E-stops act immediately, while DCS interlocks have adjustable delays.

An E-stop or pull wire is pulled by a person who has seen danger: someone caught, a fire, a belt about to fail. Any delay could mean injury. Protection relays also need to clear electrical faults fast to prevent damage.

These devices are not affected by process noise because they are deliberate human actions or electrical protection with their own timing built in. So there is no reason to delay them, and every reason not to.
f: What is the difference between a pull wire and an E-stop?
How quickly does a conveyor stop after a pull wire?
Do protection relays have their own time delays?

f.q: What is a nuisance trip and why does it matter?
f.a:
A nuisance trip is a trip caused by a false or momentary condition rather than a real problem. General term, not in the reference.

They matter for several reasons. Each trip costs production and can cause knock on effects, like settling in slurry lines or a mill restart needing power supplier approval. Repeated nuisance trips also train people to distrust interlocks, which leads to requests for bypasses, and that removes real protection.

The adjustable delays on DCS interlocks in the reference exist largely to stop nuisance trips.
f: How are nuisance trips tracked on site?
What should I do if an interlock keeps tripping falsely?
Can instrument filtering replace interlock delays?

f.q: How is a sensible delay value chosen?
f.a:
The reference says delays are set during commissioning but does not give the values or method.

In general, the delay has to be long enough to ride through normal noise and short events, but short enough that real damage cannot occur before the trip. Engineers look at how fast the equipment can be damaged, for example a pump deadheading, versus how noisy the signal is.

It is like choosing a fuse rating: high enough to carry the starting current, low enough to protect the cable. PI trends of the signal help find the right balance.
f: Who sets interlock delays during commissioning?
Can delays be changed after commissioning?
How are delay changes approved on site?

Why do DCS interlocks have an adjustable.q: What would you see in the alarm log if the delay were set too short?
Why do DCS interlocks have an adjustable.a:
General reasoning, as the reference does not cover this.

You would see repeated trips on the same interlock, often with no lasting problem found. The first out would keep pointing to the same condition, and the PI trend of that signal would show short spikes crossing the trip limit and returning quickly.

The drive would restart and run normally until the next spike. Operators would grow frustrated and may ask for a bypass. That pattern is the sign the delay needs review, or the instrument needs attention, rather than the equipment.

f.q: How would you tell a bad delay from a bad instrument?
f.a:
Look at the signal trend in PI. A healthy instrument with real but brief process spikes, such as level slosh, suggests the delay may be too short. Erratic jumps, dropouts to zero, or a frozen signal suggest an instrument fault.

Compare with related measurements. If a flow switch trips but the pump power and discharge pressure stay steady, the flow switch is suspect.

This is general fault finding practice, not in the reference. An instrument technician can test the device, and the process control engineer can review the delay.
f: How do instrument technicians test a flow switch?
What does a frozen signal look like on a PI trend?
Which related tags help check a pump flow switch?

f.q: What does a delay set too long risk?
f.a:
The opposite problem: real faults are not caught in time. A pump running against a closed valve, or a conveyor with a blocked chute, could suffer damage before the interlock acts.

The reference says the blocked chute switch is microwave with a time delay to avoid false trips, which shows the balance being made. Too long a delay means the chute overfills and spills.

This is a consideration whenever delays are lengthened to stop nuisance trips. The fix should not create a bigger risk.
f: Why use microwave sensors for blocked chutes?
What damage does a blocked chute cause on a conveyor?
How is the blocked chute delay set?

f.q: Who should I tell if an interlock keeps nuisance tripping?
f.a:
The reference does not cover the reporting process. In general, tell the CRO and shift supervisor, and raise a work order for the instrument through the maintenance system so an instrument technician can check it.

If the instrument is healthy and the delay seems wrong, the process control engineer or control systems engineer would review it. Changes to interlock delays are configuration changes and should go through the site's change control process.

Avoid the temptation to bypass. Fix the cause.
f: What is the site management of change process?
How do I raise a maintenance work order?
Who is the process control engineer for my area?

Why do DCS interlocks have an adjustable.q: How would you find out what delay time is set for a given interlock?
Why do DCS interlocks have an adjustable.a:
The reference uses XX seconds as a placeholder and says delays are set during commissioning, so the values are not in the reference.

Options in general: ask the CRO, who may be able to see the delay on the drive faceplate or interlock detail; ask the control systems engineer, who can read it from the DCS configuration; or check the commissioning records and the control narrative or functional specification for that area.

Remember the documented value and the live configured value can differ if changes were made after commissioning. The DCS configuration is the truth for what is running now.

f.q: What is a control narrative or functional specification?
f.a:
General engineering term, not in the reference. A control narrative or functional specification describes in words how each piece of equipment is controlled: modes, interlocks, permissives, sequences, alarms and setpoints.

The control philosophy documents the reference is condensed from, Plant General Process Control Philosophy Stage 1 and Stage 2, are the higher level version of this. Detailed functional specifications for each area would add the specifics such as tag numbers and delays.

They are written before configuration and updated after commissioning, ideally to match what is actually in the DCS.
f: Where are the control philosophy documents stored?
How are functional specs kept up to date after changes?
What is in the Stage 2 control philosophy?

f.q: Why might documented delays differ from what's configured?
f.a:
General reasoning. Commissioning engineers adjust delays on site to suit real process noise, and post commissioning changes are made as operations learn the plant. If the documents are not updated each time, they drift from the DCS configuration.

Good change control should keep them aligned, but in practice there is often a lag.

So for anything important, such as investigating a trip, check the live configuration in the DCS rather than the document. The control systems engineer can do that.

Can I view interlock settings on the OIS myself?
Who signs off DCS configuration changes?

f.q: Are delays on the same type of interlock usually the same?
f.a:
Not necessarily. The reference says delays are adjustable and set during commissioning, which suggests they are tuned per interlock.

The same type of interlock on different equipment may see very different signal noise. A level switch in a turbulent slurry hopper needs more delay than one in a calm water tank. Equipment damage speed also differs: a large cyclone feed pump may justify a different delay to a small sump pump.

Starting from a standard value and tuning per case is common practice, but check the actual configuration.
f: Why is level measurement noisy in slurry hoppers?
What level instruments are used in slurry hoppers?
Do the big pumps have shorter or longer trip delays?

What is 'first out' on a trip?.q: Why does first out matter more when several alarms come in at once?
What is 'first out' on a trip?.a:
When one drive trips, the effects ripple through the circuit within seconds. A cyclone feed pump stopping, for example, leads to low cyclone pressure, a rising hopper level, low flow on downstream loops, and possibly trips on interlocked equipment like the FIM mill transfer pumps, which the reference says are interlocked if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running.

The CRO then sees a flood of alarms, most of them consequences. The reference says first out records which condition tripped the drive first, so you can find the root cause.

It is like a gearbox failure: the vibration, temperature and motor overload alarms all come in, but only one of them started it.

f.q: What is an alarm flood and why is it dangerous?
f.a:
General alarm management term. An alarm flood is when more alarms arrive than an operator can sensibly handle, often defined as more than about ten in ten minutes in ISA-18.2 guidance.

It is dangerous because the important alarm gets buried. The CRO may spend time acknowledging consequences while the cause, or a new real problem, goes unnoticed.

The reference says the site follows ISA-18.2, masks alarms when equipment is not running and records first out on trips. All three help keep floods manageable and point the CRO to what matters.
f: How does alarm masking reduce alarm floods?
What is alarm shelving and is it used on site?
How are alarm floods reviewed after an upset?

f.q: Why are the FIM mill transfer pumps tied to the cyclone feed pump?
f.a:
The reference says the FIM mill transfer pumps move existing FIM SAG discharge from its hopper to the new primary cyclone feed hopper at about 60 percent solids, and they are interlocked if the primary cyclone feed pump is not running.

If the cyclone feed pump stops, nothing is drawing from the primary cyclone feed hopper. Continuing to pump the FIM SAG discharge into it would overfill it and spill slurry.

It is a classic process interlock: stop feeding a vessel when its outlet stops, a bit like stopping a fuel transfer pump when the day tank outlet is closed.
f: What happens to the FIM SAG when its transfer pumps stop?
Are the FIM mill transfer pumps duty and standby?
How big is the primary cyclone feed hopper?

f.q: Can first out be misleading in a fast cascade of trips?
f.a:
It can, in general. If two conditions occur within the DCS scan time, the system may not resolve which truly came first. And a slow signal, such as a level, may cross its limit after the real cause even though it started changing earlier.

Also, first out records which interlock tripped the drive first, not necessarily the root cause of the upset. A pump might trip on low gland flow because the gland water pump tripped, which in turn had an electrical fault.

So first out is a strong starting point, but combine it with PI trends and the alarm history. The reference does not give the scan time.
f: What is a DCS scan time?
How do I combine first out with PI trends?
What is root cause analysis in maintenance?

What is 'first out' on a trip?.q: What would a handover comment about 'first out' actually tell you?
What is 'first out' on a trip?.a:
A note like 'cyclone feed pump tripped, first out low gland flow' tells you the pump stopped because the gland water flow condition triggered first. Per the reference, low gland flow on a running slurry pump trips it after a set delay.

That directs your follow up: check the gland water supply, Maric valve, flow switch or flowmeter, and isolation valves, rather than the pump motor or the process.

If a note says first out unknown or blank, that suggests either a hardwired trip outside the DCS logic or an unusual event, and is worth asking about directly.

f.q: Why might a trip have no first out recorded?
f.a:
The reference does not cover this, so this is general.

Possible reasons: the trip came from a device outside the DCS logic, such as a motor protection relay or VSD fault that only shows as a run feedback loss; the drive was stopped by a command rather than an interlock; or power was lost to the starter.

In those cases, look at the electrical protection relay records, the VSD fault log, and the operator action log for any stop command. An electrician can read the relay or VSD history.
f: How do I read a VSD fault log?
Does a protection relay trip show on the OIS?
What causes a loss of run feedback alarm?

f.q: What follow up should a first out entry trigger?
f.a:
General practice. Check the device named in the first out: is it a real process condition or an instrument fault? Look at the PI trend to see whether the signal changed gradually, which suggests a real condition, or jumped, which suggests a fault.

If real, fix the cause before restarting, such as restoring gland water or opening a valve. If an instrument fault, raise a work order. If it repeats, record it in the shift log so patterns become visible.

The reference provides first out to help find root cause; using it consistently is what makes it valuable.
f: How do I record a repeat trip in the shift log?
What is a bad actor alarm?
Who analyses repeat trips on site?

f.q: Is first out recorded for valves as well as drives?
f.a:
The reference mentions first out detection on trips in the control system general section, mainly in the context of drives. It does not say whether valves have first out.

It does say valves have a watchdog timer that faults fail to open or fail to close and holds the sequence, plus flags for both limit switches on or off together. So valve faults are clearly alarmed, even if not presented as first out.

For how this is shown on the OIS, ask a CRO or the control systems engineer.
f: What does a valve fail to close alarm mean?
What does both limit switches on indicate?
Do valves have interlocks like drives?

What is 'first out' on a trip?.q: Where in the DCS would you go to check the first out record?
What is 'first out' on a trip?.a:
The reference says the DCS records first out on trips, but does not describe where it is displayed.

In general on a Centum VP system, the first out indication is usually on the drive's faceplate or an interlock detail window, and the alarm summary and history show the sequence of events with time stamps.

The quickest way to learn is to ask a CRO to show you a tripped drive's faceplate and the alarm history on this site. That saves guessing between screens.

f.q: What is a drive faceplate on the OIS?
f.a:
General DCS term. A faceplate is the small pop up window for one item of equipment, opened by clicking its symbol on a graphic. For a drive it typically shows the mode (Auto, Manual or Local, per the reference), run status, start and stop buttons, interlock and permissive status, and alarms.

Because the site uses standard templates for new and old plant, every drive faceplate should look and behave the same way, which is one of the benefits of standardising.

Ask a CRO to open one for you; it is the main tool for understanding why something is or is not running.
f: What does a PID loop faceplate show?
Can a field engineer open faceplates in read only mode?
How are interlocks listed on a drive faceplate?

f.q: How long is the DCS alarm history kept?
f.a:
The reference does not say. In general, Centum VP keeps an alarm and event history for a limited period on the system, and many sites also archive alarm events to the historian or a separate alarm management database.

The reference says data is logged to a PI historian for trends; whether alarm events also go there is not stated.

Ask the control systems engineer how far back alarm history can be retrieved, especially before you plan an investigation into an older event.
f: Can PI show alarm events alongside process trends?
Is there an alarm management database on site?
How do I export alarm history for an investigation?

f.q: Can field staff see first out without going to the control room?
f.a:
The reference does not say. Field LCSs have start and latch off stop buttons only, with no display described, so first out is not visible in the field.

Some sites give engineers read only OIS access or web based viewers from office PCs. Whether that exists here is not covered.

In practice, radio the CRO, who can read the faceplate and tell you the first out. Ask the control systems engineer about read only access if you need it regularly.
f: Is there a read only OIS in the maintenance office?
What does the LCS show about the drive?
How do engineers request DCS viewing access?

What are the three loop controller modes.q: Why have three loop modes instead of just manual and automatic?
What are the three loop controller modes.a:
Manual and Automatic cover the basic case: the operator sets the output, or the PID drives the process variable to an operator setpoint. The reference adds Cascade, where the setpoint comes from a master controller instead of the operator.

Cascade needs its own mode so the slave loop knows whose setpoint to follow. In Automatic it holds the operator's setpoint; in Cascade it follows the master.

The reference example: thickener bed pressure sets the underflow flow setpoint, and the flow loop drives the pump VSD. Switching the flow loop out of Cascade to Automatic lets the CRO hold a fixed flow while the bed pressure instrument is checked, for example.

f.q: When would a CRO drop a cascade slave back to Automatic?
f.a:
General practice, as the reference does not list cases. Common reasons: the master loop's instrument is faulty, such as a bed pressure transmitter reading wrong; the master is being retuned; or the CRO wants a steady flow while investigating a downstream problem.

In Automatic the slave holds the operator's fixed setpoint, so the fast inner loop still rejects disturbances like pump wear. That is better than going straight to Manual on the pump speed.

Once the issue is sorted, the slave goes back to Cascade so the master can again adjust it.
f: What happens to the master loop when the slave leaves Cascade?
How do I know a master instrument is faulty?
Who retunes loops on site?

f.q: What do PV, SV and CV mean on a loop faceplate?
f.a:
From the reference: PV is the process variable, what you measure; SV is the setpoint value, what you want; CV is the controlled variable or controller output, the signal to the valve or VSD.

For a pump hopper level loop, PV is the hopper level, SV the target level, and CV the pump speed command.

In Manual the CRO sets CV directly. In Automatic the CRO sets SV and the PID calculates CV. In Cascade a master loop sets SV. Note that some textbooks call the output MV, the manipulated variable, so watch the naming.
f: Why does the site call the output CV instead of MV?
How do I tell if a loop output is saturated?
What does the PID do with the PV and SV error?

f.q: Does a loop in Manual still have alarms active?
f.a:
The reference does not say specifically. In general, process alarms such as high and low PV alarms stay active in loop Manual, because the process still matters. The reference does say alarms are masked when equipment is not running, which is about equipment status rather than loop mode.

So if a loop is in Manual and the level drifts, the high level alarm should still come in. That is part of why a loop accidentally left in Manual is usually caught eventually.

Check with a CRO for this site's configuration.
f: What is the difference between PV alarms and deviation alarms?
How are alarms masked when equipment stops?
Why might a loop be left in Manual by mistake?

What are the three loop controller modes.q: What would you see on the OIS if a loop was stuck in Manual by mistake?
What are the three loop controller modes.a:
The loop's mode indicator would show Manual, and the output CV would stay fixed while the PV drifts away from the SV.

In PI or on the trend, the CV line is flat while the PV wanders, rather than the CV moving to correct the PV. Over time, a high or low alarm on the PV may come in.

The reference defines loop modes as Manual (operator sets the output), Automatic and Cascade, but does not describe how the OIS displays mode. Ask a CRO to show you how modes appear on faceplates; it is worth checking loop modes on your area screens on a quiet shift.

f.q: Why does a flat CV with a drifting PV suggest Manual?
f.a:
In Automatic the PID constantly adjusts CV to bring PV back to SV. So if PV moves, CV should move in response.

If CV is perfectly flat while PV drifts, either the loop is in Manual, the output is saturated at its limit, or the controller has been set with very slow tuning. Manual is the most common cause.

It is like seeing a car drift out of its lane while the steering wheel is not turning at all: either nobody is steering, or the wheel is jammed. General control knowledge.
f: What does output saturation look like on a trend?
How does slow tuning differ from Manual on a trend?
What is integral action in a PID controller?

f.q: Are there reports that list loops not in their normal mode?
f.a:
The reference does not mention any. Some sites run loop performance or mode reports that flag loops out of their normal mode, often through the historian or a separate control performance tool.

It is a useful practice because loops left in Manual quietly reduce plant performance and protection.

Ask the process control engineer whether such a report exists here, and if not, PI can usually show loop modes over time if the mode tag is historised.
f: Is loop mode recorded as a PI tag?
Who monitors loop performance on site?
What is control loop performance monitoring?

f.q: What harm does a loop left in Manual actually do?
f.a:
General reasoning. In Manual the loop no longer corrects disturbances. For a hopper level loop, level drifts until it alarms or overflows, or runs low and the pump sucks air. For a density loop, density drifts and affects downstream performance, such as cyclone cut size or flotation.

It can also defeat cascade structures. If a slave is in Manual, its master's adjustments do nothing.

There is a production cost too: many loops exist to hold the process at an optimum, and in Manual it drifts away.
f: How does cyclone feed density affect cut size?
What happens when a slurry pump sucks air?
Why do cascade masters stop working when a slave is in Manual?

What are the three loop controller modes.q: How would you tell a Cascade loop is actually following its master?
What are the three loop controller modes.a:
The slave loop should show Cascade mode, and its SV should be changing over time as the master adjusts it, rather than sitting at a fixed operator value. The slave's PV should then follow that changing SV.

In PI, trend the master output against the slave SV; they should match or be closely related. For the reference example, the thickener bed pressure controller output and the underflow flow setpoint should move together.

If the slave SV is flat while the master output moves, the cascade is broken somewhere, such as the slave being in Automatic.

f.q: Why does the cascade break if the slave is in Automatic?
f.a:
In Automatic the slave uses the operator's setpoint instead of the master's output. The reference defines Cascade as the mode where the setpoint comes from a master controller.

So the master keeps calculating outputs, but nobody is listening. If the master has integral action, its output may wind up to a limit because its own PV is not responding.

Well configured DCS loops handle this by making the master track the slave so there is no bump when Cascade is restored. That is general practice; the reference does not detail it.
f: What is integral windup in a master loop?
How does master tracking work in a DCS?
Can a CRO put the master in Manual while the slave is in Cascade?

f.q: What other cascade loops does the plant use?
f.a:
From the reference: thickener underflow pumps in cascade from bed pressure or density to flow to VSD on the flotation tails thickener; pump hopper level cascading to a flow controller that sets pump speed; the cyclone feed hopper level controller adjusting the cyclone pressure setpoint; the concentrate pre-leach thickener underflow pumps cascading from bed pressure or density; and in Stage 1, flocculant cascaded from bed level.

The pattern is always a slow process target on the outside and a fast flow or pressure loop on the inside.
f: How does the cyclone pressure cascade open and close cyclones?
Why did flocculant control change in Stage 2?
What is bed pressure in a thickener?

f.q: How fast should the slave be compared to the master?
f.a:
General control knowledge. A rule of thumb is that the slave loop should respond at least three to five times faster than the master. Otherwise the two loops interact and can oscillate.

In the reference example, the underflow flow loop responds in seconds to pump speed changes, while thickener bed pressure changes over minutes to hours. That gives a good separation.

It is like a power steering system: the hydraulic assist responds almost instantly to wheel input, while the driver's steering corrections are much slower.
f: What causes two cascade loops to oscillate together?
How is loop speed measured during tuning?
Why is thickener bed pressure so slow to change?

What's a cascade loop, in mechanical ter.q: Why use a cascade loop instead of controlling flow directly on setpoint?
What's a cascade loop, in mechanical ter.a:
Because the real target is not a flow; it is the thickener bed. The reference example has thickener bed pressure setting the underflow flow setpoint, with the flow loop driving the pump VSD.

If you only controlled flow to a fixed setpoint, the bed would build up or deplete as feed solids changed. If you controlled bed pressure directly on pump speed, every pump wear or head change would disturb the bed before the slow bed loop noticed.

Cascade gives both. The inner flow loop handles fast disturbances such as pump wear or head change, and the outer loop handles the slow process target. It is like a thermostat setting the flow on a heating valve, with the valve's own flow loop absorbing pressure swings.

f.q: What does thickener bed pressure actually measure?
f.a:
The reference lists bed pressure, also called bed mass, among the thickener vendor signals, along with bed level from a SmartDiver, rake torque, rake height and overflow clarity.

Bed pressure is usually measured by a pressure transmitter near the base of the thickener. Since slurry is denser than water, more settled solids above the sensor means more pressure. It indicates the mass of the bed rather than just its height.

It is like measuring the contents of a tank with a load cell rather than a level gauge: you get weight, which is what matters for underflow density.
f: What is a SmartDiver and how does it measure bed level?
Why is rake torque monitored on a thickener?
What happens if the thickener bed gets too deep?

f.q: Why is underflow density sometimes used instead of bed pressure?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation tails thickener underflow pumps cascade from bed pressure or density to flow to VSD, so either can be the master.

Density directly measures what downstream wants: underflow at nominal 56 percent solids, range 50 to 62. Bed pressure is a more indirect but steadier measure of solids inventory.

In general, density control responds faster to changes in underflow quality, while bed pressure control gives a more stable inventory. Which is used at any time is an operating choice; ask the area metallurgist.
f: How is underflow density measured on site?
Why does CIL4 care about thickener underflow density?
What happens to the thickener if underflow is too dilute?

f.q: What does the thickener underflow feed to in Stage 2?
f.a:
In Stage 2, per the reference, all flotation tails thickener underflow goes to CIL4. CIL4 feed is the thickener underflow plus CIL3 tails plus a portion of spent eluate, about 3,164 t/h solids.

In Stage 1, a portion went to existing CIL2 and CIL3, flow controlled to their capacity, with the balance to final tails.

So the underflow cascade directly affects CIL4 feed rate and density, which in turn affects leach residence time, design 3.2 h for leach. These are design figures, not live values.
f: Why is CIL4 leach residence below the ideal 14 hours?
What does CIL4 do with flotation tails?
How does feed density affect CIL4 residence time?

What's a cascade loop, in mechanical ter.q: What would you see if the slave flow loop couldn't keep up with the master?
What's a cascade loop, in mechanical ter.a:
General control behaviour, applied to the reference example of bed pressure cascaded to underflow flow.

The master would keep asking for higher flow, but the slave's PV would lag below its SV, and the pump VSD output would rise to its maximum speed. On the trend you would see the slave CV pinned at 100 percent and a growing error between slave SV and PV.

Meanwhile the bed pressure would keep rising, because the underflow cannot remove solids fast enough. Causes include a worn pump, a partial blockage, or a feed rate higher than the pump capacity. The reference gives duty/standby underflow pumps at about 3,329 m3/h total.

f.q: What does it mean when a VSD output is pinned at maximum?
f.a:
It means the controller is asking for more than the pump can give. The CV has hit its upper limit, so the loop has lost control authority. Any further disturbance cannot be corrected.

Common causes: pump wear, higher than usual head from a partial line blockage or higher density, or a demand beyond the pump's design capacity.

It is like a car at full throttle going uphill and still slowing: the engine is giving everything it has. General knowledge, worth flagging to the area metallurgist or maintenance planner.
f: How is pump wear distinguished from a line blockage?
Why does higher slurry density raise pump head?
What is the design speed range of the underflow pump VSD?

f.q: What happens to a thickener if underflow can't keep up?
f.a:
General thickener behaviour. The bed builds up, bed pressure and rake torque rise, and eventually the rakes can overload. Overflow clarity may worsen as the bed approaches the feedwell.

The reference lists rake torque, bed level, rake height and bed pressure among vendor signals. Rakes typically lift to reduce torque, and very high torque can trip the rake drive.

A bogged thickener is a serious recovery job, so operators act early: increasing underflow, cutting feed or adjusting flocculant.
f: Why do thickener rakes lift on high torque?
How is overflow clarity measured?
What does a bogged thickener take to recover?

f.q: Can the standby underflow pump be run to help?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation tails thickener has duty/standby underflow pumps, total about 3,329 m3/h, with recycle to feed on start up or low flow. Duty/standby usually means one runs and one is spare.

Whether both can run together is not stated. In general, duty/standby pumps on separate lines can sometimes run together briefly, but if they share a line, running both may not add much flow and can upset the system.

Ask the area metallurgist or CRO whether running both is allowed on this thickener.
f: How is a duty/standby changeover done on slurry pumps?
Why recycle underflow to feed on start up?
Do the underflow pumps share a common discharge line?

What's a cascade loop, in mechanical ter.q: How would pump wear over time change the cascade's behaviour?
What's a cascade loop, in mechanical ter.a:
In the reference example the inner flow loop handles fast disturbances such as pump wear or head change.

As the impeller and throatbush wear, the pump delivers less flow at the same speed. The flow loop sees flow drop and increases VSD speed to compensate. The bed pressure master never notices, because the flow loop holds its setpoint.

So on PI you would see VSD speed slowly rising over weeks for the same flow. That is a useful condition monitoring signal: when speed approaches its maximum, the loop will soon run out of authority, and pump maintenance should be planned. It is like watching fan speed creep up as a filter clogs.

f.q: What wears in a slurry pump and how fast?
f.a:
General slurry pump knowledge. The main wear parts are the impeller, the throatbush or suction side liner, and the casing liner or volute. The gland area and shaft sleeve also wear.

Wear rate depends on slurry abrasiveness, particle size, density and pump speed. Cyclone feed duty, with coarse dense slurry, is one of the hardest. Wear parts may last from weeks to many months.

The reference does not give wear lives. The area maintenance planner will know the replacement intervals for each pump.
f: What is a throatbush and how is it adjusted?
Why does cyclone feed duty wear pumps so fast?
How are slurry pump rebuilds scheduled?

f.q: Can impeller adjustment restore pump performance?
f.a:
General knowledge. On many slurry pumps, the gap between impeller and throatbush can be adjusted by moving the bearing assembly. Closing that gap reduces internal recirculation and restores some lost performance.

This is often done as routine maintenance, extending wear part life. After adjustment you would expect VSD speed to drop for the same flow.

The reference does not cover pump maintenance. The area maintenance planner or pump fitter can tell you the procedure and frequency here.
f: How often are slurry pump impeller gaps adjusted?
Does impeller adjustment need the pump isolated?
Which slurry pumps on site have adjustable throatbushes?

f.q: How would I track pump wear using PI?
f.a:
Trend VSD speed against flow for the pump. As wear increases, speed rises for the same flow. Normalising for density helps, because denser slurry also needs more speed.

Useful tags, by naming convention, include the flow transmitter FIT plus area plus loop, density DT, and the VSD speed and power. The reference says slurry mass flow is measured by mag flowmeter plus nucleonic density.

Plotting speed over several weeks, ideally at similar flow and density, gives a clear wear trend.
f: How do I find a pump's VSD speed tag in PI?
What is a nucleonic density gauge?
Can PI calculate a ratio trend from two tags?

How is level normally controlled in a sl.q: Why trim pump speed for level instead of just running it flat out?
How is level normally controlled in a sl.a:
Running flat out would empty the hopper, then the pump would suck air, lose prime and cavitate. You would end up cycling it on and off, which is bad for slurry systems because lines settle when flow stops.

The reference says the level controller trims the pump VSD speed. Matching pump output to inflow keeps the hopper at a steady level, flow downstream steady, and the pump running smoothly.

It also saves power and wear. Slurry pump wear rises steeply with speed, so running only as fast as needed extends impeller life. It is like a variable speed fan holding air pressure rather than a fixed speed fan with a damper.

f.q: What happens when a slurry pump sucks air?
f.a:
General pump knowledge. Air entering the suction reduces the pump's ability to generate head and flow, and in severe cases the pump loses prime entirely. Flow becomes erratic, vibration and noise increase, and the pump can surge.

For slurry, losing flow means the discharge line velocity drops, solids settle, and the line can sand up.

That is why hopper level loops hold a minimum level, and why some hoppers have dual level control to add water when inflow drops, per the reference.
f: How do dual level controllers keep a hopper from emptying?
What is a vortex in a pump hopper?
How does air entrainment affect flowmeter readings?

f.q: Why does slurry pump wear rise so much with speed?
f.a:
General knowledge. Wear in slurry pumps is dominated by abrasive particles hitting and sliding over surfaces. Wear rate rises roughly with velocity to a power of about two to three, so a modest speed increase gives a large wear increase.

Running a pump faster than needed, and throttling the excess away, wastes energy and wears the pump. VSD level control avoids that.

It is one reason slurry pumps are usually sized to run at modest speeds with VSDs rather than at fixed high speed.
f: How are slurry pumps sized for their duty?
What liner materials resist slurry wear best?
Why are throttling valves avoided on slurry lines?

f.q: What alarms tell the CRO hopper level is out of range?
f.a:
The reference says hopper level alarms warn the CRO when level drifts outside range, and analogue alarms follow LL, L, H and HH.

So you would expect L and H alarms as early warnings, and LL and HH for more serious conditions. A LL may stop the pump to protect it from running dry. A HH may stop feed to prevent overflow.

The actual setpoints and actions for each hopper are not in the reference; they would be in the area functional specification or DCS configuration.
f: What does a hopper HH alarm usually trigger?
How are hopper level alarm setpoints chosen?
Which hoppers in milling have LL pump trips?

How is level normally controlled in a sl.q: What would you see on the OIS if the hopper level kept drifting high?
How is level normally controlled in a sl.a:
The level PV would rise above its SV, and the controller would push the pump VSD speed up. If the speed reached maximum and level still rose, the H alarm would come in, then possibly HH.

The reference says hopper level alarms warn the CRO when level drifts outside range.

Causes in general: inflow higher than the pump can handle, pump wear, a partly blocked discharge, high density raising head, or the loop not in Automatic. The CRO would check the pump speed, flow and density, and might reduce upstream feed.

f.q: How would you tell pump wear from a blockage as the cause?
f.a:
General fault finding. With wear, speed rises gradually over weeks for the same flow. With a blockage, discharge pressure rises and flow falls more suddenly, often with a jump in pump power or a change in sound.

Check the PI history. A slow creep in speed suggests wear. A step change suggests blockage or a valve problem.

A blockage is more urgent, because it can lead to deadheading. Ask the field operator to check valve positions and the dump valve too.
f: What does a discharge pressure trend show for a blockage?
Can a partly closed valve look like a blockage?
How are slurry line blockages cleared safely?

f.q: What can the CRO do to bring a high hopper level back?
f.a:
General options, as the reference does not give a procedure: check the loop is in Automatic and its output is not saturated; start the standby pump if the arrangement allows; reduce upstream feed, such as SAG feed rate, if the hopper is in the grinding circuit; or reduce water addition that is adding volume.

The right action depends on which hopper. For the cyclone feed hopper, the reference mentions Fast tuning to protect equipment in upsets.

Ask a senior CRO how they handle this on each hopper.
f: When is Fast tuning used on the cyclone feed hopper?
Does reducing SAG feed affect the cyclone feed hopper quickly?
Can water addition be cut to reduce hopper level?

f.q: What happens if a slurry hopper overflows?
f.a:
General. Slurry spills into the area bund or floor, usually draining to a sump. The sump pump then starts on high level and returns it to the process. The reference says sump pumps run in Auto on high level.

Large overflows can exceed sump capacity, spread across walkways, and create slip hazards. In cyanide areas, spills are an environmental and health concern.

The HH level alarm or interlock is there to prevent this. Cleanup is time consuming, so early action on level drift saves a lot of work.
f: Where does sump pump discharge return to?
How are spills in cyanide areas handled?
Why do reagent sumps have different rules?

How is level normally controlled in a sl.q: Why add a flowmeter into the cascade instead of controlling on level alone?
How is level normally controlled in a sl.a:
The reference says with a flowmeter, level can cascade to a flow controller that sets pump speed.

Without the flowmeter, the level loop drives speed directly. Any pump wear or head change makes flow vary at the same speed, and the level loop only corrects after level has moved, which is slow.

With the inner flow loop, those disturbances are corrected in seconds before they upset level. Downstream also sees a steadier flow, which matters when the hopper feeds something sensitive like the cyclones or flotation. It also lets the DCS enforce a minimum flow to keep line velocity above settling velocity.

f.q: What flowmeter is used on slurry lines and why?
f.a:
The reference says slurry mass flow is measured by mag flowmeter plus nucleonic density, with operator entered solids SG.

Magnetic flowmeters have no moving parts or obstructions in the pipe, so slurry does not wear or block them. They measure velocity by the voltage induced as conductive fluid moves through a magnetic field. Process water here is saline, so conductivity is high, which suits mag meters.

The density gauge then converts volumetric flow to solids mass flow.

f.q: Why does minimum flow matter for slurry lines?
f.a:
Below a certain velocity, solids drop out of suspension and settle in the pipe. The reference says dual level controllers keep line velocity above the settling velocity so slurry lines do not sand up.

If settling continues, the bed builds up, reducing pipe area and eventually blocking the line.

So slurry pumps are controlled not just to match inflow but to keep at least a minimum flow. When inflow is low, water is added to make up the volume. It is a key difference from water pumping, where low flow is just low flow.
f: How is settling velocity estimated for a slurry?

f.q: Is every hopper on site cascaded to a flow loop?
f.a:
The reference says level normally trims pump VSD speed, and with a flowmeter it can cascade to a flow controller. So it depends on whether the pump has a flowmeter.

The reference does not list which hoppers are cascaded. Larger or more critical pumps are more likely to have flowmeters; the big pumps, cyclone feed, tails thickener underflow and final tails, are mentioned with mag flowmeters for gland water and on their duties.

Check the P&ID for each hopper to see the instruments, or ask the process control engineer.

Some hoppers have 'dual level controller.q: Why does the low setpoint add water instead of just slowing the pump further?
Some hoppers have 'dual level controller.a:
Because the pump can only slow so far before line velocity drops below the settling velocity and the slurry line sands up.

The reference says loop B adds water at a lower setpoint when inflow drops below the pump's minimum flow, to keep line velocity above the settling velocity.

So below a certain inflow, the pump holds its minimum speed and water makes up the volume. Solids concentration drops, but the line keeps flowing. It is like a minimum flow recirculation on a boiler feed pump: you protect the pump and line by keeping flow up even when demand is low.

f.q: What is the downside of adding water to a slurry hopper?
f.a:
General reasoning. Adding water dilutes the slurry, which downstream may not want. For example, cyclone separation depends on feed density, and flotation residence time depends on volume.

It also uses process water, which here is saline bore water at SG 1.07 per the reference, and in the grinding circuit the extra water must eventually be removed, such as in the thickener.

So loop B is a protection measure for low inflow periods, not the normal operating mode. The higher loop A setpoint keeps water addition off during normal running.
f: Why does cyclone performance depend on feed density?
Where does process water come from on site?
How does added water reach the thickener?

f.q: What sets the minimum pump speed?
f.a:
The reference says loop B adds water when inflow drops below the pump's minimum flow, but does not give the minimum speed or flow values.

In general, the minimum is set by line velocity: the pump must deliver enough flow to keep velocity above the settling velocity for that slurry and pipe size. There may also be a minimum for the pump itself, to avoid running too far back on its curve.

The values would be in the DCS configuration and design calculations. Ask the process control engineer.

Why should a pump not run too far back on its curve?
Where is the minimum flow value set in the DCS?

f.q: Which hoppers on site have dual level control?
f.a:
The reference says some hoppers have dual level controllers but does not list which ones.

In general, they are found on hoppers where inflow can drop well below the pump's minimum flow, such as during start up, shutdown or low throughput periods, and where the downstream line is long or carries coarse slurry.

Check the P&IDs or the area functional specification, or ask the process control engineer which hoppers have them.
f: How do I spot dual level control on a P&ID?
Why do start up periods have low hopper inflow?

Some hoppers have 'dual level controller.q: What would happen if setpoint B was accidentally set above setpoint A?
Some hoppers have 'dual level controller.a:
The reference says setpoint A must be above setpoint B or the loops fight each other.

If B were above A, loop B would add water whenever level fell below B, while loop A would speed up the pump whenever level rose above A. Since A is lower, there is a band where both act at once: water is being added and the pump is speeding up to pull level down. They work against each other.

The result is a continuous water addition, wasted pumping, diluted slurry, and possibly an oscillating level. It is like a heating and cooling system with overlapping setpoints running at the same time.

f.q: How would two fighting loops look on a PI trend?
f.a:
General control behaviour. You would see water addition valve open and pump speed high at the same time, with level sitting between the two setpoints rather than near either.

Often the outputs oscillate: water valve opening and closing as level crosses B, pump speed rising and falling as level crosses A, with each correction triggering the other.

Density downstream would also be low and possibly swinging. Overlaying the two loop outputs on one PI trend makes it obvious.

What other loops on site could fight each other?
How is loop interaction prevented in design?

f.q: Can the DCS prevent setpoint B being set above setpoint A?
f.a:
The reference does not say. Some DCS configurations include setpoint limits or logic that stops an operator entering conflicting values.

In general, good practice is to put high and low limits on operator setpoints so they stay in sensible ranges. Whether this site has such a check for dual level loops would be in the DCS configuration.

Ask the control systems engineer. It is a reasonable improvement suggestion if it is not there.
f: What are setpoint limits on a PID block?
How do I suggest a DCS improvement on site?
Who approves DCS logic changes?

f.q: What is the cost of the loops fighting for a long time?
f.a:
General reasoning. Water is continuously added and then pumped away, wasting pumping energy. Slurry is diluted, which may upset downstream equipment, such as reducing cyclone efficiency or shortening flotation residence time.

Extra water in the circuit also loads the thickener and water system. The pump runs faster than necessary, increasing wear.

It is a quiet loss that might go unnoticed unless someone checks the trends.
f: How does extra water affect flotation residence time?

Some hoppers have 'dual level controller.q: How does settling velocity relate to the minimum pipe flow needed here?
Some hoppers have 'dual level controller.a:
Settling velocity, or more strictly the deposition velocity in a pipe, is the flow velocity below which solids start forming a bed in the bottom of the pipe. Above it, turbulence keeps them suspended.

The reference says the dual level controllers keep line velocity above settling velocity so slurry lines do not sand up. The minimum pipe flow is therefore the deposition velocity multiplied by the pipe area, plus a margin.

In general it rises with particle size, particle density and pipe diameter. Coarse, dense slurry in a large pipe needs a higher velocity. The reference does not give values for specific lines.

f.q: Why does pipe diameter affect deposition velocity?
f.a:
General slurry engineering. In larger pipes the turbulent eddies near the bottom are relatively weaker compared to the pipe size, so it takes a higher average velocity to keep particles lifted. Correlations such as Durand's show deposition velocity rising roughly with the square root of pipe diameter.

That is why designers do not simply oversize slurry lines. A larger pipe lowers friction loss but raises the minimum velocity needed, so at low throughput it is more likely to settle.

It is a balancing act much like sizing a duct for both air velocity and pressure drop.
f: What is Durand's equation for slurry flow?
Why are slurry lines often smaller than water lines?
How does slurry viscosity affect deposition?

f.q: Does the saline process water change settling behaviour?
f.a:
General knowledge, as the reference does not discuss it. Process water here has an SG of 1.07 per the reference, slightly higher than fresh water. A denser liquid gives a little more buoyancy, slightly reducing settling velocity.

Salinity can also affect how fine particles flocculate or disperse, which changes slurry viscosity. That effect is usually more important than the density change.

Overall the difference is modest, but metallurgists account for it in design calculations.

f.q: How would you notice a line starting to sand up?
f.a:
General signs: discharge pressure rises for the same flow, pump speed rises to hold flow, and flow may become unsteady. In the field, you may hear a change in sound or feel vibration in the pipe.

In PI, a gradual rise in pressure or speed with no change in density suggests a growing bed.

Catching it early lets the CRO raise flow or add water to flush it before it blocks. A fully blocked line is a major job to clear.

Why do slurry pump dump valves fail open.q: Why is failing open safer than failing closed for a dump valve?
Why do slurry pump dump valves fail open.a:
The reference says dump valves fail open on power loss to drain the line so slurry does not settle and bog the pump and pipe.

On a power failure the pump stops. If the dump valve stayed closed, the slurry in the line would sit still and settle, possibly blocking the line and burying the impeller. Restarting against a settled bed is hard and may need the line dismantled.

Failing open lets the line drain to a sump or launder while the solids are still suspended. It is like draining a water line in freezing weather: you remove the stuff that could cause damage when it stops moving.

f.q: Where does slurry go when a dump valve opens?
f.a:
The reference does not say where each dump valve discharges. In general, dump valves drain to a nearby sump, bund or launder, from where a sump pump returns the slurry to the process once flow resumes.

The reference says sump pumps start on high level in Auto, so a dump event would likely trigger the area sump pump.

Check the P&ID for the specific pump to see where its dump valve drains.
f: How large are area sumps compared to line volume?
What happens if a sump pump is down during a dump?
Do dump valves drain by gravity alone?

f.q: How does a valve fail open without power?
f.a:
General knowledge. Air actuated valves usually have a spring that drives them to a safe position when air or the control signal is lost. For fail open, the spring opens the valve and air pressure holds it closed.

On a power failure, the solenoid that supplies air to the actuator de-energises, the air vents and the spring opens the valve.

It is the same principle as a fail safe brake held off by air. The reference states the dump valves fail open on power loss but does not detail the actuator type.

Do dump valves have air receivers for backup?
How is a spring return actuator sized?

f.q: Are there slurry valves that fail closed on site?
f.a:
The reference does not list the failure positions of other valves. In general, the failure position is chosen for each valve based on what is safest. Feed valves to tanks often fail closed to prevent overflow; dump and drain valves often fail open to prevent settling.

The failure positions are shown on P&IDs, usually as FO for fail open, FC for fail closed or FL for fail last.

Check the P&ID for any valve you are working on.
f: What do FO, FC and FL mean on a P&ID?

How is valve failure position chosen during design?

Why do slurry pump dump valves fail open.q: What would you find in the line if the dump valve failed to open on trip?
Why do slurry pump dump valves fail open.a:
General reasoning. If the dump valve stayed closed after the pump stopped, slurry would stay in the line and start settling. Over minutes to hours the solids compact on the bottom of the pipe and around the pump impeller.

When you try to restart, the pump may not turn, or it may run against a partly blocked line with high pressure and low flow. You might find a hard settled bed that needs flushing or dismantling.

The reference says the valves have proximity switches so the DCS would see that the valve did not reach its open position, and the watchdog should raise a fail to open alarm.

f.q: How is a settled slurry line cleared?
f.a:
General practice. First try flushing with water from the pump end or a flush connection, often in short bursts to break up the bed. If that fails, the line may need to be opened at flanges and dug out, or rodded through.

It can be slow, dirty work, so it requires isolations and a permit, especially as pressure can be trapped behind a blockage.

The reference does not describe site procedures. Ask the area maintenance planner or supervisor.
f: Why can pressure be trapped behind a slurry blockage?
Are there flush water connections on slurry lines?
How long does it take to clear a blocked line?

f.q: What alarm would the DCS raise for a dump valve fail?
f.a:
The reference says actuated valves have a watchdog: if the limit switch does not confirm open or closed within a set time, it faults fail to open or fail to close and holds the sequence. It also flags both limit switches on or off together.

So a dump valve that does not open on trip should raise a fail to open alarm.

Whether this alarm has a special priority on dump valves is not stated. Check the alarm configuration with the control systems engineer.

Can the CRO retry a dump valve from the OIS?
How do proximity switches confirm valve position?

f.q: Why does a settled impeller make restarting hard?
f.a:
General pump knowledge. When solids settle around the impeller, they pack into the gaps between the impeller and casing. The motor then has to overcome that packed material to start turning, which can exceed starting torque or trip the motor on overload.

Even if it turns, the pump may not generate flow until the material is cleared.

That is why dump valves fail open, and why restart sequences include checks on pumps and dump valves, as mentioned in the reference.

Why do slurry pump dump valves fail open.q: How do the proximity switches confirm the valve position to the DCS?
Why do slurry pump dump valves fail open.a:
The reference says the duty/standby pump valves have proximity switches, interlocked so a pump cannot run against a closed valve except briefly on start or changeover.

In general, an inductive proximity switch senses a metal target on the valve stem or actuator when the valve reaches a position, without physical contact. Typically there is one switch for open and one for closed, each giving an on or off signal to the DCS.

The watchdog then checks the right switch comes on within a set time after a command. Both on or both off at once flags a fault, per the reference.

f.q: Why use proximity switches instead of mechanical limit switches?
f.a:
General knowledge. Proximity switches have no moving parts or contacts, so they handle dirt, vibration and water better than mechanical switches with levers and rollers. That suits slurry areas.

They are also sealed and less prone to being knocked out of adjustment, though they still need their targets set correctly.

The reference mentions both proximity switches on pump valves and limit switches more generally on actuated valves. Either way, the DCS logic is the same: open and closed position signals.

What causes a proximity switch to fail?
Do any valves have continuous position feedback?

f.q: What does both switches on at once indicate?
f.a:
The reference says the watchdog flags both limit switches on, or both off, together, which means a switch or valve fault.

A valve cannot be fully open and fully closed at the same time, so both on means at least one switch is wrong: misadjusted, faulty or wired incorrectly. Both off for a long time can mean the valve is stuck mid travel, or a switch has failed.

It is a simple plausibility check, like an engine management system rejecting a sensor reading that makes no physical sense.

f.q: Why allow a pump to run briefly against a closed valve?
f.a:
The reference says pumps are interlocked so they cannot run against a closed valve, except briefly on start or changeover.

On start, the pump may need to begin turning before the discharge valve fully opens, partly to avoid a surge and partly because valves take a few seconds to travel. On changeover, the outgoing and incoming pumps' valves are moving at the same time.

The brief window is controlled by timers. After that, the interlock trips the pump if the valve has not confirmed open.

What makes up a pump's gland water arran.q: Why use a Maric valve instead of just a fixed orifice for gland water?
What makes up a pump's gland water arran.a:
The reference says the Maric valve gives a set flow regardless of supply pressure.

A fixed orifice gives a flow that depends on the pressure drop across it. When the gland water header pressure swings, for example as other pumps start, the flow changes too. Too little lets slurry into the gland; too much wastes water and dilutes the process.

A constant flow valve has a flexible element that deforms with pressure, shrinking its opening as pressure rises, so flow stays roughly constant. It is like a pressure compensated flow control valve in a hydraulic circuit.

f.q: How does a Maric valve actually work inside?
f.a:
General knowledge. A Maric flow control valve uses a flexible rubber ring or washer in an orifice. As upstream pressure increases, the rubber deforms into the orifice, reducing the open area. The higher pressure through a smaller hole gives about the same flow.

Each valve is rated for a specific flow and a working pressure range. Outside that range, flow is no longer constant.

The reference only says the Maric valve gives a set flow regardless of supply pressure.

f.q: What happens if gland water pressure is below the slurry pressure?
f.a:
General pump knowledge. Gland water must be at a higher pressure than the pump casing at the gland, so it flows into the pump rather than slurry flowing out. If gland water pressure is too low, slurry enters the packing, wearing the shaft sleeve and packing.

The reference says the Raw Water Tank supplies LP and HP gland water pumps. The HP supply suits pumps with high discharge pressures.

So gland water flow alone is not the whole story; pressure must also be adequate.

f.q: Why is gland water a separate clean supply?
f.a:
Gland water must be clean, because any solids in it would wear the packing and shaft sleeve themselves. The glossary defines gland water as clean seal water to slurry pump glands.

The reference says the Raw Water Tank lower portion supplies LP and HP gland water pumps, fed from the Bore Water or Saline Dam 3 via booster pumps. Using raw water rather than process water avoids the suspended solids and reagents in process water.

It is like using filtered oil for a bearing: dirty lubricant defeats the purpose.

What makes up a pump's gland water arran.q: What would low gland water flow look like on the OIS or in a handover?
What makes up a pump's gland water arran.a:
On the OIS: a low flow alarm on the pump's gland water flow switch, or a falling value on the mag flowmeter for the big pumps. If the pump is stopped, the permissive is not met so it will not start. If running, it trips after a set delay, and first out shows low gland flow, per the reference.

In a handover, you might read 'cyclone feed pump tripped on low gland flow, Maric valve replaced' or 'gland flow permissive bypassed, switch faulty'.

Either way it points to the gland water arrangement: manual isolation valves, actuated valve, Maric valve, flow switch or meter, or the supply header.

f.q: What usually causes low gland water flow on a single pump?
f.a:
General causes: a blocked Maric valve from debris or scale, a closed or partly closed manual isolation valve, the actuated valve not opening, a blocked line, or a faulty flow switch giving a false reading.

If several pumps alarm at once, suspect the supply: the gland water pumps or the header.

The reference describes the arrangement but not failure modes. A field check of each component, starting with the Maric valve and isolation valves, usually finds it.

f.q: What if several pumps alarm low gland flow at once?
f.a:
That points to a common cause: the gland water supply. The reference says LP and HP gland water pumps draw from the lower portion of the Raw Water Tank.

Possible causes: a gland water pump trip, low Raw Water Tank level, a header valve closed, or a burst line.

This is serious because many slurry pumps could trip at once. The CRO would check the gland water pumps and tank level immediately. A field operator would check the header.

f.q: Does the gland water valve open before the pump starts?
f.a:
Yes. The reference says the actuated valve opens as part of the pump start sequence, and low gland flow blocks the start.

So in a normal start, the sequence opens the gland water valve, waits for the flow switch or meter to confirm flow, then starts the pump. That way slurry never contacts a dry gland.

When the pump stops, the valve may close to save water. The reference does not state the stop behaviour.

What makes up a pump's gland water arran.q: Why do only the big pumps get mag flowmeters instead of flow switches?
What makes up a pump's gland water arran.a:
The reference says the big pumps, cyclone feed, tails thickener underflow and final tails, get mag flowmeters instead of switches.

These pumps are the most critical. Cyclone feed stops the grinding circuit if it fails. Thickener underflow affects CIL4 feed. Final tails sends all plant tailings to the TSF. A trip on any of them is costly.

A flowmeter gives a continuous value, so you can see gland flow drifting down before it trips and fix it in a planned way. A switch only tells you when it has already crossed the limit. For smaller pumps the simpler switch is good enough. It is a standard cost versus criticality decision.

f.q: Why is the final tails pump so critical?
f.a:
The reference says the final tails tank receives CIL4 tails, acid wash waste and fine carbon waste, about 3,164 t/h at 54.5 percent solids, with tailings pumps duty/duty/duty/standby to the TSF.

Everything leaving the plant goes through those pumps. If they cannot run, the final tails tank fills and the plant must stop.

That is why there are three duty pumps and a standby, flowmeters and density and pressure on each line, and a second flowmeter near the deposition end for leak detection.
