General effects: temperature rises quickly, the impeller recirculates internally causing wear and vibration, seals and bearings suffer, and with slurry the abrasion is concentrated.

The reference says a minimum number of cyclones must be open before the cyclone feed pump starts, to prevent overpressuring the cluster and deadheading the pump. It notes this is the same principle as a minimum flow path on any centrifugal pump.

f.q: Why does the cyclone feed pump matter so much?
f.a:
Cyclone feed is the heart of the grinding circuit. The reference says the cluster takes about 13,233 m3/h at 62 percent solids, about 14,400 t/h of solids. If the pump stops, the cyclones stop classifying, the ball mill loses its feed, and the FIM mill transfer pumps are interlocked off because the primary cyclone feed pump is not running.

Its gland water is monitored by a mag flowmeter rather than a simple switch, reflecting how critical it is.

In mechanical terms it is the main circulating pump on which the whole circuit depends.
f: How many cyclone feed pumps are there?
What VSD controls the cyclone feed pump?
Why are FIM transfer pumps interlocked to cyclone feed?

f.q: What is a minimum flow path on a pump?
f.a:
General. A minimum flow path, or recirculation line, lets a centrifugal pump keep some flow even when the main discharge is closed, protecting it from deadheading. It is common on boiler feed pumps and clean water pumps.

For slurry pumps, recirculation lines are less common because low velocity in the line lets solids settle and block it. Instead, interlocks such as the minimum number of cyclones open serve the same purpose by making sure there is always an open discharge path.

The reference draws exactly this comparison.
f: Why are recirculation lines avoided on slurry pumps?
Do any slurry pumps on site have recycle lines?
How is minimum flow set for a slurry pump?

f.q: How quickly does a deadheaded slurry pump get damaged?
f.a:
The reference does not give a figure, and it depends on the pump size and duty.

In general, a large centrifugal pump at zero flow turns most of its input power into heat in a small trapped volume, so temperature climbs fast. Seal and gland damage can start within minutes, followed by bearing damage from the vibration of internal recirculation.

That is why interlocks allow only a brief window. The reference says pumps cannot run against closed valves except briefly on start or changeover, and the cyclone feed pump needs a minimum number of cyclones open before it starts.
f: What temperature damages pump seals?
What vibration does deadheading cause?
How is deadheading detected?

Why must a minimum number of cyclones be.q: What would the OIS show if the pump tried starting with too few cyclones?
Why must a minimum number of cyclones be.a:
The reference says a minimum number of cyclones open is required before the cyclone feed pump starts. This acts as a start permissive.

So the pump would not start, and the faceplate would show the permissive not met. If a sequence was running, it would pause and alert the operator.

The CRO would then open more cyclones before trying again. The exact number required is not in the reference.

f.q: How many cyclones must be open before start?
f.a:
The reference does not give the number, only that a minimum number must be open before the cyclone feed pump starts.

In general, it would be chosen so that the pump at its minimum start speed can deliver flow without exceeding the cyclone pressure limit or deadheading. It is a function of pump curve, pipe system and cyclone capacity, set during design and commissioning.

Ask the CRO or process control engineer for the configured value; it may be visible as a permissive on the pump faceplate.
f: How is the minimum cyclone number calculated?
Can the CRO open cyclones manually before start?
Does the expert system manage cyclone numbers?

f.q: Can cyclones close during running and deadhead the pump?
f.a:
The reference says cyclones close one at a time when feed pressure stays low for a set time. Closing a cyclone on low pressure raises pressure, so the control is self limiting: it should not keep closing cyclones while pressure is rising.

In general, a well configured system would also enforce a minimum number open while running, but the reference does not explicitly say this. A valve failing closed, or several faulting at once, would be the more likely risk.

Ask the process control engineer whether a running minimum is configured.
f: Is there a minimum open count while running?
What protects the pump if cyclone valves fail closed?
How is cyclone pressure limited at high flow?

f.q: What is the start sequence for the cyclone feed pump?
f.a:
The reference does not give the full sequence. It mentions that gland water opens as part of a pump start sequence, that a minimum number of cyclones must be open, and that pump valves are confirmed by proximity switches before running.

In general, the sequence would open gland water and confirm flow, open the required cyclones, confirm suction and discharge valves, close the dump valve, then start the pump at low speed and ramp up while watching pressure and flow.

The exact steps are in the milling area control documentation.
f: Why start a slurry pump at low speed?
How long does the cyclone feed pump take to ramp up?
What confirms the pump has started successfully?

Why must a minimum number of cyclones be.q: Is there a minimum flow recycle line as a backup to this interlock?
Why must a minimum number of cyclones be.a:
The reference does not mention a minimum flow recycle line on the cyclone feed pump.

In general, slurry pumps often do not have recycle lines because low velocity recycle lines can settle and block. Protection usually relies on interlocks, minimum cyclones open, and the pump VSD.

Check the P&ID for the cyclone feed pump, or ask the process control engineer.

f.q: Why are recycle lines risky on slurry pumps?
f.a:
General. A recycle line carries flow only some of the time. When it is idle or flowing slowly, solids settle and can block it, so when you actually need it, it may not work. It also needs a valve in abrasive service, which wears.

Some thickener underflow pumps do recycle to the thickener feed on start up or low flow, per the reference, but those are designed for it with suitable velocities and flushing.

For the cyclone feed pump, interlocks are used instead.
f: How do thickener underflow recycle lines work?
How are recycle lines kept clear?
Which pumps on site have recycle lines?

f.q: What other protection does the cyclone feed pump have?
f.a:
The reference mentions gland water with a mag flowmeter, a minimum number of cyclones open before start, and the general pump interlocks that stop a pump running against closed valves.

In general, a pump this size would also have motor protection relays, VSD protection functions such as overcurrent and overtemperature, and possibly bearing temperature or vibration monitoring. The reference also says VSD E-stops act through Safe Torque Off.

The full list would be on the pump P&ID and in the area functional specification.
f: Does the cyclone feed pump have vibration monitoring?
What VSD protections apply to large pumps?
How does motor protection relay work on big pumps?

f.q: Where would I find the cyclone feed pump P&ID?
f.a:
The reference does not say where P&IDs are kept. In general, they are held in the project or site document control system, filed by area.

The cyclone cluster and its feed pump are in the milling area, F13 in the numbering spec, so the P&ID would be in the F13 drawing set. New Growth Project equipment numbers start at 401, which helps when searching.

Ask the document controller or your supervisor for access if you do not have it yet.
f: How do I access the document control system?
What is the F13 area?
How do I read a pump P&ID?

What sets the SAG feed rate?.q: Why use mill weight as well as tonnage in the feed rate control?
What sets the SAG feed rate?.a:
The reference says reclaim feeders are controlled to a tonnage setpoint or mill weight through the SAG feed weightometer, normally set by the mill expert system.

Tonnage control sets how much ore goes in. But the mill's grinding performance depends on its load, which changes with ore hardness and size. Soft ore grinds fast, so load drops; hard ore builds up.

Mill weight control adjusts feed to hold the load at an optimum, avoiding overload, which wastes power and can damage the mill, or underload, which lets balls hit liners directly.

It is like controlling a furnace by temperature rather than fuel flow: the target is the condition inside, not the input.

f.q: How is SAG mill weight measured?
f.a:
The reference mentions mill weight as a control variable but not how it is measured.

In general, SAG mill weight is measured either by load cells under the mill bearing pedestals, or inferred from the hydrostatic bearing oil pressure, which rises as the charge gets heavier. Both give total weight, including the shell, liners, balls, ore and water, so the useful information is the change from a known baseline.

Ask the mill maintenance planner or process control engineer which method is used here.
f: What is bearing oil pressure on a SAG?
How accurate is SAG mill weight measurement?
Does mill weight include the ball charge?

f.q: What happens if a SAG is overloaded?
f.a:
General. An overloaded SAG has too much charge, so it no longer cascades and tumbles properly. Power draw can actually fall as the charge centre of gravity moves, grinding efficiency drops, and the discharge grates and pulp lifters can choke with slurry. In severe cases the mill locks up and must be stopped.

The expert system uses load, speed, power and noise to avoid getting there, cutting feed when weight climbs.

It is like a ball mill version of flooding a distillation column: more feed reduces output.
f: How does SAG noise indicate load?
What is a locked charge in a SAG?
How is an overloaded SAG recovered?

f.q: What is the SAG feed weightometer?
f.a:
The reference says the SAG feed weightometer measures tonnage on the conveyor to the SAG. Weightometers have calibration chains, totals per 12 hour shift and day from 5:00 am, and convert wet to dry tonnes using a moisture input.

General: a weightometer uses load cells under idlers to weigh the belt and a speed sensor to calculate tonnes per hour.
f: How is a weightometer calibrated?
What is the moisture input used for?
Why do totals reset at 5:00 am?

What sets the SAG feed rate?.q: What would the OIS show if the deadband was too small for the lag?
What sets the SAG feed rate?.a:
The reference says a deadband allows for the lag between feeder speed change and the weightometer seeing it.

If the deadband were too small, the controller would keep changing feeder speed before the previous change reached the weightometer. On the trend, feeder speed and tonnage would oscillate, overshooting above and below setpoint.

It is a classic dead time problem, like adjusting a shower temperature before the hot water reaches you: you keep overcorrecting. General control knowledge applied to the reference's description.

f.q: What is dead time in a control loop?
f.a:
General. Dead time is the delay between a control action and when its effect is first seen by the measurement. Here, ore leaving the reclaim feeder takes time to travel along the conveyor to the weightometer.

Dead time makes control harder, because the controller cannot see the effect of its actions straight away. Controllers must be tuned slower, or use special techniques.
f: How do you measure dead time on a conveyor?
What is a Smith predictor?
How does dead time limit control speed?

f.q: How would you tune a loop with long dead time?
f.a:
General control knowledge. Use gentler tuning, with lower gain and a longer integral time, so the controller waits for its actions to show up before correcting again. A deadband, as the reference mentions for SAG feed, stops the controller chasing small errors.

Advanced methods such as model predictive control or a Smith predictor explicitly model the delay, so the controller can act on what it expects to happen.

The expert system may do some of this, but the reference does not say.
f: What is model predictive control?
How does the expert system handle dead time?
What gain is used for feeder control?

f.q: Can a large deadband cause problems?
f.a:
General. A large deadband means the controller ignores errors up to that size, so tonnage can sit well away from setpoint before any correction is made. Over a shift, that can add up to a noticeable shortfall or overshoot against the daily target.

It can also make control feel sluggish to operators, who may then intervene by hand.

So the deadband is a compromise: large enough to cover the conveyor lag between the reclaim feeders and the weightometer, small enough to hold tonnage close.
f: How is deadband size chosen?
Does deadband affect daily tonnage targets?
Who adjusts feeder deadband settings?

What sets the SAG feed rate?.q: How do the two reclaim feeders coordinate when run in ratio mode?
What sets the SAG feed rate?.a:
The reference says feeders can be run as a ratio, or one fixed and one trimming.

In ratio mode, both feeders get speed setpoints in a fixed proportion, such as 50:50 or 60:40, from the tonnage controller. When the controller asks for more ore, both speed up together.

In fixed and trim mode, one feeder runs at a fixed speed and the other adjusts to hold tonnage. That is useful if one feeder has a problem or one side of the stockpile is low.

The ratio lets operators draw evenly from the stockpile or favour one side.

f.q: Why draw evenly from the stockpile?
f.a:
General. Drawing evenly from both feeders helps keep the stockpile drawdown symmetrical, avoiding rat holing on one side where a narrow hole forms above one feeder and the rest of the live ore hangs up.

It also blends ore from different parts of the pile, since stockpiles segregate with coarse rocks rolling to the edges and fines staying in the centre.

The reference gives the new stockpile live capacity as about 12,035 m3 at a 60 degree drawdown, and two reclaim apron feeders.
f: What is rat holing?
How does stockpile segregation affect SAG feed?
Can feeder ratio change ore blend?

f.q: When would one feeder be fixed and one trimming?
f.a:
The reference mentions this option but not when it is used, so this is general reasoning.

Typical reasons: one feeder has a mechanical limitation or is due for maintenance, one side of the stockpile is low or hung up, or operators want to pull more from one side to blend coarse and fine ore. The fixed feeder sets a base rate and the trimming feeder does the control work.

Ask a CRO which mode they normally use and why.
f: How do operators decide the feeder mode?
What happens if one feeder trips?
Can a single feeder supply full tonnage?

f.q: Can one reclaim feeder supply the SAG alone?
f.a:
The reference says each reclaim apron feeder is designed for 2,017 t/h, which is 110 percent of nominal, while new SAG feed is 1,833 t/h nominal.

So on paper one feeder can supply nominal feed, though it would run near the top of its range and draw unevenly from one side of the stockpile.

These are design values. Whether operations actually run on one feeder for long periods is an operating choice; ask a CRO.
f: What is the new SAG nominal feed rate?
How fast can a reclaim feeder run?
What happens to the stockpile if one feeder runs alone?

What does the milling expert system use.q: Why combine noise monitoring with camera size analysis for the SAG?
What does the milling expert system use.a:
They measure different things. The reference says the expert system uses the SAG feed camera size analyser, the SAG noise monitor, mill load, speed and power.

The camera tells you what is going in: the size distribution of feed ore. Coarse feed needs more grinding and acts differently in the mill.

The noise monitor tells you what is happening inside: whether balls are hitting liners directly, which happens when the mill is underloaded or speed is too high. That is a sign of liner damage risk.

Together they give feed forward and feedback information, like an engine management system using both intake air sensors and knock sensors.

f.q: Why does SAG noise indicate liner damage risk?
f.a:
General. When the mill is properly loaded, balls thrown up by the lifters land on the toe of the charge, which cushions them. When the mill is underloaded or turning too fast, balls fly further and strike the bare liners directly, making a loud ringing impact noise.

Those impacts crack liners and break balls. The noise monitor in the reference detects this, and the expert system responds by adding feed or reducing speed.

It is a bit like a knock sensor on an engine.
f: How does SAG speed affect ball trajectory?
How is SAG noise measured?
What does a liner impact sound like?

f.q: How does feed size affect SAG throughput?
f.a:
General. A SAG mill uses large rocks in its own feed as grinding media alongside steel balls. Too fine a feed reduces that autogenous grinding. Too much mid size rock, the so called critical size, is too small to break other rock and too big to be broken quickly, so it builds up in the mill and limits throughput.

The pebble crushing circuit handles critical size material. The reference gives crusher product P80 130 mm and SAG pebble ports of 75 mm.
f: What is critical size material in a SAG?
How do pebble crushers help SAG throughput?
Why does crusher product size matter to the SAG?

f.q: What camera size analyser is used?
f.a:
The reference says there is a SAG feed camera size analyser, and that particle size analysers are vendor packages with their own PLC reporting to the DCS. It does not name the make or model.

In general, these systems use cameras over the conveyor with lighting and image analysis software that estimates the size distribution of rocks on the belt surface.

Ask the process control engineer for the details of the system installed here.
f: How does a camera size analyser work?
Where is the camera mounted?
How accurate are camera size analysers?

What does the milling expert system use.q: What would a handover mean by 'expert system dropped out, running manual'?
What does the milling expert system use.a:
It means the milling expert system stopped controlling the circuit, and the CRO is setting feed rate, water and other targets by hand.

The reference says the expert system controls feed rate, water addition, mill weight, cyclone feed flow and pressure, solids concentration, SAG speed and grind size. Without it, the CRO has to manage all of those using normal loop controls.

Common reasons for dropping out, in general: a key input failing, such as the noise monitor or camera, a communications fault, or the system detecting conditions outside its operating range. Ask why, and whether a fault has been raised.

f.q: Does throughput drop when the expert system is off?
f.a:
Often, in general. Expert systems are designed to push the mill closer to its limits safely, adjusting feed, water and speed every few seconds based on many inputs. Without one, operators naturally run more conservatively to avoid overloading the mill.

The reference does not quantify the benefit here. Metallurgists and process control engineers usually track expert system uptime and throughput with and without it.

Ask them for the site's figures.
f: How is expert system uptime tracked?
What is the benefit of an expert system?
Who supports the expert system on site?

f.q: What inputs failing would cause dropout?
f.a:
The reference lists the expert system inputs as the SAG feed camera size analyser, SAG noise monitor, mill load, speed, power and other measured variables. It does not describe the dropout logic.

In general, expert systems check that key inputs are healthy and within plausible ranges. If a critical one, such as mill weight or power, fails or goes bad quality, the system may drop to a safe state and hand control back to the operator.

Ask the process control engineer which inputs are critical.
f: How does the expert system validate inputs?
Can the expert system run with some inputs failed?
How is an input fault alarmed?

f.q: How does the CRO control the mill in manual?
f.a:
General. The CRO sets the feed tonnage or mill weight setpoint on the reclaim feeder controller, water addition setpoints, SAG speed within its 60 to 83 percent range per the reference, and other loop targets directly, while watching mill power, weight and noise.

The underlying DCS loops are the same as in expert mode; only the supervisor setting their targets changes, from software to a person.

It is busier and usually more conservative, which is why getting the expert system back is a priority.
f: What targets does the CRO watch most closely?
How often does the CRO adjust feed in manual?
What is the SAG speed range?

What does the milling expert system use.q: How does the expert system's output actually reach the feeder VSDs?
What does the milling expert system use.a:
The reference says reclaim feeder speeds are controlled to a tonnage setpoint through the SAG feed weightometer, normally set by the mill expert system.

So the expert system sits on top of the normal DCS loops. It writes a tonnage or mill weight setpoint to the feed rate controller. That controller, in turn, adjusts the reclaim feeder VSD speeds.

It is a supervisory layer, like a building management system setting thermostat setpoints. If it drops out, the loops keep running with the last setpoint and the CRO takes over.

f.q: Is the expert system part of the DCS?
f.a:
The reference does not say whether it runs inside the DCS or on a separate computer.

In general, mill expert systems often run on separate servers and talk to the DCS over a network link, reading measurements and writing setpoints. That keeps the complex optimisation away from the core control system.

Ask the process control engineer which arrangement is used here.
f: What platform does the expert system run on?
How does it communicate with the DCS?
Who maintains the expert system?

f.q: What happens to setpoints if the expert system fails?
f.a:
General. In most designs, the DCS loops hold the last setpoint written by the expert system, or revert to an operator setpoint, and an alarm tells the CRO the expert system is no longer in control. The plant carries on, but nobody is optimising it.

The reference says feed rate is normally set by the expert system but does not give the failure behaviour.

Ask the process control engineer how the hand back is configured here.
f: How does the CRO know the expert system has failed?
Can setpoints jump when the expert system drops out?
Is there an alarm for expert system failure?

f.q: Does the expert system control other areas?
f.a:
The reference describes a milling expert system and a separate flotation expert system. The flotation system uses OSA data, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to adjust cell level (froth depth), air and reagents.

So each area has its own supervisory layer on top of its DCS loops, tuned for that process. The milling one handles feed rate, water, mill weight, cyclone flow and pressure, solids concentration, SAG speed and grind size.

The reference does not mention expert control in the leach circuits.
f: How does the flotation expert system work?
What is an OSA?
What are launder velocity cameras?

How are grinding balls added?.q: Why hold mill weight instead of just dosing balls on a timer?
How are grinding balls added?.a:
The reference says balls are added automatically, either to a kg/t setpoint or to hold a preset mill weight.

A timer adds the same balls regardless of what the mill is doing. But ball consumption depends on throughput, ore hardness and abrasiveness. Feed more tonnes or harder ore and balls wear faster; a timer would let the ball charge shrink. Feed less and a timer would overcharge the mill.

Dosing to kg/t ties addition to tonnes milled, so it tracks throughput. Dosing to mill weight goes a step further and targets the condition inside the mill. It is like topping up oil by level rather than by calendar: you add what the machine actually needs.

f.q: What does kg/t mean for ball addition?
f.a:
kg/t is kilograms of grinding balls added per tonne of ore milled. If the setpoint is a given kg/t and the mill processes more tonnes, the system adds proportionally more balls.

The reference says ball addition is automatic to a kg/t setpoint or mill weight, but it does not give the kg/t value. Grinding media for the SAG are 125 mm balls, per the reference.

In general, kg/t is set from measured ball wear rates, which metallurgists track by comparing balls added with tonnes milled over a month or more.
f: How do metallurgists measure ball consumption?
What ball size goes into the ball mill?
Why does harder ore wear balls faster?

f.q: How are balls physically added to the mill?
f.a:
The reference says ball addition is automatic but does not describe the equipment.

In general, balls are stored in a bunker or kibble and fed by a ball feeder, often a rotating or vibrating device that releases a counted number of balls onto the mill feed conveyor or into the feed chute. A counter or weigh system tells the DCS how many have been added.

Ask the mill maintenance planner or area operator to show you the ball addition system on site.
f: How are ball bunkers refilled on site?
Can ball addition be done manually if the feeder fails?
How does the DCS count balls added?

f.q: Why does mill weight include balls and ore together?
f.a:
Mill weight, however measured, is the total mass in the mill: shell, liners, balls, ore and water. The reference says ball addition can be controlled to hold a preset mill weight.

The catch, in general, is that weight alone cannot tell you how much is balls and how much is ore. A heavy mill could have too many balls or too much ore. That is why metallurgists also do periodic ball charge measurements during shutdowns, and why the expert system combines weight with power, noise and speed.

The reference gives SAG ball charge 10.5 percent v/v and total load 27 percent.
f: How is the ball charge measured during a shutdown?
What does ball charge percent by volume mean?
How do power and weight together show charge make up?

How are grinding balls added?.q: What would you see on the OIS if ball addition fell behind the kg/t setpoint?
How are grinding balls added?.a:
The reference says ball addition is automatic to a kg/t setpoint, but does not describe the display.

In general you would expect the ball addition totaliser to show less than the target for the tonnes milled, perhaps with a deviation alarm. More slowly, the effects show in the mill itself: the ball charge falls, so power draw drops at the same mill weight, and grinding performance worsens.

Common causes would be an empty ball bunker, a jammed ball feeder, or a counting fault. Ask a CRO which screen shows ball addition and whether a deviation alarm exists.

f.q: Why does SAG power drop when the ball charge falls?
f.a:
General mill knowledge. Steel balls are much denser than ore, so they make up a large share of the charge mass. Mill power depends on the mass of the charge and how it is lifted and tumbles.

As balls wear away and are not replaced, the charge gets lighter and lower in density, so the motor draws less power at the same speed. Less power means less grinding.

The reference gives the new SAG at 20 MW installed with pinion duty about 16.8 MW, and ball charge 10.5 percent v/v.
f: What is pinion power on a mill?
How quickly does a SAG ball charge wear down?
Why does SAG power limit throughput?

f.q: What happens if the ball bunker runs empty?
f.a:
General. Ball addition stops, but nothing happens immediately. The mill keeps grinding with its existing charge, which wears down over hours to days. Throughput or grind quality slowly worsens.

The reference does not describe bunker level monitoring. Many sites track bunker inventory and order balls by delivery schedule.

Ask the area operator how the ball bunker is monitored and refilled.
f: Who orders grinding balls for the site?
How many balls are in a full bunker?
Is ball bunker level shown on the OIS?

f.q: Can too many balls be a problem?
f.a:
Yes, in general. Overcharging the SAG with balls increases liner wear, raises the risk of balls hitting liners directly, increases power draw, and wastes steel. Above certain limits it can overload the motor or the mill structure.

The reference gives the new SAG ball charge as 10.5 percent v/v, total load 27 percent, and structural limits of 18 percent balls and 35 percent total. The ball mill normally runs at 28.5 percent ball charge, maximum 31, structural 38.

Those structural limits are design values that must not be exceeded.
f: Why is there a structural limit on ball charge?
What happens if total load exceeds 35 percent?
How is overcharging detected?

How are grinding balls added?.q: Why does the ball mill run at a fixed speed while the SAG speed varies?
How are grinding balls added?.a:
The reference says the ball mill normally runs at a fixed speed of about 75 percent of critical, with a 60 to 78 percent range, while the SAG range is 60 to 83 percent.

The SAG feed changes constantly in size and hardness, so varying speed is a key tool to manage its load and protect liners. Faster speed lifts the charge higher for more impact breakage; slower speed reduces impacts when the mill is light.

The ball mill grinds already reduced material, cyclone underflow, which is much more consistent. A fixed speed suits it, and its variable range is mainly for optimisation or liner wear changes. It is like a variable speed primary pump and fixed speed booster.

f.q: What is critical speed for a mill?
f.a:
General. Critical speed is the rotational speed at which the charge would centrifuge, sticking to the shell instead of tumbling. It depends on mill diameter: larger mills have lower critical speeds in rpm.

Mills run at a percentage of critical, here 60 to 83 percent for the SAG and about 75 percent for the ball mill, per the reference. Below that the charge cascades and tumbles to grind ore.

The glossary defines %Cs as percent of mill critical speed.
f: How is critical speed calculated?
Why does mill diameter affect critical speed?
What happens if a mill runs near 100 percent critical?

f.q: How does SAG speed affect liner wear?
f.a:
General. At higher speeds, the charge is lifted higher and balls can be thrown onto bare liners instead of landing on the charge toe, causing impact damage. At lower speeds, the charge cascades more gently, reducing impacts but also reducing grinding power.

The expert system uses the SAG noise monitor to detect liner impacts and adjust speed, per the reference. The SAG has steel liners.

Operators balance throughput against liner life.
f: What liner material does the ball mill use?
How often are SAG liners replaced?
How does liner wear change the charge trajectory?

f.q: Why does the ball mill have a speed range if it runs fixed?
f.a:
The reference gives the ball mill a 60 to 78 percent critical speed range, normally fixed at about 75 percent.

The range is useful, in general, because as liners wear, the effective lifting changes, and speed can compensate. It also allows reduced speed for inching or start up, and optimisation trials.

The ball mill is 20 MW with Poly-Met liners per the reference.
f: What are Poly-Met liners?
How does inching work on a ball mill?
Why might metallurgists trial a different ball mill speed?

Why does the cyclone feed hopper have 'F.q: Why can't one tuning setting satisfy both stability and protection?
Why does the cyclone feed hopper have 'F.a:
Because the two goals pull in opposite directions. The reference says Slow (detuned) tuning keeps flotation feed flow smooth in normal running, while Fast tuning protects equipment in upsets by quickly restoring minimum hopper level.

Slow tuning lets the cyclone feed hopper level float, using its volume as a buffer, so the pump flow to the cyclones and on to flotation stays steady. Fast tuning moves the pump hard to correct level, which protects the pump from running dry but sends flow swings downstream.

It is the classic surge tank trade off: use the tank as a buffer, or hold level tight. A single tuning would be either too sluggish to protect equipment or too aggressive for flotation.

f.q: What is surge tank or averaging level control?
f.a:
General control knowledge. In averaging level control, the level controller is deliberately tuned slowly so the level rises and falls within a wide band, absorbing inflow changes while keeping outflow steady. The tank acts as a buffer, like a hydraulic accumulator smoothing pump pulses.

Tight level control, by contrast, holds level exactly by passing every inflow change straight to the outflow.

The Slow tuning on the cyclone feed hopper, per the reference, is averaging control for the sake of flotation feed stability.
f: How wide can the hopper level band be in Slow tuning?
What is the cyclone feed hopper volume?
Which other hoppers use averaging level control?

f.q: Why does flotation care about steady feed flow?
f.a:
General flotation knowledge with reference values. Flotation performance depends on residence time, cell level and froth depth, and reagent dosing ratios. Feed surges change all three: residence time drops, levels swing and reagent ratios go off target.

The reference gives rougher residence of 15.1 min and scavenger 21.4 min, with flotation feed 3,146 t/h at 34.4 percent solids. Level controls on cells with dart valves would have to work hard to absorb surges.

So smooth feed means better recovery.
f: How does a feed surge affect froth depth?
How are reagents dosed against feed flow?
What is the rougher residence time at design?

f.q: What is detuning a controller?
f.a:
General. Detuning means making a controller less aggressive: lower gain, longer integral time, so it responds more slowly to errors.

The reference calls Slow tuning detuned. It lets the process variable drift further before correcting, which smooths the output.

It is like softening a car's suspension: more body movement, but a smoother ride for the passengers, which here is flotation.
f: What PID parameters change in detuning?
How does detuning affect overshoot?
Can detuning cause level alarms?

Why does the cyclone feed hopper have 'F.q: What would you see downstream if Fast tuning stayed on during normal running?
Why does the cyclone feed hopper have 'F.a:
General reasoning from the reference's description. Fast tuning moves the cyclone feed pump hard to hold hopper level, so every inflow change is passed downstream.

You would see cyclone feed flow and pressure swinging more, cyclones opening and closing more often, overflow density and flow to flotation varying, and flotation cell levels working harder to compensate. Grind size could vary too.

The reference says Slow keeps flotation feed flow smooth in normal running, so staying in Fast is likely to reduce flotation performance. It is like driving with the brake and accelerator always at extremes.

f.q: How would flotation cell levels respond to feed swings?
f.a:
General. Each cell's level controller, using dart valves per the reference, opens or closes to hold level. A feed surge raises level, so the darts open; a drop lowers level, so they close.

If swings are frequent, the level controllers chase them, and froth depth varies. That affects concentrate grade and recovery.

The flotation expert system also adjusts level and air, but it works best with steady feed.
f: How do dart valves control cell level?
What happens to grade when froth depth changes?
How fast do cell level loops respond?

f.q: How does cyclone cycling affect grind?
f.a:
General cyclone behaviour. Each time a cyclone opens or closes, the same feed flow is spread over one more or one fewer unit, so pressure in all the others steps down or up. That briefly changes the cut size, sending a pulse of coarser or finer material to flotation and a matching change in circulating load back to the ball mill.

The reference says cyclones open when feed pressure stays high for a set time and close when it stays low. Bigger flow swings from Fast tuning mean more frequent cycling, more grind variation and more wear on the knife gate valves.
f: How often do cyclones cycle in normal running?
Does cyclone cycling wear the knife gates?
How is grind size measured online?

f.q: Could you spot Fast tuning left on in PI?
f.a:
Yes, in general. Trend the cyclone feed hopper level and the pump speed. In Slow, level moves through a wider band while speed is smooth. In Fast, level is held tight while speed moves a lot.

Also trend flotation feed flow: more variation suggests Fast. If the tuning mode is historised as a tag, it would show directly.

Ask the process control engineer if the mode is in PI.
f: Is the tuning mode logged as a PI tag?
How do I compare flow variability on two trends?
What is the cyclone feed hopper level tag?

Why does the cyclone feed hopper have 'F.q: Who decides when to switch the hopper between Fast and Slow tuning?
Why does the cyclone feed hopper have 'F.a:
The reference describes Fast and Slow tuning but does not say who switches or whether it is automatic.

In general, some systems switch automatically based on level: if level drops below a threshold, Fast kicks in to restore minimum level; once recovered, it returns to Slow. Others leave it to the CRO.

The phrase quickly restoring minimum hopper level suggests an automatic trigger, but this is not confirmed. Ask the process control engineer or a senior CRO.

f.q: What triggers an upset that needs Fast tuning?
f.a:
General. Upsets that drop the cyclone feed hopper level include a sudden loss of SAG or ball mill discharge, a mill trip, a feed interruption, or a surge in pump flow. The FIM mill transfer pumps also feed this hopper per the reference, so their trip would drop inflow.

Rising level upsets come from a cyclone feed pump problem or a surge from the mills.

Fast tuning restores level to protect the pump.
f: What happens to the hopper if the FIM SAG trips?
How quickly does the cyclone feed hopper empty?
What protects the pump if level gets too low?

f.q: Why protect minimum hopper level so strongly?
f.a:
General. If the hopper runs too low, the cyclone feed pump can suck air, cavitate, lose prime and surge, damaging the pump and upsetting the whole circuit. It could also trip on low level, stopping the cyclones and ball mill feed.

The cyclone feed pump is one of the most critical in the plant, so protecting it is a priority.

The reference says Fast tuning quickly restores minimum level.
f: What is the hopper low level trip setpoint?
How does a vortex form in a pump hopper?
What happens to cyclones if the feed pump trips?

f.q: Is Fast and Slow tuning used on other hoppers?
f.a:
The reference mentions Fast and Slow tuning only for the cyclone feed hopper. Elsewhere it describes dual level control on some hoppers, which is a different technique: loop A trims pump speed at a higher setpoint and loop B adds water at a lower setpoint to keep line velocity up.

Other hoppers may well use averaging level control ideas, since it is a common technique wherever a downstream process values steady flow, but the reference does not say.

Ask the process control engineer which loops have selectable tuning sets.
f: What is dual level control on a hopper?
Which hoppers have dual level control?
How do Fast and Slow tuning differ from dual control?

What makes the pebble bin bypass gate op.q: Why trip the bypass on metal detection rather than just stopping the feeders?
What makes the pebble bin bypass gate op.a:
The reference says the pebble bin bypass gate opens on metal detected in the pebble crusher feed.

Tramp metal, such as broken grinding balls, liner bolts or drill steel, would damage a cone crusher. Stopping the feeders would protect the crusher, but pebbles would still keep coming from the SAG discharge screen, about 375 t/h oversize per the reference. With nowhere to go, the conveyor and bins would fill and the SAG would have to stop.

Opening the bypass sends the metal laden pebbles straight back to the SAG, protecting the crusher while keeping the mill running. It is like a relief valve that diverts flow instead of shutting the system down.

f.q: Where does tramp metal in pebbles come from?
f.a:
General. The SAG mill contains steel balls and steel liners, per the reference. Worn balls break into fragments small enough to pass the pebble ports, which are 75 mm. Liner bolts, broken lifter pieces and occasionally drill bits or other mining steel also appear.

These are the most common source of tramp metal in pebble circuits, and they can seriously damage cone crushers.

Magnets and metal detectors are used to remove or divert them.
f: Why do grinding balls break in a SAG?
Are there magnets on the pebble conveyor?
What damage does tramp metal do to a cone crusher?

f.q: What damage would tramp metal do to the pebble crusher?
f.a:
General. A cone crusher with a tight CSS, here 7 mm per the reference, cannot crush steel. Metal jams between the mantle and bowl liner, causing huge force spikes. That can damage liners, the main shaft, bearings and the hydraulic system, or trip the crusher on overpressure.

Most cone crushers have hydraulic tramp release, but repeated events still cause wear and damage.

The pebble crushers are 2 XL7 SH-HD cones, 375 kW each.
f: What is hydraulic tramp release on a cone crusher?
How often do pebble crusher liners need changing?
What is CSS and why is it so tight here?

f.q: How long does the bypass stay open after metal detection?
f.a:
The reference says the bypass opens on metal detection, but not how long it stays open.

In general, the bypass stays open for a set time to let the detected metal pass, then closes and normal feed resumes. The time would cover the conveyor travel from the detector to past the diverter.

Ask the CRO or process control engineer for the setting.
f: Where is the metal detector mounted?
Can the bypass be closed manually?
How often does metal trigger the bypass?

What makes the pebble bin bypass gate op.q: What would a handover mean by 'pebbles on bypass since last shift'?
What makes the pebble bin bypass gate op.a:
It means the pebble bypass gate has been open for a long time, sending SAG pebbles straight back to the SAG instead of through the pebble crushers.

Per the reference, the bypass opens on metal detection, bin High with both feeders stopped, or bin High-High. If it has stayed open for a shift, something is likely wrong: both pebble crushers may be down, the feeders stopped, the bin stuck at High-High, or the metal detector giving repeated triggers.

The effect is that pebbles, critical size rock, build up in the SAG, reducing throughput. Ask why and when it will be fixed.

f.q: What happens to SAG throughput when pebbles bypass?
f.a:
General. Pebbles are critical size material, too small to act as grinding media, too large to be broken quickly. When they return uncrushed, they build up in the SAG, taking up space and reducing throughput.

The reference says pebbles are 16.6 to 28 percent of new feed. Losing pebble crushing is a significant hit to SAG capacity.

The expert system or CRO may need to reduce feed rate.
f: What is critical size material?
How does pebble crushing increase SAG throughput?
What is the pebble crusher product size?

f.q: Why would both pebble crushers be down at once?
f.a:
General reasons: planned maintenance on one while the other faults, a common upstream problem such as a conveyor trip, a metal detector fault holding the bypass open, or a power issue.

The reference says the crushers are duty/duty, meaning both normally run. Each is rated at 305 t/h, 610 t/h total, allowing for worn pebble ports.

Ask the CRO for the cause.
f: What does duty/duty mean for the pebble crushers?
Can one pebble crusher handle all pebbles?
How are pebble crusher liners changed?

f.q: How does the bin High-High open the bypass?
f.a:
The reference says the pebble bypass gate opens if the pebble crusher feed bin reaches High-High, or if it is at High with both feeders stopped.

That protects against the bin overfilling and spilling. If pebbles keep arriving from the SAG discharge screen faster than the crushers take them, the bin fills, and at High-High the bypass diverts the pebble stream straight back to the SAG.

It is the same idea as a tank overflow piped to a safe destination. The feed bins are 2 x 65 t per the reference, which is only a few minutes of buffer at about 375 t/h of pebbles.
f: How large are the pebble crusher feed bins?
What level instrument is on the pebble bins?
Why do feeders stop on bin low level?

What makes the pebble bin bypass gate op.q: How does sending pebbles back to the SAG affect its feed rate control?
What makes the pebble bin bypass gate op.a:
The reference says the SAG feed rate is controlled through the SAG feed weightometer, normally set by the mill expert system, and pebbles on bypass go straight back to the SAG.

Returning pebbles add to the mill's load without passing the SAG feed weightometer on the reclaim conveyor, depending on where they rejoin. Uncrushed pebbles build up as critical size material, so mill weight rises and power may change.

If feed is controlled on mill weight, the controller would reduce fresh feed to compensate. If on tonnage, mill weight may climb until the expert system or CRO cuts feed. Either way, fresh throughput tends to drop.

f.q: Where do pebbles rejoin the SAG feed?
f.a:
The reference says pebbles on bypass go straight back to the SAG, but it does not say exactly where they rejoin.

In general, pebble return conveyors deliver onto the SAG feed conveyor or into the SAG feed chute. Whether that point is before or after the SAG feed weightometer matters, because it decides whether returning pebbles are counted as fresh feed tonnes.

Check the F13 milling PFD or ask the metallurgist to trace the pebble return route for you.
f: Is there a weightometer on the pebble return conveyor?
How are pebble tonnes measured?
What is the F13 milling PFD?

f.q: Why does mill weight rise with uncrushed pebbles?
f.a:
General mill behaviour. Pebbles are the hard, rounded, mid size rocks that the SAG struggles to break. They are too small to act as useful grinding media and too large to be ground quickly, so when they are returned uncrushed they accumulate instead of leaving through the grates.

The mill therefore holds more material and mill weight rises. The expert system typically cuts fresh feed to keep weight in range, which is where the throughput loss comes from.

Normally the pebble crushers reduce them to P80 12 mm, which the SAG can then grind easily.
f: What is the pebble crusher feed size F80?
How does the expert system respond to rising weight?
Why are pebbles so hard to grind?

f.q: Does the expert system know when pebbles are on bypass?
f.a:
The reference does not say whether the expert system takes bypass gate status as an input. It lists the inputs as the SAG feed camera size analyser, SAG noise monitor, mill load, speed, power and other measured variables.

Even without a direct signal, it would see the effects through rising mill weight and changing power and noise, and respond to those.

Whether bypass status is one of the other measured variables is a question for the process control engineer.
f: What other variables does the expert system use?
Can the CRO tell the expert system about bypass?
How does the expert system handle sudden load changes?

How does the grinding circuit run during.q: Why can't the plant just shut down completely during a mill reline?
How does the grinding circuit run during.a:
Because each reline takes days, and stopping the whole plant would lose that production. The reference says the plant runs with alternative configurations during relines: new SAG alone (single stage) while the ball mill is relined, new SABC while the FIM SAG is relined, and FIM SAG plus ball mill while the new SAG is relined.

All at reduced throughput, but still producing gold. The SAGs and ball mill have separate relines, so having two SAGs feeding one ball mill gives flexibility.

It is like having parallel compressors: you service one while the others carry a reduced load.

f.q: Why does the plant have two SAG mills?
f.a:
The reference says Stage 1 added a new SAG in parallel with the existing FIM SAG, both feeding a new ball mill. The FIM SAG is 10.97 m by 4.27 m EGL, 12 MW. The new SAG is 10.97 m by 8.38 m EGL, 20 MW.

The new SAG feeds 1,833 t/h nominal and the FIM SAG 1,313 t/h, total 3,146 t/h. The old FIM circuit alone was 10.5 Mtpa; the combined plant is 25.5 Mtpa nominal.

Two SAGs also give reline flexibility.
f: How does the FIM SAG discharge get to the new cyclones?
Why is the new SAG longer than the FIM SAG?
What happened to the old FIM ball mills?

f.q: What is SABC?
f.a:
From the glossary, SABC means SAG, Ball mill, pebble Crusher circuit. The SAG does primary grinding, pebble crushers crush critical size pebbles from the SAG discharge screen, and the ball mill grinds cyclone underflow to the final size.

The reference says the grind target is P80 180 um.

During a FIM SAG reline, the new SAG, ball mill and pebble crushers run as a full SABC circuit.
f: What is the role of pebble crushers in SABC?
What does single stage mean?
How is grind size controlled in SABC?

f.q: How long does a SAG mill reline take?
f.a:
The reference does not give reline durations.

In general, a large SAG reline takes several days, depending on the number of liner pieces, whether a relining machine is used, crew size, and how much other work is bundled into the same shutdown. Shell and discharge end liners often have different lives, so not every reline replaces everything.

Ask the mill maintenance planner for the typical durations of each mill's reline on this site.
f: What is a relining machine?
How often are SAG liners replaced?
What crew size does a SAG reline need?

How does the grinding circuit run during.q: What would you expect throughput to look like during a single stage week?
How does the grinding circuit run during.a:
Single stage means the new SAG running alone without the ball mill, per the reference and glossary, while the ball mill is relined.

Throughput would be reduced. The reference says all reline scenarios are at reduced throughput but does not give a figure. In general, single stage SAG operation gives a coarser grind because there is no ball mill to finish grinding. To hold grind reasonably close to target, feed rate is cut.

Flotation may also see coarser feed and lower recovery. Ask the metallurgist for actual single stage targets.

f.q: Why is grind coarser without the ball mill?
f.a:
General. The ball mill grinds cyclone underflow, the coarse fraction, down to the final size. Without it, only the SAG grinds, and SAGs are less efficient at fine grinding.

So the SAG product is coarser, and to get finer grind, feed must be cut so material stays longer in the SAG.

The reference grind target is P80 180 um, max 250 um.
f: How does SAG product size compare to ball mill product?
What is the max P80 allowed?
How does coarse grind affect flotation recovery?

f.q: Where does cyclone underflow go in single stage?
f.a:
The reference does not describe single stage flows in detail, only that the new SAG runs alone while the ball mill is relined, at reduced throughput.

In general, without the ball mill, cyclone underflow must go somewhere other than the ball mill, typically back to the SAG, or classification is arranged so the SAG product goes forward with its coarse fraction recycled.

The actual configuration is a question for the metallurgist or process control engineer, and would be shown in the reline operating procedure.
f: Does single stage use the cyclones at all?
How is SAG product classified in single stage?
What controls are changed for single stage?

f.q: Does single stage affect gravity recovery?
f.a:
General reasoning. The gravity circuit takes its feed from cyclone underflow through the 2 gravity duty cyclones and their scalping screens, per the reference, with Knelson tails returning to the primary cyclone feed hopper. If cyclone underflow flows or sizing change in single stage, gravity feed changes too.

The reference does not say how gravity is run during a ball mill reline. The scalping screen oversize normally goes to ball mill feed, which would not be available.

Ask the metallurgist how gravity is managed in single stage.
f: How do the gravity cyclones get their feed?
What is gravity recovery at design?
What happens to Knelsons in single stage?

How does the grinding circuit run during.q: How does the mill reline schedule get coordinated with maintenance planning?
How does the grinding circuit run during.a:
The reference describes the reline scenarios but not the scheduling process.

In general, relines are planned months ahead based on liner wear measurements and predicted life. Maintenance planners coordinate liners, crews, relining machines and cranes, and production planners adjust targets for reduced throughput. The three mills are usually staggered so only one is down at a time.

Ask the mill maintenance planner for the reline schedule.

f.q: How is liner wear measured to plan relines?
f.a:
General practice. Liner wear is measured during shutdowns by physical gauging at set points, ultrasonic thickness readings, or laser scanning of the whole mill interior. The thickness data is tracked over time to predict when each liner will reach its minimum allowable thickness.

Some sites also use wear sensors built into liners, or track wear against tonnes milled.

The reference does not cover this. Ask the mill maintenance planner which method is used here.
f: What is laser scanning of mill liners?
What is minimum liner thickness?
How often are liners measured?

f.q: Why stagger relines between the three mills?
f.a:
General reasoning with reference scenarios. Staggering keeps two of the three mills running during any reline, so the plant keeps producing. The reference gives three reline configurations, each with one mill down: new SAG single stage, new SABC, or FIM SAG plus ball mill.

It also spreads the demand for specialist reline crews, relining machines and cranes.

Relining two mills at once would cut throughput far more, or stop the plant.
f: Can two mills share a relining machine?
How many relines happen each year?
What is the throughput in each reline scenario?

f.q: Who decides when a reline happens?
f.a:
General practice, as the reference does not cover this. Relines are usually decided jointly by maintenance, based on liner condition and predicted wear, and operations, based on production targets and ore supply. Final approval typically sits with senior maintenance and processing management, inside a longer term shutdown plan.

The decision also has to fit with power, crew and contractor availability.

Ask the mill maintenance planner how the reline plan is built and approved on site.
f: What is the maintenance superintendent's role?
How are shutdowns scheduled on site?
What is a major shutdown versus a reline?

Why do flotation cell agitators normally.q: Why is sanding in the rotor gap such a big risk for these agitators?
Why do flotation cell agitators normally.a:
The reference says if the cell holds slurry or water and the agitator stops, solids settle and sand in the rotor. It also says the air valve interlocks closed if the agitator stops to prevent sanding the rotor/stator gap and protect the bearings.

The rotor sits near the bottom of a 630 m3 rougher cell or larger scavenger cell, with a tight gap to the stator. When the slurry settles, a compact bed of sand fills that gap and buries the rotor.

Restarting against that bed can overload the motor, damage the drive, or require draining and digging out the cell. It is like trying to start a mixer with set concrete around the paddle.

f.q: How long does it take for solids to settle in a flotation cell?
f.a:
The reference does not give settling times.

In general, the coarsest particles start dropping within seconds to minutes of agitation stopping, and a compact bed around the rotor can form within hours, depending on solids concentration, particle size and density. Flotation feed here is 34.4 percent solids per the reference, ground to P80 180 um, so there is a lot of solid to settle.

That is why the reference says agitators keep running whenever the cell holds slurry or water.
f: How does particle size affect settling rate?
Can a sanded cell be recovered without draining?
What is flotation feed density?

f.q: How is a sanded flotation cell recovered?
f.a:
General practice. Options include carefully bumping or inching the rotor if the drive allows, adding water and using air or water lances to loosen the bed, or in severe cases draining the cell and digging it out.

All of this is slow, labour intensive work that needs isolation and permits, and may involve confined space entry if people must go inside.

The reference does not cover recovery procedures. Prevention, by keeping agitators running, is strongly preferred.
f: Can flotation cells be drained quickly?
What is a cell drain valve?
How long does it take to clean out a sanded cell?

f.q: What is the rotor/stator in a flotation cell?
f.a:
General. The rotor is the spinning impeller near the bottom of the cell that suspends solids and disperses air into fine bubbles. The stator is a fixed ring of vanes around it that breaks up the swirl and helps disperse bubbles.

The gap between them is critical for bubble generation.

The reference says the roughers are FLS forced air tank cells.
f: How are rotors and stators replaced?
What is forced air flotation?
How does air get to the rotor?

Why do flotation cell agitators normally.q: What would a handover mean by 'agitator visually checked before starting'?
Why do flotation cell agitators normally.a:
It means a field operator physically inspected the flotation cell agitator before the CRO started it from the OIS, as the reference requires.

The check confirms the area is clear of people and tools, guards are in place, the drive looks ready, and possibly that the cell has slurry or water at a suitable level. It may also check for signs of sanding if the agitator has been stopped.

The handover note tells you the step was done, so the start was correct.

f.q: Why must agitators be checked before starting from the OIS?
f.a:
The reference says agitators are started from the OIS after a field visual check. It does not say why.

In general, agitators are large drives that may have been stopped for maintenance, so the check confirms people and tools are clear, guards are on, and the cell is in a suitable state. Starting a sanded agitator could damage it.

It is a safety and equipment protection step.
f: What guards are on flotation agitators?
How does a field operator check for sanding?
Who starts flotation agitators?

f.q: What does the field operator look for on an agitator?
f.a:
General. The field operator checks that nobody is working on the cell, guards are fitted, the drive belt or gearbox looks normal, no oil leaks, and the cell level is suitable.

If the agitator has been off for a while, they may check whether the rotor turns freely if possible, to detect sanding.

Ask the area operator for the site checklist.

f.q: Is the visual check recorded?
f.a:
The reference says agitators are started from the OIS after the field operator has checked them visually, but it does not say how the check is recorded.

In general, sites record such checks in the shift log, on a pre start checklist, or by a radio confirmation that the CRO notes. A record helps if there is later a question about why an agitator was damaged on start.

Ask the area supervisor how agitator start checks are documented here.

Why do flotation cell agitators normally.q: What damage results if an agitator starts against settled solids?
Why do flotation cell agitators normally.a:
General. Starting against a compacted bed puts a huge torque on the drive. Possible damage: motor overload or burnout, gearbox or belt damage, shaft bending, coupling failure, and rotor or stator damage.

The motor protection relay may trip it first, but repeated attempts can still damage the drive train.

The reference says agitators keep running to avoid sanding, and the air valve closes on agitator stop to prevent sanding the rotor/stator gap and protect the bearings. All of this is to avoid this situation. It is like starting a pump with a seized impeller.

f.q: What protects an agitator motor from overload?
f.a:
The reference says LV DOL starters have electronic overloads on Modbus TCP, VSDs sit on a field network, and protection relays are critical interlocks that act in every mode.

In general, an overload relay trips the motor if current stays too high for too long, following a time curve. A VSD can also limit torque and trip on overcurrent.

Which starter type the flotation agitators use is not stated in the reference. The electrical drawings or an electrician would confirm.
f: Do flotation agitators use DOL or VSD?
What is an electronic overload relay?
How does a VSD limit torque?

f.q: Can a VSD help start an agitator against settled solids?
f.a:
General. A VSD can start the motor slowly with controlled torque, which may help work a lightly settled bed loose without a shock load. But a heavily compacted bed still needs mechanical clearing, and forcing it with torque risks shaft or gearbox damage.

The reference does not say which flotation agitators have VSDs. It only says the drives are reversible for even rotor wear.

Ask the electrical engineer or flotation maintenance planner what drive type is fitted.
f: Are flotation drives reversible VSDs?
What is a soft starter?
How much torque can a VSD give at low speed?

f.q: Why do agitator bearings get damaged by sanding?
f.a:
The reference says the air valve interlocks closed when the agitator stops, to avoid sanding the rotor/stator gap and damaging the motor bearings.

In general, a sanded rotor means heavy, uneven loads on the shaft when restarted, because the bed resists one side more than the other. Those side loads and shock loads travel up the long shaft into the bearings, which are designed mainly for steady running loads, and can dent races and damage rollers.

Protecting the bearings avoids costly repairs and cell downtime.
f: How are agitator bearings lubricated?
What are signs of bearing damage?
How often are agitator bearings replaced?

Why are flotation cell drives reversible.q: Why alternate direction instead of just replacing rotors sooner?
Why are flotation cell drives reversible.a:
The reference says flotation cell drives are reversible to even out rotor wear by running in both directions, with direction picked on the OIS based on how long it has run each way.

A rotor wears mainly on the leading face of its blades. Running one way only wears one side, so the rotor is scrapped while half its material is still good. Reversing periodically uses both faces, roughly doubling life.

Rotors are large, expensive castings and changing them needs the cell drained and a crane. Doubling life halves those costs and downtime. It is like rotating tyres on a car.

f.q: How long does a flotation rotor last?
f.a:
The reference does not give rotor life.

In general, it depends on slurry abrasiveness, solids concentration, particle size and tip speed, and can range from months to a few years. Reversing direction, as the reference describes, is one of the main ways to extend it.

Ask the flotation maintenance planner for typical rotor and stator life on these cells and how wear is inspected.
f: What material are flotation rotors made from?
How is rotor wear measured?
Can worn rotors be repaired?

f.q: What does changing a flotation rotor involve?
f.a:
General practice. The cell is drained, isolated and made safe under the permit system. The drive, shaft and rotor assembly are lifted out by crane, the rotor and often the stator are replaced, and the assembly is reinstalled and aligned before refilling and restarting.

On large cells like the 630 m3 roughers in the reference, this is a significant job needing crane time and a cell outage.

The reference does not cover maintenance procedures; ask the flotation maintenance planner.

What crane is used on flotation cells?
Can the cell run without a rotor?

f.q: Does reversing affect flotation performance?
f.a:
General. Rotors intended for reversible service are designed with symmetrical blades so they suspend solids and disperse air similarly in either direction, though small differences in power draw or air dispersion are possible.

The reference says the drives are reversible for even rotor wear, but does not mention performance effects.

If you want to check, compare cell power draw and OSA results either side of a reversal, or ask the metallurgist whether they have seen any difference.
f: Are FLS rotors designed for both directions?
How is air dispersion measured?
Does direction affect power draw?

Why are flotation cell drives reversible.q: What would you see on the OIS that tells you which direction a cell is running?
Why are flotation cell drives reversible.a:
The reference says direction is picked on the OIS based on how long the drive has run each way, so the OIS must show the current direction and the run time in each direction.

In general, the agitator faceplate would show a forward or reverse status and run hour counters for each direction, alongside the normal mode, run status and interlock information.

Ask a CRO to open a flotation agitator faceplate for you; it is quicker than hunting for it.

f.q: How are run hours tracked for each direction?
f.a:
General. The DCS counts the time the drive runs in each direction and displays the totals on the faceplate. The CRO uses those totals to decide when to reverse, per the reference.

The counters may also be historised in PI, which would let maintenance compare wear against run hours over the life of each rotor.

Ask the process control engineer whether the direction run hours are logged in PI.
f: Are run hour counters stored in PI?
Can run hours be reset?
Who monitors run hours?

f.q: Can the direction be changed while running?
f.a:
General. Reversing a large motor while it is running would cause a severe torque shock to the motor, gearbox and shaft. So direction is changed with the agitator stopped, then it is restarted the other way.

The reference does not say when reversals happen. Since agitators normally keep running whenever the cell holds slurry or water, reversals are likely done at planned stops, which also need a cell that will not sand in the time it is stopped.

Ask a CRO how it is done here.

How long does a reversal take?
Is reversal part of a planned shutdown?

f.q: Is direction shown on the field LCS?
f.a:
The reference does not say. LCSs are described as having start and latch off stop buttons, with no mode selector, and direction is selected on the OIS.

In the field, you can usually tell direction by watching the shaft or coupling turn, or from a direction arrow on the drive guard, but that needs care around rotating equipment.

Ask a field operator whether the flotation LCSs show direction locally.

Why are flotation cell drives reversible.q: How does the operator decide when it's time to reverse a cell?
Why are flotation cell drives reversible.a:
The reference says direction is picked on the OIS based on how long it has run each way.

So the CRO looks at the run hours in each direction and reverses when one side gets ahead, aiming to keep them roughly equal over time. The exact rule, such as reverse at a set hour difference or at each planned stop, is not in the reference.

Ask a senior CRO or the flotation maintenance planner for the site practice.

f.q: Is there an automatic reversal schedule?
f.a:
The reference does not say. It states that direction is picked on the OIS based on how long it has run each way, which suggests an operator decision guided by run hour counters rather than an automatic schedule.

Some systems do reverse automatically at each start, which keeps hours balanced without anyone thinking about it.

Ask the process control engineer whether any automation is configured here.

How often do flotation agitators start?
What triggers a planned agitator stop?

f.q: What if one direction gets far ahead?
f.a:
General. The rotor wears more on one face, so it reaches its replacement limit sooner than it would with balanced running, and some of its useful material is wasted. Badly uneven wear can also change how the rotor disperses air.

It would be worth reversing at the next planned stop and flagging it to the flotation maintenance planner.

The reference does not give a limit for the imbalance.

Can uneven wear affect performance?
Who decides on rotor replacement?

f.q: Do Jameson cells have reversible drives too?
f.a:
No. The reference says Jameson cells have no agitators and no blowers; the jet does the work. So there are no rotors to reverse.

The reversible drives are on the FLS forced air tank cells, the three roughers and four scavengers.

In a Jameson cell the wear points are instead the nozzles and downcomers, and the feed pump. Those are inspected and replaced on a schedule rather than evened out by reversing.

What happens to a flotation cell's air v.q: Why interlock the air valve instead of relying on the operator to close it?
What happens to a flotation cell's air v.a:
The reference says the air valve interlocks closed when the agitator trips, to avoid sanding the rotor/stator gap and damaging the motor bearings.

A trip can happen at any time, often during an upset when the CRO is busy with many alarms. If the air stayed on with the rotor stopped, air would keep blowing into the stopped rotor zone, pushing solids around and packing them into the rotor/stator gap. Waiting for the operator to notice and close it could take minutes.

An interlock acts in seconds. It is like a fuel shutoff valve that closes automatically when an engine stalls, rather than relying on the driver.

f.q: How does air flow cause sanding in a stopped cell?
f.a:
General reasoning. With the rotor stopped, nothing keeps solids in suspension. If air keeps blowing down the shaft and out through the rotor, it disturbs the settling slurry locally and can carry solids into the rotor/stator gap and air passages, where they pack. Air channelling can also let solids settle unevenly around the mechanism.

The reference says the air valve interlocks closed when the agitator stops to prevent sanding the rotor/stator gap and protect the bearings.
f: What happens to air passages when sanded?
How is air delivered to the rotor?
Why are bearings affected by sanding?

f.q: Is the air valve interlock a critical or process interlock?
f.a:
The reference does not classify it.

In general, it would most likely be a process interlock, because it protects equipment and the process rather than people. Critical interlocks in the reference are E-stops, pull wires and protection relays.

If it is a process interlock, it trips in Auto and Manual and could be bypassed by named users one at a time. Ask the control systems engineer for its actual classification.
f: Can a process interlock be bypassed?
What are examples of critical interlocks?
How are interlocks classified?

f.q: What other flotation interlocks exist?
f.a:
The reference mentions: agitators started from the OIS after a field check, agitators kept running when the cell holds slurry or water, the air valve interlocking closed on agitator stop, blowers on VSDs holding header pressure, and dart valve split range level control.

Other interlocks, such as on the flotation feed or concentrate pumps, would follow the general pump rules in the reference, but specific flotation interlocks are not detailed.

Ask the process control engineer for the flotation functional specification.

What is the flotation functional specification?
How do dart valves control level?

What happens to a flotation cell's air v.q: What would happen to the motor bearings if air stayed open after a trip?
What happens to a flotation cell's air v.a:
The reference says the air valve interlock protects the motor bearings by avoiding sanding the rotor/stator gap.

In general, if air stayed open and the rotor gap became sanded, the next start would put heavy shock loads through the shaft into the bearings. Uneven loading could also bend the shaft or misalign it. Bearings could suffer damage to races and rollers, leading to early failure.

The interlock prevents this chain of events.

f.q: How long do agitator bearings normally last?
f.a:
The reference does not say.

In general, bearings on large flotation agitators can last several years with good lubrication, sound seals and no shock loads. Sanding events, misalignment and contamination are the usual causes of early failure.

Bearing life is usually tracked against run hours and condition monitoring results rather than a fixed calendar. Ask the flotation maintenance planner for typical bearing life and the change out strategy on these cells.
f: How are agitator bearings monitored?
What lubrication do agitator bearings use?
Can bearings be changed without removing the rotor?

f.q: What are signs of bearing damage on an agitator?
f.a:
General. Signs include rising vibration, a change in noise such as grinding or rumbling, higher bearing housing temperature, and wear metals or discolouration in the oil or grease.

Vibration monitoring can detect early defects months before failure, which lets the change be planned into a shutdown.

The reference does not cover condition monitoring. Ask the reliability engineer whether flotation agitators are on a vibration route.
f: Is vibration monitoring used on flotation agitators?
What is bearing temperature limit?
How is oil analysis used?

f.q: Can shaft misalignment come from sanding?
f.a:
General. Yes. Starting against a sanded rotor, or air pushing a rotor partly buried in solids, can apply a large side load to the shaft. On long agitator shafts that can bend the shaft or shift its alignment.

The result is vibration, uneven rotor and stator wear, and faster bearing wear.

The reference does not detail shaft design, but the air valve interlock it describes is partly there to prevent this.

What is a long shaft agitator?
Can a bent shaft be repaired?

What happens to a flotation cell's air v.q: Why does the vendor want the air controller in Auto before the agitator starts?
What happens to a flotation cell's air v.a:
The reference says the vendor recommends having the air controller in Auto at a low setpoint before starting the agitator.

In general, a low air flow during start helps keep the rotor clear of solids and reduces start up load, while not overwhelming the rotor with air before it is turning. In Auto, the controller holds the low flow steadily, rather than an operator having to manage it by hand.

Once the agitator is running, the setpoint can be raised to normal.

f.q: Why start with a low air setpoint?
f.a:
General reasoning. A small air flow keeps the rotor passages clear and stops solids packing in during start, without flooding the rotor with air before it is turning fast enough to disperse it. Too much air on a slow rotor can form large air pockets, cause sloshing, and reduce power draw unevenly.

The reference says the vendor recommends the air controller in Auto at a low setpoint before starting the agitator. Once running, air is raised to the normal setpoint.
f: What is normal air flow per cell?
How is air flow measured?
Why can too much air hurt flotation?

f.q: What controls air flow in each cell?
f.a:
The reference says air to each cell is set by a flow controller with a mass flow meter, and the LP flotation blowers have VSDs holding header pressure.

So each cell has its own air control valve controlled to a flow setpoint, drawing from a common air header. The blowers keep header pressure steady so one cell's valve moving does not disturb the others.

It is like a compressed air system with a pressure controlled compressor and flow controlled users.
f: How do blowers hold header pressure?
What is a mass flow meter?
How many blowers are there?

f.q: Who sets the air setpoint during normal running?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation expert system uses the OSA, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set level (froth depth), air and reagents.

So during normal running, the expert system adjusts cell air setpoints, and the per cell flow controllers hold them. The CRO can also set them directly, for example if the expert system is offline.

Ask the metallurgist how air profiles across the rougher and scavenger banks are chosen.
