How is rougher and scavenger cell level.q: Why use two dart valves per cell instead of one larger valve?
How is rougher and scavenger cell level.a:
The reference says rougher and scavenger cells have two discharge dart valves per cell on a split range level controller, run in series or in parallel.

In general, two valves give better control over a wide flow range. In split range, one valve handles low flows with fine control, and the second opens for higher flows. A single large valve would be coarse at low flows.

Two valves also give redundancy: if one sticks, the other can still control level. It is like having a small and a large control valve on a steam line.

f.q: What is split range control?
f.a:
General control knowledge. Split range control uses one controller output to drive two valves in sequence. For example, 0 to 50 percent output strokes valve A from closed to open, and 50 to 100 percent strokes valve B.

The reference says the two dart valves per cell are on a split range level controller.

This gives fine control at low flow and full capacity at high flow, like using a small and a large bypass valve together.
f: How is the split point chosen?
Can split range cause control problems?
What other loops use split range?

f.q: What is a dart valve?
f.a:
From the glossary: a dart valve is a flotation cell discharge valve for level control.

In general, it is a cone shaped plug, the dart, on a vertical stem that moves up and down in a seat at the bottom of the cell or discharge box. Raising the dart lets more slurry out, lowering cell level.

It suits slurry because it is simple, has a short flow path and the moving plug tends to keep the seat clear.
f: How is a dart valve actuated?
How do dart valves wear?
How is dart valve position measured?

f.q: What happens if one dart valve fails?
f.a:
General. With two valves per cell, the other can usually keep controlling level, though with reduced range: if the failed one is stuck shut, the cell may not pass high flows; if stuck open, low flows may be hard to hold.

The CRO would see level deviating from setpoint or the controller output moving into an unusual range.

The reference does not describe dart valve failure handling; ask the CRO or metallurgist.
f: How is a dart valve failure alarmed?
Can a cell run on one dart valve?
How is a dart valve repaired?

How is rougher and scavenger cell level.q: What would the froth look like if a discharge dart valve stuck shut?
How is rougher and scavenger cell level.a:
General reasoning. If a dart valve stuck shut, slurry could not leave the cell fast enough, so cell level would rise. Froth depth would decrease as the pulp rises towards the lip.

In severe cases, pulp would overflow into the concentrate launder, diluting the concentrate. The froth would look wetter, less stable and lower grade.

The reference says level sets froth depth, so a stuck valve directly affects froth.

f.q: Why does pulp in the launder dilute concentrate?
f.a:
General. The pulp below the froth contains mostly gangue minerals that did not float. If cell level rises until pulp spills over the lip into the concentrate launder, that gangue mixes with the concentrate and lowers its grade.

That sends more mass and less valuable material to the cleaners, and on to concentrate handling.

The reference says level sets froth depth, which is why level control matters so much.
f: What is concentrate grade?
How is launder overflow detected?
What do launder velocity cameras measure?

f.q: How does froth depth affect grade and recovery?
f.a:
General flotation knowledge. A deeper froth gives more time for entrained gangue and water to drain back to the pulp, which raises grade but lowers recovery, since some weakly attached valuable particles also drop out. A shallower froth gives higher recovery but lower grade.

The reference says level sets froth depth, and the flotation expert system adjusts level using OSA, froth camera and launder velocity camera data.

It is a constant balancing act.
f: How does the expert system choose froth depth?
What is froth drainage?
What grade does the cleaner need?

f.q: How would the CRO detect a stuck dart valve?
f.a:
General. If cell level keeps rising while the level controller output asks for more opening, the valve is not responding. If valve position feedback exists, the measured position would not match the command.

The reference does not say whether the dart valves have positioners or position feedback.

A field check of the actuator, air supply and dart movement would confirm it.

What is the cell level alarm?
How is a stuck dart valve freed?

How is rougher and scavenger cell level.q: What's the difference between dart valves run in series versus parallel?
How is rougher and scavenger cell level.a:
The reference says the dart valves can be in series or in parallel but does not explain.

In general, in parallel both valves discharge from the cell at the same time, adding capacity. In series, one valve feeds into the next, perhaps through a discharge box, giving finer control or a second stage.

The arrangement depends on the cell design and flow.

f.q: Why would series be chosen?
f.a:
The reference says the dart valves can run in series or in parallel but does not explain the choice, so this is general reasoning.

In a series arrangement, slurry passes through one valve then the next, for example from cell to discharge box to the next cell. Splitting the head drop over two valves can reduce wear and give smoother control, since each valve does part of the job.

Which cells use which arrangement here is a question for the metallurgist or process control engineer.
f: Which cells use series dart valves?
How does series affect level response?
What is a discharge box?

f.q: Why would parallel be chosen?
f.a:
The reference says the dart valves can run in series or in parallel but does not explain the choice, so this is general reasoning.

In parallel, both valves discharge from the cell side by side, so their capacities add. That suits high flows and gives redundancy, because either valve alone can still pass some flow if the other fails. With split range, one valve trims at low flow while the second opens only when needed.

Ask the metallurgist which arrangement each bank uses.
f: Which cells use parallel dart valves?
Can parallel valves fight each other?
How is flow split between parallel valves?

f.q: Can the arrangement be changed?
f.a:
The reference does not say whether the series or parallel arrangement can be changed in operation.

In general, changing between them would mean piping or discharge box changes, or changing how the controller sequences the valves, which is a configuration change needing management of change.

Ask the process control engineer whether it is a fixed design or a selectable option.

How is air controlled in the Jameson cel.q: Why size air on total downcomer flow rather than measure air directly?
How is air controlled in the Jameson cel.a:
The reference says Jameson cell air depends on total pumped flow through the downcomers, and the feed pump VSD is on flow.

In a Jameson cell, air is naturally aspirated: the slurry jet plunging down the downcomer draws air in, like a venturi or ejector. The amount of air drawn in depends on jet velocity, which depends on the flow through the nozzles.

So controlling total flow controls air. Measuring and controlling air separately would not make sense, since there is no blower or air valve to manipulate. It is like controlling an ejector's suction by controlling its motive flow.

f.q: How does a Jameson downcomer work?
f.a:
General. Slurry is pumped through a nozzle at the top of a vertical downcomer, forming a high speed jet. The jet plunges into the slurry in the downcomer, entraining air and shearing it into fine bubbles. The aerated mixture flows down and out into the cell, where bubbles rise and form froth.

The glossary calls it a plunging jet flotation cell with no blower.
f: What is a downcomer nozzle?
How many downcomers in a B6500/24?
What wears in a downcomer?

f.q: Why recycle cleaner tails to keep downcomer flow constant?
f.a:
The reference says cleaner tails are about 50 percent recycled to the cleaner feed hopper, and this external recycle keeps downcomer flow constant.

A Jameson cell's air entrainment depends on jet velocity through the nozzles. If new feed drops, recycled tails make up the flow, so jet velocity, bubble generation and air rate stay steady.

It is like a minimum flow recycle on a pump: the machine needs constant throughput to work properly, whatever the process supply is doing.
f: What happens if downcomer flow drops?
How is recycle flow controlled?
What is the cleaner feed hopper?

f.q: What is natural aspiration?
f.a:
General. Natural aspiration means air is drawn in by the flow itself, without a blower or compressor. In a Jameson downcomer the high speed slurry jet creates a low pressure zone that pulls air in through an inlet at the top, in the same way an ejector or venturi pump draws a secondary fluid.

The reference says the cleaner uses natural aspiration via downcomers.

The air rate is set by the jet, not by an air valve.
f: How is aspirated air measured?
What limits air entrainment?
Why use natural aspiration?

How is air controlled in the Jameson cel.q: What would you see in the froth if the feed pump VSD flow drifted off setpoint?
How is air controlled in the Jameson cel.a:
General reasoning. If flow dropped, jet velocity would fall, so less air would be entrained. Fewer bubbles mean less froth, and a thinner, weaker froth layer. Recovery would drop.

If flow rose, more air and froth, possibly too much, with more entrainment of gangue.

The reference says Jameson air depends on total downcomer flow and the feed pump VSD is on flow control.

f.q: What is gangue entrainment?
f.a:
General flotation knowledge. Entrainment is when non floating gangue particles are carried up into the froth with the water between bubbles, rather than by attaching to bubbles. It is worst for fine particles and wet froths.

It lowers concentrate grade. More air and water in the froth generally means more entrainment.

Cleaner stages, like the Jameson cleaners in the reference, exist partly to reject entrained gangue and lift the grade.

What is froth washing?
How does the cleaner improve grade?

f.q: How would the CRO see flow drifting?
f.a:
General. The Jameson feed pump flow PV would move away from its SV, the pump VSD output might climb to its limit if the pump could not keep up, and a deviation alarm might come in if configured.

The reference says the feed pump VSD is on flow control, so normally the loop corrects drift quickly. Persistent drift points to pump wear, a blocked nozzle or a hopper level problem.

Trending flow and VSD speed in PI would show which.
f: What is the Jameson feed pump flow setpoint?
What alarms are on the feed pump?
How is flow measured?

f.q: Does the expert system adjust Jameson flow?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation expert system adjusts level, air and reagents using OSA, froth camera and launder velocity camera data. It does not say whether it adjusts Jameson feed flow.

Since Jameson air depends on downcomer flow, adjusting flow would effectively adjust air, so it is plausible, but not confirmed.

Ask the process control engineer which Jameson setpoints the expert system writes.
f: What does the expert system control in the cleaner?
How is Jameson cell level controlled?
What is the cleaner mass pull?

How is air controlled in the Jameson cel.q: Why don't Jameson cells need agitators or blowers like conventional cells?
How is air controlled in the Jameson cel.a:
The reference says Jameson cells have no agitators and no blowers; the jet does the work.

In conventional forced air cells, the agitator keeps solids suspended and disperses blower air into bubbles. In a Jameson cell, the plunging jet in the downcomer does both: it entrains air and creates intense mixing and fine bubbles in a small volume. The cell tank is mostly a separation zone where bubbles rise.

This reduces moving parts and power. It is like the difference between a stirred tank reactor and a jet mixer.

f.q: What are the advantages of Jameson cells for cleaning?
f.a:
General. Jameson cells generate fine bubbles with intense particle to bubble contact in a compact unit, which suits fine particles and high grade cleaning. They have no agitator or blower, so fewer moving parts.

The reference says the cleaner and cleaner-scavenger are Glencore Jameson B6500/24 cells, with a cleaner froth area of 22.2 m2 and stage sulphur recovery of about 93 percent.

These are design figures.
f: Why are fine bubbles good for fine particles?
How big is a B6500/24?
What is the cleaner froth area?

f.q: What maintenance do Jameson cells need?
f.a:
General. The main wear items are the nozzles at the top of each downcomer and the downcomers themselves, which see high velocity slurry. They need regular inspection and replacement. Nozzle wear opens the orifice, lowering jet velocity and air entrainment.

The feed pump needs normal slurry pump maintenance.

The reference does not cover maintenance. Ask the flotation maintenance planner for the inspection routine.
f: How often are Jameson nozzles changed?
What causes nozzle wear?
Can a downcomer be isolated?

f.q: Do Jameson cells use more pump power?
f.a:
General. Yes, the feed pump must supply enough pressure to form a high velocity jet at each nozzle, so pumping power is higher than for feeding a conventional cell. Against that, there are no agitator or blower motors, and the external recycle adds pumped volume.

Whether total power is lower than an equivalent conventional cleaner depends on the duty.

The reference does not give power figures for the Jameson feed pumps.

The OSA measures gold and iron. How does.q: Why is pyrite the basis for inferring sulphur instead of measuring it directly?
The OSA measures gold and iron. How does.a:
The reference says the OSA measures gold and iron, and sulphur is inferred from iron because the sulphide is mainly pyrite (FeS2).

In pyrite, iron and sulphur are in a fixed ratio, so measuring iron lets you calculate sulphur. OSAs based on X-ray fluorescence measure heavier elements like iron well, but sulphur is light and harder to measure accurately in slurry.

The assumption is that most iron is in pyrite. If other iron minerals are present, the inferred sulphur would be off. It is like inferring flow from pump speed when you know the pump curve: valid if conditions match.

f.q: What is the ratio of iron to sulphur in pyrite?
f.a:
General chemistry. Pyrite is FeS2. Iron has an atomic mass of about 56 and sulphur about 32, so one formula unit is about 120. That makes pyrite about 47 percent iron and 53 percent sulphur by mass.

The OSA can calculate sulphur from iron using that fixed ratio, which is what the reference means by sulphur inferred from iron.

It only holds if most of the iron is actually in pyrite.
f: Are there other sulphides in the ore?
How does pyrrhotite differ from pyrite?
What is the head grade sulphur?

f.q: Why is sulphur hard to measure by XRF?
f.a:
General. Sulphur is a light element. Its characteristic X-rays are low energy and are absorbed strongly by water and the slurry matrix before they reach the detector, so the signal is weak and sensitive to density and particle size.

Iron is heavier and gives much stronger, more penetrating X-rays, so it is measured more reliably.

That is why the reference has the OSA measure gold and iron and infer sulphur.
f: How does XRF work?
What elements can an OSA measure?
How is the OSA calibrated?

f.q: Why does sulphur matter for this ore?
f.a:
The reference says the ore is refractory: much of the gold is locked in sulphides, mainly pyrite, and tellurides. So recovering sulphur to concentrate largely means recovering the gold that would otherwise go to tails.

Flotation sulphur recovery is 85.1 percent nominal (max 90), and concentrate goes on to ultra fine grinding to release the gold before leaching.

That is why sulphur on each stream is such a useful control signal.
f: What is refractory gold?
What are tellurides?
How does UFG help release gold?

The OSA measures gold and iron. How does.q: What would a handover mean by 'OSA sulphur reading looks off on stream three'?
The OSA measures gold and iron. How does.a:
It means the inferred sulphur value on the third sampled stream does not match expectations, such as lab results or other streams.

Per the reference, the streams are flotation feed, rougher 1 con, rougher 2/3 con, scavenger con, scavenger tails, cleaner feed, cleaner-scavenger tails, final con and final tails. Stream three in that order would be rougher 2/3 concentrate, though the site's numbering may differ.

Possible causes: OSA calibration drift, sample line blockage, non pyrite iron changing the ratio, or a real process change. The metallurgist would compare with lab assays.

f.q: How is the OSA checked against the lab?
f.a:
General practice. Shift or daily composite samples from the same streams are assayed in the laboratory and compared with the OSA readings over the same period. Consistent differences show calibration drift, and the OSA is then recalibrated.

The reference says the OSA samples nine streams and returns samples in separate high grade and low grade hoppers, but does not describe the calibration routine.

Ask the metallurgist how often OSA checks are done.
f: Who runs the lab assays?
How often is the OSA recalibrated?
What are the high and low grade return hoppers?

f.q: What causes OSA sample line blockages?
f.a:
General. Coarse particles, trash, scale or settled solids can block sample lines and cutters, especially at low flow or after a stop. A blocked line gives stale, wrong or no readings, which can look like a process change.

Regular flushing and cleaning of sample cutters and lines is part of normal OSA maintenance.

The reference says the OSA is a vendor package with its own PLC, but does not describe the sample lines.
f: How are OSA sample lines flushed?
How long are sample lines?
Who maintains the OSA?

f.q: Could the ore have changed rather than the OSA?
f.a:
General. Yes. If the ore carries more non pyrite iron, such as iron oxides or other iron bearing minerals, the iron reading rises without a matching rise in sulphur, so the inferred sulphur reads high. A real change in mineralogy or head grade could also explain an odd reading.

The metallurgist would compare with lab sulphur assays, which measure sulphur directly, to separate an ore change from an analyser fault.
f: What iron oxides might be in the ore?
How does mineralogy affect flotation?
How is ore blend tracked?

The OSA measures gold and iron. How does.q: Why sample nine separate streams instead of just feed and final tails?
The OSA measures gold and iron. How does.a:
The reference lists nine streams: flotation feed, rougher 1 con, rougher 2/3 con, scavenger con, scavenger tails, cleaner feed, cleaner-scavenger tails, final con and final tails.

Feed and tails alone would tell you overall recovery, but not where losses happen. Sampling each stage shows how each bank performs, so the expert system and operators can adjust each section.

It is like having pressure gauges at each stage of a multistage pump rather than only at suction and discharge.

f.q: How does the expert system use OSA data?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation expert system uses OSA data, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set level (froth depth), air and reagents.

In general, the stage assays show where recovery or grade is slipping, for example rising gold in scavenger tails, and the system adjusts that bank's air, level or reagent dose in response.

Ask the process control engineer for the main rules it uses.
f: How often does the OSA update?
What reagents does the expert system adjust?
What do froth cameras measure?

f.q: How often does the OSA analyse each stream?
f.a:
The reference does not say.

In general, an OSA with one analyser cycles through its streams in turn, so each stream is measured every several minutes, with a cycle covering all nine streams taking longer. Some streams may be measured more often than others.

Ask the metallurgist or OSA technician for the cycle time here, since it sets how quickly the expert system can react.
f: How long does each OSA analysis take?
Can the OSA prioritise streams?
What is the OSA cycle time?

f.q: Why are samples returned to high and low grade hoppers?
f.a:
The reference says samples return in separate high grade and low grade hoppers.

In general, returning them separately means concentrate samples go back to a concentrate stream and tails samples go back to tails, rather than mixing them. Mixing would send valuable concentrate to tails, losing gold, or dilute concentrate with tails.

It is a small flow, but sampled continuously, so it adds up.
f: Where do the return hoppers go?
How much sample flow is taken?
What is a sample return pump?

How are reagent doses set?.q: Why use g/t dosing instead of a fixed flow rate for reagents?
How are reagent doses set?.a:
Reagents like copper sulphate, PAX and frother are consumed in proportion to the ore going through, so the dose that matters metallurgically is grams per tonne of solids, not litres per hour.

Throughput is not constant. Nominal flotation feed is about 3,146 t/h but it moves with SAG performance, relines and ore hardness. A fixed flow would underdose when tonnage rises and waste reagent (and upset the froth) when it falls.

The g/t value goes into a calculation block that multiplies it by the measured tonnage to make a flow setpoint. A flow controller then trims the dosing pump VSD. Think of it like fuel injection metered to air mass flow: a ratio controller feeding a fast inner loop.

f.q: Where does the tonnage signal for the g/t calculation come from?
f.a:
The plant has two kinds of tonnage measurement: weightometers on conveyors (wet tonnes converted to dry with a moisture input) and slurry mass flow from a magnetic flowmeter plus nucleonic density gauge with an operator entered dry solids SG.

The condensed reference does not say which signal each reagent loop uses, so check the P&ID or control philosophy for that loop.

The practical point: the dose is only as good as the tonnage signal. A wrong SG entry or a drifting weightometer feeds straight through into the reagent flow setpoint, so if consumption looks odd, check the tonnage first.
f: What happens to reagent dosing if the tonnage signal fails?
Who maintains the weightometer calibration on site?
How is a wrong SG entry usually spotted?

f.q: When would the CRO pick a direct flow setpoint instead of g/t?
f.a:
The reference only says both options exist: a g/t setpoint through the calculation block, or a direct flow setpoint to the flow controller.

In general practice a direct flow setpoint is used when the tonnage signal is unreliable or out of service, during start up when tonnage is low and unstable, for trials where the metallurgist wants a fixed addition, or for dose points that are not tied to a clean tonnage measurement.

It is a bit like taking a cascade loop out of cascade and running the slave loop on a local setpoint. It works, but the dose no longer follows the ore, so it needs watching if throughput changes.
f: Is a direct flow setpoint logged differently in the historian?
What risks come with leaving a reagent on direct flow too long?
Who sets the reagent g/t targets for each shift?

f.q: Does the flotation expert system adjust the reagent setpoints?
f.a:
Yes, according to the plant reference. The flotation expert system uses the onstream analyser (Au and Fe, with S inferred from Fe), froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set cell level (froth depth), air and reagents.

So in normal running the expert system sits above the g/t or flow setpoints, acting like an outer supervisory loop, and the dosing flow controllers carry out its requests through the pump VSDs.

The reference does not detail the exact rules or limits it uses. If you want to know how far it can move a given reagent, the flotation metallurgist or the control systems engineer who tunes it would know.
f: What happens to dosing if the expert system drops out?
Can the CRO limit how far the expert system moves a reagent?
How does the OSA data reach the expert system?

How are reagent doses set?.q: What would you see on the OIS if a reagent dosing pump VSD lost its trim?
How are reagent doses set?.a:
The flow loop would stop holding its setpoint. On the OIS you would see the flow PV drifting away from the SV, and the controller output (CV) either pinned at 0 or 100 percent or frozen if the loop has dropped to Manual.

If the VSD has lost its speed reference or faulted, flow will follow whatever the pump is doing: falling as the tank level drops or rising as line pressure changes. A deviation or low flow alarm should come up, as configured.

The process effect shows later: grade and recovery shifting on the OSA, or froth looking different. It is just like a cooling water loop where the valve actuator has failed: the controller keeps asking but nothing responds.

f.q: What makes a dosing flow loop saturate at full output?
f.a:
Saturation means the controller is asking for more than the pump can give. Common causes are a partly blocked suction strainer or line, a worn pump, an empty or low supply tank, air locking, a closed manual valve, or a setpoint above the pump's capacity.

A flowmeter reading low when actual flow is fine will also push the output to 100 percent, so a bad instrument looks the same as a bad pump from the control room.

Mechanically it is like a hydraulic pump at full stroke that still cannot hold system pressure: the control is fine, the hardware or supply is the limit.
f: How would you check a dosing line for blockage safely?
Why can air in the line upset a small dosing pump?
What would integral windup do when the fault clears?

f.q: How would the CRO tell a flowmeter fault from a pump fault?
f.a:
Compare independent signals. If the VSD shows normal speed and current but the flowmeter reads zero, suspect the meter. If speed is at maximum and motor current is low, suspect suction starvation or air locking. If the supply tank level is still falling at the usual rate, the reagent is probably getting through and the meter is the likely problem.

A field check confirms it: pump running, discharge pressure normal, no leaks.

This is general troubleshooting rather than a plant procedure, so follow the area's normal fault reporting through the control room and maintenance.
f: Can tank level trends be used as a backup flow check?
What does low motor current on a running pump suggest?
Who fixes a faulty reagent flowmeter on site?

f.q: How quickly would underdosing PAX show up in the flotation results?
f.a:
PAX is the collector, so less of it means fewer sulphide and gold particles made hydrophobic. The rougher cells react within minutes, but you will usually notice it first as a thinner, less loaded froth on the froth cameras and then as falling mass pull and rising gold or sulphur in the scavenger tails on the OSA.

Combined rougher plus scavenger residence is about 36.5 minutes at design, so a full effect on final tails builds over roughly that time.

Exact sensitivity depends on the ore and is something the flotation metallurgist tracks.
f: Why does overdosing PAX also cause problems?
Which OSA stream shows a collector problem first?
How do froth cameras detect a change in froth loading?

How are reagent doses set?.q: Why is antiscalant dosed manually, unlike other reagents?
How are reagent doses set?.a:
The reference says antiscalant comes in IBCs and is dosed by manually set metering pumps, while the main reagents have VSD pumps on flow control.

The likely reasons are general ones. Antiscalant demand follows the water stream it protects rather than ore tonnage, so there is nothing useful to ratio it against. Doses are small and steady, and a modest overdose costs little. Building a full tank, VSD and flow loop around a product that arrives in IBCs would not pay back.

It is like a set and forget chemical injection quill on a cooling tower compared with a fuel system on closed loop control.

f.q: What does antiscalant protect in a saline water plant?
f.a:
Process water here is saline bore water (SG about 1.07), and recycled water is heated and concentrated in places. Dissolved calcium, carbonate and sulphate then come out as hard scale on pipe walls, valve seats, heat exchanger surfaces, elution heater tubes and pump internals.

Antiscalant interferes with crystal growth so the salts stay in solution or form soft deposits that wash through.

Mechanically, scale is like fouling in a heat exchanger: it cuts flow area, raises pressure drop and reduces heat transfer. The reference does not list every antiscalant dose point, so check the reagent P&IDs.
f: Where in the plant is scaling usually worst?
How does scale affect elution heater performance?
What scale removal methods are used during shutdowns?

f.q: How would you know an antiscalant IBC is running low?
f.a:
The reference does not describe level monitoring on the antiscalant IBCs, and with manual metering pumps there may be no DCS signal at all.

In practice that usually means a routine field check by the area operator on their rounds, with a log of IBC changeovers. Some sites mark the IBC level each shift so consumption can be checked against the pump setting.

For the actual arrangement and who owns the changeover, ask the reagents area operator or the shift supervisor.
f: Who orders and changes out antiscalant IBCs?
What happens if antiscalant dosing stops for a day?
Is antiscalant consumption tracked in the plant reports?

f.q: Who adjusts the antiscalant metering pump setting?
f.a:
The reference does not say. Generally, the dose rate for a water treatment chemical is set by the metallurgist or a water treatment chemical supplier based on water analysis, and the area operator sets the pump stroke or speed to match.

Because the pumps are manual, any change is a field adjustment, not an OIS setpoint, so it should be recorded so that consumption can be reconciled.

Check with the process metallurgist or the reagents area supervisor for the site practice.
f: How is an antiscalant dose rate worked out?
Why record manual pump settings in a log?
Does the chemical supplier review scale on site?

How are cyanide and caustic distributed?.q: Why use a ringmain with a back pressure valve rather than a direct feed?
How are cyanide and caustic distributed?.a:
In a ringmain the pump circulates reagent from the tank around a loop and back to the tank. Each dosing point draws off the loop. The mechanical back pressure valve on the return holds loop pressure, so every take off has supply pressure no matter how many points are drawing at once.

This lets simple DOL pumps run at constant speed while the valve absorbs the changes in demand. Continuous circulation also stops reagent sitting still in dead legs, which matters for caustic that can crystallise.

It is the same idea as a fuel rail with a pressure regulator returning excess to the tank, or a hydraulic header held by a relief valve.

f.q: Why use DOL pumps on the ringmain rather than VSDs?
f.a:
With a back pressure valve holding loop pressure, the pump does not need to vary speed. It just has to deliver more than the total draw off, and the excess returns to the tank. That makes a DOL starter the simplest and most robust choice.

The reference confirms DOL pumps on the cyanide and caustic ringmains, with flow measured at each dosing point.

Mechanically it is a constant displacement pump plus a pressure regulating valve, rather than a variable pump. You trade a little wasted pumping energy for fewer components and simpler control.
f: Is there a standby pump on the cyanide ringmain?
How much spare flow does a ringmain pump need?
What happens to the ringmain if the duty pump trips?

f.q: How is each dosing point's flow controlled off the ringmain?
f.a:
The reference says flowmeters sit at each dosing point. For CIL4, cyanide is flow controlled at the front end, with the setpoint from the operator or a g/t ratio on thickener underflow tonnes, and trimmed by the cyanide analyser.

In general that means a control valve at the take off, driven by a flow controller using that point's flowmeter. Because the ringmain holds a steady supply pressure, each valve sees a stable upstream pressure and the loops do not interact much.

For the exact valve and loop at any given dose point, check the reagent P&IDs.
f: Why does stable ringmain pressure help the dosing valves?
What happens if two dosing points open at once?
How are dosing valve failures flagged on the OIS?

f.q: What pressure does the ringmain back pressure valve hold?
f.a:
The reference does not give the setting. It only states that a mechanical back pressure valve sits on the return line and that discharge and return pressures are monitored.

In general the setting is chosen so the farthest dosing point still has enough pressure to deliver its maximum flow through its valve and line, plus a margin, and it is set and confirmed during commissioning.

For the actual figure, check the vendor data or ask the reagents area maintenance planner or commissioning engineer.
f: How is a mechanical back pressure valve adjusted?
What happens if the back pressure valve sticks open?
Why is the valve on the return and not the supply?

How are cyanide and caustic distributed?.q: What would falling return line pressure on cyanide ringmain tell the CRO?
How are cyanide and caustic distributed?.a:
Falling return pressure means less flow is getting around the loop to the back pressure valve. The reference says discharge and return pressures are there to warn the operator of loss of flow.

Possible causes include a pump problem, a blockage, a leak somewhere along the loop, very high draw off at the dosing points, or the back pressure valve failing open.

Reading it with discharge pressure helps: discharge high with return low points to a restriction; both low points to the pump or a big leak.

With cyanide, a leak is a serious hazard. Any field check must follow the site cyanide procedures and the HCN gas monitor warnings, never shortcuts.

f.q: How does discharge pressure help tell a blockage from a leak?
f.a:
Think of the ringmain as a pump feeding a pipe circuit with a pressure regulator at the end.

A blockage partway round adds resistance: the pump sees higher discharge pressure while the return side, downstream of the blockage, drops.

A large leak gives an easy path out: the pump runs further out on its curve, so discharge pressure falls along with return pressure.

A failing pump also lowers both, so check motor current and tank level too. A tank level dropping faster than the metered dosing would explain is a strong sign of a leak.
f: How does a pump curve explain the pressure changes?
Why does tank level help confirm a leak?
What would a back pressure valve failure look like?

f.q: What happens at the dosing points if ringmain pressure drops?
f.a:
Each dosing valve needs a pressure difference to push the reagent through. If loop pressure falls, the flow controllers open their valves further to hold setpoint. Once a valve is fully open, the flow falls below setpoint and the deviation alarms come up.

The farthest points or those at higher elevation fail first, because they see the lowest pressure.

For cyanide in CIL4 that means underdosing leach tanks, which the cyanide analyser would then see as low free cyanide. Gold extraction suffers if it is not fixed quickly.
f: Which CIL4 tanks would lose cyanide first?
How fast would the cyanide analyser see a shortfall?
What does the CRO do while waiting for repairs?

f.q: What safety steps apply before checking a cyanide ringmain leak?
f.a:
The reference notes HCN gas monitors in cyanide areas with beacons and sirens. Beyond that the detailed response is a site procedure, so treat this as general guidance only.

Typically you would not approach a suspected cyanide leak alone or without the required PPE and gas monitoring. You report it to the control room, follow the area's cyanide emergency procedure, and only trained people do any isolation work under the permit system.

Never try to bypass alarms or isolations to keep dosing going. Ask the shift supervisor or the site emergency response team for the exact procedure.
f: What PPE is normally required in cyanide areas?
Where are the HCN gas monitors located in CIL4?
How is a cyanide spill cleaned up on site?

How are cyanide and caustic distributed?.q: How do individual dosing point flowmeters help isolate a ringmain leak?
How are cyanide and caustic distributed?.a:
Flowmeters at each dosing point let you do a running mass balance on the loop. The tank level shows what is actually leaving the system, while the dosing meters show what is being used on purpose. If tank consumption is higher than the sum of metered dosing, the difference is going somewhere unmetered, which suggests a leak.

The location narrows down further. A flow reading that jumps at one point without any setpoint change suggests a leak downstream of that meter, such as a split hose or failed fitting.

It is the same logic as finding leaks in a compressed air network by comparing compressor output with the metered users.

f.q: Can tank level drop be used to check total ringmain use?
f.a:
Yes, in general. Over a steady period, the volume drop in the storage tank (level change times tank area) should match the sum of the dosing point flows, as long as no tanker is unloading and nothing else draws from the tank.

The reference confirms tanker unloading is a manual field job, so you would exclude those periods.

Short term the check is noisy because level readings move with temperature and agitation, so it works better over hours than minutes. It is a good independent check on both leaks and drifting flowmeters.
f: How often is the cyanide tank refilled from tankers?
Why does level measurement get noisy in reagent tanks?
Could temperature change the apparent tank volume?

f.q: Why would one dosing flow read high without a setpoint change?
f.a:
If the flow controller is in Auto, it holds its setpoint, so a high reading usually means the controller is not in control: it is in Manual, or the valve has failed open or is passing.

The other possibility is a leak downstream of the meter, such as a split hose or broken fitting between the meter and the injection point. The extra reagent passes through the meter but never reaches the process.

A meter fault, such as a build up on the electrodes of a mag flowmeter, can also give a false high. A field check settles which it is.
f: How does build up affect a magnetic flowmeter reading?
What does a passing control valve look like on a trend?
Why put the flowmeter close to the injection point?

f.q: Who should walk the line if a ringmain leak is suspected?
f.a:
The reference does not name roles for this. On most gold plants, the area field operator does the first inspection, but only with the PPE, gas monitoring and buddy rules the cyanide or caustic area requires, and after telling the control room.

Any repair or isolation goes through maintenance under a permit.

For the exact responsibilities at FIM, ask the shift supervisor or the reagents area supervisor.

How are reagent lines labelled in the field?
Who signs off a ringmain repair before restart?

Why does the caustic tank have an immers.q: Why does concentrated caustic crystallise instead of just getting more viscous?
Why does the caustic tank have an immers.a:
Concentrated caustic soda solution is not a single liquid that simply thickens as it cools. It is sodium hydroxide dissolved in water near its solubility limit. As temperature drops, the solution can no longer hold that much NaOH, and solid sodium hydroxide hydrate crystals form. That is a phase change, like water turning to ice or wax coming out of diesel in winter.

For the common 50 percent strength the crystallisation point is around 12 C, which is general industry data, not a plant figure. The reference does not give the site concentration.

Crystals settle in the tank, block strainers and choke small lines, which is why the tank is heated.

f.q: What caustic concentration is delivered to site?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not state the caustic concentration. It only says caustic is distributed by a pressurised ringmain and the tank has an immersion heater that switches on below about 20 C and off above about 25 C.

The heater suggests a strong solution, since dilute caustic does not crystallise at normal winter temperatures, but that is an inference.

Check the reagent PDC section or ask the reagents area supervisor or the metallurgist for the supplied strength.
f: Why does the freezing point depend on concentration?
Is caustic diluted on site before dosing?
Where is caustic used in the CIL4 circuit?

f.q: Would diluting caustic avoid the freezing problem?
f.a:
In general, yes. Caustic at lower concentrations has a much lower crystallisation point, so a dilute solution would not need heating in a winter.

The trade off is volume. Diluting means more tank space, more truck deliveries or a dilution system, and bigger pumps for the same amount of NaOH. Some processes also need the strong solution, such as the caustic cyanide pre-soak in elution.

So sites often store it strong and heat it, which is cheaper than handling the extra water. The FIM design choice is not explained in the reference.
f: How much caustic does the elution pre-soak use?
Why does caustic give off heat when it is diluted?
What PPE is needed when handling strong caustic?

f.q: Do the caustic lines need heat tracing as well as the tank heater?
f.a:
The reference only mentions the immersion heater in the tank. It does not say whether the ringmain lines are traced or lagged.

In general, a continuously circulating ringmain helps a lot, because moving warm liquid from the heated tank keeps the lines warmer than stagnant pipework. Dead legs and small bore dosing lines are the usual weak spots, and some sites trace those.

Check the reagent P&IDs for trace heating symbols, or ask the electrical or reagents area maintenance planner.
f: Why is a dead leg more likely to freeze?
How is trace heating normally controlled?
What does lagging do on a pipe in cold weather?

Why does the caustic tank have an immers.q: What would you see in the field if the caustic tank heater failed in winter?
Why does the caustic tank have an immers.a:
The tank would cool toward ambient overnight, and once it passed the crystallisation point you would start to get solid caustic settling on the tank floor and walls.

In the field that shows up as the ringmain pump losing flow or cavitating as the suction strainer blocks, low ringmain pressures, dosing point flowmeters reading low and small lines choking. The OIS would likely show a low tank temperature as well, if that alarm is configured.

Downstream, processes that use caustic, such as the elution caustic cyanide pre-soak, would be short.

Winter nights on site can get close to freezing, so this is a realistic risk, not a theoretical one.

f.q: Which processes would suffer first if caustic stopped flowing?
f.a:
From the reference, caustic is used in the split AARL elution pre-soak, where carbon is soaked in caustic and cyanide before stripping. Without it, elution efficiency drops and more gold stays on the carbon going back to the circuit.

Caustic may also be used for pH adjustment in other spots, but the main CIL pH control uses milk of lime, so the leach itself would keep running.

The exact list of caustic users is in the reagent P&IDs; the metallurgist would know which matter most on the day.
f: Why does the pre-soak need caustic as well as cyanide?
What happens to gold left on carbon after a poor strip?
Can an elution run be delayed if caustic is short?

f.q: How do you safely recover crystallised caustic in a tank?
f.a:
The reference does not give a procedure, and this is not something to improvise. Strong caustic causes severe burns, and heating or diluting it releases heat.

In general, recovery means slowly reheating the tank so the crystals redissolve, with circulation once the pump can run safely, and inspecting strainers and lines afterwards. Any line clearing or strainer work is done under isolation and permit with the right PPE.

Ask the reagents area supervisor or the maintenance planner for the site method.
f: Why does dissolving caustic release heat?
What isolations are needed to clean a caustic strainer?
How long would reheating a full caustic tank take?

f.q: How would you test that the immersion heater is working?
f.a:
The simplest check is the trend. On the PI historian, tank temperature should flatten out or rise once it drops below about 20 C, and the heater should switch off around 25 C. A temperature that keeps falling with the heater called on suggests a fault.

An electrician can check the heater current at the starter or MCC, which confirms it is actually drawing power.

Those setpoints are design values confirmed at commissioning, so check the live values with the control room. Any electrical testing must be done by qualified people under the site isolation rules.
f: How do you find the heater's run status on the OIS?
What makes an immersion heater element fail?
Why check heater current rather than just the run signal?

Why does the caustic tank have an immers.q: Why is there a temperature deadband instead of a single on/off setpoint?
Why does the caustic tank have an immers.a:
A single setpoint would make the heater switch on and off every time the temperature crossed it, which could be many times an hour. That wears out contactors and heater elements and gives no real benefit.

With a deadband (on below about 20 C, off above about 25 C) the heater runs for a decent period, warms the tank, then stays off until the tank cools by several degrees. It is the same hysteresis a home thermostat or a compressor pressure switch uses.

The 20 and 25 C values are design figures to be confirmed during commissioning, so the live settings may differ.

f.q: What does short cycling do to contactor and heater life?
f.a:
Every time a contactor closes on load, its contacts arc slightly and wear. Contactors are rated for a set number of operations, so switching every few minutes uses that up quickly.

The heater element also suffers from repeated heating and cooling, which flexes the sheath and the internal wire and can lead to cracking.

It is like a motor that is started far too often: the starts, not the running hours, end up deciding its life.
f: How many operations is a typical contactor rated for?
Why does thermal cycling crack heater elements?
Would a solid state relay avoid contact wear?

f.q: Why switch the heater on at 20 C if caustic freezes lower?
f.a:
It gives margin. The tank temperature reading is at one point, but the tank floor, walls and connected lines can be colder, especially overnight. Starting at 20 C keeps the coldest spots well clear of crystallisation.

Heating a big tank also takes time, so you want to begin before you are close to the limit, just as you start a standby pump before the duty one has fully failed.

The exact crystallisation point depends on the strength supplied, which the reference does not give.
f: Where in a tank does the coldest liquid usually sit?
How long does a heater take to recover the tank?
Does the tank have an agitator to mix the heat?

f.q: Could a PID controlled heater do better than simple on/off?
f.a:
It could hold temperature tighter, using a thyristor controller to vary power. But the task here is just keeping caustic above its crystallisation point, not holding a precise temperature, so a 5 degree band is perfectly adequate.

On/off is simpler, cheaper and easy to maintain, with fewer things to fail. Proportional control is worth it when the process is sensitive to temperature, such as an elution heater, where the eluate temperature directly affects the strip.

So the choice matches the duty, as you would pick a simple relief valve over a servo valve where precision is not needed.
f: How is the CIL4 elution temperature controlled?
What is a thyristor power controller?
When does on/off control become a problem?

What does the flotation tails thickener.q: Why does the vendor panel run rakes locally instead of from the DCS?
What does the flotation tails thickener.a:
The reference says the rakes and rake lift are run from the field panel in local mode, while the vendor panel passes signals such as rake torque, bed level, rake height, bed pressure and overflow clarity to the DCS.

The reasons are mostly general. The rake drive and lift are a vendor package with its own torque protection built in, and they are tuned and warrantied as a unit. Lifting or lowering rakes is an operation where you want someone at the thickener who can see and hear what is happening.

The DCS still monitors the thickener and handles the underflow pumps and flocculant, so control of the process stays central.

f.q: Does the DCS get a signal if the thickener rakes stop?
f.a:
The reference lists rake torque among the vendor panel signals to the DCS, and the restart sequences include checks on the thickener rakes, so the DCS knows the rake status.

It does not detail whether a rake stop trips the underflow pumps or the feed. In general, a stopped rake is serious because the bed can set solid, so sites alarm it urgently and stop or reduce feed while it is sorted out.

For the exact interlocks, check the thickener control philosophy or ask the CRO.
f: How long can thickener rakes stay stopped safely?
Why do restart sequences check the rakes first?
What does a bogged thickener take to recover?

f.q: What does rake lift do when torque climbs too high?
f.a:
In general, rake lift raises the rake arms out of the densest part of the bed when torque passes a set level, reducing the load on the drive. As torque falls the rakes lower again. At a higher torque the drive will cut out to protect the gearbox.

It works like a torque limiting coupling on a conveyor drive, protecting the mechanical parts while the process is corrected.

The reference confirms rake height is a vendor panel signal and rake lift is run from the field panel, but the exact torque settings are vendor specific.
f: What causes thickener rake torque to rise slowly?
Why can lifting the rakes too far cause problems?
Who sets the vendor torque limits?

f.q: Who runs the rake panel during a thickener restart?
f.a:
The reference only says the rakes and rake lift are operated from the field panel in local mode, and that the DCS restart sequences check the thickener rakes.

That implies a field operator at the thickener working with the CRO, who controls the underflow pumps and flocculant from the OIS. The CRO waits for the rakes to be running before releasing the rest of the restart.

For the exact steps and who signs off, ask the thickener area operator or the shift supervisor.
f: Why start the rakes before the underflow pumps?
What does the CRO check before restarting thickener feed?
How are rake panel faults reported to the DCS?

What does the flotation tails thickener.q: What would rising rake torque with steady bed level suggest is happening?
What does the flotation tails thickener.a:
Rake torque is the load on the drive from dragging the rakes through the bed. If torque rises while bed level stays steady, the bed is getting harder to rake, not higher.

Likely causes: the bed is compacting and getting denser (higher bed mass for the same height), coarse or sandy material is building up, an island or ring of solids is forming, or something such as scale or debris is fouling the rakes. Lower underflow draw also leaves more solids to consolidate.

Check bed pressure, underflow density and flow trends. Bed pressure rising with steady level is the classic sign of compaction.

f.q: What is a thickener 'island' or 'doughnut' and why is it bad?
f.a:
An island or doughnut is a mound of consolidated solids that forms on the floor and rotates with the rakes rather than being moved to the underflow cone. It grows over time because the rakes ride over it rather than through it.

It raises rake torque, reduces effective thickener volume and can eventually stall the drive or force the rakes to lift.

The usual causes are coarse material, poor rake speed or too little underflow draw. It is a bit like a sediment ridge in a settling tank that the scraper keeps riding over.
f: How is a thickener island usually broken up?
Why does coarse material make islands more likely?
Can bed pressure detect an island forming?

f.q: How would underflow flow changes relate to the rising torque?
f.a:
If underflow draw is reduced, perhaps because the density loop is holding back flow, more solids stay in the thickener. The bed gets heavier and denser, and torque rises.

The cascade control (bed pressure or density setting the flow setpoint) is meant to catch this, increasing flow as bed mass rises. If the pump is at its limit, or the line is partly blocked, it cannot, and torque keeps climbing.

So look at whether the underflow flow controller is at maximum output. That tells you the pump is the limit rather than the control.
f: What limits the underflow pump's maximum flow?
Why can a denser underflow be harder to pump?
When does the standby underflow pump start?

f.q: When would rakes be lifted rather than pumping harder?
f.a:
In general, rake lift is the vendor's protection when torque passes a set limit; it is automatic or done by the field operator from the local panel. It buys time, but it is not a fix.

Pumping harder is the process fix: pulling more solids out reduces bed mass. Usually both happen together: rakes lift to save the drive while the CRO increases underflow draw.

The reference does not detail the torque limits or response steps; the thickener area operator or metallurgist would know the site practice.
f: How quickly can increased pumping cut bed mass?
What risk comes from leaving rakes lifted too long?
Is floc dose changed during high torque events?

What does the flotation tails thickener.q: Why measure bed pressure as well as bed level if a SmartDiver gives both?
What does the flotation tails thickener.a:
A small correction first: the reference says bed level is measured by a SmartDiver or Manta sub, and lists bed pressure (bed mass) as a separate vendor panel signal. It does not say the SmartDiver gives both.

The two measure different things. Bed level is the height of the interface between clear liquid and settled solids. Bed pressure is the weight of solids above the floor, which depends on density as well as height.

The same level can hold very different inventory if the bed compacts. It is like knowing a tank's level but not the fluid's density: hydrostatic pressure tells you the mass, level alone does not.

f.q: Why is bed mass a better variable for underflow density?
f.a:
Underflow density comes from how compressed the bed is at the bottom. A heavier bed squeezes more water out, so bed mass (bed pressure) links closely to the density you can pull.

Bed level can rise with a fluffy, poorly flocculated bed that holds lots of water, giving a false sense of inventory.

That is why the underflow pump cascade uses bed pressure or underflow density as the master, not level. The flotation tails thickener design underflow is about 56 percent solids (range 50 to 62), a design value, not a live reading.
f: What makes a thickener bed fluffy instead of compact?
How does a bed pressure transmitter work?
Why does CIL4 care about underflow density?

f.q: How does a SmartDiver actually find the bed interface?
f.a:
In general terms, a SmartDiver is a sensor lowered on a cable into the thickener. It moves down through the liquid, using a sensor such as an optical or ultrasonic detector to find where clear water changes to dense slurry, and reports the depth. It then retracts and repeats.

A Manta sub, also named in the reference, is another bed level sensor.

Exact sensing principles vary by vendor and model, so check the vendor manual for details on the units installed.
f: What can foul a submerged bed level sensor?
Why do sensors retract between readings?
How often is the bed level updated on the DCS?

f.q: What would falling bed level with rising bed pressure mean?
f.a:
It means the bed is compacting: the same or more solids squeezed into a smaller height, with water forced out.

That usually comes with higher underflow density and often higher rake torque. Causes include good flocculation, time for consolidation, or reduced underflow draw.

It is mostly fine if rake torque stays acceptable, and it suits CIL4, which wants a dense feed. But if torque climbs too, it can be the start of bogging, so the CRO would raise underflow flow.
f: How much rake torque margin is normal?
Why does a dense feed help CIL4 residence time?
Can bed compaction be too fast?

How is thickener underflow pumping contr.q: Why cascade off bed pressure or density rather than controlling flow alone?
How is thickener underflow pumping contr.a:
The goal of a thickener is to hold inventory and deliver dense underflow, about 56 percent solids at design (range 50 to 62) for CIL4. Flow alone tells you nothing about either; you could pump a steady flow while the bed empties or builds up.

So bed pressure or underflow density acts as the slow master loop and sets the flow setpoint. The fast flow loop drives the pump VSD to hold that setpoint, quickly rejecting pump wear, line resistance and head changes.

Mechanically it is like a cascade where tank temperature sets the steam flow setpoint: the outer loop holds the process target, the inner loop handles fast disturbances.

f.q: When would bed pressure be chosen over density as the master?
f.a:
The reference allows either. In general, density is the direct target because it is what CIL4 receives. But a nucleonic density gauge can be off with build up or calibration drift, and density reacts after the fact.

Bed pressure gives an earlier view of inventory and helps protect against bogging the rakes. Some sites run bed pressure normally and use density as a limit, or switch masters when one instrument is in doubt.

The metallurgist or control engineer decides which is in use on the day, so check with the CRO.
f: How does build up affect a nucleonic density gauge?
Can both masters be used together with a selector?
Who decides which master loop is active?

f.q: What happens to CIL4 if underflow density drops for a shift?
f.a:
Lower density means more water with the same solids, so more volume flows into CIL4. CIL4 residence time is already tight at design: about 12.8 hours total against an ideal of 14 hours. More volume shortens it further, which can cut gold extraction.

Reagent concentrations also dilute, so more cyanide and lime are needed for the same targets. Process water balance changes too.

These are design figures, not live values, but they show why underflow density matters downstream.
f: How does residence time affect CIL4 extraction?
Why does lower density need more cyanide?
Does CIL4 have a way to recover lost residence time?

f.q: Why have duty and standby underflow pumps on VSDs?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation tails thickener has duty/standby underflow pumps, about 3,329 m3/h total. If the underflow stops, the bed builds and the rakes can bog within hours, so a standby pump is essential.

VSDs let the flow controller vary pump speed to match the cascade setpoint, avoiding a control valve in an abrasive slurry line, which would wear quickly.

It is the same thinking as variable speed fans rather than dampers: less energy, less wear and better control.
f: How is standby pump changeover handled?
Why do control valves wear fast in slurry?
What does underflow pump gland water protect?

How is thickener underflow pumping contr.q: What would you see on the OIS if underflow density read too low?
How is thickener underflow pumping contr.a:
If underflow density reads low, the master controller sees less dense slurry than it wants and cuts the flow setpoint. On the OIS you would see the density PV below SV, the flow setpoint falling and the pump VSD slowing.

If it keeps reading low, flow can approach the minimum and the recycle to feed might come into play.

The causes can be real or instrument. Real: low bed inventory, rat holing (water channelling through the bed), or low flocculant. Instrument: a nucleonic density gauge fault. Compare with bed pressure and bed level trends before acting.

f.q: What is rat holing in a thickener underflow?
f.a:
Rat holing is when the underflow pump draws a channel of thin slurry or water through the bed rather than pulling evenly from the dense layer. The bed around the channel stays put while the pump sucks diluted material from above.

It shows up as a sudden drop in underflow density with bed level and bed pressure still high.

It usually follows pumping too hard for the bed's compaction state, or poor rake action around the cone. The fix is generally to slow the draw and let the bed reconsolidate.
f: How do rakes help prevent rat holing?
Why does rat holing happen more at high draw rates?
Can rat holing damage the underflow pump?

f.q: How would you tell a bad density gauge from a real low density?
f.a:
Cross check. If bed pressure and bed level are steady or high while density reads low, suspect rat holing or the gauge. If bed pressure is also falling, the bed really is emptying.

Pump motor current rises with denser slurry at the same speed and flow, so steady current with a falling density reading points to the instrument.

A manual sample, weighed on a density scale, gives a direct check. Nucleonic gauges are radiation sources, so only licensed people work on them.
f: Why does pump current change with slurry density?
How is a slurry density sample taken safely?
Who is licensed to work on nucleonic gauges?

f.q: What limits how slowly the underflow pump can safely run?
f.a:
Slurry lines need a minimum velocity to keep solids suspended. Below that settling velocity, solids drop out along the pipe floor, the line sands up and the pump can block.

So there is a minimum flow or speed. When demand falls below it, the underflow recycle to feed keeps the line moving without draining the bed. Dump valves that fail open on power loss do a similar job on a trip.

The actual minimum is set during commissioning; ask the CRO or control engineer.
f: What decides a slurry pipe's settling velocity?
Why do dump valves fail open on power loss?
How is minimum flow protected in the DCS?

How is thickener underflow pumping contr.q: Why recycle underflow to feed instead of just slowing the rakes?
How is thickener underflow pumping contr.a:
Recycling solves a pipe problem, not a rake problem. The underflow line needs a minimum flow to stop solids settling and sanding it up. If you simply cut flow during start up, shutdown or low throughput, you would either drain the bed or block the line.

Recycling sends underflow back to the feed, so the line keeps moving while the solids stay in the thickener, holding bed mass.

The rakes need to keep turning regardless. Slowing them would let the bed consolidate and increase torque. It is the same idea as a minimum flow recirculation line on a centrifugal pump.

f.q: What happens to a slurry line if flow stops with solids in it?
f.a:
Solids settle to the bottom of the pipe and pack down. On restart the pump faces a plug, and in a long line it might not be able to push it through, ending in a blocked line that has to be flushed or dismantled.

That is why slurry pumps have dump valves that fail open on power loss, and why minimum flows and flush sequences are built into restart logic.

It is like letting sand settle in a hose: easy to prevent, hard to clear once packed.
f: How long does slurry take to settle in a stopped line?
How is a blocked slurry line normally cleared?
Why do restart sequences include flushing steps?

f.q: How is the underflow recycle valve opened: by sequence or the CRO?
f.a:
The reference only says the underflow can recycle to the feed during start up, shutdown or low flow. It does not detail whether that is automatic in the sequence, triggered by low flow logic, or a CRO action.

In general, plants put the recycle into the start and stop sequences and may also open it automatically on low flow, with the CRO able to select it.

For the exact logic, check the thickener control philosophy or ask the CRO.
f: What would trigger an automatic recycle on low flow?
Can recycle be left on during normal running?
How does the OIS show the recycle valve position?

f.q: Does recycling underflow change the bed level over time?
f.a:
Yes, generally. With underflow recycled, no solids leave the thickener, but feed keeps coming in if the plant is running. The bed builds up and bed pressure rises, which is fine for a short time and useful on start up to rebuild inventory.

If it goes on too long, bed mass and rake torque climb, so recycle has to end and underflow has to go forward to CIL4.

It is a holding pattern, like recirculating a hydraulic pump to tank while the actuators wait.
f: How long can recycle run before torque becomes a risk?
Why rebuild bed mass before sending underflow forward?
What does CIL4 do while thickener underflow is on recycle?

How is flocculant dosing controlled on t.q: Why split flocculant dosing into two different control strategies?
How is flocculant dosing controlled on t.a:
It is not two strategies running side by side. It changed between project stages. In Stage 1, flocculant dosing was cascaded from bed level, measured by a Manta sub. In Stage 2, it runs to a flocculant to feed solids ratio setpoint.

The reasons are not explained in the reference, but in general a ratio is feedforward: floc follows the solids coming in, so the dose responds immediately to throughput changes. Bed level feedback is slow and can overdose to drive the level down.

In Stage 2 all flotation tails thickener underflow goes to CIL4, so steady, predictable operation matters more. Bed mass is handled by the underflow pump cascade.

f.q: Where does the feed solids tonnage for the floc ratio come from?
f.a:
The reference does not name the instrument. Generally a thickener feed tonnage is calculated from a magnetic flowmeter and density gauge with an entered solids SG, the same slurry mass flow method used across the plant.

Feed to this thickener is about 3,071 t/h at 33 percent solids at design, from scavenger tails plus cleaner-scavenger tails.

Check the F17 P&ID for the actual feed instruments, or ask the control systems engineer.
f: Why do thickener feed density gauges need regular checks?
How is the feed SG value kept current?
What happens to floc dosing if the feed meter fails?

f.q: Can bed level still trim the floc ratio in Stage 2?
f.a:
The reference does not say. It describes Stage 2 floc control as a ratio to feed solids, with bed level still measured and shown on the vendor panel.

In general, many plants run a ratio with a slow trim from bed level or overflow clarity so the dose adapts to ore changes. Whether FIM does this is a control configuration question.

Ask the control systems engineer or the CRO what the live strategy is.
f: What would a slow bed level trim do to the dose?
Why can bed level feedback overdose floc?
How does ore type change floc demand?

f.q: What units is a floc ratio setpoint usually in?
f.a:
Normally grams of flocculant per tonne of dry feed solids (g/t), the same way other reagent doses are set in this plant through a calculation block that turns g/t into a flow setpoint.

Because floc is made up as a dilute solution, the calculation also needs the solution strength to convert grams of dry floc into litres of solution.

The actual g/t target is not in the condensed reference; the metallurgist sets it.
f: How is flocculant solution strength controlled?
Why is floc made up as a dilute solution?
What does a typical floc plant consist of?

How is flocculant dosing controlled on t.q: What would overdosed flocculant look like in the thickener overflow?
How is flocculant dosing controlled on t.a:
Counterintuitively, overdosing does not give an even clearer overflow. Excess floc can form loose, fluffy aggregates and leave unadsorbed polymer in the water. Overflow clarity can actually get worse, with fine floc carried over, and the overflow may look slightly viscous or stringy.

At FIM this matters a lot because the overflow mainly feeds the Process Water Tank. Residual floc returns to grinding and flotation, where it can hurt froth behaviour and recovery.

In the thickener, overdosing also builds a dense, sticky bed that raises rake torque and is harder to pump. It is wasted reagent with knock on costs.

f.q: How does residual floc in process water affect flotation?
f.a:
Flocculant is a long chain polymer designed to bridge particles together. If it comes back in process water, it can flocculate fine particles in the flotation feed, trap gangue in the froth and change froth stability.

The result can be lower concentrate grade or recovery, harder to control froth and odd OSA readings.

Since process water at FIM is mostly flotation tails thickener overflow, floc dose and overflow quality are directly linked to flotation performance.
f: Why does process water recycle make reagent build up?
How would the metallurgist detect floc in process water?
Can bore water top up dilute residual floc?

f.q: Why does overdosed floc raise rake torque?
f.a:
Too much floc makes the aggregates bind into a stiffer, stickier network. The bed resists shearing, so the rakes need more torque to move through it, and the underflow can become more viscous and harder to pump.

The bed may also hold more water than a well flocculated one, giving a misleading bed level.

It is like adding too much thickener to paint: it stops flowing nicely and takes more effort to stir.
f: How does bed rheology affect underflow pumping?
Can high torque be fixed by cutting floc alone?
Why can an overdosed bed hold more water?

f.q: How is overflow clarity measured on the vendor panel?
f.a:
The reference lists overflow clarity as one of the vendor panel signals but does not say how it is measured.

In general, clarity is measured with a turbidity sensor or a clarity meter that sends light through the overflow and measures scattering or absorption, giving a reading related to suspended solids.

Check the thickener vendor manual or ask the instrument technician for the actual device.
f: What fouls a turbidity sensor in thickener overflow?
How is overflow clarity used in floc control?
Why does overflow solids content matter for process water?

How is flocculant dosing controlled on t.q: Why dilute flocculant again just before the thickener, not dose it neat?
How is flocculant dosing controlled on t.a:
Flocculant is made up as a viscous polymer solution. Concentrated solution does not spread well through a large slurry stream; it forms lumps, and much of the polymer never contacts particles, so you need more of it.

Diluting it again in an inline mixer just before the thickener gives a thinner solution that disperses quickly and evenly into the feed. The particles bind more uniformly, so you get better settling with less reagent.

It is like atomising fuel in a burner: the same fuel, but finer distribution gives much better combustion. Neat floc would be like pouring fuel in a puddle.

f.q: What water is used for the secondary floc dilution?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not state the dilution water source for the inline mixer.

In general, floc make up prefers clean water because salts can reduce polymer performance, but secondary dilution often uses process water for practical reasons. FIM process water is saline (SG about 1.07).

Check the F17 P&ID or ask the metallurgist which water is used and whether it affects floc consumption.
f: How does saline water affect flocculant performance?
Where is the floc plant located relative to the thickener?
Why is clean water preferred for floc make up?

f.q: Why not make floc weaker at the floc plant instead?
f.a:
Weaker solution would need much more storage and much bigger pumping, since you would be moving mostly water from the plant to the thickener.

Dilute floc solution also has a limited life and can degrade with time and shear, so storing it ready diluted is not ideal.

Making up a moderate strength solution and diluting at the point of use keeps tanks and pumps small and the floc fresh. It is the same reason concentrated chemicals are delivered and diluted locally.
f: How long does made up floc solution stay effective?
What does the floc plant's wetting head do?
Why does shear damage flocculant chains?

f.q: How do you know flocculant is being sheared too much?
f.a:
Polymer chains break if they pass through high shear, such as tight valves or fast pumps. Broken chains lose bridging power, so settling slows and overflow clarity drops even though the dose looks normal.

The signs are rising floc consumption for the same result, poorer overflow and a fluffy bed.

Mixers and pumps are chosen to limit shear. The metallurgist can check by comparing settling tests on floc sampled before and after the mixer.
f: Why are low shear pumps used for flocculant?
How is a cylinder settling test done?
Can inline mixers be adjusted for shear?

UFG feed hopper water addition does two.q: Why does an IsaMill heat up more than a conventional ball mill?
UFG feed hopper water addition does two.a:
An IsaMill is a horizontal stirred mill. The UFG 2 and 3 mills draw about 3.5 MW each into a fairly small chamber, spinning discs that stir fine ceramic media at high speed. Almost all that energy ends up as heat in the slurry.

The specific energy is high: about 116.5 kWh/t at design to reach P80 9 um, compared with about 9.68 kWh/t for the ball mill at 180 um. Grinding to ultrafine sizes takes a lot of energy per tonne, packed into a small volume.

It is like running a large hydraulic pump against a relief valve into a small reservoir: the oil heats up fast.

f.q: Why does finer grinding take so much more energy per tonne?
f.a:
Breaking particles creates new surface, and the surface grows fast as size drops. Halving particle size roughly doubles the surface area per tonne, and you need energy to break each new bond.

Small particles are also harder to catch between media, so many collisions do little useful work.

Empirical laws such as Bond's show energy rising steeply as target size falls. Going from about 180 um in the ball mill to about 9 um in the IsaMill needs over ten times the energy per tonne on these design figures.
f: What does the Bond work index measure?
Why does ultrafine gold need such fine grinding?
How is IsaMill grinding efficiency judged?

f.q: What gets damaged if an IsaMill runs too hot?
f.a:
In general, heat attacks the softer parts. Mill liners and discs on stirred mills are often rubber or polyurethane, which soften and wear faster when hot. Shaft seals and bearings also suffer.

Hot slurry can change the chemistry downstream, and may affect leach and pump seal performance.

That is why the UFG feed hopper adds water to cool the mill when discharge exceeds 60 C, which is the design value. Which parts are most sensitive on this model is vendor information.
f: What materials are IsaMill discs made from?
How is IsaMill shaft seal life monitored?
Does hot slurry affect the downstream cyclones?

f.q: What water is added to the UFG feed hopper?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not say which water type goes to the UFG feed hopper. It does say scheme water is used for gland seals in UFG.

Possible sources are process water or another plant water service, but that is a guess, not a fact from the documents.

Check the F28 P&ID or ask the UFG area operator or metallurgist which water is used.
f: Why is scheme water used for UFG gland seals?
How does saline water affect fine grinding?
What other water services feed UFG?

UFG feed hopper water addition does two.q: What would you see on the OIS if discharge temperature crept toward 60 degrees?
UFG feed hopper water addition does two.a:
You would see the mill discharge temperature trend climbing toward 60 C, which is the design trigger. As it does, the feed hopper water addition shifts from holding feed solids to cooling: the water valve opens further, and feed density drops.

The feed pump stays on flow control, so more water means less solids at the same flow. Power draw may change as feed density changes, and the media addition loop responds to hold its power setpoint.

There would likely be a high temperature alarm. Remember 60 C is a design value from the control philosophy; check the live setting with the CRO.

f.q: What if adding water doesn't stop the temperature rising?
f.a:
The reference does not describe a temperature trip or the next step. It mentions hardwired motor interlocks and shell vibration monitoring on the mill.

In general, if cooling fails the CRO would reduce power by cutting media addition or reducing feed, and the mill would ultimately be stopped before damage. A trip on high temperature is common on stirred mills.

For the actual trip settings and response, ask the CRO or the UFG area metallurgist.
f: How fast does IsaMill discharge temperature respond?
What hardwired interlocks protect the IsaMill motor?
Who decides to stop a UFG mill on high temperature?

f.q: Why would mill discharge temperature creep up at all?
f.a:
Common reasons: power draw rising (more media or denser feed), lower slurry flow through the mill so the same energy goes into less slurry, hotter feed or water in summer, or higher ambient temperature.

It is a simple heat balance: temperature rise equals power in divided by the slurry's mass flow and heat capacity. Cut the flow or raise the power and the temperature climbs.

Summer heat on site makes this more likely in warmer months.
f: How does feed density change the heat capacity?
Does recirculating cyclone underflow add heat?
How does ambient temperature affect cooling?

f.q: How does lower feed density affect IsaMill grinding?
f.a:
In stirred mills, solids concentration matters. Diluting the feed means fewer particles between the media, so more collisions do no useful work. Higher volumetric flow also shortens residence time.

The result is usually a coarser product at the same power. Grind target is P80 9 um (9 to 12) at design.

The online particle size analyser on UFG shows the effect, and the metallurgist balances cooling against grind.
f: How does the online particle size analyser sample?
What feed solids concentration suits an IsaMill?
How does residence time affect product size?

UFG feed hopper water addition does two.q: How does hopper water addition compete with keeping solids concentration up?
UFG feed hopper water addition does two.a:
They pull in opposite directions using the same valve. Normal duty is holding feed solids concentration for efficient grinding. Cooling duty adds extra water when discharge passes 60 C. Extra water dilutes the feed, so the mill grinds less efficiently and the product gets coarser.

So when temperature is high, cooling wins and grind suffers a bit. In control terms that is usually done with an override or high select, where the cooling demand takes over the water valve from the density loop.

The reference does not describe the selector logic in detail, so check the control philosophy for the exact arrangement.
