f.q: What is a high select override in a control loop?
f.a:
Two controllers both want to drive one valve. A high select block passes the larger output to the valve. Here, the density loop asks for some water to hold feed solids; the temperature loop asks for more when temperature is high. Whichever wants more water wins.

It is the same as a boiler where a pressure override takes over feed control near limits.

The losing controller must have anti windup so it does not run away while overridden.
f: What is integral windup in a PID controller?
Why use a low select on some overrides?
How does the OIS show which loop is in control?

f.q: How would a coarser UFG product hurt concentrate leach recovery?
f.a:
Much of the gold is locked in sulphides, mainly pyrite, and tellurides. UFG grinds the concentrate to about 9 um so cyanide can reach that gold in CIL2.

A coarser product leaves more gold locked inside particles cyanide cannot reach, so extraction falls. Design concentrate leach extraction is about 90 percent for CIL2/3.

Since the concentrate carries most of the plant's gold, small grind losses can cost real ounces.
f: Why is FIM ore described as refractory?
How does CIL2 handle high cyanide demand?
What fraction of gold reports to concentrate?

f.q: Does the online particle size analyser help the CRO here?
f.a:
Yes. The reference lists an online particle size analyser on UFG. It lets the CRO and metallurgist see the effect of feed density or cooling water on product size, rather than waiting for lab results.

If cooling is making the product coarse, they can respond, for example by adjusting power, feed rate or media, or by addressing the cause of the heat.

Analyser readings need checking against lab sizing periodically.
f: How often is the UFG analyser checked against the lab?
What does UFG cyclone overflow solids show?
Can feed rate be cut to improve grind?

How is IsaMill media added?.q: Why control on mill power draw instead of dosing media on a fixed rate?
How is IsaMill media added?.a:
Mill power draw is a direct measure of grinding work being done, and in an IsaMill it rises with the amount of media in the chamber. Media wears away continuously, so a fixed dosing rate would let the charge drift up or down over time.

Controlling on power means the knife gate valve adds media only when needed to hold the setpoint, keeping the mill working at its intended intensity. Design draw is about 3.5 MW on the 3.8 MW installed motor.

It is like holding a gearbox at rated torque by feedback rather than guessing the load: you use the motor to tell you what is happening inside.

f.q: How fast does ceramic media wear in a UFG mill?
f.a:
The condensed reference only says UFG uses ceramic media. It does not give consumption rates.

In general, stirred mill media wears by attrition, and consumption is expressed in grams per kWh or grams per tonne, depending on media quality, feed hardness and mill operation.

Ask the UFG metallurgist or the media supplier for site consumption figures.
f: How is ceramic media quality assessed?
What happens to worn media in the circuit?
Why does harder feed wear media faster?

f.q: What does the positioning knife gate do between additions?
f.a:
In general, a positioning knife gate meters media from a hopper into the mill feed. It opens partially to let media flow at a controlled rate and closes when the power setpoint is met.

Between additions it stays closed, holding back the media in the hopper.

The reference describes it as positioning, so it can open to intermediate positions rather than just open or closed. Check the vendor manual for details.
f: How is the IsaMill media hopper refilled?
What happens if the media gate sticks open?
Why use a knife gate rather than a rotary valve?

f.q: Why would the metallurgist change the power setpoint?
f.a:
Power sets grinding intensity. Raising it gives a finer product, at more energy, media and heat. Lowering it saves energy but coarsens the grind.

The design target is P80 9 um (range 9 to 12) at about 116.5 kWh/t. If feed tonnage changes, or the analyser shows product off target, the metallurgist adjusts the setpoint.

Temperature limits and motor capacity also cap how high it can go.
f: How does feed tonnage affect specific energy?
Why is the IsaMill motor rated above design draw?
What trade off does finer grind create downstream?

How is IsaMill media added?.q: What would rising IsaMill power draw with steady media addition suggest?
How is IsaMill media added?.a:
If power rises with steady media addition, something other than media is loading the mill. Likely causes: denser feed slurry, more viscous slurry, harder or coarser feed, or media accumulating in the chamber because less is leaving with the product.

Mechanical causes such as bearing drag are possible but less common.

The control loop will respond by closing the media knife gate to hold the power setpoint. If power keeps rising even with no media added, the cause is not media, and the CRO should look at feed density and flow first.

f.q: How does slurry viscosity change IsaMill power draw?
f.a:
Thicker, more viscous slurry resists the spinning discs, so the motor works harder. Power goes up even with the same media load.

Viscosity rises with solids concentration and very fine particles, and can change with ore mineralogy.

It is like a pump handling a thicker fluid: more torque needed at the same speed. That is why feed density control matters for stable power.
f: What affects slurry viscosity besides density?
Can high viscosity reduce grinding efficiency?
How is feed density measured on UFG?

f.q: What would the power loop do in response to this rise?
f.a:
It would see power above setpoint and close the media knife gate, stopping additions. As media wears, power slowly falls back.

If the rise is from feed density, closing the gate does not fix it, and power stays high. The CRO would then look at feed solids and adjust water.

That is the limit of a single loop: it only has one handle, media, so other causes need operator attention.
f: How long does it take for media wear to drop power?
Why can a single loop not fix every disturbance?
When would the CRO step in on the power loop?

f.q: Could media be building up inside the mill, and why?
f.a:
Yes. Stirred mills retain media using a separator at the discharge end. If the separator or discharge screen wears or blocks, media retention changes. A blocked outlet can cause media buildup, and with it, higher power.

Feed rate changes can also shift media distribution.

This kind of mechanical issue is something the UFG maintenance planner or vendor would diagnose during inspections.
f: How does an IsaMill product separator work?
What does worn media look like when removed?
How are IsaMill internals inspected?

How is IsaMill media added?.q: Why fit shell vibration monitoring in addition to the power control loop?
How is IsaMill media added?.a:
The power loop controls the process; vibration monitoring watches the machine. They catch different things.

Shell vibration picks up mechanical faults such as imbalance, bearing wear, loose or damaged discs and liners, or misalignment. Power draw would not show these until they were severe.

It is the same as fitting condition monitoring on a large gearbox even though its load is controlled: control keeps it working, monitoring tells you if it is breaking. The reference lists shell vibration monitoring and hardwired motor interlocks on the mill.

f.q: What faults typically show up first as shell vibration?
f.a:
In general, imbalance from uneven disc wear or broken disc pieces, bearing deterioration, loose fasteners, and misalignment between motor, gearbox and mill.

Vibration analysis can separate these by frequency: imbalance at running speed, bearing faults at specific defect frequencies.

Trending is key. A slow rise warns of wear; a sudden jump means something has broken.
f: How does vibration frequency show the fault type?
What is trended for condition monitoring?
How often are IsaMill discs replaced?

f.q: Does high shell vibration trip the IsaMill or just alarm?
f.a:
The reference does not say. It lists shell vibration monitoring and hardwired motor interlocks, but does not state whether vibration is part of the trip logic.

In general, large mills alarm on high vibration and trip on high-high.

Ask the CRO or the UFG maintenance planner what the settings and actions are.
f: Who reviews IsaMill vibration trends?
What is the usual response to a vibration alarm?
Are the vibration sensors hardwired or networked?

f.q: Why are the IsaMill starters on a vendor PLC?
f.a:
The reference says the IsaMill has liquid resistance starters on a vendor PLC, which reports to the DCS.

A liquid resistance starter limits starting current and torque on large slip ring motors, by varying resistance through an electrolyte. The vendor supplies it with its own control logic, so it is easier to keep it as a package.

Big loads like the 3.8 MW IsaMill motor need a soft start to protect the power system and drive train.
f: How does a liquid resistance starter work?
Why do large motors need soft starting?
What does the DCS see from the starter PLC?

How is CIL4 pH controlled?.q: Why let tank 2's loop take over rather than just alarm and stop dosing?
How is CIL4 pH controlled?.a:
Lime keeps the pulp alkaline. If pH falls, more cyanide turns into HCN gas, which is a safety hazard and wastes cyanide. If tank 1's loop stops and nothing takes over, lime dosing stops.

Tank 2's loop taking over keeps the lime going, with alarms still active on abnormal high or low pH in both loops.

The CIL4 leach design pH is 8.8 to 9.3, close to the point where HCN forms readily, so continuous control matters. It is like having a backup sensor for a critical loop rather than shutting down when the primary fails.

f.q: Why is CIL4 leach pH only 8.8 to 9.3 when CIL2 is near 12?
f.a:
The reference gives these as design values but does not explain the difference.

In general, raising pH costs lime, and CIL4 treats about 3,164 t/h of tails compared with about 104 t/h in CIL2, so lime consumption would be huge at pH 12. Saline process water may also buffer pH.

Ask the CIL4 metallurgist why the lower range was chosen.
f: How much lime does CIL4 consume at design?
What does saline water do to pH control?
How does pH affect cyanide consumption?

f.q: What makes the HCN gas risk rise as pH falls?
f.a:
Cyanide in water exists as cyanide ion and HCN. The balance depends on pH. HCN has a pKa around 9.2 to 9.3, meaning at that pH about half is HCN. As pH falls, more becomes HCN, which can escape as gas.

At pH 11 nearly all is ion; at pH 9, a large share is HCN.

So the CIL4 range of 8.8 to 9.3 needs careful monitoring, and the HCN gas monitor with beacon and siren is a key safeguard.
f: Where is HCN gas most likely to collect in CIL4?
How does temperature affect HCN release?
What is the exposure limit for HCN?

f.q: How does control pass from tank 1 to tank 2?
f.a:
The reference says tank 2's controller takes over if tank 1 is down. It does not say whether that switch is automatic or a CRO action.

In general, it could be done by automatic selection on loss of tank 1, or by the CRO selecting tank 2 as the active controller.

Check the CIL4 control philosophy or ask the CRO.
f: What would make tank 1 count as 'down'?
Does the CRO get an alarm when control swaps?
How does the OIS show which tank is in control?

How is CIL4 pH controlled?.q: What would a handover mean by 'CIL4 running on tank 2 pH control'?
How is CIL4 pH controlled?.a:
It means the pH loop on leach tank 1 is not in use, so the milk of lime valve at the CIL4 feed distribution box is driven by the controller on leach tank 2.

That could be because tank 1 is bypassed or out of service, or its pH probe has failed.

Control from tank 2 is slower and looser, because there is more volume and time between lime addition and measurement. Tank 1 pH is not controlled directly, so it can swing. The next shift should find out why and when tank 1 can be restored.

f.q: Why is control from tank 2 slower than from tank 1?
f.a:
Lime goes in at the feed distribution box. To reach tank 2's probe, the slurry passes through tank 1 first, a 5,600 m3 tank with about 1.6 hours of residence at design.

That extra volume adds lag and smoothing, so the loop sees changes late and must be tuned slower to stay stable.

It is like measuring temperature far downstream of a heater: the control works, but with sluggish response.
f: How is a pH loop retuned for longer dead time?
Can pH overshoot when control is slow?
Why does residence time smooth pH swings?

f.q: How often are CIL4 pH probes calibrated or cleaned?
f.a:
The reference does not give a schedule.

In general, pH probes in slurry foul and drift quickly and are cleaned and calibrated often, sometimes daily or several times a week, with auto cleaning systems on some installations.

Ask the instrument technician or CIL4 area operator for the site practice.

Probe condition matters more than usual here because CIL4 runs at pH 8.8 to 9.3 at design, close to where HCN forms, so a drifting probe can quietly push the leach into a less safe range.
f: What fouls pH probes in lime slurry?
How do auto cleaning probe systems work?
How is a pH probe calibrated in the field?

f.q: What does the Carbon Scout add to CIL4 pH monitoring?
f.a:
The reference says the Gekko Carbon Scout MK6 samples all adsorption tanks for carbon concentration and the leach tanks for dissolved oxygen, pH and solids.

So it gives an independent pH reading in the leach tanks, a useful cross check if the main probe is in doubt.

It is periodic sampling rather than continuous, so it is a check, not a replacement for the control probe.
f: How often does the Carbon Scout sample each tank?
What does carbon concentration per tank show?
Can Carbon Scout data feed control loops?

How is CIL4 pH controlled?.q: Why put pH control on leach tank 1, not the feed distribution box?
How is CIL4 pH controlled?.a:
Lime needs time to dissolve and react. At the feed distribution box, slurry and lime have just met, and the pH there would swing wildly and not represent the leach.

Tank 1 is where the reaction has mostly completed, so its pH represents what the leach actually sees. The feed box is also turbulent and harsh on probes.

It is like measuring temperature after a mixing tank rather than right at a steam injection point: you want a stable, mixed reading. The control philosophy puts the probe on tank 1 with tank 2 as backup.

f.q: Why add lime at the feed box rather than directly into tank 1?
f.a:
Adding at the feed box mixes lime into the whole feed stream as it splits, so it arrives evenly in the tank. It also gives a little extra contact time before the tank.

Adding straight into a big agitated tank can leave local high pH zones near the dose point.

The reference confirms the milk of lime valve is at the CIL4 feed distribution box.
f: How is milk of lime delivered to CIL4?
What does the feed distribution box do?
Why can high local pH be a problem?

f.q: How long between lime addition and the tank 1 pH reading?
f.a:
The reference does not give a dead time. In general it would be tens of minutes or more, depending on feed box transit, mixing in the 5,600 m3 tank and lime dissolution.

Tank 1 leach residence at design is around 1.6 hours (3.2 hours for both leach tanks), so the full effect takes time.

That is why pH loops on big tanks are tuned slowly. The control engineer would know the real figure.
f: How is dead time measured on a real loop?
Why can slow loops still control well?
Does lime slaking quality change response?

f.q: Why does milk of lime need time to react before pH reads true?
f.a:
Milk of lime is a suspension of calcium hydroxide particles. They need to dissolve before they raise pH, and dissolution takes minutes.

Coarse or poorly slaked lime dissolves more slowly. Some of it also reacts with acid producing minerals in the ore.

So pH keeps rising for a while after addition. Measuring too close would mislead the loop.
f: How does the lime plant make milk of lime?
Why does slaking quality affect reactivity?
What ore minerals consume lime?

How is CIL4 cyanide added?.q: Why base cyanide dosing on thickener underflow tonnes rather than slurry flow?
How is CIL4 cyanide added?.a:
Cyanide is consumed by the solids: gold, sulphides and other cyanide consuming minerals in the ore. Slurry flow mixes solids and water, and the split changes with density.

Dosing on dry tonnes means the cyanide follows what actually needs leaching. The tonnes come from the thickener underflow slurry mass flow, using a magnetic flowmeter, nucleonic density gauge and operator entered solids SG.

It is like dosing a fuel additive per tonne of fuel rather than per litre of a fuel and water mix.

f.q: How is thickener underflow dry tonnage calculated?
f.a:
Slurry mass flow is measured by a magnetic flowmeter plus a nucleonic density gauge, with an operator entered dry solids SG in a DCS calculation.

Volume flow times slurry density gives slurry mass, and density with solids SG gives the solids fraction. Multiply and you get dry tonnes.

A wrong SG entry gives wrong tonnes, and therefore a wrong cyanide dose.
f: How sensitive is the tonnage to SG errors?
Who updates the solids SG value?
What fouls a magnetic flowmeter in slurry?

f.q: What happens to cyanide dosing if the SG entry is wrong?
f.a:
If the SG is too low or high, the DCS calculates the wrong dry tonnage. Since cyanide is dosed on g/t of thickener underflow tonnes, the flow setpoint follows that error.

The cyanide analyser trim would partly correct it by measuring free cyanide in the tanks, but persistent trim in one direction is a hint something upstream is off.

Check the SG entry when cyanide use or tonnage looks odd.
f: How much trim range does the cyanide analyser have?
How would the metallurgist spot a bad SG?
Do other loops use the same SG entry?

f.q: Why does CIL3 tails bring cyanide into CIL4 already?
f.a:
CIL3 tails come from concentrate leach and adsorption, where cyanide targets are high (up to 6,500 ppm in later CIL2 tanks). The tails carry residual cyanide.

The reference says CIL3 tails go via a hopper with cyanide water added to the CIL4 feed box. So CIL4 feed already contains some cyanide.

That reduces the fresh cyanide needed, and the analyser trim accounts for it.
f: How much cyanide does CIL3 tails carry?
Why is cyanide water added to the CIL3 tails hopper?
Does residual cyanide vary much shift to shift?

How is CIL4 cyanide added?.q: What would a handover mean by 'cyanide analyser trimming hard on CIL4'?
How is CIL4 cyanide added?.a:
It means the cyanide analyser on the leach tanks is applying a big correction to the base dose from the g/t setpoint. The measured free cyanide is well off target.

Possible causes: ore changes with more cyanide consuming minerals, a change in CIL3 tails residual cyanide, a wrong base g/t, a tonnage or SG error, or an analyser fault.

The next shift should check analyser calibration, the base setpoint and the tonnage signal, and ask the metallurgist about ore changes.

f.q: What in the ore consumes cyanide besides gold?
f.a:
Copper minerals are the classic cyanicides, forming copper cyanide complexes. Sulphide minerals, especially reactive ones, consume cyanide by forming thiocyanate. Some iron species also react.

FIM ore is refractory, with gold locked in pyrite and tellurides, which affects cyanide demand.

The metallurgist tracks these through cyanide consumption and assays.

Silver and other base metals also form cyanide complexes. When consumption jumps without a change in throughput, a shift in ore source is the usual suspect.
f: How does copper affect cyanide consumption?
What is thiocyanate and why does it matter?
How do tellurides respond to cyanide leaching?

f.q: How would you check the cyanide analyser is reading right?
f.a:
In general, compare it against a lab titration of a manual sample, usually silver nitrate titration for free cyanide. Analysers are recalibrated if they drift.

Sample lines can block, giving false readings. Steady readings that never change are a warning sign.

The instrument technician or lab handles the check; follow cyanide safety rules when sampling.
f: How is a silver nitrate titration done?
What fouls an online cyanide analyser?
How often is the analyser calibrated?

f.q: Is there a limit on how far the analyser can trim the dose?
f.a:
The reference does not give trim limits.

In general, analyser trims are clamped so a faulty analyser cannot drive dosing to zero or to maximum. Trim at its limit is usually alarmed.

Ask the control systems engineer or the CRO what limits are configured on CIL4 and what the OIS shows when the trim is at its limit.
f: Why clamp an analyser trim?
What alarms when trim hits its limit?
Can the CRO turn off the analyser trim?

How is CIL4 cyanide added?.q: Why do leach tanks and adsorption tank 3 need extra addition lines?
How is CIL4 cyanide added?.a:
Cyanide is consumed as slurry moves down the train, so free cyanide falls. The extra lines let the CRO top up where needed.

The leach tanks are where most extraction happens, so they need cyanide to stay at target. Adsorption tank 3 is partway down, so a top up there keeps free cyanide up in the adsorption section.

The reference does not explain why tank 3 specifically. The lines also help when a tank is bypassed and the front end dose point no longer feeds it. The metallurgist would know the reasoning.

f.q: Why might free cyanide fall along the CIL4 train?
f.a:
Cyanide reacts with gold, sulphides and other minerals, and some is lost to HCN volatilisation, especially at the low CIL4 pH of 8.8 to 9.3. It can also be adsorbed or decomposed.

Over 12.8 hours of total residence at design, these losses add up.

Top up points keep cyanide adequate for leaching through the train.
f: How much cyanide is lost as HCN at CIL4 pH?
Does carbon adsorb cyanide too?
How does residence time affect cyanide loss?

f.q: What does the HCN monitor do at high-high, and who responds?
f.a:
The reference says an HCN gas monitor in the area triggers a beacon and siren at high-high.

Who responds and how follows the site cyanide emergency procedure, which is not in the reference. In general, people leave the area upwind and the control room starts the emergency response.

Ask the shift supervisor or emergency response team.
f: Where should you go when the HCN siren sounds?
How are HCN monitors tested?
What does the low HCN alarm level trigger?

f.q: How do bypass gates change where cyanide should be added?
f.a:
If a tank is bypassed using the pneumatic slurry bypass gates, slurry skips it. Cyanide added into that tank would not reach the flow.

The extra addition lines let the CRO move cyanide to where slurry actually goes.

Bypass gates are operated locally only, so the field operator and CRO need to coordinate on dosing.
f: Why would a CIL4 tank be bypassed?
How does the CRO know a tank is bypassed?
Does bypassing change carbon movement too?

How is oxygen added in CIL4?.q: Why add oxygen at both the leach tanks and adsorption tanks?
How is oxygen added in CIL4?.a:
Gold dissolves in cyanide only if oxygen is present, so oxygen is a reagent just like cyanide. In CIL, leaching does not stop when the slurry reaches the adsorption tanks. Gold keeps dissolving there while carbon picks it up.

In CIL4, the main oxygen goes in at the two leach tanks through VSD injection pumps with flow control valves, plus side lances. The first two adsorption tanks also get side lances, keeping dissolved oxygen up where leaching is still active. Sulphides in the tails also consume oxygen as they go.

Think of it like a heat exchanger train: you add duty where most of the work is still being done.

f.q: What reaction makes oxygen necessary for gold leaching?
f.a:
The usual summary is the Elsner equation: gold, cyanide, oxygen and water react to form the gold cyanide complex and hydroxide. Oxygen is the oxidant that takes electrons from the gold surface.

Without enough dissolved oxygen, the reaction slows, no matter how much cyanide is present. It becomes like a combustion process starved of air.

That is why CIL4 has oxygen injection and DO analysers, and why oxygen is supplied from a dedicated plant.
f: Can too much oxygen ever hurt the leach?
Why is dissolved oxygen solubility so limited?
How does cyanide strength interact with DO?

f.q: Why stop oxygen addition after the first two adsorption tanks?
f.a:
The reference only states where oxygen is added: injection pumps on both leach tanks, and side lances on the leach tanks and the first two adsorption tanks.

The general reasoning is that most of the dissolution happens early in the train. By the later adsorption tanks, the remaining leachable gold is small, so extra oxygen gives little benefit for the cost.

The metallurgist who set the CIL4 design basis would know the specific reasoning.
f: How much CIL4 extraction happens in the leach tanks?
Is there room to add lances on later tanks?
What does DO typically look like down the train?

f.q: Where does the CIL4 oxygen come from?
f.a:
The reference says oxygen comes from a new oxygen plant using pressure swing adsorption (PSA), with liquid oxygen as well, supplying CIL2/3 and CIL4.

A PSA plant separates oxygen from air by passing compressed air through beds of adsorbent that hold back nitrogen. Liquid oxygen is typically stored as a backup or top up.

For details on capacity and how backup is triggered, ask the oxygen plant operator or the utilities area maintenance planner.
f: How does a PSA oxygen plant work?
When does liquid oxygen take over from PSA?
How is oxygen shared between CIL2/3 and CIL4?

How is oxygen added in CIL4?.q: What would low DO alarms on CIL4 suggest is limiting recovery?
How is oxygen added in CIL4?.a:
Low DO alarms mean the leach could be oxygen limited, slowing gold dissolution and putting the CIL4 design extraction of about 38 percent at risk.

Possible causes split into two groups. Supply side: oxygen plant output or header pressure low, an injection pump tripped, or lances blocked. Demand side: more reactive sulphides consuming oxygen, higher temperature or saline water reducing oxygen solubility.

The DO analysers alarm high and low, so the next step is checking oxygen flows, pumps and lance pressures against the DO trend.

f.q: Why does saline water hold less dissolved oxygen?
f.a:
Dissolved salts take up space among water molecules and reduce how much gas can dissolve. This is called the salting out effect. Seawater, for example, holds noticeably less oxygen than fresh water at the same temperature.

FIM process water is saline, SG about 1.07, so the oxygen ceiling is lower than with fresh water. Warm slurry reduces it further.

That makes oxygen addition more important here.
f: How does temperature change oxygen solubility?
Does saline water affect cyanide leaching too?
Why is FIM process water so saline?

f.q: How would you tell supply problems from high oxygen demand?
f.a:
Check the supply side first. If oxygen flows to the injection pumps are below setpoint, header pressure is low or a pump has tripped, it is supply.

If flows and lance pressures are normal but DO still falls, demand has risen, often from a change in ore with more reactive sulphides.

The PI historian helps: compare DO trends with oxygen flows and plant feed changes. The metallurgist would review ore changes.
f: How do lance pressures show blockage?
What ore changes raise oxygen demand?
Can higher cyanide make up for low DO?

f.q: How does the Carbon Scout help confirm low DO readings?
f.a:
The reference says the Gekko Carbon Scout MK6 samples the leach tanks for DO, pH and solids, and the adsorption tanks for carbon concentration.

That gives an independent DO reading to compare with the fixed DO analysers. If both agree, the low DO is real; if they disagree, suspect the analyser.

Carbon Scout samples periodically, so it is a cross check rather than continuous control.
f: How often do DO analysers need calibration?
What fouls a DO probe in slurry?
Does the Carbon Scout sample adsorption tank DO?

How is oxygen added in CIL4?.q: Why check lance pressure against vendor curves, not just flow?
How is oxygen added in CIL4?.a:
A lance's pressure and flow are linked: for a clean lance there is a known pressure for a given flow, which is the vendor's pressure flow curve.

If pressure is higher than the curve for the flow, the lance is partly blocked. If pressure is lower, the lance may be worn, broken off or leaking. Flow alone cannot show which.

The reference says lance pressures are checked on local gauges against these curves. It is like checking a spray nozzle: pressure against flow tells you if the orifice is blocked or worn.

f.q: What blocks an oxygen sparging lance in slurry?
f.a:
In general, slurry backing into the lance when oxygen flow drops, then settling and setting inside. Scale from saline water or lime can also build up at the tip.

Low or stopped oxygen flow is the main risk, because it lets slurry in.

Sites often keep a minimum flow through lances or purge them for that reason. Check the vendor guidance.
f: How are blocked lances cleared?
Why keep a minimum flow through lances?
Does lime scale affect lance tips?

f.q: Why read lance pressures on local gauges, not the DCS?
f.a:
The reference says lance pressures are checked on local gauges. It does not explain why.

In general, adding transmitters on every lance is costly, and lance checks are routine field rounds rather than continuous control.

Ask the CIL4 area operator how often lance checks are done.

The DO analysers, which do report to the DCS and alarm high or low, give the CRO the process view. The local gauges are the mechanical check that tells the field operator which lance is the problem.
f: How often are CIL4 lance checks done?
What does a field operator record on rounds?
Who replaces a damaged lance?

f.q: What are the safety concerns with oxygen in the plant?
f.a:
Oxygen does not burn, but it makes other things burn much more fiercely. Oil, grease and some plastics can ignite easily in enriched oxygen.

That is why oxygen pipework must be cleaned for oxygen service, and why you never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings.

Follow site rules for oxygen areas and permits.
f: What does cleaning for oxygen service involve?
Why is grease dangerous in oxygen lines?
Where is oxygen pipework routed in CIL4?

What's a 'carbon detection meter' on the.q: Why put a reference probe at the carbon-free front end?
What's a 'carbon detection meter' on the.a:
The meter's reading depends on the slurry as well as any carbon in it, things like solids content, mineralogy and water chemistry. To pick out carbon, you need to know what the same slurry reads without carbon.

The front end of CIL4, the leach tanks, carries no carbon, so a probe there gives that baseline. Comparing tails against the reference cancels out the slurry effects and leaves the carbon signal.

It is like a compensating strain gauge, or a differential pressure measurement: you subtract the common effects to see the one you care about.

f.q: How does a carbon detection meter sense carbon in slurry?
f.a:
The reference does not explain the sensing principle.

In general, carbon detectors exploit a property that differs between activated carbon and the ore slurry, often electrical, since carbon conducts electricity differently from mineral particles. The meter picks up a change as carbon particles pass.

Check the vendor manual or ask the instrument technician for the specific principle on the installed unit.
f: Why does carbon conduct electricity differently?
What can cause false carbon readings?
How is a carbon detection meter calibrated?

f.q: Why are the CIL4 leach tanks kept carbon free?
f.a:
CIL4 has two leach tanks then six adsorption tanks. Carbon is held only in the adsorption tanks.

In general, starting with leach only lets gold dissolve before carbon is present. Carbon added later sees a higher gold concentration.

It also reduces the carbon inventory needed. The exact reasons for the CIL4 layout were set in design; the metallurgist would know.
f: Why does a high gold concentration help adsorption?
How much carbon does CIL4 hold?
What would happen if carbon reached the leach tanks?

f.q: What happens to the reading when slurry density changes?
f.a:
Without a reference, a density change could look like a change in carbon. The reference probe sees the same density change, so comparing the two cancels it out.

That is the point of the reference probe.

If density differs between front end and tails, some error remains, which the vendor setup should account for.
f: Does slurry density change along CIL4?
How often is the reference reading updated?
What would a reference probe fault look like?

What's a 'carbon detection meter' on the.q: What would rising readings on the tails carbon detector mean for the TSF?
What's a 'carbon detection meter' on the.a:
Rising readings mean carbon is escaping to the tails and on to the TSF. That carbon carries gold. The reference notes lost carbon carries loaded gold to the TSF, so it is lost value.

Common causes: a worn or damaged intertank screen (Kemix, 1.0 mm wedge wire) letting carbon through, or carbon breaking into fines that pass the screen.

It is worth acting quickly, because loaded carbon in the tails is gold leaving the plant. The future carbon safety screens would add another line of defence.

f.q: What usually lets carbon escape past the last intertank screen?
f.a:
In general: screen mesh wear or damage, a seal or gasket failure around the screen, or overflow if the screen blinds and slurry bypasses.

Carbon attrition also makes fines small enough to pass the 1.0 mm screen.

Field inspection of the final tank screens is the first step. Ask the CIL4 maintenance planner about screen inspection frequency.
f: How are Kemix intertank screens cleaned?
What causes carbon attrition in CIL tanks?
How often are intertank screens replaced?

f.q: Is fine carbon lost to tails as costly as coarse carbon?
f.a:
Fine carbon carries gold too, often at similar loading. But fine carbon losses are partly unavoidable through attrition, and they are expected.

Coarse carbon in tails usually means a screen failure, which can lose much more carbon quickly.

Both matter, but the response differs. The metallurgist tracks carbon losses.

Tracking fresh carbon additions against the circuit inventory gives the best measure of total carbon loss over a month.
f: How much carbon loss is normal per tonne?
Where else does fine carbon leave the circuit?
Can fine carbon be recovered from acid wash?

f.q: What are the future CIL4 carbon safety screens for?
f.a:
The reference lists future carbon safety screens for CIL4, 4.27 x 7.93 m, 0.85 x 18.5 mm apertures.

They would catch carbon escaping in the tails before it reaches the TSF, a backstop to the intertank screens.

They are listed as future, so they may not be installed yet. Check with the project team.
f: Why are the carbon safety screens listed as future?
What happens to carbon caught on safety screens?
Do CIL3 tails have safety screens?

What's a 'carbon detection meter' on the.q: How would the CRO respond to a high carbon-in-tails alarm during a shift?
What's a 'carbon detection meter' on the.a:
The reference does not give a response procedure, so this is general practice.

First, confirm it is real: check the trend, compare with the reference probe and look for related alarms. Then send the field operator to inspect the final adsorption tank screens and the tails area. Let the metallurgist know, since carbon loss means gold loss.

If a screen has failed, the repair goes through maintenance under isolation. Never bypass the alarm to clear it. Ask the shift supervisor for the site procedure.

f.q: How would a field operator check an intertank screen?
f.a:
In general, they would look for carbon in the downstream tank or launder, check the screen for visible damage or blinding, and check that slurry levels are normal.

A tank level higher than normal upstream suggests a blinded screen.

Any work on screens goes through isolation and permits. Ask the CIL4 area operator for the standard check.
f: What does a blinded intertank screen look like?
Why do tank levels rise when a screen blinds?
How are intertank screens isolated for repair?

f.q: How is lost carbon estimated after a screen failure?
f.a:
In general, by sampling the tails for carbon over the period, estimating the rate, and multiplying by time. Carbon inventory in tanks also gets checked via the Carbon Scout readings.

The reference says the Carbon Scout samples all adsorption tanks for carbon concentration, which helps track inventory.

The metallurgist would estimate losses for accounting.
f: How does Carbon Scout measure carbon per tank?
How does carbon inventory affect adsorption?
How is lost gold valued in accounting?

f.q: Can carbon lost to the TSF be recovered?
f.a:
In general, not practically. Once spread on a tailings dam, it mixes with tails and is hard to retrieve.

Some sites reprocess old tailings years later, but that is a separate project with its own economics, not a way to recover a shift's carbon loss.

That is why prevention matters: sound intertank screens, the carbon detection meter on the tails with its reference probe, and the future carbon safety screens.
f: Has FIM ever reprocessed old tailings?
Why does carbon in tailings still hold gold?
How is TSF deposition managed?

How are CIL4 tails sampled for accountin.q: Why take a shift composite rather than a single grab sample?
How are CIL4 tails sampled for accountin.a:
Tails grade moves around through a shift as ore blend, throughput, cyanide strength, oxygen and carbon loading change. A single grab sample captures one moment, which could be well above or below the shift average.

A shift composite builds up many small increments cut at regular intervals over the shift, so the result represents the average tails grade for the tonnes that actually passed. That is what the recovery calculation needs.

It is like judging a pump's efficiency from a full day of energy and flow totals rather than one reading off the gauges. Averaging over time removes the noise.

f.q: How does a three stage sampler cut a representative sample?
f.a:
In general, the primary cutter travels right across the falling slurry stream at set intervals and takes a full slice of it. That slice is still far too big to send to the lab, so a secondary cutter takes a share of the primary stream, and a tertiary cutter reduces it again to a manageable mass in the composite container.

Each stage must cut the whole stream evenly and at constant speed, or the sample becomes biased toward coarse or fine material.

The reference confirms a three stage station on CIL4 tails but not its design details.
f: Why must a sample cutter cross the full stream?
What makes a slurry sampler biased?
How is a composite kept from settling?

f.q: Why is the sampler placed before the final tails tank?
f.a:
The final tails tank does not only receive CIL4 tails. According to the reference it also takes acid wash waste and fine carbon waste, about 3,164 t/h at 54.5 percent solids in total at design.

Sampling before the tank gives CIL4 tails on their own, without those other streams diluting or contaminating the result. Fine carbon carrying gold, for example, would distort the tails assay.

So the position gives a clean measure of what CIL4 left behind, which is what the recovery calculation needs.
f: Where does acid wash waste come from?
Why does fine carbon carry gold to tails?
How are the tailings pumps controlled?

f.q: How often is the CIL4 tails composite collected?
f.a:
The reference says the sampling station takes a shift composite, so one composite is built up over each shift and then sent to the lab for assay. The shift totals elsewhere in the plant run on 12 hour shifts starting at 5:00 am, so the composite most likely lines up with those shifts.

The exact collection time, labelling and handover to the lab are site procedures not covered in the reference.

Ask the CIL4 area operator or the lab supervisor how the composite is handled.
f: How quickly does the lab return tails assays?
How are composites labelled and tracked?
Who collects the composite at shift end?

How are CIL4 tails sampled for accountin.q: What would a handover mean by 'tails sampler blocked, missed the composite'?
How are CIL4 tails sampled for accountin.a:
It means the sampler stopped working properly during the shift, so no valid composite was collected. That shift has no reliable tails assay.

The recovery calculation for that period then has a gap. The metallurgist will have to estimate or flag the tails grade, which makes recovery for the day less certain.

The practical actions are to get the sampler repaired before the next shift, through the normal maintenance request, and to make sure the metallurgist knows. A blocked sampler that keeps recurring is worth raising as a defect, since every missed composite weakens the plant's accounting.

f.q: What usually blocks a slurry sampler?
f.a:
In general, the cutter slot or sample lines catch coarse material, trash, wood fibre or scale, or solids settle in the sample lines when flow is low or the sampler sits idle.

Saline process water also encourages scale build up over time, which narrows lines and cutter openings.

Regular cleaning and flushing, and keeping cutter openings at the right size, reduce blockages. The maintenance planner would know the service schedule for the CIL4 tails sampler.
f: How are sampler cutters cleaned?
Why does low flow cause sample line blockages?
Does trash get past the trash screens into CIL4?

f.q: How is a missing tails assay handled in the accounting?
f.a:
The reference does not describe the accounting method.

In general, metallurgists fill a gap with an estimate based on adjacent shifts, other process data such as leach conditions and solution assays, or a backup grab sample if one was taken. The value is flagged as estimated so it can be reviewed during month end reconciliation.

Ask the plant metallurgist how FIM handles missing tails assays and who signs off the daily figures.
f: Who signs off the daily metallurgical accounting?
How are estimated values flagged in reports?
Is a backup grab sample ever taken?

f.q: Can the OSA or Carbon Scout stand in for a missed sample?
f.a:
Not for gold grade. The OSA measures gold and iron on the flotation streams, from flotation feed to final flotation tails, not CIL4 tails. The Carbon Scout measures carbon concentration in the adsorption tanks and DO, pH and solids in the leach tanks. Neither measures gold in CIL4 tails.

They can help explain what happened, for example low DO or low carbon in a tank, but they cannot replace the assay.

So a missed composite leaves a real gap in the tails data.
f: Which streams does the OSA measure?
Does CIL4 have any online gold analysis?
How useful is a manual grab sample here?

How are CIL4 tails sampled for accountin.q: How does the tails assay feed into the plant's daily recovery calculation?
How are CIL4 tails sampled for accountin.a:
The lab assays the shift composite to give the tails grade in grams per tonne. In broad terms, recovery is gold in minus gold out in tails, divided by gold in.

Gold out is the tails grade multiplied by the dry tails tonnes. Gold in comes from the feed grade and feed tonnes, measured by weightometers and slurry mass flow instruments.

The reference confirms the tails assay provides the grade for the recovery calculation, but it does not set out the full method. The plant metallurgist runs that calculation and can show you how the daily report is put together.

f.q: Why does tails grade matter so much at 84 percent recovery?
f.a:
At the design nominal case, total gold recovery is about 84 percent, so about 16 percent of the gold leaves in the tails. Because the tails grade is a small number, a small absolute error in it moves recovery noticeably.

With a nominal head grade of about 1.58 g/t, tails grades are fractions of a gram per tonne, so precise sampling and assaying really matter.

These are design values from the PDC, not live operating figures.
f: How precise is a gold assay at low grade?
What raises CIL4 tails grade most often?
Why is CIL4 extraction so much lower than CIL2?

f.q: How is plant feed grade measured for the recovery calculation?
f.a:
The condensed reference does not describe head grade sampling or where the feed sample is taken.

In general, plants sample the feed after grinding, often at cyclone overflow or flotation feed, because a slurry stream is easier to sample representatively than coarse ore. Weightometer tonnes then give the gold in.

The OSA also measures gold in flotation feed, but for accounting a lab assay is normally used. Ask the plant metallurgist about the FIM head sampling.
f: Why sample head grade after milling?
How are weightometer tonnes used in accounting?
Does the OSA flotation feed reading match the lab?

f.q: What is the difference between calculated and actual recovery?
f.a:
Calculated recovery comes from samples and tonnes: feed grade, tails grade and the measured tonnages. Actual recovery is based on gold actually produced, meaning doré poured in the goldroom plus changes in gold held in the circuit.

The two differ because of sampling and assay errors, weightometer errors, gold locked up in circuit inventory on carbon and in solution, and timing between production and pours.

Reconciliation compares them over a month or longer. The plant metallurgist manages this.
f: What is gold in circuit inventory?
How often is reconciliation done?
Why does pour timing affect recovery?

How are slurry bypass gates between CIL4.q: Why keep the DCS out of control for these bypass gates?
How are slurry bypass gates between CIL4.a:
The reference says the pneumatic slurry bypass gates between CIL4 tanks are operated locally by the plant operator, and DCS control of them is inhibited.

The reason is not stated, but it is easy to see. Bypassing a tank changes where slurry and carbon go and affects levels in the tanks either side. You want someone standing there who has checked the tank, the levels and the gate position before and after the change. Bypasses are also rare, done for maintenance rather than routine control.

It is like a manual isolation valve on a process line: deliberate, infrequent changes are made by a person in the field.

f.q: When would a CIL4 tank need to be bypassed?
f.a:
In general, for maintenance or inspection: agitator or gearbox work, intertank screen changes, tank repairs, liner inspection or clearing settled solids.

Bypassing lets the rest of the train keep running while one tank is out, rather than stopping CIL4 completely.

The cost is residence time. CIL4 design total residence is about 12.8 hours, already below the 14 hour ideal, so losing a 5,600 m3 tank reduces extraction. Bypasses are kept short for that reason.
f: How much residence time does one CIL4 tank give?
How is a CIL4 tank drained for maintenance?
Can two CIL4 tanks be bypassed at once?

f.q: What happens to tank levels when a bypass gate opens?
f.a:
When a bypass opens, slurry takes the easier path around the tank. The bypassed tank stops receiving feed, so its level stays put or falls if it is being drained, and the downstream tank receives the flow directly.

The upstream tank level may drop slightly because the bypass path offers less resistance than flowing through the tank and its intertank screen.

These swings are why the gate is operated locally with someone watching levels. The exact level instruments and alarms are in the CIL4 P&IDs.
f: How are CIL4 tank levels measured?
Why can a gate change cause a level surge?
What alarms cover CIL4 tank levels?

f.q: Does the DCS still see the bypass gate position?
f.a:
The reference only says the gates are operated locally and DCS control is inhibited. It does not say whether position feedback is shown on the OIS.

In general, local only devices often still have limit switches wired back so the control room can see the position, even though it cannot command them. That helps the CRO understand the slurry route.

Ask the CRO what the OIS shows for the CIL4 bypass gates.
f: How do limit switches report a gate position?
Why inhibit DCS control but keep feedback?
Who checks gate positions on field rounds?

How are slurry bypass gates between CIL4.q: What would a handover mean by 'spool piece changed to route tank 3 to CIL5'?
How are slurry bypass gates between CIL4.a:
The reference does not mention a CIL5. CIL4 has two leach tanks and six adsorption tanks (F21-TK-411 to 418), with space for a future extra tank. So "route tank 3 to CIL5" does not match the documents, and you should check what the writer meant.

What the reference does say is that loaded carbon routing between CIL4 tanks is changed with removable spool pieces in the central pipe rack. So a spool change note normally means the carbon transfer path between tanks has been altered, perhaps to skip a tank that is bypassed.

Ask the CRO or the person who wrote the note what was changed and why.

f.q: What is a removable spool piece in a pipe rack?
f.a:
A spool piece is a short flanged length of pipe. Unbolting it and fitting it in another position, or swapping it for a blank, changes which lines are connected.

The big advantage is positive routing: you can see which path is made up, and a removed spool gives a physical break that cannot leak through the way a closed valve can.

Changing one means draining and isolating the lines, so it is done under a permit.
f: Why does a removed spool give positive isolation?
How are spool changes documented?
What tools are needed to change a spool?

f.q: Why is loaded carbon pumped from the first adsorption tank?
f.a:
In CIL, carbon moves counter current to the slurry. Slurry flows from the first tank to the last, while carbon is pumped back from the last tank toward the first. The first adsorption tank meets the richest solution, so its carbon carries the highest gold loading.

The reference says loaded carbon is pumped from the first adsorption tank to the loaded carbon screen and transfer vessel, then to elution. Barren carbon returns to the last tank through the carbon sizing screen.

It is like a counterflow heat exchanger: the outgoing medium leaves at its richest.
f: How does counter current carbon flow work?
How often is loaded carbon transferred?
What does the loaded carbon screen do?

f.q: What checks happen before a carbon routing spool is changed?
f.a:
The reference does not give a procedure.

In general, the lines involved are isolated from pumps and tanks, drained and flushed of slurry and carbon, and a permit is issued before anyone unbolts a flange. Cyanide is present in CIL slurry, so the work also needs the cyanide precautions for the area.

Ask the CIL4 area supervisor for the site procedure.
f: Why must lines be flushed before spool changes?
Who issues the permit for a spool change?
What cyanide precautions apply to line breaks?

How are slurry bypass gates between CIL4.q: Why use removable spool pieces instead of an actuated valve for carbon routing?
How are slurry bypass gates between CIL4.a:
Activated carbon is fragile and abrasive. Pushing it through an actuated valve means it is crushed between closing parts and ground against seats, which makes fines and wears the valve fast.

A spool piece gives a full bore, smooth path with nothing in the flow to break carbon. It also gives positive routing, so there is no risk of a passing valve quietly sending carbon the wrong way.

Routing changes are infrequent, so the effort of swapping a spool is acceptable. It is the same logic as using a blind or removable spool instead of a valve where positive isolation matters more than convenience.

f.q: Why does carbon breakage matter so much in CIL?
f.a:
Broken carbon produces fines. Fines are small enough to pass the intertank screens, so they drift down the train and leave in the tails still carrying gold. They cannot be recovered practically once they reach the TSF.

Every tonne of fines also has to be replaced with fresh carbon, which costs money.

So breakage hurts recovery and operating cost at the same time. Gentle handling, careful pump choice and sizing screens on the barren carbon return all help.
f: How is carbon attrition measured?
What carbon particle sizes are used in CIL?
Why is fresh carbon conditioned before use?

f.q: How often is carbon routing changed in CIL4?
f.a:
The reference does not say how often spool changes happen.

In general, carbon routing changes are rare and tied to events such as bypassing a tank for maintenance or changing the carbon transfer arrangement, rather than routine operation.

Ask the CIL4 area operator or supervisor how often it happens and whether the changes are recorded in a log or on a status board.
f: Why would routing change when a tank is bypassed?
Who decides on carbon routing changes?
How is the current routing shown in the field?

f.q: How is loaded carbon pumped without breaking it?
f.a:
In general, CIL plants use recessed impeller (vortex) pumps for carbon. The impeller sits back from the flow path, so it creates a vortex that drives the slurry while most carbon particles never touch the vanes.

Some plants use airlifts, which lift carbon with injected air and no moving parts in the slurry.

Pump speeds are kept modest and pipework avoids sharp bends. Check the CIL4 equipment list for the actual pump type.
f: How does a recessed impeller pump work?
What is an airlift and where is it used?
Why do sharp bends damage carbon?

What runs the CIL4 elution?.q: Why does elution need such a tightly staged sequence instead of one long soak?
What runs the CIL4 elution?.a:
Each step does a different chemical job, and some of them must not mix. Acid wash with dilute HCl removes scale and inorganic foulants. A water rinse clears the acid. The caustic cyanide pre-soak loosens the gold cyanide on the carbon. Elution with lean eluate and then scheme water strips the gold off. Cooling with scheme water brings the carbon down before it leaves.

Acid and cyanide must never meet, because together they release HCN gas. So the steps run in a set order with rinses in between.

The sequence uses level, temperature and pressure to confirm each step, like a machine program that checks each position before the next move.

f.q: Why must acid be rinsed out before the cyanide pre-soak?
f.a:
Cyanide in acidic conditions converts to hydrogen cyanide, a highly toxic gas. If acid remained in the column when the caustic cyanide pre-soak arrived, HCN could be generated inside the column and vented.

The water rinse step flushes out the acid first, and the sequence must confirm it before stepping on. The caustic in the pre-soak also keeps pH high.

This is one of the main safety reasons the elution runs as a strict sequence.
f: How does the sequence confirm the rinse is complete?
Where could HCN escape from an elution column?
What gas monitoring covers the elution area?

f.q: Why is the elution column pressurised?
f.a:
The reference says the column is pressurised to stop flashing. Elution runs hot because gold strips faster at higher temperature. If the hot eluate were at atmospheric pressure, it could boil and flash to steam, disrupting flow through the carbon bed and damaging equipment.

Holding pressure raises the boiling point, so the solution stays liquid at the working temperature.

It is the same principle as a pressure cooker or a pressurised cooling system on an engine.
f: What temperature does CIL4 elution run at?
What happens if the column loses pressure hot?
How is column pressure held during elution?

f.q: Why use a single duplex stainless column for acid and elution?
f.a:
The reference says CIL4 has a single SAF2205 duplex stainless steel column for both acid wash and elution. Duplex stainless combines good strength with strong resistance to chloride and acid corrosion, and it also handles hot caustic conditions.

Using one column means carbon does not have to be transferred between an acid column and an elution column, which saves equipment and reduces carbon breakage.

The trade off is that the sequence must switch chemistries safely in the same vessel.
f: Why is duplex stainless good against chlorides?
How long does one CIL4 elution cycle take?
How is carbon transferred into the column?

What runs the CIL4 elution?.q: What would a handover mean by 'elution paused on temperature fault'?
What runs the CIL4 elution?.a:
It means the elution sequence has stopped partway because a temperature condition did not confirm within its transition time, or the heating system raised a fault. Possibilities include the LPG burner management system tripping, a temperature transmitter fault, or the eluate temperature controller not reaching setpoint.

Carbon is sitting in the column waiting, and loaded carbon may start backing up in CIL4.

The fault has to be found and cleared properly. Burner trips are reset per the vendor and site rules once the cause is known, never by bypassing the protection.

f.q: What does the LPG burner management system protect against?
f.a:
In general, a burner management system prevents explosions and unsafe firing. It purges the combustion chamber before lighting, proves the pilot and main flame, checks that gas valves are closed and not leaking, and shuts off fuel immediately on flame failure or other faults.

The reference says the CIL4 elution heater is an LPG fired package with its own burner management system, linked to a temperature controller on the eluate line.

It is a safety system, not just a controller, so it must never be bypassed.
f: Why purge a burner before lighting it?
How does flame detection work on a gas burner?
Who is allowed to reset a burner trip?

f.q: What happens to carbon left in a paused elution column?
f.a:
In general it just waits in the column. If the pause happens mid strip, some gold is still on the carbon and the column may cool.

When the fault is cleared, the sequence normally resumes or repeats steps to finish the strip. Restarting from cold can reduce stripping efficiency, so some gold may stay on the carbon and return to CIL4.

How the CIL4 sequence handles restarts is in the control philosophy; the CRO or metallurgist would know the practice.
f: Can a paused strip resume mid step?
How is a poor strip detected afterwards?
What happens to gold left on returned carbon?

f.q: How does delayed elution affect CIL4 carbon loading?
f.a:
If loaded carbon cannot be sent to elution, carbon in the adsorption tanks stays longer and keeps loading. Loading climbs toward and above the normal range, which is about 332 to 579 g/t at design.

Highly loaded carbon adsorbs gold less efficiently, so more dissolved gold can slip through to tails. Adsorption efficiency at design is about 88 percent.

The metallurgist would plan catch up elutions once the fault is cleared.
f: Why does high loading cut adsorption efficiency?
How is CIL4 carbon loading measured?
Can loaded carbon transfers be skipped?

What runs the CIL4 elution?.q: Why follow lean eluate elution with scheme water elution?
What runs the CIL4 elution?.a:
Lean eluate is partly spent solution saved from earlier elutions. Using it first does the bulk of the stripping while saving water, reagents and heat, since it is already warm and carries some caustic and cyanide.

Scheme water, fresh pipeline water with SG 1.00, then finishes the strip. AARL stripping works best with low salt water, so clean water pulls off the remaining gold that the lean eluate leaves behind.

The reference says pregnant eluate fills the CIL4 eluate circulation tank, and when it is full the flow diverts to the lean eluate tank for the next cycle. About 5 bed volumes of eluate are used.

f.q: Why does AARL need low salt water for the strip?
f.a:
Gold cyanide is held on activated carbon more strongly when the solution has a high concentration of dissolved salts. Low ionic strength water reverses that and lets the gold come off.

FIM process water is saline, with SG about 1.07, so it would strip poorly. That is why elution uses scheme water, the fresh pipeline supply with SG 1.00.

It is one reason the plant carries several separate water services.
f: Where does FIM scheme water come from?
What happens if saline water enters elution?
How much scheme water does one elution use?

f.q: What is a bed volume in elution?
f.a:
A bed volume is the volume taken up by the carbon bed in the column. Elution flows are expressed in bed volumes so the same recipe can be applied to columns of different size.

The reference says about 5 bed volumes of eluate are used in the CIL4 elution.

It is like specifying a flush as a number of system volumes rather than a fixed number of litres.
f: How many tonnes of carbon fit in the CIL4 column?
Why measure flow in bed volumes per hour?
Does carbon swell when wet?

f.q: Where does pregnant eluate go after elution?
f.a:
The reference says pregnant eluate goes to the CIL4 eluate circulation tanks, and once they are full the flow diverts to the lean eluate tank.

From the circulation tanks the solution feeds CIL4 electrowinning, which has two split feed cells with VSD pumps on flow control, running batches by sequence or manually.

The gold plates onto the cathodes in EW and then goes to the goldroom.
f: How do the CIL4 EW cells recover gold?
What does split feed mean for an EW cell?
How is the end of an EW batch decided?

Who controls the CIL4 carbon regeneratio.q: Why let the kiln run on a separate vendor PLC instead of native DCS control?
Who controls the CIL4 carbon regeneratio.a:
The reference says the kiln package (screw feeder, kiln and local panel) runs on a vendor PLC, which is tied to the DCS through an overall regeneration sequence.

The kiln has its own heating, feed and protection logic, which the vendor designs, tunes and warrants as a unit. Keeping that on their PLC makes commissioning, troubleshooting and safety sign off easier, and the vendor supports it directly.

Standalone PLCs need Owner approval on this project, so it is a deliberate exception. It is like a packaged compressor with its own controller that still reports to the plant system.

f.q: What does a carbon regeneration kiln actually do?
f.a:
After elution, carbon is still fouled with organics such as oils, flotation reagents and humic matter that block its pores. The kiln heats the carbon in a low oxygen atmosphere so these burn or volatilise off without burning the carbon itself, restoring its adsorption activity.

Fouled carbon adsorbs gold poorly, so regeneration keeps CIL adsorption efficient.

At FIM the regenerated carbon goes to a quench tank, then back to CIL4 via the carbon sizing screen.
f: What foulants reduce carbon activity most?
How hot does a regeneration kiln run?
How is carbon activity measured?

f.q: What signals pass between the kiln PLC and the DCS?
f.a:
The reference says vendor packages with their own PLC report to the DCS for Monitor or Control, and that the kiln is tied in through the overall regeneration sequence. It does not list the individual signals.

In general you would expect running status, faults, key temperatures, permissives and start or stop commands from the sequence.

The interface signal list in the project documents gives the actual signals; the control systems engineer would have it.
f: What is a PLC to DCS interface list?
Can the CRO start the kiln from the OIS?
How are kiln alarms shown on the OIS?

f.q: Why must mercury abatement run whenever the kiln runs?
f.a:
Ore contains trace mercury, which dissolves in cyanide and adsorbs onto carbon along with gold. At kiln temperatures, mercury left on the carbon volatilises.

The abatement system captures that mercury vapour from the kiln off gas, protecting workers and the environment.

The reference says the abatement system must run whenever the kiln runs, so its drives are included in the same regeneration sequence.
f: Where else does mercury show up in the gold circuit?
What exposure limits apply to mercury vapour?
How is captured mercury disposed of?

Who controls the CIL4 carbon regeneratio.q: What would happen if abatement tripped while the kiln kept running?
Who controls the CIL4 carbon regeneratio.a:
The kiln would keep driving mercury off the carbon with nothing capturing it, releasing mercury vapour to the atmosphere and possibly the work area. That is a health and environmental hazard.

That is exactly why the reference says the abatement system must run whenever the kiln runs, and why its drives sit in the same regeneration sequence. The design intent is that loss of abatement stops the kiln or its feed. The exact trip logic and timing are not stated in the reference.

Never bypass that protection to keep regeneration going. Ask the CRO or control systems engineer for the actual interlock.

f.q: Where does mercury on the carbon come from?
f.a:
Trace mercury in the ore dissolves in cyanide solution during leaching, much like gold, and adsorbs onto the activated carbon.

It then comes off partly in elution, ending up in eluate and EW, and partly in the kiln, where heat drives it off as vapour.

That is why gold plants manage mercury at several points: elution, electrowinning, the goldroom and regeneration.
f: Does mercury end up in the EW cells?
How is mercury tested in plant streams?
How is mercury handled in the goldroom?

f.q: What does a mercury abatement system usually consist of?
f.a:
In general, off gas from the kiln is cooled, sometimes in a condenser that drops out some mercury as liquid, then passed through beds of sulphur impregnated activated carbon. The sulphur binds mercury as a stable compound.

Spent beds are handled as hazardous waste.

The specific design of the FIM system is vendor information not covered in the reference.
f: Why does sulphur capture mercury so well?
How often are abatement carbon beds replaced?
Who handles mercury waste on site?

f.q: Who is notified if mercury abatement fails?
f.a:
The reference does not say.

In general, the CRO would see the alarm and inform the area supervisor, and environmental or health and safety staff would be involved if there was any chance of release, since mercury emissions can be reportable.

Ask the shift supervisor or the site environmental team for the actual notification process.
f: Is an abatement failure a reportable incident?
How are kiln mercury emissions monitored?
What PPE applies near the regen kiln?

Who controls the CIL4 carbon regeneratio.q: Why tie the vendor PLC into an overall DCS sequence at all?
Who controls the CIL4 carbon regeneratio.a:
Regeneration involves more than the kiln. Barren carbon is educted to a dewatering screen and kiln feed hopper, passes through the kiln, drops into a quench tank and is pumped back by the barren carbon pump. The mercury abatement system must run alongside.

Much of that equipment sits outside the vendor package, so something has to start and stop it all in the right order and stop the kiln if a supporting item fails. The overall DCS sequence does that, and gives the CRO one view with first out alarms.

It is like a plant start sequence that includes packaged units.

f.q: What does the quench tank do after the kiln?
f.a:
Hot carbon leaving the kiln drops into water in the quench tank and cools quickly.

Fast cooling stops the carbon burning when it meets air, and gives a slurry that the barren carbon pump can move to the sizing screen and back to CIL4.

The reference lists the quench tank as part of the overall regeneration sequence.
f: Why would hot carbon burn in air?
What water supplies the quench tank?
What happens to fines in the quench tank?

f.q: Why is barren carbon screened on the way back to CIL4?
f.a:
The reference says barren carbon returns to the last CIL4 tank via the CIL4 carbon sizing screen.

Regeneration and pumping break some carbon. The sizing screen removes fines before they enter the circuit, because fines would pass the 1.0 mm intertank screens and carry gold to tails.

So it protects both recovery and the carbon inventory.
f: What aperture does the carbon sizing screen use?
Where do carbon fines go after screening?
How much carbon is lost as fines each year?

f.q: How is fresh carbon added to the CIL4 circuit?
f.a:
The reference says fresh carbon is added via a hoist, bag splitter and quench hopper.

Bulk bags are lifted by the hoist, split open over the hopper, and the carbon is wetted in the quench hopper before entering the circuit. Fresh carbon replaces losses from attrition and fines.

In general, new carbon is often conditioned to knock off fragile edges before use. Ask the metallurgist about FIM practice.
f: Why condition fresh carbon before use?
How much fresh carbon does CIL4 use?
Who decides when to add fresh carbon?

How do weightometers totalise tonnes?.q: Why reset the totals at 5:00 am instead of midnight?
How do weightometers totalise tonnes?.a:
The reference says weightometers total wet tonnes per 12 hour shift from 5:00 am, per day from 5:00 am, and keep a running total.

The 5:00 am start most likely lines up with site shift change, so each shift's total matches the crew that produced it and handovers can quote one clean number. A midnight reset would split a shift across two reporting days.

It is like aligning maintenance work orders with shift rosters: records are easier to use when they match how people actually work.

f.q: How do the totals relate to the plant's 12 hour shifts?
f.a:
With totals running per 12 hour shift from 5:00 am, the day shift total covers 5:00 am to 5:00 pm and the night shift total covers 5:00 pm to 5:00 am. The daily total covers 5:00 am to 5:00 am the next day.

That gives each crew a tonnage for its own shift, which suits handover notes and shift reports.

Confirm actual shift times with the CRO, since rosters are not in the reference.
f: When are the shift handovers at FIM?
How are shift tonnes reported to management?
Who checks the totals each shift?

f.q: Why would totals at another time confuse reconciliation?
f.a:
If tonnage totals reset at midnight but shifts and lab sampling run 5:00 am to 5:00 am, one shift's production gets split across two reporting days, and the tonnes no longer line up with the shift composites and assays.

Recovery and accounting need tonnes and grades for the same period. Mismatched periods add errors that are hard to untangle later.

Aligning every total to the same 5:00 am boundary keeps it clean.
f: How are lab shift composites timed?
What is a reconciliation period?
How is the running total used?

f.q: Where can you see the weightometer daily totals?
f.a:
The DCS shows the totals on the OIS, and the plant data historian (PI) logs DCS data, so shift and daily totals and their history can be pulled from PI trends and reports.

Production reports normally draw on PI rather than people reading screens.

Ask the CRO or the metallurgist where the standard daily report lives and how to access PI.
f: How do you pull data from the PI historian?
Are weightometer totals in the shift report?
Can totals be corrected after the fact?

How do weightometers totalise tonnes?.q: What would a handover mean by 'weightometer moisture input needs updating'?
How do weightometers totalise tonnes?.a:
The weightometers weigh wet ore. To get dry tonnes, the DCS applies a moisture input. If that input is out of date, the dry tonnes are wrong, and so is anything calculated from them.

Ore moisture changes with rain, ore source, stockpile time and dust suppression water, so the input needs updating when lab moisture results change.

The note means someone noticed the value no longer matches recent samples. The metallurgist or lab normally provides the new value; the reference does not say who enters it.

f.q: How is ore moisture measured for the weightometer input?
f.a:
In general, a representative sample is taken from the belt or stockpile, weighed, dried in an oven at around 105 C until its weight stops changing, then weighed again. The weight lost as a fraction of the wet weight is the moisture percentage.

The lab does this routinely. The reference does not give the sampling frequency or location at FIM.

Ask the lab supervisor or metallurgist how moisture samples are taken.
f: How often is ore moisture sampled?
Why dry samples at about 105 C?
Who takes the moisture samples?

f.q: How much does a 1 percent moisture error affect dry tonnes?
f.a:
Dry tonnes equal wet tonnes times one minus the moisture fraction. So a 1 percentage point error in moisture gives roughly a 1 percent error in dry tonnes.

At the new crushing circuit's nominal rate of 2,634 t/h, that is about 26 t/h, or more than 600 t over a day. That is a design figure, not a live one.

Since dry tonnes feed accounting and some g/t calculations, a stale moisture value adds a steady bias.
f: How does a tonnage error affect recovery figures?
Do any reagent doses use weightometer tonnes?
How is moisture variation tracked over time?

f.q: Why does rain change crushed ore moisture so much?
f.a:
Crushed ore stockpiles are open to the weather. Rain soaks into the surface and runs down through the pile, and fines hold water by capillary action.

Ore reclaimed after rain can be noticeably wetter than normal, and it may stay that way for a while as the wet zone is drawn down.

That is when the moisture input most needs updating. Wet, fine ore can also cause chute and feeder problems.
f: How does wet ore affect chutes and feeders?
How long does stockpile moisture take to settle?
Is the crushed ore stockpile covered?

How do weightometers totalise tonnes?.q: Why do the new conveyors get permanent calibration chains but not the old ones?
How do weightometers totalise tonnes?.a:
The reference only says permanent calibration chains are fitted on the new conveyors. It does not say the old conveyors lack them, so do not assume that.

A permanent chain sits in a cradle above the belt and can be lowered onto it for a check, then lifted away. That avoids people manually laying heavy loose chains on a belt, which is slow and a manual handling and moving machinery risk. Easier checks also tend to be done more often, so weightometer accuracy is better.

Ask the maintenance planner how the existing conveyors are calibrated.

f.q: How is a weightometer chain check done?
f.a:
In general, the belt runs empty, and a calibration chain of known weight per metre is lowered onto the belt over the weigh idlers. The weightometer should read the chain's equivalent load. The reading is compared with the expected value and the span adjusted if it is outside tolerance.

A zero check with the empty belt usually comes first.

The site procedure, tolerances and who signs it off are not in the reference.
f: Why do a zero check before a span check?
What tolerance is acceptable on a weightometer?
Who records weightometer calibration results?

f.q: Why is a permanent chain safer than a loose one?
f.a:
Loose calibration chains are heavy and have to be carried, laid on the belt and removed by hand. That means manual handling strain and working close to a conveyor that has to run for the test.

A permanent chain is stored in a frame above the belt and lowered or raised with a winch or actuator, so nobody has to handle it near the moving belt.

Less exposure to moving machinery is the main benefit.
f: What are the main hazards near a running conveyor?
How is a permanent chain raised and lowered?
Can chain checks be automated from the DCS?

f.q: How often should a plant weightometer be checked?
f.a:
The reference does not give a frequency.

In general, plants do zero and chain checks on a regular routine, often weekly or fortnightly, with occasional material tests where a known mass of ore is weighed separately and compared, because chains do not reproduce real loading perfectly.

Ask the maintenance planner or metallurgist for the FIM schedule.
f: What is a material test on a weightometer?
Why do weightometers drift over time?
How does belt tension affect a weightometer?

How is slurry mass flow measured?.q: Why use a nucleonic density gauge instead of just a flowmeter for mass flow?
How is slurry mass flow measured?.a:
A magnetic flowmeter only measures volume flow, cubic metres per hour of slurry. Mass flow needs the slurry density as well, and to get dry solids tonnes you also need the solids SG.

The nucleonic density gauge measures density through the pipe wall without touching the slurry, which suits abrasive, saline slurry that would wear or foul an intrusive sensor.

The DCS then combines volume flow, slurry density and the operator entered dry solids SG to calculate dry tonnes. It is like combining a volumetric fuel meter with a densitometer to get mass flow.

f.q: How does a nucleonic density gauge measure through a pipe?
f.a:
A small sealed radioactive source on one side of the pipe sends gamma radiation through the pipe and slurry to a detector on the other side. Denser slurry absorbs more of the radiation, so fewer counts reach the detector.

The count rate is converted to density using a calibration, usually done against water and a known slurry sample.

Because nothing enters the pipe, there is no wear from abrasive slurry.
f: How is a nucleonic density gauge calibrated?
What can cause a nucleonic gauge to drift?
Why does build up on the pipe wall matter?

f.q: What safety rules apply around nucleonic gauges?
f.a:
They contain sealed radioactive sources, so they are licensed and managed under radiation safety rules. Only trained and authorised people may work on them or near the beam, and the source shutter is closed and locked before any work on the pipe or gauge.

Gauges carry radiation warning signs. Normal work nearby is safe if you respect the signage.

Ask the site radiation safety officer for the FIM rules.
f: Who is the radiation safety officer on site?
Why is the shutter closed for pipe work?
How are nucleonic gauges inspected?

f.q: Why can't a magnetic flowmeter measure density itself?
f.a:
A magnetic flowmeter applies a magnetic field across the pipe and measures the small voltage generated as the conductive slurry moves through it. That voltage depends on velocity, not on how heavy the slurry is.

So it gives volume flow only, and a separate density measurement is needed for mass flow.

The upside is no moving parts and no obstruction, which suits slurry well.
f: How does a magnetic flowmeter work in detail?
What fluids can a magnetic flowmeter not measure?
Why do magnetic flowmeters suit slurry?

How is slurry mass flow measured?.q: What would a handover mean by 'tonnes look wrong, check the SG entry'?
How is slurry mass flow measured?.a:
It means someone suspects the dry solids SG typed into the DCS calculation is wrong, and that is skewing the tonnage.

The DCS uses that SG to work out how much of the slurry mass is solids. A typo, an old value or a change in ore with more or less sulphide shifts the answer.

The wrong tonnes then feed anything built on them, such as CIL4 cyanide dosing on g/t of thickener underflow tonnes and the plant accounting. So checking the SG entry is a sensible first step when tonnages look odd.

f.q: Why does solids SG change between ore types?
f.a:
Different minerals have different densities. Pyrite has an SG of about 5, while common gangue minerals like quartz sit around 2.6 to 2.8. More sulphide in the solids raises the overall SG.
