That is why flotation concentrate, which is rich in pyrite, has a design SG of about 3.93, far above whole ore.

When ore blend or sulphur grade changes, the solids SG shifts.
f: How does sulphur grade affect solids SG?
Why is concentrate SG so high?
How often does the FIM ore blend change?

f.q: Which control loops depend on slurry tonnage calculations?
f.a:
From the reference: CIL4 cyanide addition can be set as a g/t ratio on thickener underflow tonnes, and CIL2 cyanide is ratioed to solids mass flow on the CIL2 feed. Other reagents use g/t setpoints converted to flow in a calculation block, depending on which tonnage signal they use.

Any error in slurry tonnage therefore passes straight into these doses.

Check the P&IDs to see which tonnage feeds each loop.
f: How does CIL2 cyanide dosing work?
Which reagents use g/t control at FIM?
How would an SG error show in cyanide use?

f.q: How does saline process water affect the density calculation?
f.a:
Working out the solids fraction from slurry density needs both the solids SG and the liquid SG. FIM process water is saline, with SG about 1.07. If the calculation assumed pure water at 1.00, the solids fraction would be overestimated.

The reference does not say which liquid SG the DCS uses.

Ask the control systems engineer or metallurgist whether 1.07 is built in.
f: How is liquid SG handled in the DCS?
Does water SG vary across the plant?
How has process water salinity changed over time?

How is slurry mass flow measured?.q: How often does the dry solids SG value normally get updated?
How is slurry mass flow measured?.a:
The reference does not say how often the dry solids SG is updated. It only says the value is operator entered and a wrong entry gives wrong tonnes.

In general, metallurgists review the solids SG when lab tests show a change, when the ore blend shifts, or on a routine basis such as weekly or monthly, and the value is then updated in the DCS.

Ask the plant metallurgist who owns these values and how often they are reviewed.

f.q: How is dry solids SG measured in the lab?
f.a:
In general, with a pycnometer: a small flask of accurately known volume. It is weighed empty, then with the dry sample, then with the sample topped up with water, and then with water alone. From those weights you calculate the volume of the solids and so their SG.

Gas pycnometers do the same using helium instead of water.

It is a routine lab test; ask the lab supervisor about FIM practice.
f: What is a gas pycnometer?
How accurate is a pycnometer SG test?
How is a sample prepared for an SG test?

f.q: Who enters the SG value in the DCS?
f.a:
The reference only says the dry solids SG is operator entered. It does not say who has permission to change it.

In general, values like this sit behind access levels, and the CRO enters them on instruction from the metallurgist, or the metallurgist does it directly, with a log of the change.

Ask the CRO how SG changes are made and recorded at FIM.
f: Are DCS value changes logged?
Who can change DCS configuration values?
How is a wrong SG entry usually found?

f.q: How big a tonnage error does a small SG error cause?
f.a:
As a general worked example: for slurry at SG 1.5 in plain water, changing the solids SG entry from 2.8 to 2.9 changes the calculated solids fraction by about 2 percent, so dry tonnes shift by about 2 percent too.

On a stream like CIL4 feed at about 3,164 t/h solids at design, 2 percent is over 60 t/h.

Small typing errors can therefore matter a lot.
f: How is solids mass fraction calculated?
Why is slurry density more sensitive than SG?
What slurry SG is typical for thickener underflow?

What's the difference between emergency.q: Why not just have emergency generators for everything on site?
What's the difference between emergency.a:
The reference distinguishes emergency power, a generator that starts automatically on outage, from essential power, where an operator starts a generator manually. It does not list which loads are on each.

In general, automatic generators are kept for loads where seconds matter, such as life safety. Making everything automatic would need much bigger generators and complex automatic load shedding, since many large motors starting at once would overload a generator.

Essential loads can wait a few minutes while an operator starts the set and brings loads on in a controlled order. It is like starting a big compressor house one machine at a time.

f.q: What kinds of loads usually go on essential power?
f.a:
In general, essential power covers equipment that will cause damage or a long recovery if left stopped for too long, but can tolerate a few minutes of outage. Typical examples are thickener rakes, tank agitators where slurry would settle, key sump pumps and some lube systems.

The reference does not list FIM's essential loads.

Check the electrical single line diagrams or ask the electrical maintenance planner.
f: Why do CIL tank agitators need backup power?
How long can thickener rakes stay stopped?
Who decides which loads are essential?

f.q: Why must essential loads be restarted in a controlled order?
f.a:
A generator has limited capacity, and induction motors draw several times their running current when they start. Starting several at once can drag the generator voltage and frequency down and trip it.

Bringing loads on one at a time, biggest or most important first, keeps the generator within limits.

It is the same reason large plant motors are started in sequence rather than all together.
f: What is motor inrush current?
How is a standby generator sized?
Can a generator trip on overload?

f.q: Why is emergency lighting rated for at least 90 minutes?
f.a:
The reference says emergency lighting lasts at least 90 minutes. That is a common requirement in lighting standards, giving enough time for people to evacuate safely and for initial emergency response or power restoration.

Emergency lights normally have their own batteries, so they work even if generators fail.

Ask the electrical maintenance planner how FIM emergency lighting is tested.
f: How is emergency lighting tested?
Where is emergency lighting fitted in the plant?
What powers emergency lights during an outage?

What's the difference between emergency.q: What would you expect to happen to the DCS screens during the changeover gap?
What's the difference between emergency.a:
The reference says the DCS and field RIO panels ride through on UPS. So the control system, screens and field I/O stay alive, and the CRO keeps visibility through the outage.

What changes is the plant. Drives without power stop, so the OIS would fill with trips and alarms. First out records help find the original trip. Alarms on stopped equipment are masked, which helps reduce the flood.

Emergency lighting comes on, and emergency generators start automatically while essential ones await an operator start.

f.q: How long can the DCS UPS carry the system?
f.a:
The reference does not give UPS battery duration.

In general, UPS units are sized to carry the control system until generator power is back, often between 30 minutes and a few hours, with margin.

Ask the electrical maintenance planner for the FIM UPS ratings and how battery health is checked.
f: What happens when UPS batteries run flat?
How is UPS battery health checked?
Is the UPS fed from emergency power?

f.q: What would the alarm screen look like after a power outage?
f.a:
A large burst of alarms as drives trip, flows stop and levels move. Without management that would be an alarm flood, which makes it hard to see what matters.

The plant follows ISA-18.2 alarm management, with priorities from Logging to Urgent and alarms masked when their equipment is not running. That cuts the flood down to the important ones.

First out records then show where the trip started.
f: How does alarm masking work in the DCS?
What does ISA-18.2 cover?
How does first out help after a blackout?

f.q: Why must the field RIO panels be on UPS too?
f.a:
Remote I/O panels connect field instruments and drives to the DCS controllers. If the screens and controllers stayed powered but the RIO panels lost power, the DCS would lose all its field signals and go blind.

Keeping them on UPS means the CRO still sees levels, pressures and drive status during an outage, which matters for a safe restart.

It is like keeping a car's dashboard powered when the engine stalls.
f: What is a remote I/O panel?
How do RIO panels connect to the DCS?
What happens if one RIO panel loses power?

What's the difference between emergency.q: How is essential power tested to make sure it will start when needed?
What's the difference between emergency.a:
The reference does not describe how essential power is tested.

In general, standby generators are tested by regular run tests, often monthly, where the set is started and run for a period, plus periodic load bank tests that load it to near rated output. Battery, fuel and control checks are part of routine maintenance.

The aim is to make sure it starts and carries load when needed. Ask the electrical maintenance planner for the FIM schedule.

f.q: What is a generator load bank test?
f.a:
A load bank is a set of resistors, sometimes with reactors, that absorbs a generator's output as heat. Connecting it lets you run the generator at or near its rated load without depending on plant loads.

It proves the engine and alternator can deliver full power, and burns off deposits that build up when diesels run lightly loaded.

It is like a dyno test for an engine.
f: Why do diesels suffer when lightly loaded?
How often are load bank tests done?
Who carries out load bank tests?

f.q: Who schedules generator testing on site?
f.a:
The reference does not say.

In general, generator testing is planned by the electrical maintenance team through the maintenance system, with the operations team agreeing timing so tests do not disrupt the plant.

Ask the electrical maintenance planner how it is scheduled and where results are recorded.

Test results usually go into the maintenance system against the generator's asset number, so you can look up when it last ran under load.
f: How are generator test results recorded?
What happens if a generator test fails?
Are generator tests done during normal operation?

f.q: What usually stops a standby generator from starting?
f.a:
In general, the common causes are flat or weak starting batteries, fuel problems such as contaminated or old diesel or blocked filters, failed starter motors, and control or sensor faults.

Most are caught by regular run testing, battery checks and fuel management.

That is why untested standby generators often fail when they are needed.
f: How are generator batteries maintained?
How is stored diesel quality checked?
What alarms does a standby generator raise?

What do switchroom sprinklers interlock.q: Why interlock sprinklers to the lube and hydraulic pumps at all?
What do switchroom sprinklers interlock.a:
Lube and hydraulic pumps push oil under pressure. If a fire damages a hose or fitting, the pump keeps spraying oil, feeding the fire with a fine, easily ignited mist.

Stopping those pumps when the sprinklers operate removes that fuel. The reference says the interlocks cover lube and hydraulic pumps, plus conveyor drives with external lube or hydraulic systems.

Mills are the exception: their lube pumps stop on a timed delay so the mill can stop safely first. It is like isolating the fuel supply to an engine fire.

f.q: Why is hydraulic oil such a fire risk near switchrooms?
f.a:
Hydraulic and lube oil is flammable, and under pressure a small leak sprays a fine mist that ignites far more easily than a pool of oil.

Switchrooms contain electrical equipment, such as switchgear and drives, which can provide an ignition source through arcing or overheating.

Together that is a serious fire hazard, which is why fire detection, suppression and oil pump interlocks are linked.
f: What is a spray fire and why is it so intense?
How are oil lines protected near electrical gear?
Where are the mill lube units located?

f.q: Are lube pump stops a critical or a process interlock?
f.a:
The reference does not classify the sprinkler interlocks.

In general, fire protection interlocks are treated as safety functions and are hardwired rather than relying on DCS logic. The reference notes the switchroom fire alarm is hardwired to the DCS.

Ask the control systems engineer how these interlocks are classified, and never try to bypass them.
f: What makes an interlock critical in this plant?
How are fire interlocks tested?
Who owns the fire system maintenance?

f.q: What suppression is fitted inside the switchrooms?
f.a:
The reference says each switchroom has a hardwired fire alarm on the DCS with siren, beacon and suppression, and that sprinklers interlock with lube and hydraulic pumps. It does not name the suppression type.

Switchrooms often use gas or water based systems depending on the equipment.

Check the fire protection drawings or ask the site fire or electrical maintenance team.
f: What suppression types suit switchrooms?
How is switchroom suppression triggered?
What should you do if suppression activates?

What do switchroom sprinklers interlock.q: What would you see if a switchroom fire alarm triggered during a mill stop?
What do switchroom sprinklers interlock.a:
The switchroom siren and beacon would go off, the hardwired fire alarm would come up on the DCS, and suppression would activate as designed.

The mill lube pumps would keep running for their timed delay so the mill can finish stopping safely, then stop. Conveyor drives with external lube or hydraulic systems would stop.

People should follow the site evacuation procedure for the switchroom. Do not go in to check or reset equipment while the alarm is active.

f.q: What should people in a switchroom do when the alarm sounds?
f.a:
The reference does not give the procedure.

In general, leave immediately by the nearest exit and go to the muster point, especially if gas suppression is fitted, since many gas systems make the room unsafe to breathe. Report to the control room or emergency response.

Follow the FIM site emergency procedure; your induction or area supervisor will cover it.
f: Why can gas suppression be dangerous to people?
Where are the muster points for the mill area?
Who responds to a switchroom fire alarm?

f.q: How does the DCS get the fire alarm if the switchroom burns?
f.a:
The reference says each switchroom has a hardwired fire alarm on the DCS. Hardwiring means a dedicated signal, not a shared network that could be damaged or delayed.

The DCS and RIO panels are also on UPS, so the alarm path keeps working even if the switchroom power is lost.

It is like a dedicated hardwired E-stop compared with a network command.
f: Why is hardwiring more reliable than a network?
Where does the hardwired fire signal terminate?
Is the fire alarm panel on UPS?

f.q: Why does stop timing matter more on a mill than a pump?
f.a:
A pump stops in seconds. A large mill has a huge rotating mass, with the shell, liners, media and charge together, and takes much longer to coast down. The new SAG and ball mill each have about 20 MW installed.

The bearings need an oil film the whole time the mill turns. Cut the oil too early and the bearings run dry while still rotating.

So mills need their lube pumps to keep going a little longer than other drives.
f: How heavy is a SAG mill with its charge?
What bearings do large grinding mills use?
Can a grinding mill be braked to a stop?

What do switchroom sprinklers interlock.q: Why give mills a timed delay before their lube pumps shut down?
What do switchroom sprinklers interlock.a:
Large mills take time to coast to a stop. While turning, their bearings rely on a pressurised oil film. If the lube pumps stopped instantly, the bearings could run dry and wipe, causing major damage and a long outage.

The timed delay lets the mill stop with oil still flowing, then the pumps stop to remove the fire fuel. It balances fire risk against bearing damage.

The reference gives the principle but not the delay; check with the control systems engineer.

f.q: What happens to a mill bearing that loses oil while turning?
f.a:
Without an oil film, metal surfaces touch. On a babbitt lined bearing, the soft lining smears or melts, which is called a wiped bearing. Damage happens within seconds to minutes and can score the trunnion journal too.

Repair can mean days or weeks of downtime and expensive parts.

That is why oil pressure and bearing temperature protections are standard on mills.
f: What is babbitt and why is it used?
How is mill bearing temperature monitored?
How long does a bearing repair take?

f.q: How long does a large mill take to coast to a stop?
f.a:
The reference does not give coast down times for the FIM mills.

In general, it depends on mill size, charge and speed, and can range from tens of seconds to a few minutes.

Ask the CRO or the mill maintenance planner, who will have seen it during commissioning and trips.
f: Do grinding mills have brakes?
What is mill inching used for?
How is coast down monitored on the OIS?

f.q: Why do mills use hydrostatic lift on start up?
f.a:
In general, at very low speed there is not enough rotation to build an oil film by itself. Hydrostatic lift pumps push high pressure oil under the trunnion to lift it slightly before the mill starts turning and while it slows to a stop.

That prevents metal to metal contact at start and stop, when bearings are most vulnerable.

Check the mill vendor manuals for the FIM arrangement.
f: What is a mill trunnion?
How is hydrostatic lift pressure monitored?
What happens if lift pressure fails at start up?

How do LV motors talk to the DCS?.q: Why use Modbus TCP for DOL overloads but a different network for VSDs?
How do LV motors talk to the DCS?.a:
The reference only says DOL starters have electronic overloads (EOL) on Modbus TCP and VSDs have a field network link. It does not name the VSD protocol or explain the choice.

The general reasoning: an electronic overload has a small, simple data set: run status, motor current, thermal state and trip cause. Modbus TCP is cheap, common and good enough for that.

A VSD carries more, and more time sensitive, data: speed reference, speed and torque feedback, control words and detailed fault codes. Drive vendors usually support an industrial Ethernet fieldbus that handles that better. It is like using a simple tachometer cable for one machine and a full CAN bus for another.

f.q: What data does an electronic overload send to the DCS?
f.a:
In general, an electronic overload relay measures motor current on each phase and models motor heating. Over the network it typically reports run and trip status, phase currents, thermal capacity used, trip cause (overload, phase loss, imbalance, earth fault) and the state of any inputs wired to it.

At FIM, the reference says field start, latched stop healthy, pull wire and float switch status are hardwired to the EOL or VSD I/O, so those come through it too.

Check the motor control drawings for the exact signal list.
f: How does an overload relay model motor heating?
What is phase imbalance and why trip on it?
Where are the EOLs physically mounted?

f.q: What does the VSD field network carry that Modbus doesn't?
f.a:
In general, a drive fieldbus carries a cyclic control word (start, stop, reset), a speed reference, and feedback such as actual speed, current, torque, power and status words, refreshed quickly and deterministically. It can also carry detailed fault and diagnostic data.

Modbus TCP could carry much of this, but industrial Ethernet protocols used by drive vendors handle fast cyclic data and diagnostics more neatly.

The reference does not name the protocol used at FIM; check the network architecture drawings.
f: Why does a speed reference need fast updates?
What is deterministic communication?
How are VSD faults shown on the OIS?

f.q: What happens to a VSD if its network link drops?
f.a:
It depends on how the drive's communication loss action is set. In general, drives can be configured to stop, ramp down, hold the last speed or go to a preset speed when they lose the network.

For most process drives, stopping or a controlled ramp down is the safe choice, but it is set case by case.

The reference does not say how FIM drives are configured. Ask the control systems engineer or the electrical maintenance planner.
f: Why would a drive hold last speed on comms loss?
How would the CRO see a VSD comms fault?
How quickly does a drive detect comms loss?

How do LV motors talk to the DCS?.q: What would 'lost comms to the EOL, hardwired status only' mean?
How do LV motors talk to the DCS?.a:
This is not a phrase defined in the reference, so read it as general practice.

It suggests the Modbus TCP link to a DOL motor's electronic overload has dropped. The DCS has lost the networked data: motor current, trip cause and probably the ability to start and stop the motor remotely.

The reference says field start, latched stop healthy, pull wire and float switch status are hardwired into the EOL. So those devices still act directly on that starter in the field, but the DCS may not see them until comms return.

Check with the CRO what the writer meant and get the electrician to restore the link.

f.q: Can the CRO still start a DOL motor if EOL comms are lost?
f.a:
In general, no. If start and stop commands go to the starter over the network, losing the link removes the CRO's control of that motor, and the DCS also loses its run feedback.

Some sites wire a backup run signal or have local start options, but the reference does not describe that for FIM.

Ask the CRO how the plant handles a motor with lost EOL comms, and treat it as a fault to fix rather than something to work around.
f: Does a running motor keep running on lost comms?
How does lost run feedback affect sequences?
Who restores a failed Modbus link?

f.q: Why wire pull wires and stops into the starter, not the DCS?
f.a:
Wiring safety devices directly to the starter or drive means they act on the motor without depending on the DCS, the network or software. If the network or controller fails, a pull wire or stop button still stops the motor.

That matches the reference's approach: critical interlocks such as E-stops and pull wires trip in every mode and cannot be bypassed, and VSD E-stops are wired to Safe Torque Off.

It is like a mechanical overspeed trip that works even if the governor electronics fail.
f: What is a latched stop at a field LCS?
Why must pull wires be reset in the field?
How does a float switch protect a pump?

f.q: How would an electrician find a Modbus TCP comms fault?
f.a:
In general, they work from the physical layer up: check the network cable and connectors, switch port lights and link status, then confirm the device's IP address and settings, and use a laptop to ping or poll the device.

Common causes are damaged cables, failed network switches, a replaced device with the wrong address, or power loss to the device's comms module.

Any work inside the starter cubicle is done under the site electrical isolation rules.
f: What is an IP address conflict?
Why do network switches fail in switchrooms?
How is a replaced EOL configured?

How do LV motors talk to the DCS?.q: Why wire E-stops to Safe Torque Off rather than just cutting VSD power?
How do LV motors talk to the DCS?.a:
Safe Torque Off is a certified safety function built into the drive. When triggered, it removes the gate signals to the drive's output transistors, so the motor cannot produce torque. It acts in milliseconds and its circuitry is designed for safety duty.

Cutting incoming power is slower and less certain: the drive's DC bus capacitors stay charged and can keep the motor running briefly. Repeatedly switching the supply also wears contactors and means long restarts while the DC bus recharges.

Important: STO stops torque, but it is not an electrical isolation. Maintenance still needs proper isolation and lockout. The reference confirms VSD E-stops are wired to STO.

f.q: Is Safe Torque Off enough isolation for mechanical work?
f.a:
No. STO prevents the motor producing torque, but the drive and motor terminals can still be live, and the DC bus can hold a dangerous charge. Also, STO does not stop a load that can move by gravity or stored energy.

For mechanical or electrical work, the equipment must be isolated at the proper isolation point, locked out, tested for dead and any stored energy released, following the site isolation procedure.

STO is for stopping in an emergency, not for making equipment safe to work on.
f: What does test for dead involve?
Why can a DC bus stay charged after power off?
What stored energy exists on a conveyor?

f.q: What happens to a running motor when STO activates?
f.a:
The drive stops supplying torque immediately, so the motor coasts to a stop under its own friction and load. It is not braked by the drive.

For high inertia loads, such as a big fan or a loaded conveyor, coasting can take a while. Where a faster stop is needed, drives can use a controlled ramp first, then STO, or a mechanical brake.

The reference does not say which stop category each FIM drive uses.
f: What are safety stop categories 0 and 1?
When does a conveyor need a mechanical brake?
How long does a big fan take to coast down?

f.q: How is an STO circuit tested?
f.a:
In general, by operating the E-stop with the drive running or enabled and confirming the drive reports STO active and cannot produce torque, then resetting and confirming normal function. This proves the full chain: the button, wiring and drive input.

Safety functions are usually tested at commissioning and then periodically, as set by the safety requirements.

Ask the electrical maintenance planner for the FIM test frequency and procedure.
f: Why test the full chain rather than just the button?
Who records safety function tests?
What is a safety integrity level?

What are the four DCS alarm priorities?.q: Why need four priorities instead of just alarm and no alarm?
What are the four DCS alarm priorities?.a:
Not every alarm needs the same response. Four priorities tell the CRO what to deal with first, especially when several come in at once.

Urgent means act now to avoid serious consequences. High means act soon. Low means attention is needed when time allows. Logging means the event is recorded but not normally annunciated, which is useful for later analysis.

The reference says alarm management follows ISA-18.2, which bases priority on how severe the consequence is and how much time the operator has to respond. It is like triage in an emergency department.

f.q: What decides whether an alarm is High or Urgent?
f.a:
Under ISA-18.2 practice, each alarm is rationalised: the team looks at the consequence if the operator does not respond (safety, environment, equipment damage, production) and the time available to respond. Severe consequences with little time get the top priority.

So a fire alarm or HCN gas alarm would typically be Urgent, while a slowly rising tank level might be Low or High.

The reference does not list individual alarm priorities; the alarm database holds them.
f: What is alarm rationalisation?
Who maintains the FIM alarm database?
How often are alarm priorities reviewed?

f.q: What happens to a Logging priority alarm?
f.a:
In general, Logging alarms are recorded in the event or alarm history but do not sound or flash on the operator's main alarm list. They are there for diagnosis, reporting and trend analysis, not for immediate action.

Examples might be minor status changes or events that only matter when you look back over a shift.

The reference names Logging as one of the four priorities but does not list which alarms use it.
f: Where can you see logged events in the DCS?
Why record events nobody is alerted to?
Can a Logging alarm be promoted later?

f.q: How do analogue LL, L, H, HH levels map to priorities?
f.a:
The reference says analogue alarms have LL, L, H and HH levels, and separately lists the four priorities. It does not say how they map.

In general, the outer limits (LL and HH) often carry a higher priority than L and H because they are closer to a trip or damage. But each alarm is set on its own merits, so no fixed rule applies.

Check the alarm database or ask the CRO for a specific tag.
f: Why have both an alarm and a trip on one tag?
What deadband stops alarms chattering?
How does the CRO see an alarm's priority?

What are the four DCS alarm priorities?.q: What would a flood of Low priority alarms during startup suggest to a CRO?
What are the four DCS alarm priorities?.a:
During startup, equipment changes state quickly, flows and levels move through abnormal ranges, and many conditions briefly cross alarm limits. A burst of Low alarms then is common.

It can mean alarms are not masked properly as equipment starts, or that some alarms are nuisance alarms needing better limits, delays or state based logic.

The CRO's job is to keep watching for High and Urgent alarms and not let the noise hide them. Repeated startup floods are worth raising for an alarm management review under the plant's ISA-18.2 approach.

f.q: What is an alarm flood under ISA-18.2?
f.a:
ISA-18.2 guidance treats an alarm flood as more alarms than an operator can reasonably handle, often defined as more than about 10 alarms in 10 minutes for one operator.

During a flood, the risk is that an important alarm is missed among many less important ones.

Plants track flood frequency as a key alarm performance measure and work to reduce it.
f: How is alarm performance measured?
What tools help during an alarm flood?
What is a standing alarm?

f.q: How are nuisance alarms fixed at a plant like this?
f.a:
In general: find the worst offenders from the alarm history, then fix the cause. Options include correcting a faulty instrument, adjusting limits, adding a deadband or on delay so short spikes do not alarm, suppressing alarms based on equipment state, or removing alarms that need no operator action.

Each change goes through management of change.

The reference confirms ISA-18.2 alarm management and masking when equipment is not running.
f: What is an alarm on delay?
Why use management of change for alarm edits?
Who approves changes to alarm limits?

f.q: Why is startup often the worst time for alarm floods?
f.a:
Alarm limits are usually set for steady running. During startup, tanks fill from empty, pumps run below normal flows and temperatures and densities are far from normal, so many measurements sit outside their normal band.

Equipment also changes from stopped to running in quick succession, and if masking or state based logic is not perfect, alarms fire as each item starts.

That is when the CRO is busiest too, which makes alarm quality matter most.
f: What is state based alarming?
How long does a full plant restart take?
Can alarm limits change with plant state?

What are the four DCS alarm priorities?.q: Why mask alarms on equipment that isn't running?
What are the four DCS alarm priorities?.a:
If a pump is stopped, its low flow alarm will be active, but that is expected and tells the CRO nothing useful. Leaving those alarms visible fills the alarm list with noise.

Masking alarms on equipment that is not running keeps the list focused on real problems. It also guards against alarm fatigue, where operators learn to ignore alarms because so many are meaningless.

The reference confirms alarms are masked when their equipment is not running, in line with ISA-18.2. It is like turning off a low oil pressure warning while the engine is switched off.

f.q: How does the DCS know equipment is not running?
f.a:
It uses the run feedback from the starter or drive. The reference says DOL motors report through electronic overloads on Modbus TCP and VSDs through a field network, so the DCS knows each drive's run state.

The masking logic links each alarm to the relevant equipment state and suppresses it when the drive is stopped.

If run feedback fails, masking can go wrong, so feedback faults matter.
f: What happens to masking if run feedback fails?
Can masking be linked to valve positions too?
How is masking logic tested?

f.q: Could masking ever hide a real problem?
f.a:
Yes, in principle. If equipment is stopped but something is still wrong, such as a leaking valve filling a tank or a seal leaking on a stopped pump, alarms masked with that equipment may not show it. A faulty run signal could also mask alarms on equipment that is actually running.

Good design masks only alarms that are truly meaningless when stopped, and leaves others active.

Field rounds and trend checks help catch what masking hides.
f: Which alarms should stay active on stopped equipment?
How do field rounds complement alarms?
What is a shelved alarm?

f.q: What is alarm fatigue and why does it matter?
f.a:
Alarm fatigue is when operators see so many alarms, especially nuisance ones, that they become desensitised and start acknowledging or ignoring them without thinking.

It matters because the alarm that does matter can then be missed. Several major industrial accidents have involved operators overwhelmed by alarms.

Good alarm management, including masking, rationalisation and priorities, aims to make every alarm meaningful.
f: What industrial incidents involved alarm floods?
How many alarms per hour is manageable?
How do operators acknowledge alarms safely?

How do the primary crusher 'traffic ligh.q: Why let both radar and manual crusher control room input drive the lights?
How do the primary crusher 'traffic ligh.a:
The automatic inputs give consistent protection for conditions sensors can measure: truck radar, ROM bin level, discharge chamber level and high-high switch, crusher running and rock breaker position. The lights go red whenever one of these says tipping is unsafe or would overfill.

Manual input from the crusher control room covers what sensors cannot see: people or vehicles near the dump pocket, a bridged rock, an inspection or a developing problem the operator can see on CCTV.

Together they act like an interlock with an operator stop added on top: automatic protection plus human judgement.

f.q: What does the truck radar detect at the dump pocket?
f.a:
The reference lists truck radar as an input to the traffic lights but does not describe what it detects exactly.

In general, a radar at a dump pocket detects a truck in the tipping position, so the system knows a truck is there and can stop a second truck tipping on the same side, or hold green until the bay is clear.

Ask the crusher control room operator how the radar logic works at PC2.
f: How many trucks can tip at PC2 at once?
What happens if the radar fails?
How do drivers know which side to tip?

f.q: Can the operator override an automatic red to green?
f.a:
The reference does not say.

In general, automatic red conditions exist to protect equipment and people, such as a full ROM bin or the rock breaker over the pocket, so allowing an operator to force green would defeat them. Most sites only allow overrides under formal bypass control, if at all.

Ask the crusher control room operator or the crushing supervisor for the FIM rules.
f: Who authorises bypasses at the primary crusher?
What happens to trucks waiting at a red light?
How are traffic light faults reported?

f.q: Why does the dump pocket tip from two sides?
f.a:
The reference says the dump pocket is direct tip from two sides, sized for CAT 793F trucks with about 250 t payload, with 179 m3 live volume on one side.

Two sides let one truck tip while another positions on the other side, cutting truck waiting time and keeping the crusher fed at its design rate of over 3,000 t/h.

It is like having two loading bays on a warehouse dock.
f: How long does a CAT 793F take to tip?
What limits the crusher's tipping rate?
How many trucks per hour feed PC2?

How do the primary crusher 'traffic ligh.q: What would 'traffic lights stuck red, checking ROM bin level' mean?
How do the primary crusher 'traffic ligh.a:
It means the traffic lights are holding red so trucks cannot tip, and the person writing suspects the ROM bin level as the reason.

Either the bin really is full because the crusher is not drawing ore down fast enough, or the level instrument is reading falsely high, for example from dust, build up or a fault.

If the crusher is running with an empty bin and the lights stay red, it is likely an instrument problem. The fix is checking the level reading against CCTV and a field look, then getting the instrument repaired. Trucks meanwhile queue or go elsewhere.

f.q: What measures the ROM bin level at the crusher?
f.a:
The reference lists ROM bin level as a traffic light input but does not name the instrument.

In general, dusty crusher bins use radar level sensors because they cope well with dust, though ultrasonic sensors are also used.

Check the F12 instrument list or ask the instrument technician for the actual device.
f: Why does radar cope better with dust?
How is a bin level sensor cleaned?
Where is the bin level sensor mounted?

f.q: What happens to truck haulage when the lights stay red?
f.a:
Trucks queue at the crusher, losing haulage productivity. Mine dispatch may send trucks to the existing gyratory (PC1), which the reference says runs in parallel with the new crusher, or to a ROM stockpile.

Long delays affect mine plans and plant feed.

So a lights stuck red problem is quickly a mine and plant issue, not just a crusher one.
f: How do mine dispatch and the crusher communicate?
Can PC1 handle all the ore if PC2 stops?
What is a ROM stockpile used for?

f.q: How would dust affect a bin level sensor?
f.a:
Dust can coat an ultrasonic or radar sensor's face, weakening the signal or giving false echoes. Dense dust clouds while trucks tip can also scatter the signal briefly.

The result can be a falsely high or erratic level.

Sensor choice, mounting, air purges and cleaning help. The wet scrubber and dust extraction at PC2 also reduce dust.
f: What does the PC2 wet scrubber do?
Why use air purges on level sensors?
How often are crusher instruments cleaned?

How do the primary crusher 'traffic ligh.q: Why does the rock breaker position feed into the traffic light logic?
How do the primary crusher 'traffic ligh.a:
The rock breaker arm works over the dump pocket to break oversize rocks and clear bridges. If it is deployed over the pocket and a truck tips, the load could hit or bury it, damaging it badly.

So the lights stay red unless the rock breaker is in its parked position. The reference says it is run remotely by camera and parks itself when not in use, which helps the lights return to green.

It is like a guard interlock on a machine: one action cannot start while another part is in the danger zone.

f.q: Why is the rock breaker run remotely by camera?
f.a:
It keeps the operator away from the dust, noise, flying rock and moving trucks at the dump pocket. The reference says PC2 is run from the existing crusher control room with CCTV, and the rock breaker is operated remotely by camera.

Remote operation also lets one operator in the control room run both the crusher and breaker.

The trade off is depth perception, which good camera placement helps.
f: How many cameras cover the PC2 dump pocket?
What happens if the camera feed fails?
Who is trained to run the rock breaker?

f.q: What does the rock breaker auto park function do?
f.a:
The reference says the rock breaker parks itself when not in use. In general, auto park moves the boom to a safe, folded position clear of the dump pocket after a set idle time or on command.

That clears the traffic light interlock so trucks can tip again, and avoids leaving the boom exposed to falling rock.

It is like a robot returning to a home position.
f: How does the breaker know it is parked?
What if auto park fails midway?
Can trucks tip while the breaker parks?

f.q: What oversize rocks need the rock breaker at the crusher?
f.a:
The reference gives ROM feed as F80 450 mm and F99 1,000 mm, so some rocks approach a metre or more. The new gyratory is 1300 x 1900, which handles most, but slabby or very large rocks can bridge over the crusher opening.

The rock breaker breaks those or rearranges them so they feed.

Frequent oversize usually points to blasting, which the mine manages.
f: How does blasting affect ROM size?
What does F99 mean for crusher feed?
How is bridging cleared safely?

How is the new primary crusher gap adjus.q: Why use a camera based analyser instead of measuring crushed product directly?
How is the new primary crusher gap adjus.a:
A small correction to the premise: the camera based analyser does measure crushed product. It sits on the stockpile feed conveyor, downstream of the crusher, and looks at the ore on the belt.

The point is that it measures continuously and without contact. Manual sampling and screening of large crushed rock, with a nominal P80 of 130 mm at over 2,600 t/h, would be slow, heavy and dangerous, and would give occasional results only.

The camera gives a running size trend that the control system uses to adjust the crusher gap automatically. It is like using an online sensor instead of taking parts to the inspection room.

f.q: What can fool a camera based particle size analyser?
f.a:
In general, a camera only sees the surface of the ore on the belt. Fines tend to settle under coarse rocks, so the analyser may underestimate fines. Dust, wet or muddy ore, poor lighting and overlapping rocks also cause errors.

Vendors use algorithms and calibration against screened samples to correct for these.

So trends are more reliable than absolute numbers, and periodic calibration checks matter.
f: How is a camera analyser calibrated?
Why do fines hide under coarse rock?
How does lighting affect camera sizing?

f.q: Why does crusher gap change as liners wear?
f.a:
As the mantle and concaves wear, the gap between them widens, so the crusher setting opens and the product coarsens. The crusher compensates by raising the mainshaft to close the gap back to target.

Automatic adjustment from the size analyser helps keep the product steady as wear happens.

The reference gives the new crusher's OSS as 165 mm.
f: How often are gyratory liners changed?
What is the difference between OSS and CSS?
How is liner wear measured?

f.q: What product size is the new crusher designed for?
f.a:
The reference gives a design product P80 of 130 mm (145 mm in the high throughput case), with simulated P80 of 122 mm and P100 of 229 mm.

The crusher is an FLS 1300 x 1900 gyratory, OSS 165 mm, 600 kW.

These are design values; actual product varies with ore and liner wear.
f: How does product size affect SAG throughput?
What is the difference between P80 and P100?
How does OSS relate to product size?

How is the new primary crusher gap adjus.q: What would the OIS show if gap adjustment lagged behind feed size?
How is the new primary crusher gap adjus.a:
The reference does not describe specific OIS displays for this, so treat it as general.

You would see the product size trend from the analyser rising above target while the gap setting changed slowly or not at all. The cause could be adjustment rate limits, a hydraulic issue, or the control in manual.

Downstream, a coarser product would reach the stockpile and later the SAG, which the milling expert system sees through the SAG feed camera size analyser and may handle by adjusting feed rate.

f.q: How does a coarser crusher product affect the SAG mill?
f.a:
In general, coarser feed is harder for the SAG to break down. Mill load rises and throughput may need to drop to hold mill weight, or power rises.

The milling expert system uses the SAG feed camera size analyser, noise monitor, mill load, speed and power to adjust feed rate and other variables.

So crusher product size directly affects plant throughput.
f: How does the SAG expert system respond to coarse feed?
What is SAG critical size material?
Why does fine feed help SAG throughput?

f.q: How is gyratory crusher gap physically adjusted?
f.a:
In general, the mainshaft sits on a hydraulic piston. Raising the shaft closes the gap between mantle and concave; lowering it opens the gap.

The control system adjusts hydraulic oil volume to move the shaft.

The FLS arrangement details are in the vendor manuals.

Because the mantle and concave are cone shaped, a small vertical movement of the shaft gives a meaningful change in the gap, which is what makes automatic adjustment from the size analyser practical.
f: What protects a gyratory from tramp metal?
How fast can the gap be changed?
What happens to the gap under overload?

f.q: Why can't the gap be closed as far as you like?
f.a:
A tighter gap means more crushing work, higher power and more force on the crusher. Close it too far and the crusher overloads, packs or trips, and the throughput drops.

The new crusher is 600 kW. The control has to balance product size against power, pressure and throughput.

It is like a gearbox: you can trade speed for torque only within limits.
f: What is crusher packing?
How is crusher power monitored?
Why does tight gap reduce throughput?

How is the new primary crusher gap adjus.q: Why tie the apron feeder to tonnage instead of running it flat out?
How is the new primary crusher gap adjus.a:
The reference says the discharge apron feeder is speed controlled to a tonnage setpoint on the stockpile feed weightometer, with a design rate of 3,135 t/h.

Running to tonnage evens out the flow onto the stockpile feed conveyor, avoiding surges that could overload the belt, spill or trip it. It also keeps some ore in the discharge chamber, cushioning the feeder from rock impacts.

The feeder is interlocked to the discharge conveyor running, discharge chamber low-low level and head chute high-high. It is like metering fuel to an engine rather than flooding it.

f.q: Why keep ore in the crusher discharge chamber?
f.a:
In general, a bed of ore in the discharge chamber cushions the feeder pans from large rocks falling straight from the crusher, reducing wear and damage.

The reference says the apron feeder is interlocked on discharge chamber low-low level, protecting it if the chamber empties.

It is like keeping a liquid level in a pump sump to avoid cavitation.
f: What damage can rocks do to apron feeder pans?
How is discharge chamber level measured?
What happens if the chamber overfills?

f.q: What trips the discharge apron feeder?
f.a:
The reference says the apron feeder is interlocked to the discharge conveyor running, discharge chamber low-low level and the head chute high-high.

So it stops if the conveyor stops, if the chamber empties, or if the head chute blocks.

These protect the feeder and stop spills.

Together they act like the permissives on a pump: no discharge path, no suction cushion or a blocked outlet each stop the feeder before it can cause a spill or damage.
f: What does a head chute high-high switch detect?
Why stop the feeder when the conveyor stops?
How is a blocked head chute cleared?

f.q: How does the weightometer signal reach the feeder speed?
f.a:
The stockpile feed weightometer measures tonnes per hour on the belt. The DCS compares this with the tonnage setpoint, and a controller adjusts the apron feeder VSD speed to match.

There is a time lag between feeder speed change and the weightometer seeing it, so the loop is tuned to avoid oscillation.

The same principle drives reclaim feeders on SAG feed.
f: Why does transport lag matter in feeder control?
What is a deadband in feeder control?
How accurate is the stockpile feed weightometer?

What stops the stockpile feed conveyor o.q: Why use two separate signals instead of just one level switch?
What stops the stockpile feed conveyor o.a:
The reference says the stockpile feed conveyor is interlocked to both the stockpile high-high level switch and the high-high alarm on the stockpile level indicator.

Two independent signals give redundancy: if one fails, the other still stops the conveyor. They usually use different principles, a point switch and a continuous level instrument, so a single cause such as dust or build up is less likely to defeat both.

It is like having both a high level switch and a level transmitter on a fuel tank: belt and braces against overfilling.

f.q: What would happen if the stockpile was overfilled?
f.a:
In general, ore would build up around the conveyor head and tripper or discharge point, burying the head pulley and blocking the chute. It can damage structures, idlers and the belt, and spill onto walkways.

Clearing it takes time and earthmoving equipment, causing downtime.

That is why two independent signals guard against it.
f: How is a buried conveyor head cleared?
What structural loads does overfill cause?
How is the stockpile feed point designed?

f.q: What type of level instrument usually watches a stockpile?
f.a:
In general, radar level sensors are common on stockpiles because they handle dust and long ranges well. Point level switches, such as tilt switches or radar point devices, detect the high-high.

The reference does not name the FIM devices.

Check the F12 instrument list.

Using different principles for the trip switch and the continuous reading means one failure mode, such as dust on a sensor face, is unlikely to defeat both.
f: How does a tilt switch work?
Why does radar work in dusty areas?
How is stockpile level shown on the OIS?

f.q: Why does a continuous level reading help beyond the HH trip?
f.a:
A continuous level gives a trend, so the CRO sees the stockpile filling well before high-high and can adjust feed or reclaim rates.

It also shows how much live ore is available for the mills.

The HH switch only reacts at the limit.

A switch is like a high level float in a tank: it only tells you that you have arrived. The transmitter is the gauge that lets you plan ahead, and a drift between the two can also reveal an instrument fault.
f: How does the CRO balance crushing and reclaim rates?
What is live stockpile capacity?
How is stockpile inventory reported?

What stops the stockpile feed conveyor o.q: What would 'stockpile feed interlocked out on high-high' mean?
What stops the stockpile feed conveyor o.a:
It means the stockpile feed conveyor has been stopped by its interlock because the stockpile reached high-high level, on the switch or the level indicator alarm.

Either the stockpile is genuinely full, because reclaim is lower than crushing, such as a SAG mill being down, or a level signal is reading falsely high.

When the conveyor trips, upstream interlocked equipment stops too, so crushing on PC2 stops. Once level drops below the limit, the conveyor can restart.

f.q: What stops upstream when the stockpile feed conveyor trips?
f.a:
The reference says a conveyor trip stops interlocked upstream equipment, and the discharge apron feeder is interlocked to the discharge conveyor running.

So the apron feeder stops, then the crusher backs up and trucks get red lights as levels rise.

That chain protects equipment from overfilling.

First out on the DCS records which device tripped first, which helps the CRO tell a genuine high-high from a pull wire or belt fault further along the conveyor.
f: Does the crusher trip or just stop being fed?
How long until trucks see red lights?
How is the crushing restart sequenced?

f.q: How long does the new stockpile last if crushing stops?
f.a:
The reference gives the new crushed ore stockpile live capacity as about 12,035 m3, around 20,460 t at 1.70 t/m3, with residence about 11 hours.

So in principle the new SAG can keep running for several hours without crushing, depending on reclaim rate and how full the stockpile was.

These are design figures.
f: How is stockpile residence time calculated?
What happens when the stockpile runs low?
How does dead capacity affect live time?

f.q: Can the existing crusher keep feeding the plant meanwhile?
f.a:
The reference says the existing gyratory, PC1, runs in parallel with the new crusher, feeding the existing coarse ore stockpile and FIM SAG.

So the old circuit can keep running while PC2 is stopped, but it does not directly feed the new stockpile.

Ask the CRO how the two circuits are balanced.
f: How much ore does the existing crusher handle?
Do the two stockpiles connect?
How is ore split between PC1 and PC2?

What stops the stockpile feed conveyor o.q: Why does CCTV monitoring matter if the level interlock is already automatic?
What stops the stockpile feed conveyor o.a:
Interlocks prevent overfilling, but they cannot show everything. CCTV lets operators see the stockpile drawdown shape, rat holes, hang ups, people or vehicles near it, and loader work at the emergency feeder.

It also lets operators confirm instrument readings when they disagree or look wrong.

The reference says CCTV watches the stockpile drawdown. It is like an operator's eyes complementing the instruments.

f.q: What is rat holing in a coarse ore stockpile?
f.a:
Rat holing is when ore draws down only directly above the reclaim feeders, forming a vertical hole while the rest of the pile stays put.

Live capacity drops, and the pile can collapse suddenly into the hole.

CCTV helps spot it early.

Wet, sticky or fine ore makes it more likely because the material holds itself up at a steep angle. Never approach or walk on a stockpile to clear a hang up; that is a known fatal hazard at mine sites.
f: Why does ore form rat holes?
How dangerous is a collapsing rat hole?
How is a hung stockpile cleared?

f.q: When is the emergency apron feeder used?
f.a:
The reference says there is one emergency apron feeder, fed by a CAT 992K or 994K loader.

It feeds the mill when normal reclaim cannot, such as during reclaim feeder failure or to draw dead stockpile ore.

Loader feeding is slower and needs careful coordination.

It is a fallback rather than a normal route, so its use usually appears in handover notes and on the CCTV view of the stockpile.
f: How fast can a loader feed the emergency feeder?
What safety rules apply near the emergency feeder?
Who decides to use the emergency feeder?

f.q: Why does a stockpile have live and dead capacity?
f.a:
Live capacity is ore that flows to the reclaim feeders by gravity. Dead capacity sits outside the drawdown cone and needs a loader or dozer to move.

The reference gives live capacity as 12,035 m3 at a 60 degree drawdown angle.

Dead ore is a buffer but takes work to use.
f: What sets the drawdown angle?
How is dead ore recovered?
Why build stockpiles so large?

Where does raw water for gland seals com.q: Why keep gland seal water on a separate tank from process water?
Where does raw water for gland seals com.a:
Gland seal water needs to be clean. It flushes the gap between the pump shaft and packing, keeping slurry out. Dirty water carries fines that wear shaft sleeves and packing.

Process water at FIM is mainly flotation tails thickener overflow, which can carry fines, residual flocculant and reagents. A separate Raw Water Tank, fed from Bore Water/Saline Dam 3, gives a cleaner, dedicated supply that is protected from process water upsets.

The reference says the lower part of the new Raw Water Tank feeds the LP and HP gland water pumps. It is like having a dedicated lube oil system instead of using process fluid.

f.q: What does gland water do inside a slurry pump?
f.a:
Gland water is fed into the stuffing box at a pressure above the pump's internal pressure. It flows inward past the shaft into the pump, preventing slurry escaping outward through the packing and flushing abrasive particles away from the shaft sleeve.

Without it, slurry gets into the packing and quickly wears the shaft sleeve and packing, causing leaks.

It also cools the packing.
f: How is gland water pressure set?
What is a shaft sleeve?
How often is pump packing replaced?

f.q: Why are there both LP and HP gland water pumps?
f.a:
Gland water must be at a higher pressure than the pump it seals. Some slurry pumps run at low discharge pressure and others at high pressure, such as cyclone feed and tailings pumps.

Separate LP and HP gland water systems supply the right pressure without wasting energy or over pressuring low head pumps.

The reference confirms both LP and HP gland water pumps.
f: Which pumps need HP gland water?
What happens if gland pressure is too low?
How is gland pressure monitored?

f.q: What happens to a slurry pump if gland water fails?
f.a:
The reference says low gland flow blocks a pump start, and on running pumps trips after a delay. Gland water has a flow switch or mag flowmeter.

Without gland water, slurry gets into the packing and wears the shaft and packing fast.

The delay gives time for short drops without tripping.
f: Why trip after a delay rather than instantly?
What does a Maric valve do?
How do big pumps measure gland flow?

Where does raw water for gland seals com.q: What would falling gland water pressure suggest is wrong with Dam 3 supply?
Where does raw water for gland seals com.a:
The Raw Water Tank is fed from Bore Water/Saline Dam 3 via booster pumps. If that supply fails, the tank level falls, and eventually the gland pumps lose suction and pressure drops.

But falling gland pressure could also be a gland pump fault or a header leak. Check the Raw Water Tank level first: if it is falling, the supply is the likely problem, such as booster pumps or Dam 3 level. If it is steady, look at the gland pumps.

The reference gives the supply route but not the instruments.

f.q: What would the OIS show first if Dam 3 supply failed?
f.a:
In general, the Raw Water Tank level would start falling, with low level alarms. The booster pumps might show trips or low flow.

Gland pressure would only drop later once the tank got low.

The exact alarms depend on the configured instruments.

That gives the CRO time to act before any pump loses gland water, which is why watching the tank level trend is more useful than waiting for a gland flow alarm on a pump.
f: How long does the Raw Water Tank last without supply?
What alarms protect the gland water pumps?
How are booster pumps monitored?

f.q: Is there a backup supply to the Raw Water Tank?
f.a:
The reference does not say.

In general, plants often have an alternative supply, such as scheme water, for critical gland water.

Ask the water services maintenance planner or CRO.

Gland water matters because low gland flow blocks pump starts and trips running pumps after a delay, so losing it would affect many slurry pumps at once. That makes it worth knowing what the fallback is before it is needed.
f: Can scheme water feed gland seals?
How is water supply redundancy planned?
Who manages site water supply?

f.q: Why draw gland water from the lower part of the tank?
f.a:
The reference says the lower part of the Raw Water Tank feeds the gland water pumps. It does not explain why.

In general, priority users draw from low in a tank so they keep supply as the level falls, while less critical users draw higher up and lose supply first.

Ask the process engineer for the design intent.
f: Who else draws from the Raw Water Tank?
How do priority draw offs work?
What is a tank reserve?

Where does raw water for gland seals com.q: Why does Process Water rely mainly on thickener overflow, not bore water?
Where does raw water for gland seals com.a:
Water is scarce in the Goldfields. The flotation tails thickener recovers a large volume of water from the tails, and the overflow goes to the Process Water Tank for reuse.

That saves bore water and pumping costs. Top up comes from Bore Water Dam 2 (South Dam) by three DOL saline pumps that trip on dam low-low level.

It is like recirculating cooling water rather than using once through water.

f.q: What happens to process water when the thickener struggles?
f.a:
If the thickener overflow carries solids or residual floc, that goes into process water. Solids wear pumps and nozzles, and floc can affect flotation.

The reference says overflow clarity is one of the vendor panel signals.

So thickener performance affects the whole water circuit.

Because the process water circuit is largely closed, problems recirculate: solids and floc go round again through grinding and flotation rather than leaving the system.
f: How does solids in process water affect pumps?
What overflow clarity is acceptable?
Can process water be treated?

f.q: Why do South Dam pumps trip on low low dam level?
f.a:
The reference says the three DOL saline pumps trip on dam low-low level. In general, this protects the pumps from running dry or drawing in air and silt, which would damage them.

Running a pump dry overheats the seals.

It is a standard protection.

Running dry also damages bearings and impellers quickly, so the trip protects the pumps, which are simple DOL units with no speed control to back off.
f: What does a vortex at a pump intake do?
How is dam level measured?
What restarts the pumps after LL clears?

f.q: Where else does saline water come from for the plant?
f.a:
The reference lists saline sources including the Kaltails borefield (N02), Eastern Borefield and the offsite roaster saline transfer dam.

Process water SG is about 1.07 because of this salinity.

Different sources feed different dams.

Bore Water/Saline Dam 3 feeds the Raw Water Tank, and Bore Water Dam 2 (South Dam) tops up the Process Water Tank. Ask the water services team how the borefields feed each dam.
f: What is the Kaltails borefield?
How does salinity vary between sources?
Who manages borefield operations?

How do the flotation air blowers hold pr.q: Why hold header pressure instead of controlling blower speed to total demand?
How do the flotation air blowers hold pr.a:
Holding a constant header pressure gives every cell's air flow controller a stable supply to work from. Each cell then takes the air it needs through its own control valve, and the blower VSD speeds up or slows down to keep header pressure steady as total demand changes.

If blower speed were set directly to total demand, every change at one cell would disturb the others.

It is like a compressed air system with a pressure controlled compressor: users draw what they need and the compressor keeps the pressure up. The reference confirms VSDs on the blowers hold header pressure.

f.q: What happens to blower power as header pressure setpoint changes?
f.a:
Higher header pressure means more work to compress air, so blower power rises. Lower pressure saves energy but must still be enough to get air through the cell valves and into the slurry at the cell depth.

The setpoint is chosen to just meet the worst case cell demand.

Energy savings from a lower setpoint can be significant on big blowers.
f: How is the header pressure setpoint chosen?
How much power do flotation blowers use?
What limits how low the setpoint can go?

f.q: Why use VSDs rather than inlet guide vanes or blow off?
f.a:
VSDs vary blower speed to match demand, saving energy at partial load. Inlet guide vanes and blow off valves waste energy by throttling or venting.

VSDs also give smooth control and soft starts.

The reference confirms VSDs on the blowers.

Fan and blower power falls roughly with the cube of speed at reduced flow, so even a modest speed reduction saves a lot of energy compared with throttling. It is the same reason VSDs replaced dampers on large fans.
f: How much energy do VSDs save on blowers?
What is blower surge?
How are blowers started?

f.q: How many cells does the flotation air header feed?
f.a:
The reference lists 3 rougher cells (F16-CF-411 to 413) and 4 scavenger cells (F16-CF-414 to 417), all FLS forced air tank cells. So the header feeds 7 cells.

The Jameson cleaner and cleaner-scavenger cells do not use blowers; they draw air naturally through the downcomers.

Each forced air cell has its own air flow controller.
f: Why don't Jameson cells need blowers?
How big are the rougher cells?
How is air distributed in a forced air cell?

How do the flotation air blowers hold pr.q: What would the OIS show if header pressure dropped as cells opened valves?
How do the flotation air blowers hold pr.a:
As cells opened their air valves, more air would flow out of the header. The blower VSD would speed up to hold pressure. If the blower reached maximum speed, header pressure would sag.

On the OIS you would see header pressure below setpoint, blower speed at maximum, and cell air flow controllers fully open but below setpoint.

The cells would be air starved, hurting flotation. It points to blower capacity limits, a standby blower needed, a leak or a blower fault.

f.q: What does air starvation do to flotation recovery?
f.a:
Air bubbles carry the hydrophobic particles to the froth. Too little air means fewer bubbles and less mineral carried, so recovery falls.

Froth may thin and mass pull drops.

The flotation expert system would see this through froth cameras and OSA.

Gold carried in pyrite that misses the froth goes to the flotation tails thickener and then to CIL4, which only extracts about 38 percent at design, so air problems cost real recovery.
f: How does air rate affect froth depth?
What is bubble surface area flux?
Can too much air hurt flotation?

f.q: Why can cell flow loops and the header loop interact?
f.a:
When one cell valve opens, header pressure drops slightly, which reduces flow in other cells, which then open their valves too. Meanwhile the header loop speeds up the blower.

If the loops are tuned too aggressively, they chase each other and oscillate.

Tuning the header loop faster than the cell loops usually helps.
f: What is loop interaction?
How are interacting loops tuned?
What does oscillation look like on a trend?

f.q: Is there a standby flotation air blower?
f.a:
The reference says the blowers have VSDs holding header pressure, but does not state how many are installed or whether one is standby.

Ask the CRO or check the F16 equipment list.

In general, flotation air is critical enough that plants usually install spare blower capacity, because losing air stops the forced air cells from floating anything. Air valves are also interlocked closed if an agitator stops.
f: How are blowers changed over?
What maintenance do blowers need?
What happens if all blowers trip?

How do the flotation air blowers hold pr.q: Why give each cell its own flow controller if header pressure is already held?
How do the flotation air blowers hold pr.a:
Header pressure only ensures air is available. Each cell needs its own air rate, set to suit its duty and froth conditions.

Without individual control, air would split according to the back pressure at each cell, which depends on slurry level and froth depth, not on what the process needs.

The reference says each cell has an air flow controller with a mass flow meter and control valve, and the flotation expert system sets air.

f.q: Who sets the air flow setpoint for each cell?
f.a:
The reference says the flotation expert system uses the OSA, froth cameras and launder velocity cameras to set level, air and reagents.

So in normal running, the expert system sets each cell's air setpoint, and the flow controllers carry it out.

The CRO can take over if needed.

The air valve on each cell is also interlocked closed if its agitator stops, which overrides any setpoint to protect the rotor, stator and bearings.
f: How do froth cameras guide air setpoints?
Can the CRO override expert system air?
What limits does the expert system use?

f.q: Why do roughers and scavengers need different air rates?
f.a:
Roughers treat fresh feed with faster floating particles, while scavengers chase slower floating and finer particles.

Air rates are set to suit froth stability, mass pull and grade in each stage.

The metallurgist and expert system tune them.

Rougher 1 at design pulls about 4.4 percent of feed mass at around 15 percent sulphur, while scavengers pull about 1.1 percent at around 5 percent sulphur, so their froths behave very differently.
f: What is mass pull in flotation?
Why do scavengers float slower particles?
How is froth stability measured?

f.q: How does a thermal mass flow meter measure air?
f.a:
In general, a thermal mass flow meter heats a sensor and measures how much heat the passing air carries away. More mass flow cools the sensor more.

It measures mass flow directly, unaffected by pressure and temperature changes.

The reference says each cell has a mass flow meter but not its type.
f: Why measure air as mass rather than volume?
What fouls an air flow meter?
How are air flow meters calibrated?

What's a 'vendor package' and how does i.q: Why require Owner approval for a standalone vendor PLC?
What's a 'vendor package' and how does i.a:
Every standalone PLC adds a different platform to maintain: separate spares, software licences, programming tools, skills and cyber security management. It also adds an interface to the DCS that can fail.

The owner has standardised on the Yokogawa Centum VP DCS, with new and old plant built to the same site templates so they operate as one plant. Requiring approval for standalone PLCs keeps exceptions to cases where the vendor package really needs one.

It is like a fleet manager limiting truck models to keep spares and training simple.

f.q: What does a vendor PLC need to stay maintainable on site?
f.a:
In general: current program backups, the right software version and licences, trained technicians, spare hardware and vendor support.

Without those, a fault can mean long downtime waiting for the vendor.

Sites track these in an asset register.

Engineering laptops with the right software version are a common weak point: if the only copy sits with the vendor, a simple fault can take days. Ask the control systems engineer how FIM manages this.
f: How are PLC programs backed up?
What happens when PLC hardware goes obsolete?
Who supports vendor PLCs on site?

f.q: Why standardise both plants on one DCS platform?
f.a:
The reference says new and old plant are configured to the same site templates, so they look and operate as one plant.

That means one set of operator screens, training, spares and engineering tools.

It also reduces errors when operators switch between areas.

Data from both plants also goes to the same PI historian, so trends and reports cover the whole site in one place.
f: How are site DCS templates maintained?
What is a Field Control Station?
How is the PI historian linked to the DCS?

f.q: What cyber security issues do vendor PLCs bring?
f.a:
In general, vendor PLCs can have default passwords, remote access connections for vendor support and outdated firmware, all of which can be weak points.

Each one needs managing under the site's cyber security rules.

Fewer standalone PLCs means fewer weak points.

Industrial control systems are increasingly targeted, so a PLC reachable from outside the plant network is a real risk, not a theoretical one. Ask the control systems engineer about site rules for vendor access.
f: How is vendor remote access controlled?
What is network segmentation?
How are PLC firmware updates managed?

What's a 'vendor package' and how does i.q: What would 'vendor package reporting Monitor only' mean for the CRO?
What's a 'vendor package' and how does i.a:
The reference says vendor packages with a PLC report to the DCS for either Monitor or Control.

Monitor only means the DCS can see the package status, alarms and key values, but the CRO cannot start, stop or adjust it from the OIS. Any change must be made at the vendor's local panel, usually by a field operator.

So the CRO coordinates with the field rather than acting directly.

f.q: Which vendor packages are usually Monitor rather than Control?
f.a:
The reference does not list which packages are Monitor and which are Control.

In general, packages that run on their own with minimal operator input, such as compressors or chillers, are often Monitor only.

Ask the CRO or check the DCS interface list.

The reference lists rock breaker, OSA, particle size analysers, compressors, chillers, samplers, IsaMill starters and the regen kiln as vendor packages that report to the DCS.
f: How are compressors controlled at FIM?
Why monitor a package you cannot control?
Who decides Monitor or Control?

f.q: How does the CRO get a Monitor only package restarted?
f.a:
In general, by asking a field operator to go to the local panel and restart it, following the vendor procedure.

The CRO then watches the DCS signals to confirm it is running.

Radio coordination is key.

The field operator also checks why it stopped before restarting, since a package that tripped on its own protection may trip again or be damaged if restarted blindly.
f: What radio protocols are used on site?
How are package faults reset?
How long does a field restart take?

f.q: Does Monitor only still show package alarms on the OIS?
f.a:
Generally yes. Monitor means the DCS reads status and alarms from the package PLC, so the CRO sees faults.

The exact alarms shown depend on the interface.

Check the interface list.

If the comms link to the package PLC fails, the DCS loses that view too, so a communications fault alarm is normally configured to warn the CRO that the package status shown may be stale.
f: How are package alarms prioritised?
What if the package PLC comms fail?
Can package alarms be masked?

What's a 'vendor package' and how does i.q: Why are the big units controlled directly by the DCS, not vendor PLCs?
What's a 'vendor package' and how does i.a:
The big units are the core of the process and must be tightly integrated with sequences, interlocks and the expert systems for milling and flotation. Running them directly on the DCS gives one platform, one operator interface and no gateway between controller and plant.

The reference says SAG, ball mill, flotation cells, thickener, Knelsons, ILR, EW cells and Jameson cells are DCS controlled.

It is like keeping the main engine on the ship's own control system rather than a separate box.

f.q: How do the expert systems talk to the DCS?
f.a:
The reference says the milling and flotation expert systems set feed rate, water, air, level and reagent setpoints, but does not say how they connect.

In general, expert systems run on a separate server and write setpoints to the DCS over a standard interface.

Ask the control systems engineer.
f: What happens if the expert system server fails?
How are expert system setpoints limited?
Who tunes the expert systems?

f.q: What does the DCS gain from controlling the SAG mill directly?
f.a:
Direct control lets the SAG sit in the same sequences and interlocks as feeders, pumps and cyclones, with no gateway delays.

The milling expert system can adjust SAG speed and feed directly.

It is simpler to maintain and troubleshoot.

The CRO also gets consistent faceplates, alarms and first out records for the mill, the same as every other DCS drive, which matters during a trip when time is short.
f: How does the SAG start sequence work?
What interlocks protect the SAG?
How is SAG speed controlled?

f.q: Why is the IsaMill partly on a vendor PLC but the SAG not?
f.a:
The reference says the IsaMill liquid resistance starters are on a vendor PLC. That starter is a specialised package supplied with its own logic.

The IsaMill process control, such as feed, water and media addition, still sits in the DCS.

Ask the control systems engineer for the exact split.

What does the IsaMill vendor PLC report?
How is the SAG motor started?
